The cedar burns behind my ribs, desperate and wild, and I force it down one more time while Saelis guides me toward the lie we'll tell together.

* * *

The briefing room smells like stale coffee and fear.

I step through the side door behind the podium, my dress blues crisp enough to cut glass. The bio-wards hum beneath my collar bone—white-lilac and fresh cedar, burning with that absolute purity they taught us at the Academy. It should feel right. Protective. Instead, it feels caged in this sterile, air-conditioned box of corporate lies.

Forty-three news cameras are trained on me. Their red recording lights form a constellation of evil across the darkened room. Beyond the bulletproof windows, a fleet of black '99 Crown Vics sits idling in the lot, their exhaust making the air taste like ozone and gasoline. Someone's idea of intimidation.

"Commander Vance." The head of BATC Public Relations—a woman whose smile doesn't reach her eyes—gestures toward the podium like she's presenting a prize bull at the county fair. Her perfume fights a losing battle against the underlying scent of magic in here. Mine. Everyone's.

I take position. The microphone picks up every breath.

"Good morning," I say, because that's what they paid for. "My name is Commander Mara Vance, Field Lieutenant designation Echo-Seven. As of this week, I've been promoted to oversee all metropolitan response units. We're here today to address concerns about water toxicity in the Newark Bay watershed."

A hand shoots up from the front row. AP News. A man whose face looks carved from old leather.

"Lieutenant, can you guarantee these rumors are false? The numbers coming out of Kearny Marshes don't lie."

The bio-wards flare hot against my sternum. Not anger. Not exactly. More like... warning.

"I can tell you we've deployed enhanced detection protocols throughout the affected zones." Smooth. Corporate. I hate how easily the words come now. "Any contamination would be identified within hours."

Another reporter leans forward, his voice dripping with skepticism. "Your predecessor disappeared three weeks ago. His truck was found abandoned near Sub-Station Seven. You want to comment on that?"

My jaw tightens. Command said not to engage on Petrov. But lying to reporters who aren't stupid enough to believe it...

"The investigation is ongoing. Next question."

Before anyone can follow up, there's movement behind me. A side door opens and two paramedics wheel in a gurney. On it sits a Dwarf—real short, real broad-shouldered, his Local 405 union patch visible even under the hospital gown. His left forearm is wrapped in sterile bandaging, but I can smell it from here: scorched hair, ozone, burnt flesh. Genuine plasma-torch injury.

This wasn't in the briefing notes.

The Dwarf meets my eyes as they position him between the podium and the cameras. He doesn't smile. His beard is braided with what might be wire, might be chain. Definitely a machinist. Those hands could build engines or break skulls equally well.

"Showtime," he mutters just loud enough for me to hear.

I step down from the podium. The flashbulbs become a strobe light nightmare. Every click of the shutter feels like a gunshot in my peripheral vision. I crouch beside the gurney, ignoring the cameras, focusing entirely on the Dwarf.

His forearm is bad. Not life-threatening, but angry red tissue and blistered skin around the edges of the burn. Third-degree at the center where the torch actually touched him.

"I don't need your pity, copper," he says quietly. "Just get this over with."

"Keep your head down," I whisper back.

My hands hover over the wound. The bio-wards surge upward—not the clean white-lilac they want to see, but something raw and immediate. Fresh cedar floods through the room, cutting through the perfume and fear. The reporters lean forward.

Light spills from my palms.

It's not performance. Despite everything this is, despite the cameras and the scripted bullshit, the magic responds to pain. Always does. My grandmother taught me that before the Academy ever existed—magic finds suffering like water finds low ground.

The Dwarf's burn begins to knit together. Skin pulling closed, pink new flesh forming beneath the old scar tissue. It takes maybe thirty seconds. Forty. The whole time, he doesn't make a sound except for controlled breathing through his nose.

When I pull away, the forearm is healed. Perfectly. Just a faint red mark where the worst of it was.

The camera flashes go absolutely insane.

But in that moment before I stand up, while everyone else is focused on their lenses, the Dwarf catches my eye again. His expression hasn't changed. Still that same flat assessment.

"Tell your bosses the South Side ain't buying the spin, though," he says, quiet enough that only my enhanced hearing picks it up.

I stand. Straighten my jacket. Turn back to the podium.

"You've all seen our commitment to metahuman integration," I say, because that's what they wrote for me to say. "BATC stands ready to serve every citizen of Newark regardless of origin or ability."

More questions. More flashes. But underneath it all, I'm aware of the Dwarf being wheeled back toward the side door. Aware of how his words settled into my gut like lead.

Outside, the Crown Vics continue idling. Their exhaust creeping under the door seals. Ozone and gasoline and the metallic taste of coming storms.

Someone hands me a bottle of water. BATC logo on the label.

I don't drink it.

* * *

The briefing room's air conditioning died the moment I stepped out. My lungs filled with something thick and recycled, tasting like corporate carpet and expensive cologne. The makeup they'd cake-d over my scars was already starting to crack, pulling at the tender skin beneath.

I ripped the microphone pack from my collar before anyone could stop me.

The Velcro shrieked against my uniform as I yanked it free, tossing the whole goddamn assembly—mike, battery pack, transmitter—into an empty trash can. It landed with a satisfying metallic clang. Let them sue me. Let Director Kellerman have my ass for insubordination on camera day. Fuck it.

The locker room was mercifully empty, all fluorescent lights still off in this early hour. I splashed cold water across my face, watching the pink-tinted runoff swirl down the drain. Beneath the theatrical foundation, my skin looked gray. Exhausted. The bio-wards that normally hummed along my spine felt muted here, strangled by the sterile concrete and sealed windows. Just a dull buzz of static trapped in my ribcage.

My reflection stared back at me from the mirror above the sinks—a woman in a crisp EMT uniform with lieutenant bars pinned to her shoulders, but whose eyes held nothing but emptiness. They'd dressed me up like some kind of golden saint. Fed me lines about "proactive community outreach" and "transparency initiatives." Made me smile while I lied straight-faced about the purity of Newark Bay's water supply.

The Nextel pager on my belt vibrated.

Not a gentle buzz. A violent, grinding shudder that made the metal bench beneath it rattle. Cold porcelain pressed against my palms as I gripped the sink's edge, heart suddenly hammering. That specific frequency meant encrypted. Direct contact. Burner number routing through three dead drops minimum.

I grabbed it before the vibration stopped, thumbing open the monochrome LCD screen. Green phosphorescent glow lit my face in the dimness:

**COORDINATES: 40.7218° N, 74.1653° W**
**SUBSTRATE: SOUTH SIDE PARKING GARAGE (LEVEL C)**
**MESSAGE: THEY BURIED YOUR WATER SAMPLES.**
**MESSAGE: COME ALONE.**

The cadence. Those precise intervals between words. The way 'buried' was capitalized like an accusation. I knew that pattern. Had memorized it during sleepless nights in our cramped apartment when I was twelve, watching Mom tap out messages on her old Motorola brick phone to contacts who never called back.

*Lysandra.*

My mother had been silent for four years. Radio silence since she disappeared into the Kearny Marshes the night of the Pulaski Skyway incident, taking every piece of family history with her except what I could carry in my head. And now this. A direct page that no one—not even BATC's signal intelligence division—could have intercepted without triggering every alarm system we possessed.

The bio-wards flared hot and sharp in my chest.

White-lilac smoke curled from my fingertips as adrenaline flooded my system. My keys were already in my hand before conscious thought caught up. The locker room door slammed open under my palm, rattling on its hinges.

They buried your water samples.

Which meant the samples I'd personally logged and sealed three weeks ago—the ones showing anomalous crystalline compounds in the bay water, the ones Director Kellerman had ordered "re-evaluated" by his own team—hadn't just been misinterpreted or lost in bureaucracy.

Someone had actively hidden them. Destroyed evidence that proved the toxicity rumors weren't rumors at all.

And if Lysandra was breaking radio silence to tell me about it...

I hit the stairwell at a run, my boots echoing against concrete. The South Side coordinates put her near the old textile district, blocks from where County General ER processed most of the exposure cases. If there was rot inside BATC, it ran deeper than I'd ever imagined. Deeper than the marsh waters themselves.

My truck was parked in the restricted lot behind High-Spire, engine already warming when I reached it. I peeled out onto the street without looking back.

---

## CHAPTER 12: APEP'S BLACK VENOM

The Crown Vic's engine block ticks like a dying heart as I kill the ignition, plunging us into the sodium-yellow half-light of the subterranean garage. My fingers stay wrapped around the steering wheel for an extra second—the leather still warm against my palms, grounding me in something real before whatever nightmare Lysandra has called this meeting to unleash.

I step out into the damp chill that rises from the cracked concrete floor, carrying the distinctive stench of motor oil mixed with something worse. Something organic. Decayed. The smell hits my nostrils and immediately my white-lilac aura flares defensively, trying to purify what can't be purified, to ward off what shouldn't exist in breathing air.

She steps from behind a pillar on the second level—my mother, though calling her that feels increasingly like naming some ancient, vengeful god. Lysandra Vance looks like she hasn't slept since our last encounter, which was... when? Three weeks? Four? Her trench coat hangs loose on her frame, the left shoulder sagging where she'd torn it climbing through that warehouse window in Harrison. A lit cigarette trembles between her fingers, sending spirals of acrid smoke into the already toxic atmosphere.

"Look at you," she rasps, taking a drag that makes the ember glow like a warning light. "The Golden Saint. They dressed you up in silver bars while they slit the city's throat behind your back."

My hand instinctively moves to my EMT uniform—the County General insignia visible even in this dim light. I don't need the reminder about the promotion to Commander. That feeling of accomplishment tastes bitter now, like ash on my tongue.

"I submitted the water samples, Mom. I pushed it up the chain." My voice comes out more defensive than I intended. "They said it was a localized heavy-metal leak. Chromium-6 from an old manufacturing site. I followed protocol."

Lysandra barks a laugh that echoes off the concrete pillars, hollow and bitter as November wind through broken windows. She takes another pull from her cigarette, and I notice her hand shaking—not just from nicotine or fear, but from something else. Rage, maybe. Or the kind of bone-deep exhaustion that comes from knowing too much truth that nobody wants to hear.

"A leak?" She steps closer, the flickering sodium lamps casting dancing shadows across her face that make her look gaunt, hollow-eyed. "Mara, they opened the damn floodgates."

The words hang in the air between us, thick with implication. My aura flares brighter, responding to the emotional spike, and suddenly I'm aware of how exposed we are down here—three levels beneath street level, no witnesses, nothing but dying lights and our breathing filling the cavernous space.

"You're going to have to be clearer than that," I say, keeping my voice low and controlled despite the knot tightening in my stomach. "What floodgates? What are you talking about?"

She flicks ash onto the concrete, watching it scatter like dying stars. When she speaks again, her voice drops to barely above a whisper, urgent and paranoid.

"Three years ago. 1997. The Newark Bay Treatment Plant expansion. You remember—the one everyone called the 'miracle' because it came in under budget." Her eyes lock onto mine, searching for recognition. "They didn't come in under budget, Mara. They came in under budget because they skipped the containment protocols on Sector Seven's holding tanks. Eight hundred thousand gallons of industrial waste. Heavy metals, PCBs, mercury compounds so concentrated they'd eat through steel. They dumped it all into the Newark Bay aquifer system under the cover of night."

I feel the blood drain from my face. Eight hundred thousand gallons. The number echoes in my skull like a death knell. No wonder the water samples were off the charts. No wonder Danny Reyes had started convulsing the moment that contaminated water touched his skin.

"And nobody stopped them?" My voice comes out hoarse. "No inspections? No environmental oversight?"

Lysandra takes another drag, smoke curling around her face like spectral fingers. "Oh, there was oversight. There was even an investigation." She smiles without humor. "It went nowhere. Files sealed. Investigators reassigned. A few conveniently-timed retirements. The kind that happen when certain county executives have too much to lose."

The cooling engine block continues its rhythmic ticking behind me, counting down seconds I can't afford to waste on disbelief. But my mind is already racing through the implications—eight hundred thousand gallons seeping through the groundwater table, contaminating the Undercity's makeshift water mains, poisoning anyone who drank unfiltered tap water or showered in infected buildings.

"This is... this is catastrophic," I breathe, my medical training warring with my need to maintain composure. "How many people are we talking about? How long has this been happening?"

"Happening?" Lysandra's laugh is sharp as breaking glass. "Sweetheart, it's done. Finished. Baked into the city's foundation now. That black sludge you're pulling out of the bay? That's not runoff anymore. That's the fucking cancer, and it's everywhere."

She moves closer still, close enough that I can smell the cigarette smoke mixed with stale coffee and the distinctive cedar scent that used to mean 'safety' but now means 'complicity.' My mother, who knew about this. Who'd been trying to expose it for years while I played by the rules, followed protocols, trusted the system that had just handed me a promotion as a consolation prize for being too blind to see what was happening beneath my feet.

"You need to get out of there," she says quietly, urgency bleeding through every word. "County General is sitting on top of one of the worst contamination sites in North Jersey, and they know it. They've known since day one." She flicks her cigarette onto the concrete where it sputters and dies. "The question isn't whether you can fix this, Commander. The question is whether you'll survive knowing you wore their uniform while they poisoned everyone you swore to protect."

* * *

I watch Lysandra's fingers, steady despite everything, pop the latches on a ruggedized Panasonic Toughbook resting on the hood of my Crown Vic. The New Jersey state police emblem has been carefully ground off. She cracks it open and the screen boots up with a soft chime, casting a harsh green glow over our faces that makes us look like corpses.

"Hold this," she says, shoving a cigarette between my lips without asking. I don't smoke, but I take it anyway. My hands are shaking. The garage smells like damp concrete and motor oil, but underneath that is something else—a sickly-sweet decay that I now recognize for what it is. Corrupted water mains. Poisoned earth.

She pulls up something called BATC Telluric Engineering logs. Green terminal text scrolls past, reflecting in my wide eyes.

"There," Lysandra points with a stubby finger, ash falling onto the keyboard. "Pylon #4. You see those numbers?"

I lean closer. The flow-rate data from October 3rd, 2000. My medical mind kicks into gear even as my stomach turns. I start doing calculations—gallons per hour, dispersion rates through municipal systems, absorption coefficients for pulmonary tissue...

"Jesus Christ," I whisper.

"Eight hundred thousand gallons, Mara." Her voice is flat, dead. "It's coating the lungs of every Orc dockworker and Dwarven machinist down here. Malvourne and Morvain signed the order. It's a culling."

The cigarette burns between my fingers. I drop it, crush it under my boot.

"The black-iron flecks in their sputum..." My voice breaks. "The pneumoconiosis we've been seeing. It's not a mutation. It's chemical warfare."

Lysandra doesn't say anything. She just keeps scrolling. There are names on the manifest—technicians who loaded the tanks, engineers who calculated trajectories, executives who approved budgets. Names I recognize from County General fundraisers. People who clink champagne glasses at the Sterling Manor country club while their waste products kill working-class metahumans by inches.

"How did you get this?" I ask, though I already know. The weight of what she's done sits heavy in the garage air, pressing down like a physical thing.

"My father had a safe deposit box. Insurance policy." She taps another key. A separate file opens—memos between Lord Malvourne and Director Elias Morvain. The language is corporate, sanitized, but the meaning is clear:

*...maintenance of caste hierarchy through targeted biological suppression... experimental compound designation 'Apep's Black Venom' shows promising results in reducing labor agitation among lower-tier demographics... projected reduction in medical infrastructure demands by Q2 2001...*

"Lower-tier demographics," I repeat, tasting bile. "Is that what they call our patients?"

The temperature in the garage drops suddenly, as if someone's opened a window into winter. My white-lilac aura flares defensively around me, trying to purify the toxic air, but there's too much corruption here. Too much death. The cedar-scented wards I maintain for Danny Reyes seem fragile now—paper-thin against what's coming.

"How many people are we talking about? How many died?"

"Not enough." Lysandra's eyes meet mine and there's something hollow behind them. "Not nearly enough to stop it."

She pulls up another document. A map of Newark's water distribution system with red circles marking contamination zones. Pulpaski Skyway. Kearny Marshes. The South Side Grid where Sub-Station Seven draws its power.

"This isn't just happening here," I say, following the lines on her screen. "This is the whole damn region."

"Worse. Morvain's got contracts in six states." She scrolls again. More maps. More circles. More deaths.

I think of Danny Reyes in his coma, his lungs filling with black slime. Of the other patients at County General—the Orc security guard who can't breathe without a tank, the Goblin bartender with the hacking cough, the Dwarven foreman whose X-rays look like rust. All of them casualties of business decisions made in boardrooms three hundred miles away.

"What do we do?" The question sounds pathetic even to my own ears.

Lysandra closes the Toughbook with a sharp click. In the sudden darkness, I can barely see her face.

"We expose it. We burn their empire down."

* * *

The Toughbook snapped shut with a sound like a coffin lid. My mother's hands trembled as she closed it, fingers drumming once against the cracked plastic before falling still.

"We're out of time," Lysandra said, and the words came out flat, final. Her eyes—those same green eyes I saw in my mirror every morning—had gone distant, calculating something far beyond this concrete tomb we'd made of ourselves. "The High-Spire already knows. They know what I took."

The air in the garage suddenly felt too thick, too wet. My white-lilac aura flared without conscious thought, rippling outward in defensive waves, trying to cleanse the space between us even as my cedar wards strained at their boundaries. But there was no purifying fear. No scrubbing away the weight of what we now knew.

"Mom—"

"I'm ghosting tonight." She cut me off with surgical precision, already moving toward the service elevator like a woman who'd memorized her own funeral march. "There's a nurse. Elena Reyes. Human, fierce as broken glass, works the South Side clinics. She's setting up a shadow operation. Underground. For the poisoned ones."

My boots scraped against oil-stained concrete as I followed her. "What poison? What are you talking about?"

Lysandra paused at the elevator doors, pressing her palm against the metal like she could feel its coldness one last time. When she turned back, shadows pooled beneath her cheekbones, and I caught it—the smell. Stale tobacco smoke clinging to wool, ozone from her hurried teleportation, and underneath it all, that uniquely human scent of sheer terror.

"The 800,000 gallons they dumped into Newark Bay three years ago," she said quietly. "Apep's Black Venom. It didn't dissolve. It didn't disperse. The currents funneled it down through the old sewer lines, into the foundation water mains. The whole Undercity is sitting on top of a goddamn poison bomb, Mara, and nobody knows except the people who put it there."

The elevator dinged. Doors opened on nothing but darkness beyond.

"Danny Reyes—Elena's husband—he got sick six months ago. Liver failure, they said. But he's not the only one. There are dozens. Hundreds maybe, if we count the slow rot." Her hand found mine, squeezed hard enough to hurt. "I'm going to help them. And then I'm disappearing before Morvain's hunters find me."

"You can't just—" My voice cracked.

"I have to." Lysandra pulled me into an embrace that felt less like love and more like a life raft in a hurricane. Her body shook against mine, and my aura surged white-lilac around us both, desperately trying to calm her racing heart even as my own threatened to explode from my chest. She smelled wrong. Terrified. "Play the good soldier, baby girl. Use your 'Golden Saint' status. Let them think you're clean, loyal, pure. It'll be your shield."

Her hands found my face, thumbs brushing away tears I hadn't realized were falling.

"And Mara?" Those green eyes locked onto mine with an intensity that burned. "Never trust Director Morvain. Not for one second. He knew about the dumping. Might've ordered it himself."

The elevator light flickered behind her.

"Mom, please—"

"Go back upstairs. Do your job. Be perfect." She kissed my forehead once—a ghost-touch, already distant. "And if anyone asks, you never saw me tonight."

Then she was gone, swallowed by shadow and the yellow-sick light of the garage's failing bulbs, moving toward that waiting elevator like death itself had come calling for an old friend.

I stood alone in the poisoned air, my white-lilac aura flickering weakly against concrete walls that reeked of damp rot and motor oil and all the things that should not have been mixed together. The Toughbook lay discarded on the ground between us, its dark screen reflecting nothing but my own stricken face.

Above me, somewhere fifteen stories up, County General ER waited with its fluorescent lights and sterile halls and all those people I'd sworn to save.

Below me, in darkness older than the city itself, something black and terrible spread through water mains like a promise kept too long.

And I—the Golden Saint, Commander Vance, the woman who could heal anything with a touch—stood at the center of a secret that would kill us both if I made even one wrong move.

The elevator dinged again, patient as a coffin door closing.

---

## CHAPTER 13: THE VIADUCT ARC-BOMB

The beeping was wrong.

I stared at the cardiac monitor mounted above the driver's compartment—its rhythmic *bip-bip-bip* cutting through the rain-slicked darkness like a question mark. Self-test mode. The whole goddamn rig was running diagnostics while I sat there in the passenger seat of Rig 42, watching droplets race down the windshield. Graveyard shift. Tuesday night. November seventeenth, two-thirty AM.

"Christ, Vance," Garcia muttered from behind the wheel, his breath fogging the interior mirror. "You been checking those bandages for twenty minutes. They ain't gonna breed."

He was right. The telluric gauze packets lined up neat as soldiers in their compartment—sterile white, barely glowing with residual charge. Medical grade. Expensive. I ran my thumb across the packaging anyway, feeling the embossed warnings, the lot numbers, anything to keep my hands busy.

The epinephrine amps rattled when I opened that compartment. Four syringes left. Should've been six. Someone forgot to reorder Monday. I made a note on the clipboard even though I knew it wouldn't matter. Nothing mattered except the rhythm of the work—the inventory, the checks, the routine that kept the *other* thoughts from crawling out of whatever hole I'd shoved them into three days ago.

Three days since they told me about Mom's car. Three days since I'd stopped by her apartment in Sterling Manor and found the place empty, dishes still drying in the rack, her reading glasses on the kitchen table. Three days since I learned she'd gone underground.

The radio crackled. Static. Then:

"—Code Three dispatch. All units respond. Ten-thirty-three. Nine Street Viaduct. Suspected arc-car detonation. Multiple casualties reported. Requesting BATC interceptor immediately—"

My hand froze on the clip-board.

"—vehicle identified as late-model sedan, plate Victor-Alpha-Niner-Seven-Niner-Tango. Repeat: Vict—"

"Victor-Alpha-Niner," I whispered.

Garcia's eyes flicked toward me in the rearview. "Vance?"

I wasn't listening anymore. Wasn't thinking. My legs were moving, muscle memory throwing open the driver's side door before Garcia could process what was happening. Rain hit me like ice water—cold November downpour soaking through my uniform in seconds.

"Dispatch, this is Rig 42. We're on it." My voice came out steady somehow. Professional. "Commander Vance responding to 9th Street Viaduct. Requesting clearance for high-speed pursuit protocol."

The siren wailed before Dispatch could acknowledge.

"No, Mara—" Garcia's protest got swallowed by the horn as I threw the rig into drive, tires screaming against wet asphalt. The Ford trauma-ambulance lurched forward like a bull charging red. My heart hammered against my ribs hard enough to bruise.

*Hold on, Mom. Just hold on.*

The Pulaski Skyway loomed ahead—a concrete beast cutting through Newark Bay's industrial sprawl. I ran it at sixty-five, seventy, the rig fishtailing around the few cars brave enough to be out this late. Red and blue lights painted everything crimson and shadow.

"Dispatch reports structure collapse on the viaduct span," Garcia shouted over the siren. He'd moved up front without me noticing, his big hands gripping the dash rail. "Police are establishing perimeter. Estimated arrival time?"

"Two minutes." My knuckles were white on the wheel. "One minute if God feels generous."

The smell hit me first—burning rubber mixing with something worse. Something chemical. Iron-gall residue, thick and acrid, coating the back of my throat. Then the smoke rose above the viaduct's silhouette, black and greasy against the rain-darkened sky.

I killed the siren fifty yards out. Let the engine's whine carry us in.

The scene was chaos.

Police cruisers blocked both ends of the bridge, officers in telluric-resistant gear waving us through. The viaduct itself looked like a wound—the center span collapsed, twisted steel jutting upward at wrong angles. And there, hanging suspended between intact roadway and ruin: a sedan, half-swallowed by the breach.

Victor-Alpha-Niner-Seven-Niner-Tango.

My mother's car.

"Mara!" Garcia grabbed my arm as I jumped from the rig. His grip was iron. "You can't go out there! Whole thing could come down!"

But I was already running toward the collapsed section, boots slipping on wet pavement. The heat from the detonation made my skin prickle even through three inches of concrete separating me from the wreckage. Blue-black scorching marks radiated outward from where the arc-car had blown—a perfect circle of destruction that told me this wasn't random.

This was targeted.

I could see movement inside the car. A figure slumped against the driver's side window.

*Mom.*

"Ladder!" I screamed at Garcia. "We need a goddamn ladder and a rescue harness!"

The figure didn't move when the light hit them. Didn't flinch. Just... sat there, rain streaming down the glass, blood trickling from somewhere I couldn't make out from here.

My white-lilac weave flared without conscious thought—threads of protection spiraling around my forearms, my chest, my head. Triage armor. The old instincts kicking in because the new ones were shattering into pieces I couldn't afford to acknowledge right now.

"Commander Vance!" A cop ran up, face twisted with concern. "You can't—it's not stable! The whole span could—"

"I'm going." My voice cut through his protest like a scalpel. "Get that ladder. Now."

He hesitated one second. Saw something in my eyes that made him nod instead of arguing. Smart man.

The ladder came down heavy, metal rungs cold and slick under my hands as I climbed out over empty space. Forty feet above Newark Bay's polluted waters. Thirty-five feet above the rubble-pile where my mother's car hung suspended like a prayer.

* * *

The rig wheels lock as I throw us into a controlled slide, the sound of screeching brakes cutting through the November rain. Everything moves in slow motion. Through the windshield, I see it—a sedan completely consumed by flames that burn wrong. Too blue. Too violet. Arc-fire.

"No," I breathe, but my hands are already moving, releasing my harness, grabbing my trauma kit from behind the seat.

"Commander!" Reyes calls after me, but I'm already slamming the passenger door open, boots hitting pavement that sizzles under my feet. Blue-black residue coats everything—iron-gall. The smell hits me next: burning rubber, scorched asphalt, and something else. Something chemical that makes my eyes water and my lungs burn even through the filtered air of the viaduct.

The heat is immediate. A wall of it. I can feel my skin tightening, the sweat on my face evaporating instantly. The fire roars like a living thing, feeding on metal and plastic and flesh, spitting showers of blue-white sparks that hiss when they hit the wet concrete.

"Lieutenant Vance!" An Orc tactical officer steps into my path, his body armor gleaming under the emergency lights. His MP5 is raised, not aimed at me yet, but ready. The barrel pointed somewhere near my chest. "Class-1 Hazard Zone. You need to fall back."

I try to push past him. He doesn't budge. Just a solid mass of muscle and ceramic plating.

"My mother's car," I say, and my voice sounds foreign. Raw. "That's her car."

"Ma'am." He uses the formal term, but there's no respect in it. Just distance. Protocol. "There's nothing left. BATC sweep confirmed secondary arc-charges in the chassis. We're waiting for EOD."

"She could still be alive!"

My white-lilac weave flares without conscious thought. Cedar-warding magic crackles around my fists, the scent of crushed cedar bark mixing with the toxic iron-gall smoke. The Orc's eyes widen behind his gas mask. He raises the MP5 properly now, training it on center mass.

"Stand down! That's an order!"

But I'm already moving. Not thinking. Just reacting. My arm sweeps out in a desperate arc, raw power exploding from my palm. The concussive blast catches the Orc square in the chest plate, sending him stumbling backward into two of his teammates. The perimeter tape snaps as I crash through it, my medical kit clutched against my chest like a shield.

The heat intensifies. My skin feels like it's melting. I can see through the fire now—well, almost. The sedan's frame is still visible, twisted and blackened. And there, in what used to be the driver's seat...

No. No body. No blood. Nothing that looks like Lysandra Vance.

Just fire. So much fucking fire.

I drop to my knees ten feet from the wreckage, ignoring the screaming protests from my thighs, the rain soaking through my uniform pants. My hands shake as I fumble with the trauma kit latch. Come on, come on, come on.

The tactical officers are shouting behind me. Heavy boots on wet concrete. More Orcs. Maybe Street-Elves. I don't look back.

"You need to get clear!" someone yells. "We're evacuating the whole viaduct!"

"There might be survivors!"

But even as I say it, I know. I can feel it in my bones. In the way the fire burns too hot, too blue, consuming everything. In the iron-gall residue eating through the concrete itself, creating small pits that hiss and smoke.

Lysandra never believed in the old gods. She called them "fairy tales for superstitious mundanes." But she knew about the weaves. Knew enough to teach me the basics when I was young. How to sense magical currents. How to shield myself from psychic probing.

If she were alive, I'd feel something. Even through the arc-fire, even through whatever dark shit caused this, I should feel her presence like a weight against my chest. Like a second heartbeat.

There's nothing.

My white-lilac weave flares brighter, desperation making it unstable. The air around me shimmers with raw power. I can taste copper on my tongue. Feel my pulse hammering in my ears, drowning out the roar of the flames.

"Commander Vance! Last warning!"

I ignore them all. My fingers find the handle of the trauma kit again—when did I dropped it?—and I start pulling supplies. Tourniquet. IV fluids. Burn gel. Everything I'll need if by some impossible miracle there's anyone left to save.

Except there isn't.

The sedan frame groans, metal stress-screaming before it collapses inward with a sound like God's own thunderclap. A gout of blue-violet flame erupts skyward, and the heat slams into me like a physical blow. I throw one arm up to shield my face, feeling my eyebrows singe.

When I lower it, blinking water and sweat from my eyes, the driver's side is gone. Completely consumed. There's no seat. No dash. Just molten metal and fire that shouldn't exist in our world.

This wasn't an accident.

Someone did this. Someone staged this. And they made damn sure there would be nothing left to identify.

I should stand. Should retreat back behind the perimeter line before the tactical officers decide I'm more threat than victim. Before EOD arrives with their bombs and their cold professionalism.

Instead, I crawl forward another foot. Then another. Until I'm close enough to feel the arc-fire licking at my boots, until I can see individual droplets of iron-gall residue sizzling on the asphalt like living things.

My mother taught me how to be strong. How to survive. But she also taught me hope was just another word for delayed pain.

Right now, kneeling in the rain and the smoke and the impossible blue flames, I understand what she meant.

"Lysandra," I whisper, but the wind steals her name, carrying it away across the viaduct where emergency vehicles are backing up, where tactical teams are forming perimeters, where my entire world just collapsed into ash and iron-gall residue.

The white-lilac weave around me flickers. Fractures. And for the first time since I learned to sense its presence, I feel it starting to unravel—not from any outside force, but from within. As if even magic cannot bear the weight of what just happened.

I close my eyes.

And when I open them again, everything has changed.

* * *

The heat hits me like a physical wall.

I'm fifteen feet from the wreckage now, close enough to feel my skin tighten and crack beneath my helmet. Close enough to smell it—the burning rubber, the scorched asphalt, something else underneath. Something chemical. Sweet and acrid at once.

"Commander! Vance!" Someone shouting behind me. I don't turn around.

My knees hit the wet pavement hard enough to jar my teeth. The cold rain soaks through my pants immediately, but I barely register it. My hands are already outstretched, fingers spread wide above the twisted metal skeleton of what used to be my mother's car.

The white-lilac flame erupts from my palms without conscious thought.

It's different this time—fractured, desperate. My weave tears itself apart trying to reach deep into the inferno, searching for cellular structures, for heartbeats, for anything living that needs healing. The flame flickers wildly between colors—lilac fading to angry violet, sparks of pure white shooting out like dying stars.

There's nothing there.

Just metal. Molten plastic. And underneath it all, coating everything in a thick, greasy residue that makes my magical senses scream warnings my brain can't process yet. The residue smells like copper and rotting flowers, and when my weave touches it, it recoils like flesh burned by acid.

"No." The word comes out strangled. "No, no, no—"

I push harder, driving more power into my search. The heat is unbearable now. Paint on my helmet is cracking with audible *pops*. Sweat pours down my face inside the mask. But I don't care. I can't stop. There has to be something. A heartbeat. Lung tissue. Bone structure. Anything.

*Find her. Find her find her find her—*

My weave screams. It's like shoving my hands into an open wound, except the wound is everywhere and nowhere at once. The feedback echoes hollowly through my skull—the sound of my magic bouncing back untouched, unspent, useless.

Empty.

The flames lick higher as if mocking me, fed by whatever accelerant was used. They consume what remains of the car—of her—and there is nothing left but ash and twisted steel and that god-awful chemical sweetness.

"VANCE!" Strong hands grab my shoulders. Someone from BATC, their uniform dark with rain. "Commander, you're going to burn yourself alive! Pull back!"

I try to jerk away but they hold firm. Behind them, I see other responders keeping their distance, watching the inferno with professional wariness. One of them—a veteran paramedic named Rodriguez I've worked with before—is talking into his radio, calling for fire suppression.

But none of that matters. None of it.

Because my mother is in those flames.

And I couldn't save her.

My weave pulses erratically, white-lilac light flickering across the wet pavement in agonizing waves. Each pulse feels like a heartbeat torn from my chest. My breathing comes in ragged gasps, fogging up my helmet's interior until everything blurs.

"Please," I whisper, though I don't know who I'm begging. God? The universe? Myself? "Please..."

Another wave of power surges from me involuntarily—my grief given form as wild magic that has no discipline, no control. It lashes out at the flames like a drowning man grabbing at straws. The fire flares bright blue for a moment where it touches my weave, then settles back down.

As if laughing at my weakness.

"There's nothing there, Commander." Rodriguez's voice is gentler now, laced with pity. "You have to step back."

I finally look at him—really look—and see the way he's holding himself ready to restrain me again if needed. In his eyes: fear. Pity. And underneath both: certainty.

He already knows what I'm refusing to accept.

My hands are shaking so badly I can barely keep them steady. Slowly, mechanically, I pull them back toward my body. The white-lilac flame dies down to a weak glow around my fingers before sputtering out entirely.

For the first time since I developed my gift, my healing weave goes completely dark inside me.

Cold.

Empty.

Like ash.

I stare into the flames without seeing them anymore. Somewhere in those coals and melted metal is what remains of Lysandra Vance—the woman who raised me alone after my father died, who taught me medicine when she should have been resting after double shifts, who never once complained about the sacrifices she made.

And I let this happen.

I was supposed to protect her. That was my job—to heal, to save, to be the shield between life and death.

But when it mattered most, I wasn't there fast enough. Wasn't strong enough. Wasn't *anything* except late.

My throat closes up. Tears spill hot and bitter down my cheeks, mixing with rainwater that drips from my helmet brim.

Behind me, someone starts crying too—a witness maybe, or another first responder overwhelmed by the scene. But their grief sounds distant compared to mine.

This isn't just loss.

This is failure crystallized into nightmare fuel that will haunt every moment of every day for the rest of my life.

As BATC medics finally haul me backward, away from the wreckage, something catches my eye on the asphalt near where my mother's car came to rest.

A piece of silver chain—melted beyond recognition but still unmistakably hers because I gave it to her last Christmas. It hangs from a twisted clump of blackened metal like an accusation.

Without thinking, I wrench free from the medics' grip long enough to snatch it up.

The metal sears my palm immediately—still hot from the fire, burning me in the same way everything else in my life has suddenly burned away.

I close my fingers tight around it anyway.

Let it brand me.

Let it mark what I've lost and what I couldn't prevent and how utterly broken I am right now in this moment on this viaduct under this freezing November rain.

The pain is welcome.

At least it means I'm still alive while she isn't.

---

## CHAPTER 14: TRIAGE ARMOR

The fluorescent lights overhead hum their sterile hymn as I move between cots, my boots tracking red across the linoleum. Three weeks since Mom's funeral. Twenty-two days since they told me it was a heart attack, not what really happened—what she became when that liche-touched artifact finally consumed her from the inside out.

I don't think about it.

Can't afford to.

"Bed seven, massive subcutaneous hematoma," someone calls from behind the triage desk. I'm already moving before the words fully register, muscle memory taking over where thought ends. My tactical headset crackles with vital signs—I let the numbers wash through me, let the rhythm override everything else.

The South Side ER has become a battlefield casualty station. Metahuman workers from the docks are flooding in after hours hauling black-iron ore, their bodies rejecting the toxic shit like living filters. They come in coughing up sludge that smells of burnt motor oil and necrotic flesh, their skin mottled with veins that pulse with unnatural darkness.

I kneel beside an Ogre-Kin whose chest cavity has collapsed inward from a falling shipping crate. He's twelve feet of gray-hide bulk reduced to wet, ragged breathing. His eyes are wide with terror and pain.

My hands hover above his torso. The white-lilac light begins to gather at my fingertips—not warm, not comforting. Just pure, clinical power. Cedar sharpness cutting through the copper stench of blood and the acrid burn of disinfectant.

I press my palms flat against his sternum.

His ribs are pulverized, fragments floating in the magical field I've constructed around them. I can feel each one individually—the micro-fractures, the shattered bone edges threatening to puncture lung tissue. My magic doesn't ask permission. It simply reorganizes reality according to my will.

The bones snap back into place with six distinct cracks that echo through the triage tent.

The Ogre-Kin screams, a sound like grinding metal.

"Sedation, now," I say without looking up. A nurse appears at my elbow with a syringe. I don't acknowledge her presence beyond taking the instrument and driving it into his shoulder muscle. The scream cuts off mid-wail.

The white-lilac glow intensifies until it's nearly blinding, washing out the world beyond my immediate focus. I'm weaving tendrils of bio-magic through torn muscles, knitting flesh, sealing ruptured vessels. Each movement is precise. Mechanical. Perfect.

Just like they taught me to be.

"Commander Vance." Nurse Patterson's voice carries the careful tone people use when addressing something volatile. "You need to rest. You've been on shift for—"

"Forty-six hours," I finish, still not looking at her. "I know."

"And you haven't slept."

"Sleeping would imply I'm tired." My hands continue their work, pulling damaged cells back together molecule by molecule. "I'm not tired. I'm functional."

The Ogre-Kin's breathing stabilizes. His eyes have rolled back, unconscious now. Good. Can't hear him gasping if he's unconscious.

A junior medic stumbles over a pile of blood-soaked gauze, catching himself against a cot. "Jesus Christ, Commander. Did you see what she just did? That was—"

"That was necessary," I cut him off, straightening from the patient. The white-lilac light fades from my hands, leaving only the harsh fluorescent glare. "Move him to recovery. Bed seven has priority."

Nurse Patterson exchanges glances with someone behind the desk. They're talking about me again—I can feel it like static on my skin. Whispered words I don't let myself parse:

"...hasn't slept in three days..."

"...just keeps pulling them back..."

"...doesn't feel anything anymore..."

They think they're being discreet. They're wrong, but I don't correct them.

What would I say? That I feel everything so intensely that I've had to build walls around it until even I can't find the doors? That every time I close my eyes I see Mom's body on that slab in the morgue, and the thing wearing her face trying to speak through lips that had started to rot?

Better to be the Mechanical Saint. Better to be perfectly functional.

My headset crackles with another alert: **BED FOUR - TELLURIC DEFIBRILLATOR NEEDED IMMEDIATELY**

"Less talking," I bark at the clustered staff, already moving toward bed four where an Elf-Kin convulses on the gurney, his body arching in seizure-like spasms. "More gauze. Prep the telluric defibrillator for bed four. Move."

The ER staff scatters like startled birds.

I kneel beside bed four without breaking stride, palms already beginning to glow that cold, sterile white-lilac. The Elf-Kin's vital signs are collapsing into cardiac arrest territory—his heart struggling against something in his system. Black-iron poisoning, most likely. Toxic magic that conventional medicine can't touch.

I place one hand over his chest, feeling the chaotic electrical storm raging through his circulatory system.

And I begin to calm it. Rhythm by rhythm. Beat by beat.

Mechanical. Perfect.

Empty.

The hum of the tactical headset fills my ears, drowning out all other sound.

* * *

The Ogre-Kin's breathing steadied beneath my hands, each inhale a measured pull of air through reconstructed lungs. The flesh knitted itself together under my touch—another miracle of white-lilac magic that tasted like nothing anymore. Just empty precision.

I withdrew my fingers from the wound and stepped back. My boots crunched on the dirt floor of the triage tent, still damp from last night's rain that seeped up from the Kearny Marshes. Somewhere beyond the canvas walls, a generator coughed and sputtered, then caught its rhythm.

Tap-tap-tap.

My index finger struck the side of my Aegis tactical headset—the gesture automatic, practiced until it became muscle memory. The volume cranked higher. Dispatch flooded my ear:

"...Code Three to County General...patient DOA on arrival...estimated time of death..."

The synthetic crackle filled my skull. I welcomed it. Let the radio static wash over me like industrial solvent, stripping away anything soft, anything human. Ten-codes followed in clinical succession. The rhythmic cadence of emergency codes became a mantra:

Ten-forty-one.
Ten-ninety-nine.
Ten-seventeen.

Numbers without context. Problems without faces.

*Beep-beep. Beep-beep.*

The cardiac monitor beside me pulsed its steady metronome. One heartbeat per second, mechanical and perfect. Not like the frantic thrumming of the Ogre-Kin moments ago. Not like—

No.

I adjusted the earpiece again, turning until the beeping and the dispatch voices merged into one cohesive hum. It was all armor now. If I stopped listening to the numbers, if I let the silence creep in for even one second, I would hear something else.

The roar of fire on the Pulaski Skyway viaduct.

The crack of structural steel giving way.

The scream that wasn't mine but somehow was.

"Commander Vance." 

The voice came from my six. Male, clinical. One of the junior paramedics I'd trained myself to forget names. "Next patient is ready."

"Copy that," I said, not turning around. My eyes remained fixed on the EKG readout, watching the little peaks climb and fall with mathematical predictability. Safe. Controllable. Dead inside.

But not dead enough.

A small hand tugged at my jacket sleeve. Soft. Insistent.

"Hey, lady?"

I glanced down. A Goblin boy, maybe eight or nine standard years, his green-grey skin sallow in the fluorescent light filtering through the tent's canvas roof. His yellow eyes were red-rimmed, wet. Behind him, on a cot near the back wall, a female Goblin lay covered in blankets. Even from here I could sense the fever radiating off her—that distinctive heat-signature of marsh sickness.

"The other docs wouldn't even look at us 'cause of the sludge," the boy said, his voice trembling between bravado and fear. The kind of street-kid cadence I'd heard a thousand times in Newark Bay. "Said we were 'contaminated.' Said to go home and die quiet-like."

My hand moved before I consciously decided. Not compassion—just efficiency. A quick burst of cedar-warding magic, sharp and precise, aimed at the mother's cot. The fever broke instantly. The magical energy dissipated into the air like steam over hot asphalt.

There. Done.

I looked back at the boy, but my eyes didn't quite focus on him. They passed through him, finding purchase on something behind, something distant and cold.

"Keep her hydrated," I said flatly. "Next patient."

"But—"

"Did you hear me?" My head turned now, slowly, mechanically. The boy flinched. I watched his face contort with disappointment that quickly hardened into resentment. Good. Resentment was easier than gratitude. Gratitude meant connection. Connection meant feeling.

And I had locked that away three weeks ago when they told me about Mom.

The boy backed away, dragging his feet across the dirt floor. His small leathery hand slipped from my jacket sleeve without resistance.

I walked toward the next cot without looking back. The tactical hum in my ears grew louder:

"...multiple casualties...gunshot wounds...trauma team standing by..."

*Beep-beep.*

Mechanical.
Sterile.
Safe.

If I kept moving, if I kept healing, if I kept listening to the numbers...

Maybe I wouldn't have to feel anything at all.

* * *

The fluorescent lights overhead flickered once—twice—then settled into their humming vigil. I sat on the cold metal bench of the ER locker room, my BATC jacket still damp with someone else's blood that wasn't mine. The scent of antiseptic couldn't quite mask it.

Silence pressed against my eardrums like cotton soaked in formaldehyde.

I fumbled for my locker combination, fingers moving through the sequence without thought. Three-left, two-right, one-full-turn. The lock clicked open, and I reached inside, pulling out the small evidence bag sealed at the top with red tape. Inside, nestled against the transparent plastic, was what remained of my mother's silver necklace—the locket that had hung around her neck since before I could remember.

Or what used to be a locket.

Now it was a twisted, melted blob of silver slag, scorched black at the edges where whatever force had torn through the bridge had caught it. The chain had fused into a single strand of metal, warped and blackened. I held it up to the harsh light, watching how the charred surface reflected nothing—not even my face.

*She's gone,* I thought, and the words felt like swallowing ground glass.

My white-lilac magic whispered at the edge of my consciousness, but it came cold now. Sterile. Like touching ice instead of water. Cedar and lilac, but hollow—empty of warmth. I'd learned to weaponize that hollowness over the past seventy-two hours. Every call became mechanical. Every patient just another set of vital signs. Heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory function. The rhythm of it all became armor.

The hum of my tactical headset had become my anchor. The crackle of dispatch calls, the rhythmic beeping of monitors, the synchronized breathing of patients sedated and stable—all of it created a wall between me and the thing trying to claw its way up my throat every time I closed my eyes.

I watched my reflection in the locker door. A stranger stared back—dark circles under eyes bloodshot from exhaustion and unshed tears I wouldn't let fall. My hair stuck out at angles I didn't have the energy to fix. There was a streak of dried blood across one cheek that I hadn't noticed until now.

The evidence bag crinkled as I shifted it in my palm.

Just one tear. Just one. But if I started, I knew I wouldn't stop, and there wasn't time for breaking down. Not when whoever had done this was still out there, walking around free while my mother burned in whatever hellhole they sent her soul to after what they did on that bridge.

I exhaled hard through my nose, forcing my heart rate to slow. My magic answered the command immediately—not from any deep emotional connection anymore, but from sheer force of will. I was training it like a dog. Obedience without love. Efficiency without passion.

*You're not Mara Vance,* I told myself. *Not right now.*

I was something else. Something harder. Something BATC could use.

The Golden Saint.

I placed the charred necklace back into the evidence bag with deliberate care, sealing it again even though the seal was already perfect. Then I dropped it back into my locker and slammed the metal door shut.

**BANG.**

The sound echoed through the empty locker room like a gunshot. Final. Absolute.

I zipped up my BATC jacket with sharp, decisive movements, smoothing down the patches and insignia. Commander Mara Vance, Tactical Medic Unit. BATC Response Division. The letters felt different on my uniform now—not just letters, but a promise. A weapon.

My Nextel pager buzzed against my hip, its vibrating alert cutting through the silence.

I pulled it off the clip, squinting at the LCD screen:

**SUMMONS - HIGH-PIRE DIRECTOR E. MORVAIN. IMMEDIATE ATTENTION REQUIRED. SUB-STATION SEVEN.**

Elias Morvain. Head of the High-Spire itself. The man who signed off on tactical deployments and sanctioned operations that made my stomach turn when I read the briefings in my commander's portfolio.

He wanted to see me. Immediately.

I clipped the pager back onto my belt, standing straight. My magic settled into its cold, mechanical rhythm—steady pulses of white-lilac and cedar that moved with clinical precision rather than instinct. No warmth. No connection.

Just power.

"Let them come," I whispered to the empty locker room. "Let them all fucking come."

I grabbed my helmet from the bench and headed for the exit, my boots echoing in the fluorescent-lit corridor beyond. Whatever Morvain wanted, whatever the High-Spire needed—they were about to get exactly what they'd created.

I was ready to burn the whole system down if that's what it took.

And if I had to become a monster to do it?

Fine by me.

---

## CHAPTER 15: THE DIRECTOR'S OVERWATCH

The elevator doors slide open with a pneumatic sigh that echoes through an impossible silence.

I step onto the eighty-second floor of the BATC High-Spire, and the world changes. Gone is the chaos of County General—the screaming patients, the copper-salt stench of blood and antiseptic, the electric urgency that crackles through every shift. Here, there is only silence so complete it has weight.

Black marble floors stretch before me, polished to such a mirror finish I can see my reflection fractured across its surface. My white EMT jacket looks out of place, contaminated, bleeding reality into this sterile environment. The lighting is muted, indirect—expensive lighting designed to make powerful men look benevolent. It doesn't work on me.

My boots click against the marble as I walk down the glass corridor toward Director Morvain's office. Through the walls, I can see into meeting rooms where High-Spire executives sit in their expensive suits, speaking in voices too soft to carry. Their faces are carved from the same cold stone as these floors.

Then I pass a doorway left ajar.

The room beyond is a server farm, all steel racks and humming equipment. But these aren't ordinary servers. IBM ThinkPads stacked in towers, their asset tags gleaming under harsh fluorescent lights. And between the racks move figures in bespoke suits—not the cheap off-the-rack affairs worn by most corporate drones, but tailored silk that speaks of old money and older power.

High-Spire Elves.

They're running arcane-magnetic scrubbers over the hardware, handheld devices that crackle with barely visible energy. The sound is wrong—a high-pitched whining squeal that makes my teeth ache, like nails on a chalkboard translated into pure sonic torture. Each pass wipes another layer of data, erasing gigabytes of information into digital nothingness.

I know those asset tags.

Lysandra's research. Her notes on the Newark Bay water toxicity. The Apep's Venom logs she'd been compiling, cross-referencing infection rates with corporate shipping manifests. All of it, disappearing into the electronic void one hard drive at a time.

An Elf adjusts his silk tie while speaking into an earpiece, his voice carrying just enough for me to catch:

"Wipe the redundant backups. If anyone asks, Vance was a rogue contractor. Total scrub."

My hands clench into fists inside my jacket pockets. The white-lilac flame burns steady in my chest, its warmth the only thing keeping me from freezing solid in this tomb of marble and silence. I keep walking. Eyes forward. Triage armor locked down tight around every emotion, every reaction.

"They're burying her twice," I whisper, so low even I can barely hear it beneath the scrubbing machines' scream.

Because there was Lysandra the woman—the researcher who died believing she could make a difference. And then there was Lysandra the legend we built around her corpse, the martyr whose death meant something, who changed something.

Now they're taking even that away.

The Director's office looms ahead—double doors of polished oak banded with gold, the kind of entrance designed to intimidate before you even meet whoever sits behind it. A receptionist I didn't notice until now stands beside it, an older woman with silver hair pulled back severely, wearing a suit that probably costs more than three months of my rent.

"Commander Vance." Her voice is professionally warm but her eyes are flat. "Director Morvain will see you now."

She opens one door without waiting for my response, gesturing me through into an antechamber. Beyond, through another set of glass doors, I can see him.

Elias Morvain. Director of BATC Operations, puppet master extraordinaire, and apparently the man responsible for erasing his own daughter's legacy from existence.

He sits behind a desk that could serve as a landing strip for small aircraft, surrounded by windows that offer a god's-eye view of Newark Bay below. Even from here, I can feel his attention focus on me like a predator tracking prey.

The flame in my chest burns brighter, casting shadows across the marble floor that shouldn't be possible in this lightless place.

I push through the second set of doors, my boots clicking against more black marble, and meet his gaze directly. My face is perfectly blank. My triage armor is holding firm.

Whatever game he's playing, whatever role he's written for me—I won't make it easy.

"Director Morvain," I say, my voice steady despite everything. "You wanted to see me about the Gold-Bismuth Seals."

His smile doesn't reach his eyes. It never does.

"You have no idea what you've walked into, Commander."

"Enlighten me."

He gestures to a chair opposite his desk—an invitation that feels less like courtesy and more like placing a pawn on a chessboard where all the other pieces belong to him.

Behind me, I hear the soft hiss of the doors closing. Locking, maybe.

The interview has begun.

* * *

The elevator doors hiss open onto a different world.

Where Sub-Station Seven had been all concrete and fluorescent hum, all the sterile practicality of emergency response, this place is something else entirely. The executive level of BATC High-Spire feels less like an office and more like a tomb carved into the sky—all polished marble floors that reflect nothing but your own pale face back at you, walls of frosted glass that whisper secrets to themselves, and a silence so profound it has weight.

My boots click against stone that's been made to look like marble. White-lilac flame flickers at my fingertips, casting dancing shadows across the corridor. It should feel comforting. Instead, it feels small. Insignificant.

The receptionist doesn't even look up as I pass. Her head is bowed over paperwork, but I can feel her eyes tracking me in the reflection of her desk's glass surface. Waiting. Watching.

Director Morvain's office takes up half the floor.

The door is already open when I reach it—a deliberate choice, I'm sure. Another power play in a room full of them. Beyond the threshold, floor-to-ceiling windows dominate the far wall, looking out over Neon Hollow like God's own judgment seat. The city sprawls below in a grid of sodium-vapor lights, an electric web that pulses with the sickly yellow-green glow of arcane contamination. From up here, the whole thing looks like a wound.

And standing before that window, silhouetted against the neon abyss, is Elias Morvain.

He doesn't turn when I enter. Just stands there, hands clasped behind his back, gaze fixed on the sprawling corruption beneath us. For a long moment, he says nothing. Lets the silence stretch until it feels like it might crack.

Then: "Lieutenant Vance."

His voice is smooth. Baritone. The kind of voice that belongs on corporate training videos and late-night talk radio shows, promising solutions to problems you didn't know you had.

"You're earlier than expected." He finally turns, and I get my first good look at him.

Morvain is tall—taller than me by a solid six inches—and built with the lean muscle of someone who maintains their physique not for health but for appearance. His suit is charcoal gray, perfectly tailored, probably costs more than three months of my salary. His hair is silver-white, swept back from a face that would be handsome if it wasn't for the eyes. Those eyes are cold. Calculating. They look at me the way a predator looks at prey.

"Directors don't keep appointments waiting," I say flatly.

A smile ghosts across his lips. "No. I suppose they don't."

He gestures toward a seating area near the windows—a leather sofa and two armchairs arranged around a low table bearing a crystal decanter and glasses. Ice clinks softly as he pours himself a drink. Bourbon, judging by the amber color.

"I've been reviewing your file," he says, settling into one of the chairs with predatory grace. "Extensive field experience. Commendations from Sector Command. And lately..." He swirls the bourbon in his glass, watching the liquid catch the light. "...you've been involved in some rather interesting incidents down in Pulaski Skyway."

My hand doesn't move to the med-kit at my belt, but I'm aware of its weight. Aware of everything in this room—the distance between us, the angles, the exits, the way his body language suggests controlled power without quite revealing its source.

"The Gold-Bismuth Pylons were compromised," I say. "I responded. That's what I do."

"Mm." He takes a sip of his drink, those cold eyes never leaving my face. "Your mother did similar work, you know. Lysandra Vance was... exceptional at her job."

The name hits like a physical blow, but my expression doesn't flicker. Won't. Can't.

"What happened to your mother was tragic," Morvain continues smoothly, as if discussing the weather rather than the woman whose death set me on this path. "An accident during a routine maintenance procedure. The official report says she lost control of the resonance matrix before it could be properly grounded."

His smile is thin. Predatory.

"But then, official reports have a tendency to gloss over inconvenient details, don't they?"

"Director—"

He holds up a hand, and despite myself, I stop. Not because I have to, but because something in that gesture carries the weight of absolute authority.

"Please. Sit." It isn't a request.

I remain standing.

Morvain's smile widens by a fraction. "Stubbornness. Good. You'll need that where you're going."

I stay silent.

"You have her talent," he says after a moment, setting down his glass with a soft clink against crystal. "Lysandra's resonance signature was remarkable—pure white flame, just like yours. But..." He tilts his head slightly, studying me like I'm a specimen under glass. "...she lacked discipline. Let herself get distracted by moral ambiguities."

"You didn't call me here to discuss my mother's career choices."

"No." His gaze sharpens. "I called you here because you've been selected for a specialized command track. Gold-Bismuth Seals, Lieutenant. The keys to Neon Hollow's telluric grid."

The air goes cold. My flame sputters once before steadying.

Those words shouldn't mean what they sound like they mean.

"They're myth," I say. "Legends from before the Breach. Something Sector Command doesn't even acknowledge exists."

"The Aegis Directive acknowledges many things behind closed doors," Morvain replies softly. "And yes, Lieutenant—the Seals are real. Hidden away in secure facilities throughout the city, waiting for someone worthy enough to bear them."

Worthy. The word hangs between us like poison in the air.

"I don't understand why you're telling me this."

His smile is chilling now, showing teeth.

"Because you're going to secure them for me, Mara. One by one. It's your destiny."

The way he says my name—like it belongs to him rather than my mother—makes something primal curl in my gut. Rage. Fear. Recognition of danger that has nothing to do with arcane contaminants and everything to do with the man sitting across from me.

"What I do or don't do for the Directorate," I say carefully, evenly, "depends on orders. And so far, you haven't given me any."

For the first time, something flashes across his face. Surprise? Amusement? Hard to tell.

"You really are forged from stronger iron than she was," he murmurs. Then, louder: "Very well. Consider this your official briefing, Commander Vance."

The promotion hits harder than it should.

"...Commander?"

"You'll need the rank to access certain facilities without raising questions." He stands, moving back to the window as if the conversation is settled. As if he just handed me my entire future and expects me to accept it without comment.

"But there will be conditions," he adds over his shoulder. "Rules you must follow. And failures you cannot afford to make."

My white-lil

* * *

The oak doors closed behind me with a sound like a coffin lid settling into place.

I stood there in the glass elevator, watching Morvain's silhouette recede upward through the transparent walls of his office. He hadn't moved from behind his desk, just watched me descend like some specimen under observation. The promotion papers sat in my jacket pocket—Commander Vance, they said—and I could feel the weight of them like stones.

The elevator hummed its frictionless descent. Floor after floor blurred past outside the glass: the glittering offices where people typed away at computers, completely unaware that magic was real and that monsters walked among us. The BATC High-Spire was a lie wrapped in chrome and glass, all of it built on foundations of blood.

My mother's face flashed behind my eyes. Lysandra Vance, the woman who'd tried to protect this city from exactly what I'd just agreed to serve.

I pressed my palm against the cool glass and felt nothing but emptiness on the other side.

The air changed as we dropped lower. That sterile, vacuum-tight atmosphere of the executive levels gave way to something more honest—the faint chemical tang of recycled air, the distant wail of sirens from the streets below. By the time we reached ground level, I could smell the Undercity proper: ozone from the marsh, exhaust fumes, rain on pavement.

The doors pinged open.

And there it was. County General ER. My home for the last six years, now officially my command post in this war nobody else even knew had begun. The lobby was chaos incarnate—the usual Tuesday night madness of hypochondriacs, junkies, and genuinely sick people all pressed together in fluorescent hell. Some teenager with a skateboard trick gone wrong was screaming about his ankle. A woman in a bloodstained dress rocked back and forth muttering prayers to a saint who wouldn't answer. Two cops were arguing with an EMT about a gunshot victim they wanted processed faster.

They all looked up when I stepped out.

Maybe it was the way I moved. Maybe it was the shift in my bearing after that meeting with Morvain. Or maybe—just maybe—they could sense the white-lilac flame burning just beneath my skin, brighter than it had any right to be inside the BATC tower without me incinerating half the building.

Dr. Reyes caught my eye from the nurses' station and did a double-take. She'd worked with Lysandra too, back in the old days before everything went sideways. Before my mother became "that rogue elemental" in the official reports.

I nodded at her. Just once. Let her see that yes, I knew exactly what I was doing when I walked into that lion's den today.

My hand went to my pocket, fingers brushing the seal Morvain had given me. Gold-bismuth, he'd called it. A key to their network. Access to resources that could save lives—or end them.

The long war begins, I thought, watching a paramedic wheel another stretcher past me toward trauma bay two. Someone else's emergency. Someone else's pain.

But they didn't know yet. Morvain and his circle of directors, all those smiling faces in their pristine offices—none of them understood what they'd just done.

They killed my mother.

They poisoned this entire city with their greed and lies.

And now they'd handed me the weapons I needed to burn every last one of them to ash.

I looked down at my hands and watched the white-lilac flames dance across my knuckles, invisible to everyone but me. Pure. Uncontaminated by their cedar-dreams or their honeyed promises of order.

The Golden Saint is dead, I told myself, feeling something cold and hard settle in my chest where warmth used to live.

Let the avenging angel rise.

The ER waited for its commander. Newark waited for its reckoning.

And somewhere above, in his ivory tower, Elias Morvain was probably already moving pieces on his board, thinking he'd won.

He had no idea what was coming.
