## CHAPTER 3: CHAPTER 3

The city breathes its last gasp of the twentieth century through my cracked windshield, and I'm already counting the seconds like they're bullets in a revolver I can't fire fast enough.

The Pulaski Skyway stretches ahead of me—a concrete serpent choking on darkness. Every light dead. Every car stalled. The Y2K bug wasn't some computer nerd's wet dream; it was real, and it had just bitten Newark in the throat hard enough to crush its larynx.

I slam the Ford's transmission into neutral, coasting until momentum dies, then I'm out and running before the metal even stops rocking. My steel-toed boots hit pavement that's still warm from the day's heat, but the air? Christ, the air tastes wrong. Like copper pennies and burning plastic.

Behind me, the gridless city groans.

Emergency lights sputter in the distance—County General probably, the only place that might still have backup generators worth shit. But Danny isn't there. Danny's at home, where I left him an hour ago watching MTV with a bowl of Cocoa Puffs, oblivious to the fact that the whole fucking world was about to tear itself apart at the seams.

My lungs burn. The cold doesn't touch me yet—the way it should, the way it would if I were normal—but sweat stings my eyes as I cut across someone's lawn, vault their chain-link fence, and hit South Street running again.

The apartment building looms four stories of peeling brick and rust-stained fire escapes. Emergency lights flicker in the stairwell windows like dying stars trying to remember how to shine.

I don't slow down.

Mrs. Gable is already in the hallway when I hit the third floor. She's crying, her hands pressed against her face, and for a second—I swear to God—for a second she looks human. Then her jaw cracks sideways, bones shifting beneath skin that's turning the color of spoiled meat.

"Stay away from the sinks," I yell, shoving past her hard enough to send her stumbling back into her apartment door. "Don't drink anything! Don't—"

But she's already changing, and I can hear others doing the same. All over this side of Newark. All over North Jersey. The tap water. It's not safe anymore. Nothing is.

I take the last flight of stairs three at once, my shoulder crashing against the wall when I misjudge the landing. The door to our apartment—my apartment, since Mom's been gone six years—stands open just a crack.

Just enough.

Danny's not in the living room.

The TV still plays, soundless now without electricity, frozen on some commercial for pizza that probably tastes like ashes even if you could get them to deliver. His Cocoa Puffs sit on the coffee table, milk going warm and flat.

Then I see it—the glass by the sink. Broken. Water spreading across the linoleum floor, catching the moonlight through the window like spilled blood.

My stomach drops into my boots.

"Danny?"

The bathroom door is closed.

I know what I'm going to find before I turn the knob. I know it with every fiber of my being because this is how stories like mine always start—with something precious poisoned, with a choice that wasn't really a choice at all.

The iron in me wakes up then, slithering through my veins like liquid mercury, and the temperature in the hallway plummets so fast I can see my breath fogging in front of my face.

* * *

The door splintered off its hinges as I kicked it open, the rotten wood giving way like tissue paper. The apartment was black—pitch dark except for the moonlight slicing through the frosted windows.

"Danny?" My voice cracked. Sounded wrong in my own ears.

Silence. Then—a drip. Drip. Drip.

Water running.

I moved through the living room, hands outstretched, fingers brushing against familiar furniture. Coffee table. Couch. The TV stand with Mom's picture sitting crooked on top, her smile frozen from before everything went to hell.

The dripping got louder as I rounded the corner into the kitchenette. The faucet was on full blast, water pouring out but it wasn't clear. It was *wrong*—thick as motor oil, sluicing down the drain with a gurgle that made my teeth hurt. The smell hit me next: sulfurous rot, like something dead had been sitting in the pipes for months.

And there he was.

My little brother stood on our mother's wooden stool, the one she used to reach the high cabinets, his oversized New York Giants pajamas hanging off his skeletal frame. He looked so small up there, eleven years old and already too thin, his dark hair wild around his face. 

In his hand: a glass tumbler filled with tap water.

But it wasn't water.

It was black. Not brown, not gray—*black*. An iridescent, oily black that seemed to swallow the moonlight instead of reflecting it. Little motes of light swirled inside like dying stars.

"Cole?" Danny's voice was sleepy, confused. "The faucet wouldn't turn off. I'm thirsty."

"No." The word ripped from my throat. "Danny, NO!"

I launched myself across the linoleum floor, arms stretched, desperate. Too far. Always too fucking far.

He blinked once at me. Then his lips parted. Then—

He drank.

Swallowed that poison like it was fresh lemonade. The black liquid disappeared down his throat. His eyes widened for just a second, pupils dilating until there was no white left, just two pools of midnight staring into nothing.

"Danny!" My hands caught him as he crumpled, the empty glass slipping from his fingers. It shattered against the floor with a sound like breaking bones—*CRACK-CRACK-CRACK*—and the shards scattered across the yellowed linoleum.

He convulsed in my arms, back arching unnaturally. A wet, rattling cough exploded from his mouth, and what came out wasn't spit or bile.

It was *iron*.

Flecks of rust-red metal spraying across my face, stinging like acid, sticking to my skin where blood should have been. His lungs were filling up. I could feel it—the weight of iron settling inside him like ballast.

The apartment temperature plummeted. My breath became clouds in front of me. Frost crawled across the kitchen windows, spreading like veins, like death creeping inward.

"Mom," Danny whispered, blood trickling from his nose now, mixing with the iron dust on his upper lip. "Cole... can't... breathe..."

My magic didn't ask permission. It didn't think. It just *was*.

Heat flooded through me—not the warm kind but the burning kind, the kind that felt like swallowing molten glass. Power surged outward in desperate waves. I slammed both palms against Danny's chest, trying to pull, trying to draw that iron *out*, trying to reverse whatever the fuck had happened.

But you can't put iron back once it's in your lungs. You can't unwring the towel.

The frost spread faster, covering every surface. The running water froze solid mid-drip, icicles forming and shattering, forming and shattering. My hands burned ice-cold as they pressed into my brother's collapsing ribcage.

"Please," I begged something—I don't know what, God or devil or the universe itself. "Please please please *please*—"

Danny's eyes rolled back until only white showed. Then even that went gray, turning ash-colored, lifeless.

The faucet finally stopped running. The last droplet of black water froze in mid-air between the spigot and the sink, suspended like a tear, like a promise, like everything I'd failed at crystallized into one perfect moment before it shattered on the floor with all the rest.

And my little brother stopped breathing altogether.

* * *

The air in my lungs burns colder than January wind off the bay.

Danny's body goes rigid against me, a seized engine locking up mid-torque. His spine arches backward with a sound like tearing fabric and snapping cable. I barely catch him before his head cracks against the linoleum.

"DANNY!"

My voice splits the apartment.

He convulses once, twice—a marionette with cut strings jerking on invisible wires. Then his mouth opens and that *thing* comes out.

A spray of arterial red hits the wall behind him, but it's wrong, all wrong—the blood runs thick and viscous, speckled with fragments that catch the overhead light like crushed glass. Black glass. Metallic shards that scatter across our kitchen floor with the sound of breaking machinery.

I drop to my knees without thinking, grabbing him by the shoulders. His skin feels wrong under my palms—too hot where it should be cold, fever-burning through the chill already spreading from my hands. Because they're glowing now. That same frost-cobalt light that killed the men at Sub-Station Seven is bleeding from my fingers, casting dancing shadows across Danny's face.

His breathing makes a noise like grinding gears.

No—worse than gears. Like someone trying to breathe through a fistful of rusted nails.

"Shit, shit, SHIT—"

I slam my glowing hands against his chest, right over his heart. The contact point erupts with crystalline frost that spreads outward in fractal patterns, freezing the grease stains on our countertop, frosting the edge of the sink. The temperature must be dropping twenty degrees per second because I can see my breath now, can feel ice forming along my eyebrows.

The magic pours out of me like blood from a severed artery.

I can *feel* it inside him—the iron, the sludge, whatever the fuck that was. It's moving through his alveoli, reacting violently with living tissue, crystallizing into rigid black-iron structures that are turning his lungs into stone. Each breath forces more air against those calcifying surfaces, accelerating the process. A feedback loop of suffocation.

"No no NO—Danny, listen to me, you gotta—"

He's not listening. Can't listen. His eyes roll back white and blue, lips parting around another wet cough. More black-spotted blood spatters between us.

My hands dig deeper into his chest cavity, not physically but magically, reaching with that new sense I barely understand how to control. I'm feeling for the iron deposits, tracing their paths through bronchial tubes, finding where they've already formed solid barriers.

And then I start pulling.

Not the iron—Jesus Christ, there's too much of that, it would tear him apart—but the heat. The reaction energy fueling the calcification. I'm drawing thermal mass away at a rate my body shouldn't survive, channeling all of it into frost spreading across every surface of this kitchen we grew up in. The refrigerator door is sheathed in ice three inches thick. The window above the sink has frosted over completely.

His breathing slows. Becomes shallower.

Less desperate.

"Stay with me, Danny. Stay. With. Me."

The words come between clenched teeth because my jaw won't stop chattering—not from cold, but from exertion. Using magic like this feels like running a marathon while holding your breath underwater. My vision tunnels. Spots dance at the edges.

But I keep pulling.

Can't reverse what's already happened—those crystals are permanent now, embedded deep in lung tissue. But I can stall it. Keep his airways just flexible enough for those agonizing, shallow breaths. Each one sounds like velvet being torn apart slowly, deliberately, but at least they're *happening*.

Danny's eyelids flutter. For a moment his pupils focus on me, blue-gray and wide with terror and pain.

"Cole..." His voice cracks like breaking ice. "Can't... breathe..."

I gather him into my arms, lifting him like he weighs nothing even though he's a growing boy, all sharp elbows and knees. Frost coats his hair as I press him against my chest where the glow is brightest, trying to share warmth I don't have to give, stealing it instead from the apartment itself.

"I know," I whisper into his ear. "I know, buddy. We're going. We're getting you help."

But even as I say it, I understand: my magic isn't medicine. It's brute force and desperation. I've bought us time—I don't think I can buy anything else.

Danny shivers violently in my arms, lips turning that horrible shade of blue-green that means lack of oxygen. His breathing has become almost imperceptible now, each inhale taking longer than the last.

The truck keys. They're on the counter by the door where Mom left them this morning before her double shift started. Seems like years ago now, not hours.

I'm moving before I decide to move, carrying Danny through the dark apartment, kicking open the front door hard enough to dent the drywall. The January night hits us like a wall of knives—cold, clear, indifferent to whatever fresh hell has just unfolded inside 1423 Clinton Street.

My boots crunch on frozen puddles as I sprint toward the rusted F-150 parked cockeyed in our driveway. Danny's head lolls against my shoulder with each step, and I can feel how shallow his pulse has become, fluttering under my fingers like a dying bird's wing.

Elena. Dr. Elena Volkov runs an underground clinic out in Kearny, handles cases County General won't touch or can't figure out. She owes me favors from Sub-Station Seven—owed everyone still standing after what happened there.

She'll have machines. Oxygen. Whatever medical bullshit can fight what I've managed to hold back.

*Please let me be fast enough.*

The truck roars to life beneath me, Danny slumped across the passenger seat while I throw it into reverse without looking, not caring about the fence post I clip or the neighbor's mailbox that explodes in my rearview mirror. We're already peeling out onto Clinton when the engine catches fully, tires screaming against asphalt slick with frost that radiates out from wherever I touched the ground.

Newark Bay slides past my window—a black mirror reflecting nothing but darkness and my own wild eyes staring back at me from the glass.

Danny makes another sound. Half cough, half choke.

"HOLD ON!" I scream at him even though he can't hear over the engine. "FUCKING HOLD ON!"

The Pulaski Skyway rises ahead of us like a concrete bridge to nowhere good, its shadows swallowing whole cars disappearing into New Jersey night.

---

## CHAPTER 4: CHAPTER 4

The tires screamed against wet asphalt as I wrenched the wheel hard left, sending gravel spray across the parking lot of the South Side Community Clinic. My knuckles were white on the steering wheel, every muscle in my body coiled tight as a spring.

"Hold on, kid," I muttered, shoving the truck into park so hard the whole chassis shuddered.

Danny's breathing was shallow, rattling like loose change in a jar. The frost-cobalt magic pulsed beneath my palm, that familiar cold burn spreading from my chest down into my arm, maintaining its death-grip on his failing lungs. It was keeping him together—barely—but he needed a real doctor. Now.

I kicked the door open and hauled him out without ceremony, one arm hooked under his knees, the other supporting his back. His head lolled against my shoulder, lips cracked and bleeding that same black-iron sludge he'd been coughing up since we found him in those marshes.

The moment we cleared the truck, the smell hit me like a punch to the face.

Bleach. Blood. And underneath it all—that sulfurous, metallic stench that made my eyes water and my nose burn. The smell of poison. The smell of something wrong in ways that went deeper than just chemistry.

The clinic's waiting room looked less like a medical facility and more like a triage tent in some third-world warzone. Fluorescent lights buzzed overhead, casting everything in harsh white glare that showed off every stain, every smear of blood on the linoleum floor, every desperate face.

Bodies packed the space wall-to-wall. Humans pressed alongside newly-awakened Dwarves, their gray skin mottled with sickness, and Orcs who were supposed to be tough as iron but now hunched over themselves, gasping for air they couldn't seem to catch. A young woman—couldn't have been more than twenty-five—clutched her stomach while another victim beside her retched up a thick stream of that black shit onto the floor where it hissed faintly against the tile.

"Doc! Doc, please!" An Orc near the front desk was on his knees, clawed hands wrapped around his throat. His voice came out like gravel being ground through a garbage disposal. "My chest is turnin' to concrete, I swear to god. Can't breathe, can't—"

A nurse rushed past me without a word, already dragging a gurney toward him, but the desperation in his eyes said she wouldn't get there fast enough.

"Cole?"

I turned. My mother stood at the doorway to the examination area, still wearing those same scrubs from earlier, now soaked through with sweat and god knew what else. Her dark hair had come loose from its bun, strands plastered to her face. But it was her eyes that gutted me—that look of exhausted horror mixed with professional determination.

She saw Danny cradled in my arms. Saw the way he wasn't moving right. Saw the frost spreading across my hand where it touched his shirt, just barely visible in the harsh light.

"Jesus Christ," Elena whispered, then louder: "Here! Get him here! Now!"

Two orderlies appeared from somewhere, moving with the practiced efficiency of people who'd already seen too much tonight. They took Danny from me—gently, as gently as could be managed—and lifted him onto a gurney. One started slapping monitors onto his chest while the other wheeled him toward an exam room.

Elena grabbed my arm before they disappeared down the hall. Her grip was iron-hard.

"You feel it?" she asked quietly, urgently. "The magic? Is it spreadin'?"

"Not yet." I shook my head. "But Danny's not gonna last another hour without real help."

Her jaw tightened. She looked like she wanted to say something else, but instead she released my arm and spun back toward the chaos of the waiting room. Her voice cracked through the noise like a whip:

"Triage by severity! Anyone coughing up black fluid, this way!" She pointed to a makeshift area cordoned off by hanging sheets. "Everyone else, stay seated. We'll get to you as fast as we can."

An old Human woman near the back started wailing, rocking herself back and forth. "My grandson... where's my grandson? They took him back there an hour ago and nobody's told me anything—"

A different nurse appeared at her side, murmuring soothing nonsense while guiding her toward some chairs that weren't already overflowing with the sick and dying.

I stood there for a moment, watching my mother become the thing she'd trained to be. Clinical. Efficient. Unemotional despite the tears tracking down her cheeks.

"Cole," she called out without looking at me, already moving toward another patient—a young Dwarf whose breathing sounded wet and awful. "Go home. Lock your doors. This isn't random."

"But Mom—"

"This wasn't an accident!" She finally turned to face me fully now, eyes blazing with something I couldn't quite name. Fear? Anger? Both? "Those respirators were stolen from our supply closet three days ago. The ones we ordered specifically because of the marsh contamination reports."

The words hit like a physical blow.

"Someone knew," Elena continued quietly enough that only I could hear. "Someone knew this was coming."

* * *

The centrifuge whirs like a dying insect trapped in glass. I keep one hand pressed against Danny's chest, feeling the cold spread through my palm—frost-cobalt spreading through his ribs in crystalline fractals, forcing those lungs to stay flexible when they want nothing more than to turn to stone.

"Hold still, kid," I mutter. "Just breathe what you can."

Elena works fast, her movements sharp and precise even as her knuckles go white around the syringe. She scoops the black sludge from Danny's mouth—thick as tar, glistening with an oily sheen under the fluorescent lights. The stuff stinks of sulfur and burnt chemicals, that same god-awful smell from the creek near Kearny Marshes.

"Pressure's not enough," she says, adjusting the oxygen mask over Danny's nose and mouth. He gasps, but it's shallow, rattling. The iron crystals in his lungs are already forming, I can feel them through my magic—hard and jagged, cutting his airways from the inside out. "Cole, we need to crack him open just to get any real airflow in there."

I shake my head. "Too risky. He won't survive the surgery if we can't stop the crystallization first."

She doesn't argue. Instead, she slides the sample tube into the centrifuge—a sleek silver machine bolted to the counter, its motor humming steadily. While it spins, she boots up the Panasonic Toughbook sitting next to the trauma bay equipment. The rugged laptop's screen flickers green and black, a command-line interface scrolling past chemical codes I barely recognize.

The centrifuge timer beeps. Three minutes exactly.

Danny shudders beneath me. His eyes flutter open—those brown irises clouding over with flecks of metallic gray. "Mr. Reyes..." His voice cracks. "It hurts. It feels like... like swallowing glass."

"I know." My hand stays cold against him, maintaining pressure, keeping those crystallized ribs from puncturing his heart. "Just hang on. Elena's gonna figure this out."

She glances at the Toughbook screen, her jaw tight. "Son of a bitch."

"What is it?"

The centrifuge clicks off automatically. Elena retrieves the separated sample tubes, slides one into the analyzer port. The Toughbook processes for three seconds flat before the readout pops up full-screen.

Mass spectrometry analysis. Chemical compound breakdown. And there, highlighted in angry red text: **APEP'S VENOM - SYNTHESIZED HEAVY-METAL COMPOUND**.

Elena's hands ball into fists. When she looks at me, her eyes are burning with something I haven't seen since that night at County General when she had to tell a mother her daughter wasn't coming back from surgery.

"This isn't some industrial accident," she says, her voice trembling but controlled. "This is Apep's Venom. It's a corporate defoliant. Someone dumped this into the water supply on purpose."

I keep my hand on Danny's chest, watching the frost-cobalt magic pulse through him in slow waves. The crystals have stopped growing for now, held in check by the cold. But they're still there, sharp and deadly inside him.

"Sterling-Voss," I say flatly. "Their PMCs did it. I saw them near the Newark Bay treatment plant last week. Black vans, chemical tanks, the whole operation. They were dumping barrels into the main intake."

Elena's breath catches. She swipes through the Toughbook's files—company records cross-referenced with the chemical composition. Her finger stops on a document marked **PROJECT CHIMERA - Q4 1999**.

"Oh God." She pulls up another file. Then another. A whole directory of corporate communications between Sterling-Voss executives and their private military contractors. Authorizations for disposal. Cost-benefit analyses. One memo stands out: *"Liquidation of toxic assets via municipal waterways - Project Chimera Phase Two. Estimated cleanup costs: $28M. Projected liability reduction: $730M."*

"They knew exactly what they were doing," Elena whispers. "They calculated the cost of poisoning people versus the cost of proper disposal. And they chose to poison us."

Danny coughs, a wet, rattling sound. Blood flecks his lips, mixed with more black sludge. "It's spreading..." he gasps. "Can feel it... in my throat..."

The Toughbook screen flickers. Elena scrolls frantically through medical databases, searching for any protocol, any treatment for weaponized heavy-metal compounds. There's nothing. Apep's Venom is classified as a next-gen chemical agent—the kind that doesn't just kill, but transforms living tissue into synthetic metal from the inside out.

"We need to get him to County General," she says. "Their tox lab might have something."

"No time." I can feel Danny fading beneath me, his heartbeat weakening despite my magic holding his ribs together. The frost-cobalt is keeping him alive, but it's not healing him. It's just slowing down the death sentence Sterling-Voss wrote for him when they decided to dump their garbage into our water.

Elena meets my eyes across the trauma bay. We both know what comes next.

"There's only one way to pull this stuff out fast enough," she says quietly. "Emergency thoracotomy. Crack his chest open, physically remove the crystallized tissue, then hope like hell we can stitch him back together before he bleeds out."

I nod once, grim and certain. "Do it."

She already has the surgical tray open—scalpel, rib spreader, sutures, clamps. Her hands are steady as she begins cutting, opening Danny up so we can fight Sterling-Voss's poison on their terms.

But this time, we're fighting back.

* * *

The monitor shrieks.

That flat, electronic wail that means everything stops. I watch the green line on Danny's screen go horizontal—a dead straight line across the dark display. Three seconds. That's how long his heart stays stopped before my frost-cobalt magic surges through my palm and into his chest cavity, sending a shock of ice-blue electricity that arcs across the bed like frozen lightning.

His back bows off the mattress. The line spikas up and down, erratic as hell, but alive. Alive.

"Jesus Christ, Cole!" Elena's hand slams against the wall for support, her face gone pale beneath the fluorescent lights. "What the fuck was that?"

"Not enough," I say, keeping both hands pressed to Danny's sternum now, feeling that cold burn in my bones. The magic is spreading through his ribcage like frost on glass, maintaining some kind of perverse life support. But it's not working right—can't get the sludge out while also keeping him stable. It's a catch-22 that's gonna kill us all if we don't do something different.

Elena's already moving, ripping open cabinets in the treatment room with desperate efficiency. "Standard oxygen won't work—the particulate size is too fine, it gets past the membranes." Her fingers are bleeding from tearing at medical tape. "We need something industrial grade. Something that'll force air *through* the poison instead of around it."

She turns, eyes wild with the same thing I'm feeling—that clawing terror that comes when you're watching someone die and medicine isn't enough. "There's an experimental shipment came in yesterday. High-pressure pneumatic respirators. Military contract stuff—supposed to be locked down tight in supply storage."

"The ones for toxic environment PMC gear?" I ask, still holding pressure on Danny's chest. The monitor's keeping its rhythm, but barely.

She nods, frantic. "Yeah. They run at 40 PSI, got filtration systems that can handle chemical warfare agents. If anything can push air *through* whatever the hell this sludge is, those can." She grabs my arm. "But they're in secure storage. Biometric lock, steel door, the whole nine yards. We'd have to break in."

I look at Danny. His skin has gone translucent, veins visible beneath as dark threads of contamination spread from his lungs outward. The magic in me is cold as a tomb, and getting colder. I can feel my own heart stuttering now, the price of channeling so much power through such a small area.

"Which way?" I say.

---

The supply closet is on the third floor, tucked away behind what used to be the maternity ward before budget cuts turned it into dead space. Elena leads me there through back corridors, past nurses who don't ask questions and janitors who've seen worse than two people sneaking through a clinic at 2 AM.

The door is exactly what she described: steel, heavy-duty hinges, a digital keypad beside a biometric scanner. And underneath, old-school but effective—a simple deadbolt with a steel plate.

"You know how to pick locks?" Elena whispers.

I shake my head. "Better." My frost-cobalt magic coils in my right hand, gathering cold until my fingertips burn white with frozen fire. I press my palm against the deadbolt and let it go.

The flame spreads across the metal like water finding cracks in glass. No sound. Just that silent blue-white inferno that eats through steel like tissue paper. Thirty seconds and the bolt drops out with a metallic clunk onto the linoleum.

Inside smells sterile—antiseptic and plastic packaging. Rows of metal shelving units packed with medical supplies in their original boxes. But Elena's already moving toward the back wall where three large black cases sit stacked on a dolly, each one marked with military transport stickers.

She rips open the first case, revealing a respirator system that looks more mechanical than medical. Heavy rubber hosing, metal valves, a faceplate that'd look at home on a deep-sea diver. "This is it. This has to work."

We grab three of them, shoving everything into a duffel bag Elena finds in another cabinet. The weight alone tells you these aren't standard equipment—they're built for people operating in environments where regular gear would kill you.

"Elena," I say as we're packing the last unit. "These aren't gonna be enough. Even with the pressure, he needs something more. A chamber. Some kind of sealed environment around his chest to maintain consistent atmospheric pressure while the respirators push air through the poison."

She stops, looks at me with those same desperate eyes from before. "Can you build something like that?"

"No." I zip the bag closed. "But I know someone who can."

---

Danny's still breathing when we get back to the treatment room, though every breath sounds like gravel grinding against concrete. I wrap him in thermal blankets, trying to keep him stable while I pack up what little gear we have left.

"He's not going to make it here," Elena says quietly, watching me work. She's already called ahead to clear us out without questions—one of the perks of being family in a place like this.

"I know." I lift Danny carefully, settling him against my shoulder. He weighs almost nothing now, all the fluids in his body replaced by poison. The monitor we're unplugging shows one final heartbeat before the screen goes dark.

The pneumatic respirators thump heavy in the duffel bag. Three chances. Maybe four if we can figure out how to repurpose parts between units.

"We're taking him to Local 405," I tell her. "It's a machinist union hall down near the docks. There's a guy there named Bram Kovacs—he's got a workshop that'd make NASA jealous. If anyone can build whatever the hell we need to keep Danny alive, it's him."

Elena grabs the keys to an old Crown Victoria parked out back. "I'll drive. You stay with him."

We move fast through the parking lot, cutting across the South Side streets toward Newark Bay. At 2 AM on New Year's Day, the city feels empty but not peaceful—just holding its breath waiting for something to happen.

Local 405 sits in a converted warehouse district, yellow lights spilling from windows that shouldn't be lit at this hour. But Bram works weird hours. Always has.

"Cole Reyes!" His voice booms across the shop floor when we burst through the door, carrying Danny and our stolen gear. "What the fuck you done now?"

I don't have time for explanations. Just drop the duffel bag at his feet and point at Danny. "Need a pressure chamber. Need it yesterday. And it has to integrate with these."

Bram looks at the respirator systems, then at Danny's chest where my frost-cobalt magic is still maintaining that fragile heartbeat, then at me. His eyes narrow with understanding.

"Christ on a crutch." He slams both hands on his workbench, making tools jump. "Alright. Get him on that table over there. I'll see what I can

---

## CHAPTER 5: CHAPTER 5

The metal door screams on its rollers as I kick it open. Cold January air rams into the heat-soaked interior of the Union hall's chop-shop, carrying snow flurries that melt instantly against hot machinery. The smell hits me first—WD-40 mixed with three days' worth of stale cigarette smoke and the acrid tang of metal shavings.

Bram Kovacs doesn't even look up from where he's hunched over the main workbench. His union coveralls are stained dark with machine oil, sleeves rolled past elbows thick with calluses that've earned every millimeter through thirty years of turning wrenches at the Bayonne refineries. He takes another drag off his Marlboro, the cherry glowing orange in the dim light of a single overhead fixture.

"Door's got a closer," he grunts without looking. "You're letting the heat out."

I don't answer. Can't waste breath explaining. Danny's getting heavier by the second, his breath rattling like loose change in a tin cup. I lay him down on the cleared workbench space—Bram had apparently been working through the night already, because there's fresh cuts of brass piping scattered across the surface, along with pneumatic hoses coiled like sleeping snakes.

"Kid looks like he swallowed a spark plug, Cole." Bram finally turns, stubbing out his cigarette in an overflowing ashtray. His eyes go wide when he sees what I'm doing to keep Danny alive—the frost-cobalt aura spreading from my palms into the kid's chest, making his ribs shift with mechanical precision. "Jesus Christ. What the hell is *that*?"

"The lung's calcifying inside him. Black Iron. Turned him into a goddamn pressure vessel." My voice sounds wrong even to me—flat, clinical. The kind of calm you get when your hands are moving but your mind has gone somewhere else entirely. "I'm keeping him ventilated manually until we build something permanent."

Bram steps closer, squinting at where my fingers press against Danny's collarbone. The cold magic makes little clouds of vapor rise from contact points, frost spreading in delicate crystalline patterns that would be beautiful if they weren't keeping a seventeen-year-old boy from drowning in his own blood.

"You want me to build a pressure-casing around his ribs?" Bram asks, running one calloused hand over Danny's compressed torso. The touch is professional, gentle despite looking like it could strip paint. "That's gonna take brass, heavy pneumatics, and a prayer."

"Get started. Now." I pull back from Danny, watching his chest collapse before I force another breath cycle through the frost. My hands are shaking—not from cold or fear, but from the exhaustion of maintaining this constant rhythm. "He's been breathing on his own for maybe two hours total since yesterday morning."

The big Dwarf nods once, already moving toward his tool wall—a massive assembly of organized chaos that most people would call a disaster zone but that he can navigate blindfolded. He grabs a caliper first, then an old-fashioned drafting compass.

"We're talking about building him an artificial ribcage that won't collapse," Bram mutters, more to himself than to me. "Gotta measure thoracic expansion, calculate tidal volume, figure out what kind of pressure differential we need to maintain..." He glances back at Danny, then at the respirators I'd dumped on the workbench. "Those things any good?"

"Stolen from County General ER. Figured we'd need them as backup." Or as replacements when Danny dies and we try again with someone else. Not that I'm thinking that. Not consciously.

Bram grunts approval and starts taking measurements, recording numbers in a grease-stained notebook. His movements have the practiced economy of someone who's built thousands of custom machines—hydraulic lifts for garbage trucks, specialized valves for chemical plants, whatever weird contraption some engineer dreamed up and needed fabricated.

"You got a name for this thing?" he asks while marking dimensions along Danny's compressed torso.

"Iron-Lung." The words come out like they've always existed, waiting for someone to speak them into reality. "Danny's gonna be the prototype. If it works, if it keeps him alive, then we build more."

"More of *what* exactly, Cole?" Bram straightens up, eyeing me the way he used to eye union reps trying to sell us on contract concessions. "You're talking about turning kids into metal-lungs. That ain't right, even by Breach standards."

"It's not about being right." My voice drops lower, colder than the frost magic still crackling around my fingers. "It's about surviving. There are five hundred kids in Newark alone who inhaled Black Iron yesterday. By tomorrow there'll be a thousand. A week from now? Nobody knows. We can either watch them suffocate one by one, or we get creative."

The silence stretches between us, broken only by Danny's rattling breaths and the distant wail of sirens heading toward the hospital district. Outside, the new year is already three hours old—a fresh millennium, a clean slate except for the fact that reality itself has torn open like a rusted seam.

Bram looks at his hands, spreads the thickened fingers wide. Since the Breach hit yesterday, every machinist in Union territory has noticed something different—their tools responding better, their intuition for mechanical systems sharpening until they can almost *feel* where bolts should go, how stresses will distribute through materials.

"Alright," he says finally. "Let's build your Iron-Lung."

I force another breath cycle through Danny's collapsed chest, watching the ribs shift with that horrible grinding sound. The kid's eyelids flutter—no consciousness yet, just reflexes firing across synapses that may never fully wake again.

"If this works," I tell Bram while reaching for the brass cuttings, "we're going to need more shops. More machinists. More union halls willing to work without asking questions."

Bram lights another cigarette, takes a long drag. "Local 405 doesn't ask questions. That's in the bylaws." His grin shows tobacco-stained teeth. "We just make things that shouldn't exist and hope nobody notices."

"Good enough."

* * *

The forge roars behind me, its heat hammering against my back while ice crawls up my forearms. My hands glow that familiar cobalt blue now—colder than they should be, but precise. Dead steady.

"Hold the angle," Bram shouts over the din. His voice cuts through the industrial chaos of the chop-shop. "Twenty degrees off the sternum line."

I don't answer. I just *feel*—the way the brass sheet wants to buckle under the heat, the molecular structure singing to me in frequencies only my frost-touched senses can read. The plasma cutter screams somewhere to my left, throwing those blinding white sparks across Danny's unconscious body spread out on the makeshift surgical table we've welded together from scrap.

Bram's lathe whines down to a mechanical purr. The first section of the Iron-Lung slides into place over Danny's chest—brass ribbing that catches the firelight like copper bones. He's been breathing on his own for six hours straight now, but barely. Each breath is a war he's losing by inches.

"This is gonna hurt him more than help if you slip," Bram says. Not warning me. Stating fact. His calloused hand comes down on my shoulder, squeezing hard enough to remind me there's weight to this. Real consequences. "Pressure's gotta hold at eight hundred PSI minimum. Runes need to be perfect."

My fingers tremble—just slightly—but the frost-cobalt flame doesn't waver. It licks along the seam where two sheets meet above Danny's heart, and I can feel it: the metal wanting to fuse, wanting to become something new. Something necessary.

"The valves fit?" My voice sounds wrong. Flat. Like I'm reading lines someone else wrote.

"Fitted 'em myself. Third time." Bram's already moving back to the lathe, feeding another sheet through. "You're welding the seams. I'm cutting the next section. We got maybe two hours before his vitals tank again."

The ozone smell hits me—that sharp electric burn that means magic and machinery are dancing too close together. Brass smoke rises in thin blue-gray wisps. Somewhere in the Union Hall beyond our improvised workshop, New Year's revelers are still partying. Drinking cheap beer. Making resolutions they'll break by morning.

Danny's making a different kind of resolution right now. Written in pain and pressure gauges and desperate improvisation.

I lean closer to his chest, feeling the shallow rise and fall. Barely there. The stolen pneumatic valves—a scrap-yard find from some defunct factory up in Paterson—sit nested in the brass framework like mechanical lungs waiting for their first breath. They'll force air into his stiffening respiratory system. Break through whatever arcane rot is turning him to stone from the inside out.

"Temperature steady at minus forty," I murmur, more to myself than Bram. The cobalt blue intensifies around my fingertips. "Starting the fusion sequence."

The weld begins with a sound like ice cracking on frozen water, but hot. Impossibly hot. The brass glows orange-white where my flame touches it, then cools instantly to that deep metallic sheen. The seam holds. Perfect fusion.

Bram lets out something between a grunt and a laugh. "Jesus Christ, Cole. You seeing what I'm seeing?"

I am. The runes he's etched into the brass—not the old ways, not anything mystical or inherited, just pure engineering principles transferred to glyphs—are glowing faintly under my frost-touched gaze. Structural reinforcement. Pressure distribution matrices. All of it working because *we* made it work. Because we were desperate enough to forget the rules.

"We're gonna kill him trying this," I say.

"We're already killing him by doing nothing." Bram doesn't look up from his lathe. Just keeps cutting, feeding metal, shaping salvation from industrial scraps. "Hold the temperature. Gonna need another section welded before we test the pressure seals."

My hands move without conscious thought now. The magic flows through me like cold current, precise and merciless. No hesitation. No second-guessing. Just the perfect fusion of opposing forces: heat and cold, magic and machinery, hope and despair compressed into brass and steam.

Danny's eyes flutter beneath closed lids.

"Cole."

Bram's voice cuts through the trance. I lift my head, breaking contact with the weld. My hands are shaking now—for real this time. The adrenaline is catching up with everything else.

"What?"

"He sees you."

I look down at Danny. His eyes are open. Not quite focused. But aware.

"Can't... breathe..." It's barely a whisper. Barely sound at all.

"It's okay, kid." My throat closes around the words. "We got you. We got something that'll help."

The plasma cutter screams again. Brass sheets slide together over Danny's chest, forming a cage that might save him or kill him or do both in some terrible order. I raise my hands, feeling the frost-cobalt gather in my palms.

"Let's finish this," I say.

* * *

The Iron-Lung shudders to life with a sound like a dying god's last breath—a wet, rhythmic *THUD-HISS* that fills the chop-shop with mechanical urgency. Brass pipes groan under pressure as pneumatic pistons slam forward and back in brutal syncopation.

Danny's chest cavity convulses beneath the apparatus Bram and I just bolted around his tiny torso. The glass casing fogs instantly with condensation, obscuring my view of those fragile ribs expanding and contracting—faster than any human lungs should have to work. But work they do. Air rushes into my brother's mouth. His eyes snap open wide, pupils dilated with pain so pure it makes my teeth ache.

"Jesus Christ," Bram mutters, wiping grease from his temple with a rag that leaves black streaks across his forehead. He doesn't look at Danny. Can't. Instead he monitors the pressure gauge on the side panel, watching the needle bounce between amber and red zones. "Hold on, hold on..."

I can't move. Frozen against the workbench, still slick with Danny's blood—the dark arterial stuff mixed with motor oil and transmission fluid from when I dragged him here through three blocks of South Side pavement. My knuckles are split. Shattered. The right hand won't straighten fully anymore; something in the finger joints gave way while I was carrying him.

But I don't care about that.

The frost-cobalt aura clings to my skin now like a second layer of muscle, ten degrees below zero, numbing the cuts that should be screaming. It came over me during the surgery, this cold focus, seeping from somewhere deep inside where rage calcifies into something harder and quieter. Something permanent.

*THUD-HISS.* *THUD-HISS.*

Each piston stroke echoes through the cramped garage. The smell is overwhelming—melting brass, ozone from overtaxed electrical components, cutting fluid evaporated under heat lamps we rigged up to keep Danny warm during the operation. Underneath it all: the copper tang of blood. Always the blood.

Danny's gasping settles into a desperate rhythm matching the machine's brutal cadence. His hands clutch at the glass casing, leaving smeared prints in the moisture. Those fingers are so small. Too small for adult-sized bolts and military-grade hardware.

"It'll hold him," Bram says finally, voice tight as guitar strings ready to snap. He won't meet my eyes. Instead he jabs a thumb toward the valve assembly mounted beside the power supply—a cluster of brass fittings and rubber gaskets stolen from an old refrigeration unit. "Standard issue. Burn out in a month. Maybe less."

My jaw clenches so hard the muscle spasms in my temple. A month. Forty weeks. Three thousand hours of watching those pistons pump air into lungs already half-destroyed by black-iron residue from the Four Heads' thermite bomb.

"Military-grade Telluric pressure-valves," Bram continues, pulling out his cigarette pack with trembling fingers. Lights one without offering me the second. Smart man. "You're talking Union County Cartel suppliers or scrapyard raiders who hit Defense contractor warehouses down in Secaucus. Either way means getting wet with people who'd gut you for spare change."

I push off from the workbench, joints popping audibly. My reflection catches in the glass of Danny's Iron-Lung—eyes hollow, face carved from marble dipped in ash. The frost-cobalt aura pulses faintly around me like bioluminescence, cold enough that my breath mists even though we're standing ten feet from forge heat still radiating off the main workstation.

A sliver of justice.

The thought arrives fully formed, clear as broken glass cutting through water. I don't question it. Can't afford to anymore.

It doesn't scrape the black iron out of his lungs—that poison will sit there permanently now, grinding against alveoli every time he inhales machine-assisted oxygen. It doesn't undo what happened at that clinic on Bergen Street. Doesn't bring back Elena or any of the other names I'm too numb to remember right now.

But it's something.

And something is better than nothing when nothing is all the world has offered your little brother since midnight last night.

*THUD-HISS.*

"Where do I get them?" My voice sounds wrong—flat and distant, like someone speaking through a long tunnel.

Bram takes a long drag, exhaling smoke toward the ceiling where shadows pool thick between hanging light fixtures. "That kind of hardware? You're talking about entering conversations with metahuman enforcers, Cole. People who collect teeth as payment. Who've got black magic running through their veins thicker than blood."

"You're telling me this because you won't help me?"

"No." He stubs out the cigarette on an engine block, crushing it until tobacco juice seeps into metal. "I'm telling you because once you step into that game, you never step out clean again."

The pistons continue their relentless rhythm. Danny's breathing steadies slightly—the Iron-Lung doing its brutal work, forcing life into a body that wants to surrender.

I look down at my hands: still shaking slightly from adrenaline dump, knuckles ground raw against concrete during the three-block carry, frost-cobalt aura climbing up my forearms in crystalline patterns.

A sliver of justice isn't enough. It's not even close to enough.

But for right now—in this moment, in this garage lit by forge-glow and desperation—it'll have to be enough.

Because if I don't start somewhere, if I don't push forward instead of collapsing here beside my dying brother, then everything Elena sacrificed at that clinic fire was wasted.

And I can't live with that weight.

Not anymore.

"I need names," I say quietly, meeting Bram's eyes for the first time since we finished bolting the apparatus together. "Give me names or get the fuck out of my way."

He studies me for a long moment, seeing something in those hollow spaces behind my pupils that makes him flinch. Whatever he finds there—whatever cold calculation has crystallized into doctrine—makes him reach for his phone instead of the door handle.

"The Threefold Cord," he says finally, thumbs moving across the screen. "Penance. Revenge. Justice."

My breath catches despite the numbness coating everything else. He said it aloud—that silent equation forming in my mind as I watched brass bolts tighten around Danny's chest cavity like a coffin lid designed to keep death at bay through sheer mechanical violence.

*THUD-HISS.*

"Yeah," I whisper, watching condensation drip down glass casing. "The Threefold Cord."

Bram nods slowly, reading the finality in my tone—the unbreakable equation settling into bone deep certainty. He reads it because he recognizes what I'm becoming: someone who weighs lives on scales tipped toward vengeance, who measures worth in slivers instead of wholes.

Someone who won't stop until every head of the Four Heads hangs from Pulaski Skyway overpasses like garlands made of failure and regret.

His phone buzzes. Once. Twice.

"Got a contact," he mutters. "Independent metahuman contractor runs junk hauls through Kearny Marshes

---

## CHAPTER 6: THE SEWAGE MANIFEST

I slipped through the alley behind the South Side Free Clinic just past eleven forty-five, my boots crunching on frozen puddles that reflected the sickly orange glow of the sodium-vapor lamps. The thermos in my left hand had gone lukewarm despite the blood-iron heat humming beneath my skin—that low, anxious warmth that never quite went away anymore, like standing too close to an acetylene torch.

The back door was propped open with a rusted fire extinguisher, same as always. I ducked inside, shaking off the February cold, and immediately caught the familiar cocktail of smells: rubbing alcohol sharp as a cut, stale coffee gone bitter, and underneath it all that electric ozone scent that meant someone had been running equipment too hard for too long.

"Mom?" My voice echoed down the narrow hallway.

No answer. But I could hear it—the distinctive clack-clack-clack of an IBM ThinkPad keyboard, frantic and insistent, coming from Elena's office at the far end. And beneath that, the screech of a dial-up modem pulling data across copper wires, that digital warbling that made my teeth hurt even when I was half a block away.

I found her hunched over the salvaged laptop, her dark hair pulled back in a tight bun that had started coming loose, strands stuck to her forehead with sweat. The screen's blue light carved deep shadows under her eyes. She didn't look up when I entered, didn't acknowledge me at all—just kept typing, her fingers flying across keys that should have been replaced two years ago but never were because we couldn't afford them.

"The battery," she said without looking around, voice tight and clipped. "Left pocket."

I set down the thermos and fished out the replacement pack, heavy with lithium cells I'd harvested from a wrecked Honda civic last week. As I swapped it out, the modem finished its connection with a final beep, and Elena immediately navigated away from the clinic's intranet into something else entirely—a black terminal window full of green text scrolling past faster than I could read.

"What are you looking at?"

Her head snapped toward me, and for a second I saw real fear in her eyes—not the professional distance she wore like armor, but raw, gut-deep terror. "Cole, close the door. Lock it."

I did, though my hand hesitated on the bolt. "Mom, what's going on?"

She turned the screen toward me. A document filled the display: SEWAGE MANIFEST #734-B, dated three weeks ago. The numbers blurred together at first—too many zeros, too many fields of data—but then I caught the words:

*EXPERIMENTAL SLUDGE - 800,000 GALLONS*
*AUTHORIZED FLUSH - SOUTH SIDE MAINS*

My blood went cold. My hand went to the welding torch lighter in my pocket.

"Elena." My voice came out wrong, hoarse. "Where did this come from?"

She was pointing now, her finger shaking slightly as it traced down the authorization seals at the bottom of the page. Three names burned themselves into my retinas:

STERLING
VOSS
MORVAIN

"The hospital network is locked down," Elena said, still in that rapid-fire whisper. "But there's a Gnome in the IT department who owed me from when we treated his daughter last year. He bypassed the firewall using an old dial-up line they forgot about. This manifest... Cole, this isn't contamination. This isn't an accident."

* * *

The Nextel hit my palm like a dead fish—warm, slick with Elena's sweat, that stupid little green LED blinking its coded death-rattle. I caught it on reflex when she snatched it from my belt, and for one heart-beat I thought maybe she'd just forgotten it was there, that she'd press it back into my hand with an apology about being jumpy lately.

Then I heard the voice bleeding through the speaker.

"Mrs. Reyes." Crisp as broken glass, female, clipped consonants that made my teeth ache. High-Spire elf, no question—I'd heard enough of them skulking around Sterling Manor during my chop-shop days to recognize that particular brand of educated cruelty. "BATC internal security has flagged your access logs. The manifest download wasn't clean."

Elena's face went gray. Not pale, but *gray*—like someone had sucked all the color right out through her pores and left only ash behind.

"The Shadow Serpent Four Heads have been notified," the voice continued, unhurried despite the death sentence hanging in every syllable. "Clean-up team dispatched. ETA thirty minutes. You, your son, and the machinist are loose ends requiring termination. We suggest you cooperate with sterilization protocols."

"Who is this?" Elena's voice came out strangled, thin.

"The Voice of Sterility. Lysandra Vance, BATC Internal Affairs Division." A pause. Static crackled across the frequency like Gnome interference, those little green bastards scrambling signals down in their sewer-grates and utility tunnels. "You have ten minutes before the team arrives at the clinic address. Your cooperation determines whether we breach quietly or loudly. Choose wisely."

The line went dead.

I watched Elena's hands shake as she keyed the power button, tried again. Nothing. The Nextel was a brick now, its secrets locked tighter than a virgin on prom night.

"Cole." Her eyes were huge in her skull, pupils blown wide. She grabbed my wrist—harder than I'd ever felt her touch before. "You need to go. Now."

"What? No, we need to—"

"The backup drive." She was already moving, yanking open drawers at the clinic's ancient filing cabinet, papers scattering like autumn leaves. Her movements were frantic, desperate. "It's not done. The encryption took longer than expected. Go to Danny. Guard him. Don't let anyone near that workshop."

"I'm not leaving you here alone." My jaw set stubborn. South Side pride, stupid and thick as concrete.

"You don't have a choice!" She slammed a canvas tote shut, shoved it into my chest hard enough to knock me back a step. "Danny is alone with the Iron-Lung. If the power dips, he suffocates. *Go!*"

I wanted to argue. Every fiber of my being screamed to stay, to fight, to do something other than run away while my mother faced down assassins in a freezing clinic that smelled like disinfectant and desperation. But I heard the hum of Danny's lung in my head—that constant mechanical wheeze, the rhythm I'd memorized during those long hours welding arcane iron, keeping it stable, alive.

"If anything happens to—"

"It won't." Her smile was terrible, brave, broken. "I'll be right behind you. Just... ten minutes. Finish the backup. Then I'm coming."

She pushed me toward the door. I stumbled backward, caught myself on the frame. Through the dusty window I could see nothing but darkness pressing against the glass, the city holding its breath.

"Elena..."

"Ten minutes, mijo." She turned away from me, bent over her laptop, fingers flying across keys like she was conducting some kind of digital exorcism. "Then we run together."

The fire-door swung shut behind me with a heavy thud that echoed through my bones. The lock clicked home. I pressed my palm against the cold metal, feeling the vibrations of footsteps inside—the frantic rustle of papers, the desperate click-clack of keys—but couldn't make myself turn the handle again.

Couldn't bring myself to look at her face one more time.

The March wind cut through my jacket like knives made of ice and regret as I ran toward Kearny, toward Danny, toward the workshop that suddenly felt miles away instead of blocks. Behind me, somewhere in that darkened clinic, my mother faced down the Shadow Serpent's Four Heads with nothing but a laptop and a lie about backing up files.

I didn't know then that I would never hear her voice again.

I didn't know that when I finally made it back to the South Side with police sirens wailing in the distance behind me, that the clinic would be dark, empty, the smell of copper hanging thick in the air where Elena Reyes had breathed her last.

But the blood-iron magic humming in my veins knew.

It sang its warning in metallic dread even as I ran, faster, desperately, toward a future that had just been rewritten without her in it.

* * *

The February air hits me like a slap across the face when I burst out of the clinic's back door. Cold. Sharp. Real. Unlike whatever the fuck I just saw on that screen.

My boots splash through puddles in the alley—black water reflecting the sodium lights that bleed orange against the brick walls. The '99 Crown Vic sits there like an old friend, dented hood and all. I yank open the driver's side, and the engine coughs to life with a deep V8 rumble that shakes the whole frame.

I don't bother with seatbelts. Just slam it into drive and floor it.

The South Side blurs past my window—a kaleidoscope of flickering neon signs advertising check cashing places, bodegas selling dream books and loose cigarettes, and the occasional flicker of arcane light from some occultist's shop front. Rain starts coming down harder now, streaking the windshield with dirty water. I wipe it manually. No cruise control in this beast, no fancy wipers that actually work right.

My hands grip the steering wheel until my knuckles go white. And beneath that pressure, I can feel it—that humming warmth starting to spike. Blood-iron magic doesn't ask permission. It responds to adrenaline, to fear, to rage. Right now it's all three.

"Fuck," I mutter, loosening my grip slightly. The wheel creaks as I ease off.

The city stretches out before me, a maze of industrial decay and desperate hope. Pulaski Skyway looms in the distance, its concrete arches disappearing into the rain-soaked night. Somewhere under there, Danny's mother is probably still working double shifts at County General ER. Still fighting battles she doesn't know are already lost.

I think about what I saw. Those documents. Sterling Manor on the manifest. The High-Spire Elves' signatures. And underneath it all—that symbol. The one that matches the brand on Danny's back.

Coincidence? Bullshit. There's no such thing in a world where magic bleeds through reality like rust through iron.

Twenty minutes later—I'm not counting anymore—I pull up outside the chop-shop garage. The bay doors are half-open, just enough for my Crown Vic to squeeze through. Inside, the space smells like motor oil and brass shavings, hot metal and ozone. My workshop. My sanctuary.

"Danny?" I call out, killing the engine. The sudden silence feels wrong. "Elena?"

No answer except the rhythmic *hiss-thump, hiss-thump* coming from downstairs. The Iron-Lung never stops. Can't stop. Not while Danny needs it breathing for him.

I take the stairs two at a time down to the sub-basement, flashlight beam cutting through the gloom. Water drips somewhere in the darkness—plumbing issues I haven't had time to fix—and my footsteps echo off concrete walls lined with my tools and spare parts.

The Arcane Iron-Lung dominates the space. Brass tubes gleam dully in my flashlight beam. Glass chambers fogged with condensation. Pressure gauges clicking softly as they cycle through their measurements.

And inside... Danny. Small form curled up in the main chamber, suspended in that artificial womb of arcane engineering. His chest rises and falls with each mechanical breath the machine provides.

"He's stable," I whisper, checking the gauges anyway. Needles hovering right where they should be. For now.

But I can feel it—that spike in my blood-iron magic getting stronger. Like something's calling to me from deep inside this machine, or maybe from deeper inside myself.

My Nokia pager vibrates on my belt. 911 code from Elena.

Then—a sound from above. A muffled *THUMP* that rattles every window in the garage.

The glass chambers of the Iron-Lung sing in response, tiny fractures spiderwebbing across one pane.

"Shit."

I grab my phone before I even process what I'm doing.

## CHAPTER 7: THE NECRO-THERMITE PROTOCOL

My boots slammed against concrete as I burst from the machine shop's fire exit, the metallic tang of blood still coating my tongue. Behind me, the steel door clanged shut—locked down tight, the way Elena taught me. No witnesses. No loose ends.

The Crown Vic sat where I'd left it, engine ticking as it cooled in the February chill. I yanked open the driver's side door hard enough that the latch popped, threw myself behind the wheel, and fired the ignition.

The V8 roared to life like an angry god waking from sleep.

I didn't bother with seatbelts. My hands—still shaking slightly from the adrenaline dump back at Sub-Station Seven—gripped the leather-wrapped steering wheel as I floored it out of the alley. Tires screamed against wet asphalt, leaving twin trails of black rubber that stank of burned synthetic compounds. The Crown Vic lurched forward with violent acceleration.

"Come on, come *on*," I muttered through clenched teeth, slamming the shifter into third. A beat-to-shit Honda Civic ran a yellow light ahead of me—I didn't slow down. Horn blaring, I cut hard right around them, hornet-stitching through the intersection as their headlights painted my interior in strobing white flashes.

The South Side streets blurred past, neon signs bleeding into watercolor smears against rain-slick pavement. Budget Motel 6. Check Cashing. All-Night Diner with its flickering "OPEN" sign. Each landmark meant distance covered, seconds shaved off whatever was happening at the clinic.

My Nextel crackled to life on the passenger seat. I snatched it up one-handed while swerving around a pothole the size of a bathtub.

Static. Then screaming—no, not screaming. Something worse. A signal caught between dimensions, raw quantum noise that made my teeth ache and my left eye twitch. Whatever number I'd dialed, it wasn't connecting.

"Fuck." I threw the device back onto the seat, knuckles going white again on the wheel.

Then I saw it: rising above the rooftops like a tombstone made of night itself—a column of smoke unlike anything natural. Blue-black and writhing, pulsing with a rhythm that suggested something breathing inside it. Necro-Thermite. The stuff Elena had whispered about once during a three-day bender, when we were both too drunk on cheap whiskey to care what we said.

"The only fire that burns cold," she'd slurred, tapping ash from her Camel Light. "Burns away flesh without heat. Turns bone to powder, leaves the soul trapped in the residue."

I slammed my palm against the steering wheel hard enough to set off the horn—that ugly mechanical blare cutting through the night. My heart hammered so hard I could feel it in my throat, taste copper blood again.

A Razor-Wire Street-Elf on a crotch-rocket screamed past going the wrong way down a one-way street, his yellow eyes reflecting in my mirror for just a second before he vanished into an alley. Didn't even register whether he was friendly or looking to peal my skin off for sport.

The smoke plume grew thicker as I approached, spreading across the sky like bruised clouds pregnant with storms. My foot stayed pinned to the accelerator. The Crown Vic's engine howled in protest, pushing sixty through neighborhoods where fifty was aggressive.

A semi-truck—one of those industrial haulers pulling double-wides stacked with shipping containers—loomed suddenly around a corner. Its halogen headlights turned night into noon, blinded me with their glare reflecting off rain-slick pavement. I jerked the wheel left, tires losing grip, fishtailing across two lanes before I caught it.

"Shit! *SHIT!*"

The trucker laid on his air horns—a deep, mournful sound that shook my bones—and swerved wide. In my rearview, I saw him brake lights flaring red as he slowed to navigate around the madness in his path.

Another vehicle was coming *toward* me now, cutting through the opposite lane. A trauma-ambulance, all chrome and brutalist angles, its emergency lights painting everything in strobing reds and blues. Behind the wheel sat an Ogre-kin paramedic, his massive frame hunched over the controls, heading straight for the same destination I was racing toward.

We passed each other like bullets, close enough that I could see his face—furrowed brow, tusks glinting, eyes locked forward with grim determination. He didn't slow down either.

Then the smell hit me.

Burning copper. Chemical accelerants. That unique stench of necromantic combustion bleeding through the Crown Vic's ventilation system, turning the recycled cabin air toxic and wrong. I killed the AC with a jab of my finger, but the smell clung to everything—the upholstery, my clothes, the inside of my nose.

I turned the final corner onto the clinic's block and slammed on the brakes.

The wall of heat hit my windshield like a physical blow—dry, suffocating, unnatural in its intensity despite the blue-black smoke promising cold fire. The Crown Vic skidded sideways, nose pointed at the burning building, tires screaming their protest against asphalt.

And there it stood: Dr. Elena Volkov's clandestine medical facility, half-consumed by flames that shouldn't have been possible, surrounded by a perimeter I couldn't yet see but felt pressing against my awareness like static electricity before lightning strikes.

I threw open the door and ran into hell itself.

* * *

I slammed the car door and ran.

The clinic was burning.

Not just burning—the whole three-story brick building was *writhing* under a writhing blanket of flame that shouldn't exist in nature. Blue-black tendrils shot up from shattered windows like frozen lightning, spitting jagged spatters of residue that sizzled when they hit the pavement. The sound wasn't crackling wood or roaring gas—it was a *screaming*, a high-pitched metallic shriek that made my teeth ache.

"MAMA!"

My voice tore raw from my throat. I was already twenty feet past where I'd abandoned the Buick, engine still running, hazard lights blinking uselessly at the destruction ahead.

This wasn't fire.

The flames were wrong—too sharp-edged, too hungry. They clawed across brick and mortar like iron gall etching copper, leaving behind charred tracks that glowed white-hot before crumbling into ash. A parked sedan thirty feet from the building's front entrance had its paint bubbling black in sheets. Another one had collapsed on melted tires.

I could feel it even from here—the cold. My breath came out frost-white. The temperature around me dropped ten degrees as my magic flared in panic, ice crystals forming and dissolving along my fingertips. Something primal had triggered deep in my bloodstream, the first stage of the shift I couldn't control, wouldn't control because all I could think about was her being inside that hellish crucible.

"ELENA!"

Two figures in yellow turnout gear materialized from the smoke-laden night, moving with surprising speed for their size. Dwarven firefighters, Local 405 South Side—I recognized the patches even through my tunnel vision. One grabbed my shoulders while the other moved to block my path forward.

"You're dead if you go in there, kid!" The one holding me grunted, his grip like iron clamps. "It's an arcane burn! You'll be vapor before you hit the—"

"I don't *care*!" I struggled against him, but he had a firefighter's strength and years of experience wrestling panicked civilians. His partner moved closer, ready to help subdue me if needed.

"She's in there!" I screamed at them. "My mother is inside!"

The lead firefighter's helmeted head shook. Through the gaps in his gear, I caught the glint of eyes that had seen too much, knew too much about what necro-thermite could do to flesh and bone.

"The whole structure's compromised," he said, voice muffled by his breathing apparatus. "Second floor just collapsed. We can't get close enough to—"

A tremendous *WHUMPH* cut him off.

The clinic's second story—which I'd known as Elena's office space, where she kept those hard drives with all our secrets—exploded outward in a shower of molten glass and superheated debris. The blue-black flames roared higher, fed by whatever chemical cocktail was making this hellfire possible. The explosion threw chunks of burning brick across the street like shrapnel.

"COLE REYES!" someone else shouted from the growing crowd of emergency responders. A female voice, sharp and commanding. "Stand down or we'll sedate you!"

I stopped fighting then, but only because the dwarf's grip would've broken my collarbone if I'd continued. My knees buckled. He eased me down to the wet asphalt while I stared at what used to be my mother's clinic, her sanctuary, the place where she'd healed people who couldn't afford County General.

Now it was a tomb.

And I hadn't been fast enough to save her.

* * *

The moment my boots hit pavement, I knew something was wrong. The air tasted like copper and ozone, thick enough to choke on. My lungs burned with each breath—part panic, part the metallic tang of blood-magic running hot through my veins.

"Elena!" Her name tore from my throat raw and broken.

The Clinic—a squat concrete box that had seen better days even before tonight—was already screaming. Not people screaming. The *building* screaming as flames licked up its sides, feeding on something far more than wood and plaster. The fire moved wrong. Too hungry. Too deliberate.

I ran hard toward the entrance, my vision tunneling red at the edges. My fingers were starting to numb—the first sign of frost-cobalt kicking in when adrenaline spiked too high. Magic always found a way to fuck me over at the worst possible moment.

Then they hit me.

Two masses of solid muscle slammed into my ribs from either side, driving the air from my lungs in a wet gasp. We went down in a tangle of limbs, my head cracking against asphalt hard enough to see stars. Dwarven firefighters—both of them, easy 250 pounds of dense muscle packed with weave-resistance training.

"Easy! Easy!" one shouted, but I wasn't hearing words anymore. Just the roar of blood in my ears and the sick certainty that Elena was in there dying while I wrestled with—

My knuckles connected with something solid. Cartilage crunched. The dwarf grunted, his grip loosening just enough. That's all I needed.

Pure desperation turned my right fist into a meteor. Blood-iron magic flared hot through my arm—the metal rings under my skin glowing dull blue through my skin—and I caught the second dwarf square across the jaw. He flew sideways, crashing into a parked car with enough force to dent the door.

The other one recovered fast, wrapping both arms around my torso in a bear hug that squeezed the remaining air from my lungs. "Stop it! Stop it now!"

"LET ME GO!" I screamed, bucking like a madman. My elbows found soft spots—solar plexus, throat, temple. The dwarf coughed, stumbled, but didn't release. His helmeted face swam in front of mine, voice muffled by smoke and distance.

"It's too late! The structural—"

*CRACK.*

The sound cut through everything else. Concrete groaning. Steel beams shrieking as they lost integrity. And then—

The roof collapsed inward.

It happened slow-motion and all at once. The center section gave way first, pulling down sections like dominos. The fire roared in response, feeding on oxygen, sending up a column of blue-black smoke that climbed toward heaven like an accusation. Slag dripped from the frame, white-hot and hissing where it hit wet pavement.

"No," I whispered. "No no no no—"

The dwarf was still holding me, but his grip had changed. Less restraint. More support. When he spoke again, his voice carried genuine sorrow. "Nothing left in there, son. The weave-fire ate it all. I'm sorry."

I stopped fighting.

My knees buckled. The dwarf eased me down gently onto asphalt slick with rainwater and worse things. Somewhere nearby, Ford trauma-ambulances pulsed their lightbars—strobe-red painting smoke, turning it into hellish tapestry.

I stared into the inferno.

Blue flames danced along what remained of load-bearing walls—Necro-Thermite doing exactly what it was designed to do: ensuring nothing biological survived. No bodies. No DNA. Nothing but slag and memory.

Elena was gone.

Lysandra was gone.

And I...

"Cole." The dwarf's hand came down on my shoulder, heavy as judgment. "Cole, you need to—"

I looked up at him blankly. My mouth tasted like ash and iron. My eyes reflected the blue flames back at him—I could see them in the black pupils if I squinted just right.

"Danny," I said hoarsely. "There's... there's still Danny."

But even as I said it, the words felt hollow. Because Elena had made her choice. Lysandra too. They'd staged this—they'd *wanted* this—to protect their boys from whatever was coming next.

Now I was alone with one kid while the other burned somewhere in that white-hot furnace.

The Clinic collapsed another foot inward with a sound like God breathing out. Sparks scattered upward like dying stars.

And I knelt in the cold February night, surrounded by firefighters and first responders who couldn't help because there was nothing left to save, watching everything burn until morning.

---

## CHAPTER 8: ASH AND IDENTIFICATION

The cold bites through my jacket like teeth finding skin. I don't feel it anymore—that's how you know you're deep in shock. Your body stops bothering with things that don't matter.

Dawn comes up over Neon Hollow like someone dragging a dirty rag across the sky. Gray light filters through the perpetual smog that hangs over the South Side, painting everything in shades of ash and regret. The Clinic Ruins spread out before me, still smoking in places, though the fire burned itself out hours ago. Necro-Thermite doesn't need anything—no oxygen, no fuel. It just *takes*. Burns so hot and clean that by the time it's done, there's only slag and silence.

I duck under the yellow police tape. A beat cop, this big Uruk named Grask who used to buy coffee at Mom's place every Tuesday morning, shifts his weight and starts toward me. He takes one look at my face—my eyes probably reflecting that dead-winter-ice color they get when the blood-iron retreats—and stops. His hand drops from the radio clipped to his shoulder.

"Reyes," he says, voice flat as week-old beer. "You shouldn't be here."

"It's my mother's clinic." My own voice sounds distant, like I'm hearing it through water. "I should probably see what's left."

Grask looks past me at the ruins, then back at my face. Whatever he sees there makes him flinch. "Ain't nothing left to contaminate anyway," he mutters into his radio. "Yeah. Let the kid walk." Then to me: "Don't touch anything. Don't take anything. Just... look if you gotta look."

I nod. Walk past him. The crunch of pulverized brick and melted glass echoes through the footprint where the building stood. Everything is gray and black and white-hot in patches—the slag from the Necro-Thermite still glowing faintly orange in the pre-dawn gloom. It stinks of iron-gall residue, that acrid chemical burn smell mixed with something worse. Something organic.

The wind cuts through the devastation, carrying ash and debris across the South Side. Police tape snaps in the gusts, a sound like breaking bones.

I navigate by memory. This was Mom's space—forty years she worked here, healing people the system discarded. I know every doorway, every support beam, every window. Even now, with everything collapsed and melted and scattered, I can map it in my head. Second floor, northwest corner—that's where Elena's office was. Where her second bedroom connected to her secret lab.

Now it's just a crater in the earth.

My boots find the right spot. Here, where the foundation gave way. Here, where the second story imploded down into the basement. I stop at the edge, looking into the collapse. Melted steel I-beams jut up at impossible angles, twisted like pretzels. The concrete has turned to dust and fused slag.

And there—buried under three tons of wreckage—I see red.

Not blood. Worse than blood.

Ceramic shards, painted the color of arterial spray. Pieces of the containment vessel Elena used for her research. The one she swore was stable. The one that burned clean and hot enough to melt steel in seconds flat.

"You stupid fucking woman," I whisper to the ruins. "You beautiful, brilliant, dead idiot."

The words taste like copper. Like I'm chewing on old coins.

My hands are shaking—not from cold, not from fear. From the blood-iron magic coiling tight inside me, retreating deeper and deeper as shock sets in. It wants to help. Can't. There's nothing left to heal. Nothing living to pull back from death's edge.

Just ash and slag and the acrid stench of failure.

I drop to my knees at the crater's edge. Dawn light catches the white-hot slag, makes it gleam like diamonds. Beautiful. Deadly. Final.

Somewhere behind me, Grask coughs into his radio. The city wakes around us—the distant sound of traffic on the Pulaski Skyway, the rumble of early-morning trains crossing Newark Bay. Life goes on.

For everyone else.

I dig my fingers into the pulverized brick. Feel it sift through my grasp like sand. Like time. Like all the moments I should have spent here instead of out there, playing vigilante, thinking I could make a difference.

"Cole."

* * *

The dawn comes cold and gray over the ruins. I can't feel it.

My breath clouds white in front of my face as I stand at the edge of what was the Clinic. The fire's gone out—burned itself into exhaustion sometime in the last few hours—but the ashes are still alive with heat. Hundreds of degrees. Hot enough to melt glass, hot enough to fuse steel. I can see the glow of it pulsing beneath the gray surface like the heartbeat of something dying.

I drop to my knees without thinking about it. The impact sends a jolt up through my legs, but I barely register it. My hands hang above the ash, trembling slightly. They're covered in soot already, black streaks running down my wrists, under my shirt sleeves. My knuckles split somewhere during the night—I don't remember when—and there's dried blood caked around the cuts.

Then the change starts.

It always begins the same way. A coldness that has nothing to do with temperature, spreading from deep inside my chest outward. My blood-iron magic responding to something. Fear? Grief? Rage? I don't know anymore which emotion triggers it. Maybe all three at once. The warmth that kept me going through the night—the fever-bright certainty that pushed me through the smoke and flames—dries up like spit on summer pavement.

And then the frost comes.

My skin begins to pale, starting at my fingertips and creeping up toward my elbows. That familiar cobalt hue spreads across my hands like veins of ice beneath the surface.
