My pencil stops its rhythm.

The pipe doesn't connect to the municipal treatment facilities. That's the first red flag. Should've been obvious from the start—no way Newark's water department would process sludge this toxic without raising alarms. But it doesn't terminate at a storm drain either. On the digital map, it simply dead-ends at a massive grayed-out block in the Foundry District's industrial sector.

Accessing property records requires three password entries and patience I don't have. The browser churns for nearly a minute before pulling up the file.

Decommissioned arc-alchemy processing subsidiary. Official shutdown date: March 1998. Ownership transferred to a shell corporation. I drill down into the ownership chain, watching the corporate names cascade downward like a pyramid scheme built by accountants who understood magic better than morality.

Sterling-Voss.

Of course it's Sterling-Voss.

The phone in my pocket vibrates. My Nokia—the clamshell model with the green backlit screen, all business with none of the sleek pretensions of what's coming next decade. I pull it out, see Torque Kaelen's name on the caller ID.

I hit send before he can hang up.

"Torque. That sludge we found in the trench at 4th and Pike. Does the runoff main there connect to the old Sterling-Voss processing plant in the Foundry District?"

His intake of breath tells me everything before his words do. "Yeah. Why? Doc, tell me you ain't poking around Sterling's old garbage."

"I'm not poking." I'm already standing, grabbing my Aegis jacket from the back of my chair. My keys jangle as I scoop them from the desk drawer. "I'm going to take a sample."

"You're gonna get yourself killed!" His voice rises to that particular pitch that means genuine fear, not just cop bravado. "That whole district's off-limits since the cleanup operations. Sterling-Voss has private security that makes us look like—"

I snap the phone shut mid-sentence, cutting him off. He'll understand eventually. They always do, once they see the pattern too clearly to ignore.

The map stays open on the screen behind me as I leave. Forty-seven cases. Two miles of poison. One corporate signature at the end of every chain leading backward into the dark.

The clinic's ancient HVAC unit hums its mechanical prayer. The smell of antiseptic and desperation hangs thick in the morning air.

I lock the door behind me and head for my truck.

---

## CHAPTER 4: CHAPTER 4

The rain hammers against the Crown Vic's roof like a thousand angry fists. I kill the engine two blocks out, watching the Sterling-Voss subsidiary disappear behind sheets of water that cascade down the windshield. The Foundry District looks like something dug up from the bottom of Newark Bay—all skeletal steel frames and broken promises.

I grab my gear from the trunk. Flashlight. Sampling kit. Service weapon. The weight settles familiar against my hip as I shoulder through the driving rain toward the perimeter fence. Chain-link rises ahead, topped with razor wire that glints dully in the occasional flash of distant lightning.

There—a gap, maybe six feet across where the fence has collapsed inward. I slip through without a sound, boots landing in thick mud that sucks at my soles. The smell hits me immediately: wet rust and something chemical underneath, like old motor oil mixed with something sweeter, more organic. Something wrong.

My white-lilac weave stays coiled tight. Barely a whisper of arcano-energy, just enough to keep my senses sharp but not enough for any decent sensor array to flag. Stealth mode. Medical leave be damned—I'm investigating now.

"Perimeter breach," I mutter into the micro-recorder tucked inside my jacket collar. "Site should be cold since ninety-eight. But I've got active power signatures. Someone's keeping the lights on in the graveyard."

The settling tanks loom overhead, massive cylinders of corroded steel that block out what little starlight manages to penetrate the storm clouds. Their shadows are pooling oil slick across the flooded ground. My tactical boots crunch over gravel, each step deliberate, controlled.

Fresh tire tracks cut through the mud. Deep ones. Heavy vehicle. Recent.

I round the first tank, flashlight beam cutting through fog so thick it feels solid. Then another shape—towering smokestacks, their brick exteriors stained black with decades of exhaust, rising like industrial monuments to corporate indifference.

A low hum vibrates through the air. Telluric generators. Active ones.

"You've got to be fucking kidding me," I whisper.

The hum grows stronger as I push deeper into the site. Past a row of chemical vats, their observation windows cracked and clouded. Around a conveyor system frozen mid-motion, belts sagging with accumulated debris. This place shouldn't have power. Shouldn't have anything.

But here we are.

Then—the sound cuts through everything else. Boot heels on concrete. The subtle click of someone adjusting their grip on a weapon.

I freeze behind a support column, pressing myself against rust-slicked metal. The white-lilac weave flares just enough to let me extend my awareness, feel for the signature ahead.

Not human. Not quite.

Elf. High-Spire corporate security by the look of the equipment. And they're not here to protect empty buildings.

I pull back, retracing my steps. Need to get eyes on this guard without being seen. Need to know what Sterling-Voss is really doing in their supposed "abandoned" facility while the county dumps sludge that makes people forget how to breathe.

* * *

I press my spine against the settling tank, feeling the cold seep through my jacket. The metal is slick with something I don't want to identify. My breath catches in my throat as I angle the broken mirror from my med-kit around the corner.

There are four of them.

High-Spire security personnel—Elves by the look of their crystalline features and those predatory eyes that glow faint yellow in the dark. They move like oil through water, perfectly synchronized, their boots barely making a sound on the cracked concrete. No comm chatter, no hand signals. They just *know* where each other will be.

My white-lilac weave pulses once, a warning. I clamp down hard, coiling it tighter until it's barely a whisper in my chest. Can they sense it? The thermal optics mounted to their helmets sweep the area in methodical arcs, the motors whining quiet and mechanical.

The lead Elf—tallest one, silver hair pulled back tight enough to hurt—lifts his wrist to his mouth. "Sector four clear," he says, voice crisp, educated, dripping with that High-Spire superiority. "Tell the shift boss the runoff levels are holding. We don't need another 2000 spill on our hands."

My blood goes ice.

A direct admission. Sterling-Voss knew about the sludge dump. They covered it up. And now I'm standing in the evidence, soaking wet and probably about to get ventilated.

The Elf lowers his arm, and all four of them pivot toward the southern perimeter. For three seconds, maybe four, they're facing away from me.

I drop to my knees and crawl.

The trench runs along the base of the settling tank, filled with several inches of black water that reeks of chemical runoff and something organic I really hope isn't what I think it is. It seeps through my pants immediately, cold burning against my skin. My heart hammers so loud I'm convinced they can hear it over whatever tech they're running.

Keep moving. Don't look back.

The thermal optics keep sweeping. Left to right. Left to right. I time my movements to their rotation, crawling when they're aimed elsewhere. Twenty feet. Fifteen. Ten.

One of the Elves stops. His head cocks slightly, like an animal catching a scent.

Shit.

I freeze mid-crawl, half-submerged in the filth, willing myself invisible. The mirror shard tumbles from my fingers into the toxic slurry with a soft *plink* that sounds like a gunshot in the silence.

He doesn't move. Just stands there, weapon raised, barrel pointed at where I was three seconds ago. The others have gone still too, forming a loose perimeter.

My weave writhes against its binding. It wants out. Wants to light up like a goddamn lighthouse and either save me or kill us both.

"Movement in sector four-B," the first Elf says calmly. "Investigating."

They spread out, weapons trained on the darkness. One of them—shorter than the rest, scar on his jawline—is heading straight for my position.

I make my choice.

Rolling forward into deeper shadow, I splash through the trench toward the main outflow pipe. The sound is wrong. Too loud. Water sloshing. Metal grating shifting under my weight as I scramble to my feet and run.

A metal screech—high-pitched, echoing across the compound—that wasn't supposed to happen.

All four weapons snap toward me at once.

"Contact!" someone shouts.

I'm already moving, diving behind the outflow pipe as the first shots punch through where I stood. Suppressed rounds, quiet pops in the night, but each one hits like a fist. I can hear them ricocheting off concrete, spanging off steel.

My hands fumble in my jacket pocket while staying low. The sampling vial falls out, rolls halfway across open ground toward them. Toward death.

"Hold fire! Interrogate first!" That's the lead Elf again, voice sharp with command.

I lunge for the vial, snag it just before the thermal optics sweep over my position again. They're re-calibrating, narrowing their search pattern. Smart. Efficient. Fucking Elves.

Can't stay here. Can't go back.

There's an access ladder bolted to the side of the outflow pipe, leading up to some kind of maintenance walkway maybe thirty feet above. It's exposed, suicide territory, but it's my only play.

I sprint for it, vault onto the bottom rung, and climb.

The weapons track upward. More shouting. Boots on concrete, getting closer.

Halfway up. My muscles scream. My lungs burn.

Something impacts the pipe inches from my hand—a suppressed round, maybe, or some kind of non-lethal stunner. It sends vibrations rattling through my bones.

Three-quarters up. Almost there.

Another impact. Closer this time.

My fingers find the top rung just as something slams into my calf, hard enough to make me cry out. Pain explodes up my leg, hot and immediate. Blood, probably. Definitely blood.

I haul myself over the edge onto the maintenance walkway and don't look back.

Behind me, the four Elves are already climbing.

Ahead of me, nothing but darkness and a choice: follow the walkway deeper into the plant, or risk jumping down to ground level where I might actually lose them in the maze of decommissioned machinery.

My weave pulses again, harder this time. Urgent.

*Use me,* it whispers. *Let me help.*

But if I light up now, they'll know exactly what I am. BATC Aegis Commander or not, that makes me a target. Sterling-Voss won't hesitate. Corporate sovereignty means they answer to no one except their stockholders.

I take the vial—still intact, miraculously—and tuck it inside my jacket next to my heart.

Then I run toward the darkness, limping bad but moving forward, because stopping means dying, and I didn't survive County General ER to get gunned down in a toxic waste dump by High-Spire watchdogs.

The pain in my calf is a fire. The cold water soaking my clothes feels like ice forming under my skin.

And behind me, I hear the soft, terrifying whisper of four weapons tracking my every move.

* * *

I hit the trench as the first rounds sang overhead, depleted-bismuth tearing rust from steel with that distinctive *zick-zick-zick* of suppressed fire. Cold water surged over my shoulders, shockingly frigid even through my tactical vest, and I slammed the collection vial downward into the viscous sludge pooling at the outflow pipe's mouth.

The glass was warm when I sealed it—still hot from being handled without gloves—but that heat didn't last. The sludge inside had already begun its strange luminescence, a sickly green-yellow glow pulsing faintly against the amber prescription label I'd hastily scribbled earlier.

"Contact east trench! Move move move!"

The Elf commander's voice carried that crisp military precision that made my jaw clench. Their flashlights swept across the corrugated steel above me like hunting beams, and I could hear boots slamming down on the grated walkways overhead. Five, maybe six operators. Sterling-Voss security, probably ex-military themselves, hired muscle who knew what they were protecting and why.

I couldn't outrun them through open ground. Couldn't fight my way clear without exposing myself, revealing what I was, burning everything.

So I did what I wasn't supposed to do.

My white-lilac weave had been coiled tight since entering the Foundry District, dimmed to almost nothing—just enough residual magic to keep my arcano-signature from spiking on their sensors. Now I unspooled it fast, pulling threads of power from the stagnant water around me. Chemical runoff, industrial waste, things that had no business holding magical current, but they did anyway. Everything held potential if you knew how to look.

*"Thermos."*

The word came out as breath, barely a whisper, and the effect was instantaneous. The sluggish water in the trench flashed-boiled in an expanding sphere of superheated steam. The shockwave of temperature change hit me like a hammer—sudden, intense, painfully hot even at distance—and the entire outflow trench erupted into a massive cloud of dense white vapor.

The Elves' flashlights disappeared. So did their shouts. For ten seconds, fifteen at most, the thermal baffling would blind every sensor and eye in a hundred-foot radius.

I scrambled up the muddy embankment, fingers slipping in the slick earth, boots finding purchase where there shouldn't be any. The vial in my chest pocket thunked solidly against my ribs with each heartbeat. Evidence. Proof. A chemical signature I could take directly to the Board of Inquiry.

"West side! West side!"

They were already adapting, shouting positions. Smart. They'd expect me to run east toward the Crown Vic.

I vaulted the chain-link fence separating the Sterling-Voss property from the old railroad bed, landed hard enough to drive the air from my lungs, and kept running. My boots splashed through puddles that reeked of motor oil and something worse, some chemical cocktail that made my eyes water. The fog—the natural kind, rolling off Newark Bay two blocks south—was thick here, a blessing I hadn't anticipated.

Behind me, the steam cloud was already dissipating, and I heard the snap of branches as the Elves breached into the railroad cut.

But I was faster than they expected. Faster than men who spent too much time behind desks chasing paper targets instead of running through North Jersey's industrial wastelands.

The Crown Vic appeared ahead, parked under a sodium light that flickered like a dying star. I yanked open the driver's door, slid inside, and slammed it shut without looking back.

My hands were shaking when I pulled out the collection vial. Just slightly. Adrenaline and exhaustion and the sharp relief of success all mixed together in ways that made my vision swim.

I held the sample up to the streetlight, turning it slowly in the amber glow.

The sludge inside had separated, forming layers of different densities. And at the top, where it met the glass, there was that telltale sizzle—a faint reaction between the chemical compounds and the borosilicate surface. A blue-black residue spreading across the interior, iron-gall byproducts crystallizing out of suspension.

My breath caught.

I'd run forensic chemistry on forty-seven victims. Forty-seven Black-Iron Lungs cases over three years. Every single one showed this exact chemical signature: trace elements of cobalt-60 contamination, specific polymer binders used only by Sterling-Voss subsidiaries, and this particular iron-gall compound that no other manufacturer employed.

This sample from 2000 matched them all perfectly. Not similar. Identical.

They'd been dumping radioactive waste slurry into the Kearny Marshes while knowing—*knowing*—it would eventually migrate into the aquifer. Into the water supply. Into lungs.

And High-Spire Corporation had covered for them. Had paid the hush money, buried the reports, ensured the BATC investigation went nowhere because the evidence was "inconclusive" and the witnesses were "unreliable."

I started the engine, feeling the familiar rumble as the V8 came to life beneath me. The vial went into a sealed evidence pouch, then into the locked box in my trunk where it belonged. Chain of custody, even if I had to maintain it off the books.

The Elves behind me were still shouting, but they weren't running anymore. They'd lost their target. Their perimeter had been breached, and they knew it.

I pulled away from the curb, heading south toward the Pulaski Skyway and home. My hands were steady now, gripping the wheel with professional control.

Sterling-Voss. High-Spire. The names burned in my mind like brands.

I had them.

Now I just needed to figure out how to use this without getting myself killed.

The city lights of Newark spread out before me, a million points of light reflecting off rain-slicked streets. Somewhere down there, the marshlands were still bleeding poison into the ground. Still killing people who never knew why their lungs turned black and iron-hard.

But not for long.

---

## CHAPTER 5: CHAPTER 5

The elevator ride up to Director Morvain's office had been silent except for the pneumatic hiss of the car ascending through High-Spire's crystalline tower. I clutched the Panasonic Toughbook against my chest, feeling its weight—both physical and metaphorical. Inside that machine was everything we needed to bring down the architects of the South Side plague.

The doors opened onto an entirely different world than Sub-Station Seven.

Morvain's office occupied the entire eastern apex of the building. Floor-to-ceiling windows revealed Newark Bay sprawling below like a circuit board of neon and steel, the morning sun painting everything in shades of amber and gold. The air tasted filtered, expensive—the kind of climate control that cost more per hour than most people made in a week.

"Commander Vance." Elias Morvain stood from behind a mahogany desk that could have served as a conference table in most offices. Human, mid-fifty, custom-tailored suit that probably cost more than my monthly salary. His eyes were the color of winter sky just before snow—pale blue, emotionless. "You requested this meeting urgently."

I set the Toughbook on his desk with deliberate care, then placed beside it a sealed glass vial containing the blue-black sludge we'd extracted from the contaminated main lines. The substance moved with sentient malice inside its prison, leaving faint scorch marks where it touched the glass.

"I have indisputable proof, sir." My voice echoed in the cavernous space, swallowed by plush carpet and sound-dampening panels. "Sterling-Voss Chemical subsidiary, designated SV-734, illegally dumped approximately eight million gallons of experimental arc-alchemy waste into the South Side water mains between March 2000 and August 2001. They've been covering it up ever since."

Morvain poured himself espresso from a machine that looked like it belonged in a museum. The hiss of pressurized steam cut through our conversation. He didn't look at the evidence. He looked at me.

"The 47 cases of Black-Iron Lung currently in County General ER are directly traceable to this contamination." I opened the Toughbook, its screen illuminating the forensic models we'd built over six months of investigation. "This isn't conjecture, Director. It's mathematical certainty. We have chemical signatures, timeline analysis, witness testimony from three former SV-734 employees who've fled the state. Sterling-Voss knew exactly what they were doing."

"Continue." One word. No inflection. He sipped his espresso.

"We need to raid the SV-734 facility immediately. Confiscate their records. Arrest the executives. And issue a citywide health mandate for the affected zones—South Ward, Ironbound, the Kearny Marshes outskirts." My magic flared beneath my skin, white-lilac light flickering around my fingertips without conscious summoning. Righteous anger always triggered my caste's gifts. "Forty-seven people are dying, sir. Some of them children."

The words felt hollow even as I spoke them. I'd watched too many die already. Watched lungs turn to black glass from the inside out. Watched families burn through savings on quack alchemists and faith healers while the real culprits laughed behind gated communities.

Morvain finally glanced at the Toughbook screen. Then back at me. His expression hadn't changed—not even a micro-expression of concern or outrage.

"Do you understand the economic impact of such an action?" he asked.

My jaw tightened. "I understand that seven people died last week alone. That there will be more this week. That children—"

"The Slag-Rush contract." Morvain set down his espresso cup with surgical precision. "Do you know how much revenue Sterling-Voss generates for this city? Their waste disposal operations employ twelve thousand people. Their chemical refining keeps the port competitive against New York and Boston. The Slag-Rush alone accounts for thirty percent of BATC's annual budget."

"You're talking about people dying."

"I'm talking about systemic stability, Commander." He stepped closer, invading my personal space in a way that screamed authority and privilege. "You present evidence of criminal negligence. I see a potential cascade failure if we disrupt the most lucrative inter-caste partnership in North Jersey history."

The vial of sludge sizzled on his desk. My magic pulsed brighter, making the office wards hum in response—the High-Spire's sterile, oppressive containment systems pushing back against my caste's power like oil and water.

"Sir, with respect—I don't understand what you're saying."

Morvain smiled. Not warmly. It didn't reach those winter-sky eyes.

"Commander Vance. Do you understand what the Slag-Rush is currently achieving for this city?"

The question hung in the filtered air between us. Below, Newark Bay continued its indifferent rotation around the sun, unaware that forty-seven people were slowly suffocating because someone had decided profit mattered more than human life.

And in that moment, standing in Director Morvain's immaculate office while holding the evidence that would save—or condemn—hundreds of lives depending on which side of the ledger they fell on, I realized something terrible:

I was going to lose this argument.

"Explain it to me, sir," I said quietly, though every fiber of my being wanted to scream.

* * *

The air in Director Morvain's office tastes like expensive leather and stale ambition. My magic coils beneath my skin—that white-lilac flare of righteous fury—pressing against the sterile wards that keep this entire floor bottled and contained.

Morvain stands at his window, hands clasped behind his back, looking down at the city spread below us like a circuit board lit by morning sun. His suit is charcoal today, perfectly pressed. No wrinkle. No weakness.

"They were dumping Telluric copper into the Kearny Marshes," I say, my voice harder than I intended. "Sterling-Voss. Two years running. And they buried forty-seven South Side metahumans under slag to hide it."

I don't move from where I stand near his desk. The manila folder sits between us like an accusation. Inside: soil samples tagged with chain-of-custody seals. Autopsy reports. Photographs of bodies wrapped in copper shavings, preserved in metal graves.

Morvain doesn't turn immediately. When he does, his reflection catches mine in the soundproof glass—the both of us suspended above a city we're supposed to protect.

"You've done thorough work." His voice is smooth as silk pulled across a blade. "Exceptional, even. That South Side district has been a blind spot for years."

"The Slag-Rush." I step forward, placing both palms on his desk. "It started right after those bodies went missing. Three months of continuous construction, retrofitting the entire Newark Bay grid with their 'donated' copper. The city council calls them heroes. Meanwhile, they were literally burying people to make room for more product."

The hum of traffic filters through the glass—muffled, distant, a constant reminder that three million lives pulse below this sterile perch. Morvain moves away from the window, circling behind me. I can smell his cologne now. Something expensive. Old money.

"Sit down, Mara."

"I'd rather stand."

He smiles—that thin, reptilian expression that never reaches his eyes. "You understand what's at stake here, don't you? Truly understand?" He picks up the manila folder, weighs it in his hands. "Sterling-Voss and their subsidiaries have invested eight hundred million credits into the 2002 infrastructure overhaul. Eight. Hundred. Million. Every transformer station, every substation, every telluric relay from the Meadowlands to the Hackensack River."

My magic flares again, reacting to the words like oil to flame. White-lilac sparks dance across my knuckles before I clamp them down.

"If I authorize a raid on Sterling-Voss," he continues, moving back to the window, "the copper stops flowing. The grid fails. Thousands lose their jobs, and the South Side burns in riots. Forty-seven lives, Mara, against the stability of three million." He turns, meeting my eyes with something cold and absolute. "It is a terrible equation, but it is the one we are paid to balance."

"You're calling forty-seven dead metahumans a 'write-off'?"

"They died because Sterling-Voss prioritized profit over environmental protocols." His voice remains steady, reasonable, utterly sociopathic. "A tragedy. But exposing this now would destroy two years of fragile alliance-building between corporate interests and municipal government. Inter-caste stability—"

"It's not stability if it's built on bodies!" My fist slams onto the desk, rattling the blotter. "Those people had names, Elias. Families. They weren't numbers on your fucking spreadsheet."

The wards in this office pulse in response to my magic—they don't want me here any more than Morvain wants to hear what I'm saying. The air pressure shifts, oppressive.

He walks back to his desk slowly, picking up not just the folder, but also that vial of contaminated soil and a floppy disk containing my digital backup.

"Your diligence is commendable, Mara. Truly." He sets them all into a drawer, closes it with a soft click. "But this investigation is officially closed."

I stare at him. At the locked drawer. At the casual way he just erased everything—the evidence, my work, forty-seven lives.

"What did they pay you?"

* * *

I watched him walk to that vault like I was watching my soul get locked away in cold storage.

The thing took up most of one wall—four feet tall, maybe six wide, all brushed steel etched with corporate runes that made my teeth ache just looking at them. Morvain didn't even glance back at me as he approached it. His fingers moved across a biometric panel I couldn't see from where I stood, and I felt the air pressure change.

Then came the magic.

It wasn't anything like mine—that bright, clean white-lilac that tasted like ozone and justice. This was heavy. Dense. The kind of weave that felt like swallowing gravel, all restrictive bindings and bureaucratic chains. It sank into the vault door's lock mechanisms, and I heard the tumblers shift with a series of metallic clanks that echoed through the office like hammer blows against my ribs.

The door swung open.

Morvain placed our evidence inside with the casual indifference of someone tossing yesterday's newspaper into recycling. First the vial—the sludge that had killed three people in Newark Bay last week, the stuff we'd risked our lives collecting proof about. Then the floppy disk containing my full report, every word of testimony from witnesses who'd seen BATC contractors dumping toxic waste into the marshlands. Finally, the physical files. Years of documentation we'd pieced together.

Just... gone. Erased. Buried under tons of steel and corporate will.

He shut the door, and those locking mechanisms engaged again—*clank, clank, clank*—each sound feeling like another nail in some coffin I couldn't quite identify yet but knew was mine to lie in eventually.

My magic flared beneath my skin without permission, that familiar white-lilac heat surging up through my chest, sharp cedar smell filling my nostrils. It wanted to *do* something. Wanted to burn. Wanted to break that fucking vault open and drag every piece of evidence back into the light where it belonged.

But I was Aegis. I was a soldier. I was a good goddamn soldier who followed orders.

So I swallowed it down until my throat burned.

"Salute," I said, voice tight as piano wire. The gesture was stiff, mechanical. My hand came up to my temple, fingers pressed hard enough to leave indentations in my skin.

I turned on my heel before he could see whatever expression was trying to crack through my professional mask. The office door felt miles away even though it was only twenty feet. Each step weighed more than the last.

"Young commander," Morvain called out, and I stopped with my hand on the cold brass doorknob. Didn't turn around. Couldn't trust what might show on my face if I did.

"Do not let this sour you, Mara. You are meant for great things in Aegis." His voice carried across the room, smooth as river stones but just as likely to crush your foot if you stepped wrong. "Keep your eyes on the future, not the mud of the past."

The future. Right. Some future where I got promoted after being ordered to bury the truth about corporate crimes that had killed civilians under our protection.

"Yes, Director," I managed. Got the door open. Stepped through without looking back.

The hallway beyond felt suffocating—all those executive wards still pressing down on my magic, making it hard to breathe properly. I made it to the elevator and rode down in silence, watching the floor numbers descend like they were counting down to something inevitable.

By the time I reached precinct level, my hands were shaking.

The locker room stank of sweat and stale coffee and bad choices. I went straight to my metal locker, spun the combination lock, yanked the door open hard enough to make it rattle on its hinges.

My civilian jacket hung inside where I'd left it this morning—a lifetime ago, felt like. Underneath, folded neatly on top of my spare uniform and equipment bag, sat a blank black floppy disk.

And a note. Torn piece of paper, handwritten scrawl that looked like someone had been writing in a moving vehicle:

*THEY BURIED YOUR REPORT. WE CAN SHOW YOU WHAT ELSE THEY BURIED.*

*- THE WATCHING PARTY*

I stared at it. The metal locker suddenly felt cold against my palm where I gripped the door. My white-lilac magic sputtered weakly around me, confused, seeking a target it couldn't find.

"Who the fuck..." I started, then stopped.

Because I knew. Someone had been there. In Morvain's office when we weren't supposed to be disturbed. Someone had access to things they shouldn't have access to. Someone who knew what happened in that vault and didn't like it any more than I did.

Someone dangerous.

I picked up the floppy disk between two fingers like it might bite me. Turned it over—nothing written on the other side. No label. Just... a disk.

And an invitation into whatever rabbit hole came next.

My phone buzzed in my pocket. Probably Thornton wondering where I'd disappeared to. Or maybe it was real work, actual crimes needing attention, the kind of shit that made being Aegis feel less like complicity and more like... well, if not exactly righteousness, then at least purpose.

But I stood there in that smelly locker room with evidence of institutional betrayal burning behind my eyes and this mysterious gift in my hand, and all I could think was:

*What now?*

---

## CHAPTER 6: CHAPTER 6

The locker room stinks of wet wool and institutional bleach, that particular smell that makes my teeth ache. I'm sitting on the wooden bench between rows of dented metal lockers, still wearing my tactical blacks, boots laced tight despite being off-duty hours ago. The fluorescent lights overhead buzz like trapped hornets, casting everything in that sickly green-white glow that never quite illuminates anything properly.

My head's been a mess since Morvain locked up my Black-Iron Lung report. Not filed, mind you—just *locked*. His vault. Behind three different security weaves. When I pushed back, he gave me that smile, the one that doesn't reach his eyes, and told me to "let the brass handle it, Commander." Brass. Right. Corporate red tape wrapped around a corpse and sold as policy.

I run my hand over my face, feeling the exhaustion settle into my bones like sediment. Three days straight of chasing shadows through Kearny Marshes for nothing. The Council wants results they can present at their quarterly shareholder meetings. What they get is me wading through toxic runoff while some mutant with a stolen bio-weave laughs at us from the darkness.

I need to decompress. Clear my head before I do something stupid—like go back to Morvain's office and pick that vault lock myself.

The locker door screams open—a sound like tearing metal—and I grab my civilian jacket, the leather worn soft at the elbows from too many late nights like this one. But when I pull it free, something catches my eye.

Taped to the inside of the locker door.

A floppy disk. 3.5-inch. Completely black, not the standard beige or blue. And etched into the plastic casing, just above where the write-protect tab would be, is a single stylized eye. Pupil dilated. Watching.

I freeze.

The locker room is empty—has been since I came in here fifteen minutes ago. Just me and the smell and the dying fluorescent tube that keeps sputtering overhead. I glance up quickly. No cameras. This section was retrofitted last year; they never bothered reinstalling surveillance after the rehab.

My heart hammers against my ribs.

I reach out slowly, fingers hovering over the disk. Could be nothing. Prank. Some tech-wonk leaving a dead drop for someone else who happened to use this locker. But my gut tells me different. My gut tells me whoever left this knew exactly whose locker it was.

I snatch it up, feel the weight of it—surprisingly substantial for plastic—and turn it over. Blank on the other side except for a serial number stamped so small I'd need a magnifier to read it.

"Everything alright down here?"

I nearly jump, spinning around. It's just the janitor—a human, older, name tag says MARTINEZ. He's pushing a wheeled trash bin, looking tired enough to drop.

"Fine," I say, voice coming out rougher than intended. I clear my throat. "Just pulling a double. You know how it is."

Martinez nods like he does know, which probably means he doesn't but won't argue with a BATC commander at midnight. "Those lights been bugging you too?" He gestures at the sputtering tube. "Maintenance said they'd fix it. That was Tuesday."

"Thursday now." I tuck the disk into my jacket pocket where it presses cold against my hip.

He pushes his cart past, muttering about union negotiations and minimum wage. I wait until his footsteps fade down the corridor before I pull the disk back out.

The eye seems to stare at me.

Standard sweep first—I cast a low-level diagnostic weave, white-lilac flame flickering from my fingertips without conscious thought. The magic smells clean, fresh cedar cutting through the locker room stench. The weave spreads across the disk's surface like morning dew, probing for explosives, biological agents, anything that might turn my hand into pink mist or worse.

Clean. No traps. But there's encryption layered on this thing like sedimentary rock—arcano-ciphers stacked on standard crypto, weaving together in patterns I don't immediately recognize. Someone spent serious money on this security.

And someone went to serious effort to put it in my locker.

I close my fist around it, feeling the rigid plastic edges dig into my palm. Standard tech-ops would just bury this. File it as unknown origin, let it gather dust in evidence control while Morvain signs off saying all protocols were followed. By the book.

But whatever's on this disk ended up in my locker because someone knew I wouldn't play by the book.

The fluorescent light above me dies with a final sputter, plunging everything into shadow for half a second before the backup kicks in with an electronic whine. In that darkness, I swear I hear something—a whisper, maybe, or just the building settling.

When the lights return, I'm already standing, jacket in hand.

I know exactly where to go.

There's a place under the Pulaski Skyway, in what used to be an industrial loading dock before the Undercity expanded to swallow it whole. The Gnome hardware-brokers run operations out of there—technomancers who deal in black-market data and equipment that the BATC officially doesn't acknowledge exists. They have slicers who can crack anything short of Council-level security.

They also have memories longer than their moral compasses and prices that make you wonder if you're paying for goods or absolution.

I check my sidearm out of habit, though I won't wear it into the Wire-Tap proper. The brokers have rules, and breaking them means more than getting banned. It means they'll remember your face.

The disk feels heavy in my pocket as I head for the exit. Behind me, the lockers clang shut one by one, like teeth.

Someone wanted me to find this.

Now I need to figure out why.

* * *

The rain had turned the Pulaski Skyway into a river of light, each sodium-vapor streetlamp bleeding halos across the wet asphalt. I killed the Crown Vic's engine in front of a defunct laundromat in Kearny, its windows painted over with spray-painted circuit boards and glowing sigils that hurt to look at too long.

"The Wire-Tap" wasn't exactly on any map.

I grabbed the manila envelope from the passenger seat—Morvain's buried report, the floppy disk inside sealed tighter than a tomb. My hand smelled like fresh cedar when I touched it, that white-lilac flame crawling up my fingertips before I reined it back. Patience. Control. Everything Morvain had taught me about keeping the Aegis line pure.

The basement door was hidden behind a rusted dumpster, the kind of place where the concrete still remembered boot heels and blood. Down three flights of stairs slick with condensation, past walls tagged with running code that made my eyes water if I stared too long. The smell hit me first—ozone and rosin from soldering irons, stale coffee gone bitter, and underneath it all that metallic tang of electronics that'd been pulled from dead bodies.

Digits O'Malley was exactly where intel said he'd be: hunched over a workbench cluttered with gutted Nokia pagers, their circuit boards spread out like dissecting frogs. He didn't even look up when I came in, just kept clicking away at some mechanical keyboard that sounded like nails in coffins.

"Got a lockout job?" His voice scraped gravel. Gnome accent, thick as mud. "Got a waiting list, Commander. Try again next week."

I slapped the envelope down next to his PalmPilot graveyard. The twenties peeled out from under the plastic sleeve like dead leaves. "This isn't a negotiation, Digits."

Now he looked up. Eyes too big for his face, pupils dilated in the green glow of a dozen monitors mounted ceiling-high around his cramped workshop. The Panasonic Toughbook on his main bench was Frankenstein's monster—a Frankenstein built by someone who thought monstrosity was an art form. Wires ran everywhere, disappearing into holes drilled through the aluminum frame.

"You bringing BATC heat into my shop?" He stood, hands coming up fast but not threatening. Defensive. "What happened to 'no official business after midnight'? That rule still kick, or did Morvain retire your brain along with your badge?"

"Morvain buried this." I tapped the floppy disk. "You're going to crack it. You're going to show me what he tried so hard to hide."

Digits whistled low through his teeth. "Razor-Wire encryption, Vance. Street-Elf grade, probably off-the-books High-Spire hardware. Whatever's on there, it's not just locked—it's *poisoned*. Every hacker in three counties has been trying to breach Watching Party comms since they surfaced. Nobody's made it past the first layer."

"The second layer is broken," I said. Not asked. Stated. Because I could smell it—that cedar-clean scent of pristine magic meant someone with my training had already been here, had already opened the door before slamming it shut again.

Digits stared at me for a long moment, then shrugged and slumped back into his chair. "Fine. Fuck it. Let's see what your old mentor didn't want you seeing."

He plugged the floppy drive into the Panasonic, fingers flying across that clicking keyboard. The screen lit green-black, cascading text flowing like water. My breath caught.

*WATCHING PARTY [CLASSIFIED]*
*OPERATION: GHOST DANCE*
*SUBJECT: MILLENNIUM BREACH CONTAINMENT*

"No, no, no..." Digits muttered, pulling up a terminal window. His fingers danced across keys faster now, some kind of cryptographic assault program blooming across the secondary monitor. "This is Tier-Nine security, Vance. This isn't just encrypted—it's got a self-destruct protocol wired into the file headers. One wrong move and this whole thing evaporates."

"Then don't make a wrong move."

He shot me a look that could curdle milk, but his hands never stopped moving. The progress bar appeared onscreen, crawling forward millimeter by agonizing millimeter. 3%... 7%... 14%...

The rain hammered harder against whatever windows existed in this underground tomb. Somewhere above us, a car alarm screamed. Someone shouted words in High Speech that made the air taste like copper.

28%... 45%...

"I'm in," Digits breathed. Then louder, panic creeping into his voice: "Vance, I'm *in*—"

The screen flooded white.

When my eyes cleared, they weren't looking at encryption anymore. They were looking at blueprints. Structural diagrams. Architectural schematics for something massive buried beneath Newark Bay, its foundations sinking into the marsh mud where Kearny used to bleed into Pulaski.

And symbols. God help me, symbols carved into those concrete walls with magic older than Morvain, older than the Aegis itself. Older than anything we'd been trained to contain.

Digits went pale as death, pushing back from the workbench hard enough to send his chair rolling into a stack of fiber-optic cables. "Vance..." His voice cracked. "What the hell are your bosses building down there?"

The progress bar hit 100%.

I didn't answer him. Couldn't answer him. Because I recognized those symbols from somewhere deep in my training manuals—the kind of knowledge you're taught to forget because once you see it, you can't unsee it.

Once you know what's sleeping under the city, you can never pretend it isn't there again.

* * *

I lean forward over the Toughbook, my shadow falling across Digits' face in the cramped darkness of his nest. The screen's pale glow reflects in my eyes as I watch the corrupted file unfold—partial schematics, heavily redacted, but unmistakable in their implications.

Five massive structures. Subterranean. The Pylons.

The data streams past in technical jargon that would make most operators' heads spin, but I've been reading telluric signatures since my Academy days. These aren't standard grid retrofits. They're unauthorized taps, drawing power levels that make my stomach clench with something between fear and professional horror.

"Jesus Christ," I breathe out, watching the numbers cascade down the screen. This is far beyond what any sanctioned operation should be pulling from the earth's ley-lines.

Digits shifts beside me, the Toughbook balanced precariously on his knees. His fingers hover over the trackpad like he wants to shut it down, bury it, pretend we never saw this. But he doesn't move. He can't look away either.

There—a cluster of coordinates highlights in the margin. Foundry Sector. Deep in the Undercity's bowels, where the light doesn't reach and the only law is whatever you're strong enough to enforce.

"The sewage plumes," I say quietly, connecting threads my subconscious has already woven. Those toxic clouds that swept through County General ER, poisoning patients like Danny Reyes. The environmental reports blamed industrial runoff, municipal negligence. But this...

My white-lilac flame flickers at my fingertips without conscious thought, a bio-ward responding to my spike in adrenaline. The scent of fresh cedar cuts through the stale air of Digits' sanctuary, sharp and clean and utterly alien to this place.

I reach out and eject the floppy disk with more force than necessary. The black square pops free and lands in my palm—heavy, innocent-looking, containing secrets that could burn half the BATC command structure to ash.

"I'm not keeping this on the hard drive," Digits says, and there's something almost apologetic in his tone. "You understand. If someone cracks this machine..."

I do understand. In the Undercity, digital ghosts live forever if you're stupid enough to leave traces.

"Any chatter?" I ask him, watching his face as much as listening to his words. "On the wire about the Foundry? Movement, activity, anything?"

He leans back against the corrugated metal wall, running his hands through hair that probably hasn't seen water in days. When he talks, it's measured, careful. "Corporate mercs. Moving in heavy all week. Armed for bear." He pauses. "Using cheap muscle to clear tunnels. Displaced workers mostly. Offering cash for demolition work."

Translation: They're clearing the way, making sure nobody asks questions when the real operation starts up. Making the Undercity a little more empty, a little more desperate, one paycheck at a time.

My Nextel pager is already in my hand. I hit speed-dial for Aegis Squad—the number's burned into muscle memory, third knuckle, middle finger, same spot every time.

"Suit up," I say when the line connects. "We're going off-grid. Undercity. Bring breathers and telluric dampeners."

There's a pause on the other end. Then: "Commander, are you sure—"

"Now, Corporal."

I hang up before they can question me further. Because questions mean hesitation, and hesitation means dead indigent patients in County General ER waiting rooms. Means Danny Reyes with froth on his lips and no explanation except toxic clouds that came from somewhere.

The floppy disk sits in my palm like a loaded gun.

And somewhere deep beneath Newark Bay, in the dark places where the Pylons draw their power, something ancient is waking up hungry.

---

## CHAPTER 7: CHAPTER 7

The elevator groans like dying metal as we descend through layers of concrete and neglect. Four levels down and the temperature's already climbing—can feel it baking through my tactical vest, making sweat run cold between my shoulder blades.

"Sub-Level 3 approaching," I mutter into the comm, watching the IBM ThinkPad's screen flicker green phosphorescence across my face. The portable spectrometer's needle jumps wildly now, tracking telluric spikes that shouldn't exist this deep. Shouldn't exist at all without proper permits, oversight, basic human decency.

The elevator lurches. Someone coughs—a wet, rattling sound. That's when I know we've hit the bad air. Can taste it myself now: sulfur cutting through the filter, like licking an old battery. Stagnant water underneath that, and something else. Ozone. Electrical discharge.

"Sealing atmosphere protocols engaged," says Chen, our tech specialist, his voice distorted by the respirator. Good man. Former paramedic before he signed on to Aegis. Knows how to keep people alive in impossible situations.

We pass Sub-Level 3 without stopping. The coordinates from that floppy disk were clear—sub-level four, sector seven, maintenance quadrant C. Deep in the Undercity Foundry, where Neon Hollow's forgotten workers actually make things happen.

The elevator gates grind open onto a maintenance tunnel that smells like a battlefield. Wet concrete, cordite residue, and beneath it all that chemical tang that means someone's been burning off industrial waste again. Probably one of the foundries trying to bypass environmental monitoring.

I raise my hand, signal the team to spread out. Three points of cover, tactical spacing. Standard infiltration protocol.

"Check your filters. We're walking into a high-toxicity zone," I say quietly, though the words barely carry over the dripping sound echoing down the tunnel. Water runs in sheets along cracked pipes overhead. Somewhere distant, machinery thrums—regular, rhythmic, mechanical.

We move single file, weapons ready but holstered. This isn't a combat op. Not yet. We're here for intelligence gathering first. Document the illegal operations. Secure civilian safety. Then escalate if necessary.

The sodium-vapor work lights start appearing around the third junction—orange flickering that cuts through the perpetual gray like bleeding wounds. Each one illuminates more decay: rust-cored piping, buckled floor plates, electrical conduits running exposed and dangerous.

And then I hear it.

*Thud-thud-thud.*

Automatic weapons fire, muffled by distance but unmistakable. Heavy caliber. Military-grade or close enough. The rhythm is wrong though—not controlled bursts, not even sustained fire. Just random, panicked discharge punctuated by screams.

My hand goes to my sidearm automatically. The team tenses around me.

"I need eyes on that firing line," I whisper into the comm. "Chen, can you get me a thermal read?"

"Working on it, Commander." His fingers fly across his equipment. "Lot of heat signatures downrange. Twenty, maybe thirty meters beyond next intersection."

I signal forward with two fingers. We creep past another junction, moving silent as shadows. The gunfire's getting louder now—closer. Can feel each round discharging in my chest cavity, sympathetic pain from years of active duty.

Around the corner, the tunnel opens onto a catwalk overlooking a cavernous junction. And there it is: a massive copper busbar, at least four inches thick, illegally tapped and running hot with telluric energy that makes my wards hum like angry hornets. The busbar itself glows orange-white in places where the connections are overloading, throwing hellish light across—

I freeze.

Look down from the catwalk rail.

See what they're protecting.

Three bodies sprawled on the concrete floor below, barely recognizable as human anymore. Another figure stumbles backward, trying to raise a pistol with shaking hands before someone off-screen cuts him down with a three-round burst center mass. His body hits the ground hard enough to crack audible against the concrete.

They're slaughtering them.

The illegal tap workers—the metahumans working the foundry sector without permits, without protections, without rights. Meat-shields for whoever's running this operation. They're dying because some corporate overlord needs cheap energy and cheaper labor.

And I'm standing here watching it happen.

"Commander?" Chen's voice cracks through the comm. "We have to do something. We have to—"

"I see them," I cut him off, voice tight as steel wire. My white-lilac wards flare bright around me suddenly, cutting through the sulfur-choked air like a beacon. Like a promise. Like a threat.

Someone screams below—not pain, but recognition. Of the wards. Of Aegis presence.

Time to stop being observers.

Time to start being the law.

* * *

The stench hits me before I see anything—a toxic cocktail of sulfur, cordite, and something worse. Something organic and wet. My wards flare white-lilac in the gloom as I drop down the maintenance ladder, boots hitting slick concrete four stories below ground level.

Sub-Level 4 of the Undercity Foundry Sector breathes like a dying lung.

The catwalk groans under my weight as I move forward, weapon raised. Below, the telluric tap coordinates weren't bullshit after all. But what I find makes my stomach clench.

They're using them as meat-shields.

The Elves wear tactical suits that probably cost more than most people's houses—bespoke armor with optical-camo cloaks that shimmer and blur at the edges. High-Spire corporate security, their insignias barely visible through the smog. They stand behind a wall of flesh.

Goblins. Ogre-Kin. Chained to reinforced posts driven into the concrete floor, their wrists bound in iron that weeps blue-black residue onto the ground. The smaller ones—the Goblins—are screaming, their voices high-pitched and desperate. The bigger ones—the Ogre-Kin—roar defiance even as blood mats their gray-green skin.

"HOLD THE LINE!" The Elf Commander's voice cuts through the gunfire like a scalpel. He doesn't shout—doesn't need to. There's something in his tone that suggests he's said this a hundred times before. "Let the grunts eat the shrapnel! Keep the tap secure!"

His mercs don't hesitate. Rune-etched MP5s buck against their shoulders, the weapons glowing faintly blue where arcane runes spiral around the barrels. Brass casings dance across wet concrete, smoking hot. The rounds punch through the clustered laborers without slowing down.

A Goblin takes one center-mass. His body jerks, and then another round catches him in the throat. Blood sprays in an arc, catching the lilac light of my wards.

An Ogre-Kin bellows, fighting against his chains. "I AIN'T DYIN' DOWN HERE FOR YOUR DAMN COPPER! GET OFF ME!"

The Elf behind him just fires over the massive metahuman's shoulder, using his body as cover. The Ogre-Kin's roars turn to screams as shotgun slugs from the rival syndicate tear into his back. Blue-black iron-gall residue burns into his flesh, sizzling, smoke rising in thin wisps.

There must be twenty of them. Twenty working-class metahumans chained and bleeding while corporate mercs use them for cover.

My finger tightens on the trigger.

But I don't fire yet.

Need intel first. Need to know what they're protecting down here besides their pathetic lives.

The telluric tap is there, visible past the firing line—a cluster of crystalline nodes pulsing with captured lightning, feeding power up to High-Spire through conduits that disappear into the ceiling. Illegal as hell. This whole operation is a violation of every treaty signed after the Breach.

And they're willing to kill their own people to protect it.

A rocket-propelled grenade screams through the smog.

I see the trail of fire arcing toward a cluster of Goblins, all chained together, too terrified to run. The warhead will vaporize them.

Mara Vance doesn't hesitate.

I vault the catwalk railing.

* * *

The coordinates led us down through layers of concrete and despair until the air itself turned thick with the taste of sulfur and old blood. Sub-Level 4 of the Foundry Sector was where Neon Hollow kept its dirty secrets—the kind that didn't appear on any city planning documents or official maps.

My boots hit wet concrete as I dropped through the maintenance hatch, Aegis Squad following behind in controlled chaos. The first thing that registered wasn't the workers or the weapons, but the *sound*—a wet, rhythmic thudding like meat being pounded against stone.

"Commander!" Reyes' voice crackled through my comm. "We've got hostiles at three o'clock—"

I saw them before he finished. High-Spire Elves, their armor gleaming even in the sickly yellow light filtering through decades of accumulated grime. They weren't here for salvage or territory. Their rifles were trained on a group of laborers chained to the wall—Ogres, Trolls, a few desperate humans—and one of those rifles had an RPG round already locked and loaded.

The world went sharp and clear.

My hands erupted in white-lilac fire so bright it burned away the smog around me like a surgical incision through diseased tissue. The flames sang up my arms, spiraling into a bio-ward that expanded outward in a perfect hemisphere. Pure. Clean. Everything about it screamed *official BATC intervention*.

"You want to start this dance?" I called out, my voice cutting across the underground chamber. "Because I guarantee you won't like how it ends."

The Elf commander—a tall bastard with silver hair and enough ritual scars to make him expensive—froze. His eyes tracked the glow of my wards, then widened as he recognized what he was looking at. Not some street mage. Not even regular BATC enforcement.

Aegis Commander.

His rifle lowered fractionally. Behind him, two more elves moved, optical-camo cloaks beginning to shimmer around their forms. Smart. They knew exactly what those cloaks meant—they could vanish into the shadows and make this whole thing disappear, no witnesses, no incident reports, just another night in the Undercity where people who didn't matter got disappeared.

But they hadn't counted on my squad dropping through every maintenance hatch within a hundred meters. Non-lethal suppression rounds began pinging off concrete around them, not quite hitting but making it crystal fucking clear that we had them surrounded.

"Stand down!" The Elf's command was sharp, precise. To his men: "Cloak. Fall back. We abort."

And just like that, they were gone. Optical-camo hummed and faded, leaving nothing but empty air and the acrid smell of cordite mixing with something sweeter, cleaner—that fresh cedar scent that always accompanied major magical expenditure.

I dropped to my knees beside the nearest laborer without thinking, my hands already shifting from combat weaves to medical triage. White-lilac light traced over an Ogre-Kin with a gut wound so bad I could see bone through the tear in his hide. Blood slicked my medical gloves hot and wet.

"Triage! Now!" I barked to my squad. "Reyes, you've got three more casualties over there—start compression. Martinez, get me the field trauma kit!"

The Ogre grabbed my arm with surprising strength for someone bleeding out. His eyes were wide, pupils blown wide with shock and pain. "They... they just pushed us in front..." he gasped, each word a struggle. "Said we were cheaper than Kevlar..."

My jaw tightened so hard my teeth hurt. Rage wanted to burn through my veins, wanted to pour itself into a retaliatory strike, but I forced it down into something useful. Controlled. Focused.

"I've got you," I said, my voice tight as I applied a glowing white-lilac cauterizing weave across the worst of the damage. The smell changed again—cedar and ozone overwhelming even the blood and sulfur. "Stay with me. You're going to make it."

Behind him, chained to the same wall, another worker—a Troll with half his face missing—wasn't so lucky. Reyes was already shaking his head at me. Can't save them all. Never can.

But you try anyway.

That's what separates us from the monsters who'd chain people up as meat shields.

As I worked on stabilizing the Ogre, my peripheral vision caught something that made my stomach drop. Stamped on the heavy chains binding these workers: a Sterling-Voss corporate insignia, clear as day.

Not Morvain.

The Board of Directors.

*Shit.*

This wasn't some rogue operation. This was sanctioned. Official. Someone high up had decided that Undercity laborers were disposable resources, and Sterling-Voss had provided the chains to make it legal.

I looked down at the dying Ogre-Kin, at his eyes finding mine with desperate hope as my weaves knit his flesh back together. Whatever came next—I'd deal with it. But first, this man survived. All of them who could be saved would survive.

Because that's what Aegis does in the dark places where no one else wants to look.

We bring the light.

---

## CHAPTER 8: CHAPTER 8

The coffee tasted like regret and burnt filters, but I'd drunk worse. Much worse. The mug sat cold between my palms while I stared at the rusted iron chain links sprawled across my desk—evidence from the Undercity raid, evidence that Sterling-Voss had been moving blood-iron through the sewer systems for months now. Maybe years.

My office smelled like cedar and old paper, the lingering scent of my own magic clinging to everything I touched. The warmth was familiar, comforting even, after three days of processing what we'd found down there. Bodies. So many fucking bodies.

The Motorola Nextel on my desk started buzzing.

I didn't recognize the number, but I recognized the code that flashed across the tiny screen: **187-Arcane**. Homicide with metaphysical components. My jaw tightened as I reached for my medical kit—the leather bag felt heavy with its contents, bandages and antiseptic and more arcane materials than any field commander should have to carry.

"Vance." The dispatcher's voice crackled through the speakerphone. "Foundry District. Behind the old textile mills on Penn."

"I know where it is."

"You need to see this one yourself. Cops are spooked. Says the crime scene's... freezing over." She paused. "And Vance? Forensics won't touch it. They're calling it active magic."

Active. That meant the working wasn't finished. The spell was still running.

I grabbed my coat—a heavy wool thing that had seen better decades—and headed out into the October rain.

---

The Crown Vic's tires sang against wet asphalt, rhythmic and hypnotic. Rain hammered the windshield in sheets, the wipers barely keeping pace. I merged onto Route 1 & 9, lights cutting through the darkness, and thought about Sterling-Voss. About chains and blood and whatever fresh hell was waiting for me behind those textile mills.

Forty minutes later, I pulled up to a cluster of patrol cars, their emergency lights painting everything in strobing yellow and red. Cops huddled under awnings, shoulders hunched, breath visible in clouds despite the temperature gauge on my dash reading fifty-two degrees.

I killed the engine and stepped out into the downpour.

"Commander Vance?" A young cop—couldn't be more than twenty-five, face pale beneath his cap—approached with a flashlight extended like an offering. His hands were shaking. "Forensics won't go near it, ma'am. Says the magic on the vic is still active. It's..." He swallowed hard. "...it's quiet. Too quiet."

I took the flashlight without responding and ducked under the yellow police tape.

The moment I crossed that line, something changed.

The rain stopped hitting me.

I looked up, watching droplets freeze mid-air a few feet ahead, suspended like crystalline beads before transforming into sleet and continuing their fall. The temperature plummeted—I could feel it in my lungs, each breath suddenly sharp and cold. Ten degrees. Maybe fifteen. The air itself felt wrong, dense and heavy and somehow *listening*.

My cedar-scent magic pushed back automatically, warmth radiating from my chest as I activated my wards reflexively. But this wasn't normal arcane work. This was something else.

I clicked on the flashlight and walked forward.

The alley was narrow, walls of crumbling brick pressing inward like a throat. Garbage cans overflowed with refuse, and somewhere water dripped with that particular emptiness of abandoned places. My boots splashed through puddles that shouldn't have been frozen at fifty degrees, ice forming in fractal patterns where they touched the ground.

Then I saw him.

A man—middle-aged, business suit torn and soaked, face twisted in an expression that was neither surprise nor pain but something beyond both. He lay sprawled against the wall, one arm outstretched toward the mouth of the alley like he'd been reaching for help or escape or just air when whatever happened, happened.

But it wasn't the body that made my stomach clench.

It was the frost spreading across the pavement around him, creeping outward in intricate geometric patterns. And the silence. God, the silence. No birds, no traffic noise filtering from the street beyond—just the soft hiss of sleet hitting the ground and my own breathing.

"Fuck," I whispered.

This was Cole Reyes's work. Had to be.

I'd read the reports from Sub-Station Seven, seen the aftermath of his confrontation with the Undercity gangsters. The way metal had frozen solid mid-air. The way blood turned to iron filings before anyone's eyes. But reading about it and seeing it were two different things entirely.

I knelt beside the body, cedar magic flaring bright as I established a perimeter ward. The cold hit me immediately—not the ambient temperature drop, which my wards could handle, but something deeper. A wrongness that sank into bone marrow and made my teeth ache.

The victim's skin was blue-tinged, frost forming on his eyelashes. But there was no blood. None. His chest had been opened—cleanly, surgically—and whatever had been taken was gone. Only the cavity remained, perfectly smooth edges that shouldn't have existed without massive hemorrhage but somehow didn't bleed at all.

"Christ," I breathed, leaning closer.

There, in the center of the wound, where a heart should have been: a single chain link, no bigger than my thumb. Frost-cobalt. The same material Sterling-Voss had been moving through the Undercity.

And it was still pulsing with active magic.

My pager buzzed again. Same number as before.

*You wanted proof, Commander.*

*Look closer.*

* * *

The rain hammers against my back as I step into the alley's mouth, boots squelching in the oil-stained puddles. October in North Jersey should smell like wet pavement and dying leaves. Instead, my nose fills with something else—a metallic tang that makes my teeth ache.

"Commander Vance." The uniform who flagged me down looks green around the gills. Smart kid. He stays at the alley entrance while I push deeper into the shadows.

My Maglite cuts through the darkness like a lighthouse beam. The warmth from its handle seeps into my palm—solid, electric, real. I need that reality right now because what the light illuminates is anything but normal.

An Elven male, tall even in death, pinned to the brick wall by his own hand. Literally. A jagged spike of something dark and crystalline erupts through his right palm, driving straight through his chest cavity. The point of impact is a perfect circle of frozen tissue, black ice radiating outward in spider-web patterns across his lab coat. Sterling-Voss corporate logo barely visible under all the frost.

I pull out my micro-cassette recorder, voice steady despite the cold knifing through my wool coat.

"Victim is a High-Spire Elf. Estimated age two-hundred-sixty, maybe older. Cause of death appears to be massive arcane trauma. The hex... it's blood-iron metallurgy. But I've never felt a weave this cold."

I move closer, beam tracking over the details. No pooled blood. None. What should have been gallons of lifeblood has flash-frozen into this grotesque sculpture of ice and iron. The surface shimmers with an oily blue-black sheen—cobalt mixed with something else. Something wrong.

"There's no residual anger in the magic. It's just... absolute zero."

The words feel inadequate. My cedar-scented wards always run warm, protective, alive with purpose. This thing that killed him? It's the opposite. Dead-cold precision without malice or passion or any human emotion whatsoever.

And the ledger.

A thick black leather journal sits wedged against his sternum, perfectly parallel to his ribs. The cobalt spike drives clean through its center pages before penetrating flesh. The pages aren't just stuck—they're welded to the wound, fused by some impossibly hot-and-cold process simultaneously.

Frost coats my eyelashes as I lean in. Each breath clouds white in air that shouldn't be this frigid. My thermal vision would normally show heat signatures, but around this body there's just... absence. A void where warmth should be.

"The execution was performed at close range," I continue recording. "No defensive wounds. Victim likely didn't see it coming or couldn't react. Point-of-origin suggests the attacker stood approximately three feet distance, right-hand dominant."

* * *

The rain falls wrong tonight.

I kneel beside the corpse in the alley behind the Foundry District, watching droplets hit the ground ten inches away where they should fall on me instead. The temperature plummets—ten degrees in three steps, like crossing an invisible wall. My breath clouds white while the world beyond stays November-wet and autumn-cool.

The victim's name was Marcus Webb. Forty-seven years old, former vice president of waste management at Sterling-Chem. His body lies pinned to a brick wall by what looks like an icicle made from liquid mercury that forgot how to flow. Frost spreads from the wound points, crystalline patterns that eat into his suit jacket, his flesh, the mortar between bricks.

No blood. That's the first thing you notice—should be arterial spray, pooling, dripping down the wall. Instead there's just... absence. A cold so deep it sucks heat from everything around it.

Cole Reyes did this.

I've seen his work before—every Aegis Commander has—but never up close. Never when the air still tastes like frozen void. I extend my right hand slowly, summoning the white-lilac flame that marks my magic. Cedar scent blooms warm around me, fighting against the sterile nothingness radiating from those cobalt spikes.

The smell helps. Always does. Fresh cedar means life, growth, the way things should be. Whatever Cole is, he's the opposite of that.

My fingers stop six inches from the nearest spike. Even through the flames, I feel the wrongness—the psychological residue baked into the weave. This isn't malice exactly. It's colder than that. More disciplined.

*Justice*, whispers something in my bones. *Penance. Necessity.*

I don't let myself dwell on it. Analysis can come later. First priority: evidence preservation.

Using my free hand, I trace bio-wards in the air—a complex pattern of protective sigils that cost me half my remaining stamina for the night. The frost recedes fractionally where they intersect with Cole's work. Just enough.

"Someone is hunting the people who poisoned the South Side," I mutter to the corpse, carefully working my magic to thaw the frozen blood without damaging whatever's underneath. "And they aren't asking questions."

Steam hisses as my white-lilac flames touch the cobalt frost. Ice cracks with sounds like breaking glass. The leather ledger pinned under Webb's left shoulder begins to emerge—stiff, waterlogged, but intact.

I slide it free. Open it.

Shipping manifests. Dates from 2000. Sterling-Chem Experimental Sludge Unit, Batch 734-B through 812-G, all dumped into the Undercity sewer network between March and June. The same sludge that caused the Black-Iron Lung epidemic. The same poison that killed two hundred families down south while the company filed paperwork claiming 'controlled agricultural runoff.'

My stomach turns. Not from the death—I've seen worse—but from what this means.

Footsteps echo at the alley entrance. I look up fast, hand already moving to my sidearm before I register the BATC Internal Affairs badges.

Two men in suits, faces I recognize from headquarters briefings but whose names I can't place right now. They're here for the body. Here for *me*.

"Commander Vance," says the taller one, not smiling. "We need you to come in. Now."

---

## CHAPTER 9: CHAPTER 9

The elevator ride up was silent except for the pneumatic hiss of hydraulics and the soft chime of each passing floor. I watched my reflection in the polished chrome walls—blood crusting on my cheekbone, the BATC insignia on my soaked uniform stained crimson instead of regulation black. Someone had tried to clean the elevator since my last visit. They'd failed.

The doors opened onto the 80th floor.

IA.

Internal Affairs didn't have offices. They had sanctuaries. Glass walls separated the briefing room from the rest of the Spire's sterile expanse, but I could see the elves moving like ghosts through the cubicles beyond—high-society metas in pressed suits, their pointed ears catching the fluorescent light. The air smelled wrong. Too clean. Ozone-purified. Expensive cologne mixed with the electric tang of equipment that cost more than a Kearny tenement building.

Vane Thorne stood by the panoramic window overlooking Neon Hollow. Sunrise painted the city in shades of bruised plum and sickly orange, the chemical plants belching smoke over the marshlands. He turned as I entered, his smile razor-thin and utterly cold.

"Commander Vance," he said, voice smooth as silk pulled across broken glass. "You look like you've been wrestling hogs in the slaughterhouse."

I didn't move closer. Let him come to me if he wanted something.

"The chemist is still warm enough to smell," I replied. "Your people should hurry if they want first dibs at the autopsy."

Thorne poured himself water from a crystal decanter, ice cubes clinking like tiny bells against the glass. His suit was immaculate—a charcoal grey that probably cost more than my monthly salary. Not a wrinkle. Not a stain. Perfectly groomed hair, perfectly manicured nails. Everything about him screamed High-Spire superiority.

"You recovered a ledger." Not a question. He took a measured sip, those elven eyes never leaving mine. "The one the deceased was so carelessly clutching when you arrived."

My hand instinctively went to my belt pouch. The leather felt wet and heavy.

"That's evidence."

"We are all evidence, Commander." Thorne set down his glass on a tray beside an IBM ThinkPad that looked fresh from the factory floor. "The chemist—Marcus Thorne, Sterling-Voss division—was killed with blood-iron hexwork during what appears to be a corporate dispute. This makes it *our* matter."

"Bullshit."

His smile widened, showing too-white teeth. "Excuse me?"

"He died in my sector. In my city. With a hex signature that matches three separate attacks on BATC infrastructure over the past month." I took two steps forward, boots squelching on the imported Persian rug. "Someone's testing our defenses. Someone's good enough to walk through wards that should've stopped a goddamn nuke. That makes it my problem."

"And yet," Thorne gestured lazily toward the door behind me, where two IA enforcement officers stood with their arms crossed, "you're here. Speaking to me. Which suggests someone above your pay grade disagrees with your assessment."

I hated this. Hated every inch of polished marble and climate-controlled air. Hated how clean everything was while the city below rotted in its own filth. Hated that he was right—I'd been summoned like a dog on a leash.

"Give me the ledger, Commander. You can consider yourself... temporarily reassigned."

"What's that mean?"

"It means," he turned back to his laptop, fingers dancing across keys with unnatural speed, "that you're going to find whoever killed Mr. Thorne. But you'll do it under our supervision. Our rules." The projector hummed to life behind him, bathing the room in cold white light. A file folder appeared on screen: *OPERATION MECHANIC - EYES ONLY*.

"We have a name for your suspect."

The image changed. A grainy surveillance photo from one of Newark Bay's cargo terminals—too dark to make out features clearly. Male. Tall. Moving with the precise economy of motion I recognized from combat training.

"The Mechanic," Thorne said softly, dimming the lights until we were both bathed in the monitor's glow. "Cole Reyes. Former Sterling-Voss security contractor. Discharged for 'excessive zeal' after an incident in 2001. Since then, he's been a ghost. Three years of silence. Then suddenly..." He clicked again. More images. Security footage showing impossible feats of strength, hexwork that violated fundamental laws of arcane physics.

"He didn't just kill the chemist," Thorne continued, voice dropping lower. "He broke into Sterling-Voss's primary research server. Stole proprietary data on blood-iron weaponry. Data that could level this entire city if deployed improperly."

"Why?"

That smile again—that predatory, corporate smirk.

"That, Commander, is what you're going to discover."

* * *

The briefing room sits thirty stories above Newark Bay, all chrome and smoked glass that reflects nothing. I feel like I'm breathing through a straw.

Vane Thorne stands at the control panel, his perfectly pressed suit the color of charcoal smoke. Behind him, the projector hums—an old-school Epson that smells like burning dust and ozone. Click-clack. Click-clack. The carousel advances.

"Commander Vance." His voice is smooth as river stones. "Thank you for coming."

I don't respond. My fingers find the armrest of my chair, dig in slightly. The leather creaks.

"The Mechanic," Thorne begins, and already I hate the nickname. Criminals get nicknames when they escape us, when they become myths instead of men. "Real name Cole Reyes. Thirty-two years old. Former BATC contractor, dismissed 2001 for insubordination during the Kearny Marshes cleanup."

Click-clack.

The first image slams onto the wall—a photograph so grainy it looks like an x-ray. A man slumped over a steering wheel in some Lincoln Town Car, frost spreading across the windshield in crystalline fractals. Ice crawls down the driver's face, turning his expression into something frozen between rage and surprise.

"Victim number one. Anthony Scavo. Union boss, 43rd Street Waterfront Coalition. Found November 3rd, 2001. Body temperature was minus-17 degrees Celsius."

Thorne gestures with his pen, laser-pointer dot dancing across the ice-crystal patterns on the glass. "Notice anything?"

I notice everything. That's my job.

"The frost," I say quietly. "It didn't melt. Even after we found him, even when he'd been dead for hours. Forensic team said it was like... like the cold was still there. Still clinging to him."

"Precisely." Thorne clicks again. Click-clack.

Another photo: a Black-Circuit smuggler impaled against a warehouse wall, iron rebar punched clean through his chest. Blood has frozen in rivers down his torso, black as tar in the flashbulb glare.

"This is Viktor Kozlov. September 8th, 2002. Same signature—body temp at discovery, minus-23. And here..." He pauses, lets the silence stretch. "...here's where it gets interesting."

The carousel slides to the next shot. My stomach drops.

The chemist from the alley. The one I watched Cole walk away from, back in August. He's sprawled in what looks like a meat locker, flesh blue-white, lips pulled back in a silent scream. But this time I can see more—the context. A laboratory freezer, equipment scattered, chemical formulas scrawled in his own blood before it froze solid.

"He killed the chemist," Thorne says unnecessarily. "Three weeks ago. August 24th. Burned the lab, but not before our analysts recovered enough data to trace his supply chain all the way back to the Pylon Project."

My knuckles whiten around the armrest.

Thorne turns, and for the first time, something flickers across his face—not quite concern, not quite fear. Ambition, maybe. Or calculation.

"You know about the Pylon Project, Commander?"

"The deep-level infrastructure contract." My voice stays flat. "Undercity renovation, wastewater management, slag reclamation. Twenty-billion-dollar federal grant."

"And who won that contract?"

"Sterling Manor Consolidated."

He smiles—that practiced, corporate smile that belongs on magazine covers and never near real violence.

"Yes. Sterling Manor. Which means..." He pulls up another image: a schematic of some massive underground structure, all cylinders and conduits and glowing nodes. "This is Phase Two. Not just cleaning up the Undercity. This is weaponizing it. Turning the entire Northeast Corridor's waste disposal system into an arcane power grid. The Mechanic understands what he's interrupting."
