My fingers found the top button of my work shirt. Pop. Second button. Third. The fabric fell away from my shoulders, pooling around my boots. In the full-length mirror mounted on the wall, I caught sight of myself—ribs prominent against pale skin, the old scars looking like raised silver rivers across my torso. I looked like something dug up from the Kearny Marshes after a long winter.

The Nextel in my hand felt heavy as a brick. I pressed send, watching the screen light up with its green glow before the speakerphone crackled to life with static.

"Yeah," came Grimjaw's voice, rough as sandpaper dragged across bone. "Cole?"

"Got ten minutes before they take me in," I said, staring at my reflection. My voice sounded flat, distant—not even my own anymore. Just echoes bouncing off cold surfaces. "You listening?"

"Christ, Cole. You sure about this? 'Cause once you're under their knife, there's no—"

"I'm sure." I interrupted. No point in dancing around it. We both knew what was happening here. What I was trading for Danny's next breath. "The remaining crates are under the old Pulaski overpass. Section seven, third support beam from the east end."

Silence stretched out except for the hiss of static.

"Grimjaw."

"I hear you." His voice had gone tight. Controlled. That way cops have when they're watching someone walk toward certain death and can't stop them.

"They want them delivered to Sub-Station Seven by midnight tomorrow. Sterling Manor address—the one on the waterfront, where the marsh meets the bay. The one with the rusted crane."

"You're selling your soul to monsters, man. You know that, right?" He wasn't asking. Just stating facts he thought I needed to hear.

I unbuttoned the last few buttons of my shirt, letting it hang open. My chest rose and fell with measured breaths. In the mirror, I looked hollow. Emptied out.

"Maybe," I said. "Doesn't matter."

"What happens if you die during the operation? Huh? They just toss your body in the river? Or do they keep you alive somehow, some fucked-up way, as their puppet forever?"

My hand went to my sternum, pressing against the bone beneath skin. Cold. Solid. For now.

"If I die, Danny gets a shot at living. That's the deal." I paused, running through it again in my head—not because I needed to remember, but because saying it made it real. Made it undeniable. "They fuse the Geas into my bone marrow. Lead and bismuth, laced with whatever dark shit makes magic stick to meat. It'll poison me slow. Kill me slower than the cancer would've killed him. But while it works, while the spell holds..."

I trailed off, fingers still pressed to my breastbone like I could feel the future growing there already—something cold and heavy taking root in the marrow of my ribs.

"So what, you're just gonna let them carve you up? Let those syndicate butchers install some kind of magical killing clock inside your chest?"

"Not just any magic." I closed my eyes. When I opened them again, my reflection looked different somehow. Harder. Resigned. "Frost-cobalt weave bound to his lungs. Every breath he takes pulls heat from my life-force. Keeps the tumors dormant. Buys him time."

"Time for what?" Grimjaw's voice had gone quiet. Dangerous quiet.

"Time to see his daughter graduate high school. Time to hold his grandkids. Time to wake up one morning without coughing blood."

The line crackled. I heard him breathing on the other end—fast, angry breaths.

"And all that costs is your life," he said finally.

I laughed then. Hollow sound that didn't belong in my throat. "Grim, listen to me carefully. I know what I'm doing here. Penance, revenge, and a sliver of justice. You want the breakdown? Here it is: Danny went down for a crime the Syndicate committed. They framed him because he wouldn't pay their protection money—some bullshit about his auto shop being too successful, drawing attention they didn't want. So they burned him. Made sure the evidence stuck. Five years at Rahway State. By the time he got out, lung cancer eating him from inside out."

My fingers traced the pattern of my ribs through skin.

"I went after them. Should've known better than to think one guy could take down an organization like that. But I tried anyway." The memory came sharp as broken glass—Newark Bay at midnight, the cold water closing over my head, the weight of failure dragging me under until Grimjaw pulled me back. "They caught me. Broke every bone in both hands. Left me in a drainage ditch by County General with a message taped to my chest: *Next time, we don't miss.*

"That was two months ago. Danny has maybe six left. Maybe eight if we're lucky."

I stepped closer to the mirror, studying the face looking back at me. This wasn't cowardice wearing courage's mask. This was something else entirely. Something that had calcified in the darkest parts of my chest long before tonight.

"A sliver of justice isn't enough," I continued, talking more to myself now than to Grimjaw. "It won't scrape the black iron out of Danny's lungs. It won't bring back the twelve other guys who died waiting for appeals. Won't return the twenty million they stole from pension funds or stop them from flooding the streets with product that turns kids into husks before they hit eighteen."

The fluorescent lights seemed brighter somehow, burning holes through my retinas.

"But it's better than no justice at all. And it'll keep him breathing. That's all that matters."

"Cole..."

"The crates contain enough raw material for three operations. Maybe four if they're careful. They want you to deliver them because they know you'll come after me eventually. Gives them leverage. Insurance policy." I buttoned my shirt back up, one slow button at a time. "So here's what you do: you deliver like they asked. Then you disappear. Go south. Florida, maybe. Someplace warm where their reach doesn't extend."

"You think I'd—"

"I know you will. Because you're smart and you're loyal and you've got a daughter who needs her father alive." My reflection had gone still as stone in the mirror. "This is my choice, Grim. Mine alone. Don't make it harder by trying to talk me off it."

Silence stretched between us except for static and breathing.

Finally: "What happens to you? After?"

"Lead poisoning. Bismuth toxicity. Frost-cobalt magic eating away at whatever's left when the Geas burns out

* * *

The steel beneath my spine feels like I'm lying on ice. It's actual ice, I realize after a second—they've frozen the entire operating table to numb me just enough without knocking me unconscious.

Can't pass out for this. Won't.

Four leather straps bite into my wrists and ankles, pulling taut as the dwarf surgeon—I refuse to look at his name tag, refuse to give these motherfuckers any piece of me beyond what they're about to carve out—tightens each one with mechanical precision. His hands are steady despite their tremor, despite the way he can't quite hide the pity in his eyes before the mask goes on.

"Bite down," he says, shoving a thick leather strap between my teeth. "When the Lead-Bismuth hits your marrow, your magic is gonna fight back. Don't let it, or you'll stroke out on the table."

I taste rubber and old blood.

The overhead lights burn white-hot through my closed eyelids. Somewhere in the clinic—a converted meat-packing facility if the rust-streaked floor drains are anything to go by—the machinery hums like dying gods. 1980s trauma monitors beep an erratic rhythm that makes my teeth hurt through the leather gag.

*Beep-beep-beep.*

They're watching my vitals. Making sure I don't die before they finish whatever fresh hell they've got planned.

An elf with fingers too long and graceful for this work approaches with a stainless steel tray. The smell hits me first—iodine so strong it makes my eyes water, mixed with something else. Something metallic and wrong. Copper-sulfate stench layered over burning sugar.

"Iron-gall residue from the casting," the elf says conversationally, noticing my reaction. Her voice carries that musical lilt all her kind have, but there's no warmth in it. Just professional detachment. "It burns when we apply it directly to bone. Standard procedure for embedding geas-work deeper than subcutaneous."

She begins painting my sternum with the solution. It feels like someone dragging broken glass across my skin even through the cold. Blue-black fluorescence spreads across my chest in spreading circles of light, making the hollow of my throat glow like a damned nightlight.

My frost-cobalt magic stirs in response. Cold pressure builds behind my ribs, instinctive defense mechanism screaming at me to lash out, to freeze these bastards where they stand.

*No.* I clamp down on the feeling, bite harder into the leather strap until my jaw aches.

The dwarf surgeon powers up the bone saw. That whining scream cuts through everything else—that specific sound of grinding metal against diamond-coated edge, the same one I heard three years ago when I had to amputate my own fingers after that job in Paterson went sideways.

He positions the saw blade just above my sternum. Through the fluorescent glow of the arcane iodine, I can see the compliance runes etched into the metal, each one a tiny prison cell waiting to be burned into my bones.

"Deep breath in," the surgeon instructs. "Let it out slow."

I do. The air tastes like rust and ozone.

"Here we go, kid. This is gonna hurt worse than anything you ever felt."

* * *

The bone saw sings its horrible song—a high-pitched whine that cuts through flesh and bone like butter. I don't scream. Not yet.

My vision whites out.

The first incision burns cold as liquid nitrogen. My body convulses against the leather restraints bolted to this stainless-steel table. Below me, tiles of white ceramic stretch into infinity under the merciless glare of surgical lamps. I smell antiseptic. Burnt hair. Iron.

Then the pain hits—not as a wave but as an explosion.

*SNAP*

Something gives way beneath my ribs.

"HOLD HIM!" A woman's voice, harsh with strain. Footsteps. Hands pressing down on my shoulders, my hips, pinning me to the table as my back arches involuntarily. "Cut deeper! We need access to the aorta!"

The saw bites again. Deeper now. I taste copper. Salt. The copper of my own blood mixed with the salt of sweat pouring from every pore. My teeth clench so hard I feel something crack in my jaw.

White light behind my eyelids. Consciousness fraying at the edges like burnt paper.

"Clear the field—GODDAMMIT, CLEAR IT!"

Something cold splashes across my chest. Ice water. It should shock me awake. Instead it just adds another layer to the agony—the sharp sting of frozen needles sinking into already-flayed skin.

I open my eyes.

Three figures loom over me, faces obscured by surgical masks and magnifying goggles. One holds the bone saw—still running, still dripping red. Another has forceps. The third, smaller figure with elven features that even the mask can't hide, cradles something metallic and ticking.

The Lead-Bismuth Geas Coil.

It's beautiful in a grotesque way—a spiral of leaden metal veins threaded through blocks of solidified bismuth, all wound around a central mechanism that pulses with sickly amber light. Each tick reverberates through my sternum where the bone saw has carved its path of destruction.

"No sedation?" I gasp the words between shallow breaths. "Thought you wanted me... conscious."

"We do." The elf doesn't look up from her work. Her fingers dance across the Geas surface, tracing arcane sigils that glow hot-pink against the grey metal. "Can't bind the magic if the host is dreaming. Needs to know what's being taken from him."

The surgeon with the saw leans closer. "Last chance for prayer or whatever bullshit you believe in, machinist."

My frost-cobalt blood-iron magic stirs in response to the threat—that ancient gift passed down from some forgotten ancestor who made a deal with powers that shouldn't exist. It coils in my core like a sleeping serpent, cold and patient and waiting.

"Don't..." The word comes out strangled as they spread my chest cavity wider. Ribs crack. Something wet sloshes inside me. "Don't touch it..."

Too late.

The elf lowers the Geas Coil directly into the opening.

The moment metal touches flesh, my magic EXPLODES.

Frost-cobalt energy erupts from my chest—crystalline ice formations shooting outward, freezing the blood pooling on my sternum, turning it to crimson glass that shatters under the surgical lamps' heat. The temperature plummets. Frost spreads across the table legs. The monitors behind us crack, their screens going white then black.

*SNAP SNAP*

Two leather restraints burst apart, frozen solid.

"AHHHHH—!"

I thrash upward, breaking one more restraint with my shoulder, but three hands slam me back down. The pain of the impact sends fresh agony through my body—my shattered ribs grinding together, muscles tearing at their attachments.

"The binding!" The elf's voice cuts through my screaming. "Force it! NOW!"

"What are you doing to ME?!" I choke the words out between gasps as the elf presses her palm flat against my chest, right where the Geas Coil sits nestled in my exposed heart tissue. Her skin glows faintly blue—the telltale sign of flesh-weaver magic, that old-world art of manipulating living matter like clay.

She begins to chant in a language predating English by centuries. Each syllable makes my flesh crawl, makes the frost-cobalt magic writhe and rebel against this violation.

"NO—get it OUT—GET IT—"

Her fingers dig into my chest cavity. I feel something tear—something vital—and then there's pressure. Overwhelming pressure. My heart stutters. Skips a beat. Stutters again.

The Lead-Bismuth Geas pulses in time with Danny's Iron-Lung now—I can hear it somehow, the synchronization clicking into place like tumblers in a lock. *Thump-hiss. Thump-hiss.* 

"No no NO—"

"Hold him STRAIGHT! Don't let him throw the alignment!"

They're wiring it directly into my myocardial tissue. I can feel each thread of arcane binding sink into muscle fiber, wrapping around arteries, embedding itself in the electrical pathways that control every heartbeat. My body bucks violently, muscles spasming beyond my control.

Frost-cobalt energy surges one final time—a desperate, dying gasp from deep within—but it's not enough. The elf's magic is stronger than mine here, in this space where metal meets flesh, where life force is bent to serve.

*THUD*

A heavy, wet impact that echoes through my skull like a headstone being dropped on a coffin. The fusion completes.

Everything goes black.

---

I wake to silence.

Not peaceful silence but the absence of sound—the kind that presses against your eardrums until you think they'll burst. A recovery cot. White sheets rough as sandpaper under my palms. Fluorescent lights overhead casting everything in harsh grey illumination.

My chest...

I touch it cautiously. Feel the thick, raised scar running vertical down my sternum, still tender despite whatever healing accelerants they pumped into me while I was unconscious. The skin beneath feels wrong—not just sore but *foreign*. Like there's something living inside that shouldn't be there.

Beneath my palm: two heartbeats.

One organic and familiar—the steady thrum-thrum of my own pulse. But underneath it, slightly offbeat:

*Thump-hiss.*

Mechanical. Regular as clockwork. Ticking out Danny's breaths on his Iron-Lung.

The Geas is wired to him now. As long as Cole Reyes obeys, Danny breathes.

As long as Cole disobeys—

I don't finish the thought.

My eyes shift color without conscious effort—frost-cobalt bleeding away the warm brown until my reflection in the nearest monitor shows dead-silent irises that could freeze fire itself.

The Syndicate didn't just bind me to them.

They created their greatest monster.

---

## CHAPTER 6: FROST-COBALT ON THE GLASS

The Crown Vic's door clunks shut behind me like a coffin lid. Sodium vapor turns everything orange—building facades, the puddles on cracked asphalt, Grimjaw's scarred face as he checks his load. My breath clouds white in air that shouldn't be this cold for Newark in February.

My palm finds the vault door's surface. Durasteel, supposed to be impervious. I feel it already—the familiar burn-rush of blood-iron flooding my veins, the taste of copper and ozone coating my tongue. The metal beneath my hand screams silent warnings.

Frost-cobalt spreads from my touch point. Not ice. Something colder. Something that remembers what absolute zero *feels* like when matter stops moving entirely. Blue-black crystalline patterns race across the reinforced steel, each fractal branching with mathematical precision. The locking mechanisms inside freeze first—not frozen solid, but *beyond* solid into something else. Something brittle.

Grimjaw's pack fans out behind me, their weapons ready. The younger ones tense, watching my hand work its dark magic. They've seen it before, but they never get used to how the temperature drops ten degrees just being near me. How the frost-cobalt leaves those spreading veins of impossible cold that make normal ice look like fire.

"Vault's popped, boss." Grimjaw keeps his voice low, that South Side rasp barely above a whisper. "Two minutes before High-Spire response teams ping the perimeter."

I don't answer. Can't. My focus narrows down to the molecular structure of durasteel, to the precise temperature at which its crystalline lattice will shatter rather than bend. One degree too warm and it holds. One degree too cold and the entire door becomes powder.

The deadbolt freezes. 

I kick.

The door explodes inward with a sound like a freight train hitting a wall. Chunks of durasteel—each piece still bearing those terrifying blue-black crystalline veins—tumble into darkness beyond. Alarms start screaming somewhere in the building's guts, but we're already past them.

"That's our window," I say, voice flat. Dead-eyed. "Jax?"

A suppressed cough-echo from the rooftop position where our Razor-Wire Street-Elf sniper painted the perimeter guards. Clean shots through optical-camo, bodies dropping without enough time for screams. Professional.

The vault yawns open before us, darkness within. Grimjaw's pack moves forward with practiced efficiency, flashlights cutting through blackness. I follow, my bare hands still trailing those faint wisps of frost-cobalt mist.

We're expecting cash. Sterling-Voss logistics means product movement, and product means money changing hands. Easy score. Simple breach.

The first guard appears around a corner twenty feet inside. His eyes widen when he sees me—not Grimjaw or the pack, but *me*. Sees the way the air frosts around my shoulders. The blue-black sheen on my knuckles.

His gun comes up anyway. Brave bastard.

He never gets off a shot.

The vault opens not to stacks of currency or sealed crates of contraband, but to muzzle flashes. Automatic weapons fire stutters out of the darkness ahead, a full squad's worth. Sterling-Voss corporate security, all tactical gear and cold-blooded professionalism. They've been waiting.

"AMBUSH!" someone shouts.

Grimjaw drops behind cover, his MP5 already returning fire. The young enforcers scatter like leaves in a hurricane. My hand comes up instinctively, frost-cobalt erupting from my palm in a shielding arc—

* * *

The temperature drops when I move through the corridor, my breath crystallizing in clouds that taste like pennies and rust. The frost-cobalt state settles over me like a second skin, every nerve ending singing with metallic resonance. My Lead-Bismuth Geas Coil pulses hot against my sternum—that damned Syndicate brandmark thrumming with Danny's vitals, reminding me why I'm here. Why I've become this.

Grimjaw takes point, his Ogre-Kin frame blocking most of the hallway as we breach into the logistics hub's main server farm. Behind him, two more union breakers fan out, their MP5s already up and tracking. The ambient lighting cast everything in sickly red emergency mode, turning blood to black oil on the linoleum.

"Movement at three o'clock," one of the breakers hisses.

I don't respond. Can't afford to split focus. My attention fractures across multiple planes—the physical space before me, the iron signatures embedded in the walls' rebar, the ghost-signal of Danny's consciousness feeding back through the geas coil. He's stable. For now.

The first corporate guard rounds the corner and Grimjaw's MP5 coughs twice. Center mass. The man goes down hard, but he's already screaming into his shoulder-mic, words garbled by copper-wire static.

"—red team compromised, northeast sector—"

Grimjaw's boot comes down on the mic with a wet crunch. "Cancel the cab, suit. You're staying local."

More guards pour around the corner. Four, maybe five. Their tactical armor gleams under the red lights—I can see the iron mesh woven through the Kevlar panels, designed to stop bullets and blades. They don't know about what I do.

My right hand sweeps out in an arc, fingers trailing frost-cobalt residue that hangs in the air like deadly calligraphy. The Lead-Bismuth Geas Coil flares and my blood-iron hexes lock into place.

The nearest guard's eyes widen behind his visor as I pull.

It happens fast—too fast for screams. I yank the metallic threads from his armor's weave, from the rivets holding his plates together, from the steel-toed boots on his feet. All of it responding to my will, drawn out like taffy until the melting point, then beyond. The iron doesn't just separate; it crystallizes into razor-sharp shrapnel that erupts from inside his armor in a cloud of freezing metal fragments.

He disassembles from within.

His companions open fire, their MP5s stuttering death in the enclosed space—the reports deafening, muffled, absolute. Bullets ping off concrete, tear through server racks, punch holes in drywall. Grimjaw and his Ogre-Kin brothers form a phalanx, their bodies absorbing the incoming fire while they return devastating bursts of their own.

I'm already gone, moving through the chaos like smoke. My footfalls leave frost patterns on the floor. Another guard turns toward me, muzzle flash illuminating his terrified face, and I'm there before he can adjust his aim.

My forearm slams across his throat—not hard enough to kill, just enough to crush his windpipe and drop him. As he falls, choking and clawing at his neck, I plant my palm against his chest plate where the iron mesh sits beneath Kevlar. The frost-cobalt state surges through my hand.

Ice spreads across his armor in crystalline fractals. Then the iron mesh itself begins to freeze, expanding as it solidifies, cracking apart under the stress. The sound is like breaking glass multiplied by dozens—tink-tink-TINK—before the whole panel shatters inward with a wet crunch. Blue-black iron-gall residue sprays across the linoleum, sizzling where it hits.

The dying man's scream cuts off mid-gasp.

More shots. More shouting. The Nextel pager vibrates rhythmically against my hip—Danny's heart rate, steady and strong. That focus becomes my anchor as the firefight spirals into controlled chaos around me. Grimjaw's voice booms commands that I don't hear. The breakers are singing in their guttural tongue, probably praying to whatever gods listen to hired guns and muscle-for-hire.

Two more guards down. Their armor twisted into fatal shrapnel clouds. The air reeks of gunpowder and ozone and blood.

Then silence. Sudden and complete except for the crackle of cooling metal and someone's death rattle.

I approach the primary objective—a secure server rack, its locked doors hanging open on broken hinges. Someone's already been here. Recent. The access lights still blinking amber.

Grimjaw joins me, breathing hard, MP5 slung across his chest. "Status?"

"Wiped." I run my fingers across the server faces. Empty slots. Erased drives. But something catches my eye—a small compartment at the bottom, barely visible behind a loose panel.

Inside: a single data chip sealed in evidence-grade plastic. No label. Just a serial number etched into the casing.

Behind us, the bodies cool in pools of their own blood and blue-black residue. Frost spreads from each corpse like macabre halos.

My Nextel vibrates again. Danny's heart rate hasn't changed.

I pocket the chip and turn toward the exit. Whatever's on this drive is why they wiped the servers. Why they left it behind instead of destroying it with everything else.

The Syndicate will want answers.

And I'll deliver them, same as I delivered death tonight.

Same as I'll deliver it every night until Danny wakes up or the geas coil finally stops pulsing against my sternum.

Which comes first is anyone's guess.

* * *

The server room tastes like copper and ozone.

I stand in the center of what used to be Sterling-Voss Logistics' primary data hub. Now it's just another crime scene I've contaminated. The bodies are already stiffening—not from rigor, but from the frost-cobalt that leaked from my palms ten minutes ago. Each corpse wears a rime of crystalline blue-white ice across their faces, their mouths open in silent screams that never made it past their frozen throats.

The temperature in here must be below zero. My breath comes out in thick, heavy clouds that hang suspended before dissolving into nothing. The air itself feels wrong—too dense, too cold for human lungs. But I don't feel it. Can't feel it. Not anymore.

The geas makes sure of that.

My blood-iron hexes have locked down hard into dead-silent mode. Zero remorse. That's what the Syndicate needs—I can hear it in the binding, a whisper against my skull that drowns out everything else except the mission. *Erase this. Erase them. Leave no trace.*

The server tower itself is encased in a shell of ice, its blinking lights frozen mid-blink beneath half an inch of frost. Whatever data was on those drives is now scrambled beyond recovery—thermal shock does nasty things to electronics, turns silicon chips into brittle glass shards. I made sure of that too. Pulled the heat right out of every component, every cable, every fucking transistor.

The room looks like something pulled straight from a morgue freezer.

"Cole."

Jax drops from the ceiling rafters with a soft *thud*, his boots crunching on the frozen floor. He's wearing thermo-optic gear—expensive shit that should keep him warm—but even through that I can see him shaking. His breath plumes just as hard as mine.

"Spire-blood cops are two blocks out," he says, voice tight. "We gotta bounce. It's too damn cold in here anyway."

I don't blink. Don't turn. Just stare at the frozen corpses, at the blood pooled beneath them now solidified into black-red glass shards that crack and tinkle when I shift my weight.

"Let them come," I say. My voice sounds hollow, distant even to me. The geas makes it easy—not to be cold, but not to care about being cold. "They'll only find ice."

Jax's eyes dart around the room, taking in what I've done. The ice coating every surface. The way the temperature dropped so fast the air crystallized. This is what they're calling me now behind closed doors: the Syndicate's Butcher. The cleaner who doesn't just erase evidence—he erases everything. Makes scenes so sterile, so impossibly cold, that forensic teams have nothing to work with except frozen bodies and shattered electronics.

He swallows hard, then nods toward the exit. "Still gotta check for anything we missed before—"

That's when I see it.

Tucked into the server rack's ventilation grate, half-hidden beneath a frozen cable bundle. A small package, maybe six inches square, wrapped in black thermal paper. Not frozen. Somehow untouched by the frost-cobalt wave I unleashed across this entire fucking room.

My hexes scream warnings—I can feel the arcane signature from here. Whatever's in that package isn't supposed to exist. Not in this place. Not after what I did to everything else.

"Cole?" Jax follows my gaze. His hand instinctively goes to his sidearm—a gesture as useless as everything else right now.

---

## CHAPTER 7: THE WATCHING PARTY DEAD-DROP

The sky bleeds rust-orange over Newark Bay as I pull the Crown Vic into the chop-shop's yard. Ice crystals cling to my coat sleeves, melting slow in the pre-dawn heat radiating off Bram Kovacs' work bay. The dwarven machinist doesn't even look up from his welding rig, but I can feel his eyes tracking me anyway—he always knows when something's wrong.

Which means everything's wrong.

"Kid's stable," Bram grunts before I can ask. His welding mask flips up, revealing a face scored with oil stains and something harder—concern. "Telluric core's pulling clean energy from the ley lines. Better than anything we had in the old country."

I don't respond. My boots crunch on broken glass as I pass through the main bay, past rows of stripped ambulances and police interceptors waiting for their illicit modifications. The smell hits me next—ozone burning sharp in my lungs, mixing with machine oil and that sterile antiseptic scent that never quite leaves medical equipment.

Danny's room sits in the back, separated by a chain-link curtain that rattles in the draft. The Arcane Iron-Lung dominates the space like some brass cathedral organ built inside a coffin. Danny's small body lies suspended in the glass chamber, tubes running from the Telluric Core Compressor—a Syndicate device I stole from Sub-Station Seven—pulsing with amber light through his black-iron lungs.

*Whoosh-click. Whoosh-click.*

The rhythm is steady now. Regular.

I press my palm against the warm glass. Frost-cobalt energy recoils at the heat, retreating down my arm, and for just a second I let the hearth-coal warmth seep into my bones. Danny's pale face floats in the amber glow, his chest rising and falling beneath the mechanical bellows' patient rhythm.

"The price is mine to pay, Bram," I say without turning around. "Just keep him breathing."

Behind me, metal clangs against concrete. The welding torch sputters out.

"Julian Sterling's name came up in the server logs," Bram says quietly. "Before you ask. Before you do what I know you're gonna do."

My reflection stares back at me in the glass. Dark eyes. Hollowed out. Old beyond my thirty-two years.

"I know."

I leave them there as dawn fully breaks over the South Side, casting long shadows across the chop-shop's yard. My Crown Vic waits at the curb, engine ticking as it cools. Inside the passenger footwell, wrapped in oil-stained canvas, sits the dead-drop package I pulled from Sub-Station Seven's server rack during last night's raid.

I haven't opened it yet.

But I will.

Because Julian Sterling has been watching. Waiting. And now the Watching Party wants something from me that goes deeper than simple revenge. The kind of debt that costs more than blood.

I rip open the canvas wrapping with frozen fingers.

Inside: blueprints. Maps. And a photograph of a man I thought was already dead.

* * *

The Crown Vic's engine rumbles beneath my ass, a steady *thrum-thrum-thrum* that vibrates through the driver's seat into my bones. Heat blasts from the vents, fighting off the winter pre-dawn chill that clings to Neon Hollow like a dying breath. I killed the headlights an hour ago—don't need any Spire-patrol cruisers curious about why a South Side machinist is parked outside Bram Kovacs' chop-shop at 0530 on a Tuesday.

The package sits on the passenger seat beside me, wrapped in oil-tanned leather that smells like saddle-work and copper wire twisted tight as a tourniquet around the whole mess. My tactical knife lies across my lap, matte-black blade still wet with machine oil from picking the lock on Sub-Station Seven last night. The blade catches what little ambient light seeps through the windshield—streetlamps struggling against the coming dawn, their halos bleeding orange through the perpetual smog that hangs over the Under-City like a cheap shroud.

I reach for the package.

The leather feels wrong under my fingers. Too warm for something sitting in a dead-drop box overnight. Warm, and faintly vibrating. Telluric residue, maybe. Or worse—the kind of arcane static that makes your teeth ache if you hold it too long.

*SNIK.*

The copper wire parts clean where the knife bites. Two pieces of wire drop onto the seat, already coiling back on themselves like they want to spring closed again. I shake off the thought. Just metal. Just physics. But even as I think it, my fingers tingle with frost-cobalt energy that won't quite dissipate from last night's work in the Kearny Marshes.

Inside the leather wrap: vellum. Heavy as bible pages, sealed shut with wax so black it seems to drink the light instead of reflect it.

An eye. Surrounded by thorns. The seal presses cold into my palm when I lift the packet, and not just winter-cold. This is *dead* cold. The kind of cold that comes from places deep underground or from things that have forgotten how to be alive.

"Watching Party."

Grimjaw's voice rumbles from outside the passenger window. Didn't hear him approach over the engine noise. His yellow eyes are wide behind the cracked safety glasses he wears to keep the grease out of his vision. The Orc leans against the door, his massive frame casting a shadow across the interior dashboard lights.

"The fuck you talking about?" I ask, though I know damn well what he means. Everyone knows the stories. Street-runners whisper about them around late-night oil fires. Spire-bloods who venture too far South come back telling tales of shadows with eyes, ghosts that see through walls and remember names of people who've been dead for generations.

"Thought they were just bedtime stories," Grimjaw says, his gaze locked on the seal in my hand. "Something to scare the kids away from the Pulaski Skyway after dark." He taps the glass with one thick finger—tap-tap-TAP. "But if they're real enough to leave *you* a package..." He trails off, meaning clear: then we're all in deeper shit than we thought.

I run my thumb over the wax seal. The eye stares back at me, unblinking. The thorns twist like living things under my touch, but when I pull my hand away, there's no residue. No warmth where the cold should be melting. Just that same tombstone chill that makes my breath fog inside the car despite the heat running full blast.

"They're real," I say. "And they left this for me."

The question is why. And more importantly: what price am I going to have to pay for whatever comes next?

* * *

The ledger paper crinkles under my fingers as I spread it across the Malibu's dashboard, the overhead light cutting through pre-dawn darkness. My breath fogs the interior in rhythmic pulses—I haven't noticed the cold biting at my lungs until now.

Numbers. Rows upon rows of them, printed in that precise bank font that screams legitimacy wrapped around illegitimacy. Routing codes from places that don't show up on maps unless you're looking for trouble. Cayman Islands. Panama. Liechtenstein. Each one stamped with dates from '99 and early 2000, right when the Sludge was hitting hard.

And the sums. Jesus Christ, *the sums*. Seven figures. Eight figures. Money that could buy politicians, build armies, poison entire city blocks.

At the top of the page, written in script so elegant it might as well be calligraphy, is a name that turns my blood to ice before any Telluric current ever could:

**Julian Sterling.**

The name sits there like a brand. Like an accusation. Like a goddamn death sentence.

My vision tunnels. The frost-cobalt doesn't wait for conscious thought—it just *happens*, spreading across the inside of the windshield in crystalline fractals, spiderwebbing from the spot where my hand touches the glass. The metal dashboard beneath the ledger begins to weep condensation, tiny droplets freezing into pinpricks of ice.

"Fuck," I whisper, but it comes out wrong, strangled by the constriction in my throat.

Danny died because of this man. Elena burned because of this man. How many others? How many names are buried under this ledger, under these routing numbers that trace back to the architects of the Flush?

I snatch the paper, nearly tearing it in my grip, and stalk toward Grimjaw's position by the chop-shop entrance. He's leaning against the concrete wall, his massive frame somehow making even exhaustion look dangerous.

"Grimjaw." My voice is flat, dead. "Wake the kid up."

He blinks slowly, those predatory eyes focusing on me with reluctance. "Cole, he needs his rest. You saw what happened in there—"

"I need to know what these connect to." I shove the ledger at him. "And the encryption on that MiniDisc"—I pull the iridescent disc from my jacket pocket, holding it between two fingers like it might bite—"is beyond anything I can crack."

"Still doesn't mean—"

"My eyes are dead, Grimjaw. Devoid of warmth." I step closer, close enough to smell the machine oil clinging to his fur. "We all do. Starting now."

He studies me for a long moment, then sighs—a sound like rocks grinding together. "You're going to get him killed, Cole."

"Maybe." I don't look away. "But not today."

The watchman-turned-bouncer shuffles toward where Danny's slumped against a stack of tires, still unconscious but breathing steady. Grimjaw kneels down, gently shaking the kid's shoulder.

"Danny. Hey, kid. Time to work."

No response.

"Danny, come on. Cole found something you need to see."

A groan. Then movement as consciousness drags the hacker back from wherever his mind had fled during the Telluric feedback. Danny's eyes flutter open, unfocused, pupils dilated.

"What... what happened?" His voice is thin, cracked.

"You burned through three layers of security that should've taken a mainframe team six months," Grimjaw says gruffly. "Now you gotta wake up and break some bank encryption."

"That's—that's not how it works—" Danny tries to sit up, winces, catches sight of me standing over them both with the MiniDisc held between my fingers like an offering to vengeful gods.

He sees the expression on my face.

"What did you find?"

I walk past them into the chop-shop proper, the smell of ozone still sharp in the air despite hours passing since the breach. The lights Bram installed are harsh, fluorescent, cutting through shadows that seem to cling around the machinery anyway.

"Julian Sterling," I say without looking at either of them. My voice echoes off the concrete walls. "Head #1. Architect of the Flush. And this"—I turn, holding up the ledger—"is how he paid for it."

Grimjaw helps Danny to his feet, the kid wobbling but standing. They follow me deeper into the space where Bram's body was just hours ago, where the bloodstains still darken the floor.

Danny takes the ledger with trembling hands. His eyes scan down the columns, widening with each number. "Jesus... Cole, these routing numbers..."

"I know what they mean." My jaw is tight enough to crack teeth. "What I need to know is *where* they go. What accounts they're tied to. Who else signed off on these transfers."

"The MiniDisc?" Danny's gaze shifts to the iridescent surface I'm still holding. "That might have the decryption keys, but the coding..."

"It's beyond you?"

"No." He shakes his head quickly, then immediately regrets the motion, grimacing. "No, I can break it. Just... give me time. Give me access to a real terminal."

"How much time?"

His answer comes after a long pause, watching those numbers like they hold secrets to the universe itself. "Forty-eight hours. Maybe less if I can piggyback through some unsecured networks." Another pause. "Assuming nobody traces my access and tries to kill me again."

"Fair assumption." I pocket the MiniDisc carefully, almost reverently. "You get me everything on this disc—every transaction, every signature authorization, every goddamn detail—and I'll keep the death attempts to a minimum."

"Real encouraging," Grimjaw mutters.

But Danny's already focused, that technical brilliance burning through whatever pain remains from tonight's work. "I'll need a secure location. Somewhere with redundant connections and physical security."

The chop-shop is out—the heat's too high here now, Bram's death having lit up every alarm in Sterling's organization. Sub-Station Seven would be suicide with all three of us there. The docks are too exposed.

Then it hits me: Sterling Manor. Julian's own fortress. And within it, a ghost.

"I know a place."

---

## CHAPTER 8: THE IRON-LUNG HACKER

The cylinder looms before me like something torn from Verne's fever dreams—a brass-and-glass monstrosity that shouldn't exist outside of Victorian illustrations, yet here it sits in Bram Kovacs' cluttered workshop, humming with impossible energy. Steam vents through ornate copper pipes along its curved surface, condensation dripping in rhythmic patterns that echo the beat of my own heart.

Inside, suspended in the amber glow of the Telluric core, sits my son.

Danny's fifteen now, though he looks smaller—wasted thin by whatever poison still courses through his blood. The specialized mask covers half his face, tubes snaking back into the cylinder's apparatus. But his eyes... those are still his mother's eyes, dark and sharp and defiant as hellfire.

"Got it," I say, holding up the MiniDisc case between thumb and forefinger. The plastic is scuffed, probably dropped in some gutter during one of my midnight runs. Don't matter. Inside this Sony 74-minute jewel is more than stolen data—it's leverage against Sterling-Voss.

I slide open the maintenance hatch Bram welded onto the cylinder's side last month. The mechanism *clicks*, and compressed air whistles out in relief. Through the thick glass panel mounted on the interior wall, I can see the ThinkPad already booting up, its green power LED blinking steady as a heartbeat.

"Careful, Pops." Danny's voice crackles through the speaker system Bram installed. "Don't want you contaminating my sterile environment."

I can't help the smile that tugs at my lips. There's my boy—the same smart-ass who once tried to reprogram our VCR to order pizza.

The ThinkPad's keyboard sits recessed in a custom mount, wired directly into the external Sony drive unit. I feed the MiniDisc into the slot, feeling the satisfying *whirr* of motors engaging, the gentle *clunk* as the disc locks into place. The display flickers to life, showing directory listings in a cascade of green-on-black text.

Danny's fingers dance across the chunky rubber keys with surprising speed—those pale, thin digits moving like he's playing a concerto. The *clack-clack-clack* echoes inside the brass chamber, syncopated with his labored breathing.

"Encryption is heavy, Dad. High-Spire corporate grade. Sterling-Voss proprietary." His voice is muffled through the mask but clear enough. "This isn't some small-time operator shit."

I lean closer to the glass, close enough to see my own reflection ghosting beside his face. "Can you crack it, Dan?"

His head tilts, and there—just for a second—that ghost of Elena's smile crosses his features. "Give me ten minutes and a direct line to the Undercity trunk."

My hand goes to the leather satchel at my hip. Inside: a stolen SIM card from a Verizon payphone in Kearny, still warm from its extraction. "You'll have both."

He doesn't look up from the screen as his fingers continue their furious dance. Numbers scroll past faster than any human eye should track. The amber light from the Telluric core casts everything in shades of rust and blood.

"Tell me what you're seeing," I say.

"The usual bullshit." *Clack-clack-clack.* "Financial records encrypted under three layers of public-key infrastructure. But here..." A new window opens on his display, lines of code cascading downward. "Here's something interesting. Packet headers stamped with Port Newark timestamps. They're routing traffic through the container yards."

The Kearny Marshes flash through my mind—the way fog clings to those industrial waterways after dark, how easy it is to lose someone among the stacks of shipping containers. "Smuggling routes?"

"Or dead drops. Hard to say without decrypting the payload." He pauses, one finger hovering over the keyboard. "Dad... this encryption protocol. I've seen it before. In Sterling-Voss corporate documentation that got leaked last year."

I feel the weight settle deeper into my bones. "What kind of documentation?"

"The kind that deals with asset management." His eyes finally lift to meet mine through the glass. "Human assets."

My fist tightens around nothing. The workshop suddenly feels too small, the cylinder too transparent. Every breath Danny takes sounds amplified, mechanical—like he's breathing through a straw at the bottom of some black ocean.

"I need you to be careful," I hear myself saying.

Danny laughs, that wet, metallic rattle of a cough following immediately after. "Too late for careful, Pops. Been living in an iron lung since I was twelve. This is just... another level."

He turns back to the screen, and I watch his reflection fragment across the curved glass panels. Outside Bram's shop, the winter sun barely penetrates the grimy windows. Somewhere past the rust-stained brick walls, Newark is waking up—a city of ghosts and monsters that don't know they're myths.

The MiniDisc drive *whirs* louder, spinning faster as it processes data streams I can't begin to understand. Green text scrolls upward like some digital waterfall.

Then everything stops.

The display flashes red. Error messages cascade downward in rapid succession—hexadecimal strings that might as well be ancient runes.

"Shit." Danny slams his palm against the ThinkPad's trackpoint. "Firewall. It's trying to wipe the drive."

"What do you need?" I'm already moving toward where Bram keeps his tool kits, toward anything that might help.

"A miracle." He's typing now, fingers flying desperate patterns across the keys. "Or someone who knows Sterling-Voss's internal network structure better than their own goddamn IT department."

I stop mid-step. There's only one person I know who fits that description—and she wants nothing to do with me anymore.

"Fuck," I breathe.

Danny looks up again, and this time there's no smile. Just fear, raw and honest and so much like his mother when she knew we were about to lose something we couldn't afford to lose.

"I need backup, Dad. Real backup. The kind that doesn't come from stolen payphone SIM cards."

My hand goes to my phone. The number hasn't changed since I last used it—not that she ever answered anyway.

The firewall's countdown appears on-screen: **00:02:47**.

"Hold on, Dan," I say, though whether to him or to myself, I'm not sure anymore.

* * *

The Nextel pager squats between Danny's fingers like some chrome insect. He hits the push-to-talk button.

*CHIRRRRP.*

The sound echoes through the confines of the Iron-Lung, all brass pipes and glass chambers. It's too loud in here. Everything is too loud.

"Fizz," Danny says into the crackling void. His voice sounds smaller than fifteen should be allowed to sound. "It's me. Danny."

Static. Then: *"Kid? Jesus Christ, is that you? Thought you were—"* The voice cuts out, replaced by white noise that makes my teeth ache even from where I'm standing outside the chamber.

Danny jiggles the antenna—an old-school trick he picked up somewhere between his hospital bed and whatever digital hellhole he crawls into these nights. The connection snaps back.

"It's me," he repeats. "Dad needs the Gnome. Can you get on this?"

More static. Then: *"Fuck me sideways, kid. You know what time it is? Your old man owes me big for this one. BIG."*
*"He knows."*

I watch through the glass panel as Danny's fingers find the ThinkPad keyboard. The green phosphor glow illuminates his face, casts shadows under his eyes that shouldn't exist on someone his age. The laptop fan whirs—that same death-rattle sound of stressed silicon we heard last summer when we pulled those Sterling-Voss server logs.

"Alright, alright," Fizz's voice comes through clearer now, layered with urgency. *"Listen good. We're going ghost-routing through Sterling-Voss infrastructure. Their ICE is industrial-grade shit, kid. One wrong move and they'll trace this back before you can say 'motherfucker'."*

"I can handle it," Danny says.

*"Can you? Last time we tried this, you crashed three BATC satellites and nearly fried my whole rig. Remember?"*

The smell hits me then—the acrid tang of overheating electronics mixed with antiseptic and rust. The Iron-Lung pumps its steady rhythm, each compression making the thinkpad screen flicker.

Danny's typing already, code scrolling past faster than I can read. Those fingers moving like they've got their own minds.

*"Okay, okay—I'm in,"* Fizz chatters rapidly over the speaker. *"Bouncing your signal off the Kearny Marshes repeater. Hold on while I crack the first layer..."* Click-click-click-clack from Danny's side. *"Got it. Jesus, look at this firewall. This is some serious corporate-grade bullshit."*

"My dad said you owe him."

*"Don't remind me."*
*"He said it was for Millie."*

Long pause. Just static and the hum of the Iron-Lung.

*"Fuck."* The word comes out different somehow—softer. More resigned. *"Alright kid. Alright. Let's do this. You see that proxy list I sent you? The one with all the shell accounts?"*

"Yeah."

*"You're gonna want to hit the Cayman one first. It's got the weakest encryption. We bounce through there, maybe we can slip under their radar."*

I press closer to the glass. Watching my son—no, my kid, Christ, he's just a kid—type with fingers that know more about the digital world than most adults twice his age will ever learn. His face is illuminated by green text cascading down black screens. He looks like something out of a fever dream. Too young. Too knowledgeable.

The smell intensifies. Copper burning now mixed with melting plastic.

*"Kid, they're onto us!"* Fizz's voice spikes higher. *"Reroute NOW! Use the dead BATC satellite! The one I showed you last week!"*

Danny doesn't hesitate. His hands blur across the keyboard.

*"Good! Good! Now hit the VPN tunnel!"*

The ThinkPad screen goes white for a second—just a flash—and then:

*"Oh shit. Oh SHIT. They're collapsing the firewall. Danny, get out, get OUT!"*

But he doesn't move. Keeps typing.

*"DANNY!"*

Then the screen erupts in data.

Green text flooding up at impossible speeds. Numbers. Coordinates. Dates. All of it pouring into the machine like someone cracked open a dam. The fan screams. Danny's breath fogs against the inside of his chamber. Outside, the Iron-Lung pumps steady as a heartbeat.

And there on the screen, emerging from the chaos:

**DATE: 02/14/2005**
**GPS: 40.7319° N, 74.1768° W**
**SUBJECT: OPERATION IRON-CHEST**

More coordinates appear below it. A pattern forming.

"Danny." My voice cracks through the speaker system—some engineer's mercy built into this prison. "Get out of there."

He glances up at me. Just for a second. Then back to the screen where more data cascades down into infinity.

*"Fizz?"* he says into the Nextel.

Static answers him.

But the screen keeps filling with truth that Sterling-Voss tried very hard to bury.

* * *

The monitor's glow cut through the pre-dawn darkness like a lighthouse beam through fog—a single point of sterile blue in Kovacs' industrial hell-scape. I stood at the glass partition separating my son's iron lung from the rest of the world, watching the numbers cascade down Danny's screen.

The boy—no, he wasn't a boy anymore, not after what he'd done last night—had his headset on, fingers dancing across a keyboard suspended in a mechanical spider-crash of cables and tubing. The medical equipment hummed its constant mechanical prayer around him, but he was somewhere else entirely. Somewhere in the digital veins of North Jersey's municipal infrastructure.

"Got something," he muttered, not looking up. His voice came muffled through the respirator, tinny and distant.

I leaned forward. "Talk to me."

"The GPS coordinates from that satellite feed... they're cross-referencing with old city records. Public works permits, sewer maintenance logs..." He paused, and even through the glass, I could see his shoulders tense. "Dad, these dates go back to winter '99."

My hand found the edge of the console. The brass fixtures in this room were cold as grave markers, worn smooth by decades of Kovacs hands before mine. "Keep going."

"They match. Every single one." Danny pulled up another window, and suddenly I saw it—a map of the South Side, dotted with red indicators like bleeding wounds on a corpse. Neon Hollow. Kearny Marshes. The access points to Newark Bay. All the places where the Experimental Sludge had been flushed into our water supply five years ago.

"My treatment schedule..." Danny's voice cracked. "It started the week after these dumping dates."

Grimjaw materialized beside me, his massive frame blocking what little light filtered through the chop-shop's skylights. The Orc's tusks gleamed as he stared at the screen, his green skin taking on a sickly pallor under the monitor's glow. A low growl built in his chest, starting deep and resonating up through his throat like an earthquake warning.

"Show me the authorizations," I said quietly.

Danny's fingers flew. Routing numbers appeared on screen—transfers from Sterling-Voss accounts dated January 14th, 1999 through March 2nd, 1999. Each one marked "HAZARD PAYMENT - WASTE DIVISION." And below each entry, a signature: Julian Sterling.

The room seemed to tilt.

"That son of a bitch," Grimjaw rumbled. The words came out wrong, twisted by his non-human vocal cords, but the meaning was clear enough.

I watched those names scroll past. The waste engineer who'd cashed those checks, the foreman who'd signed off on the manifests... they were all ghosts now, but their ledgers survived. Their digital fingerprints burned bright on Danny's monitor.

My hand tightened on the console until my knuckles went white.

Danny looked up through the glass, his eyes finding mine. Behind the respirator mask, behind the tubes and monitors and medical hardware that had kept him alive through five years of Sterling's poison, there was something new in his expression. Not fear anymore. Resolution.

"Dad... it's the flush. These are the payouts for the night I got sick. Julian Sterling signed the checks."

The silence that fell over Kovacs' shop was absolute. Even the machinery seemed to hold its breath. That frost-cobalt feeling started in my boots again, creeping up through my legs, spreading across the concrete floor like a stain.

I turned away from the glass.

"I need the name of the waste engineer who cashed those checks," I said. My voice dropped ten degrees colder than it already was. "And I need it now."

---

## CHAPTER 9: THE SLIVER OF JUSTICE

The Crown Vic idles at the curb, engine ticking as it cools. Through the windshield, the Meat Locker rises like a monument to cold storage—a pre-war brick monstrosity squatting at the edge of the Kearny Marshes where the South Side bleeds into industrial wasteland. No lights. No movement. Just concrete and corrosion under a sky the color of bruised meat.

"You sure about this?" Grimjaw's voice rumbles from the passenger seat, his tusks catching what little light bleeds across the dashboard. He's still wearing his security guard uniform—dark blue polyester, name tag reading "JAVIER"—stained with someone else's blood we'd cleaned off poorly.

"Trenchard works out of here," I say, pulling the folded Sterling-Voss payroll schedule from my jacket pocket. The paper crinkles wetly between my fingers; frost-coal magic always leaves things damp when it settles. "Waste engineer. Handles the off-the-books disposal. The kind that makes bodies disappear."

Grimjaw grunts, cracking his knuckles. His hands are the size of hams, knuckles scarred from decades of factory work before he went full-time muscle-for-hire. "Off-the-books means no witnesses. Means clean."

"Means we go in hard." I kill the ignition. The sudden silence presses against our ears. Out here, away from the city's electric hum, you can hear the marsh breathing—reeds clicking, water lapping, things moving through the darkness that don't belong in any ecology textbook.

The abattoir's main entrance faces the road, but I know better than to use the front door. Always the service entrance, always the blind spot. We circle around back through mud that sucks at our boots, past dumpsters overflowing with guts and bones wrapped in blood-soaked plastic. The smell hits like a physical blow—copper and decay, sweet-rotted meat left too long in summer heat.

A steel door, padlocked. Grimjaw doesn't bother picking it. He just takes two steps back and kicks. The lock shrieks. Metal buckles. The door swings inward on protests of rusty hinges.

Cold washes over us immediately—not natural cold, but the mechanical death-chill of commercial refrigeration. It sinks into bone, settles deep where warmth should live. Our breath fogs. Footsteps echo on concrete, amplified by the warehouse cathedral beyond.

Inside: rows of hanging carcasses, sides of beef suspended from overhead rails, swinging gently in drafts that smell of ammonia and blood. Fluorescent tubes flicker overhead, casting everything in sickly white light punctuated by pools of shadow. The floor is slick with ice and something darker. Meat hooks dangle empty from chains above. This place hasn't processed livestock in years. Now it just stores corpses for Sterling-Voss clients who need problems to vanish.

"Split up?" Grimjaw asks.

I shake my head. "Together. Watch each other's back."

We move between the hanging meat, boots crunching on frozen detritus. My frost-coal magic coils tight in my chest—a familiar weight, like swallowing ice. It wants out. Wants to spread this cold until everything stops moving, until the whole building becomes a tomb.

Then I hear it. Voices. Male. Coming from deeper inside, past the hanging slabs, toward what must be an office or storage area.

Grimjaw nods. His hand goes to the revolver tucked behind his belt—illegal as hell, but effective at close range when you can't risk a rifle shot.

We round a corner stacked high with crates of frozen mystery meat.

And there he is. Marcus Trenchard. Recognizable from the photo Grimjaw lifted from Sterling-Voss security files: mid-forties, wiry build, expensive suit that doesn't match the surroundings, motor oil stains on the cuffs he can't quite get clean. He's standing over a workbench covered in paperwork, arguing with someone on a silver Motorola Razr.

"...should've been disposed three days ago. I don't care if it was a priority shipment—" He pauses, listens. Then: "Fine. I'll handle it myself. Same dump site as last time."

He snaps the phone shut with finality and shoves it in his breast pocket. His hands are shaking slightly—not from cold, but from whatever pressure Sterling's putting on him. Waste engineers don't normally have to personally oversee disposal. That means whatever they're hiding lately is big enough to scare senior management.

I catch Grimjaw's eye. He gives me the signal: *Now.*

He steps out first—a massive silhouette blocking the corridor entrance. Trenchard spins around, eyes going wide.

"Who the—"

Grimjaw's backhand catches him across the jaw with the sound of splitting wood. The Razr flies from Trenchard's pocket, skittering across concrete. Grimjaw stomps down on it. Once. Twice. Metal cracks, plastic shatters into pieces.

Trenchard hits the floor hard, dazed.

That's when the bodyguards come running.

Two elven mercenaries, High-Spire contract muscle based on their customized tactical gear—body armor over designer suits, mag-locked sidearms, comms earpieces. They burst through an office door at the end of the hall, weapons drawn before their brains fully process the situation.

"Hands where we can see them!" the first one barks, accent clipped and proper, like he learned English from BBC dramas instead of South Side streets.

I drop backward off the metal catwalk above—I'd climbed up while Grimjaw distracted Trenchard—and come down hard on the nearest guard. My frost-coal magic erupts instantaneously, flash-freezing his holstered pistol mid-draw. Ice crystals spread across the weapon's frame in a heartbeat, locking it solid.

His eyes go wide. He tries to pull anyway. The gun won't budge.

I slam my tactical baton into his knee. Bone crunches. He goes down screaming, clutching his leg as ice spreads from the frozen weapon to his hand.

The second guard brings his pistol up fast—faster than I expected—so I redirect my magic. Frost explodes outward in a cone, hitting his face mask. Ice crusts over the lenses. He fires blindly, rounds punching holes in hanging meat sacks that explode in showers of blood and tissue.

Grimjaw catches him with a haymaker that sends him sprawling unconscious into the workbench, papers scattering like snow.

"You're dead, street-trash," the kneeling elf gasps through split lips, spitting blood onto concrete. "Sterling will mount your head on a pike outside High-Spire Gate. You understand? Your family, your friends—they'll all—"

I kick him in the jaw.

Teeth crack. His words cut short. He slumps sideways, out cold.

"Sterling is next," I say to his unconscious form anyway.

Trenchard's trying to crawl away, leaving a bloody smear trail toward an emergency exit. Grimjaw steps on

* * *

The door seals behind me with a pneumatic hiss, and immediately the air turns crystalline. My breath plumes in clouds that shouldn't be possible—not yet—but here they are anyway, ghosting out in silver-blue wisps that catch the single swinging bulb above us. That sodium-vapor thing hangs by a chain thick as my thumb, casting long shadows that writhe across the walls like dying things.

Trenchard's already shaking when I step into the light.

The meat locker stinks of ammonia and old blood, but underneath that is something worse—the smell of terror, sharp and metallic. Rows of hanging beef carcasses sway gently on their iron hooks, suspended in the cold dark. They're frozen solid now, coated in a thin layer of frost that wasn't there when we dragged him in twenty minutes ago.

That was before my magic started working.

"Please," he stammers through chattering teeth, head lolling against his shoulder. His expensive charcoal suit—probably cost more than most people on this side make in a year—is already stiff with ice crystals. "I don't know anything! Just... just a logistics manager. Supply chain. That's all."

Grimjaw steps forward from the darkness near the back wall, his bulk making the floorboards groan. The troll's yellow eyes fix on Trenchard with predatory interest, one clawed hand resting on the grip of his rusty hatchet. His tusks catch the light as his lips pull back in something that might be amusement.

"Lie again, suit," Grimjaw rumbles, voice like gravel tumbling down a metal chute, "and I'll eat your liver while it's still warm."

I raise one hand.

Silence.

The temperature drops another ten degrees. I can feel it happening—not because I command it directly, but because the geas pulsing in my sternum wants to hurt this man. Wants to peel him apart molecule by molecule until he gives me what I need. The cold is just how it chooses to start.

Trenchard's shivering becomes violent, convulsive. Ice forms along the edges of his hair, spreading downward across his forehead in delicate crystalline patterns. His breath comes in ragged gasps now, each exhalation freezing in the air between us.

"December 14th, 1999," I say quietly. My voice doesn't echo—the meat locker swallows sound whole and digests it into silence. "The South Side flush. Who gave the order, Marcus?"

His eyes go wide when I use his first name. Good. He should understand that I know everything about him already. Address, social security number, the name of his daughter's elementary school in Maplewood. All the little details that make someone human before you start taking them apart.

"I... I..." His words dissolve into another fit of shuddering. Frost spreads across his shoulders now, creeping down his arms where they're bound to the chair with zip ties that have gone brittle with cold. The ice isn't just surface-level anymore—my metallurgy hexes are working deeper, finding the trace amounts of iron in his bloodstream and crystallizing them from within.

The frostbite must be excruciating. I've seen what it does to flesh—how it turns tissue black and necrotic, how nerves die screaming. But Trenchard doesn't scream yet. Not quite ready for that.

Grimjaw shifts his weight impatiently. "Boss, maybe we should—"

"No." Still quiet. Still controlled.

I take another step forward, and the sodium-vapor bulb swings wildly on its chain as if disturbed by some invisible wind. The shadows dance across Trenchard's face, making him look like a death mask carved from bone.

"The waste engineer," I continue, watching those blue-black flames dancing in my peripheral vision—the reflection of whatever hellfire lives behind my eyes when this thing inside me wakes up fully. "The one who designed the disposal system for County General's ER. You were his supervisor then. Before you got promoted to 'logistics manager.' Before you learned how to bury things deep enough that nobody would ever find them."

More frost. It coats the hanging carcasses now, turning them into grotesque ice sculptures suspended in our private hell. The temperature must be approaching negative forty now—not the air itself, but the *feeling* of it against skin that's starting to lose sensation at the edges.

Trenchard's lips are blue. His face has taken on that waxy pallor of severe hypothermia.

"Please..." A whisper now. Barely audible over the sound of frozen meat creaking on its hooks above us—a sound like bones snapping in slow motion.

My fingers flex slightly, and suddenly there's another drop in temperature. This one sharper than before. Deliberate.

The frostbite is reaching his chest now.

I can see him trying not to panic, failing miserably as his body betrays him completely. Violent tremors rack his frame so hard the steel chair groans under the stress of it. Ice crystals spread across his expensive tie like some perverse decoration.

"The order came from Pulaski," he chokes out finally, words slurred around swelling tongue. "Sub-Station Seven. They wanted... they wanted proof that we could handle large-scale organic disposal without trace analysis detecting it. The flush was a test run."

Grimjaw leans forward eagerly. "That all you got for us?"

But I'm already moving closer, close enough to see every pore on Trenchard's face, each individual ice crystal forming on his eyelashes.

"Not enough." My voice barely rises above a murmur but somehow fills this freezing chamber completely. "Who specifically? Give me names. Give me locations. Give me everything about what happened that night or I'll let my magic have its way with you until there's nothing left but a popsicle wearing an expensive suit."

He's crying now—tears freezing before they've traveled halfway down his cheeks.

"I'll tell you!" The scream tears itself free at last, raw and desperate and utterly broken. "I'll tell you everything! Everything about that night!"

Behind me, Grimjaw grins wide enough to show yellowed fangs.

The frost recedes just slightly—not kindness exactly, more like a brief reprieve before the real interrogation begins.

* * *

The meat locker tastes like copper and frozen blood. I stand over Trenchard—waste engineer, company man, monument to corporate indifference—and watch him shiver so hard his teeth fracture against each other. The temperature has dropped another ten degrees since we dragged him in here, my frost-cobalt seeping through the concrete floor like liquid night.

"Please," he wheezes, breath crystallizing before it leaves his lips. "I didn't know... I mean, I knew about the dump, but I didn't think—"

"You thought wrong."

My voice comes flat, mechanical. The kind of sound that doesn't belong to any living thing. I kneel down, resting my forearms on my knees, studying him the way you'd study a broken machine. Because that's what he is—just another cog in Sterling's engine of destruction. But cogs know where the gears turn.

"So let me hear it again," I say quietly. "About that night. About Julian Sterling's penthouse. About the security feeds."

Trenchard's eyes dart toward the freezer door behind us, then back to my face. What he sees there makes him shrink smaller in his plastic chair. The smell shifts—ammonia from his bladder letting go, mingling with the raw meat stench and something else. Fear-sweat freezing on his skin.

"They were all there," he spits out, words tumbling over each other. "Julian, Victoria, her whole retinue of those High-Spire bastards. They had it piped into every screen in that fucking penthouse suite." His voice cracks. "Watching the sludge pour into the Undercity like champagne flowing at a wedding."

The image burns behind my eyes. Danny, drowning in black iron. Elena, burning in her own blood. All those faces I saw in the Sludge when Grimjaw first pulled me under. Every one of them watching their world collapse while Sterling's elite sipped expensive wine and laughed.

"They laughed!" Trenchard sobs now, snot freezing to his upper lip in an icicle. "Victoria said... she said it was just flushing the rats out of the gutters! That it would cleanse the city! Please, I was just following orders! Just doing my job!"

"Following orders." 

I lean forward until our faces are inches apart. Until I can see the individual pores on his skin going white with frostbite. Until my breath—that cold, abyssal thing—mists between us like grave fog.

"You flushed the rats," I whisper. "Now the rats are coming for you."

He doesn't answer. Can't answer. His lips have frozen together.

I stand up, rotating my shoulders against the weight of what comes next. Grimjaw watches from near the door, his massive frame silhouetted against the single light bulb overhead. He hasn't said a word since we brought Trenchard down here. Doesn't need to. I know what he's thinking because I'm thinking it too.

This won't fix Danny.

It won't bring back Elena.

But as I turn toward him, frost-cobalt residue dripping blue-black and iron-gall from my fingertips onto the concrete floor, I lay it out anyway. Need to hear it spoken aloud. Need to make it real.

"You want to know why?" I ask Grimjaw, though my eyes stay on Trenchard's terrified face. "Why we do this? Why we're going after Sterling?"

Grimjaw grunts acknowledgment.

"Because justice isn't about balance sheets or corporate responsibility or any of that righteous bullshit they feed you in courtrooms." My hand clenches into a fist, knuckles cracking with ice. "Justice is a sliver. A goddamn shard of broken glass you pull out of someone's foot so they can walk again. It doesn't heal the wound. It doesn't make them whole. But it gives them a chance to keep walking."

Trenchard makes a strangled sound.

"I can't scrape the black iron out of my boy's lungs," I continue, voice hardening. "Can't resurrect Elena. Can't undo what happened that night." The words taste like acid. "But I can take these motherfuckers who watched people die for profit... and I can make sure they understand exactly what they did."

I look at Grimjaw now, dead-on.

"This won't be enough. Never will be. But it's enough to justify what comes next."

The silence hits then—not the absence of sound but something heavier. More complete. The kind of silence that exists in deep space or inside tombs. Even Trenchard stops breathing.

I leave him frozen solid in that chair, lips pulled back from yellowed teeth in a rictus scream no one will ever hear. Turn toward Grimjaw.

"We need to go down into the Sludge drains," I say. "Find where that pipeline breaks. Where the poison first hit."

Grimjaw nods slowly. Understanding passes between us without another word.

---

## CHAPTER 10: THE SLUDGE-RAT CAULDRON

The metal rungs taste like old pennies and despair as I descend into the mouth of Newark's bowels. My gloved fingers grip each one with deliberate care—the last thing we need is for the rust to give way and send us plunging into what lies below. The air hits me first, a physical blow of sulfur and rot that makes my eyes water even behind the protective goggles.

"Christ," Grimjaw mutters behind me, his voice distorted by the respirator strapped across his muzzle. "Reminds me of that abattoir job in Irvington."

I don't respond. Words would waste breath in this place. Instead, I focus on the frost-cobalt current building in my palms—that familiar prickle of arctic energy that's become my constant companion since the Breach cracked open reality back in '99. The hex responds sluggishly here, fighting against the ambient heat rising from the sludge below. It's wrong. Everything about this place screams *wrong*.

Korg goes next, his massive frame having to turn sideways to fit through the maintenance hatch. The Ogre-Kin's waders slap against his tree-trunk thighs as he drops the final few feet onto something that squelches wetly beneath him. Then there's Thorne, quieter than Korg but no less imposing—a mountain of muscle and scar tissue who hasn't spoken a word since we suited up topside.

My boots hit the surface, and immediately I feel it: the unnatural warmth seeping through the thick rubber. This isn't normal groundwater. This is Sterling's legacy, the black-iron runoff from those illegal dumps, still radiating whatever cursed vitality the old bastard infused it with before the Feds finally shut him down.

The sodium-vapor emergency lights cast everything in diseased amber, creating pools of sickly illumination separated by chasms of absolute darkness. We stand in waist-deep liquid that should be frozen solid given the winter temperatures above ground, but instead radiates a damp heat that makes my skin crawl. The surface tension is all wrong—too viscous, too alive.

"Spread out," I command, my voice barely above a whisper despite knowing the sound won't carry far over the constant *drip-drip-drip* echoing off the corroded pipe walls. "We're looking for tracks, tunnels, anything that suggests habitation."

Grimjaw hefts his razor-wire net, testing its weight. "You sure these things are even real, boss? Could be just urban legend. Another one of Jersey's tall tales."

"The chemical analysis doesn't lie." I crouch low, examining the sludge near my feet. Even through the protective suit, I can feel my frost-cobalt hex working overtime, pushing back the toxic heavy metals trying to seep into my bloodstream. Tiny crystals of ice form around my fingers as I stir the muck. "Sterling dumped enough transmuted iron and alchemical binding agents down here to create something new. Something that's been living in these pipes for five years."

Korg's nostrils flare wide, his sensitive nose working overtime despite the respirator. "Smells like dead magic and bad meat, boss. We shouldn't be down here." His tail swishes nervously behind him, betraying anxiety beneath the brute exterior.

"We're already down here," Grimjaw snaps. "Might as well finish the job. We came to catch the devil's pets, so let's hunt."

The flickering lights choose that moment to die—the nearest one sputtering twice before plunging us into darkness broken only by our headlamps cutting weak beams into the gloom. The effect is immediate: the confined space feels smaller, more oppressive. And in that sudden silence after the light dies...

A sound.

Low. Chittering. Multiplied by dozens, maybe hundreds. It echoes from deeper within the tunnel system ahead of us, accompanied by frantic splashing that sends ripples across the sludge surface. Whatever made that noise, it's big. Or there are many of them.

"Did you hear—" Thorne starts, but I'm already moving forward, my frost-cobalt hex intensifying until a blue-white glow emanates from my palms, illuminating the tunnel with cold, clean light that pushes back the disease-yellow dark.

The tracks appear almost immediately—three-toed prints pressed into the hardened sludge at the tunnel's edge where the liquid level drops lower. They're fresh. Recent. And they're leading us exactly where we need to go.

"Found them," I call back, keeping my voice steady even as my heart hammers against my ribs. "Move up. Stay alert. These things were born in poison; they won't fight fair."

* * *

The beam of my flashlight cuts through the thick, oily miasma like a knife through warm lard. The cistern stretches before us—a massive concrete cathedral swallowed by darkness and filth. Water, if you can call that black, viscous shit water, sloshes ankle-deep across the floor. The stench hits me like a physical blow: ammonia, sulfur, burnt plastic, and something else. Something alive and wrong.

"Christ Almighty," Grimjaw mutters behind me, his voice muffled by the filter mask he'd finally put on. Smart man. "You sure about this?"

I don't answer. My eyes are adjusting to the gloom, picking out shapes clinging to the walls—hundreds of them, maybe thousands. They're motionless now, but I can feel their hunger radiating off them in waves. Can smell it cutting through the chemical soup.

They're bigger than any rats should be. Bigger than dogs, some of them. The Sludge-Run of 2000 had done more than just poison the groundwater. It had rewritten the goddamn genetic code of every living thing unlucky enough to drown in it.

My frost-cobalt magic coils around my fingers like living wire, its cold blue glow pushing back against the unnatural heat emanating from the sludge below our feet. The two forces war against each other in the confined space, creating pockets of steam that writhe like ghosts.

"Light 'em up," I say quietly.

Grimjaw switches on his tactical light. The sudden brightness reveals the nightmare in full detail. The rats' fur is gone, burned away or dissolved by the toxic runoff, leaving pink, glistening skin stretched tight over bodies twisted with tumors and growths of fused metal. Their teeth—*fuck*, their teeth—are jagged things of black iron, fused directly into their jaws. Some of them have too many. Some have none at all, replaced entirely by drills of crystallized sludge.

And they're waking up.

A high-pitched shriek pierces the air—the sound of a thousand rusty hinges being torn open simultaneously. Then another. And another, until the cistern rings with their chorus of madness.

"They see us!" one of the Ogre-Kin barks, raising his pipe.

The swarm descends.

I watch them come in slow motion—a wave of starving, mutated horrors pouring down the walls like waterfalls of bone and iron. Their claws scrape concrete. Their teeth chatter together in anticipation, sparks flying from the friction.

Grimjaw's MP5 coughs twice. Two razor-rats explode in bursts of red mist and black ichor. But for every one he drops, ten more pour into the gap.

"Hold your fire!" I shout. "We need them alive!"

"What?!"

But the Ogre-Kin are already swinging those massive pipes. *CRACK.* A rat's skull collapses like an eggshell. *THUMP.* Another goes flying, limbs splaying at impossible angles. The violence is immediate and brutal, each impact echoed by the wet crunch of breaking bone and the shower of blood and Sludge.

No, not just Sludge. That black-iron mixture that had turned these creatures into living weapons.

One breaks through toward me, its mouth open impossibly wide, rows of metal teeth gleaming in Grimjaw's light. Too fast to dodge. I slam my palm against the concrete floor, sending frost-cobalt magic racing across the surface in a spreading web. The rat hits it mid-leap, its feet touching the flash-frozen patch—
