"He doesn't understand that this isn't about stopping us anymore. It's about consequences. About balance."

The frost-cobalt magic pulses harder now, responding to the weight of what's coming. The temperature drops another few degrees. Someone coughs—cold air catching in their throat.

"For the sandhogs who drowned in those sub-labs." My voice is dead-silent. Absolute. "For the Orcs who got burned alive because Julian Sterling decided some lives weren't worth the cost savings. For everyone on the South Side who ever looked up at his ivory tower and knew, with bone-deep certainty, that they were nothing but cattle to him."

Grimjaw's hand rests on his weapon. The twins have already raised theirs—silent agreement.

"We don't take prisoners tonight. We don't show mercy. We drag that son of a bitch out of whatever hole he crawls into when things get rough, and we introduce him personally to everything he's unleashed on this city."

Bram spits into the shadows.

"The first scale gets balanced tomorrow night," I finish. "All of it comes due."

Silence. Thick as smoke.

Then Grimjaw laughs—that low rumbling sound like grinding machinery—and racks his shotgun.

The Ogre-Kin follow suit. Then Bram. Then the twins.

A chorus of bolts clicking home. Magazines slamming into place. The metallic song of weapons being readied for war.

It echoes through the loading bay like a promise.

I smile.

Cut to black.

---

# BOOK #11: THE SUB-STATION SEVEN FIRE
### Prequels Cycle 3 (PA-3)

---

## CHAPTER 1: CHAPTER 1

The air down here tastes like burning copper and diesel fuel. I'm crouched in the access duct three levels up, pressed so tight against the rust-coated pipes that I can feel every vibration through my ribs. Through the perforated metal grating above me, I catch flashes of movement below—shadows moving through sodium vapor light that makes everything look diseased.

"Commander Vance." The whisper comes from my left, barely audible over the hum of transformers. Special Agent Torres. His breath fogs the cold metal inches from my face. "They're running another check on the main conduits. Looks like they're prepping for transport."

I don't move. Don't even blink. Below, the black-ops crew is working fast now, their movements efficient and brutal. The clank of chains echoes off concrete walls slick with iron-gall residue—some kind of industrial byproduct that drips in thick, sizzling streams when it hits the floor. It smells sharp and acrid, cutting through the ozone stench of raw magic.

Through gaps in the grating, I see him. Marcus Voss. Trench coat hanging open despite the heat radiating from the nearby busbars. He's got a clove cigarette wedged between his lips, the cherry glowing orange-red in the half-light as he leans over what looks like four massive tanks. Lead-lined. Heavy enough that it takes three Razor-Wire Orcs to haul them into position with industrial chains.

"They're using Liquid Isfet," Torres whispers again. "Unstable batch. Those valves won't hold past maximum pressure."

I know. I can taste it from here—that particular wrongness in the air that means someone's weaponizing pure corruption. The Isfet sloshes inside its containment vessels, dark and viscous as motor oil mixed with nightmare fuel.

Voss straightens up, brushing ash from his lapel. His voice carries down through the ductwork, flat and matter-of-fact: "Pressure readings?"

One of the Orcs—a scarred brute with tusks filed to points—consults a gauge mounted to one of the tanks. "Holding at eighty percent, Mr. Voss. Gauges are rigged to spike past critical threshold on remote trigger."

"Good." Voss pulls the cigarette from his mouth, studying the glowing tip like he's reading tea leaves. "How long until commuter traffic resumes?"

"Ten minutes," another Orc replies. This one's the foreman by the look of his faded tattoos. South Side accent thick enough to spread on bread: "Valves are stripped, boss. This shit blows, it ain't leaving ash, it's leaving shadows."

Voss doesn't even glance at him. Just flicks cigarette ash onto concrete that's already stained black with burnt residue. "Shadows work too."

The foreman grunts acknowledgment and barks orders to his crew in gutter-Orcish. Chains rattle. Metal groans under impossible weight as they position the final tank directly beneath ventilation grates that feed fresh air to the lower platform.

That's when I see him.

Elias Morvain.

He descends from a catwalk above, immaculate in a bespoke suit that somehow remains pristine despite the grime and filth coating everything else in these tunnels. The fabric is dark charcoal, tailored to razor-sharp precision. His shoes—hand-stitched Italian leather—don't make a sound on concrete slick with iron-gall residue.

Corporate. High-Spire. The kind of elf who calculates collateral damage with spreadsheet precision while never getting his hands dirty himself.

Morvain stops beside Voss, adjusting his cufflinks with methodical care. His voice carries down crisp and clear, each word articulated with boardroom coldness:

"The blast radius needs recalibration. Current parameters will compromise the upper pylons by point-zero-three percent. Unacceptable structural failure probability."

Voss shrugs. "We'll adjust. Target's priority one anyway."

"I'm not concerned with priorities." Morvain's gaze sweeps across the assembled tanks, calculating trajectories like a chess master planning fifteen moves ahead. "I'm concerned with asset preservation. Leave the pylons intact. Incinerate everything below deck level."

The Orc foreman spits into the shadows. "That's gonna take more punch than these babies can manage, boss-man. Need double the payload to guarantee platform-level incineration without touching the supports."

Morvain finally looks at him, expression unreadable behind eyes that reflect sodium light like polished glass. "Then acquire additional resources. This facility operates on a contingency budget. Adapt accordingly."

He turns away before anyone can respond, already climbing back toward the catwalk, leaving Voss to oversee the final preparations alone.

Below, the crew shifts into high gear. Industrial wrenches clanging against metal. The sharp hiss of pressure valves being manually adjusted. Voss circles the rigging setup like a shark, checking connections with practiced efficiency.

Then he pulls out a phone—heavily modified Motorola Razr, all brushed steel and red LED indicators. Flips it open with one hand while tightening a valve with the other.

"Payload is primed," he says into the device. Pause. Listening. Then: "Just waiting on the target to buy his ticket."

The line goes dead.

Torres's grip tightens on my shoulder—barely perceptible through body armor—but I feel it. Feel the weight of what just happened settling over us both.

Someone's coming down to this platform.

And four tons of Liquid Isfet are waiting to turn them into shadows.

* * *

The Toughbook's screen glows that sickly green, washing out Morvain's face as he leans closer. Static crackles through the stolen audio feed—a river of white noise punctuated by the mechanical *thump-thump* of turnstiles somewhere in the depths below. Newark Penn Station breathes around us like a living thing.

"Got him," I mutter, fingers already moving across the touchpad.

Voss doesn't look up from his own terminal, a second Panasonic perched precariously on a stack of evidence folders. His reflection stares back from the dark screen, hollow-eyed and sharp-featured in the ambient glow. "Camera three, mezzanine level. Last visual was security checkpoint two."

I pull up the feed. Grainy. Green-tinted. The kind of footage they show in detective shows when they want you to know something important is happening but can't quite afford decent equipment. Except this isn't television—this is real, and those aren't actors filtering through the turnstiles below.

A Gnome. Hard to miss him even in the crowd. He's shorter than most, stockier, clutching a briefcase against his chest like it contains his soul. Which, in a way, it does. Kix—or whatever his real name is; we've got him filed under forty-seven different aliases—is sweating. You can see it even through the shitty resolution, little beads catching the fluorescent lights above.

"Bingo," Voss says quietly.

Kix's head swivels left, then right. Paranoid. Good. Should be paranoid. The BATC doesn't take kindly to accountants who suddenly develop consciences. Especially ones who've decrypted their slush-fund ledgers and are trying to walk away with the proof.

He checks his pager. One of those old Nokia models, extended antenna stabbing upward like an accusation. A relic. Analog. Untraceable.

Except we traced it anyway.

"Marcus." I keep my voice low. We're not supposed to be here, technically speaking. Not without a warrant, which we don't have, because officially speaking, the slush fund doesn't exist and neither do the decrypted ledgers.

Morvain shifts beside me, leather jacket creaking. "Yeah?"

"Once he hits the lower platform, seal the gates."

The question hangs unspoken between us. Collateral damage. Three hundred fourteen metahumans caught underground while Kix makes his play. Local 405 Dwarven machinists heading home after a double shift at the shipyards. Office workers. Students. All of them just trying to get somewhere else before midnight.

Voss finally looks up from his terminal, meeting my eyes for half a second. He knows what I'm asking. Whether we're really going to trap all those people just to catch one rat.

His gaze drops back to the screen. Doesn't answer.

Below us, Kix descends the escalator. Each step takes him deeper into the station's throat. He disappears briefly behind a pillar, then emerges on the lower platform—platform seven, the dead-end track that only sees service during rush hour. The crowd swells around him: a sea of blue work jackets and business casual, bodies pressing together in the confined space.

"He's at the bottom," Voss says.

I watch Kix merge into the mass of commuters. Almost invisible now. Just another body waiting for a train that won't come.

My hand hovers over the keyboard. One command. That's all it takes.

*Thump-thump. Thump-thump.*

The turnstiles keep spinning, feeding more people into the trap.

"You sure about this?" Morvain asks, though he's already reaching for his sidearm, checking the magazine out of habit.

"Positive." Not entirely true. But necessary? Absolutely.

Voss types something into his terminal. The mainframe connection lights up green. His fingers find the execute key.

The steel quarantine gates slam shut with a hydraulic *bang* that echoes through every speaker in the system.

On camera three, the crowd below doesn't immediately react. They're still moving, still talking, oblivious. Then someone notices—the Dwarf near the front, looking back over his shoulder. Another person catches it. Then another.

Panic starts as a ripple. Becomes a wave.

Kix spins around in the middle of the platform, briefcase still clutched to his chest, eyes wide and white in his dark face.

He just realized he's trapped.

And so are 314 other souls.

"Now we wait," I say, killing the audio feed because I don't want to hear what happens next.

* * *

I'm slamming through the gates of the Pulaski Skyway when the call comes through on my helmet comms. The Nextel crackles—Command, but wrong. Urgent. Wrong.

"Code Black. Sub-Station Seven." The voice is Morvain's handler, but there's something underneath it. Fear? Excitement? Can't tell anymore after twelve years in BATC Aegis. "Confirmed Class-5 Necro-Plague aerosol release on the lower concourse. Seal the grid. Scramble Aegis immediately. We need thermal purge protocols."

My hands tighten on the wheel of the Interceptor. Class-5. That's not just containment—that's scorched earth protocol. Burn everything within a half-mile radius. Turn the whole sector into glass if we have to.

The Skyway stretches out ahead, rust-streaked concrete pillars disappearing into November fog rolling off Newark Bay. Behind me, the rest of my squad peels off from HQ—Jackson on his bike, Chen and Rodriguez in the second vehicle. We're a six-person rapid response team designed for exactly this kind of shit.

But something doesn't sit right.

"The hell is a Class-5 doing at Sub-Station Seven?" I key back, my voice sharp even through the helmet compression. "That's a civilian transit hub. Where'd the threat intel come from?"

Silence. Then: "Direct report from on-site security. Multiple casualties already. They're venting the station now—you'll see the signature from three blocks out."

White-lilac magic flares hot around my knuckles where they grip the steering wheel. My bio-wards are clean. Pure. Telling me nothing about what's waiting down there except that my instincts are screaming wrong.

I floor the accelerator anyway.

The Interceptor whips off the Skyway exit toward Kearny, tires screeching onto surface streets. The city bleeds past—industrial parks, rusted warehouses, the skeletal remains of the old Passaic River waterfront. Four miles. Three and a half.

"Command, what assets are we talking about?" I demand. "How many tangos on site?"

More silence. This time longer.

"They're gone," comes the reply. "Security footage shows three individuals deploying aerosol canisters from a service elevator. Lower platform. Then they vanished into the maintenance tunnels. Vance, you have eyes-on command once you arrive. Full tactical authority to execute purge protocol if necessary."

My jaw clenches so hard it aches. Tactical authority means they're betting my life that I know what I'm walking into. That my training will override whatever bullshit is waiting.

Two miles. The smell hits first—that acrid chemical burn that means Isfet contamination. But underneath it, something else. Not death exactly. Something colder.

Something planned.

"I want thermal scanners running full spectrum the second we breach," I order the squad. "Chen, Rodriguez—environmental sampling kits ready. Jackson, you're with me on initial entry. We secure the perimeter, then we clear platform by platform. No heroes, no assumptions. This could be a trap, or it could be legitimate, but either way, we do this right or not at all."

A chorus of acknowledgments crackles back through the comms. Good soldiers. Smart enough to know when their commander's worried.

Half a mile out, I kill the lights and sirens. We roll in quiet mode, engines idling rough and hungry as we approach Sub-Station Seven's surface entrance. The whole structure looks wrong somehow—inert, like someone hit pause on reality itself.

I park parallel to the station entrance, blocking it. Chen and Rodriguez immediately deploy environmental sensors while Jackson covers our six with his rifle up and trained on the dark windows above us.

"Signatures are... fuck." Chen's voice goes tight. "Commander, you need to see this readout."

I pull up short of the entrance doors, my boots crunching on shattered glass from some long-ago vandalism. The sensor display illuminates my HUD:

NECRO-PLAGUE: NEGATIVE
ISFET CONTAMINATION: MINIMAL, VENTED
THERMAL SIGNATURES: ZERO ACTIVE SOURCES

"What the hell does that mean?" Jackson mutters behind me. "If there was an aerosol release..."

"Exactly." I stare at those readings, white-lilac magic crawling up my spine now, protective and hot. "Either we got lucky as hell, or someone wanted us to think there was an attack."

The entrance doors hang open ahead. Darkness beyond them. And underneath everything—so faint I almost miss it—that distinctive mechanical hiss of pressurized vapor systems shutting down.

Someone just turned off whatever they were using to sell this lie.

"Stay sharp," I whisper into the comms. "We're going in."

My hand finds the grip of my sidearm as I cross the threshold. The station concourse yawns before us—tiled walls, flickering fluorescent lights, empty benches. No bodies. No signs of struggle. Just... nothing.

Except for the smell. That chemical burn still clinging to the air like a ghost.

And the distant sound of footsteps echoing up from below.

"Contact!" Rodriguez shouts through the comms. "Multiple heat signatures, lower platform! They're moving fast!"

My magic flares full spectrum, washing the darkness in revealing light. White-lilac fire spills from my palms, illuminating every surface as I surge forward into the station's depths.

They want a fight? Fine.

Let's give them one.

---

## CHAPTER 2: CHAPTER 2

The locker room reeks of disinfectant and old sweat, fluorescent tubes buzzing overhead like trapped insects. I'm standing at my locker, palms extended, watching the arcane current flow through my hands. Pure flame—that's what the instructors called it during basic training. White-lilac and clean, smelling of cedar shavings from some pristine forest that never existed outside my mind's eye.

It dances across my fingers without burning. Not yet. Not today.

"Still showing off for the new recruits?" Saris leans against the bench behind me, her Street-Elf features sharp in the harsh lighting. She's already geared up—light tactical armor, her modified Barrett M82 resting against the wall like an old friend.

I let the flame gutter out with a thought. "Just keeping the edge sharp."

"That flame gonna save you when we're knee-deep in Splicers?" Gart shuffles over, his Ogre-Kin frame making the doorway look smaller. He slams a depleted-bismuth magazine into his MP5 with enough force to crack bone. The metallic clatter echoes off the concrete walls. "Heard rumors about Sub-Station Seven. Whole sector went dark three hours ago."

"Rumors don't kill us," I say, closing my locker with a soft click. My hand finds the Nextel pager clipped to my tactical belt. Still silent. Still calm.

The silence doesn't last.

Klaxons split the air like angry gods. Red emergency lights strobe across every surface, turning blood into crimson waterfalls on the white tile floor. My pager vibrates violently against my hip—an aggressive buzzing that feels like insects crawling under my skin.

I yank it free, thumb pressing the LCD screen awake. Green backlit text bleeds across the display:

*CODE RED. CLASS-5 NECRO-PLAGUE. SUB-STATION SEVEN.*

My stomach drops. Class-5. Flesh-eater status. That's not just dead bodies shambling through the streets—that's people melting from the inside out, their flesh turning to black ichor while they're still screaming. That's entire blocks becoming quarantine zones overnight.

"What is it?" Saris is already moving to her gear.

I hold up the pager, watch the emergency alert scroll past again. "Sub-Seven. They've got a plague outbreak."

Gart's laugh is dry as corpse dust. "You gotta be shitting me. That station's been running cold for months. What are the odds?"

"Not our job to calculate probabilities." I'm already pulling on my MOPP-suit, the chemical-resistant fabric cool against my skin. The zipper teeth catch and pull. "Full containment protocols. Rebreathers mandatory. This isn't a reconnaissance mission."

My hands move automatically—check the seals on the suit, verify the rebreather cartridge, mag-check my sidearm. The routine calms something deep in my chest even as adrenaline sharpens my vision to razor edges.

"Sixty seconds," I say, holstering the weapon with practiced efficiency. "Garage. Now."

Saris grabs her rifle, slinging it across her shoulder. Gart's already at the door, his massive frame blocking what little light filters into the corridor beyond.

The dispatch radio mounted on the wall squawks to life before we can make it out: "...multiple casualties reported... Sub-Station Seven command center is... repeat, command center is compromised..." The voice cuts off mid-word, replaced by static that sounds like a thousand flies dying at once.

I don't wait to hear more.

My boots hit the corridor hard, sprinting toward the garage where our transport sits waiting. Behind me, I hear Saris and Gart following close—their footsteps echoing mine in perfect rhythm.

Class-5 necro-plague. Sub-Station Seven.

The words taste like copper and fear on my tongue.

* * *

The rain hits the windshield like buckshot, each drop exploding into starbursts under the strobing amber lights of the city. I'm pressed against the passenger door of our lead Crown Vic, watching Neon Hollow blur past—sodium-vapor lamps bleeding through the sheets of water, turning everything the color of old bruises. The wipers slap their relentless rhythm: thump-thump, thump-thump, thump-thump.

"Twenty seconds," growls Martinez from behind the wheel. He doesn't look at me. His knuckles are white on the steering column, veins standing out like cables on his forearms. The radio crackles with cross-talk from the three other vehicles trailing us through the downpour—a convoy of dark sedans that look like they belong to repo men instead of BATC Aegis Command.

I turn my attention to the IBM ThinkPad bolted to the dashboard, its screen glowing that sickly green that always reminds me of emergency room lighting. My fingers move across the clunky keyboard, pulling up the telemetry feed Vane Thorne's team managed to scrape together before the comms went dark at Sub-Station Seven. The numbers scroll by, clinical and terrifying:

*Bio-hazard bloom detected. Class-5 pathogen. Containment breach imminent.*

Class-5. Jesus Christ.

Saris shifts in the back seat, her optical-camo scope clicking softly as she cycles through magnification settings. She's a Street-Elf, which means she grew up navigating these neon-soaked streets before we ever recruited her. Means she knows what happens when something goes wrong in the tunnels beneath Newark Bay. "Boss," she says, her voice cutting through the wail of our sirens, "a Class-5 means a 90% mortality rate in ten minutes. If it's already in the ventilation system, we're just showing up to bag bodies."

The Crown Vic hits a pothole hard enough to rattle my teeth. I grip the edge of the ThinkPad's mounting bracket and stare at the data streaming past. The bio-signatures aren't moving. They're stationary. That's either good news or the worst news possible—depending on whether containment is holding or if everything below ground is already dead and the sensors just haven't registered it yet.

"Command says it's contained to the lower platform." My own voice sounds hollow in the cramped space. "We hold the line at the mezzanine. Thermal purge protocol is authorized if we can't secure the ventilation manifold."

Martinez finally glances at me, his reflection ghostly in the side mirror. "You believe that?"

I don't answer. Don't need to. We both know Command has been wrong before. We all do.

The other cars peel off as we approach Sub-Station Seven—their headlights sweeping across the entrance plaza like search beams at a crime scene. Which, I suppose, is exactly what this is. The rain hammers down harder now, or maybe it's just gotten louder because we've stopped moving. The sirens cut out with a mechanical whine, leaving an eerie silence broken only by water drumming against metal.

Then I see them: plumes of black smoke rising from the subway grates nearest the station entrance. Not steam—smoke. And through our windshield, barely visible through the curtain of rain, civilians are pouring out of the main doors. Their mouths are open. Screaming about gas attacks. Chemical weapons. Something worse.

Saris is already out of the car, her scope raised, scanning for hostiles. Martinez follows, his service pistol drawn but held low. Our team spreads out across the plaza in practiced formation—four more tactical units emerging from the other Crown Vics, securing perimeters, establishing a containment zone.

I step into the rain myself, the cold immediately soaking through my tactical jacket. The smell hits me next—not gas, not chemicals. Something organic and rotten, like meat left too long in summer heat. My stomach clenches.

"Vance to Command." My radio crackles. "We have visual confirmation of civilian exodus. Smoke plumes emerging from ventilation grates. Requesting immediate clarification on biological agent characteristics."

Static answers me. Then Thorne's voice, tinny and distant: "Unclear. Sensors indicate possible mutation. Proceed with extreme caution."

Possible mutation.

The words hang in the air as I watch another figure stumble from the station entrance—a man in a business suit, his face streaming with something that isn't rain. Blood? Sweat? He collapses onto the wet pavement five feet away, convulsing.

My hand moves instinctively to my sidearm.

Behind me, one of the newer recruits vomits into the gutter.

* * *

The overhead fluorescents flickered once, twice, then died completely as we hit the upper concourse of Sub-Station Seven. Emergency reds kicked on immediately, bathing everything in arterial crimson that made my squad look like demons emerging from hell itself. Which, I suppose, wasn't far from the truth.

"Commander! North side's a shitshow!" Rodriguez's voice crackled in my ear as we pushed through the first wave of commuters. The woman was human—a rare choice for Aegis work, but she'd proven herself during the Kearny Marshes incident three years back. She knew how to hold ground when the world went sideways.

I didn't answer. Couldn't waste breath. My lungs were already burning from the sprint up the emergency stairs, but there was no time for anything less than maximum momentum. The station smelled wrong—metal and ozone and something else underneath it all, something sweet-rotten that made my pure weave crawl along my spine like ice water.

The crowd thinned ahead where a handful of Newark PD officers had managed to string up yellow tape across one of the main thoroughfares. An Orc beat cop, easily seven feet tall with tusks that gleamed in the red lighting, was trying to reason with a woman clutching two kids. His voice rumbled so deep it vibrated in my sternum even from twenty feet away.

"Not safe down there, ma'am. Station's locked down."

"I need to get to Elizabeth!" She was screaming now, her face contorted. "My daughter's at daycare in Union County!"

I flared my ward.

The white-lilac light exploded outward from my chest in a perfect sphere, sixty feet across, pure and brilliant enough to make everyone within its radius cry out and throw hands over their eyes. For just one crystalline second, every eye in the concourse was on me—on the glowing sigil burning on my uniform, on the way my hair lifted in a wind that wasn't there, on the absolute certainty that whatever was happening, I was in charge of it now.

The silence lasted exactly that long.

Then I spoke, my voice carrying that particular edge that came with channeling pure weave authority: "PD! Get that tape up properly. No one crosses until I say otherwise." I turned my head slightly toward Rodriguez without breaking eye contact with the nearest officer. "Status report."

"North escalator secured," she said, already moving to enforce my order. "South still open but PD's setting up barricades."

"Captain!" I called out, spotting the human lieutenant coordinating the police effort. He looked exhausted, his weathered face tight with the kind of tension that came from watching chaos unfold and knowing you couldn't stop it all no matter how hard you tried. "Vance, Aegis Command. Brief me."

He jogged over, Motorola crackling with static from his shoulder mic. "Lower platform sealed about five minutes ago. Transit Authority shut down the mechanical gates and locked them remotely. But people are trapped between here and there—maybe three hundred souls caught in the middle sections when the alarm went off." His jaw worked. "We're getting reports of... disturbances. From below."

Before he could elaborate, my earpiece lit up with Vane Thorne's distinctive voice—that High-Spire Elven cadence that always made him sound like he was talking down to you even when he wasn't trying to. Which, given his position as BATC Internal Affairs Inquisitor, meant he pretty much always was.

*"Commander Vance."* The connection was crystal clear despite the ambient noise around us. Thorne had access to tech that made standard military comms look like tin cans on a string. *"Hold your current position at the upper mezzanine. Do not—repeat, do NOT—attempt entry into the lower platform. The necro-pathogen is demonstrating volatile expansion characteristics."*

I started walking toward the security overlook without responding. Behind me, I heard Rodriguez shouting orders, her boots heavy on the concrete as she positioned my squad to control access points. The glass barrier of the observation deck gleamed ahead, reinforced acrylic thick enough to stop rifle fire, designed so station masters could watch the trains come and go without risking getting hit by debris or derailment.

*"Commander."* Thorne's tone sharpened. *"Did you copy? We're still establishing containment protocols. Your primary objective is perimeter enforcement."*

"Copy that, Command," I said evenly, my hand already reaching for the railing leading up to the overlook. The metal felt cold through my tactical gloves. "I'm approaching the overlook now to assess the situation from elevated position."

The stairs were narrow, steep enough that someone in full gear would have trouble if they rushed them. I took them two at a time anyway. My heart hammered against my ribs—not from exertion but from the same primal instinct that had kept humanity alive when everything else tried to kill them. Something bad was waiting downstairs. Something that made even Thorne nervous, which was saying something given his usual attitude of superior indifference.

I reached the top step.

And looked down.

My breath caught.

Through the reinforced glass, the entire lower platform stretched out below like a diorama of damnation. Emergency lighting cast everything in shades of red and shadow, turning ordinary commuters into silhouettes frozen mid-action. Some were running. Others stood stock-still, staring at something out of frame. A few were on their knees, hands pressed to their faces.

All three hundred of them trapped behind the locked mechanical gates.

And between where I stood and where they waited, in the gaps between the support pillars and beneath the departures board, things moved in ways that shouldn't be possible. Shapes that were wrong—too tall, too angular, leaving trails of darkness that seemed to eat the light around them.

One of them turned toward the upper mezzanine.

Toward me.

Its face was human-shaped but all the proportions were stretched like taffy pulled too thin. Eyes like holes burned through paper stared directly upward with an intelligence that predated anything biological. When it opened its mouth, I heard nothing through the thick glass—but I saw teeth that weren't meant for chewing food, only tearing flesh and bone.

"Oh fuck," Rodriguez whispered in my ear. "Commander, you seeing what I'm seeing?"

The thing smiled.

And began climbing.

Not up the stairs or escalators—directly up the wall, fingers digging into concrete as if it were butter. Behind it, others stirred. The plague vector wasn't expanding anymore.

It had already arrived.

"The lower level is compromised," I said into my mic, voice steady even as my pure weave flared instinctively around me like a shield. "I have visual confirmation. We need evac protocols now."

*"Negative."* Thorne again, but his usual smugness was gone replaced by something closer to fear. *"Standby for extraction, Commander. Do NOT engage."*

Below me, the first creature reached the top of the wall and stepped onto the reinforced glass. It walked across the surface without breaking stride, defying physics in a way that made my academic training scream that this was impossible while my combat instincts screamed that possibility didn't matter when facing something that could kill

---

## CHAPTER 3: CHAPTER 3

The security booth reeks of stale coffee and fear. My hand trembles as I press it against the reinforced glass, feeling the vibrations of 314 desperate souls pounding from below.

"Three-one-four," I whisper, my voice cracking. "Christ."

Through the double-paned safety glass, the lower platform of Sub-Station Seven sprawls like a hell-bound waiting room. The fluorescent lights flicker overhead—one, two, three remaining bulbs sputtering their last breath before a transformer explodes somewhere deep in the station's guts. Darkness eats at the edges of the platform, creeping inward like oil spreading across water.

But even in the dying light, I can see them. All of them.

Local 405 Dwarves cluster near the locked gates, their calloused hands still hammering against the steel bars with that rhythmic, desperate percussion. Their Carhartt jackets, once the color of rust and forest green, now look gray in the emergency lighting. Somewhere in that mass, I recognize Big Jax Morrison—his wife was pregnant when I pulled him out of a collapsed building last October. His fists beat faster than the others, his mouth moving in silent screams I can't hear through the glass.

Street-Elves weave between the humans, clutching grocery bags to their narrow chests. One of them—a woman with braided silver hair—keeps looking back toward the far end of the platform where her children must be. Her pointed ears are flat against her skull, a sign of pure terror I learned to read during the Kearny Marshes incident. She knows something. They all know something, and it's turning their blood to ice.

The humans are worst of all. A teenager drops his Sony MiniDisc player, the plastic case clattering across the tile floor as he scrambles backward. It spins twice, its LCD screen still displaying the track list of some pop-punk album that will never finish playing. The kid who dropped it has his arm around a smaller figure—a sister? Little brother? They're crying now, both of them, pressed together like drowning swimmers.

Orc laborers stand at the periphery, their massive frames creating a perimeter they didn't choose. Their green skin has gone pale, almost jaundiced under the failing lights. One of them—the one with the faded prison tattoos running up his neck—has his eyes closed. He's praying. I've seen enough Orcs to know when they've accepted death.

My magic flares without conscious thought. White-lilac energy coils around my wrist, tendrils of clean cedar scent filling the cramped booth. It wants out. It *needs* to reach down there, to wrap itself around those 314 souls and yank them through the glass, through reality itself if necessary.

But magic doesn't work like that. Not even mine.

"Commander." Gart's voice rumbles from beside me, low and dangerous. His Orcish features have gone hard, all soft tissue retracted, leaving nothing but bone and muscle. "Boss."

I don't look at him. Can't tear my eyes away from the platform.

"There's kids down there," he continues, each word clipped, controlled. "Half the South Side shift is on that platform. The night crews. The ones pulling double shifts at County General because we're short-staffed."

"I see them." My knuckles are white against the glass. Blood and magic pulse in tandem through my veins.

Gart steps closer, his bulk filling half my field of vision. "The ventilation system runs underneath Platform Seven. If whatever's coming—"

"It's already here," I cut him off.

Because I can smell it now. Beneath the cedar scent of my own magic, beneath the stale coffee and ozone from the dying transformers, there's something else. Something wrong. Like burning plastic mixed with rotten meat and the acrid tang of void-touched matter.

"The gates won't hold," Gart says quietly. "Even if they were locked—and they weren't, not properly—they won't hold."

My hand drops from the glass. I grab the radio mounted to the wall, keying it open with more force than necessary. The plastic casing cracks under my palm.

"Vance to Command. Vance to any BATC unit." Static answers me. Always static these days. "You have over three hundred civilians trapped in the hot zone. Repeat: three-one-four souls. Human, Elf, Dwarf, Orc—I don't care. We need an evacuation protocol. Now."

More static. Then a voice, distorted beyond recognition, speaking words that might be English or might be something older, harsher.

"...containment protocols... breach threshold... sacrifice vector..."

"Fuck your protocols!" I slam the radio against the wall. It bounces once, twice, then settles into silence.

Below me, someone screams. A real scream this time, piercing enough that even muffled by glass and distance, it cuts through my skull like shattered mirror.

The black vapor is hissing up from the ventilation grates now, thick and malevolent, swallowing the lower half of the platform in absolute darkness. It moves with purpose, with *hunger*, spreading across the tile floor like spilled oil, consuming everything it touches.

One of the Dwarves stumbles backward into the dark. His boots scrape against concrete. He doesn't make another sound after that.

Gart's hand lands on my shoulder, heavy as lead. "Commander."

I'm already moving, magic crackling around both hands now, white-lilac light casting demonic shadows across the booth walls. Whatever comes next, whatever horror is rising from those vents, it will find me here.

And if there's one thing pure magic does better than anything else, it's remembering.

Remembering every name.
Every face.
Every soul left behind.

* * *

The monitors in my observation booth flicker to life, bathing the cramped space in sickly green phosphorescence. My fingers tighten around the radio handset as the first wisps of dark vapor appear on the platform below—thin tendrils threading through the gaps beneath the sealed gates like living smoke.

Then it begins.

A woman in a business suit drops her briefcase. It hits the concrete with a hollow thud I can almost feel through the reinforced glass. She clutches her throat, mouth opening and closing wordlessly as she tries to breathe. Others notice. Heads turn. The murmur of morning conversation dies into something worse—a collective gasp that rises into panic.

The hissing grows louder. Pressure. Escaping. That sound cuts through everything else.

I watch them press backward first, toward the far end of the platform where the stairs lead up. But there are too many bodies, too much confusion. They bunch together like cattle trapped in a pen. Then someone pushes. Someone else screams. The crowd surges forward again, this time *toward* the gates.

A figure breaks away from the mass—a Gnome, slight frame, jacked into a PalmPilot he's clutching like a talisman. He shoves his way through the panicked commuters, stylus flying across the device's screen. Green light glows against his face, casting harsh shadows in the dim station lighting.

"Move! Get back!" A Dwarf appears beside him, crowbar already wedged between gate and frame. His beard bristles with exertion as he heaves downward. Steel groans against steel. Sparks fly from the effort.

"Bypass the relay, you little shit, or we're all dead!"

The Gnome doesn't look up. His fingers work frantically over the PalmPilot's keyboard, lines of code cascading down the tiny LCD screen in rapid succession. Sweat beads on his forehead despite the autumn chill. The vapor is at their ankles now, creeping higher.

"I'm locked out! The mainframe is overriding local control!"

Another Dwarf joins the first, both of them grunting with effort as they drive their crowbars deeper, leveraging their weight against the sealed doors. Metal shrieks in protest but holds firm. The BATC engineering was built to withstand worse than desperation.

I key my radio. "Sub-Station Seven, this is Vance. I have visual confirmation of breach containment, but the civilians are—"

Static cuts me off. Not interference. Deliberate signal termination.

On the monitor, the Gnome's PalmPilot sparks violently. Blue-white flash. The device clatters to the platform, screen shattered, useless plastic and metal. The Gnome staggers backward, hands raised defensively, eyes wide with terror as he watches the black fog swallow his feet whole.

And then it stops.

The hissing cuts off mid-sound, leaving only silence and scattered coughing. The vapor continues to rise slowly, inexorably, reaching waist height now. But it's not spreading further. Contained. Quarantined.

Sealed.

I press my hand against the cold glass separating me from the scene below. My breath clouds the surface. Through it, I watch a woman collapse to her knees in the deepening fog, sobbing into her hands. Others huddle around her, arms raised protectively over their faces.

They don't know yet that what they're breathing isn't plague. They don't know it's just Isfet—deadly to metahumans, yes, but not contagion. Not the Necro-Plague that haunts our nightmares.

They think they're already dead.

The Dwarves abandon their crowbars. One slumps against the gate, face gray with resignation. The other simply walks away, shoulders slumped, disappearing into the thickening darkness below ground level.

I stare at the monitors showing the quarantine zone from multiple angles. My reflection ghosts across each screen—a woman watching people die who aren't actually dying.

"God help us all," I whisper to the empty booth.

But God doesn't answer anymore.

Only BATC does.

And BATC has just sealed those gates permanently.

* * *

I watch the red "LOCKOUT" text flash across the security booth's CRT monitors like a death sentence. My hands are still embedded in the circuit board, white-lilac energy crackling between my fingers, arcs of power jumping from copper trace to soldered joint. The smell of burning electronics fills my nostrils—a sharp, acrid scent cut through with ozone and something sweeter, like static electricity given form.

The hydraulic gates above us groan. For one heartbeat, I feel them move—an inch, maybe two. Below, on the platform, faces turn upward. Hope. God, there was hope in their eyes.

Then Thorne's voice cuts through my earpiece like a razor blade dipped in dry ice.

*"Commander Vance."*

My teeth clench so hard my jaw aches. Magic surges through me, desperate to obey, desperate to *save*, but I force it down, redirecting the flow deeper into the substation's systems. The CRT screen flickers, showing multiple camera feeds. Platform level. The crowd still packed tight, some on their knees now. Above them, the black vapor has spread wider, tendrils creeping along the ceiling like oil in water.

"I had them," I snarl into the mic, shoving more power into the circuits. Solder melts under my fingertips. A relay switch explodes with a sharp *crack*. "Thorne, open these fucking doors!"

*"You know I cannot do that." His voice is absolute, unyielding. "That vapor is aerosolized Necro-Plague. If you breach containment, you doom Newark. You doom the entire tri-state area. Stand down immediately."*

"No." The word comes out raw, broken. Sweat drips from my nose, sizzling when it hits the energized board. My left hand finds another junction box, ripping it open with fingers that are starting to shake—not from fear, from rage. Pure white-lilac light spills out, casting everything in an otherworldly glow.

The gates shift again, a mechanical whine echoing through the maintenance shaft. Another inch of movement before something deep within the hydraulics *screams* and they slam shut with a thunderclap that rattles bones.

"Vance." Thorne's tone changes, drops an octave into cold authority. "As your commanding officer and pursuant to Section 7-B of the BATC Containment Protocols, I am invoking emergency protocols. Prepare for Thermal Purge."

My breath catches. No. No no no—

*"Did you hear me, Commander?"*

I pull my hands from the circuitry with a wet sound. Power bleeds away, dissipating into the air like morning fog. On the monitors, I watch as new readouts appear. Temperature sensors. Fuel cells. Something called THERMITE CHARGES—located in the ceiling manifold above the platform.

"You wouldn't," I whisper, though I already know he would. He has before.

*"You have sixty seconds to evacuate the booth, Commander. Failure to comply will be considered insubordination under—"*

"Fuck your protocols!" I scream at the mic, smashing my fist against the console. The CRT screen shudders but holds. Below, people on the platform are stirring now, some trying to run, trapped by the closing vapor cloud. *"There are children down there! Twenty-three fucking children according to the manifest, and you want me to—"*

A new chime cuts me off. A countdown appears on every screen: **60... 59... 58...**

My stomach drops. The cedar smell of my magic curdles into something sour, something *wrong*. Because I can feel it now—the charges are real. I can sense their signature, buried deep in the station's infrastructure, waiting for Thorne's word.

The crowd below is panicking fully now, pressing against barriers that won't hold them, looking up toward cameras they can't see.

**30... 29... 28...**

Thorne's voice returns, softer somehow, almost gentle. "I'm sorry, Mara. You were always too compassionate for command."

My hand hovers over the master override panel—a final failsafe I'd overlooked in my desperation. If I can trigger the emergency ventilation system manually, create an updraft, maybe scatter the vapor enough to give them a chance—

But as soon as the thought forms, I see it: the secondary readout. Emergency vents lead directly to the city's main air circulation system. Open them, and the aerosolized plague doesn't just escape Sub-Station Seven.

It spreads to every building connected to Newark's grid.

My fingers curl into a fist. The white-lilac power still thrumming through my veins screams at me to *do something*, but my mind catalogs the impossibility with cold clarity. Every option leads to death. Every choice means sacrifice.

**10... 9... 8...**

Below, someone finally breaks through the barrier. A woman, dragging two kids behind her, stumbling toward the stairs that will never open because I can't force those fucking doors—

**5... 4... 3...**

I kill the connection. My hands move on muscle memory alone, fingers dancing across keys that shut down everything except the basic power grid. The countdown keeps counting down on screens I can no longer control.

The thermal charges ignite simultaneously.

Through the maintenance shaft windows, I watch the ceiling manifold above the platform bloom with heat signatures—first orange, then yellow-white. The vapor catches fire instantly, burning away in seconds, consuming everything beneath it in an inferno of chemical heat.

Screams echo up through the shafts, cut short by the roar of combustion.

When it's over, when the readings stabilize and the flames die down to glowing embers, I'm sitting on the security booth floor with my face in my hands, tasting copper and ash and the bitter tang of tears I didn't know had fallen.

Thorne's voice returns: *"Containment secure. Casualty estimate: three hundred forty-seven civilians, twelve BATC personnel. Prepare your after-action report."*

I don't respond. Can't respond. Because he's wrong about the numbers—they're higher than that, so much higher—and I know exactly why. In his haste to stop me from opening those gates, he activated the Thermal Purge before the full crowd could evacuate. Before the automated escape protocols could engage.

He sacrificed them to teach me a lesson about obedience.

And I let it happen.

My reflection stares back at me from the darkened CRT screen—a hollow-eyed woman with blood on her hands and magic crackling uselessly around her fingers like beautiful, terrible lightning that never struck its target.

---

## CHAPTER 4: CHAPTER 4

I slam through the security booth door, the flimsy aluminum crumpling inward like foil. My boot heels ring against the concrete, each step deliberate, heavy—marching toward the main ventilation manifold at the far end of the platform.

Behind me, Gart's radio crackles. "Commander Vance, wait."

"Stay back," I snap, my hand already reaching for the massive steel grate that feeds air directly down to the lower platform. The metal is cold even through my gloves, vibrating with the constant hum of turbines far below. Three hundred breaths, all flowing through this single point.

The Nextel on my belt chirps—encrypted channel, Command-level priority.

"Vance." It's Thorne's voice, clipped and urgent. But then another joins the line, familiar and authoritative.

"Commander." Director Elias Morvain. Smooth as silk over digital compression. "Status report."

My fingers curl around the edge of the grate. The turbines beneath are spinning up—not manual operation. Someone in Control has initiated emergency vent protocols.

"The platform is secure," I say, watching Gart and Saris stop twenty feet behind me, their weapons still lowered but ready. They can sense it too—the weight of what's coming. "Three-one-four hostiles neutralized. Civilian population intact."

A pause. Then Morvain speaks again, his tone shifting subtly. Not quite concern, but close enough to fake it. "Mara. The pathogen has reached critical mutation threshold in the vapor column. You have two minutes before it breaches the upper ventilation system and begins aerosolizing across the entire installation."

I turn from the grate, pressing the radio harder against my jaw. "Explain 'mutating.'"

"Delta-Strain Ophanim, accelerated by the heat signature from your tactical weave earlier. It's developing a chitinous spore casing—resistant to standard containment protocols. We need you to execute a White-Lilac Thermal Containment Purge."

The words hit me like ice water. My hand drops from the radio, hovering over the glowing amulet at my chest where my bio-weave reservoir pulses with stored energy.

"You want me to cast fire down there?" My voice is low, dangerous. "While three hundred civilians are on that platform?"

"Commander Vance—"

"There are children down there, Elias. Dwarves. People who didn't choose this war." My other hand clenches into a fist, and I feel it immediately—the familiar white-lilac aura beginning to bleed from between my knuckles, responding to my adrenaline spike. The stone beneath my boots cracks, spiderwebbing out in delicate patterns.

"Mara." His voice loses its professional edge for just a moment, something almost human bleeding through. "You are the only one with a thermal weave hot enough to sterilize the air column without destroying the infrastructure. If we can't contain this here, it spreads to Newark Bay. To the Kearny Marshes. We lose thousands."

"Then lose them," I snarl, marching back toward the grate. "Because I'm not—"

The radio crackles again, but it's Thorne now, his voice tight with something that might be excitement or fear or both. "Commander, wait. We're getting telemetry from Sub-Level Three. The blast doors just opened. They're evacuating into the bomb shelter. Estimated time until full clearance: ninety seconds."

I stop dead in my tracks, ten feet from the grate.

Morvain's voice returns, carefully neutral now. "Did you hear that, Mara? Ninety seconds. All they have to do is reach those shelters, and your purge becomes viable."

My eyes close. Behind my lids, I see them—faces from briefing photos. Mrs. Kowalski with her grandson. The dwarf mechanic with oil-stained hands. Kids no older than thirteen, running.

Sixty seconds.

"I need visual confirmation," I say quietly. "Get me eyes on those shelters. Now."

The turbine hum grows louder, vibrating up through the floor plates. My bio-weave reservoir pulses faster, responding to my thundering heart. White-lilac light spills between my fingers like liquid fire.

Fifty seconds.

"Feed opening in three... two..."

* * *

The air tastes like copper and burnt ozone, thick enough to coat my tongue. My palms are burning—literally fucking burning—and I can feel the white-lilac flame pooling there, coiling around my wrists like living serpents that smell of fresh-cut cedar. The sweet, clean scent cuts through the subway stench so sharp it makes my eyes water.

"Morvain," I say into the comm. Voice steady, even though my heart's hammering against my ribs like it wants out. "Your cameras are shit. Lower platform is just gray static. I'm looking at dead screens here."

I gesture with my chin toward the booth where those two techs are huddled over CRT monitors, all showing nothing but snow. The black vapor—the *thing*—had blinded them completely. Whatever the hell it was, it didn't just kill; it wiped its tracks clean.

Gart shifts beside me, his massive hand coming down on my shoulder. The weight of it is solid, real, grounding. His thumb presses once—a simple gesture that means *I've got your back*. Trust. No questions asked.

"The biometric telemetry," I continue, keeping my eyes locked on the radio tower's red blink above us. "Send it to my Toughbook. I want to see 314 individual heartbeats registering in that sub-level bunker before I even think about releasing this purge." I pause, letting the words settle. "And if you're lying to me, Morvain, if there's one civilian left down there when I fire... well. Let's just say the Manhattan Project looks like a sparkler by comparison."

The pure weave responds to my certainty—or maybe my terror. The white-lilac flames surge brighter, licking up past my elbows now, and the heat radiates across my face like standing too close to an open furnace. Cedar smoke curls from between my fingers.

Ten seconds pass. Twenty. The silence stretches thin enough to snap.

Then—*chime*.

Saris's Panasonic Toughbook lights up in her hands, screen glowing blue-white against the concrete gloom. She swipes it open, eyes narrowing as she scrolls through data streams I can't quite read from here. Behind her glasses, her pupils are wide with something that might be fear or excitement—I've never been good at telling with Saris.

"Commander Vance?" Her voice carries that weird echo on the comm. "Data packet incoming. Encrypted BATC Command signature. It's... it's clean."

My jaw clenches. "Show me."

She turns the laptop toward me. Numbers cascade down the screen—biometric signatures, all labeled and timestamped. Heart rates. Breathing patterns. Body temperatures. Three hundred fourteen distinct life signs, all clustered in the sub-level bunker. All stable.

All accounted for.

I stare at those numbers until they blur. Until I'm sure. Until I know with absolute certainty that there's no one else down there. No civilians. No children. No one who doesn't deserve what's coming.

"Gart," I whisper. He squeezes once more, then steps back.

I raise both arms, palms forward, the white-lilac fire roaring to life around my entire forearms now. The cedar smell is overwhelming, sweet and sharp and terrible. My pure weave is singing its death song.

"Morvain," I say, and my voice cracks just slightly around the edges. "Purge authorization: Vance-7-Alpha. Execute."

The manifold beneath our feet shudders like something waking up hungry.

And then the real nightmare begins.

* * *

The green glow washed across Saris's face like demonic laughter. I stood behind her, my hand still gripping her shoulder, watching the tactical display on that rugged Panasonic screen. Each little green dot represented a life. Three hundred fourteen commuters. Three hundred fourteen souls I was about to save.

"Boss," Saris said quietly, her Street-Elf ears twitching as she leaned closer to the screen. Her gloved finger traced the digital blueprint of Sub-Station Seven. "Look."

My eyes followed her motion. The dots were moving in perfect synchronization—flowing away from the lower platform like water down a drain, funneling toward the reinforced sub-level bomb shelter. One by one, they blinked out as they registered inside the bunker's sealed confines.

The platform zone began flashing.

EVACUATED - ZERO BIOSIGNATURES DETECTED

The text pulsed in harsh red-white cycles, casting strobing shadows across the cramped maintenance office where we'd set up our command post. I watched those words appear, felt them sink into my bones. Zero biosignatures. The platform was empty. They were all safe.

A sound escaped me—half-laugh, half-sob. My shoulders dropped six inches as tension drained from my spine like blood from a wound. Days of sleepless planning. Weeks of hunting Voss through the Kearny Marshes. Months of watching the plague spread through Newark Bay. All of it had led here, to this moment, and I hadn't needed to sacrifice anyone.

"We did it," I whispered. "Jesus Christ, Saris. We actually did it."

She glanced back at me, those strange golden eyes reflecting the screen's glow. "Your call, Commander. You pulled the right strings."

Thorne's voice crackled through my radio earpiece, urgent and strained: *"Commander Vance, report! What's your status? The containment field is holding but barely—"* Static cut him off for a second before he returned, more insistent: *"Mara! If those commuters aren't clear, we need to abort now! Once you ignite the purge, there's no going back!"*

I keyed the mic. "They're clear, Thorne. All biosigs are in the bunker. The platform is empty." As I spoke, I watched another cluster of green dots blink out on the Toughbook display. "Repeat: platform is clear."

There was a pause—long enough that my stomach clenched. Then Thorne's voice returned, different now. Not relieved. Something else. Urgent. *Frightened.*

*"The bunker is sealed. All hatches are locked. The platform is clear."* He paused again, and when he continued, his words came faster, tumbling over each other. *"Commander, you have to ignite the purge NOW. Before the plague breaches the mezzanine. Before Voss can countermand anything. NOW, Mara! The city depends on it!"*

Saris looked up at me from the screen, her expression unreadable.

"The magic is ready," she said simply. "It's been building since we entered the manifold chamber. When you give the word, it'll release everything you've stored."

I took one last look at the Toughbook screen. Those beautiful green dots were still blinking their steady rhythm in the bunker below. Safe. Protected. Saved by my decision.

I nodded once, sharp and final.

"Set it free."

Saris backed away from the computer station as I turned and walked into the main ventilation manifold. This space was vast—cathhedral-sized, all curved steel walls and industrial piping that snaked upward toward the skyway above. The air here tasted different. Charged. My white-lilac magic had been pooling in this contained space for the past hour, drawn and focused through arcane geometry I'd painted onto every available surface with silvered chalk.

The scent hit me first—that overwhelming aroma of fresh cedar, clean and powerful enough to make my eyes water. Then came the light.

My hands rose before me, palms open and facing outward. The magic responded instantly, spiraling up from the floor where it had been gathering like steam from a boiling kettle. It poured into my body—pure, uncorrupted energy that sang through my nervous system like electricity through live wires. White-lilac flame erupted around my wrists, cascading up my arms in sheets of impossible color.

This was the peak. Absolute apex. No corruption. No taint. Just pure Aegis power, righteous and true.

Beautiful.

Righteous.

*True.*

I raised both hands higher, feeling the magic gather between them until it formed a sphere—a miniature sun burning in my grasp. The pressure built against my sternum, against my ribs. Every molecule in my body wanted to explode outward, to release everything at once.

"For everyone who died," I whispered. "For everyone still breathing."

Then I threw my hands forward and let it all go.

---

## CHAPTER 5: CHAPTER 5

I press my palms flat against the cold iron, feeling the vibrations pulse through my bones. The grating hums beneath my touch—alive with potential, thrumming with the raw telluric current I've been channeling for the past ten minutes. My knees ache from kneeling here in the rain-soaked concrete of the upper concourse, but I can't afford to move yet.

Above us, the storm rages like something personal. Lightning splits the sky over Newark Bay, painting everything in jagged white, then dropping us back into near-darkness punctuated by emergency lights. Around me, the bio-weave burns bright—too bright to look at directly now. It crowns my shoulders in cascading sheets of white-lilac fire that don't consume but illuminate, pushing back the shadows with an intensity that makes my teeth ache.

The smell hits me first. Cedar. Fresh as if we'd just split open logs in some mountain cabin instead of standing in a transit station reeking of fear-sweat and ozone. It fills my lungs completely, driving out every other scent—the acrid tang of panic, the wet concrete, even the copper-metallic tinge of blood from where Gart cut his hand on a loose rebar earlier. The cedar is *pure*, and it's spreading.

"Goddamn," Gart mutters beside me, one arm raised across his face. His hair stands straight up, electrified by the static charge radiating off my body. "Boss, you're lighting up like a goddamn Christmas tree."

I ignore him. Can't waste focus on words when I need every ounce of concentration to hold this together. The thermal purge isn't just heat—it's precision. I close my eyes and reach deeper, feeling along the ventilation shafts like they're veins running through the station's metal skeleton. There: the main intake, two levels down. Here: the lateral cross-vents. And there, barely perceptible, the micro-filters that will help distribute...

*Grid locked.*

Vents open.

*Sterilization protocol active.*

The mantra forms in my mind, modern and mechanical despite the arcane power flowing through me. This isn't magic like the old books described—no incantations in dead languages, no robes and ritual circles. This is pure applied science with a supernatural foundation, and it requires focus sharper than any scalpel.

Saris crouches on my left, her tactical scanner held up to her face. The green readout paints her features in an eerie glow. "Plague signatures holding steady at lower platform," she reports, voice tight. Professional. She's seen what happens when we hit this thing with everything we've got. "No movement from the contaminated zones. Looks like they're dormant for now."

For now. That's the key phrase. The Necro-Plague doesn't sleep; it waits. Patience is its greatest weapon.

I draw in another breath of cedar-scented air and feel the bio-weave respond, condensing around my hands. The light intensifies until even through my closed eyelids I can see the white-lilac glow painting the inside of my skull. My heart hammers against my ribs—not from fear but from the sheer volume of energy coursing through my system.

"This is going to hurt the structure," I say quietly. More to myself than them. "Thermal shock. We might collapse sections of the lower platform."

"Better than letting those things spread," Gart replies. His voice carries the weight of someone who's watched people die too many times already.

He's right. It's always a choice between bad outcomes, and some choices you make alone.

The iron grating vibrates harder beneath my palms. I can feel the heat building now, not just in the bio-weave but in the metal itself. Soon it will be hot enough to melt steel if I don't—

*Focus.*

One final breath.

My lungs fill with that impossible cedar scent, and for a moment—for just one crystalline moment—I forget about plague-infected corpses two stories below. I forget about command responsibility and casualty projections and the fact that I'm burning through telluric reserves that took me six months to rebuild after Newark. 

In this breath, there is only purity. Only the clean, sharp scent of cedar and the feeling of sunlight-warm power flowing through every cell of my body.

I open my eyes.

And slam both hands down onto the grating with all the force of will and desperation I can summon.

* * *

I pour everything I have into my palms.

The white-lilac flame erupts like a captured star, a miniature sun that screams its way out of my flesh and bone. It's agony. It's ecstasy. My tendons burn from the inside out as the magic tears through me, desperate for release, hungry for purpose.

"Purge is away," I grunt into my throat-mic, tasting copper and ozone. "Temperature holding at two thousand degrees."

My knees are braced against the metal grating of Sub-Station Seven's ventilation access panel. The manifold beneath my hands glows cherry-red where my fingers dig in, the heat singing up through my gloves. Sweat pours down my face, my neck, my back—but it vanishes the moment it forms, flash-boiled by the inferno pouring from my body.

*"Confirmed, Commander."*

Morvain's voice cuts through the deafening roar of the magical fire rushing through tin ductwork. The sound is like a hurricane trapped in a coffin, all wind and fury and no place to go but down, down, down into the darkness of Neon Hollow below.

I feel it racing through the infrastructure—that liquid sun sensation spreading from my chest cavity down through my spine, flooding my arms, gushing from my open palms. The telluric busbars hum beneath me, massive iron conduits carrying power throughout the station. They're hot enough already, but they can take more. Have to take more if this purge is going to work.

"Hitting the lower platform... now."

The column of light shoots straight down into the black maw of the shaft. Two thousand degrees—hot enough to flash-fry anything biological that might be lurking in those vents, whether flesh or something worse. But not so hot it'll melt the load-bearing structures keeping this whole godforsaken place from collapsing into Newark Bay.

I'm doing my job.

The thought should comfort me. Should fill me with that righteous satisfaction I used to feel back when I first pinned on the Aegis Commander insignia. Back before the Kearny Marshes incident. Before Pulaski Skyway. Before I learned what really happened at County General ER in '02.

But now it just feels like another layer of dirt, another coat of blood I haven't spilled myself but still carries my name, my signature, my seal of approval.

My arms are shaking. The white-lilac fire doesn't care about my exhaustion. It wants out. Needs to burn. And I am nothing but a vessel for its cleansing rage.

Sterling Manor's ghosts whisper in the periphery of my consciousness—I've been hearing them ever since the breach opened wide in 1999. Most nights I can tune them out. Tonight they're screaming.

*"Commander Vance! You cannot! Think of the children!"*

*"It will consume everything!"*

*"The price is too high!"*

I grit my teeth and push harder.

The fire floods the lower platform.

For one perfect moment, I feel relief. Whole-body, soul-deep relief. This is working. It's going to work. Neon Hollow will be safe. No more nightmares from the Kearny Marshes. No more bodies washing up along the shoreline wrapped in telluric wire.

I begin to sever the connection.

And then—

The fire hits something wrong.

So horribly, violently wrong that my entire body goes rigid. My spine arches involuntarily as the feedback slams through every nerve ending. The white-lilac flame doesn't dissipate or fade. Instead, it *screams* back up the shaft toward me, carrying with it a sensation so profoundly alien that my mind tries to reject it entirely, to pretend it isn't happening.

But I feel it anyway.

A presence. Awakening.

Down there in the dark beneath Sub-Station Seven, something has been waiting. Something old enough to remember when Newark Bay was just another tributary of the Hudson, before the Dutch came with their bricks and their ambition and their hunger for land.

Something that has finally been given what it needs to rise.

"Morvain," I choke out, tasting blood now. "We have a problem."

* * *

The white-lilac fire touches the black vapor, and my universe ends.

Time fractures. The moment of contact—one second of ignition—stretches into an eternity while simultaneously collapsing to nothing. The thermal lance's beam catches the suspended cloud of condensed Isfet like a lit match meeting gasoline. For one microsecond, there's only silence. Then the world remembers how to make noise.

The explosion isn't a boom. It's the sound of reality tearing itself apart.

Blue-black force—a concussive wall of pure violence—roars upward from the lower platform through every ventilation shaft like God's own fist punching through floor after floor. I feel it hit before I hear it: a physical slap against my chest that knocks the air from my lungs, that sends my ribs cracking inward, that slams me backward as if I weigh nothing at all.

My body becomes weightless. Time resets. I'm airborne twenty feet above where I stood three heartbeats ago, spinning end over end, the gun still clutched in my hand, my larynx screaming wordless fury even though no sound escapes because the blast has stolen my voice along with everything else.

The iron grating of the mezzanine doesn't just buckle. It *decompresses*—the heavy plates twisting like tinfoil before they're simply torn away from their bolts and hurled aside like discarded toys. One section spirals past me in slow motion, trailing sparks, and I think distantly that there should be more time between thoughts but everything is happening at once forever.

The security booth's reinforced glass—thick enough to stop a .40 caliber round—doesn't crack or spider. It shatters. Every pane erupts into thousands of diamond-shaped fragments that rain down in a glittering cascade, each piece catching the emergency lighting in a final brilliant flash before gravity claims them and they fall forever through the darkness.

Then comes the sound. Sweet merciful Christ, the sound.

First: the boom. A deep, resonant thunderclap that vibrates through bone and marrow, a sonic punch that makes my eyes water and blood trickle from my nose. But that's just the overture.

Second: the screams. Three hundred and fourteen voices rise up simultaneously—a chorus of pure agony that drowns out thought, that freezes the blood in my veins, that crawls under my skin and scratches at my soul. They overlap and echo through the ventilation shafts, multiplying until it sounds like the entire world is burning alive all at once. Some are high-pitched and desperate. Others are guttural and wet. All of them are dying.

I hit the concrete floor hard enough to rattle my teeth loose. My left shoulder takes most of the impact, and even through the adrenaline and shock, I feel something pop in my collarbone. The gun skitters across the floor. Breath returns in ragged gasps.

"Vance! VANCE!" Gart's voice cuts through the screaming. He's on his hands and knees ten feet away, clutching his head with one hand while the other presses against his ribs. Blood runs between his fingers from a cut above his eye. His MP5 lies discarded near a concrete pillar where he must have been thrown. "What the FUCK was that?!"

I don't answer. Can't answer. My ears are ringing so loud I can barely hear myself think, let alone speak. Instead, I push myself up onto my elbows and stare at the security booth, at the shattered monitors still flickering inside despite the missing glass.

The telemetry feeds. The thermal imaging showing clear green. The radiation detectors reading null.

All lies.

My stomach drops as understanding crashes into me with the same physical force as the explosion itself. Those readings were wrong. Wrong wrong WRONG. The lower platform wasn't empty. There were people down there—three hundred and fourteen of them—and I just used the thermal lance on them like they were targets in a training simulation instead of human beings who deserved better than to be burned alive by their own Aegis Commander.

"You triggered the Isfet tanks," I whisper, though I'm not sure if the words make it past my lips. But Gart hears them—or reads them on my face—because his eyes go wide with comprehension followed immediately by horror.

"No." It's a single word, but it carries the weight of every soul I've just sent screaming into oblivion. "No no no NO—"

I'm already moving before the thought fully forms. My sidearm is back in my hand somehow—I don't remember retrieving it—but I'm sprinting for the locked stairwell door now, my boots slipping in the blood pooling beneath me (Gart's? mine?), the ringing in my ears replaced by the continuous roar of fire below and the endless, agonizing symphony of death echoing through the vents.

The door handle burns my palm when I grab it. Locked. Of course it's fucking locked.

I fire three rounds into the lock mechanism. Metal shrieks. The bolt tears free. The door swings inward into darkness that reeks of ozone and melted rubber and something worse—something that smells like meat cooking over an open flame except this isn't food and those aren't spices and the heat climbing up from below makes my skin crawl because I know exactly what caused it.

Steam rises from the stairwell entrance, thick and black and smelling of sulfur. Below, the screams continue unabated.

Three hundred and fourteen people burning alive.

And I pulled the trigger.

---

## CHAPTER 6: CHAPTER 6

I stand in the upper control mezzanine, my palms pressed flat against the primary ventilation manifold. Cold steel bites through my gloves as white-lilac magic—pure, uncorrupted—flows smoothly from my fingertips into the gratework. The bio-weave feels clean on my tongue, fresh cedar underneath the sterile antiseptic taste of my concentration.

My breath clouds in the frigid air. Behind me, the ruggedized Panasonic Toughbook's screen glows green: "ALL CLEAR - LOWER PLATFORM." Time stamp 6:15 PM. The commuter crowd, fifty-three souls according to station telemetry, has been evacuated cleanly to the bomb shelter. No casualties. No contamination spread.

"Execute the purge, Commander," Vane Thorne's voice purrs over tactical comms, smooth as polished bone. "Burn the rot."

My jaw tightens. The thermal wave gathers at my chest—a sphere of searing light that hurts to look at, even for me. White-lilac threads spiral tighter, tighter, building pressure. This is what BATC trained me for. What they made me for. Aegis Commander Mara Vance, the woman who can sterilize anything.

I push.

The apex of my spell drops down the shaft like a falling star.

For one perfect moment, everything is exactly as it should be.

Then the world *explodes*.

Not with fire—the temperature spike registers wrong on every sensor I've got. Not with sound, though my eardrums rupture from the pressure wave. The floor of the mezzanine heaves upward with a sickening groan of stressed concrete and snapping rebar. Reinforced glass in the control booth shatters outward in a crystalline storm. My body slams backward into the Panasonic Toughbook, which screeches and dies mid-crash.

"What—" My words dissolve into coughing as something acrid and chemical floods up through the broken ventilation shafts. It smells like burning plastic mixed with raw sewage and the copper tang of fresh blood, but twisted, wrong, the way a nightmare tastes when you wake up screaming.

*"Command, I have a secondary ignition!"* I'm barking into my Motorola headset, tasting blood on my tongue. *"The manifold is backdrafting! There's something else in the system!"*

"Proceed with protocol," Thorne says, his voice unnervingly calm. "The threat must be neutralized."

My thermal vision flares automatically. Through the haze of crackling energy, I see the truth: the white-lilac purge isn't just incinerating biological material. It's hitting something that *reacts*. Explosive decomposition. Chemical cascades I wasn't trained for because BATC never mentioned this possibility.

The entire station groans around me like a dying beast.

And then, impossibly, the CCTV system reboots.

CRT monitors flicker to life across the damaged control room, their picture tubes warming with a high-pitched whine. Green phosphor ghosts sweep across static before resolving into live feeds from cameras I was told had been disabled for maintenance.

Lower commuter platform.

6:15 PM timestamp still running at the bottom of the screen.

But it's not empty.

It's filled with people.

Fifty-three souls according to telemetry that was either incompetent or lying. Fifty-three souls who were supposed to be safe in the bomb shelter. Women in business suits clutching briefcases. A teenager texting on an ancient Nokia. An elderly man reading a paperback western.

All standing in the open platform.

All looking directly at Camera Seven-B, as if posing for a photograph.

As if they know I'm watching.

As if they want me to see what happens next.

The thermal wave I released—my perfect, pure sterilization spell—hits them like God's own judgment. White-lilac fire consumes everything in its path. Screams slice through the speakers but cut off abruptly, replaced by the sound of cooking meat and boiling blood.

I watch them die in real-time, frame by agonizing frame, on a monitor that shouldn't exist showing a feed that should have been offline.

BATC lied to me.

And fifty-three innocents are burning because I trusted them.

* * *

The CRTs flicker to life one by one, their electron guns painting ghostly green phosphorescence across my face. I'm still standing over the ventilation manifold, my hands trembling from the raw expenditure of power. The white-lilac purge has left me hollowed out, running on fumes and adrenaline.

Then I see them.

My breath catches.

The lower platform is not empty. It's *packed*. Shoulder-to-shoulder metahumans in late afternoon crush—the six o'clock exodus bleeding into seven. Orcs in Carhartt jackets and union pins, their tusks yellowed, their faces set in permanent scowls of working-class endurance. Dwarven mechanics clutching greasy lunchboxes, their thick fingers stained with motor oil. Street-Elves in cheap polyester suits, their too-thin frames pressed together for survival in the human tide.

314 souls according to the thermal overlay counter in the corner of Monitor Seven.

The number blinks. Mocks me.

"Commander Vance, telemetry confirms sterilization complete," the Panasonic Toughbook announces in its flat synthetic voice. "Recommended containment protocols now active."

I watch the thermal wave—my thermal wave, my pure white-lilac magic that was supposed to save everyone—I watch it hit something on the monitors. Something that wasn't there before. Hidden tanks beneath the tracks, glowing sickly amber in the thermal spectrum. Liquid Isfet. Of course. Why wouldn't they?

The detonation doesn't just explode. It *rips*.

White-hot. A hellish firestorm that tears horizontally across the locked platform like a freight train made of pure anguish. The audio feed cuts in with a half-second delay—just long enough for my brain to process what I'm seeing before it punches me with sound.

The collective scream of three hundred plus people burning alive.

It shreds through the control room speakers, a wall of agony so absolute it becomes physical. My teeth rattle. My eardrums threaten to rupture. An Orc transit worker appears center-frame on Monitor Three, his massive hands—each one bigger than my entire head—beating against the locked quarantine gates. His face is melting, skin bubbling and running like wax down his skull while his mouth opens in a silent shriek that the microphones transform into a sound like tearing metal.

*"OPEN THE FUCKING DOORS!"* He roars it again and again, each word punctuated by the wet crackle of his own flesh cooking on bone.
