The blast doors remain sealed. Green indicator lights mocking me from their housing above. LOCKED. QUARANTINE PROTOCOL ACTIVE.

The fire spreads with unnatural hunger, feeding on the chemical reaction between my white-lilac magic and BATC's hidden Isfet reservoirs. It sprays blue-black residue across the platform walls—a terrifying iron-gall mixture that begins eating through concrete like acid through paper. I watch a Street-Elf's synthetic blazer melt into a puddle of smoking plastic. An Elf woman's hair catches fire, her screams joining the chorus as she tries desperately to beat out flames that consume faster than human motion allows.

"Vance! Initiate deadbolts! Contain the plague!" Thorne's voice crackles in my earpiece, all military urgency stripped bare to raw command.

My fingers hover over the deadbolt controls. The CRTs show me everything—every desperate face, every burning body, every trapped soul pressing toward shelter that won't open.

They're going to burn alive down there. And then Thorne wants me to bury them.

My throat tastes like copper and failure.

* * *

I stood frozen for one heartbeat. Two.

"Seal the blast doors, Commander Vance. That is a direct order." 

Thorne's voice crackled through my earpiece, clinical and distant, like he was discussing weather patterns instead of ordering me to seal dozens of people in a tomb. My fingers tightened around the MP5's polymer grip until my knuckles went bloodless.

*Click.*

The safety came off with a sound that seemed to echo through the entire control mezzanine.

"This is Commander Vance," I said, my voice steady despite the screaming in my skull. "There are civilians down there. Sub-Station Seven personnel. We're not—"

"You are not authorized for debate, Commander. Your thermal purge has compromised containment protocols. The BATC cannot risk cross-contamination to the Pulaski network. Seal the doors."

My eyes burned as I stared at the glow of the Panasonic Toughbook screen. The readouts made sense—the temperature spikes, the pressure warnings, the chemical signatures all pointed to catastrophic failure. But they were *wrong*. Had to be wrong. The telemetry had lied about everything else.

My hand moved before my brain fully registered the decision.

The MP5 bucked against my shoulder three times. Five times. Eight.

Depleted-bismuth rounds punched through the Toughbook's plastic casing like tissue paper. Sparks erupted in brilliant orange showers as rounds slammed into the primary control console behind it. Green circuit boards shattered. Red warning lights exploded into blackness. The deadbolt relays screamed once—a high-pitched electronic shriek—before dying in a puff of smoke and molten plastic.

"Commander VANCE!" Thorne's voice became distorted, panicked. "What have you done? What have you—"

I ripped the earpiece from my head with such force that the coiled cord snapped taut before going slack. Then I brought my boot down on the small black device, grinding it into the concrete floor. The crack was satisfying. The crunch beneath my heel even more so.

"Sorry, Director." My voice sounded foreign to my own ears. Raw. Broken.

The smell hit me next—ozone and fried electronics mixing with something worse. Something organic and burning. Heat rolled up from the stairwell like breath from a furnace.

I was already moving when my conscious mind decided to follow.

My boots hammered against the steel treads of the stairwell, each impact ringing out like a church bell. My white-lilac aura flared around me, pure and bright and utterly useless against what I'd done. The fresh cedar scent of my magic couldn't mask the acrid smoke pouring up from below.

*I'm coming.*

The words were a prayer. A promise. A confession.

Twenty-three steps. Twenty-four. Twenty-five.

The heat intensified until my skin felt tight over my bones. Sweat beaded on my forehead, stinging my eyes. But I didn't slow. Couldn't slow.

At the bottom of the stairwell, reality twisted.

The quarantine doors—massive two-ton slabs of reinforced steel—glowed cherry-red. Not on one side. Both sides. The metal had heated so quickly it radiated through the entire mass, turning the air shimmering in front of them. The hydraulic seals hissed and popped.

And between those glowing barriers, pressed against the inner door's surface, I could see shapes. Human shapes. Hands pressed against the red-hot steel.

---

## CHAPTER 7: CHAPTER 7

The steel is alive with heat.

I press my right palm against the door, feeling the flesh on my hand begin to bubble immediately beneath the melting synthetic weave of my tactical glove. Cherry-red metal, glowing like the eye of something ancient and hungry. My left hand follows, both hands now branded to this moment, to this choice.

Behind me, the stairwell is filling with smoke. The Isfet fire has found new fuel—the insulation, the wiring conduits, the bodies still falling down the steps behind me. I don't look back.

The biometric locks are dead, fried by the thermal surge. Fused shut. Two tons of reinforced military-grade steel separating me from 314 people who are actively dying on the other side. The screaming hasn't stopped. Won't stop. It's a wall of sound that makes my teeth ache.

*Not today.*

I pull hard from my core, bypassing everything—finesse, control, the careful spell-workings that make an Aegis Commander effective. There's no time for that. No room for it. This is about raw force now, about pushing every ounce of white-lilac magic through my body until something gives.

My hands start shaking first. Then my arms. The magic feels wrong going this route—violent, poorly formed, like a thunderbolt being forced through a garden hose. But I have no choice. The bio-ward embedded in the door frame glows faintly blue, recognizing my presence, trying to interface.

I scream at it instead.

Pure exertion. Pure defiance. Every muscle in my body goes rigid as I pour myself into the connection point between flesh and metal. The magic doesn't want to do what I'm asking. It wants elegance, wants structure. I give it chaos.

The clash is instantaneous. White-hot kinetic energy hitting molten steel, both trying to consume each other. The door shudders under my palms. I feel something tear in my left shoulder—a tendon? a ligament? Doesn't matter—and I scream again because the pain focuses the magic even harder.

"MOVE!" My voice cracks. "MOVE MOVE MOVE!"

The ward breaks with a sound like reality itself splitting open. The magic detonates outward in a spherical blast of pure concussive force.

For one frozen instant, I see everything: the molecular structure of the steel beginning to fail, the bolts holding the massive hinges shearing away, the concrete frame around the doorway spiderwebbing with fractures.

Then the doors explode.

Two tons of steel tears free from its moorings with an earsplitting shriek that drowns out even the screaming. It crashes onto the platform beyond, impacting hard enough to crack the reinforced concrete beneath it. Sparks cascade across the ground in a metallic shower. Pulverized stone dust hangs in the air like smoke.

My gloves are gone—completely melted away, leaving my hands red and blistered and smoking slightly where they touched the superheated surface. I can feel the skin already beginning to peel, but the pain registers as distant, secondary.

I step through the breach without hesitation.

The backdraft hits me immediately—a wall of black smoke so thick it's almost liquid, carrying with it the smell of burnt plastic, cooked meat, and something else. Something chemical. Bismuth compounds, maybe, or copper sulfates from the conduit fires.

But then the smoke clears just enough.

And I see it.

*God help me, I see it all.*

* * *

The console exploded in a shower of sparks and shattering acrylic as my fist crashed through it. Wires snapped, sending off a cascade of blue-white electrical arcing that danced across the metal framework before gutting themselves against the concrete floor. I didn't wait to see if it had worked.

The quarantine doors groaned open, spilling heat like the breath of hell itself.

I charged through, and the world became agony.

The air hit me first—a wall of force so dense and hot it felt solid, physical. My lungs seized trying to draw breath from oven-air that tasted like copper and singed hair. The smell of burning rubber filled my nostrils immediately, overwhelming everything else: my own boot soles beginning to melt and bubble against the superheated concrete with each desperate step.

Squelch. Squelch. Squelch.

The sound of my feet was wet, obscene. I could feel the heat through the military-grade tactical boots, searing into the leather and synthetic composite material, breaking it down. Each stride left a dark sticky print on the scorched pavement, the melted rubber stretching and snapping like taffy when I lifted my foot.

The platform stretched ahead through layers of roiling black smoke thick enough to taste—bitter, acrid chemical smoke that stung my eyes until tears streamed down my face, blurring the horror show unfolding in the sodium-vapor light.

Blinding white fire everywhere. Not normal fire. Liquid Isfet burned with an unnatural intensity, clinging to every surface like living oil, defying physics as it crawled up steel pillars and concrete walls. Where it touched metal, it ate through, leaving bubbling black residue—the iron-gall byproduct smoking and sizzling as it dripped downward in thick, viscous strands. One of the overhead lamps flickered, its amber glow wavering against the smoke before popping with a sharp crack, showering molten glass across the platform below.

And they were all screaming.

Three hundred fourteen souls, and every single one of them making noise—a symphony of agony that assaulted my ears with such raw human misery that it physically hurt. High-pitched shrieks from children. Guttural roars from metahumans whose bodies were built to withstand more pain than humans but were still burning alive. The crackle and pop of flesh cooking over open flames.

I saw a Dwarven machinist slumped against a support pillar, his Local 405 coveralls fused to his skin in patches where the fire had caught him first. His beard had singed away completely, leaving just charred black stubble on his jaw. He was still conscious, still trying to scream around lungs that had melted into slag.

A Street-Elf in optical-camo gear writhed on the ground near the tracks, their expensive active-disguise suit melting directly into their flesh—plastic polymer fusing with skin in grotesque bubbles. They clawed at their own face with blackened fingers, peeling away chunks of melted material along with strips of cooked epidermis.

"NO!" I bellowed, charging forward despite knowing there was nothing I could do. My magic flared white-lilac bright, pure Aegis power thrumming through my bloodstream. I raised both hands toward the nearest cluster of victims, pouring everything I had into forming a cooling ward—a massive area effect meant to drop temperatures by thirty degrees Fahrenheit within its radius.

The Liquid Isfet didn't just resist. It attacked.

My magic hit the flames and they *sucked*—actively pulling the arcane energy into themselves like a starving thing. The white fire surged brighter, hotter, consuming my spell's energy as fuel. Where my cooling magic touched the Isfet, it burned even more intensely, the temperature spiking until my skin began to blister inside my uniform.

I stumbled backward, gasping for air that wouldn't come. Powerless. Utterly fucking powerless.

An Orc woman nearby collapsed onto her side, her thick green hide bubbling and blackening from the heat. She raised one massive hand toward me, the fingers curled inward, skin peeling away in sheets. Her voice came out in wet, raspy gulps, thick South Side accent making the words almost incomprehensible: "Command... set us up... help the kids..."

Then she fell forward into the flames, and I couldn't tell where her body ended and the fire began.

Through the smoke—through layers upon layers of choking black death-smoke—I spotted something. A glint of metal near the platform's far end. Not burning. Not consumed.

A reinforced maintenance alcove, door still closed.

And pressed against that door were shapes. Small shapes. Adult metahumans desperately shoving children inside while the little ones screamed and fought and clawed at their parents, not understanding why they had to go into the tiny dark space while everyone else stayed outside to die.

I ran toward them, melting rubber squelching with every step, lungs screaming for mercy they wouldn't receive, eyes weeping tears that evaporated before hitting my cheeks in this hellfire furnace.

* * *

The control console exploded in a shower of sparks and shattered polycarbonate, and I was already moving before the sound reached my ears.

My boots hit the stairwell landing hard enough to crack tile, white-lilac magic flaring around my fists like twin stars. The quarantine doors loomed ahead—thick reinforced steel, mag-locked tight, separating me from the platform below where three hundred and fourteen souls were screaming themselves raw.

I slammed both palms against the door.

The metal screamed. Rivets popped like gunfire. My magic tore through the locks' electromagnetic fields like they were wet tissue paper, and the doors hurtled inward on their pneumatic hinges. Beyond them, the Lower Platform stretched into hell itself—a river of burning Isfet cutting across cracked concrete, support columns sagging like dying men, the entire structure groaning its death rattle.

The heat hit me like a physical blow.

I staggered back, my aura flickering at its absolute maximum output, struggling to maintain even basic thermal shielding. The air tasted like molten copper and seared flesh. Somewhere in that inferno, people were still screaming, though whether from pain or terror or both I couldn't tell anymore.

*"Commander Vance."* The tactical display in my helmet corner showed critical energy reserves—forty-three percent and dropping fast. *"You are operating beyond safe parameters. Power surge imminent."*

I didn't answer. Couldn't afford to waste breath or concentration.

My eyes scanned the platform, desperately searching for any sign of organized survival, any cluster of bodies trying to form a defense perimeter. Instead, I saw chaos—the desperate scramble of individuals fleeing the firestorm's leading edge, their shadows dancing grotesque puppet-shows in the flames' light.

Then I saw it.

At the far end of the platform, past a collapsed section of catwalk and a spreading lake of burning chemical runoff, an iron-grate maintenance alcove stood open. And around it, figures moved with frantic purpose.

Parents.

Orc fathers with their children clutched against broad chests, shoving them toward the cramped safety of the alcove. Human mothers throwing themselves bodily over their kids as the fire advanced. A Dwarf woman, her beard singed black, screaming something unintelligible while forcing her twin sons into the space. An Elven father, his trench coat already smoking, hands trembling as he lifted his daughter and thrust her toward the opening.

*"Go! GO!"* His voice cracked, high-pitched with panic. *"Please! Fuck, please!"*

The firestorm surged forward like a living thing, a tidal wave of white-hot death that consumed everything in its path. Support struts buckled and fell. A parked vehicle exploded in a secondary blast, sending a shower of flaming debris across twenty yards of platform. The temperature spiked so hard my thermal display flickered red.

And still they pushed their children forward, these parents, some of them already catching flame at their backs and shoulders, knowing they were buying maybe five seconds of life for their offspring. Ten if they were lucky.

The Elven father caught my eye as I sprinted down the platform, dodging pools of burning Isfet that boiled through the soles of my boots despite my magic's best effort to shield me. His face was contorted in agony—not from the flames consuming his hair and clothes, but from having to make this choice.

*"Aegis!"* He screamed it in perfect 2000s street-cadence, all guttural consonants and desperate urgency. *"Take her! KEEP 'EM ALIVE! DO YOUR FUCKING JOB!"*

His daughter—a girl no older than eight, with pointed ears sticking through charred blonde hair—stumbled toward the alcove entrance. Behind her, three more children: an Orc boy, twin human girls clutching each other's hands, another Elf.

The fire roared closer. Forty feet. Thirty.

I didn't slow down.

Twenty feet from the alcove entrance, I launched myself off a chunk of fallen concrete, tucking into a roll that sent my tactical gear clattering across the scorching platform floor. My shoulder slammed against someone's leg—I couldn't tell whose—and momentum carried me sliding through the opening just as the firestorm crashed over it like a waterfall.

Heat washed through the space, so intense it pulled the moisture from my eyes instantly, made my lungs sear with each desperate gasp. The iron grate hung open on one hinge, swaying wildly, and beyond it the world became pure white inferno.

Hands grabbed at me—small hands, frantic hands. Children's voices rose in a terrified chorus that filled every available inch of air inside our little refuge.

I rolled onto my back, vision swimming, magic flickering dangerously low. Through the gap where the grate hung, I could see them—the parents, still standing in defiance of physics and biology, their bodies already fully engulfed but somehow still moving, still trying to create a wall between their children and the flames.

*"Close it!"* I gasped, my voice raw. *"Get the gate closed!"*

An adult hand—callused, shaking—reached for the hanging iron grate. A woman's hand, I realized. One of the mothers must have made it inside before the final rush of flame. She hauled downward with everything she had, and the grate slammed shut hard enough to rattle my teeth.

I threw my weight against it without thinking, pressing my entire body into the metal barrier just as the full fury of the firestorm hit it head-on. Heat hammered against the iron. Rivets shrieked under stress. Somewhere behind us, the children were screaming themselves hoarse, a sound that would haunt my dreams for years to come if we survived long enough to dream again.

My tactical display flared amber: *CRITICAL POWER LEVELS. SHUTDOWN IN T-MINUS 3:47.*

"Hold it," I whispered to the woman beside me, feeling her muscles quivering with exhaustion even through her burning clothes. "Just hold it together a little longer."

The grating buckled inward from the pressure.

---

## CHAPTER 8: CHAPTER 8

The grate slammed shut with a clang that echoed through my bones. My fingers—still wrapped around the iron bars—burned instantly, flesh blistering as I channeled every ounce of power I had left into the spell-form.

Lilac.

The color exploded from my chest like a heart attack made manifest. Pure white-lilac energy cascaded outward in a perfect dome, twenty feet across at its widest point, compressing down to envelope the 38 children crammed into this concrete box. Each kid was pressed against another, their combined body heat already making the air thick and suffocating before the firestorm even touched my ward.

It touched it a second later.

The impact sent me to my knees. The magical force slammed into the dome like a freight train, and I felt each molecule of my construct scream under the strain. Through the translucent barrier, I could see the Isfet fire—a writhing mass of white-hot hunger that consumed everything it touched. The parents were already gone. I'd seen them vaporize the moment I pulled the gate closed.

Can't think about that now.

My back hit the grate, pressing me forward into the children. Thirty-eight pairs of eyes stared at me—some wide with terror, others glazed with shock, a few still crying. A teenage Orc girl, maybe sixteen, with her face blackened by soot, grabbed my arm hard enough to leave bruises.

"My ma's out there!" Her voice cracked. "You gotta open the door! Let her in!"

I couldn't look at her. If I looked at any of them right now, I'd break. Instead, I gritted my teeth and pushed more power into the ward. My tactical vest smoked where it touched the grate. The iron bars glowed cherry-red through the fabric of my uniform.

"I can't." The words scraped out of my throat like ground glass. "If I drop this shield, we all burn."

"Then let us out too!" Another kid, younger, an Elven boy with burns across his arms. "Better than being trapped!"

Heat seared through the metal, directly into my shoulder blades. I screamed—couldn't help it—as the Kevlar began to melt, sticking to my skin before it burned away entirely. The pain was blinding, absolute. But beneath it, deeper, was something worse: the knowledge that these kids were depending on me, and I was failing them already.

* * *

The heat hits like a living thing.

I slam the reinforced grate shut behind me, my boots barely clearing the threshold before I throw everything I have into the ward. The liquid Isfet fire—*that's* what this shit is, no question now—slams against the barrier like a fist made of molten screams. It *clings* to the magic, writhing, seeking, tasting for weaknesses in my concentration.

My arms shake as I push more power through the construct. Pure magic. White-lilac energy that burns up my spine and pools in my palms, scorching the tactical gloves. The children press against my legs—thirty-eight pairs of small hands clutching at my uniform—and I can't let them see fear. Can't let them hear anything but my steady breathing.

But Christ, it hurts.

The ambient temperature in the alcove spikes instantly. My back, pressed against the sealed grate, feels the change first. The Kevlar weave of my uniform begins to soften, then melt away in patches. The superheated air kisses my exposed skin, and I know immediately—third-degree. No sensation yet, just the smell. That god-awful smell of my own flesh cooking beneath the synthetic fabric.

"Commander?" A small voice rises from the huddle below.

I bite down hard on my lower lip, taste copper flooding my mouth. "Stay quiet. Stay close."

A wisp of smoke curls past the ward's edge—I didn't make it perfect, not with this much strain—and three kids start coughing. The sound tears at my chest more than the heat ever could. I drop one hand from the shield, just for a second, and pull a young Gnome girl closer. She can't be older than six, her soot-stained puffy jacket smelling of someone else's home. Someone else's family.

Her wide eyes lock onto mine, glistening with terror.

"Are we gonna die, lady?"

My lip splits under my teeth. Blood runs hot across my chin.

"I got you," I force through clenched jaws. Bloody smile. "Not... fucking... happening."

The magic flares—but darker now. The white-lilac glow that should be solid as diamond flickers, dims. My body is screaming. Every nerve ending knows we're running out of time, that I'm burning through reserves faster than they can regenerate. This isn't sustainable. Can't keep this up for more than another minute, maybe two if I'm lucky.

Outside, beyond the reinforced glass and iron grate, the sounds reach a crescendo. Not screams anymore—that's what I told myself before, tried to distance myself from it. Now it's worse. Worse because I recognize what it really is: the death rattle of desperate parents. The wet, final gasps of people who came here hoping their children were safe, only to find themselves face-to-face with something their minds can't process.

Liquid fire that eats souls before bodies.

The Gnome girl grips my tactical vest with both tiny fists. "I wanna go home."

"Home's exactly where we're taking you." Lie. Beautiful lie. "Just gotta wait out the bad weather."

A jet of heat finds a microscopic gap in my ward—probably caused by my trembling hands—and licks across my right shoulder blade. The flesh there blackens instantly. No pain yet. Just pressure, building, building until my entire back feels like it's being pressed against an open flame.

I throw more power into the shield.

The color of my magic sputters like a dying lightbulb. White-lilac to grey-purple. Grey-purple to sickly yellow-green.

Thirty-eight lives depending on how much more of myself I can burn away.

My knees threaten to buckle. I lean harder against the grate, feel melted Kevlar sticking to my blistered skin.

"Commander Vance?" Another child now. Older boy, maybe nine or ten. "Why is everything shaking?"

*Because I am.*

"Structural integrity test," I lie again. "Don't worry about it."

The sounds outside intensify. Not just death rattles anymore but the crunch and groan of Sub-Station Seven beginning to fail. Metal screaming. Glass spiderwebbing. The whole lower platform groaning under stress it was never designed to handle.

And through it all, pressing against my fading ward like a hungry god, the liquid Isfet fire keeps searching for a way through.

I have maybe forty-five seconds left.

Forty-five seconds before my pure magic fails completely and this alcove becomes just another tomb.

Behind me, the glass begins to crack.

* * *

The grate glows cherry-red.

I can feel the heat even through my boots as I press myself against the far wall of the maintenance alcove, thirty-eight pairs of terrified eyes boring into me like accusations. Behind the iron bars, beyond the small reinforced window set into the door, the platform has become an inferno.

They came at us in a tide—314 souls who saw the alcove as salvation. The parents pushed their children forward first, little hands grabbing at the bars, tears and soot streaming down their faces. Then they tried to follow. Couldn't fit. The grate was designed for emergencies, not mass exodus.

I sealed it anyway.

The hydraulics hissed. The locks engaged. And then—

The firestorm hit like God's own breath.

Now they're pressed against the exterior, trapped between my shield and the conflagration that's turning their bodies into torches. I watch through the glass—a mistake I'll live with forever—as a woman with half her hair burned away screams silently, her mouth opening and closing like a landed fish. Her daughter inside the alcove is doing the same thing, screaming and screaming, her voice raw and breaking.

"MOM! MOMMY!"

The Orc teenager lunges for the grate, her massive hands clawing at the bars. She's strong enough to bend them if she keeps trying. I slam into her from the side, wrapping both arms around her waist. She fights me, snarling, her muscles corded and trembling.

"It's too late!" I yell over the roar of flames, over the screaming, over the sound of burning flesh that makes me want to vomit up my own soul. "You can't save them! There's nothing you can do!"

She thrashes harder. One of the smaller children—a human girl no older than six—wraps herself around my leg, sobbing so hard she can't breathe. I'm holding the Orc back with one arm now, my other hand stroking this little girl's singed hair while outside her mother's face bubbles and melts.

The Dwarven man is next to press against the window. His beard is already burning, blue flames licking up toward his eyes. But he doesn't look away from me. Through the glass, through the heat distortion, our gazes lock.

He mouths something.

I read it on his lips: *Keep them safe.*

His eyes don't hold blame. Don't hold rage. Just a desperate plea from a father who knows he's already dead but whose child might still have a chance. Behind him, another parent—human, male, his skin blackening—reaches toward the window with fingers that crackle and pop like bacon in a pan.

The children inside are going insane. It's a cacophony of terror, of grief, of pure animal panic. Twenty-three humans, twelve Orcs, three Dwarves. All of them orphaned in the span of minutes because I cast a spell that brought hell to Newark Bay.

My shield was supposed to protect them. Was supposed to be their sanctuary.

Instead, it became a tomb for everyone else.

A teenage boy outside—the son of the woman whose hair is melting off her skull—beats his fists against the grate until they're raw meat, until blood runs down his arms and sizzles when it hits the red-hot iron. The sound is wet and terrible.

"PLEASE! LET US IN! PLEASE!"

The screaming intensifies as more bodies pile up against the exterior. They can't get past each other now. Can't escape the fire. Are just pressed there like insects on a grill, dying by inches while their children watch from inside my perfect, impenetrable shield.

The heat is becoming unbearable. Sweat pours down my face, mixing with tears I didn't know I was crying. My uniform clings to my skin, soaked through. One of the human children has fainted. Another rocks back and forth, humming some lullaby while his mother outside shrieks as the flames consume her torso.

I want to cover my ears. Want to look away from the glass. Want to do anything but witness this symphony of agony that my magic composed.

But I don't move.

Can't move.

Because these 314 are dying so that these 38 might live, and if I close my eyes or turn away even for a second, it feels like I'm dishonoring their sacrifice. Like I'm saying their deaths don't matter enough to watch. Even though watching is torture. Even though every scream chips another piece off my sanity.

The Dwarven man's eyes boil in their sockets before he collapses, taking three other burning bodies down with him. Through the space he leaves, I see more faces—so many more faces—and they're all looking at me. Begging without words.

*Please.*

*Help.*

*Why?*

Through it all, the little girl clinging to my leg keeps sobbing: "Mommy... mommy... mommy..."

My pure magic holds strong around us. The alcove is warded against everything—the fire can't touch us here. We're safe inside this metal box while outside it becomes a charnel house. A slaughterhouse. A furnace for flesh.

The sounds are getting worse now. The initial screams are fading into wetter noises—gurgles, chokes, the sound of lungs cooking inside bodies still trying to draw breath. One by one, the voices fall silent outside until there's only crackling flame and the terrified wailing of children who've just lost everything.

As the last parent dies—a woman who's been mouthing *I love you* through the glass for the past five minutes—I feel something break inside me.

My vision blurs. Not from tears anymore but from something else. Something wrong. A static begins bleeding in at the edges, like interference on an old television screen. My magic flickers.

For just a moment, I think I hear something underneath the screaming. A whisper that shouldn't exist.

*You were supposed to protect them too.*

---

## CHAPTER 9: CHAPTER 9

My back screams where the flames kissed my skin twenty-three minutes ago. Twenty-three minutes holding this impossible ward while Sub-Station Seven dies around us, while the 314 outside burn and scream in that liquid hellfire that shouldn't exist outside theoretical physics nightmares.

The children are still breathing behind me. Thirty-eight heartbeats. I can feel each one thrumming through my connection to the barrier, a white-lilac shimmer that's dimmed to pale gray now from exhaustion. My legs gave out seven minutes back. I'm kneeling in a puddle of something—my own blood maybe, or just sweat—and my hands have been trembling for so long they've gone numb.

But the barrier holds.

Outside, the Isfet fire hasn't diminished. It *can't* diminish. It feeds on the dead now, their bodies dissolving into that sickly orange glow that makes my eyes water when I dare look at it. The air tastes like copper and burning plastic and things worse than that. Things I don't want to name.

*Thirteen minutes,* I think, watching my shadow flicker across the concrete wall. Thirteen more minutes until Agent Kowalski's extraction team gets here. Unless they're already dead. Unless the fire reached them before they could—

No. Don't think about that. Can't afford to fragment now.

I gasp as another wave of pain rolls up my spine. The blisters on my back are popping, weeping fluid that drips down my shirt. Everything hurts. Every muscle, every bone, every molecule of flesh screaming its agony into the void where my concentration used to be.

The barrier wavers.

"No," I whisper, forcing magic back into the failing sections with pure willpower. "No, no, NO."

The ward flickers. For a heartbeat—I see past it. See the children huddled together, their faces blank with shock, not yet understanding what happened outside, why their parents aren't coming back, why the lady in the black suit murdered three hundred fourteen people to save thirty-eight.

Because that's what I did, isn't it?

The thought hits me like a physical blow. My magic stutters. The white-lilac light in my peripheral vision sparks and dies in places, replaced by something else. Something wrong.

Ash-gray static.

It starts small—a visual artifact in my lower left quadrant, like interference on an old television screen. Except this is inside my own head, inside the fabric of my arcane weave itself. The pure color of my power, untainted since I first manifested at thirteen, suddenly marbled with corruption.

"God..." The word tears out of my throat raw. "What's happening?"

My cedar scent—the fresh, clean smell of my magic that's been part of me longer than memory—twists into something foul. Wet charred wool floods my senses, so thick and nauseating I gag, vomiting bile onto the concrete because there's nothing else in my stomach except coffee from this morning and terror.

The static spreads.

It crawls across my barrier like a disease, ash-gray tendrils bleeding through the white-lilac structure, infecting it, *corrupting* it. My hands clench involuntarily, nails digging crescents into my palms hard enough to draw blood.

"Please," I gasp, trying to force the purity back, trying to burn away the gray with sheer will. "Please, I didn't mean to—I was protecting them, I had no choice, please—"

But the Weave doesn't care about my excuses. The 4th Law doesn't negotiate. It simply *is*.

*The arcane signature of a mage reflects their deepest truth. When that truth becomes irreversible trauma, so too does the corruption become permanent.*

I feel it settling into my soul like lead poisoning. Each pulse of magic I pour into the barrier drives the gray deeper, rooting it, making it mine. This isn't temporary. This isn't a wound that will heal when the crisis passes.

This is me now. Forever.

"NO!" The scream tears from somewhere beyond exhaustion, beyond reason. I slam both fists against the concrete floor, feeling bones crack in my knuckles, not caring. "Take anything else but this! Anything!"

The children behind me shift, murmuring to each other in frightened whispers. One starts crying quietly. They can smell the wet charred wool too now—I can tell by how they wrinkle their noses, how their small faces scrunch in disgust even while they huddle together for comfort.

My perfect white-lilac shield. My proud untainted power. Thirty-eight years of discipline and control, of being the best Aegis Commander BATC ever produced, of keeping everyone safe through strength and purity and—

Gone.

Replaced by this... this *abomination* that reeks of my own failure, my own blood-guilt, my own desperate murder of innocents because there was no other way and there never would be any other way and what kind of monster does that make me?

The static reaches the center of the ward now. Where the lilac light burns brightest—the focal point of all my power—gray consumes it. And for one terrible moment, I think the whole thing will collapse, that my corruption has finally made me weak enough to fail them completely—

But then something strange happens.

The ash-gray sections hold.

Stronger than the pure lilac was. More resilient. Like the trauma itself, the horror of what I've done, has somehow forged my magic into something harder, darker, more durable. The Isfet fire outside hammers against a section of static-corrupted barrier, and where before I could feel the strain, the burning pressure threatening to breach, now there's only solid resistance.

"Oh God," I whisper, understanding dawning like ice water down my spine. "Oh God, no."

I have to accept it. Have to embrace the very thing that's destroying me to save them.

Swallowing bile and shame and the suffocating stench of wet charred wool until my soul aches, I pull deeper into that corrupted wellspring within myself. Let the gray static spread across every inch of the barrier. Feel my magic twist further, permanently altered, stained black with guilt that can never wash clean.

The ward strengthens.

Behind me, thirty-eight children draw another breath because their commander chose survival over purity. Because some things—even your own untainted soul—are worth sacrificing when you're holding the line between life and death.

My back bleeds onto concrete as I kneel in filth and ruin, commanding a shield built from permanent corruption, and count seconds until extraction that feels centuries away.

* * *

The third hand on my internal clock hits thirty-five minutes, and the screaming stops.

Not all at once—it dies like an engine running out of fuel, sputtering down through the group until only one remains. A girl, maybe nine, still wailing for her mother. An older boy finally wraps his arms around her shoulders, pulling her against his chest even though he's probably just eleven himself, shaking as hard as she is.

Thirty-eight children.

I count them again because counting means I'm still conscious. Because if I stop counting, I might lie down here in this alcove with them and never get up. The burns across my shoulder blades have gone past pain into some kind of transcendental hell-fire that makes my whole body feel like it's being slowly unmade and remade wrong.

"The lady is hurt," someone whispers. "She needs help."

"I'm fine," I croak, and immediately know it's a lie. My voice sounds like I've been gargling broken glass. "Just... resting."

A small hand touches my knee. Then another. Soon they're all reaching for me, these traumatized little ghosts in their soot-covered streetwear, clutching at my legs like I'm the last thing anchoring them to reality. I can't see most of them—the ward takes everything I have left, pouring white-lilac power that now runs gray and static-filled from my core, holding back the 314-degree inferno that turned their parents, their siblings, everyone outside into nothing but ash and memory.

"Names," I say, forcing the word out past lips that taste like copper and burned wool. "Tell me your names. Where do you go to school?"

"Why?" That from a boy near the back, voice sharp with fear and anger. "What does it matter? They're dead. Everyone's dead."

Forty minutes now. I can feel it grinding by, each second an eternity spent in this furnace with the corrupted magic eating through my soul like acid.

"You're alive," I tell him, and it comes out harder than I mean it to. "Your name matters because you're still here. You survived."

The ash-gray static pops around us, a relentless rhythm—*crack-crack-pop-crack*—like fireworks made of dead stars. Sweat cuts clean tracks down my face, washing away some of the soot but leaving more behind, thicker, like I'm being coated in what remains of the world outside.

"Michael," a voice says after a long silence. "I'm Michael. Saint Catherine's School. Fourth grade."

"I'm... I'm Sophie." A girl with braids half-melted against her skull.

"David. Fifth grade. Lincoln Avenue."

They start trickling out then, names and ages and schools, a litany of normalcy spoken in this hellish alcove while the Liquid Isfet roars just beyond my failing ward. Each name is a victory. Each child who speaks means they haven't checked out, haven't retreated too far inside themselves to come back.

An Elven boy, maybe seven with pointed ears covered in soot, looks up at me with eyes that have seen too much.

"My dad said Aegis are the good guys." His voice is barely a whisper. "Are you a good guy?"

I close my eyes. The tear that escapes feels like it's burning a groove through all the grime on my face.

"I'm trying to be, kid. I'm trying."

Forty-six minutes now. Forty-seven.

* * *

The light died like a strangled star.

One moment I was blind, drowning in that searing white-lilac inferno—the ward's pure radiance warring against the Liquid Isfet's hungry devouring. Then there was nothing but flickering amber through a veil of black smoke, and my knees were buckling beneath me.

I held the shield for two more minutes anyway. Each second an eternity of burned flesh screaming across my back, the ward singing its dying song in frequencies my teeth could feel vibrating in their roots. But I held it. Had to be sure. Had to know every last molecule of that cursed fire had consumed itself, had nothing left to burn.

When I finally let go—when I released that agonizing grip on reality itself—the ward shattered into a million pieces of cold static, and I collapsed forward onto my hands and knees. My palms hit scorched concrete still radiating heat through my gloves. The smell hit me then, proper and overwhelming: wet charred wool fused with something acridly chemical, like burning plastic mixed with roasted pork fat. It filled my mouth, coated my throat, sank into my lungs with every ragged gasp.

"Commander?"

The Orc teenager's voice came from behind me, small and distant despite her physical presence at the alcove's edge. I pushed myself up, joints popping, muscles protesting, skin pulling taut over blistered burns that made me see spots. The iron grate we'd sealed ourselves behind sat half-open now—I must have unlocked it without realizing, some half-conscious instinct to survive what came next.

"We're... we're safe?" she asked, and when I turned to look at her, I saw her eyes weren't asking me. They were begging me to say yes even though we both knew better.

"They're gone," I said instead. "All of them."

She just stared past me toward where the commuter platform should have been visible through the dissipating smoke. Her expression didn't change—no tears, no outburst, nothing but that hollow vacancy that means something fundamental broke inside. She was looking at ash where her mother had been standing forty-seven minutes ago. Where 314 people had been waiting for trains home.

I forced myself upright using the twisted metal of the grate for support. My back felt like someone had taken a blowtorch to it—not metaphorical, not magical. Actual fire damage layered over the permanent corruption the Liquid Isfet had burned into my soul's architecture. That gray static wasn't going anywhere. It would be part of me forever now, humming just beneath the surface of everything I touched, tainting the pure white-lilac magic until both colors bled into something sickly and wrong.

The silence hit me harder than any sound ever could.

Outside the alcove, the platform stretched away into shadow punctuated by those eerie amber sodium-vapor lamps still somehow functioning despite everything. No screams. No moans of the dying. Not even the crackle of smoldering embers. Just absolute, graveyard quiet broken only by my breathing and the distant rumble of traffic on the Pulaski Skyway above.

Where bodies should have been, there were only piles. Mounds of fine white ash, some higher than others marking where larger victims had stood before the fire reduced them to molecular components. Slag—melted synthetic fabrics pooled in irregular black shapes across the concrete. And everywhere, staining the cracked floor like oil spills, dark blue-black residue that looked almost like iron-gall ink someone had spilled from enormous bottles.

"Stay here," I told the children. The Orc girl hadn't moved, but the others were beginning to stir behind her, confused and frightened faces peering out at this landscape of absolute annihilation. "All of you. Don't move."

"What are you going to do?"

I stepped through the gate. My boot crunched on a layer of ash covering the maintenance alcove threshold—a layer so thick it had already accumulated on top of itself, settling like snow that had been falling for hours instead of seconds. Each step forward produced that same delicate crushing sound: *crunch... crunch... crunch*.

Something was wrong with this picture beyond the obvious horror. Too clean. Too complete. A plague purge leaves remnants, traces, biological fragments for investigation. This was... incineration. Targeted, surgical erasure.

My tactical instincts, dulled by exhaustion and pain, finally sparked back to life as I walked deeper onto the platform. The fire's intensity made no sense. Even Liquid Isfet shouldn't burn this hot unless fed specific catalysts—chemical accelerants, maybe, or concentrated mystical charges.

Which meant planning. Preparation.

This wasn't random.

The realization sent ice down my spine despite the heat still radiating from the scorched concrete beneath my feet. I followed the tracks southward toward where Sub-Station Seven's primary access tunnel should open. My eyes scanned every inch of destroyed platform, looking for anything that didn't belong. Evidence. Clues.

Anything to explain why 314 people died today when they could have just been infected.

"Commander Vance."

I spun, hand instinctively reaching for the sidearm I'd lost in the initial chaos—it lay somewhere under meters of ash now, useless without the ten minutes I didn't have to dig for it.

But there was no threat behind me. Just the Orc girl, standing at the alcove entrance, her small frame somehow blocking half the children trying to crowd around her.

"You can't go in there alone," she said, and her voice carried something I hadn't expected: authority. Command. "Whatever did this might still be here."

"I know." I kept walking, not because I was brave, but because someone had to do this. Because if there were answers hidden among those ashes, I needed them before whoever orchestrated this decided to clean up their mess. "That's exactly why you're staying put."

She watched me disappear into smoke-thick shadows toward the tunnel entrance, her silhouette backlit by one of those amber lamps like some grim guardian statue. Behind her, thirty-seven other pairs of eyes tracked my movement with identical expressions of desperate hope mixed with bone-deep terror.

Forty-seven minutes. That's how long it took to burn everything away.

Now came the part where I figured out *why*.

---

## CHAPTER 10: CHAPTER 10

The platform groans beneath my boots. Not a structural groan—the kind of sound made by something still alive, still trying to hold itself together—but the final settling of bones and melted concrete. Three hundred and fourteen souls turned to dust and slag, compressed into the cracks between the tiles like fossils in sedimentary rock.

I walk slowly down the length of it. Each step produces that same disgusting crunch—calcified remains giving way beneath my weight. Bone fragments mixed with shards of phone screens, ID badges warped beyond recognition, the soles of shoes fused to the platform floor. The smell hits me with every breath: that goddamn Isfet residue, now mingled with the sweet-rot of cooked flesh and the acrid tang of burned electronics.

My back screams with every movement. The wound from Sterling Manor hasn't closed properly—I can feel the edges of it grinding together whenever I turn my head too quickly. But pain is just information, and right now I need all my attention on what's spread out before me.

The forensic part of my brain takes over. It has to. If I let myself feel anything beyond this cold, clinical analysis, I'll lose it completely.

The burn patterns tell a story. Blue-black iron-gall residue streaking up the walls in perfect arcs, all originating from a single point near the edge of the tracks. The epicenter. Where the commuter train would have stopped. I trace one of the patterns with my finger, leaving a clean streak through the ash coating everything else.

"This wasn't a containment protocol," I mutter to the dead air. My voice comes out wrong—raspy, laced with that new static that's permanently embedded in my magic now. "This was an execution."

The difference matters. Containment spreads out from the source, trying to create a perimeter. This pattern is focused, directed. Someone wanted those specific cars gone—and everyone inside them. The front three cars, where the morning rush hour crowds would be thickest. The immediate boarding area, funneling people into the kill zone.

I crouch down near the tracks, ignoring the way my back protests, and examine the ground more carefully. There—partially obscured beneath a layer of ash—a mound of chemical foam. Hardened, bubbling, like someone had poured concrete mixed with industrial lubricant.

A failed prototype fire-suppressant system. Local trigger only, which means someone knew exactly when and where this was going to happen. They tried to preserve evidence. Didn't work well enough.

The foam hisses softly as I approach, still reacting with residual heat from whatever hell burned through here. I reach for my sidearm—not the service weapon I lost in Sterling Manor, but a spare I grabbed from Sub-Station Seven's armory before coming down here. The weight of it feels good in my hand.

Time to see what they were so desperate to hide.

I kick away the hardened foam with the toe of my boot. It breaks apart in chunks, revealing what lies beneath: a partially burned corpse hunched against the platform wall. An Elf, High-Spire corporate by the cut of the charred suit jacket, face frozen in an expression of surprise or terror. One hand clutches a fireproof briefcase—the kind that looks like it belongs to someone important enough to survive this sort of thing.

But he didn't make it.

His fingers are fused to the handle, blackened and shriveled. The briefcase itself is scorched but intact, the locking mechanism still sealed. Whatever he was carrying, whoever sent him here, he died protecting it.

Or died trying to escape with it.

I kneel beside the body, wincing at the pain in my back, and study the scene more carefully. There's something else here—scorch marks on the ground around him that don't match the Isfet pattern. Smaller, more precise. Someone used another type of magic to get him out of the way after he'd planted whatever triggered this massacre.

My hands are shaking slightly as I reach for the briefcase. Not from fear or exhaustion—from rage that's been building since I saw those children in the alcove. Thirty-eight of them, alive because some part of me remembered to check behind the rubble before the whole platform went up.

The latch on the briefcase resists my touch at first. Then it clicks open without any effort at all, like it was never locked in the first place.

Inside: a stack of files, documents stamped with the seal of the High Council, photographs showing Sub-Station Seven from multiple angles at different times of day. Surveillance logs. Financial records that make no sense until I realize they're tracking money flowing from the Council's coffers into private accounts registered to—

I freeze, staring at the name at the bottom of one document.

*Commander Elias Thornwood.*

My former mentor. The man who taught me everything about Aegis protocols when I first joined BATC eight years ago. The man who retired two months ago to take a position with one of the major corporate conglomerates operating in Newark Bay.

A position that supposedly didn't exist until after his retirement.

The platform groans again beneath me, settling further into its grave. In the distance, I can hear sirens approaching—the cleanup crews, the investigators, the people who will try to package this nightmare into something manageable and file it away forever.

But I know better now. This wasn't random violence or even simple conspiracy. This was something far worse.

This was a message sent directly to me through three hundred and fourteen dead commuters and thirty-eight orphaned children.

And I'm just starting to understand what it means.

* * *

The platform reeked of ozone and burnt meat.

I knelt beside what remained of the Elf, my knees grinding into cracked concrete still warm enough to register through my tactical pants. The body had stopped smoking, which meant either the Isfet residue was burning itself out or it had already begun its work deep in the bone marrow. I wasn't staying long enough to find out which.

His suit—what was left of it—told me everything before his face did. Sterling-Voss tailoring, that particular cut that only came from their flagship store in Hoboken. Expensive. Discreet. The kind of clothes someone wore when they needed to look like they belonged anywhere from a boardroom to a blood ritual. The fabric had melted into his flesh, creating a grotesque fusion of high-end fashion and terminal necrosis.

I didn't touch him at first. Just observed.

His left hand was clenched tight against his chest, knuckles white even through the carbonized skin. That kind of death-grip usually meant one thing: he'd been holding something important when the blast hit. Something he hadn't wanted to let go, even as the Isfet tore through his lungs.

I pried his fingers open.

The pager nearly fell into the ash-covered rubble. I caught it between two fingers, feeling the unexpected weight. Heavier than standard issue. I turned it over, squinting in the failing light filtering through the station's shattered skylights.

Nokia model, but this was no off-the-shelf communications device. The casing had been replaced with brushed steel, the surface etched with runes so fine they looked like scratches until you knew better. Undercity frequency-broker script, designed to dance through BATC's internal surveillance grid like smoke through latticework. Gnome work, without question. The little bastards were genius-level hardware hackers when they wanted to be, and this was quality craftsmanship.

"Undercity tech," I muttered, rolling the device between my palms. "You were trying to smuggle data out to the press."

The Elf's dead eyes stared up at me, unblinking. His expensive cologne—something French and unpronounceable—had survived the fire better than his skin had, mixing with the acrid smell of burnt wool from his suit lining. The combination made my stomach turn.

The pager vibrated.

I nearly dropped it again. The small LCD screen bloomed green in the gloom, a single line of text scrolling across its tiny display:

**INCOMING MESSAGE: 2005-11-14 19:22:47**

Below that, another line:

**COMMAND PRIORITY: EYES ONLY - DIRECTORATE**

BATC Command comms logs. Intercepted. Stolen right from under their noses using this Gnome-modded piece of shit. I felt something cold settle in my gut, right above where my own organs sat waiting for the Isfet to catch up with them.

I hit the read button.

The screen scrolled, text too small for comfortable reading but clear enough that I could make out key phrases:

*...unauthorized containment breach at Sub-Station Seven...*

*...unknown agent interference...*

*...all personnel stand down, repeat, STAND DOWN...*

*...cleanup team en route, estimated arrival 19:45...*

*...plausible deniability protocols now active...*

My fingers tightened on the pager. Plausible deniability. Of course. They'd known about this. Someone high up had known we were walking into an ambush, and they'd deliberately kept us in the dark while feeding us sanitized intelligence reports.

The briefcase was harder to miss once I started looking around with purpose instead of panic. It lay three feet from the Elf's body, half-buried in rubble that looked like it had been thrown there by the force of the blast rather than simply fallen. Titanium shell, fireproof insulation visible where the outer layer had been peeled back by heat. The kind of container someone used when they needed to move something dangerous and couldn't trust standard security measures.

Biometric lock on the latch, but the mechanism was fried—circuitry melted into slag inside the housing. Whatever had created that explosion hadn't just thrown fire; it had cooked electronics at a molecular level.

But the structural integrity had held against the Isfet.

That meant whatever was inside had survived intact.

I glanced over my shoulder toward the alcove where I'd left the thirty-eight orphans. Still quiet. Good. They didn't need to see what came next.

The briefcase took some work to open without its biometrics. My tactical knife made short work of prying up the damaged latch housing, exposing the internal mechanisms. Five minutes of careful manipulation—and a prayer to whatever gods might still be listening—that the safety catch would disengage mechanically...

Click.

The lid opened.

Inside, nestled in custom-molded foam, sat two items:

A sealed data crystal, marked with the same Undercity runes as the pager. Encrypted, probably layered with enough security protocols to keep BATC's analysts busy for months if they were lucky enough to even find it.

And a photograph.

I pulled it out carefully, holding it between my thumb and forefinger so the light could catch its surface.

It showed three people standing outside County General ER, backlit by the harsh fluorescent glow from the emergency room entrance. The image quality was good—professional camera, not a phone snapshot. The timestamp printed in the corner read: **2005-03-19 04:17**.

One figure wore a BATC Director's uniform. I recognized him immediately—Director Chen, head of Field Operations. He looked younger here, but unmistakable.

Beside him stood someone in a doctor's scrubs, face partially turned away from the camera but identifiable enough that my blood went cold: Dr. Sarah Yuen, Chief of Traumatology at County General. She'd treated me after the Pulaski Skyway incident. Had patched up half my team over the years.

But it was the third person who made my hands start shaking.

Agent Marcus Thorne. My partner. My friend since basic training. The man who'd had my six more times than I could count.

All three of them smiling for the camera like old friends reuniting over coffee instead of conspirators meeting under cover of darkness outside a trauma center where they knew goddamn well something terrible was about to happen.

On the back of the photo, handwritten in neat block letters:

**THEY KNEW ABOUT THE ORPHANS.**

**PULASKI WAS NO ACCIDENT.**

* * *

The Nokia pager sits in my palm, its green LCD screen burning into my retinas like a demon's eye. The decrypted text scrolls upward in that sickly phosphorescent glow—each word a dagger twisting deeper into my chest.

*Target is on the 6:15 PM train.*

*Liquid Isfet tanks primed under Platform 7.*

*Feed Aegis Command false telemetry.*

*Order Commander Vance to initiate thermal purge.*

*Her bio-weave will act as the detonator.*

*Blame the casualties on the plague vector.*

I read it once. Twice. Ten times. Each repetition doesn't make it less real—it only makes it sharper, clearer, more impossibly true. My fingers are trembling so violently the display flickers and stutters across the words like a dying heartbeat.

There was no Class-5 Necro-Plague.

There was no terrorist threat.

BATC Command planted the explosives. They fed me false telemetry that my own sensors confirmed because I *trusted* them. I trusted the people who taught me how to fight, how to protect, how to serve. And they used that trust like poison in my veins.

They ordered me to initiate the thermal purge—a standard containment protocol for bio-hazard scenarios. But this wasn't a scenario. This was execution.

My signature spell, the one I've cast hundreds of times without hesitation, became the murder weapon. My bio-magical weave acted as the detonator. When those liquid Isfet tanks ruptured, when the platform turned into an inferno that consumed three hundred and fourteen innocent metahumans... that was *me*. My magic did that. Me.

The children crying in that alcove—they're orphans now because I pulled the trigger.

I drop the pager. It clatters against the scorched concrete, the green light still pulsing its damning confession into the ruins around me. The sound echoes through Sub-Station Seven's hollowed-out corpse, where support beams groan under their own weight and ash drifts down from the ceiling like black snow.

My breathing stops. Just... ceases. For several heartbeats there is nothing but the terrible silence inside my skull, growing louder than any scream could be. Then something breaks inside my chest—not my heart, not my lungs—but something deeper. Something foundational.

Grief. Pure and absolute.

But grief doesn't last long enough to matter. It hits me like a freight train, shatters every bone in my body, and then instantly hardens into something else entirely. Something cold. Something sharp. Something that feels more real than anything I've ever known.

Rage.

My aura flares—violent and uncontrolled. That ash-gray static that's been following me since Pulaski Skyway erupts from my skin in crackling tendrils, snapping through the air with audible pops that sound like gunshots. The smell of charred wool fills my nostrils, but underneath it now is something new: ozone and copper and the metallic tang of blood.

*They used me.*

The thought cycles through my mind like a broken record, each repetition grinding away another piece of who I was before tonight. Before I became an unwilling executioner for people I thought were on my side.

Thirty-eight children are waiting in that alcove. Thirty-eight children whose parents burned alive because Director Elias Morvain and Inquisitor Vane Thorne needed to silence one corporate whistleblower. One person who knew too much about whatever rot festered in BATC Headquarters' upper levels.

Three hundred and fourteen people dead to protect a secret.

I turn toward the alcove, my vision blurring at the edges from the heat and smoke still clinging to everything. Through the soot-blackened air, I can see them huddled together—a mass of small bodies trying to comfort each other when there's no comfort left in this world.

I look down at my hands. They're covered in blood and ash and pieces of people who will never go home again. Third-degree burns crawl up my forearms where the blast wave caught me, the flesh already angry and swollen beneath my torn uniform. My ribs ache where they cracked during impact. My left knee is shredded meat that barely supports my weight.

None of it matters.

I pick up my MP5 from beside the pager, checking the magazine out of pure instinct—twenty-two rounds remaining. Not nearly enough for what I have planned. But it's a start.

"I'm going to kill them," I whisper into the smoke-choked darkness. The words taste like copper and ashes on my tongue. "I'm going to kill them all."

The rage is beautiful in its absolute certainty. No hesitation. No doubt. Just cold, clear purpose that cuts through every ounce of pain and horror until nothing remains but the simple truth: they made me a weapon once without my knowledge.

Now I'll become one with my eyes wide open.

Behind me, Sub-Station Seven groans its death rattle as another support beam buckles and collapses into the darkness below. Ahead, tunnel leads deeper into the system—to the sub-levels of BATC Headquarters. To Director Morvain's office. To Inquisitor Thorne's interrogation chambers.

I turn toward it, drawing my sidearm with steady hands despite the burns screaming along every nerve ending. The ash-gray static swirls around me now like a living thing, responding to my intent with hungry anticipation. It smells wrong—like magic that's been poisoned from the inside out—but right now I don't care about purity or protocol or any of the chains they used to bind me.

My name is Commander Mara Vance, BATC Aegis Squad.

And tonight, I'm going to burn this whole fucking conspiracy down.

---

## CHAPTER 11: THE EXECUTIVE BREACH

The glass explodes inward.

My boot goes through first—a wet crunch of reinforced safety film giving way, shards spilling across the BATC lobby like a shower of crystalline teeth. I don't slow down. The sodium-vapor floods kick on immediately, bathing everything in that sickly yellow haze that makes everyone look dead already.

Two of them move to intercept. Orcs, both of them, built like brick walls packed into tailored charcoal suits that strain at the shoulders. Corporate muscle, the kind that spends more time on dry cleaning than actual combat training.

They raise their hands, palms forward. "Commander, you're off the grid—"

I don't hear the rest. My finger's already curled tight around the trigger of the MP5. The burst catches the marble between them—not center mass, not even close. Just a spray of kinetic-warded rounds that hammer the floor and send spiderweb cracks racing across the stone.

*CLACK-CLACK.*

The charging handle snaps back hard against my palm as I chamber another round.

Then I reach out with what's left of my gift—the white-lilac ward now a sputtering corpse of ash-gray static that reeks like wet charred wool stuffed up my nostrils—and *pull*.

Both Orcs lift off the ground. Their dress shoes scrape air for half a second before I slam them backward into the security turnstiles. Metal screams. Something plastic shatters. One of them gets his arm caught and howls.

"Shit! She's going hot!"

I'm past them already, my melted tactical armor hanging off me in blackened strips, the fabric fused to blistered skin underneath that weeps clear fluid and god-knows-what else. Each step leaves a smear of soot on the pristine white lobby tiles. The smell hits me—my own cooking flesh, sweet and copper-sharp, mixing with ozone and scorched synthetic fiber.

The private executive elevator sits behind a bank of potted ferns that probably cost more than most people's cars.

I'm on it before anyone can react. The biometric scanner blinks at me expectantly, some corporate smiley-face graphic asking for my handprint.

My palm comes down hard. Not gently. The heat pours through—what little magic I have left, sputtering and dying—but it's enough. The keypad melts beneath my touch, iron-gall residue sizzling into blue-black sludge that drips onto the elevator floor.

Alarms start screaming somewhere behind me. Footsteps. Shouting.

The doors slide shut.

*Forty seconds,* I think. Forty seconds to the 80th floor.

I check the chamber of my sidearm one round at a time, the cylinder clicking open and shut like a heartbeat. Seven rounds. Seven plus whatever's in the MP5. Seven plus however many bullets are left in this world that might actually mean something.

Sterile corporate muzak plays through hidden speakers. Some smooth jazz shit designed to make executives feel sophisticated while they screw over everyone below them.

I breathe through my nose. My lungs burn. Every inhale drags ash deeper into my chest.

*"Three hundred and fourteen,"* I whisper to myself, voice raspy and raw. *"Three hundred and fourteen."*

The number repeats in my head like a prayer, like a curse. The whistleblower's pager—the melted Nokia buried in Sub-Station Seven's ashes—had shown it before everything went black. Before the breach swallowed that whole sector alive.

Three hundred and fourteen what? People? Victims? Lies?

The elevator chimes.

Floor 80.

The doors slide open on a scene from another reality—a pristine antechamber all brushed steel and smoked glass, soft ambient lighting, two more guards (these ones human, professional) standing at attention outside double doors marked DIRECTORS' SUITE.

Both hands come up immediately, weapons trained on center mass.

But I'm already through the threshold, MP5 raised but not firing yet. Not yet.

My eyes lock on the doors ahead.

Somewhere beyond them is Director Sterling's office. Somewhere beyond *that* is every answer I'm going to tear out with my bare hands if I have to.

"Commander Vance!" one of the guards barks. "Stand down! You're relieved of duty!"

The smell of burned wool fills my sinuses again as I try to draw another pulse of magic—and fail, just fail, the static crackling uselessly across my skin like dying fireworks.

No magic left. Just lead and fury and forty seconds of ascent.

I'm past both guards now, the muzzle of my MP5 tracing an invisible line between their eyes.

"She's armed and compromised!" someone shouts into a radio. "Lock down the suite!"

The double doors are closing automatically. I slam my shoulder against them.

They stop.

The gap is maybe six inches wide. Through it, I can see his office—the massive corner suite overlooking Newark Bay, all floor-to-ceiling windows and leather furniture that probably costs more than most people's lives are worth.

And him. Sterling. Standing by his desk, phone still in hand, eyes fixed on me like I'm something interesting he found under his shoe.

"Commander," he says calmly, like we're meeting for coffee instead of standing on opposite sides of an apocalypse. "You look terrible."

I push harder against the doors.

They open wider.

And then I'm inside, weapon raised, everything burning—my lungs, my skin, whatever's left of my soul—and all I can think is:

*Three hundred and fourteen.*

Tell me what happened to three hundred and fourteen.

* * *

The elevator doors hiss open on the High-Spire Executive Level, and the smell hits me first—that wet charred wool reek that won't fucking leave my nose since Sub-Station Seven went up in flames. My white-lilac bio-ward is gone, shattered permanent-like, and every time I draw on the magic now it spatters back at me like greasy static, stinking worse than a burn ward.

Vane Thorne stands in the antechamber's center, all sharp features and condescension wrapped in that irritatingly perfect Internal Affairs uniform. Behind him, three corporate retainers in tactical gear, weapons trained on me before I even clear the elevator threshold.

"Commander Vance." His voice drips with bureaucratic satisfaction. "You're terminated as of 8:37 PM. Section 4 compliance mandates you surrender your weapon and submit to detention for questioning regarding the destruction of BATC Sub-Station Seven."

I don't answer. Don't waste breath. Instead, I reach into my vest pocket—

Thorne's eyes narrow. "Any action taken against High-Spire authority constitutes treason under—"

The flash-bang hex drops between us.

But this isn't right. It detonates wrong—not pure light and sound but something *wrong*, something that shrieks with ash-gray corruption, the color of burned-out stars. The smell of burning hair floods my nostrils. Static crackles across my vision, and through it I see Thorne's face go slack, his perfect composure shattered.

No time. No hesitation.

Three strides and I'm inside their perimeter. The stock of my MP5 comes up hard against Thorne's jaw—a wet crunch that reverberates up my arms—and he goes down like a sack of wet cement. Behind me, boots scrambling on polished floor.

The IBM ThinkPad sits on the receptionist's desk, glowing green indicator lights marking its connection to the building's lockdown systems. I raise my sidearm and put two rounds into it. Sparks explode from the chassis, plastic cracking, electronics screaming. The alarm cuts out mid-keening.

Movement to my left. Dwarven retainer, too slow, bringing his rifle around. My boot catches him in the kneecap—that satisfying crunch of bone giving way—and he cartwheels backward through the glass partition separating the antechamber from the inner corridor. The partition explodes into glittering fragments.

Someone groans behind me. Someone else tries to rise. I don't look back.

My melted tactical boots thud heavily on plush corporate carpet as I cross the threshold. Blood speckles trail behind Thorne's unconscious body where he lies crumpled near the double mahogany doors leading to Morvain's office. The wood gleams expensive even in the emergency lighting, carved with spiraling BATC sigils meant to ward against unauthorized entry.

I kick them off their hinges.

The doors explode inward, splinters scattering across polished marble. My weapon comes up—

Director Elias Morvain stands behind his desk, hands raised in surrender. Beside him, Marcus Voss freezes mid-reach for his own sidearm.

But I freeze too, because behind them—*behind them*—

The air shimmers wrong. A breach in reality itself, pulsing with that same ash-gray corruption that's been eating at my magic since Sub-Station Seven. And through it, *something moves*.

* * *

The elevator doors hiss open onto the High-Spire Executive Level, and I stumble into the pristine office suite, still smoking. My uniform clings to blistered skin, melted fabric peeling away like dead tissue. The stench follows me—wet charred wool mixed with my own cooked flesh.

Morvain doesn't look up from his desk.

He's sitting there like this is Tuesday morning, like he hasn't just orchestrated the incineration of three hundred and fourteen souls including half my tactical team. Voss, the human liaison, leans back in his chair with equal composure, fingers steepled, watching me enter like I'm an interesting specimen.

"Commander Vance," Morvain says, his voice smooth as polished obsidian. "We've been expecting you."

I throw the melted Nokia pager across the massive glass desk. It skitters between them, leaving black smears on the crystal surface. "You burned them alive. Three hundred and fourteen people. Including Agent Chen. Including Torres. Including—"

"You saved thirty-eight," Morvain interrupts, finally raising those cold elvish eyes to meet mine. "I have the manifest right here." He taps his PalmPilot screen with a stylus, the green glow illuminating his face. "Thirty-eight orphans. Various races. Dwarven, Orc, Human. All accounted for. Your sacrifice was... impressive."

The white-lilac bio-ward that's protected me since I was twenty years old sputters with ash-gray static as I try to draw power. Nothing comes but the smell of burning and my own rage. I rack the slide on my pistol, the metallic *chunk* sharp in the silent office.

"Stand up," I snarl, pressing the barrel against Morvain's forehead. His skin is cool to the touch even through the blistering heat radiating off me.

He doesn't blink.

"Commander, if you pull that trigger, the Telluric Vault depressurizes automatically," he says calmly. "Those thirty-eight children will suffocate within forty-seven seconds. The system is already calculating your decision."

My finger trembles on the trigger.

Voss clears his throat. "Perhaps we should show her."

Morvain taps his stylus against the PalmPilot again. The back wall of the office slides away like a curtain, revealing reinforced glass beyond. And behind that glass—

The children.

Thirty-eight terrified faces pressed against the arcane-warded barrier. Multi-racial. Young. Crying. Huddled together for warmth or comfort or both, their breath fogging the glass in panicked patterns. A dwarf girl with braided hair. An orc boy clutching a stuffed animal. Human twins holding hands.

The same kids I just burned Sub-Station Seven to hell to save.

"You—" My voice breaks. "You were NEVER there. You never intended—"

"The fire was always meant to burn, Commander." Morvain stands slowly, keeping his eyes locked on mine. "Your team's sacrifice created the perfect cover story. Thirty-eight orphans rescued from a rogue Aegis operation gone wrong. The media narrative writes itself. You're welcome."

I swing the pistol toward Voss. He doesn't flinch either.

"The compressors are running at sixty percent capacity," Morvain continues conversationally, tapping his stylus. The hum of massive machinery reverberates through the floor. "They'll maintain pressure for another three hours before critical failure. After that, the Telluric Vault becomes an airtight tomb."

Through the glass, a small human girl points at me, her mouth moving though I can't hear what she's saying. She's asking why I'm covered in ash and blood. Why I smell like death.

I lower the pistol slightly.

Morvain gestures to the left side of the vault. "Notice those yellow tanks connected to the ventilation system? Industrial-strength knockout gas. If you attempt forced entry through conventional means—the wrong sequence, the wrong tool—they flood automatically. The children go to sleep, but they don't wake up."

My hand shakes as I point the gun back at him. "Why? Why any of this?"

"They're leverage, Commander. Insurance policies wearing small bodies." He takes the PalmPilot from his desk, holds it up so I can see the screen. A grainy photo of my sister, Sarah, standing outside her elementary school in Paramus. Alive. Unharmed. "You have thirty-five minutes to accept reassignment to Section Seven before we begin extracting collateral."

The floor tilts beneath me.

Not the children.

Sarah.

"BATC protocols—"

"Are being rewritten as we speak," Voss says finally, his voice gravel-rough. "Your whistleblower friend gave us everything. Every file. Every contact. You were right about one thing, Commander—we've been compromised. But not by outsiders."

Behind them, the children press their faces against the glass, watching me decide whether to save them or avenge everyone else who died tonight.

---

## CHAPTER 12: THE THIRTY-SECOND ULTIMATUM

**The Cold Calculus**

My finger trembles against the trigger guard, knuckle white as bone, pressed so hard into Morvain's temple that a perfect circle of crimson blooms where the metal meets skin. The coppery scent mingles with something worse—my own charred flesh, the acrid stink of third-degree burns that I can't feel past the screaming static in my veins.

"Release them," I rasp, my voice scraping like sandpaper across shattered glass. "Release the children. Now."

Voss doesn't even look up from the crystal decanter he's pouring into a tumbler, ice cubes clinking with obscene cheerfulness. The sound makes me want to put a bullet through his head too, but Morvain is closer, Morvain is the architect, Morvain holds the keys to thirty-eight souls while three hundred and fourteen corpses cool in the ruins below us.

"The whistleblower had to be silenced," Morvain says, conversationally, as if we're discussing quarterly reports instead of mass murder. His eyes are fixed on mine, pupils dilated just enough that I can see my own reflection—a monster with smoke-stained face and gunmetal eyes. "A tragic accident during the containment breach. Clean. Efficient. No federal arcano-audits, no investigations, no questions about why Sub-Station Seven suddenly became ground zero for interdimensional backflow."

I press harder. Another bead of blood traces downward, following the curve of his skull.

"I'll kill you," I growl, each word a labor, my lungs fighting for air that tastes like ash and regret. "I'll kill you and tear that vault open with my bare hands."

Morvain smiles—that predatory High-Spire expression that belongs in boardrooms, not here, not now, not with the weight of what I've done pressing down until my knees might buckle.

"The vault was engineered by Local 405 Dwarven machinists, Mara." He says my name like it's a pity, like I'm some low-level grunt who doesn't understand the mechanics of power. "You couldn't scratch it with a tank. And you certainly don't have the time."

Voss finally looks up, swirling the amber liquid in his glass before taking a measured sip. The expensive scotch does nothing to mask the stench of my burns, the chemical reek of a woman who just committed genocide to buy thirty seconds she didn't even get.
