"Stand back," I muttered, drawing a rune-etched blade from my thigh holster. The metal sang its harmonic frequency as I scored three quick passes across the threshold—blood-iron geometry, old magic married to new physics. The hex wouldn't break the locks. It would make them break themselves.

The sound was like someone snapping steel cables inside a coffin. Three sharp *CRACK-CRACK-CRACK* echoed through the empty terrace.

Mika's eyes widened in the dim light filtering from the manor's interior windows. She pulled the doors open without another word, revealing a corridor of such opulent excess it made my teeth hurt. Imported marble flooring, mahogany wainscoting that probably cost more than Bram's apartment building, recessed lighting casting everything in warm amber glow.

That warmth lasted exactly three seconds after I stepped through the threshold.

The temperature dropped like I'd walked into a meat locker. The air crystallized around my face with each exhalation. Frost began creeping up the walls immediately, spreading like a living thing along the expensive woodwork. Behind me, I heard Kovacs curse softly.

"What the fuck, Reyes?"

"Don't ask." I kept moving, MP5 raised and ready. The bismuth-depleted slugs in the magazine felt heavy in their casings—good weight, good balance. Mika slid in behind me, her own weapon covering our six. Bram took up position at the front door we'd just breached, watching for any movement outside.

We were maybe twenty feet down the service corridor when voices drifted toward us from somewhere deeper in the manor. Laughter. A cup clinking against something hard.

*"—can't believe Moretti expects us to do another sweep at midnight,"* a male voice said. *"Guy's paranoid as shit."*

*"Pay is good though,"* another answered. *"Better than the last gig."*

Human security contractors. Private muscle hired by Moretti because he didn't trust the local firms—or maybe because he needed plausible deniability. Either way, they weren't on our side.

I raised one hand, fist closed. Mika stopped. Bram went still behind us.

Three men rounded the corner ahead, still laughing among themselves. One held a steaming cup of coffee. They wore black tactical gear, but nothing that would stop what I was carrying.

They saw us simultaneously. Eyes widening. Hands dropping to weapons.

I didn't hesitate.

The MP5 bucked against my shoulder three times in quick succession—*thwip-thwip-thwip*—the sound eaten by the silencer even as blue-black iron-gall residue puffed from the barrel like smoke from an old gunpowder weapon. The depleted-bismuth slugs punched through their kinetic vests like paper, each impact spraying red mist into the suddenly frigid air.

The first guard dropped without even finishing drawing his sidearm. The second stumbled backward, blood bubbling from his lips as he collapsed. The third managed half a step before my third round caught him in the throat, severing whatever he'd been about to say into a wet gurgle.

The coffee cup fell from the dead man's fingers, shattering on the marble floor with a sharp *CRACK*. Hot liquid splashed across the white stone, and I watched it freeze solid in seconds, turning from brown liquid to a slushy crust as my aura finished doing its work.

Bram stepped over the bodies without breaking stride, his own weapon still raised and scanning. *"Kinetic wards didn't even slow the bismuth down. Good machining, if I do say so myself."*

I pointed down the hall with my free hand, not taking my eyes off the corridor ahead. The cold was getting worse now, frost spreading faster along both walls like veins of ice reaching toward something deep inside me that I refused to acknowledge.

*"Security hub is next,"* I said quietly. *"Cut their eyes."*

Mika checked her tactical display—holographic readout projected from the smart-glasses she wore. *"Reinforced oak doors, fifty feet north. Thermal signatures consistent with at least four personnel inside."*

We stacked up outside those doors exactly forty-five seconds later. Behind us lay three corpses freezing solid on expensive imported marble. Ahead waited Moretti's security team.

And somewhere beyond them was the reason we'd come.

* * *

The oak doors explode inward like matchsticks.

I don't even break stride as I channel the kinetic burst—pure mechanical precision translated into brute force. Splinters spray across marble floors, scattering like teeth. Behind me, Grimjaw moves like a shadow given muscle, two Ogre-Kin flanking him with suppressed weapons already raised.

Inside the security hub, four High-Spire elves barely have time to register our entry before their world goes red. The room reeks of that distinctive sterile-sweet scent that clings to corporate types—expensive cologne mixed with the acrid tang of fresh coffee gone cold in designer mugs.

CRT monitors dominate the far wall, their green-phosphor glow casting everything in sickly light. Four screens showing different angles of the manor's interior. Four screens about to die.

"Contact!" One elf—that's all he gets out before Grimjaw's already moving, his .45 barking twice. Center mass. The elf crumples.

The other three scramble for their sidearms holstered at their hips, but they're too slow, too comfortable, too used to guarding paper-pushers instead of actual threats. An Ogre-Kin drops one with a single shot through the throat. The second tries to bring up an expensive-looking pistol, and Grimjaw's there, driving his fist into the elf's solar plexus hard enough to crack ribs.

That leaves number four—the lead retainer, judging by his better suit and the way he was standing behind the main console. He fumbles with his weapon, panic creeping into those ice-blue eyes.

I'm already across the room, frost-cobalt bleeding from my fingertips, coating my combat knife in that telltale iridescent sheen. The temperature in here has already dropped twenty degrees; I can see my breath pluming white in front of me.

The elf fires wild as I close. The bullet shatters a monitor behind my head, sending glass spitting everywhere, but I don't flinch. Can't afford to. My left hand catches his wrist—bones crack under the pressure—and I slam his hand down on the desk.

He screams. That pretty corporate accent cracks like ice on a winter lake.

"You're dead, street-trash! Sterling will—"

Grimjaw's beside us in a heartbeat. His pistol comes around, and he smashes the butt into the elf's temple. Once. Twice. The screaming stops, replaced by wet choking sounds.

"Sterling ain't the one holding the leash tonight, suit," Grimjaw growls, then kicks the elf's legs out from under him.

I drive the frost-cobalt knife through the retainer's pinned hand, nailing it to the mahogany desk. Blood pools instantly, spreading crimson across expensive wood. And then something remarkable happens—it begins crystallizing at the edges, ice forming where the cold from my blade meets his warm flesh.

"Camera systems," I say flatly, yanking the mainframe tower open. Ripping out cables. "Hard drives."

My fingers find the array—they always build them in the same configuration, predictable bastards—and I wrench them free. Metal tears with satisfying screeching sounds. Sparks shower across my knuckles.

All four monitors flicker. Die. Plunge into static.

The manor is blind now.

Silence settles over the security room, broken only by the elf's panicked breathing and the smell of ozone from the burning electronics. There's another odor too—the copper tang of blood mixing with the acrid burn of melted plastic.

Then, faint as a ghost's whisper, drifting down from somewhere above:

A string quartet playing Vivaldi.

Champagne glasses clinking together.

The real party hasn't even noticed we're here yet.

* * *

The security hub behind us was a frozen tomb. Blood and brain matter coated the walls in dark crimson crusts, each splatter caught mid-air by my psychic bleed like insects in amber. The temperature had dropped below zero during the fight—ice crystals formed patterns across shattered monitors, across the faces of dead men who'd never seen me coming.

"Move out," I said.

Grimjaw's heavy footfalls echoed as he followed me through the carnage. Behind him, my fireteam—three ex-special forces types I'd pulled from various mercenary pools—moved with practiced silence despite their gear. They'd seen enough shit to know when to follow orders without questions.

We hit the grand staircase.

My breath plumed thick and white with each inhale. The frost wasn't natural—I could feel it emanating from my core, bleeding outward like radiation from a broken reactor. It crept up the marble steps ahead of us, transforming the ornate iron railing into something from a winter palace. The Sterling family portraits lining the wall caught my eye as we ascended. Generations of smug faces, all those Old Money bastards looking down at us with their painted superiority. Frost bloomed across their gilded frames, creeping over the oil paint itself.

I checked my pulse on the second-floor landing. Sixty beats per minute. Steady as a metronome.

No tremor in my hands. No adrenaline jitters. Just cold, pure calculation. The 4th-Law had burned away everything else.

The second floor corridor stretched before us, carpeted in plush burgundy that crunched beneath our boots with each frozen step. Ahead, massive mahogany double doors marked the formal dining room. Light spilled from underneath—the warm glow of candlelight and civilization, utterly unaware of the death that surrounded them.

Through the doors, muffled by distance but clear enough: the soft strains of a string quartet playing something classical. Bach? Vivaldi? I didn't give a fuck. Behind the music came voices—elegant, refined laughter—and the distinct clink of crystal champagne flutes.

Julian Sterling was giving a toast for his anniversary. Right now. At this exact moment.

"Stack," I whispered.

Grimjaw moved to position without hesitation, his bulk somehow silent despite his size. He racked a round into his shotgun—a beanbag load, non-lethal. Smart. The others followed suit, spreading out. One took kneeling position, another pressed against the opposite doorframe.

I looked at Grimjaw. His tusks were bared in what might've been a grin if you squinted. "Non-lethal on the family. I need them awake for the vault."

He nodded, racking another round. "Copy that, boss. We'll just bruise 'em up real good."

I placed both palms flat against the mahogany doors. The wood groaned—literally *groaned*—as my frost-cobalt magic seeped through the grain, finding every crack and seam in the hinges. Ice formed where my skin touched wood, spreading like frostbite across the surface.

Inside, the toast continued. Someone laughed—a woman's voice, probably Julian's wife.

The frost had reached the doorframes now, transforming the gold leaf into glittering crystals.

My pulse stayed steady at sixty.

I pushed.

---

## CHAPTER 4: CHAPTER 4

The mahogany doors didn't break—they *exploded*.

I put my shoulder through them like they were made of wet cardboard, and the entire frame gave way with a sound like a gunshot crack echoing through marble halls. The doors crashed down onto the polished hardwood of the Sterling Manor dining room, splintering into kindling that skittered across the floor.

Behind me, Grimjaw's bulk filled the doorway, his rust-pitted shotgun held casually across his chest. To my right, the Ogre-Kin shuffled forward, all seven feet of scarred hide and crushing fists. Their eyes burned with that same sickly green phosphorescence that marked every abyssal-crawled creature.

The temperature drop hit like a physical blow.

One moment, the dining room had been warm—overheated even, with fire crackling in some ornate mantlepiece and the body heat of too many well-dressed parasites packed around an absurdly long table. The next moment, a wall of frost-cobalt winter screamed through the shattered doorframe.

Crystal champagne flutes erupted.

Not one by one, but all at once—a cascading symphony of shattering glass as thermal shock ran through the room like a wave. Each flute, each goblet, each decanter of vintage something-or-other exploded into glittering shards. The sound was musical, crystalline, absolutely beautiful in its violent suddenness.

"Jesus Christ!" someone shrieked.

Julian Sterling stood at the head of the table, still on his feet while everyone else flinched or ducked. His bespoke Italian tuxedo probably cost more than most people made in a year. Silver hair swept back perfectly despite the chaos. His face cycled through shock to rage to the practiced corporate mask he'd worn for forty years of cutting throats.

"You South Side thugs don't know whose house you just broke into," he said, voice steady despite the tremor in his hands. "Whatever you've been paid, I'll double it. Triple it."

I didn't blink. Didn't lower the MP5. My finger rested light on the trigger guard, barrel pointed right between his eyes.

"On the floor. Now." My voice came out flat, dead. Empty.

The string quartet in the corner had already scattered, their instruments clattering to the floor. Victoria Sterling—his wife, though 'trophy' was probably more accurate—lay sprawled beneath the table in a ruin of white silk and pearls. Two younger men, his sons maybe, or nephews, still sat frozen in their chairs, veins visible beneath their skin pulsing with that tell-tale dark sludge-thickening.

I fired once.

The ceiling plastered exploded above Julian's head, raining down bits of ornate molding and white dust. The shot cracked like thunder in the enclosed space, followed by the acrid stench of gunpowder mixing with ozone from my frost-wreathed entry.

"That was your warning," I said. "Next one goes through your skull."

Julian's mask finally cracked. He stumbled backward, knocking over his chair with a clatter. His mouth worked soundlessly, like a fish gasping for air.

Then his sons moved.

Both of them roared—a deep, guttural sound that shouldn't have come from human throats—and suddenly they weren't men anymore. They were monsters fueled by premium-grade Sludge, refined in some underground lab where chemistry met demonic pacts. Their bodies swelled, clothes tearing as muscle bulked beyond natural limits. The table flipped between them like a child's toy, launching platters of roasted pheasant and glazed vegetables across the room.

They charged.

And I smiled for the first time in months.

*Let's dance.*

* * *

The eldest heir moved like lightning through honey—fast but sluggish, his muscles pumped full of some chemical abomination that gave him speed without coordination. He cleared the overturned mahogany table in one fluid motion, a silver steak knife gripped in fingers that trembled slightly around the handle.

My frost-cobalt aura flared instantaneous, responding to the threat like a coiled spring released. Time stretched that fraction of a second where instinct becomes action. I felt the temperature plummet ten degrees in my immediate vicinity as azure energy rippled from my skin, crystallizing moisture in the air into microscopic ice particles.

The blade came for my throat at an angle meant to slit deep. I sidestepped left—not far, maybe six inches—but enough. The knife whistled past my ear close enough to shave away a few strands of hair. My right leg snapped up in a front kick that would've ended any normal man's knee joint permanently.

Bone shattered with a wet crunch I could feel through the leather of my boot. The heir's scream cut short as his leg buckled sideways at an impossible angle, and he collapsed onto the Persian rug, clutching his ruined knee. Blood seeped between his fingers, dark against the cream-colored wool.

I didn't hesitate. Never give them time to recover, to adapt, to counter. While he was down, I drove the butt of my MP5 into his jaw with everything I had behind it. His head snapped back hard enough to crack against the edge of the dining table. Teeth exploded from his mouth in a spray of pink froth and red fragments. He went limp, eyes rolling white before consciousness fled entirely.

Behind me, Victoria Sterling let out a strangled cry of horror that might have been her sons' names, or might have been gibberal terror. Didn't matter. She'd made her bed when she decided to mix business with abyssal magic.

Grimjaw had already intercepted the second heir—younger, faster, but just as stupid with Sludge-fueled confidence coursing through his veins. The kid tackled the Orc like some football hero taking down a linebacker, arms locked around Grimjaw's thick waist, clearly planning to use momentum and body weight to bring him down.

The massive green-skinned metahuman barely flinched. He simply grabbed the heir by the throat with one meaty hand, fingers closing around the boy's windpipe with casual precision. Then Grimjaw raised his other hand and slammed the younger heir face-first into the glass display cabinet showcasing centuries-old Chinese porcelain.

The crash was spectacular—a symphony of breaking crystal and shattering china that echoed through the manor like thunder. Antique teacups and plates exploded into jagged shards, scattering across the carpet in glittering fragments. The heir bounced off the cabinet once, twice, then slumped sideways onto the floor, blood streaming from cuts on his forehead and cheeks where glass had embedded itself into his skin.

Grimjaw planted his heavy combat boot squarely on the heir's chest, pinning him to the ruined carpet. The Orc looked down at his captive with those flat, dead eyes that had seen too much death in too many muddy trenches.

"Rich kids," he rumbled, his voice like grinding gears. "Think a little designer Sludge makes 'em tough." He spat a wad of phlegm onto the expensive Oriental rug near the heir's head. "Ain't never fought in the mud."

I stepped over the groaning eldest son—his breath coming in wet, whistling gasps through his broken jaw—and closed the distance to Julian Sterling in three long strides. The patriarch stood frozen, his champagne flute still clutched in trembling fingers, his face drained of all color except for the purple bruise spreading across his cheekbone where my fist had connected earlier.

Without ceremony, I grabbed him by his silk lapels—the fabric expensive enough to feed half the South Side for a month—and hauled him effortlessly to his feet. My frost-cobalt aura pulsed around us both, raising goosebumps on his skin as cold magic seeped through his thousand-dollar suit.

"You wanted to play with forces you don't understand, Julian," I said quietly, my voice barely carrying over the sounds of his sons' pained breathing. "Now we're going to have a conversation about what happens when you open doors that should stay shut."

His eyes darted between mine, searching for something—mercy, reason, fear of consequences. He'd find none of them. Not tonight.

* * *

I watched Julian’s face go from purple rage to something worse—something broken—as the Local 405 crew moved in behind him. They didn't use gentle police procedures. This was raw, industrial muscle work.

"Hands behind your back," one of them growled, already pulling out the heavy-duty zip-ties from their gear belts. The sound when they cinched tight was obscene—a sharp *zzzip* followed by a meaty *click* as the teeth locked into place.

Julian struggled against the restraints, his silk shirt tearing slightly at the shoulder. "What the fuck do you think you're doing? These are assault weapons charges! Police brutality! You have no jurisdiction here!"

The second guy just laughed, a harsh bark. He grabbed Julian's other wrist and pulled it back hard enough to make the man gasp. Another *zzzip*. His ankles got the same treatment, plastic biting into flesh through expensive trousers.

Victoria was next. She fought harder, her heels scraping against the mahogany floor, but it was useless. The crew had done this before—their movements were efficient, brutal. They yanked her hands together behind her back. *Zzzip.*

"No! NO!" Her screams pierced my ears, high-pitched and desperate. "Julian! JULIAN!"

I felt nothing. Not satisfaction. Not pity. Just the cold burning through my veins like liquid nitrogen.

Then came the younger heirs. The ones who'd been bleeding from their noses, their eyes glazed with whatever euphoria that frost-cobalt shit created. They barely resisted, too far gone to care about much beyond the chemical haze in their heads.

I pulled one of the black canvas hoods from my jacket pocket—rough material meant for blocking sight, not comfort. I shoved it down over Victoria’s head without ceremony.

Her muffled shrieks intensified, fabric dampening the sound into something pathetic and small.

"COLE!" Julian's voice cracked now, the aristocratic veneer shattered completely. "Cole, wait! We can talk about this! Please!"

I ignored him. Moved to the first heir. The hood went on easy. Then the second. Both went quiet under the canvas, their struggles weakening.

Only Julian remained visible, his face twisted in an expression I'd seen on a lot of men when they finally understood that money couldn't solve everything.

"You're not a merc," he said, his breath coming in ragged pants. Sweat beaded on his forehead despite the freezing temperature my aura was pumping into the room. I could see his expensive cologne turning sour with fear-sweat, the scent degrading into something acrid. "Who sent you? Morvain? Voss? Somebody had to send you. I can give you ten million right now. Cash. Offshore accounts. Stock in BATC. Just name your price."

I leaned in close enough that he could feel the cold radiating off me like death itself. My voice came out as a low rasp, words forming ice crystals in the air between us: "My price is 800,000 gallons of sludge."

His eyes widened, comprehension dawning in them like a terrible sunrise.

"And you don't have the currency to pay it."

Julian opened his mouth but nothing came out except a strangled gasp. The arrogance had drained completely from his features, leaving behind only naked terror.

I pointed at Grimjaw without looking away from Julian’s face. "The vault."

Grimjaw nodded, his massive frame moving toward where the family knelt bound and hooded. The Ogre-Kin followed, both of them grabbing collars and hauling the prisoners up by main force.

They dragged Victoria first—her muffled protests still audible through the canvas. Then the two heirs, stumbling in their restraints. Finally Julian himself, struggling against his bindings as they pulled him toward the hidden elevator.

The sound of their movements echoed in the suddenly silent dining room. Crystal glasses trembled on the table, then began to crack from the extreme temperature drop my presence was causing. One shattered with a sharp ping.

I stood alone among the wreckage of Sterling Manor's anniversary celebration, frost spreading across the mahogany like creeping decay.

The tribunal would begin soon.

And God help anyone who got in my way.

---

## CHAPTER 5: CHAPTER 5

The elevator lurches downward, hydraulic fluid wheezing through rusted pipes somewhere in the building's guts. I can feel the descent in my knees—the sudden drop in my stomach as we pass below ground level, then the methodical grind of counterweights taking us deeper still.

Grimjaw stands across from me inside the freight car, his massive frame making the space feel claustrophobic despite its size. The three heirs are sandwiched between us—Julian Sterling in the middle, his sons flanking him. All hooded. All bound at wrists and ankles with reinforced cable ties that bite into flesh even through their expensive clothes. The fabric of their hoods is already dampening with blood from where Grimjaw rough-housed them getting them into position.

"Fucking hell," Bram mutters beside me, his voice low enough that only I catch it over the elevator's industrial groan. His black eyes scan the walls as we descend. "You see this shit? Polished steel panels. Climate control vents. This isn't just a basement, Cole. This is a *facility*."

He's right. Even muffled by canvas, I can hear the family's breathing—a synchronized panic rising with each foot we sink beneath Newark's frozen earth. The temperature drops noticeably. My frost-cobalt magic responds instinctively, coils of crystalline energy tracing up my forearms like living tattoos, but I force it down. Not yet. The cold here is different—sterile, controlled, purposeful.

The elevator slows with a mechanical whine that sets my teeth on edge.

Steel doors slide open with a pneumatic hiss, revealing the trophy vault beyond.

It hits you first—the smell. Concrete dust and cleaning solution mixed with something older, something organic and wrong. Then the light. Dozens of halogen surgical lamps snap to life automatically, their harsh white glow illuminating a chamber that stretches back maybe sixty feet. The ceiling disappears into shadows above, but the walls... Christ, the walls are covered.

Glass display cases line every surface, each one climate-controlled and carefully lit from within. Ancient grimoires bound in what looks like human skin. Dwarven forging hammers mounted alongside hunting rifles like some perverse museum. A jar containing what might be a preserved basilisk egg, its scales still gleaming despite preservation. Skulls from species that haven't walked this earth in centuries, arranged by size along one entire wall.

"Sick fucking bastard," Bram whispers now, louder. He can't help himself. "Look at this place. He's got forge-hammers from the 1800s mounted like *hunting trophies*. Sick. Fucking. Bastard."

I don't look at the artifacts. Can't afford to. My eyes lock onto the center of the vault where four heavy steel chairs are bolted to the concrete floor, restraints dangling from each armrest. And between those chairs and the elevator—a medical examination table, stainless steel and pristine, with overhead lighting that hums like an angry hornet.

Grimjaw moves first, his boots echoing as he drags Julian Sterling out of the elevator. The man tries to struggle, muffled sounds coming from beneath the hood, but Grimjaw just adjusts his grip and keeps pulling. The younger sons come next—Grimjaw hauls one while another crew member takes the other. They're lighter than their father, built different, but they fight harder. One catches his elbow on the doorframe hard enough to make me wince.

They hit the concrete floor with meaty thuds that echo through the soundproofed chamber.

The breathing under those hoods gets faster now, more desperate.

I step out last, my own boots clicking against polished concrete as I walk past the displayed atrocities toward the center of the room. My vest feels heavier tonight—the weight of what's inside it pressing against my ribs. I reach into my tactical pouch and pull out a thick manila folder, dog-eared and water-stained from too many nights in my truck.

"Strap them down," I say, my voice flat. Empty. "Get the lights on the examination table."

Someone fumbles with switches near the table. A massive light box mounted on articulated arms swings down, its surface blindingly bright even at half power. It begins to hum—a deep, mechanical vibration that you feel in your sternum.

Bram appears beside me, his expression unreadable. He knows where this is going. We all do.

Julian Sterling is already trying to speak through the gag, words distorted beyond comprehension. His sons are whimpering now, the illusion of control shattered completely.

I open the manila folder, spreading photographs across the nearest steel table like tarot cards of damnation.

"Let's begin," I say.

* * *

The Local 405 crew moved like ghosts through my vault, their efficiency cold and practiced. I watched from the center of the room as they hoisted each captive—Julian Croft first, then Victoria, followed by his two heirs—into four heavy steel chairs bolted to the concrete floor.

Julian fought hardest. His chair scraped and rattled against the bolts, metal shrieking against metal. But Grimjaw was there in an instant, one meaty paw clamping down on Julian's shoulder. The noise stopped. Straps went across his chest, arms, legs—thick leather that bit deep, held firm by iron buckles that clicked shut with finality.

I walked behind him and ripped the black canvas hood from his head.

He gasped, blinking rapidly against the harsh halogen lights that now flooded his vision. His eyes darted around the vault—my vault—taking in the steel tables, the rows of weapons, the medical equipment. Then they found me. Recognition bloomed into terror.

"Please," he whispered, his voice cracking. "My wife. My boys. Let them go. I'll give you everything."

I stepped around to face him, hands shoved in the pockets of my leather jacket. The frost-cobalt magic had receded now, leaving only a hollow, methodical calm. "Your boys are pumped full of the same refined Sludge you dumped into the South Side water table. They stay."

Victoria sobbed quietly, her face still covered. The youngest heir—couldn't be more than eleven—whimpered into his hood. The older one, maybe fourteen, sat rigid and silent, probably already calculating escape routes that didn't exist.

Grimjaw positioned himself at the door, arms crossed over his barrel chest. He said nothing, but his presence filled the space—the promise of violence held in reserve. The rest of the crew took up positions along the perimeter, watching, waiting. Their shadows stretched long under the white light.

I turned away from Julian and approached the humming medical light box near the wall. Inside was a manila folder I'd been carrying for weeks. I opened it, pulling out a series of large, black-and-white medical transparencies.

The first one showed a cross-section of the Newark Bay water table, dated 1987. Clean. Pure. Labeled with precise chemical markers showing nothing beyond standard contaminants.

The second transparency was dated 1993. New markers appeared—sulfur compounds, heavy metals, petroleum distillates. All clustered in the southern quadrant.

By 1999, the third transparency revealed, the contamination had spread like a cancer through the aquifer, reaching residential intake points. Red zones marked areas where children were developing respiratory illnesses at three hundred percent above the national average.

2005's transparency made my hands clench around the plastic sheets. The entire southern half of Newark Bay was now saturated. Cancer clusters. Birth defects. A generation born sick because men like Julian Croft decided profit mattered more than breathable air.

"These are from County General," I said quietly, holding up the latest transparency. "They've been burying these reports since '94. Paying off state inspectors. Making sure nobody connected the dots between your industrial parks and the kids dying on the South Side."

Julian stared at the images, his face draining of color. "That's... those numbers are exaggerated. We followed all regulations."

"You built the regulations." I let the transparency fall to the floor, where it landed with a soft rustle against the concrete. "Then you paid people to ignore them when they didn't work in your favor. How many bodies did it take to get this vault built? How much blood money?"

Victoria's sobbing intensified. She knew. They both knew exactly what their fortune was built on.

I pulled out another folder from the light box—not medical this time, but police files. "Detective Maria Santos spent six years investigating your company. Filing reports. Building cases. Every single file ended up 'lost' or 'inconclusive.' She died in a car accident two months after filing the last one. Her brakes failed on Pulaski Skyway during rush hour."

I looked directly at Julian as I said that last part, watching for any flicker of recognition, guilt, fear. His expression remained carefully neutral, but sweat beaded on his upper lip.

"Was it worth it?" I asked. "All of it. Was the money worth watching children choke on water you poisoned? Worth killing the one cop brave enough to fight back?"

The vault fell silent except for Victoria's muffled crying and the hum of the light box. The smell of iron-gall residue mixed with something else now—the sharp, clean scent of antiseptic from the medical equipment, a sterile odor that somehow made everything feel worse.

I walked over to the steel table and arranged the transparencies in chronological order, spreading them out like evidence at a trial nobody would ever see.

"We're going to have an audience here tonight," I told Grimjaw without looking away from my work. "Make sure the cameras are positioned properly. I want every face clearly visible."

Grimjaw grunted acknowledgment, moving to check the surveillance equipment I'd had installed throughout the vault. Multiple angles. Redundant systems. No chance of technical failure.

Julian watched me arrange my evidence, his breathing shallow and rapid. "What do you want from us?"

Everything. Nothing. Revenge doesn't quantify.

I picked up the 2005 transparency again, holding it up so he could see every detail—every red zone marking another death sentence written in chemical compounds.

"I want you to understand exactly what your legacy is before it ends."

* * *

The vault's air tasted like pennies and formaldehyde. I slapped the medical transparencies onto the glowing light box with a sound that cracked through the sterile silence—*snap*—two sharp reports like bones breaking.

Danny's lungs.

What used to be Danny's lungs.

The X-rays glowed sickly green against the cold backlighting, and there they were—the jagged crystallizations of black iron, spreading like frozen lightning through flesh that was supposed to breathe. Eleven years old. Brass-and-glass Iron-Lung in County General's pediatric ward. Third floor. Room 347. The smell of antiseptic never quite masked the metallic tang of his fear when I visited after my shifts at the machinist plant.

"Look at this," I said, my voice flat as millwork steel. "You remember 2000? You remember signing off on BATC Document 7-Gamma? Eight hundred thousand gallons of Experimental Sludge dumped into the Undercity sewers. Direct injection point Alpha-Seven."

I pulled the ledger from inside my leather jacket—the one I'd lifted from Julian's office last month during a thunderstorm that knocked out Sterling Manor's security grid for exactly four minutes. The paper crinkled as I pinned it beside the X-rays. His signature was there in blue ink, neat and professional, authorizing environmental genocide.

"I know you do." I leaned closer to where Julian hung, suspended by his own copper chains. "Because you're smart enough to remember every decision that didn't get you prosecuted."

My frost-cobalt magic had receded now, leaving behind something colder. Something more purposeful. The vault's temperature dropped another degree, but it wasn't my doing. It was just the weight of what came next.

"This won't cure my brother." My words fell like stones into still water. "It won't bring back the dead in the Undercity. The sliver of justice I take from you tonight is never going to be enough."

I reached down to my belt, fingers closing around the blood-iron pincers. They were custom work—machined from scrap metal I'd salvaged years ago, quenched in rusted motor oil and blessed under no particular god. Just tools. Sharp enough for fine work.

"But it will do for the moment."

The silence pressed against us both. Somewhere far above, through layers of concrete and earth, the world kept turning. Cars on the Pulaski Skyway. Lights in Kearny Marshes. The county hospital's ER running its endless triage. None of it mattered here.

"Bram," I called without looking away from Julian's face.

The door opened. Kovacs stepped inside carrying the copper pot from the Crown Vic's trunk. Heavy thing—sealed tight with wax that smelled like sulfur and old money. Inside, something moved. Scratched. Hungered.

The sound was frantic. Desperate.

Julian's eyes found the pot, then widened.

"No," he breathed. "Cole, please—"

"The Threefold Cord," I interrupted, straightening up and pocketing the pincers. "Penance. Revenge. And a Sliver of Justice."

I walked over to Bram, taking the pot between both hands. It was warm despite the vault's cold. Alive with hunger.

"Danny's lungs aren't getting better." Each word came measured, precise. "The Undercity didn't come back to life when the BATC executives went to federal prison for obstruction of justice. Thirty years each. They'll die comfortable. Dignified. Their families will visit. They'll have books published about their 'controversial legacy.'"

The pot trembled slightly in my grip. Whatever was inside knew what waited.

"A sliver isn't whole. A piece doesn't make a puzzle complete." I turned back to Julian, holding the pot level. "But a sliver is something. When you've got nothing else? That sliver means everything."

Kovacs produced a blowtorch from his coat—not for cutting, just for melting the wax seal.

"For Danny," I whispered. Not to Julian. To myself.

The wax hissed as it gave way.

And then—

---

## CHAPTER 6: CHAPTER 6

The vault smells like old money and older blood.

Julian Sterling blinks consciousness back into his eyes, head lolling against the high-backed leather chair that's bolted to the reinforced concrete floor. His silk suit jacket hangs open, gold cufflinks catching the sickly yellow glow of the sodium-vapor emergency lights. The binding around his wrists—standard issue zip ties, probably from one of his own security stations—digs into flesh but doesn't break skin.

His gaze sweeps the room. Familiar. Safe. The mahogany paneling absorbed decades of cigar smoke and whispered deals. Mounted heads of snow leopards watch from walls lined with climate-controlled display cases. Behind him, through reinforced glass, rests the Sterling family's crown jewel collection: artifacts pulled from dig sites across three continents, each with its own acquisition story written in redacted documents and disappeared lives.

"Comfortable?" I ask, though he can't see me yet. I'm behind him. Always good to let them think they're alone for just a moment longer than they are.

Julian's spine straightens. Corporate instinct overriding pain receptors. "Whoever hired you made a mistake."

I walk around to face him. My work boots crunch over the debris littering the Persian rug—the shattered remains of a crystal decanter, amber liquid still bleeding into the wool fibers. The temperature in here is dropping. It always does when I stop holding it back.

"You don't know who I am." Julian's voice carries that practiced boardroom confidence, like he's addressing hostile shareholders instead of whoever dragged him down here. "My son has people looking for me right now. Security teams. Private contractors. People who understand leverage."

The vault's air circulation system hums. The soundproofing makes it feel submerged, underwater. I pick up a small jade figurine from the nearest table—Song Dynasty, if the appraisal tag is accurate. Hefty thing. Solid.

"I'm not interested in your leverage," I say, and crush the figurine in my palm. Jade shards fall like emerald rain onto the broken glass already covering the floor.

Julian's composure fractures for half a second before slamming back into place. He watches me drop the fragments, jaw tightening. "Fine. You want to play tough. Who holds the contract? Voss? Morvain? The Korean syndicates finally made their move?"

I move to the steel appraisal table dominating the room's center. Maps spread across its surface—I count six different architectural schematics of Sterling properties, each marked with red ink. Property values. Asset lists. Family trees scrawled in ballpoint pen.

"Name your price," Julian says, finding his rhythm again. "Whatever they're paying you, I'll double it. Triple it. Cash. Untraceable accounts. Whatever you want. But I need to know who sent you."

I sweep everything off the table with one arm. Documents scatter like snow. A heavy Ming vase—the one centered on the table, worth more than most people see in a lifetime—hits the concrete and explodes into porcelain confetti. The sound echoes wrong in this dead-silent room, swallowing itself before it can reach the walls.

"Look—" Julian starts again, but I'm already walking away.

Toward the far corner where Julian keeps his personal collection. The really old stuff. Pre-Arcane stuff that shouldn't exist according to any official historical record but does anyway because money writes reality checks that other people have to cash.

I find what I'm looking for in a locked cabinet whose combination I learned from his son's diary—poor bastard kept it under his mattress like he was twelve years old instead of twenty-six. Inside: a Manila folder, thick with age and stained black around the edges.

Grease stains.

I carry it back to him.

Julian's eyes track my movement. He doesn't flinch when I drop the folder in his lap, just stares at it like it might bite him. "What is this?"

"Not who hired me." I pull up a chair—identical to his, also bolted down—and sit facing him. My expression doesn't change. Can't afford to let it. "Who I am."

He opens the folder. X-rays slide out first, fanned across his knees. Ribcage. Spine. Skull. Each one stamped with County General ER timestamps stretching back to 1999. Old fractures healed crooked. Metal plates holding bone together where they shouldn't be able to hold.

"You're a mess," Julian says, voice dripping contempt. "Some thug who got too ambitious."

The next page makes him pause. Photographs this time. Sub-Station Seven. Not the clean tourist version, but the Undercity—the real one beneath Newark Bay where the power actually comes from. Where machines hum with something that predates electricity. Where men like Julian Sterling send their problems to disappear.

"Recognize anything?" I ask.

His hand trembles slightly as he lifts the top photo. The image shows the substation's control room six hours ago before everything went sideways. I'm in the picture—not looking at the camera—but visible enough. Coveralls splattered with hydraulic fluid. Wrench in hand. Working on the main transformer housing like I belong there because I do.

"That's you," Julian whispers.

"Keep going."

More photos. Different angles. Different days over different years. Me working the night shift at County General's machine shop. Same hands, same grease-stained coveralls, always alone at three AM when no one else can see what needs doing.

And then—

A photograph of a girl. Maybe nine years old, standing outside an apartment building in the South Side's worst block. She's holding a metal butterfly—a piece I made for her on a lathe because she asked pretty please and how could I say no?

Julian's face drains of color. He recognizes the location even if he doesn't recognize why it matters.

"That building collapsed two months later," I tell him, watching his eyes. "Seventeen families died inside. Structural failure. The official report said faulty welds."

"You did them." His voice barely carries across the space between us.

"I did."

The temperature in the vault has dropped another ten degrees. Frost creeps along the edges of Julian's whiskey decanter, crystallizing the amber liquid inside into geometric patterns that shouldn't be possible.

"This is insane," Julian breathes, but his corporate certainty is bleeding away faster than the frost spreading across the walls. "You're... what are you?"

I stand up. Walk to where he sits bound and helpless in his own kingdom's treasure room.

"A mechanic," I answer quietly. "Same as always."

His gaze finally meets mine—and whatever he sees there makes something in him break.

The real delusion, I think, watching recognition dawn across his features, isn't money or power. It's thinking that people like me exist anywhere except right in front of you until they don't anymore.

* * *

The X-ray box hums to life with a faint electrical whine, bathing half my face in cold blue light as I pin the films against the translucent surface. The image glows through the plastic—lungs turned to crystalline nightmare, black-iron shards branching like frozen lightning through delicate tissue.

Danny Valdez. Eleven years old when he took his last breath three weeks ago.

I hear Julian Sterling shift behind me, the leather creaking of his chair restraints cutting through the vault's oppressive silence. I don't turn around. Can't afford the distraction. Not while I'm holding this particular brand of hell in my hands.

"Recognize him?" My voice sounds wrong even to me—flat, metallic, like grinding gears in a dead machine. "This is what 800,000 gallons of Experimental Sludge does to a kid's lungs. Turns them into rock candy. Black iron crystallizes in the alveoli. Every breath becomes sandpaper dragging across broken glass."

I let the films drop, watching them flutter to the mahogany floor. Then I reach into my coat pocket and pull out the ledger—water-stained, edges curled from sitting too long in the South Side flood zones where children used to play before they started coughing blood.

I slap it down on the light-box, right over Danny's ghost.

Julian's eyes track the movement. He sees the date stamps. November 2003. Authorized by J.S. Corporate seal intact. Undercity Water Flush Initiative, Phase Three. Right there in neat corporate font: *"Discharge point Delta-7, South Sector Metahuman Residential Zone. Volume: 819,456 gallons. Material: Class-4 Industrial Waste, Experimental Batch."*

"The boy was caught in the initial splashback," I say, pulling another X-ray from inside my jacket. This one smaller, more compact—an adult ribcage punctured by a steel-toothed goblin wrench, lung collapsed completely. "His mother tried to carry him to County General. Made it three blocks before she dropped. She was a sandhog at Sub-Station Seven. Worked eighteen years for Sterling Consolidated."

I feel the temperature dropping around us. Not from any climate control system. From me. The hex is taking hold now, frost-cobalt settling into bone-deep certainty that this man deserves every molecule of suffering I can engineer.

Julian stares at the medical images for a long moment. His jaw tightens. When he speaks again, his voice has shed its corporate polish entirely, revealing something rawer underneath—a man accustomed to justifying atrocities with spreadsheets and zoning maps.

"You're doing all this over a few thousand sewer-rats?" He laughs, sharp and ugly. "Look at the zoning maps, pal. Those Orcs, those Goblins, the Dwarven sandhogs—they're expendable slag. We flushed the pipes to build the Telluric grid. It's progress."

The words hang in the frozen air between us. I watch his expression, searching for even a flicker of shame or regret. Find nothing but the cold certainty of a predator who's never been challenged before.

"Progress." I repeat the word like it's a foreign language I'm trying to comprehend. "Is that what you called it when Sub-Station Seven went up? Progress?"

"That was industrial sabotage," Julian snaps back. "Some eco-terrorist cell. You think I had anything—"

"Don't." My hand comes up, fingers still stained dark with Black-Iron residue from dragging his family down here. "You authorized the dump. Your signature. Your authorization codes. Eight hundred thousand gallons of poison into drinking water because it was cheaper than proper disposal. Because the people living there didn't have lobbyists. Didn't have lawyers filing lawsuits. Didn't matter that their children would turn to stone inside their own ribs."

I step closer to where he sits bound, close enough to smell his expensive cologne mixing with sweat and fear. His eyes dart toward a sleek black laptop sitting on an adjacent desk—one of those ultra-thin models that probably costs more than most South Side families make in a year.

"There are six million metahumans in the Undercity," I continue. "Six million people your company decided were worth less than the cost of proper waste management. So you dumped your experimental chemicals into their reservoirs. You clogged their lungs with Black Iron. And when they started dying, when County General's ER became a morgue for kids with crystallized organs, you bought politicians and controlled the news cycle until it became 'industrial accident' and then 'urban renewal opportunity.'"

Julian shifts in his restraints, testing them. Finding them solid as I made them. He takes a breath, clearly calculating odds, weighing options the way men like him always do—everything reduced to assets, liabilities, and acceptable losses.

"I'm making you an offer," he says finally, voice dropping back into that corporate smoothness like switching costumes between scenes. "Name your price. Cash. Untraceable accounts. Whatever you want."

He nods toward the laptop. Some kind of transfer protocol already queued up, no doubt. Ready to buy his way out of this the same way he's bought everything else—with money that means nothing to people whose children are turning to stone in their chests.

I look at him for a long moment. Feel the frost spreading along my fingertips, creeping up my wrists.

"You think this is about money." It's not a question. "You think because I came from the slums, because I smell like machine oil and desperation, that I'll trade justice for cash."

The temperature drops another five degrees. Ice crystals begin forming on the edges of Julian's crystal whiskey decanters, catching the blue light from the X-ray box in prismatic fragments across the vault walls.

"Danny Valdez was eleven years old," I say quietly. "His mother worked eighteen years for Sterling Consolidated. And you"—I lean in close enough that he can see every detail of my face in the reflected light—"you called them expendable slag."

My hand moves fast—faster than his eyes can track. Not toward him, but toward the desk where that sleek black laptop sits waiting with its promises of easy money and moral bankruptcy.

The hex finds it first—a pulse of blood-iron that fries the circuitry instantly. Sparks spray upward like dying fireworks. The screen goes black. Dead.

Julian flinches, then swallows hard.

"No?" He tests the word like tasting something bitter. "What do you want, then?"

But I'm already turning away, heading for the door. Behind me, I hear the click-clack of chains as he struggles against his restraints, voice rising in panic now.

"What do you want?!"

I pause at the threshold, one hand on the vault door's heavy handle. Don't turn around.

"I want you to remember their names," I say softly. "Every single one. When you're down here in the dark, remember Danny Valdez. Remember Maria Valdez who carried her son three blocks before she died. Remember them

* * *

The vault goes silent except for our breathing—and Julian's breath is already turning to white mist in the air.

I stand there, watching him watch me, my blood-iron hex locked down tight as a frozen piston. Ten degrees cooler now. Fifteen maybe. The leather couches creak under the weight of the Sterling family—Julian on one knee like a supplicant, his wife cradling their daughter, both of them wide-eyed and waiting for some goddamn hero to walk through the mahogany doors.

That's not happening.

Julian spreads his hands wide, rings catching the warm amber light from the recessed ceiling fixtures that are working overtime against the cold. "Cole," he says, smooth as oil on water. "Let's be reasonable here. Let's talk about solutions."

He gestures toward an IBM ThinkPad sitting open on a pedestal near the wet bar. The screen glows that distinctive late-90s green-phosphor glow. "Right now, I can authorize a wire transfer. Ten million dollars. Routed through three corporate shells, deposited into a Cayman account. Untraceable. By morning, it's yours."

His voice carries that practiced boardroom confidence, the kind of thing he probably uses to buy politicians and bury union strikes. But this isn't a negotiation.

"You think you're a monster," he continues, still talking like we're two businessmen discussing merger terms. "But monsters don't have children. Monsters don't worry about medical bills. That kid of yours—what was her name? Maria? She needs new lungs. High-Spire clinics can do things the South Side can only dream of."

The frost-cobalt ward in my veins pulses, and the temperature drops another five degrees. The whiskey decanters on the bar start showing crystalline formations at their bases. The air tastes metallic.

I pull out my Motorola Razr—heavy, bulky, indestructible—and flip it open with a sharp *clack*. The blue backlight illuminates my face in the darkness. 11:52 PM. Sub-Station Seven is burning miles away right now. The Undercity is lighting up like the Fourth of July.

I check the time once more. Close it. The phone snaps shut with that satisfying plastic crack.

Then I look at Julian Sterling.

"You think this is a negotiation," I say, my voice coming out low and mechanical, rusted gears grinding in my throat. Pure North Jersey-noir cadence, no inflection, just statement of fact. "You think you're in a boardroom. You're not. You're in a slaughterhouse."

Julian's eyes narrow. His wife makes a small whimpering sound.

I walk over to the IBM ThinkPad. The screen shows some kind of banking software, fields waiting for authorization codes. Ten million dollars. Enough to change everything. Enough to give Maria a shot at living past eighteen.

My hand tightens around my rune-etched wrench.

And then I bring it down.

The aluminum frame cracks with a sound like a gunshot. The LCD screen explodes into a shower of sparkling glass fragments and smoking lithium-ion battery acid. Sparks pop and fizz across the mahogany pedestal. The smell of burning electronics fills the suddenly frigid air.

Julian staggers back, his breath plumming now, visible in front of his face like a ghost.

"That's your answer," I tell him, watching the smoke curl from the ruined laptop.

Without another word, I turn my back on all of them—the rich bastard on his knees, the wife clutching her daughter, the vault full of stolen treasures and empty promises. 

I walk to where I left my canvas duffel bag. Unzip it. Start pulling things out.

Blue-flame welding torch. Heavy iron tongs that clink against the floor as I set them down. A spool of braided steel cable. Industrial bolt cutters.

"Cole, wait—"

Julian's voice cuts off as he sees what I'm laying out.

This isn't about money anymore.

It never was.

---

## CHAPTER 7: CHAPTER 7

The cold is absolute now. It seeps up through the concrete floor like something alive, crawling past the cuffs around my ankles, settling into my bones. The laptop's smoking ruin still hisses in the darkness somewhere behind Julian's chair, but I'm not listening to that anymore.

I'm listening to him breathe.

Rapid. Shallow. The kind of breathing that happens when your body realizes what your mind hasn't accepted yet—that this is real, that there's no way out, that every instinct screaming *run* is just noise because running isn't an option that exists anymore.

He hasn't noticed I've stopped moving.

His eyes are locked on the ruined laptop like it was a god that just died. His hands—those manicured, pristine hands that probably haven't done honest work since before his father bought his first commission—are shaking against the armrests of that cheap metal chair.

Good.

I walk to the steel table. My boots scrape against concrete. Each step deliberate. Measured. Let him hear that. Let him count each one if he wants. There's nowhere for those sounds to go except back into his ears, bouncing off these vault walls until they're all he can hear besides his own heartbeat hammering against his ribs.

The table's surface is stained. Years of use. Blood mostly, but also oil, acid, other things I don't bother categorizing. I wipe it down anyway, dragging the rag across the metal in slow, methodical strokes. Back and forth. Like I'm prepping a workbench at Sub-Station Seven.

Because in a way, I am.

I line up my tools with the same precision I'd use on a complex assembly. The industrial zip-ties clink against the steel—a heavy, final sound. Then the leather belts, still thick and supple despite how many times I've used them. The welding torch comes next, its brass valve catching the dim light from above. And finally, the iron pincers. Raw steel, forged in some back-alley shop where questions weren't asked and quality wasn't guaranteed, just probability.

Julian's breathing hitches.

"That's... what is that?" His voice cracks. That High-Spire polish he wore like armor has started flaking away, revealing the soft, desperate thing underneath. "Cole, wait. Wait, listen to me! I have clearance codes! I have the Pylon schematics! I can give you Voss! I can give you Morvain!"

I adjust the valve on the torch. The hiss builds slowly, deliberately. Blue flame sparks to life, small at first, then growing. It's the color of frost on a window in winter, the kind that forms when something dies inside a house that nobody checks for weeks.

"I'll get to them," I say.

The words are flat. Matter-of-fact. Because they're true.

From the corner, behind Julian, there's movement. Victoria's muffled whimpers cut through the hiss of the torch. Her children—grown now, but still bound and gagged like livestock—stir against their restraints. Their eyes wide enough to see even in this half-light.

I don't look at them.

Can't.

Because if I do, if I let myself see them right now, something might crack in whatever passed for my soul before tonight. And I need that thing intact. Need it cold and sharp and unbroken.

The blue-black residue on my knuckles begins to flake. Iron-gall. The smell hits next—ozone and butane mixing with the damp concrete scent of the vault. My magic is priming itself, responding to the intention building in my chest like pressure behind a dam wall.

Julian's bravado has completely shattered now. He's actually shaking, his whole body trembling as he watches me work.

"You... you killed my wife's brother!" The accusation comes out strangled, pathetic. "You think I won't pay? You think I can't—"

"She had a choice." I set down the rag, pick up one of the zip-ties, run it between my fingers like rosary beads. "You're making yours right now."

The torch flame dances higher. I watch it reflect off the stainless steel surface of the table, casting writhing shadows across Julian's face. His expensive suit looks wrong here. Out of place. Like trying to wear silk into a knife fight.

"I have money," he tries again, desperation making him stupid. "More than you could spend in ten lifetimes! I can make you comfortable! I can make you powerful!"

I turn the torch off. The sudden silence is louder than any scream.

Walk toward him slowly.

Each step feels like walking through deep water, but I don't rush. Don't give him the satisfaction of urgency. This isn't about speed anymore. It's about completion.

About delivering what I came here to deliver.

He leans back in the chair, trying to create distance that doesn't exist. His eyes dart around, looking for exits there aren't any of. Looking for help that's not coming.

"The Threefold Cord," I say quietly. "Ever hear of it?"

His jaw works, but no sound comes out.

"It's an old concept. Before the Breach. Before magic leaked back into this world and made everything complicated." I stop just outside arm's reach. Close enough that he can smell the iron on me, taste the ozone in the air. "A mechanic's principle. Every joint needs three points of contact or it fails under pressure. Engines. Machines. Structures."

I flex my fingers. Feel the frost-cobalt state settling deeper into my bones, cold as a tomb but burning with its own terrible heat.

"You're going to learn why they call it that tonight."

* * *

I lean closer, close enough that Julian can feel the frost creeping up his expensive silk collar. My breath doesn't mist in the air—it crystallizes before it even leaves my lips, tiny shards of ice that settle on his forehead like a crown of winter.

"Let me tell you how this works," I say, my voice flat and distant, like I'm reading instructions off a sheet I memorized years ago. "There are three cords in everything I do now. Three strands twisted together so tight they might as well be one."

The ticking of the clock grows louder. Each second feels like a hammer blow against my skull.

"The first cord is Penance. That's what this started as—I told myself I was making amends for being late, for not watching him close enough, for all those years I spent in the garage instead of teaching him to throw a ball." I straighten up slightly, rolling my shoulders. The frost-cobalt aura pulses once, and the temperature drops another few degrees. I hear Julian's teeth start to chatter. "But penance is a lie we tell ourselves when we're too scared to admit the truth."

My hand reaches into the toolkit beside me. I pull out a pair of heavy-duty wire cutters, their jaws dark with old rust that's been baked onto the metal by heat so intense it left its fingerprint. The handle feels cold in my palm, but not from any magic. Just old iron.

"The second cord is Revenge. That's the easy part. Everyone understands revenge. You hurt someone, someone hurts you back. Simple transaction." I crouch down again, bringing our faces level. My reflection stares back at me from his dilated pupils—dead eyes, empty eyes, the eyes of a man who stopped feeling anything useful months ago. "But here's the thing about revenge, Julian. It's a hunger that can never be satisfied. You think cutting out your heart will make the pain stop? It won't. The hole just gets bigger."

I reach behind me without looking and grab something else from the kit. A small propane torch. I click the ignition, and a bright blue flame sputters to life with a sound like tearing silk.

"Which brings us to the third cord," I continue, holding the flame inches from Julian's face. He flinches away, but there's nowhere to go. His wrists are bound tight enough to cut off circulation. "The Sliver of Justice."

The word tastes like ash on my tongue.

"This isn't justice, Julian. Don't ever mistake what happens next for justice." I lower the flame until it hovers over the X-rays spread across his chest. The heat intensifies, and I watch as the film starts to curl at the edges, blackening. Danny's lungs begin to blur and burn. "Justice would mean my boy walks out of County General tomorrow with clean lungs. Justice would mean every metahuman you sold out comes back from under the grid, whole and breathing. Justice would mean you pay some kind of debt that actually balances the scales."

I turn off the torch with a sharp click. Smoke rises from the ruined films, carrying the acrid stench of burning plastic.

"But we don't live in that world anymore. We haven't since the day you decided profit was more important than people." My voice drops even lower, barely above a whisper. "So this is all I can offer. One sliver of something that might pass for justice if you squint real hard. One piece of accountability for a mountain of bodies."

My fingers find the wire cutters again. I squeeze them once, experimentally. The rusted jaws give a metallic screech.

"It won't fix anything. It won't scrape a single ounce of black iron out of my son's lungs. And it sure as hell won't bring back the dead you buried under the grid." Each word falls like a stone into still water. "I know that. You know that. God knows that, if there's anyone left listening up there."

The ticking clock seems to slow down or speed up—I can't tell which anymore.

"But it's what I've got."

Something shifts in Julian's expression. Fear gives way to desperation. He starts talking fast, words tumbling over each other. Money. Information. Connections. Anything he has, anything he is, laid on the table like chips in a game he's suddenly realized he's already lost.

I let him talk. Let him drown in his own futile bargaining. There's no point interrupting—he needs to hear the sound of his own voice one last time, even if it's just the prelude to silence.

Behind me, I hear it: a heavy rhythmic pounding against the vault door. Thud. Thud. Thud. Someone's here. Someone found us.

But the sound feels distant now, like it's coming from underwater. Like it doesn't quite matter anymore.

"Shut up," I say quietly.

Julian's eyes go wide.

I lean in close one final time, until our foreheads are almost touching.

"The cords are tied," I whisper. "And I'm cutting them loose."

* * *

The cold doesn't bother me anymore. It never really did, but now it's like breathing. Frost spreads across the concrete floor in crystalline fractals, each branch reaching toward the center where I stand. My knuckles crack—not from the temperature, but because something else wants out. Blue-black residue flakes off my fingers like rusted iron filings, clinging to the air before dissolving into nothing.

Julian watches me from his chair, bound by those cheap zip ties that won't hold him long once he gets his blood flowing again. Good. Let him think about escaping. Let him count the seconds until help arrives. He'll be counting for a while.

"Justice is a broken concept," I tell him, my voice flat as machine oil. The words come easy now, rehearsed a thousand times in the dark hours between midnight shifts at the plant. "You know what they taught us in school? That everyone deserves a fair trial. Due process. The right to confront your accuser." I laugh—dry, humorless. "What a fucking joke."

I pick up one of the tools from my workbench. It's heavy, cast iron, meant for shaping metal under extreme heat. The kind of thing that leaves scars you can feel in your bones when the weather changes.

"They gave your father fair trials. Three of them. Three chances to prove his innocence." I turn the tool over in my frost-numbed hands. "Didn't matter. He was guilty. We all knew it. The whole county knew it. But the system—this beautiful, sacred system—said we had to play along. Had to let him walk free twice before they finally got it right on the third try."

The room feels smaller now. Or maybe I'm taking up more space than I should. Hard to tell when you're standing outside yourself, watching your own hands.

"And what did justice get for him? Twenty years in a maximum security facility where he learned new skills. Made connections. Built an empire from behind bars." My grip tightens on the iron tool. "So when he gets out, who does he hurt first? Who does he blame?"

Julian flinches. His eyes dart toward the laptop on the floor, the screen still cracked and flickering with corrupted data.

"The system failed your father," I continue, stepping closer. Each footfall echoes like a gunshot in this frozen tomb we've made down here. "And tonight, Julian, the system is going to fail you too. Not because it's broken—because it never worked to begin with. It's just theater. A show we put on so people like you can sleep at night, thinking there are rules."

I stop two feet away from him. Close enough to see the fear in his eyes. Far enough that he might think he still has a chance.

"Your money won't save you. Your lawyers can't reach you down here. Your father's ghosts aren't coming through that door." I look past him to the heavy vault entrance. "But something else is."

The Nextel on my hip chirps—once, twice, three times. A signal, not a message. I press the call button back, holding it down until my thumb goes numb from the cold.

"Justice isn't about fairness," I say, letting go of the button. "It's about consequences. And you, Julian... you're about to face some consequences that the courts would never allow."

Hydraulics hiss—metallic, powerful, final. The vault door swings open with a groan that rattles my teeth.

Grimjaw ducks through first, seven feet of Sludge-scarred muscle barely fitting through the frame. Behind him, three more figures squeeze into the room: two Goblins with mottled green skin and yellowed eyes that glow in the dim light, and an Ogre-Kin whose head nearly brushes the ceiling.

The smell hits me like a wall—sewage water, cheap tobacco, wet fur, and something else underneath. Something hungry.

"The pot, Reyes. Rats are hungry. Sludge got 'em mean," Grimjaw spits onto the polished mahogany floor, black chewing tobacco splattering across the surface. He jerks his thumb at one of the Goblins, who shoves forward carrying a copper vessel sealed tight with iron rivets. It vibrates violently, metallic scraping sounds echoing from inside as whatever's trapped within claws against the walls.

I watch Julian's face go pale. Watch his eyes lock onto that writhing container and understand exactly what it contains.

"Because a sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone," I tell him, holding his gaze as Grimjaw drops the copper pot onto the steel table with a crash that reverberates through my bones.

The Orcs move toward Julian's chair.

And I let them.

---

## CHAPTER 8: CHAPTER 8

The air tastes like ozone and old blood when I give the nod. Grimjaw's grin spreads across that scarred face like a rust stain bleeding through cloth. He makes a gesture—I don't need to see it clearly in this half-light, I know what it means—and two of his Ogre-Kin goons move forward like wrecking balls wrapped in muscle.

Julian starts talking fast, words tumbling out in that smooth corporate veneer he thinks will save him. "Now wait, there's been a misunderstanding—my people know where I am—they have protocols—" His voice cracks higher when those meaty hands grab his lapels.

The first tear of fabric sounds like ripping canvas. Then another. The expensive silk gives way under brute force, golden thread snapping like guitar strings. The shirt follows, buttons scattering across the concrete floor like tiny white teeth. Underneath, Julian's skin is pale and unmarked, soft from years behind desks instead of on street corners.

"Please!" He thrashes now, actually struggling, which only makes it worse. The Ogres don't hesitate. One grabs each arm while Grimjaw moves to his legs. They lift him off the ground like he weighs nothing—because to them, he doesn't.

The cold slap of bare flesh against steel echoes through the vault. Julian's gasp cuts short into a strangled cry as his back meets the appraisal table. The metal must feel like ice, even through his panic. His naked body shivers, not from cold but from primal fear.

Grimjaw produces a roll of industrial zip-ties from somewhere—probably kept them handy for occasions exactly like this. The *click-click* of plastic ratchets fills my ears as they secure each wrist to the table's corners. Julian bucks hard against the restraints, veins standing out on his neck and forehead.

"Your corporate Elves are dead on the lawn, suit," Grimjaw says, that gravel-deep voice rolling over Julian like an avalanche. "Ain't nobody coming down here but us."

Julian's screaming now, incoherent words dissolving into raw sound. The Ogres work methodically, wrapping heavy leather belts around his ankles next, pulling tight until the black straps bite into skin and draw thin lines of crimson. Same with his neck—a wide strap at the throat, forcing his head back against the steel, cutting off any real movement.

When they finish, Julian is completely immobilized. Spread-eagled on that freezing table like a specimen waiting for dissection. His chest heaves with panicked breaths, his eyes wide and darting everywhere except where I'm standing at the head of the table.

I let him see it then—the faint glow starting in my palms, blue-black iron-gall residue coating my fingers like living paint. The hexes are ready. They've been waiting all night for this moment.

The copper pot sits between my feet, steam rising from its contents. Those razor-rats are stirring inside, sensing what's coming. Sensing their purpose.

I pick up the pair of raw iron pincers from the instrument tray beside me. They're cold in my grip, solid weight balancing perfectly. The metal catches what little light there is down here, throwing back shadows.

"I believe we have much to discuss, Mr. Sterling," I say quietly. My voice barely carries across the vault, but Julian hears it—hears every word—and goes still as death beneath those restraints.

* * *

The metallic tang fills my mouth—that taste of old blood and iron that means I've pushed too far, dug too deep into reserves I shouldn't be touching. My hands are slick with it now, both literal crimson and that blue-black residue from the gall-work. The frost-cobalt chill hasn't left me since I stepped into this tomb, but underneath it burns something worse: the heat of what's coming next.

Julian's breath comes in ragged, wet gasps. His head lolls against the concrete, dark hair matted with sweat and grime. The silver chains haven't moved an inch—good. Can't have him getting ideas about struggle. Not yet.

"Grim," I say without looking at her. My voice sounds like gravel scraped across bone. "Need the pincers."

I hear her footfalls, the deliberate weight of them. She sets the tools down beside me with a *clink* that echoes through the vault. Three pairs of iron implements, each one crafted by my own hands months ago for exactly this kind of work. Not the flashy stuff, not the showmanship. This is mechanics. Precision.

My pulse doesn't spike as I reach for them. Sixty beats per minute. Flatline calm.

The first pair I pick up feels right in my grip—they're meant for delicate work. I move to the workbench, firing up the small forge I set up hours ago. The coals glow orange, then white-hot as I feed them air with steady pumps. I can feel Julian's eyes on me even though he's half-conscious, that instinctive fear that tells prey when the predator is preparing something new.

Smart boy.

I hold the tips of the pincers directly into the hottest part of the flame. Blue-black iron-gall residue begins to crawl across the metal, feeding off the heat. It won't burn him—not exactly—but cold iron has ways of making itself known. Ways that bypass ordinary pain responses and go straight to nerve endings screaming.

"He's waking up," Grimjaw observes from somewhere behind me. Her voice carries that same flat affect she always uses when we're working.

"Good." I pull the pincers out. They glow faintly in the low light, wisps of gall-smoke curling from their tips. "He needs to be conscious for this part."

I return to the table where Julian lies bound. His eyes are starting to flutter open, pupils dilating as consciousness drags him back from whatever black hole his mind tried to retreat into. He sees me approaching and tries to turn away.

Bad move.

My free hand clamps down on his jaw—gentle enough not to break anything, firm enough that he can't look anywhere but at my face. At what he's made me become.

"You looked away when you dumped the Sludge," I say quietly, leaning down so our faces are inches apart. My breath must smell like copper and exhaustion. "You looked away when the Undercity drowned. You don't get to look away today."

His eyes widen. Realization hits before the physical contact does.

The pincers come up between us. He makes a strangled sound as I bring them toward his face, some animal noise of protest. But it's too late. The sterilized tips press against his left eyelid with just enough pressure to make the point.

The sizzle is immediate. Not loud, but present—a quiet *hiss* of flesh meeting purposefully treated iron. Julian's body goes rigid, muscles locking as shock overrides everything else. A wet sound escapes his throat as the cold metal bites into the delicate tissue.

"Hold still," I tell him, though I know he can't. Won't.

The right eyelid gets the same treatment. Another hiss. Another full-body convulsion against the chains. Bloodshot eyes start to bulge as tears well up immediately, unable to find relief through closed lids now.

I apply steady pressure to both upper lids until they're clamped open, then switch to the lower pairs. These ones lock in place with a soft *click*—a mechanism I built specifically for this. They'll hold position even if he thrashes. Even if he passes out again. Even if I have to walk away from him.

By the time I'm done, Julian's entire face has gone pale except where the iron touches—there it's reddened and starting to bruise around the contact points. His eyes are wide open, pupils blown so large that only thin rings of color remain. Tears stream sideways down his temples, mixing with sweat.

And he can't look away. Can't blink. Can't hide behind unconsciousness or deflection or any of those coward's tools.

His fixed stare reflects the vault lights back at me like a cornered animal seeing its death approaching.

Satisfied, I straighten up and roll my shoulders. My back protests—I've been hunched over too long. The frost-cobalt chill settles deeper into my bones.

"Grimjaw." I step back from the table, gesturing toward the floor near Julian's feet. "Show him what we brought."

She's already moving before I finish speaking, crouching by the copper pot she carried in earlier. It's been sitting there steaming slightly—not from heat but from whatever unholy thing is inside making it react to the vault's atmosphere.

Julian's breathing quickens when he sees her reach for it. He knows. Somehow, on some primal level, he knows what comes next.

The lid scrapes as she lifts it.

* * *

The copper pot lands with a sickening *thud* on Julian's bare stomach. I hear him gasp through the rag stuffed between his teeth, see his eyes clamp shut like a man waiting for execution. Good. Let him imagine the worst.

"Grim," I say, my voice steady despite the frost-cobalt burn still crawling up from my fingertips. "Steel plate."

The troll doesn't question. Just slides the heavy circular steel across the concrete floor with a metallic shriek that makes several of the gathered metas wince. It fits perfectly over the mouth of the inverted pot—copper pressed flat against Julian's pale flesh, steel creating an airtight seal above it.

For three seconds, there's silence except for Julian's panicked breathing.

Then the screaming starts.

High-pitched, wet, desperate. The sound of dozens of starved razor-rats suddenly finding purchase after being held upside-down in copper darkness. Their claws scrape against the underside of the steel plate first—a frantic pattering like fingernails on a coffin lid. Then they hit Julian's skin.

"Oh fuck," I mutter, watching a line of thin red scratches appear on his lower abdomen. Blood beads immediately, dark against white. "That's gonna leave marks."

A goblin machinist cackles from near the vault entrance, her yellowed fangs catching the dim light. "Hear 'em scratchin', corpo? They want out. They want meat." She licks her lips slowly. "Been three days since Grimjaw caught these little beauties. You know what happens to razor-rats when they go that long without feed?"

I do. I've seen it before in the Kearny Marshes, where Sterling-Morris Chemical dumped their arcane byproducts for years. The rats mutated, grew bigger, meaner, developed those razor-sharp quills along their spines. And when they went hungry...

"They get desperate," I say, picking up the heavy leather straps. "They'll chew through anything."

The goblin grins wider. "Especially when they can smell blood."

Julian's chest heaves beneath the weight of the pot, trying to buck upward. Can't move more than an inch with the restraints already biting into his shoulders and thighs.
