## CHAPTER 11: CHAPTER 11

The screaming stopped at exactly eleven forty-two.

I counted the seconds between Julian Sterling's final gasp and the moment the vault fell into absolute silence, save for that god-awful hiss—that wet, cooking sound as the copper pot settled against what remained of his torso. The cherry-red glow was already fading to dull brown, like embers dying in a forgotten fireplace.

Sixty beats per minute.

My fingers pressed against my own carotid artery, feeling the steady drum beneath skin and bone. I didn't need to check. I knew. I always knew. My heart had been beating exactly sixty times a minute since the moment I'd kicked open this vault door, and it wasn't going to change now.

Julian's eyes were clamped shut—one lid half-melted, the flesh bubbled and blackened around the edges where spray had caught him during the retribution. His mouth hung open, tongue swollen and purple. The smell hit me in waves: charred pork fat mixing with boiling copper and something else, something metallic-sweet that made my iron-gall residue flake off in blue-black crusts near the welding torch still smoking against the wall.

"Jesus fucking Christ," Grimjaw muttered beside me, his chest heaving like a bull after a dusty fight. Blood on his tusks. Blood splattered across his forearms. He spat—a thick wad that landed near Julian's outstretched hand. "It ain't enough, Reyes. Doesn't bring my brother back from the sludge-vats."

I didn't look at him. Didn't look away from those clamped eyes.

"It’s never enough, Grim." My voice came out flat, icy rasp—perfect 2000s noir if you asked me, though nobody did. "But it’s a start."

Wiping a rag across my cheek—some arterial spray had caught me when the pot went over—I moved past the corpses. Victoria Sterling lay twisted among her heirs, her designer dress torn open to reveal the defensive talisman she'd worn under her breast. Useless. All useless now. I signaled Grimjaw with a sharp jerk of my chin toward his people. They backed off the bodies reluctantly, wiping their hands on rags already soaked through.

My boots left prints in the blood-slicked mahogany floor as I circled what was left of Julian. Frost crept up the steel table legs where my feet touched, spreading like veins across the metal surface. Ten degrees colder in here now. The air tasted like frozen iron.

That Timex watch on my wrist—the analog kind, because digital couldn't be trusted anymore—ticked its way toward eleven forty-three. We were on the clock. Always on the clock since the Breach opened up the world and let all this shit pour through.

"What now?" Grimjaw asked, voice rougher than usual.

Now? Now I saw it.

The Mosler safe built into the far wall, behind that ruined oil painting—a landscape piece showing some pastoral bullshit that had been slashed down the middle by whatever weapon had killed one of the bodyguards earlier. The safe itself was massive, older than Christ, rune-etched along its door in symbols that predated the Breach but had learned new tricks after 2001.

I turned away from Julian's corpse without another glance. Without remorse. Without sadism. Just cold, mechanical balance.

"That," I said, pointing at the safe with the rag still in my hand. "We came for a reason that wasn't personal, remember?"

Grimjaw's eyes followed mine. His pupils dilated slightly—enough to tell me he could see what I meant. What Sterling had been protecting in here while his daughter died screaming and his heirs bled out on expensive carpet.

"Fuck me sideways," he whispered.

"Save it for later." I dropped the blood-soaked rag and pulled a leather case from my back pocket. Inside: picks, tension wrenches, a stethoscope that looked like it belonged in an ER—not County General, something cleaner, somewhere people actually survived their visits.

Behind me, the copper pot finally stopped sizzling.

* * *

I watch them work like they're gathering scraps after a battle—because that's exactly what this is.

The Ogre-Kin brothers move through Julian Sterling's trophy vault with surprising delicacy, their massive fingers scooping brass shell casings from the Persian rugs without disturbing the patterns of blood spreading underneath. One of them—a hulking bastard named Grendel who used to run security for the Ironbound docks—dumps a handful of spent 9mms into a canvas bag. The sound is wrong. Too soft. Like coins in a pauper's purse instead of bullets from the gun that ended Sterling.

"Bag 'em all," I say, my voice flat, distant even to my own ears. "Brass and buckshot. Everything."

The temperature in here has dropped hard. I can see it on their breath now—little clouds escaping their lips as they work. My frost-cobalt runs cold tonight, colder than usual, the iron-gall residue from Sterling's copper pot mixing with the heat-signature of three dead men upstairs. The air tastes like charred pork fat and freezing water.

A Street-Elf wire-runner near the door shifts his weight, optical-camo rig flickering around his eyes. Kid's name is Vex—I pulled him off a boost crew last month because he could thread fiber through impossible spaces.

"The Party says High-Spire retainers are still bleeding out up top," Vex reports, keeping his voice low despite the dead silence dominating the room. "Cops haven't made the perimeter yet. Wards are holding, boss. Should give us another fifteen before they start smelling something wrong."

I nod, not taking my eyes off the Mosler safe built into the wall behind what used to be Julian Sterling's liquor cabinet. The dial is slick with condensation, droplets forming and running down the heavy steel face. I pull my duffel bag closer, extracting a crowbar that weighs almost forty pounds—depleted bismuth, custom forged at Sub-Station Seven when I was still trying to figure out if I had any business being the South Side's vigilante instead of just another machinist who kept his head down.

The brass casings keep clinking into bags.

Grendel moves past me toward the safe, his shadow blocking half the light from the chandelier overhead. "You sure about this part?"

"Am I sure about any of it?" I wedge the bismuth crowbar into the seam where the Mosler's door meets its frame. Metal shrieks as I press, the sound high-pitched and angry in the frozen air. "We're past sure, Grendel. We're in the accounting phase now."

That's what Danny would have called it. Accounting. He'd been an auditor before the Syndicate decided his books didn't balance their way, before they dragged him down into the sewer tunnels and left him with black iron dust coating his lungs until he couldn't breathe, couldn't speak, could only whisper my name while blood ran from his mouth like rusty water.

Penance. Revenge. A sliver of justice.

Three parts of a cord that shouldn't hold anything together but does anyway.

This was revenge. Pure and simple. Julian Sterling got exactly what he earned, measured out in copper and lead and the same casual brutality he'd distributed across North Jersey for thirty years. But Danny's lungs are still dead. The Undercity bodies are still buried in unmarked graves scattered through Kearny Marshes. This doesn't fix any of that.

It just makes sure someone pays.

I channel frost-cobalt through the bismuth crowbar, feeling the metal scream as arcane thermal shock hits the safe's internal tumblers. There's a series of sharp cracks—tumbler one, tumbler two, tumbler three—and then the heavy door swings open on oiled hinges, revealing the vault's contents:

Ledgers. Hundreds of them, bound in leather and stacked in military precision. Behind the ledgers, sealed envelopes marked with dates and names I recognize from County General ER morgues. And beneath everything else, wrapped in oilcloth, the paper trail that connects Sterling's money to every disappeared person, every "accidental" industrial accident, every body that washed up in Newark Bay with its fingers cut off.

The Threefold Cord has one strand welded shut tonight.

That's going to have to be enough.

* * *

The safe yawned open like a wound.

I stepped into the refrigerated air, my breath crystallizing into geometric patterns that hung suspended for a moment before shattering on nothing. The frost-cobalt was singing now—loud enough that I could taste it on my tongue, metallic and clean. Julian Sterling's blood had cooled on the marble floor behind me, pooling around the copper pot like a dark halo.

Grimjaw stood at the threshold, silhouetted against the amber emergency lights from the corridor beyond. His jaw worked silently, those massive teeth grinding together as he surveyed the contents of the vault.

"Fucking Christ," he muttered.

I ignored him.

Past the neat stacks of bearer bonds—hundreds of thousands, maybe millions—I reached deeper into the reinforced compartment. My fingers brushed against velvet bags heavy with diamonds, uncut stones that caught the cold blue light and threw back rainbow fractals across the steel walls. I didn't take them. Didn't even look twice.

My hand closed around something heavier. Solid. Industrial.

An IBM ThinkPad, 1999 model, all black plastic and practical design. It felt like a brick in my hands, substantial and old-world despite its electronics. Below it, a stack of Sony MiniDiscs in their clear plastic cases, each one labeled with a handwritten number in fading marker. 001 through 023.

And then—

A leather ledger. Bound in oil-treated hide that smelled like tanned skin and telluric ink. The kind of book that high-spire executives kept off-grid because digital traces could be scrubbed but paper burned slow and left evidence.

I opened it.

The pages were thick, water-flush stock designed to resist degradation. But it wasn't the quality that made my stomach clench—it was the writing. Cramped, urgent script in fountain pen ink that shimmered faintly brown-gold under the light. Telluric residue. Magic on paper. A record that shouldn't exist according to any natural law.

Names. Dates. Transfers. Not just money, either. There were symbols here I recognized from the Under-city texts, glyphs for binding, for compulsion, for things that ate souls at the margins where reality frayed thin.

"Cole."

Grimjaw's voice cut through my focus.

I didn't answer. Instead, I reached into my coat and pulled out three sealed evidence bags—the good kind, the ones that blocked electronic scanning and thermal signatures. The ThinkPad went into the first. The stack of discs into the second. The ledger into the third, carefully, as if it might bite me.

"I said Cole." Grimjaw stepped into the vault now, his massive frame blocking what little light remained from outside. "What are you doing?"

I zipped the bags shut and turned to face him. From my pocket came another bag—velvet-lined, filled with about a quarter of the diamonds I'd seen stacked inside the safe. I tossed it underhand.

He caught it reflexively, those yellow eyes widening slightly.

"That's for the families in the Undercity," I said. "Get your people to the extraction vans. Get them clear before dawn."

"What about you?" His jaw set hard. "You ain't coming?"

I pulled a magnesium flare from my belt pouch—standard issue for demolition work, though I'd never used one quite like this before. The cardboard tube felt warm against my palm despite the freezing temperature I was projecting into the room.

"No," I said simply.

The flare ignited with a sharp *crack* when I struck it against my boot. Blinding white light exploded outward, casting long shadows that twisted across the vault walls into something nightmarish and wrong. For just a moment, every surface became a Rorschach test of death.

"Go," I told him.

Grimjaw hesitated only a second longer, then backed toward the door without another word. Smart man. The flare's heat was already making the air shimmer dangerously close to my frost-cobalt field.

I dropped the burning magnesium onto the stacks of bearer bonds.

They caught instantly—paper money burning fast and hot, the flames spreading to the velvet bags of diamonds next to them. Then to the remaining vials of sludge-vial compounds that Julian had been hoarding, their chemical compositions unknown but volatile as hell.

The fire roared to life all at once, a controlled inferno that would consume everything except what I'd already bagged and tucked safely under my arm.

I walked out of Sterling Manor carrying Julian's sins on my hip and a dead man's technology under my coat. Behind me, the trophy vault burned silent and bright in the November dark.

By morning, there would be nothing left but ash and questions.

And that ledger. God help us all, there was that fucking ledger.

---

## CHAPTER 12: CHAPTER 12

The portable generator wheezes like a dying man, its pull-start cord still warm in my grip. I set the IBM ThinkPad on the workbench, its fan already spinning up with that familiar mechanical whine—like a dentist's drill wrapped in tinfoil. The screen glows green, bathing everything in sickbay fluorescence.

"Got her running," I mutter, wiping motor oil on my jeans. The smell of ozone cuts through the garage's permanent stench of rust and stale coffee.

Bram doesn't look up from his disassembly of the MP5. His callused fingers move with the precision of a watchmaker, though he's handling hardware designed to turn people into red mist. The rune-etched magazines line up beside him like brass prayers. "Power supply stable?"

"For now." I slot the Sony MiniDisc into the external drive, hearing the satisfying *click* as the tray catches. The mechanism hums, loading data that'll probably get us killed before dawn.

The frost-cobalt aura coils low in my chest, a defensive chill that spreads across my shoulders. My breath fogs the air three inches from my face. Outside, the garage windows are frosted over—not condensation, but ice crystals forming patterns that would've made a snowflake jealous. Good. Any BATC drone passing overhead will see nothing but dead cold storage.

The ThinkPad screen flickers. DOS prompt.

`A:\>_`

I stare at it for a long moment. Bram finally looks up, squinting through cigarette smoke. "Problem?"

"It wants a telluric key." I crack my knuckles, feeling the hexes settle under my skin. Metallurgical magic—the kind of dirty work that makes pure-blood mages gag. But that's all I am. Dirty.

I slice my thumb open, just enough. Blood wells dark, almost black in this light. I let two drops fall onto a copper wire, watching them bead and merge. Then I bridge the wire to the serial port.

The ThinkPad screams—actually *screams*—a sound like metal tearing in an accident. The screen flashes white, then:

`TELLURIC BRIDGE ESTABLISHED`
`ARCANE LOCK: BRUTE-FORCED`
`DECRYPTION: 100%`

Bram whistles low. "Christ, Cole."

The screen refreshes. The green glow reflects in his eyes, making him look half-possessed. And maybe he is. We all are these days.

What appears isn't what I expected.

Spreadsheet. Goddamn spreadsheet. Rows upon rows of numbers so dense they might as well be hieroglyphs. Transaction logs. Routing numbers. Shell corporation designations.

"Drek," Bram breathes, leaning closer. His shoulder presses against mine. "That's a lot of zeroes."

I scroll down with the trackpad—rough, unresponsive little shit, but it works. Each line represents money moving. Sterling Manor wasn't just burning records; he was laundering them through every digital river in North Jersey.

"He wasn't moving it for himself." My voice comes out flat, deadpan. Professional. "He was funneling it. Look at the routing numbers."

Bram points a grease-stained finger at the screen. "All bleeding back?"

"To two shell corps." I highlight the repeating patterns, watching the numbers cascade. Financial ghost companies registered to addresses that don't exist, using names pulled from dead languages and forgotten gods.

My thumb hovers over the Enter key.

"Don't," Bram says quietly. But he doesn't move to stop me.

I hit it anyway.

The screen flickers again, refreshing. The cursor blinks once, twice, three times before the registry loads. Data flows across the CRT like mercury, pooling into legibility.

Two names appear.

The temperature in the garage drops another five degrees. Not from my aura this time—from recognition. From the sheer weight of what we're seeing.

Sterling Manor didn't burn because of some internal power struggle.

He burned because he knew.

And now, looking at these names, I know too.

"This is bigger than Local 405," I whisper.

Bram's hand finds the MP5, chambering a round with the soft *click* that sounds louder than a gunshot in the frozen silence.

"We need to call someone," he says.

But which someone?

* * *

The frost-cobalt aura hums low and steady, a defensive chill that coats the garage windows in frost, masking my thermal signature from any BATC drones that might still be sweeping for survivors of Sterling Manor's collapse. The temperature in here dropped twenty degrees when I triggered it—my body's reflexive response to what went down tonight.

Bram sits across from me in the cramped Local 405 safehouse, his massive frame making the folding chair creak like it might give up its ghost. He's got burns on his face where Sterling's security team caught him with flashbangs before I put them all down. He doesn't seem to care. One hand absently rolls a smoke between his fingers while the other scrolls through the stolen data on my laptop, the blue LED glow casting shadows across his scarred features.

"Christ, Reyes," he mutters, taking a drag from the unlit cigar, then flicking his thumb against the filter. A small spark ignites it. "You really burned that place to the ground."

"I didn't have much choice." I lean forward, pulling the laptop toward me. My hands are still shaking slightly—not from fear, but from the residual adrenaline and the cold. "Sterling had three armed teams moving in. Burning was faster than fighting."

The screen glows in the darkness of the garage. Outside, Newark Bay stretches into the pre-dawn gloom, the Kearny Marshes visible as darker smudges against the industrial skyline. It's 3:15 AM. Somewhere out there, Voss is probably already working damage control. Morvain is shipping sludge. And I'm sitting here with their names on a hard drive.

I click through the encrypted folders, watching the files decrypt one by one. The ledger appears first—a standard accounting document, except instead of product codes there are names. Operational designations. Financial transfers to offshore accounts. But two names stand out, highlighted in red text that makes my stomach clench:

**MARCUS VOSS - HEAD TWO**
**ELIAS MORVAIN - HEAD THREE**

"You seeing this?" My voice comes out rougher than intended. Bram looks up, exhaling smoke toward the corrugated ceiling where condensation drips steadily into buckets we've placed around the perimeter.

"Yeah." He takes another pull from the cigar. "Three heads. Like you said."

But it's not just the names. It's what follows—the detailed breakdown of their responsibilities within the Syndicate structure. Marcus Voss handles political cover-ups and High-Spire compliance, his network extending through BATC Internal Affairs like cancer through healthy tissue. Elias Morvain controls raw telluric distribution and the black-market sludge trade, the man who actually moves the product through the city's veins while Voss cleans up any messes he leaves behind.

"Three heads," I repeat, running a hand through my hair. It comes away damp—whether from sweat or the residual frost-cobalt effect, I can't tell anymore. "Sterling thought he was untouchable behind a copper-wire fence. He was wrong."

Bram grunts, crushing out the cigar half-smoked against the workbench. "Voss is untouchable, Reyes. Different kind of wrong. That man's got judges on speed dial and senators in his pocket. You take him down, you're looking at every law enforcement agency in three states coming after your ass."

I don't answer. Instead, I scroll further down the ledger until I reach the attachments—a series of schematic files labeled PYLON_SITE_ALPHA through DELTA. My breath catches as they load onto the screen.

Blueprints. Detailed architectural schematics showing five massive structures scattered across Neon Hollow's industrial sector. Each one designed to channel telluric energy—not the small-scale stuff that powers streetlights, but something else entirely. Something massive enough to light up the entire county if all five were activated simultaneously.

"What the fuck..." Bram leans closer, squinting at the screen. "What are those?"

"They're pylons." The word tastes metallic in my mouth. "Power conduits. And they're going into Neon Hollow."

Neon Hollow—that stretch of decayed warehouses and abandoned factories between Newark Bay and the Pulaski Skyway where BATC never bothers sending patrols after dark because even their drones get shot down. Where the Telluric currents run strongest because nobody's bothered to regulate them since the 70s.

I hit print on the dot-matrix printer—an old 1995 model we keep here for situations exactly like this. The machine screams to life with its characteristic rhythmic grind, feeding continuous-feed paper through the mechanism at a pace that seems glacial when you need information now. But it's untraceable, unlike any modern networked printer.

The physical weight of the paper is reassuring as it spools out, inch by inch. Real evidence. Tangible proof. Not some ghost-in-the-machine digital file that can be deleted with a keystroke.

CRACK.

The paper tears free as I yank it from the printer, the perforations splitting along their seams. Frost spreads across the printed pages immediately—the aura responding to my elevated pulse rate before I consciously realize I'm gripping them too tight.

"Three heads," I mutter again, folding the schematics into quarters, then eighths until they fit into my jacket pocket. "And these five pylons."

My Nextel pager buzzes on the workbench—a priority alert from the Watching Party frequency. The morning news cycle has just broken the story.

*BREAKING: STERLING MANOR DESTROYED IN FIRS SUSPECTED ARSON*

"Shit." Bram reaches for his own phone, already dialing contacts he keeps in various pockets of Newark's criminal underbelly. "Word's going to spread fast."

I look up at him through the frost-coated air between us. Somewhere out there, Marcus Voss is waking up to the news that Sterling Manor burned down with all its records inside. Elias Morvain is probably already moving to consolidate power, seeing an opportunity in chaos.

They think they're safe because they don't know about me yet. Don't know about this garage or what we found.

But that won't last long.

I pull out my phone and start making calls—not to anyone who'll help directly, but to people who need to know what's coming. The Watching Party frequency crackles with static-encoded messages as other operators come online for the day shift.

Neon Hollow. Five pylons. And three heads of a snake I've only just started cutting off.

The frost-cobalt aura pulses once—almost like a heartbeat—and I feel it settling deeper into my bones.

"Voss handles the cover-ups," I say quietly, more to myself than Bram. "Morvain moves the product. But whoever built those pylons..." I trail off, staring at where the printer continues spooling blank paper now, searching for something I can't name yet. Something larger than any three heads of a Syndicate.

Something that makes Sterling Manor look like a copper-wire fence.

* * *

The ball-peen hammer connects with a wet *CRUNCH*. Aluminum shatters. Silicon platters spider-web into fragments.

I bring it down again. And again.

The IBM ThinkPad's guts scatter across the concrete floor of the safehouse garage like mechanical viscera. Plastic casing splits. Circuit boards crack. I'm breathing hard through my nose, jaw clenched tight enough to make my teeth ache. My hands are shaking—adrenaline still dumping from Sterling Manor, from watching those flames climb the Victorian facade while something that had been wearing my father's face screamed in languages older than man.

"Cole."

Bram's voice cuts through the red haze. I stop mid-swing, the hammer hanging over the ruined drive assembly. Blood drips from my knuckles where I'd cut them on the casing. Doesn't matter. Nothing matters except scrubbing this clean.

"We need to go," he says. His weathered face is pale under the bare bulb overhead, dark circles bruised deep beneath his eyes. "Now. Trace-hounds will be—"

A dog barks. Not real. Telluric-trace equipment. BATC's hex-dogs picking up the brute-force spell I used to crack the encryption on the flyer's data. The one that lit up like a beacon for anyone listening between here and Newark Bay.

"Right." I drop the hammer. It clatters against the concrete. My frost-cobalt aura flares—just a pulse, defensive—and the temperature in the garage drops ten degrees. Ice crystals form along the windows, frothing outward in fractal patterns. Thermal signature mask: active.

I kneel beside the wreckage, fingers working fast. The hard drive platters are still intact enough. I pry them free with a screwdriver, wincing as cold metal bites into my already bleeding fingers. Two platters. That's all I need. Evidence of what Sterling was really running—not just money laundering, but something deeper. Something that made the ThinkPad's owner try to burn it before the flames took him.

The platters slide into my jacket pocket. Heavy. Warm. Dangerous.

"Ammonia," I say, standing. "All surfaces."

Bram's already got the bottle. We move through the garage like a pair of grim reapers, spraying the workbench, the file cabinets, the floor where we'd laid out the stolen tech. The sharp chemical sting hits my sinuses immediately—burns like breathing glass. My eyes water. Good. Means it's strong enough.

We're wiping our prints when Bram freezes.

"Headlights," he hisses.

Through the garage door's window, two blocks down, I see them. Unmarked vans. BATC tactical units, moving slow and deliberate down the street. Search pattern. They know someone was here. They don't know who yet, but they'll tear this place apart looking.

"How much time?" Bram asks.

I'm already calculating angles, distances, the Crown Vic's V8 rumble starting up beneath the tarp. Five seconds to reach the driver's seat. Ten more to get the engine turning over. Twenty before those vans round the corner and spot us.

"Enough." My voice sounds wrong in my own ears. Hollow. I grab the thermite charge from the supply cabinet—standard issue for clearing evidence—and slap it against the generator housing. The timer clicks. Thirty seconds.

"Go," I tell Bram.

He scrambles into the passenger side as I throw myself behind the wheel. The Crown Vic coughs once, twice, then roars to life. I slam it into gear without bothering with the headlights. My frost-cobalt spreads across the hood, coating the engine block in rime. Thermal signature suppressed. For now.

"Brace."

The tires shriek as I cut the wheel hard left, launching us backward into the alley. Bram's knuckles go white on the dashboard. We hit something—a dumpster, a crate, doesn't matter—I feel the crunch through the frame but we're moving, that's what counts. Moving fast.

Behind us, the thermite charge detonates.

White light floods the garage. Not fire, exactly. Something hotter, cleaner—the charge melting steel and concrete into slag. Destroying every trace of our presence. Burning the bridge behind us.

"Christ," Bram mutters.

We burst onto Clinton Avenue, the Crown Vic's engine howling. Sodium-vapor streetlights smear past like burning yellow eyes. I take the turns by memory—seventh left, straight through the industrial park, right at the warehouse with the rusted crane. BATC's van lights are still visible in my rearview mirror, growing smaller.

"They're panicking," I say, cutting the wheel to navigate a pothole that nearly bottoms out the suspension. "Sterling was their anchor point. Now it's gone." My hands are steady on the wheel, but my heart's trying to pound its way out of my chest. "They'll come at us hard after this."

"What about the data?"

I pat my jacket pocket where the platters sit. "We decrypt it. Then we burn it too, if we have to. Some bridges aren't meant to be crossed twice."

As we merge onto the Lower McCarter bypass, the radio crackles to life.

"—gruesome discovery this morning at Sterling Manor in Jersey City. Authorities are not releasing details pending investigation, but sources report multiple fatalities and extensive structural damage. The historic Victorian estate, owned by prominent businessman Victor Sterling, has been the subject of federal inquiries for years..."

Bram and I exchange looks. No mention of arson investigators finding anything useful. Just corpses and ash.

"Play dumb?" he asks.

I flick off the radio. Ahead, the Pulaski Skyway rises against the predawn darkness, concrete arches disappearing into low-lying fog. Somewhere beyond those arches is Newark Bay. Beyond that, the rest of our problems.

"We play dead," I correct. "Until we know what we've really got here."

The Crown Vic eats miles. Behind us, something burns in the South Side safehouse. Ahead, something worse waits in the cold New Jersey night.

---

## CHAPTER 13: CHAPTER 13

The Crown Vic's engine hummed low and steady as I guided it through the fog-thick streets of Neon Hollow. Six AM, and the world was just learning what I'd done at Sterling Manor.

I turned the dial on the AM radio, letting the local news anchor spill into the car's interior. Her voice was sharp, frantic—the kind of tone they only use when something really bad goes down.

"—scene of absolute carnage at the historic Sterling Manor. Fire crews arrived to flames consuming the estate's eastern wing, but what they found inside has authorities baffled. Multiple sources confirm that Julian Sterling, CEO of Bay Area Technology Consortium, and several family members were discovered in what police are calling a 'brutal and inexplicable assault.' The exact nature of the injuries remains undisclosed pending investigation."

The windshield wipers kept their steady rhythm against the glass. *Thump. Thump. Thump.* Fog rolled past like cotton batting soaked in diesel and rot.

"Eyewitnesses report temperatures near the manor dropping to unnatural levels during the fire, despite readings indicating the flames reached upwards of two thousand degrees Fahrenheit. Police have cordoned off the entire property, and BATC officials have refused all comment—"

I flicked to the police scanner. Dispatch chatter crackled through static:

"...all units respond Sterling Manor vicinity... reports of massive energy signatures... repeat, massive energy signatures detected pre-incident... request tactical support..."

Bram shifted in the passenger seat, the leather creaking beneath him. His eyes reflected green from the dashboard lights as he lit another cigarette, the match flare illuminating his smirk for a heartbeat before darkness swallowed it again.

"'The Butcher of Sterling Manor,'" he said, reading from a newspaper tucked under his jacket. "'Unseen assassin with possible metahuman capabilities targets BATC leadership. City on edge following gruesome slaughter.' Christ, Reyes. They're calling you a monster now."

I didn't look at him. Didn't take my eyes off the road, where sodium-vapor lamps cast everything in that sickly orange glow that made the fog look like blood mist.

"Good," I said flatly. "Let them."

The anchor's voice cut back through: "...detectives are pursuing multiple angles, including organized retaliation by South Side metahuman factions. Sources close to the investigation suggest this may be the work of vigilante elements previously thought dormant in the metropolitan area..."

My fingers tightened on the steering wheel. Cold leather against skin still faintly sticky with Julian Sterling's blood. Under my fingernails, embedded deep enough I'd need a wire brush and bleach to get it out.

*Thump. Thump.*

The scanner squawked suddenly—a different frequency, higher priority. I recognized the voice immediately. Vane Thorne. BATC Internal Affairs Inquisitor. The woman who'd been hunting me since I burned down Sub-Station Seven.

"—lockdown. Effective immediately, all metahuman registration clinics in Sector 7 through Sector 12 are to cease operations. All personnel report to central command for screening. This is not a drill. Repeat, lockdown protocols activated city-wide. Thorne out."

Bram exhaled smoke slowly, watching it curl toward the Crown Vic's cracked sunroof. "She smells blood in the water now, doesn't she?"

"Always does." My jaw was tight. Tension crawling up the back of my neck like spiders. "Makes things complicated."

"Not if you're already planning your next move." He stubbed the cigarette into the car's ashtray—already overflowing with butts from previous nights. "Morvain and Voss won't sit still after this. Sterling was their shield. Now he's meat, and they're exposed."

I pulled the Crown Vic off the bypass, heading deeper into Neon Hollow's industrial sprawl. Factories loomed through the fog like tombstones. Somewhere ahead, my chop-shop waited in its basement beneath an abandoned textile mill. The place where I could think, plan, rebuild.

Because Voss and Morvain were listening. They knew someone had crossed that line.

And now, so did everyone else.

* * *

I kill the engine in the underground lot beneath what used to be a strip mall back when Kearny still had something resembling a retail district. Now it's just concrete bones and graffiti tags that shift colors under different light.

The Crown Vic shudders into silence.

My hands are still shaking—just barely, but I feel it. The frost-cobalt weave has retracted completely now, leaving my fingertips numb and my veins feeling like someone ran cold wires through them. There's still blood under my nails from last night's work. I didn't bother washing it off.

The parking structure smells like rust and motor oil and whatever chemical shit they used to seal the floor decades ago. Fluorescent lights flicker overhead, casting everything in this sick green-yellow glow that makes the shadows move wrong.

Fizz's trauma-ambulance sits in the far corner. It's an old 1989 Ford, white with red stripes that have mostly peeled away. He converted it into some kind of mobile frequency-workshop, all antennas and rigged equipment that shouldn't legally exist. The back doors hang open, spilling blue LED light onto the concrete.

I get out of the car, leaving the door ajar. My boots echo in the cavernous space as I walk toward him.

"Cole." Fizz's voice comes out ahead of him—a high-pitched warble that echoes off the walls. He emerges from behind his ambulance, still wearing those oversized magnifying goggles that make his eyes look like they're about to pop right out of his skull. His hands are stained with solder and what might be grease or might be something more esoteric. "Shit. You actually did it."

"You sound surprised." I stop a few feet away, crossing my arms.

"Not surprised. Just..." He adjusts the goggles, pushes them up higher on his head. They leave red marks around his eyes. "Christ, Cole. The Spire is bleeding. Like really bleeding. Voss is having a full-blown meltdown on the encrypted channels. Morvain pulled every sludge-shipment off the streets. Every single one."

The air feels heavier now, charged with the kind of static that means something big just shifted in the balance of power. North Jersey's underworld runs on information, and right now, every frequency-broker and street-level operative is probably listening hard.

Fizz reaches into his ambulance and pulls out a Motorola Razr—silver, sleek, the kind of phone that costs more than most people's monthly rent. It looks absurdly clean compared to everything else in this garage.

"This was sitting on a BATC server three hours ago," he says, tossing it to me. I catch it without thinking. "I've been digging through their comms traffic all night. Thorne's got the High-Spire locked down tighter than a drum. No unregistered magic use. Lethal force authorized for anything that smells like freelance work."

I flip the Razr open. A list of decrypted messages scrolls across the screen:

*Voss (Executive): Morvain, report. We have containment breaches in Sector 7.*

*Morvain (Sludge Operations): All shipments suspended pending security audit. The source is still active.*

*Thorne (Security Chief): Lockdown protocols enacted. All clinics stand down. We hunt the source first.*

I scroll further. More panicked chatter. Voss screaming at someone about "unacceptable losses." Security chiefs trying to triangulate positions they can't locate. The whole structure of the Syndicate crumbling from the inside out because some lunatic with frost-hex decided to burn their distribution network to the ground.

"Your work last night," Fizz continues, watching my face as I read. "The clinic hits, the substation incident... they're connecting dots now. Scary fast."

I close the phone with a sharp click. "Tell the Watching Party to go dark. Forty-eight hours minimum. No wire-runs, no street-deals. Let BATC chase ghosts while we regroup."

Fizz nods rapidly, already pulling out his own burner phone to pass along the message. The frequency-brokers who run intel for smaller operations—the ones who actually keep this city's underbelly functioning—need to disappear right now. Visibility is death when the Spire decides it wants heads on spikes.

But something about Fizz's body language makes me pause. He's hesitating.

"What?" I ask.

He fumbles in his pocket and pulls out a slip of paper, creased and stained with coffee rings. Hesitates again, then extends it toward me like he's handing over evidence at a crime scene.

"Thorne didn't just lock down the clinics," he says quietly. "Sent a strike team to Sub-Station Seven ruins. Ruins, Cole. They're looking for the source of the frost-hex personally."

The paper feels heavy in my palm even though it's just cheap printer stock. I don't unfold it yet.

"When?"

"This morning. Six AM push. Full tactical." His eyes meet mine through those ridiculous goggles. "They know where you came from. Or at least, they're going to start digging through the debris soon enough."

The frost-cobalt weave pulses once in my chest—a warning shot. My hands stop shaking.

Sub-Station Seven. Where it all started. Where I learned what I could do. Where the Watching Party found me after that night in County General's ER.

And now Thorne's sending his best people to tear apart every piece of rubble, looking for whatever made me into the weapon that just burned half their operation to ash.

I fold the paper carefully and tuck it into my jacket.

"Tell them to be thorough," I say. "There won't be anything left to find."

* * *

I stare at the slip of paper for what feels like an hour, though the dashboard clock tells me it's only been three minutes. Sub-Station Seven. The name sits on my knees like a lead weight, wrapped around a half-empty bottle of whiskey I can't remember cracking open.

The Crown Vic idles in Neon Hollow, this stretch of undercity bypass that smells like diesel and despair even at six AM. Fizz leans against the driver's side window, his punk-ass grin somehow still intact after everything he's seen tonight. After watching me dismantle that Sterling Manor butcher with a precision that would make a surgeon weep.

"Clean work," he says, tapping ash from a cigarette that's probably its fifth life. "Real clean."

I hand him the stack of bills without counting them. Too tired to care if it's enough. The cash is crisp, newly printed—money from jobs I took before my hands got too full of blood to remember being anything else. Before the frost started crawling up my arms when I sleep.

"Get lost, Fizz." My voice comes out wrong. Hoarse. Like I've been screaming into a hurricane.

He doesn't argue. Smart kid. He pockets the money and melts back into the neon-soaked shadows, leaving me alone with the paper and the memory of what happened at Sub-Station Seven three months ago.

*Three months.*

Mara burned thirty-seven people alive there. Commuter train, morning rush, she turned it into a funeral pyre to stop the Orphans from flooding into Newark proper. I saw the aftermath. Walked through the ash-gray static that clung to everything like radioactive cotton candy. Smelled the wet charred wool—the signature scent of her corrupted weave, all heat and desperation and no control.

Thorne wants me to see the connection. Wants me to understand that Mara's fire and my frost are just different sides of the same coin: violence dressed up as salvation. He keeps sending me these messages, these little breadcrumbs that lead back to the places where the 4th-Law cracked wide open and bled all over North Jersey.

Sub-Station Seven.

I crumple the paper in one fist and jam it behind the brake pedal with the others. A collection of failures and warnings. A roadmap to everywhere I've tried not to look.

The Crown Vic lurches forward as I press the accelerator, tires finding their rhythm on the rain-slick pavement. The city is waking up around me—early shifts heading to County General, truckers hauling scrap metal north toward Kearny Marshes, someone's alarm clock screaming through an open window in Sterling Manor.

And there it is.

Rising from the industrial sprawl like a tombstone carved from rust and regret, Sub-Station Seven hunkers against the morning sky. The police cordon is still up, yellow tape dancing in wind that carries that smell—Christ, even now, three months later, I can smell it. Wet charcoal and something worse. Something burned that shouldn't have been.

I don't stop. Can't stop.

But I roll down the window anyway.

The cold air hits me like a slap, and for a second the frost-cobalt weave responds, crawling up my neck, trying to answer the call of all that residual psychic bleed radiating from those ruins. All that trauma soaked into concrete and rebar. Bram shifts in the passenger seat, his small hands pressed against the glass, staring at the silhouette of destruction.

"You think she's still out there?" he asks quietly. "The Fire-Starter?"

My knuckles go white on the steering wheel. Mara. The name sits in my mouth like broken glass. She's out there, yeah. Burning her way through whatever darkness has her now, fighting a war that started before either of us understood what we were carrying inside. What the 4th-Law does to people who can't control it.

"She's out there," I say, because lying would be easier but somehow feels wrong right now. "Fighting her own war."

"Does that mean—"

"We stick to ours." The words come out harder than I intend. Bram flinches, pulling back from the window, and I immediately regret it. He doesn't deserve that. None of this was his fault, finding himself caught between me and whatever Thorne wants to make me become.

The Crown Vic pulls away from Sub-Station Seven, eating distance like hunger. Behind us, the ruins shrink until they're just another blight on Newark's already fucked-up skyline. But I know better. Know that some scars don't heal just because you drive past them fast enough.

I turn down an alleyway that shouldn't exist according to any city planning documents—the kind of space that opens up when you need it and disappears when you look too hard for it. Ahead, heavy steel doors start their rumbling ascent, revealing the darkness below.

Home. Sort of.

The chop-shop basement waits like a sanctuary, filled with the tools of my trade and the ghosts of every metahuman I've tried to save by breaking every law I could find. The frost-cobalt retraction leaves me trembling as I kill the engine, exhausted in a way sleep will never fix.

Bram climbs out first, small feet hitting pavement that echoes in the confined space. I follow slower, my body remembering every strike and parry from tonight's work, every drop of blood spilled in Sterling Manor's finest room.

Above us, the city keeps waking. Unaware. Always unaware.

And beneath it all, the 4th-Law hums its endless song of consequence and collision.

---

## CHAPTER 14: CHAPTER 14

The lock clicks shut behind me like a judge's gavel. Heavy. Final. I'm alone now—truly alone—in the basement where the world can't reach me. Can't judge me. Can't ask questions I don't want to answer.

The Arcane Iron-Lung dominates everything. Its brass-and-glass cylinder rises twelve feet from the concrete floor, Danny's sleeping form visible inside like a saint in a church reliquary. The machine's rhythm never stops: *hiss-thump*, *hiss-thump*. Inhale. Exhale. Living. Breathing. Waiting.

I cross the basement without looking at the workbench. Don't need to see what's there—the bloodstained rags, the tools, the maps with their red pushpins marking problems that needed solving. My knuckles are stiff as I approach the deep-basin industrial sink bolted into the far wall.

The tap water runs cold. Always cold down here. I turn the handle hard and watch the stream hit the stainless steel basin with sharp metallic chimes. The temperature doesn't matter. Nothing matters right now except getting clean.

I grab the block of pumice soap from its hook. Rough texture, gritty smell—industrial strength, the kind mechanics use to scrub transmission fluid off their hands. Except it's not transmission fluid I'm washing away today.

Pink-tinged water spirals down the drain as I scrub. Hard. Methodical. Each knuckle gets attention. The dried blood comes off in flakes, revealing the sizzling blue-black iron-gall residue underneath—that telltale sign of the frost-cobalt burning through my veins all night long. Julian Sterling had that same residue on his neck when I left him. Except on him, it was spreading. Eating through tissue and bone.

*You think this makes you a monster,* whispers that voice in my head—the one that sounds disturbingly like my own conscience. *But monsters kill for pleasure. I kill for balance.*

The contrast of the icy water against my skin should hurt more than it does. Steam rises where my frost-cobalt meets the liquid, creating ghosts that dissipate immediately. Gone. Like everything else about tonight.

It wasn't just killing Julian. It was watching his lieutenant try to crawl toward a dropped pistol. It was putting my boot on his spine and hearing the wet crack of vertebrae. It was the silence after. That heavy, crushing silence that settles over everything like snow.

I scrub harder. The pumice scrapes skin raw at my cuticles. Good. Let it sting. Let me feel something real instead of this hollow victory that tastes like ash.

*It’s a sliver of justice.* I stare at my reflection in the cracked mirror mounted above the sink. My face looks older than yesterday. Dark circles under eyes that have seen too much. Blood speckled across my cheek—when did that happen? I wipe it away with my forearm.

*It's not enough. It will never be enough. But it will do for today.*

The pink swirls in the drain hypnotize me. All that life, all that violence, reduced to a few ounces of water circling down into darkness. I turn off the tap. Watch the last droplets fall. Listen to the *drip... drip... drip...* echoing off concrete walls.

My hands are clean now. Raw red from scrubbing, but clean.

Behind me, the Arcane Iron-Lung continues its eternal cycle: *hiss-thump*, *hiss-thump*. Danny is still there. Still breathing. Still alive because I made different choices with different people. Not monsters. Just... necessary.

I dry my hands on a rough towel hanging by the sink—gray and threadbare, probably been here since the previous owner sold this place to me. The basement smells like industrial soap now, cutting through the copper scent and smoke that always lingers in places where violence has happened.

I ball up the towel and toss it toward the laundry pile in the corner. Miss. Don't care enough to pick it up.

The brass-and-glass cylinder catches morning light filtering through the ground-level windows. Inside, Danny shifts slightly in sleep, his breathing tube moving with the rhythm of the machine keeping him alive. For now. Until whatever curse is working through his system decides whether he lives or dies.

I have work tomorrow. Regular job at the machine shop on South Street. Mr. Chen needs someone to finish the compressor rebuild. Normal life stuff. As if normal even exists anymore.

The frost-cobalt hums faintly beneath my skin, tired and sated. It got what it wanted tonight. Balance restored. Sort of.

I cross to the workbench, grabbing a rag to wipe down the tools scattered across oil-stained wood. Methodical. Clean. Order returning to chaos.

Tomorrow will bring new problems. Different faces. New names to remember or forget depending on which side they fall.

But for today—the sliver of justice is done.

* * *

The basement reeks of copper and industrial soap. My boots echo against concrete as I descend the stairs, each step sending tremors up my shins—the kind that settle deep in bone when you've pushed your frost-cobalt too hard, too long through the wet November air.

I pause at the bottom landing.

The Arcane Iron-Lung sits in the center of my workshop like a cathedral relic. Amber light bleeds through its thick glass chambers, casting long shadows across the oil-stained floor. Inside, suspended in the telluric fluid, Danny drifts. Fifteen years old. Trapped in mechanical sleep since Sterling's thugs used him as leverage—pushed him into the Kearny Marshes' sinkhole, let him drown in the black iron runoff while his lungs filled with metallurgical poison.

His chest rises and falls with that steady *hiss-click-release* rhythm of the Syndicate Compressor I jury-rigged. The heavy brass valves gleam under the workbench lights. Each one calibrated to a fraction of pressure, keeping the telluric solution circulating through his system just enough to sustain him. Not heal. Never heal. Just... wait.

I cross to the lung on legs that want to collapse.

My fingers wrap around the nearest valve—cold brass against heat-burnt skin—and I turn it fractional degrees clockwise. The compressor shifts pitch. *Hiss-click-release*. I watch Danny's face through the condensation-dotted glass. Pale as moonlight. That stupid smile he used to flash before he knew what violence looked like up close.

"One down, Danny," I rasp, voice stripped raw from the night's work. "Sterling is dead."

The words hang in the frigid basement air. I don't mention how it went down. How I found him in Sub-Station Seven, surrounded by his security detail. How my frost-cobalt burned hot enough to crack concrete when I finally had him cornered. How his eyes went wide with recognition when he saw who'd come for him.

He tried to run. They all do.

I adjust another valve, listening to the pressure gauge tick upward. One degree. No more. The telluric fluid swirls around Danny's suspended form, that warm amber glow the only color in this graveyard of machines.

"It doesn't scrape the black iron out of your lungs." My knuckles whiten against the cold glass. "Doesn't fix what was broken. Doesn't bring back the kid you were last summer before you climbed into those marshes after that goddamn dog."

The compressor breathes. *Hiss-click-release*.

"I know that. You know that. Sterling dying doesn't mean anything except one less monster in a city full of them."

I press my palm flat against the glass, feeling the vibrations of the machine pulse through my hand. Through the ice-cobalt exhaustion that's settled in my bones.

"But it's a sliver of justice. A poor substitute for a life. For yours." My throat tightens. "It's all I have left to give you right now."

Turning away costs something. Every time. Like ripping flesh.

But there are two more names on my wall. Two more men who stood by while Sterling used your body as a negotiation tactic. While they poisoned you with their industrial waste and walked away clean.

"Going to find them both," I promise the sleeping boy's reflection in the glass. "Going to burn them down too."

My boots scuff toward the far concrete wall where my investigation sprawls—newspaper clippings, polaroids from crime scenes, red string weaving connections between faces and locations. Pulaski Skyway toll booth murders. County General ER records. The Kearny Marshes toxicology reports.

Somewhere in this chaos is the next thread.

* * *

The basement reeks of industrial soap and copper residue, a metallic tang that clings to the back of my throat like I've been chewing on pennies all night. My hands are still trembling—not from fear, but from the aftershock of the frost-cobalt receding through my system. It pools in my gut now, cold and sluggish, making my stomach churn.

I stand before the concrete wall, six feet high, stained with decades of grease and grime. At the top, written in thick black grease pencil—probably stolen from some mechanic's tool kit years ago—the names form a web of connections. Julian Sterling sits at the apex, his name underlined twice. Beneath him, branching outward like poisonous roots, are Marcus Voss and Elias Morvain.

Three names. Three targets. One already crossed out.

I pick up the grease pencil from its tray, the waxy chemical smell hitting me hard as I unscrew the cap. The metal cylinder is cold against my palm, familiar weight. For a moment, I just hold it, feeling the slight vibration in my bones—a phantom echo of what I did last night at County General.

Then I raise my arm.

The line goes straight through Julian Sterling's name. Thick. Heavy. Definitive. Black ink bleeding across white concrete like a wound that won't close. I don't hesitate. Don't second-guess. The stroke is clean, decisive, final.

*He's done*, I think, lowering the pencil. *The first one is finished.*

But when I look at what remains—Voss, Morvain—I feel something different stirring in my chest. Not satisfaction. Not closure. Just the cold, mechanical understanding that this was only the beginning. An appetizer for what's coming next.

My eyes drift to the dot-matrix printout crumpled on the workbench beside me. Five Telluric Pylons, their coordinates marked in green phosphorescent ink. I smooth it flat against the concrete, positioning it carefully beneath Elias Morvain's name. Pinning it there with a rusted nail from the box near my boots.

*There you are*, I mutter to myself, stepping back to survey the board.

The rhythmic breathing of Danny's Iron-Lung fills the silence—that mechanical hiss-thump-hiss-thump that's been counting down the hours since I brought him here six years ago. It's steady now. Stable. Almost peaceful if you can ignore the fact that he needs that damn machine to keep his lungs functional.

"Voss," I say aloud, my voice cracking slightly from exhaustion. "Morvain."

You're on the clock.

The words hang in the frigid air of the basement. Somewhere above us, the November morning is trying to break through the grimy windows at street level, but down here it's perpetual dusk. The generator hums its dying song—needs fuel soon—but I don't care about that right now.

I drop into the worn leather armchair that sits in the corner, cushion long ago collapsed and shaped by my body. My head lolls back against the headrest. Every muscle aches. There's blood under my fingernails—some mine, some Sterling's—I haven't bothered cleaning yet.

The frost-cobalt pulls me down like an anchor.

"Danny..." The name escapes my lips without permission, soft and tired.

His Iron-Lung answers: *hiss-thump*. *hiss-thump*.

*It's done, kid. The first one's taken care of.*

My eyelids grow heavy as lead weights. Just for a minute, I tell myself. Just enough to reset before planning the next move.

As consciousness starts to slip away, something shifts in my peripheral vision—the shadows on the wall seem to writhe, stretching longer than they should be. The metronome of Danny's breathing begins to speed up, distorting:

*Hiss-hiss-hiss-thump-thump-thump-BEEP-BEEP-BEEP!*

My eyes snap open for just a second, catching a glimpse of fluorescent hospital lights where there should only be dim bulbs. A monitor screen flickering with vital signs that belong to 2015 instead of 2005.

Then darkness swallows everything whole.

---

## CHAPTER 15: CHAPTER 15

The darkness tastes like rust.

I'm drowning in it—not water, something thicker, heavier. My lungs burn with each attempted breath, filling with fluid that shouldn't be there. Pain radiates from everywhere at once, a symphony of agony conducted by broken bones and torn muscle. I can feel my ribs grinding against each other with every shallow inhale, the sound wet and sickening in the back of my throat.

*CRACK.*

A flash—gunfire, muzzle flashes burning themselves into my retinas. Voss's face, twisted in triumph. Then another crack—the sound of bone snapping as something heavy impacts my chest. Concrete dust fills my nose, choking me as the world goes white-hot—

I gasp.

Air. Real air, cold and sterile, flooding my lungs. Too much at once. I choke on it, coughing until my whole body convulses, each spasm sending fresh waves of pain through my torso. Something sharp digs into my arm. An IV needle, tearing through skin and vein as I twitch involuntarily.

"Easy. Easy, goddammit!"

Hands on me. Multiple sets. Rough, practiced movements. One set is warm, almost scorching hot where they press against my shoulder. Another is cooler, controlled. The smell hits me next—ozone, like after a lightning strike, mixed with antiseptic so strong it makes my eyes water. Underneath it all, cedar. Fresh cut wood.

My frost-cobalt flares instinctively.

Ice crystals form along my fingertips, spreading up my arms before someone—something—slams a wall of force down on my hex. Not blocking it, *pushing* it back inside my body like shoving a knife deeper into a wound. White-lilac light erupts behind my eyelids, warm and suffocating, wrapping around my magic and binding it tight.

"No! Don't fight it, you stupid bastard!" A woman's voice, sharp and impatient. "Your blood-iron is trying to knit your lungs back together while they're full of fluid! You'll drown yourself!"

Another flash—this one from memory or hallucination, hard to tell anymore. The Kearny Marshes at night, mist rising off the stagnant water. Voss standing in the middle of it all, his void-magic consuming everything around him. The Syndicate's soldiers falling like dominoes, their bodies twisting into impossible shapes as reality itself warped around him.

Then me, charging forward, hex blazing white-hot. My fist connecting with his jaw. His head snapping back—

And that ceiling collapsing.

The weight of tons of concrete and rebar slamming down on top of us both. The impact throwing me backward, my spine compressing against steel beams. Something cracking in my lower back. Screaming.

But not just mine.

A roar—low, guttural, Orc. The sound of something massive being torn apart. Bone crunching under pressure. Then silence.

"Lysandra! Now!"

More hands. Rougher this time. Forcing me flat onto something cold and hard. Straps clicking into place across my chest, hips, ankles. Restraints. I'm restrained.

"My sutures are holding but barely! He's still trying to heal wrong!"

Sutures? There should be frost. My frost-cobalt should be working, rebuilding, mending the damage—

*Push.*

That warm force again, stronger now, pressing down on my magic until it feels like I'm suffocating beneath its weight. Not hostile exactly, but unyielding. Absolute.

"Let go," a different voice says, softer but somehow more commanding than the first. "Cole. Let your body rest. Your blood-iron can't work if you're fighting us."

Elena.

I know her voice even before consciousness fully returns. Know it the way you know your own heartbeat. The tone she uses when she's terrified but won't show it. When she's already three steps ahead of disaster and just waiting for everyone else to catch up.

Light pierces through my eyelids—blinding white-lilac, almost painful in its intensity. It doesn't come from outside; it comes from *inside*, as if someone's opened a window directly into the sun inside my skull.

The void shatters.

My mind snaps back into my body with the force of a rubber band breaking, and suddenly I'm aware of everything at once: the sterile white ceiling above me (fluorescent lights making my eyes water), the sharp sting of IV fluids pumping into my arm (something cold and medicinal), the burning ache of dozens of deep lacerations being sealed by what must be Elena's healing magic, and underneath it all, that cedar smell getting stronger, mixing with ozone and antiseptic until it forms something new. Something protective.

"What... happened?" The words scratch out of my throat raw and broken.

"Three years happened," Lysandra says flatly, her silhouette appearing above me against those harsh lights. Her arms are crossed, one hip cocked in that way that means she's been standing there watching me die and heal and die again for God knows how long. "You've been in and out of consciousness since we pulled you out of Sub-Station Seven. That was..." She glances at something I can't see. "...two weeks ago."

Two weeks.

The word hangs in the air between us like an accusation.

I try to move, and immediately regret it as pain flares hot and bright across my entire torso. My ribs aren't the only thing broken—not even close.

"How bad?" I manage to get out this time without coughing up blood.

Elena's face swims into view beside Lysandra's—tired, drawn thin with exhaustion, but alive. *Alive.* Her hands glow faintly with that warm white light as they hover over my chest, guiding the healing processes she's orchestrated inside me.

"Seven fractured vertebrae," she says calmly, though I hear the tremor underneath. "Four cracked ribs with internal puncturing. Collapsed lung that we had to manually reinflate twice. Your right clavicle is shattered in three places." She pauses, meeting my eyes. "And your frost-cobalt nearly killed you trying to fix everything at once before we could stabilize you. You burned through so much energy that your blood-iron hasn't fully recovered yet."

The void between years stretches out behind her words—a chasm three years deep filled with violence and failure and bodies I couldn't save.

* * *

The smell hits me first—sharp, clinical, unmistakable. Iodine. Bleach. Antiseptic. My nose wrinkles involuntarily, even before my eyes decide to cooperate with consciousness.

Then the cedar. Fresh. Clean. Like a winter wind through pine forests that don't exist anymore.

"Easy now."

A woman's voice. Not young. Not old. Commanding.

My hearing kicks in next—the *beep-beep-beep* of a heart monitor, too fast, matching my pulse as it hammers against my ribs. Surgical instruments clattering on metal. The hum of fluorescent lights overhead, though when I try to locate them, my vision swims, refuses to focus.

I'm lying down. That much I know. Sterile paper crinkling beneath me with every shallow breath. Hospital blanket. Scratchy. I hate hospital blankets. They're designed for people who've accepted they're sick, and I never accepted shit.

Pain registers last—that's how you know something's wrong with the world. A deep, agonizing pull across my chest, my shoulder. Stitches. Lots of them. Someone sewed me back together while I was out.

"The frost-cobalt is spiking again," another voice says. Younger this one. More cautious. "He's fighting the integration."

Frost-cobalt. Right. My aura. My defense mechanism. It should be cold right now. Should be freezing everything within ten feet into crystalline stillness.

But there's warmth instead.

Warmth and lilac.

White-lilac wards, I realize. Pulsing. Glowing softly at the edges of my blurred vision. The kind Lysandra Vance used to weave—pure, uncorrupted, impossibly complex for someone still alive in 1999.

Which means...

"No," I rasp, my throat raw, voice coming out like gravel poured through cheesecloth. "Danny..."

"Danny is safe." The first voice again. Closer now. A hand settles on my forehead—cool, steady, not quite flesh but not quite magic either. Somewhere between. "Secure. You need to stop fighting the weave. Let the lilac do its work."

"I don't—" Another attempt to move. My limbs are leaden, unresponsive. Muscle memory screams at my brain that I should be able to roll off this table, stand, fight, *do something*. But my body isn't cooperating.

The frost-cobalt flares defensively, responding to my panic. Ice crystals begin forming on the metal tray beside me, creeping across stainless steel with familiar hunger.

And then warmth again. Not fighting it. Not pushing back. Just... accepting. Neutralizing. A counter-weave so subtle, so perfectly calibrated that it wraps around my frost like a lover's embrace, cooling without chilling, protecting without imprisoning.

That's Elena's style. My mother's magic has always been surgical. Precise. She doesn't waste energy on confrontation when she can achieve the same result through understanding.

But Elena died in 2006.

"So did you," the younger voice says, and I hear the smile beneath the words. "Technically speaking."

My eyes finally decide to open. Not all the way—the halogen surgical lamp overhead is blinding, a white-hot sun in miniature that makes me wince and turn my head sharply to the left.

Two silhouettes above me. Feminine. One taller, more angular. One shorter, curvier.

"...mothers?" The word comes out strangled.

"In a manner of speaking." The taller one leans into the light, and as my vision adjusts, features emerge. Dark skin. Silver-streaked hair pulled back tight. Eyes that gleam with an unnatural luminescence—white-lilac, just like the wards pulsing softly behind her.

Lysandra Vance. Except she should be dead. Should have burned out decades ago, her power consumed by the Breach.

"I'm not your mother," Lysandra says gently, reading my expression. "Not by blood. But I've carried the weight of yours long enough that the distinction feels academic."

The shorter figure shifts, and I catch a glimpse of familiar brown eyes, warm skin, hair now threaded with silver but still recognizably hers.

"Mom?"

* * *

The blur clears like ice breaking on a winter river.

I'm lying on my back, cold metal pressed against skin that shouldn't exist anymore. My chest rises, falls—mechanical, rhythmic, *insistent*. Somewhere close by, machines beep in Morse code I don't understand yet.

"Easy now."

My mother's voice cuts through static. Elena. But it can't be—I just left her in 2006, watching me walk into those tunnels beneath County General, thinking she'd never see me again after what I did at Sub-Station Seven.

I try to turn my head. The movement sends needles through my neck.

"What... happened?" My throat feels scraped raw.

Elena leans closer, her face swimming into focus above mine. She's wearing surgical scrubs, stained dark at the elbows and knees with blood that looks freshly spilled. A surgical mask dangles around her neck, loose fabric stained pink. Her hair is pulled back tight. There are new lines around her eyes—deep trenches carved by years I didn't witness.

Years I was gone.

"You took a hell of a hit out there, Cole." She reaches up, wipes something sticky from my cheek. When she pulls her hand back, it's smeared red-black. "Voss almost had you. Again."

Again.

That word lands wrong in my ears. Like I should remember the first time.

I force myself to look left.

The woman standing there makes no sense.

She's draped in white-lilac fire, but it doesn't burn. It *wards*—pulsing, living barriers that shimmer in geometric patterns across the air around us. Her coat is immaculate, tailored black wool with silver threading that catches the harsh fluorescent lights overhead. Beneath it, I can make out the telltale bulge of concealed weapons.

Her hands glow with that same white-lilac light, maintaining pressure points in the air that correspond to where my body lies on the table.

She meets my gaze with eyes like steel trap. Gray. Calculating.

"Your isolated crusade is over, Mr. Reyes," she says, voice carrying the kind of authority that comes from commanding rooms full of people who want you dead. Or wanted her dead once, anyway. The cadence is wrong for the Undercity—too refined, too High-Spire—but the underlying threat is pure street-level grit.

"Who—"

"The Syndicate has activated the Fourth Head." Another machine beeps faster. My heart? "It's time to wake up. We have a war to win."

I try to sit up. Can't. The wards won't let me.

Elena's hand presses gently against my shoulder. "Not yet. Lysandra's keeping you stitched together. You bleed out frost-cobalt when you're this busted up. She's maintaining the wards while we stabilize your cellular regeneration."

Lysandra.

*Mara's mother.*

The words click into place like gears I didn't know were there. Suddenly I understand why those wards feel so familiar—they're built from the same magic Mara used to save me at Kearny Marshes, back in... when was that? 2005?

My mind reels, trying to calculate the timeline.

"How long?" I croak. "How much time?"

Elena and Lysandra exchange a look—years of unspoken communication compressed into a single glance between women who have clearly worked side by side through things they'll never speak aloud.

"You've been out for three days," Elena says quietly. "It's January 17th, 2008. You've been missing since October 2006. We found you last week in what was left of Newark Bay. Voss had carved pieces out of you to study your frost-cobalt mutations."

The monitor beside my head spikes—a sharp peak that makes Lysandra adjust her wards slightly.

"He's remembering," she observes. Clinical. Measured.

"Give him a second," Elena snaps, then softens as she looks back down at me. Pride flickers across her tired features. "You did good work out there, Cole. Even if you were an idiot for going it alone."

The room smells wrong. Ozone and antiseptic fighting with something else—cedar, maybe? Fresh cut wood mixed with the metallic tang of blood and burning wards. I try to process it all but my thoughts keep slipping sideways, trying to reconcile everything I just learned.

Three years. They found me after three years. And somehow...

"How many are dead because I wasn't here?"

Lysandra's lips thin. Her wards pulse brighter—agitated or angry, hard to tell which.

"The numbers don't matter now." She steps closer to the table, tilting her head as she studies me like a specimen under glass. "What matters is whether you can fight. Whether you're willing to stop playing lone wolf and join the resistance we've built while you were frozen in ice water beneath County General."

Elena shoots her a warning glare, but doesn't contradict her.

I look between them—the surgeon covered in her son's blood, the High-Spire exile wreathed in protective fire—and finally understand what those three years really meant.

They didn't wait for me.

They built something without me.

And now they're offering me a place in it.

The machine beeps steadily behind my head. White-lilac wards intertwine with frost-cobalt sparks dancing across my skin. Somewhere far above us, 2008 New Jersey keeps spinning through its days while the Syndicate activates gods know what kind of weapon.

My mother waits for my answer, hand still on my shoulder.

Mara's mother watches with calculating eyes.

Both of them standing over the broken mechanic who thought he could win this war alone.

I swallow hard against my raw throat.

"Show me," I whisper.

---

# BOOK #01: HALO OF ASH
### Machete Core Part 1 (MA-1)

---

## CHAPTER 1: ASH AND LILAC IN THE DOWNPOUR

No. Absolutely not. I'm not sending you back in there.

The voice cuts through the rain like a blade—the gravel-and-honey cadence that means my second-in-command has actually left his post at the south perimeter and made it all the way across our staging area without me noticing. That's how deep I've slipped into the memory again.

I don't turn around immediately. Instead, I watch the flickering sodium-vapor lights play across the sealed entrance to Sub-Station Seven, watching for any sign of movement from inside those blast doors. The metal is scorched black even now, two years later. Patches of rust bloom across it like wounds that never healed.

"Commander." Cole tries again, closer this time. "Mara."

My jaw clenches. The name sounds wrong coming from him—too familiar, too soft for what we are here to do. But he uses it anyway because he knows it pulls me back from whatever fog I'm drifting into.

We're standing in hip-deep water now. The November rain hasn't let up since we arrived, turning the cracked pavement of Newark Bay's industrial sector into something resembling a shallow river. Every few seconds another flash-bang detonates somewhere inside the substation as our Aegis tactical team pushes deeper, trying to flush out the scavengers holed up in the old Y2K breach-tunnels.

"They're getting desperate," I say finally, still not looking at Cole. "The scavenger crew inside—that Goblin splice-runner we pulled out earlier said they've got kids with them. Maybe ten, twelve years old. South Side orphans who think there's food caches down in the deep tunnels."

The words taste like ash on my tongue.

Cole doesn't answer right away. He's smart enough to know when silence serves better than argument. When the wind shifts, I catch a whiff of something underneath the petrichor—the acrid stench of burning wool mixed with copper and ozone. It makes my stomach turn.

"You burned three hundred people alive here," Cole says quietly, almost gently. Like he's reminding me of basic arithmetic rather than the weight of my soul. "In 2005. During the Orphan Hostage crisis. You saved thirty-eight children by immolating an entire subway station full of commuters—human, elven, dwarven, orc—all trying to escape the Y2K breach creatures pouring through from the other side."

"I remember what I did." My voice comes out sharper than intended.

"Then you also remember that returning to this site is explicitly against your psych profile recommendations. That Dr. Chen has you flagged for traumatic memory recurrence events whenever you're within two hundred meters of ground zero."

He steps around me now, blocking my view of those cursed blast doors. Behind him, Grimjaw and his South Side sandhog crew have finished setting up the thermite charges on our perimeter fence—a message to any other scavengers considering raiding BATC Telluric sites tonight. The big Orc's voice carries across the staging area as he barks orders about load-bearing angles and detonation timers.

But all I can focus on is how close we are to Sub-Station Seven.

"Commander Mara Vance reporting to Commander Sterling's office at 06:00 hours tomorrow requires me to submit complete tactical incident reports before end-of-shift," I recite mechanically, falling back into procedure when everything else feels like it's dissolving. "Sub-Station Seven breach response falls under my command authority until relieved by Internal Affairs eligibility assessment. Which means I'm staying here."

"You're being a stubborn fool who can't forgive herself enough to move forward," Cole counters. And somehow he says it without cruelty—just observation wrapped in exhaustion. "The Geas fused to your sternum isn't going anywhere whether you stand guard over these ruins or not. Those thirty-eight children will never stop screaming under your ribs no matter how many times you relive burning their rescuers alive to save them."

My hand goes instinctively to where the Lead-Bismuth Myocardial Geas pulses just beneath my breastplate—not from external magic but from the weight of what was done to become worthy of bearing such a thing. Two years carrying phantom screams that were real once upon a time.

"The white-lilac restorative wards won't hold near this site," I say quietly, trying to explain something I barely understand myself. "Every time I try to cast healing bio-wards here, they corrupt into ash-gray static. The air smells like wet charred wool because that's what fills my lungs every night in dreams—the smoke from three hundred bodies cooking in a fire so hot the metal walls ran like wax."

Cole's expression softens slightly—rare for him. Most days his face is carved out of granite and suspicion; tonight there's almost concern there instead.

"Then don't cast them." Simple solution delivered with that same gravel-and-honey tone that could talk down a suicide jumper or convince an enemy agent to switch sides. "We've got paramedics from Newark Bay Medical already on-site. Rookie Jax took femoral shrapnel during the initial breach engagement—they're stabilizing him as we speak. Let someone else handle field medicine while you focus on commanding this operation without drowning in ghosts."

There it is again—that word. Ghosts.

But he doesn't know that standing here isn't about remembering what happened two years ago. It's about being close enough to feel if Sub-Station Seven ever wakes up hungry again. If those sealed blast doors ever crack open under pressure from inside, releasing whatever new breed of Y2K nightmare has been gestating in darkness since 1999 when the Millennium Breach first tore through Earth's ley-lines and flooded our world with everything hunting us now.

The rain keeps falling.

My Motorola Razr flip-phone buzzes against my tactical vest—a message from Sterling's office reminding me that Internal Affairs will be conducting their annual psychological evaluation tomorrow at 06:00 sharp whether I file my reports or not. As if those high-resonance corporate elites dressed in thousand-dollar suits understand anything about what burns underneath Commanders who've done what needs doing.

"You can't stop me," I tell Cole quietly. "Not from standing watch over ground zero."

"No." He agrees readily—too readily—and I suddenly realize he never intended to try forcing me back into the transport. Instead, he pulls out his own phone (some cheaper Sprint model that looks half-melted) and starts dialing. "I'm calling Grimjaw over though. The big Orc owes me favors from three years working together in Local 405 before either of us went BATC black ops. Mara Vance: The explosion hit like a thunderclap rolled through with gravel. My training kicked in before shock could—before the memory of burning commuters could rise like bile in my throat.

## CHAPTER 2: THE PRICE OF THIRTY-EIGHT
