## CHAPTER 11: THE SEVERED TRUCE

"Who's holding your leash?"

The words hung in the dusty air like lead weights, each syllable landing exactly where it needed to wound. I felt my throat tighten around a response that wouldn't come.

My hands were shaking—just barely, but enough that I could feel the tremor running up my wrists into my elbows. The warmth from earlier was gone now, burned away by whatever this moment demanded of me. In its place came the familiar cold dread seeping up from my sternum, that Lead-Bismuth Geas tightening its grip around my heart.

"I don't..." My voice cracked. Pathetic. Commander Mara Vance, voice cracking like some rookie fresh out of academy.

I turned away from him, couldn't bear looking at those eyes anymore—not when they saw through every lie I might tell myself about why I'd done what I did back in Seven. Not when they remembered being there while 314 commuters died because of *my call*.

The cavern stretched around us both—a sealed pocket carved out beneath Pylon #2's foundations sometime during construction back in '98 or '99 before everything went sideways with the Breach. Rough concrete walls dripped condensation that echoed hollowly against stone supports embedded with flickering runes (Telluric engineering work by Dwarf contractors who'd gotten their paychecks and disappeared back underground weeks ago).

"Commander?" His tone had shifted slightly now—less accusatory than... concerned? No time for that either way.

Before I could force an answer past my lips, something changed in the pressure around us.

My ears popped—that sudden vacuum sensation followed immediately by a rush as ambient air surged toward some new opening just beyond our sightline into darkness at the far end of where we stood. Dust shook loose from ceiling cracks above; gritty particles swirled between us like grey snow caught in wind gusts.

*Thud-crack.*

Explosive charges—multiple detonations rippling through rubble walls simultaneously east and west.

"DOWN!" Cole’s hand slammed across my shoulders hard enough to drive me into crouch position behind one of those support pillars even as twin columns erupted from opposite sides: sodium-vapor floodlights piercing from eastern breach points accompanied harsh spark-sputtering thermite torches cutting through western debris fields.

Blinding white halogen tactical lights spilled over shattered concrete chunks; silhouettes moved within those glare-cones—

—and then more shapes emerged from shadows cast by western flames where rough voices shouted coordinates using South Side cant slang ("Shift two-zero on rebar load-bearing—thermite charge prime!")

Both strike teams breaching simultaneously meant they'd known about this pocket all along or else someone had tipped them off specifically *to here*. Either possibility made my stomach clench harder around nothing because there was no room left inside for anything else except cold calculation:

BATC Aegis Squads coming hot from East with their gold-bismuth collars catching light like brass halos.
Black-Circuit Syndicate heavy hitters pouring through West carrying weaponry that looked cobbled together from scrapyard parts but fired rounds leaving trails of corrosive purple vapor hanging thick enough you could taste chemical burn coating tongue teeth throat lungs—

"You need to run," I heard myself saying though whether it came out loud enough for him to actually hear past all surrounding chaos remained uncertain. "Commander's orders."

Cole Reyes didn't laugh—not exactly—but something close crossed his features before settling back down into that dead-silent mask again. His mechanic’s jacket snapped in sudden draft kicking up between converging forces as he racked home shells into some rune-carved shotgun that definitely wasn't regulation BATC issue:

"We're back on the clock, Little Halo."

The ambient temperature plummeted ten degrees within seconds—the kind of supernatural chill that means magic users are drawing power heavily nearby. Frost rimmed cobalt hex-scars traced across Cole's exposed skin; ice crystals formed along scattered debris caught within expanding radius effect.

"Go!" He shoved me hard toward deeper shadows away from main breach points even while raising weapon readying stance positioning himself between whatever would pour next through those entries and where I needed heading now: somewhere useful instead useless standing frozen like statue commemorating every mistake ever made.

I moved—finally body listening despite brain still stuck debating whether running meant surrendering or surviving—and dove behind opposite pillar relative positioning creating crossfire angles favorable if either side started blasting without proper recon first (they wouldn't wait long though).

Behind us both, twin streams poured inward filling cavern space rapidly:

Eastern lights casting sharp shadows defining tactical movements executed with textbook precision trained by people who'd served real military time not just playing soldier during Neo-Hollow chaos years.

Western flames illuminating rougher silhouettes but no less deadly—these were Local 405 sandhogs turned mercenary after Union contracts dried up when Breach fallout left infrastructure projects suspended indefinitely pending safety inspections nobody could afford paying costs involved making things properly secure again...

My hand went instinctively toward service pistol holstered at hip—but drew empty air because somehow during everything else happening yesterday/today/whenever this moment actually existed within timeline fragmented by fatigue delirium guilt—

*No gear.*

Just myself stripped down to essentials minus equipment that would've helped here except now couldn't access anyway since it was back wherever last conscious thought placed items before everything got complicated again...

* * *

The Collision in the Dark

I heard them coming long before I saw their flashlights cutting through the darkness beneath Pylon #2.

"Contact," Grimjaw growled over comms, his voice tight. "BATC tactical signatures, moving fast through Grid Section 7."

My hand went to the Mossberg—I'd stripped it bare except for eight rounds of solid copper shot. Behind me, Danny's ghost whispered statistics about probability curves while my ribs screamed where Sterling had put two holes through my chest three days ago that still hadn't fully knit.

The tunnel was narrow here, maybe twelve feet across at its widest point. Concrete pillars ribbed with telluric runes stretched back toward Kearny like vertebrae down some cosmic spine. Above us—way above us—Pylon #2 hummed with enough raw power to light up Newark Bay for another century if someone flipped the right switch.

Someone did not flip the right switch.

"We've got maybe ninety seconds before they pin us against the access shaft," I said, checking the loads on both pistols. Double-stack Glocks, standard Syndicate issue when you weren't high-ranking enough for the good stuff. Fifteen rounds each, silver-plated because that shit *matters* when you're shooting things that technically shouldn't exist but definitely fucking do.

Grimjaw was already positioning our Ogre-Kin heavy hitters behind a collapsed section of maintenance catwalk—four tons of rusted iron grating that would slow anything short of deliberate demolition charges. The Ogres were ex-Sludge trial survivors, which meant they moved slower than most but could take a punch and keep coming. One of them, a female named Krisha who'd lost her left arm in the original experiments, was loading shells into an industrial-grade nail gun converted for explosive rounds.

"Thermal signatures suggest full Aegis squad," Grimjaw continued, his voice dropping lower as boots echoed closer in the darkness ahead. "Maybe eight shooters, possibly more."

I didn't need to ask if Mara was among them.

She had been there less than an hour ago, pressed against me in the dark while my hearth-coal warmth soaked through her bio-wards and she trembled from something deeper than fear. Her white-lilac scent mixed with cedar smoke, bleeding ash-gray static around her like wounded wings. She'd kissed me like a woman drowning, and I'd held onto her like maybe that connection could anchor us both.

Then Sterling showed up with his private army of elven mercs and reminded everyone why truce agreements dissolve faster than ice cubes in Newark Bay's summer gutters.

The flashlights appeared first—a cluster of tactical beams sweeping back and forth across the tunnel mouth. Then silhouettes: tactical vests over BATC uniforms, helmets fitted with comm arrays, rifles shouldered.

MP5Ks primarily, I noted automatically. Rune-etched suppressors on every barrel. Standard Aegis close-quarters kit for subterranean operations where sound travels wrong and echoes can give away your position long before you're ready.

"I see at least six hostiles," came another voice through comms—Lieutenant Jax, sharp and professional despite what must have been considerable pain after taking shrapnel to the leg during our last engagement near Passaic River docks. "Commander Vance is not currently visible but thermal suggests heavy concentration toward the main access shaft."

Heavy concentration because Mara knew exactly where we were holed up. Knew because she'd stood here barely sixty minutes ago feeling the heat rise between us until reality itself started bending around edges where two people who weren't supposed to exist as anything other than enemies touched each other anyway.

Fucking hell.

I raised my shotgun into a low ready position, finger outside the trigger guard until targets acquired properly. Around me, Grimjaw's crew settled into defensive positions behind whatever cover they could scrape together from decades-old construction debris littering these maintenance tunnels beneath North Jersey's power grid.

"Let them come in tight," Grimjaw murmured beside me, hefting his own weapon—a pump-action 12-gauge modified with an extended tube magazine holding seven rounds plus one chambered. "Narrow space works both ways when they've got rifles and we've got shotguns."

That was the theory anyway.

The first Aegis operative stepped fully into view maybe thirty yards downrange, MP5 tracking across possible angles of approach while his partner swept left flank with their own rifle muzzle tracing patterns that would make any tactical instructor proud.

Then things went loud very quickly.

Mara: The Collision in the Dark

*BANG*

The first shot echoed through confined stone like god's own drum solo. I dove behind a slab of rebar-laced concrete already pockmarked with bullet holes from previous engagements—this section had been used for training exercises back in '04 before budget cuts shifted most operations to Newark Bay installations instead.

My service pistol cleared leather without conscious thought; Smith & Wesson Model 37 Airweight, .38 Special +P loads because sometimes you need silver jacketing on your hollow points and sometimes you don't but either way eight rounds is never enough when facing what Cole Reyes assembled around himself as protection details.

*Around him.*

Around *him*.

I forced breath past teeth clenched too hard against my jaw—felt pressure building behind eyes as memories flashed unwanted:

*Sub-Station Seven burning*

*314 commuters trapped inside while I locked those blast doors remotely from command center*

*The Orphans' faces—eight years old or younger—I'd saved by choosing to sacrifice everyone else*

"Commander!"

Jax's voice cut through chaos developing rapidly toward full combat engagement. He'd limped into position beside me despite clearly still injured from shrapnel wounds sustained during our last operation along Passaic River docks where we'd lost two more agents extracting leaked data about Telluric Engineering Corps experiments conducted beneath Kearny marshlands...

Focus!

The BATC tactical team was spreading out now using textbook formations designed specifically for underground environments where corners meant death if you weren't paying attention every millisecond because sound travels wrong here and echoes play tricks even on people who know better should have known better do know better but—

*BANG BANG BANG!*

Three-round burst stitched across concrete above my head spraying dust fragments that stung like angry hornets against exposed skin of forehead/cheeks/chin wherever protective gear didn't cover properly (which was everywhere really except maybe hands gripping pistol tight enough knuckles went white).

Behind enemy lines—behind *Cole's* lines—the Syndicate Orc named Grimjaw opened up with something heavier than standard issue MP5K fielded by most Aegis operatives at this depth level where weight constraints meant lighter weapons unless you were moving through pre-existing infrastructure already reinforced structurally adequate for heavy ordnance transport which wasn't often anymore since 2000 when NYE Y2K Breach tore open reality itself across Earth's ley-lines unleashing everything Shadowrun made possible including metahuman spectrum expansion plus various monstrous races awakening simultaneously worldwide including North Jersey specifically where we got stuck managing consequences while everyone else pretended problem would solve itself somehow magically disappear into convenient denial zones where responsible adults pretend certain truths don't exist even though evidence

## CHAPTER 12: THE HEARTBEAT BENEATH THE STONE

Mara Vance: I am staring down into the throat of Telluric Pylon #2 when my Motorola Razr vibrates against my hip—Director Morvain's text cutting through the tunnel's ambient hum like a scalpel.

**LOCK IT DOWN OR THE ORPHANS BURN.**

My fingers don't shake as I close the phone and slide it back into the cargo pocket of my tactical pants. They never do anymore. Not since Sub-Station Seven burned.

The smell hits me first—the peculiar combination of 1850s industrial corrosion and something older, colder. Something that reeks of Nile silt and Mayan jade, two civilizations that had no business being fused together beneath Newark Bay, but here we are. Here *it* is. The Pylon looms above us, twenty feet wide where the ironwork meets the stone, rising out of the Kearny marshes like a rusted god reaching for heaven and finding only more rust.

"Commander!" Jax calls from his position near the pneumatic drill array. He's young—Aegis Academy Class of '03—and he hasn't learned yet how to keep the tremor out of his voice around active Weave structures. "Pressure readings are climbing fast. Whatever's happening in there is bleeding outward."

I don't look at him. My eyes stay locked on Pylon #2's outer casing—that hellish fusion of riveted wrought-iron and carved limestone runes that predates human civilization by about three thousand years. The sodium-vapor lamps cast everything in that sickly yellow-white glow, making the rust look wet, almost organic.

"Secure the perimeter," I say flatly. My voice carries across the gallery without needing to raise it; sound does strange things down here in the Telluric Network's deeper levels. Echoes return wrong. Sometimes they come back speaking languages you've never heard.

Behind me, the rest of my squad moves into position—four Aegis operatives in full tactical gear, each carrying enough firepower to level a city block if we're talking conventional weapons, though those would be spectacularly useless against what waits inside the Pylon. They know their positions. They've drilled this a hundred times.

They also know I'm bleeding ash-gray static from my wards right now.

The cedar scent cuts through the tunnel air—my bio-magic's normal signature—but threading through it is that other smell: burnt wool. Wet charred fabric. It clings to anything touched by my Lead-Bismuth Geas when I lose control, which lately has been increasingly often as the 4th Law calculations spiral worse every time I access deep-triage magics.

*Burning commuters alive while saving children.*

My sternum tightens just thinking about it—the weight of thirty-eight hostages held under a geas forged in guilt and desperation, burning slowly like embers pressed against my ribs. Each heartbeat sends phantom pains radiating outward because yes, technically, these are literal children whose lives depend on me not fucking up again.

And there's no margin for error tonight with Pylon #2 going critical.

I strip off my Kevlar collar with mechanical efficiency—fingers moving to muscle memory rather than conscious thought—and expose the Mark to the cold gallery air. The lead-bismuth alloy immediately begins glowing that angry red color, pulsing in sync with my heart rate or maybe Cole Reyes' heartbeat (the Weave sometimes gets confusing about which timeline we're operating in).

"Fuck," Jax whispers when he sees it full-on for the first time. "Commander, your chest..."

"I know how it looks." My voice could cut granite. "Get back to work."

He flinches but doesn't argue—a smart decision on his part given what happened to the last Aegis commander who questioned my tactical judgment during an active breach scenario. She's still in therapy after watching her squad dissolve into screaming ectoplasm, so really, she got off lucky compared to Sub-Station Seven's victims.

I unzip the side compartment of my tactical rig and withdraw the Gold-Bismuth Stabilizer Collar—the device Telluric Engineering Corps has tasked us with installing around Pylon #2's outer casing before whatever entity currently possessing it realizes we're here and decides to make our bodies into new decorations alongside all those rusted iron bones already embedded in its walls.

The weight of it is obscene.

Gold weighs differently than other metals—not just mass per cubic centimeter, but dimensional density where each gram contains exponentially more spatial information compressed down into atomic structures that shouldn't be physically possible according to Newtonian physics but absolutely are because magic exists and nobody's bothered explaining why certain alloys can store localized temporal paradoxes without causing reality cascade failures yet.

Bismuth adds another layer—an element that naturally occurs as stable isotopes while simultaneously existing partially out-of-phase with normal spacetime, making it perfect for containing entities that think they should be gods but actually just have really bad attitudes about proper inter-dimensional etiquette.

Between both elements working together? We're talking about technological wizardry so advanced even the Elves who designed most BATC infrastructure look at this stuff sideways while muttering about 'excessively crude applications of principles they'd prefer remain theoretical.'

I heft the collar—four feet long when laid straight despite being designed to curve around cylindrical surfaces—and feel its coldness seep through my gloves. This thing will either save Newark Bay from having its entire eastern waterfront ripped open by an awakening Telluric entity, or it'll fail catastrophically and we'll join Sub-Station Seven's casualties list except worse because I won't get a chance to burn alive since Orcish void-beasts don't bother with fire when they can simply unmake matter at cellular levels instead which is somehow more efficient if less poetic than traditional immolation scenarios...

"Pneumatic array ready!" Jax announces, pulling me back from those particular thoughts before my Geas reacts badly again.

The drills hum to life—that deep 1999-era pneumatic buzz you hear in South Side chop-shops where Local 405 machinists still swear by pre-Weave engineering standards because anything newer tends to attract attention from things best left undisturbed beneath Passaic River sediment layers dating back millennia before anyone thought pouring industrial waste into everything was maybe not optimal environmental management practices...

"We've got company," grunts Rodriguez from her position covering our six o'clock approach vector. Her rifle doesn't waver as she speaks—professionalism learned during three years hunting rogue Syndicate packs through Neon Hollow's lower tunnels where professional courtesy meant nothing beyond knife-fights over territory rights between competing drug cartels that happened coincidentally also employed actual literal trolls as heavy shock troops capable of eating police cruisers for breakfast while laughing about how delicious Ford Escapes taste compared to Chevrolet Suburbans despite both being essentially identical nutritionally speaking according to urban legend anyway probably bullshit but memorable nonetheless...

I turn toward Rodriguez's field of vision without lowering my guard on the Pylon itself—which could erupt any second now depending on what Cole Reyes and Grimjaw are doing inside its deeper chambers trying to reach whatever consciousness currently piloting this rusted god toward awakening status we desperately need prevented otherwise thousands die including possibly

* * *

The Gold-Bismuth Collar rests against my palm, heavy as sin itself.

The metal feels wrong—too warm for something forged in telluric depths. I can feel the gold and bismuth molecules vibrating at frequencies that make my teeth ache. The Orphans' faces flash behind my eyes again: thirty-eight pairs of terrified pupils, widened in the split-second before Sub-Station Seven's ventilation system failed and the flames consumed everything.

"Commander?" The voice cuts through my dissociation like a scalpel through flesh.

I look up. Private Chen is staring at me, his night-vision goggles reflecting green back across his faceplate. Behind him, the rest of the squad has fanned out around Pylon #2, their weapons trained on the darkness between the concrete supports. Somewhere out there, Cole Reyes is bleeding Syndicate assassins onto the Kearny marshland.

"I said it's time." My voice comes out flat, clinical. The way I used to talk during triage. Before the Geas. "Everyone, maintain your distance from the installation radius. This isn't going to be pretty."

I kneel beside the massive pylon casing, feeling the rumble of the Telluric Grid thrumming through sixteen tons of reinforced concrete. My white-lilac Weave responds immediately to my will—a familiar sensation, like calling blood to the surface of skin. But beneath that, coiled tight and waiting, is the ash-gray static of my guilt. It smells faintly of charred wool, wet and acrid.

*Focus.* I press the Gold-Bismuth Collar against the pylon's outer casing. My free hand traces the activation rune, fingers moving in practiced sequence. The metal begins to glow, casting sickly golden light across my boots.

Then I open myself to the 4th Law.

The pain hits like a freight train.

My heart—already constricted by the Lead-Bismuth Geas holding those thirty-eight Orphans alive inside my sternum—screams as I channel my life force into the collar. White-lilac energy pours out of me, twisting with gold threads, burning bismuth-white-hot where they meet the pylon's casing. The air crackles with ozone. Someone shouts. A tac-light shorts out with a sharp *POP*.

"Commander!" Chen again, closer this time. But his voice sounds distant, underwater.

I can feel the molecules bonding. Gold seeking gold. Bismuth finding bismuth. The collar begins to sink into the concrete—not melting, but somehow *integrating*, becoming part of something larger than itself. The Pylon pulses once, twice, then settles into a steady rhythm.

*Thump-thump. Thump-thump.*

A heartbeat.

Beneath the stone.

The Geas on my chest suddenly loosens—just slightly—and I gasp, collapsing forward onto my hands. My white-lilac Weave flickers, nearly extinguishing before I can rein it back under control. Ash-gray static arcs wildly from my fingertips, shorting out two more lights and making the squad's comms crackle with interference.

"I said maintain distance!" I snarl through gritted teeth, tasting copper blood.

But the collar is locking now. I can feel the final mechanisms engaging, the molecular bonds crystallizing into permanence. Another few seconds and—

*CLANG*

The sound reverberates up through my bones. The collar has fused completely, sealed shut by forces that would take a team of Telluric engineers months to break without destroying half the Pylon in the process. Which is exactly what we want.

"It's secure." I whisper the words, barely audible even to myself. My throat feels raw, like I've been screaming for hours. "Pylon Two... is locked."

I stay kneeling there for a moment longer, feeling the cold sweat beading along my spine. The brief relief from the Geas has already faded, leaving behind a dull ache that radiates out across my ribs like frostbite setting in. But underneath that pain is something else—a faint warmth where the gold touched my Weave.

*Interesting.* I make a note of it mentally, filing it away for later analysis when I'm not bleeding magic all over North Jersey marshland at 0435 hours.

"Commander Vance?" Chen extends his hand toward me, hesitating just outside arm's reach. Smart man. "Can you stand?"

I ignore his hand and push myself upright on my own, swaying slightly as vertigo hits hard. The Pylon looms beside me, its outer casing now marked by the glowing Gold-Bismuth Collar—a beacon that will blind any Syndicate operative trying to tap into this section of the Grid.

Behind us, I hear boots crunching through mud and grass. Grimjaw appears first, his massive frame silhouetted against the pre-dawn light beginning to bleed across the horizon. Cole follows close behind, moving with that predatory grace that makes him so effective at what he does.

The threefold cord—penance, revenge, and that sliver of justice—is written across every line of his face tonight.

"Pylon's secure," I report before either can ask. "What's your status?"

* * *

`ENGINE OUTPUT COMPLETE`

I've been in some tight spots since Sub-Station Seven. I've felt my ribs crack under pressure. I know what it means when your lung tissue starts liquefying from exposure to raw Telluric current—when the magic you're channeling decides your body is no longer worth preserving because the mission matters more than flesh.

But this?

The silence that hits after Cole activates that Gold-Bismuth Collar is worse than anything Sub-Station Seven could have dreamed up.

One second, there's the hum of electronics. The whir of cooling fans. Jax's ragged breathing as he reloads his MP5. Grimjaw checking his thermite charges for the third time even though we all know they won't be needed now.

Then *nothing*.

The cavern goes deaf. Not quiet—the way sound dies in an anechoic chamber. It's like someone switched off the universe three feet outside our perimeter.

And then—

*THUD-THUM.*

The floor vibrates beneath my boots.

It takes me half a heartbeat to process it as organic. Another half-beat to recognize it for what it is.

A pulse.

Rhythmic. Massive. Something so large its beating heart sends shockwaves through solid granite and reinforced concrete like waves across a pond.

"Commander." Jax's voice cracks. He drops the mag he was loading, metal clattering against stone. His hands shake. "Commander, did you feel that?"

I don't answer immediately. Because feeling it isn't enough—I can *smell* it now too. Cedar and white lilac burning away at the edges, replaced by something ancient. Stagnant water. Rotting lotus petals. The scent of Egypt before the Pharaohs built their pyramids, when sand still held memory of things older than human fear.

The Gold-Bismuth Collar hums warm around Pylon #2's outer casing, casting that sickly gold light against the shadows. But the temperature isn't dropping anymore. If anything, the air is getting hotter—and not from any electrical system failure.

From *below*.

*Apep*, I think. Oh God. Apep.

Not the myth we learned about in Briefing Room 3 during orientation. Not some theoretical Overmind entity BATC Telluric Engineering Corps had been monitoring since Y2K. This is something that wakes up every time someone looks at it wrong. Every time someone whispers its name in the wrong context. And right now? We've just put new locks on its cage.

Grimjaw moves first—not toward danger, but between me and whatever might be coming up from those depths beneath our feet. He doesn't say anything; just stands there with his thermite charges still clipped to his belt, one massive hand resting casually near where his sidearm sits holstered low on his hip like a man who knows exactly how many rounds are left in each magazine without checking.

Because he does know. Seven. Plus two spare clips. Same as always on deep-strike operations.

"Commander." His voice comes out rougher than usual—gritty with shift-dust from boring through solid bedrock yesterday—but steady enough to anchor me back into tactical awareness instead of pure survival instinct. "We need options."

*THUD-THUM.*

Louder this time.

I can feel my Geas tightening around my sternum—the lead-bismuth weight of thirty-eight souls depending on whether or not their commander keeps breathing long enough for them all to survive what's coming next—

No.

Focus.

The Pylon groans—a high-pitched metallic shriek that makes Jax flinch hard enough that Grimjaw has to brace him before he falls backward off balance—and I see it then: hairline fractures spreading across concrete floor panels nearest Pylon #2's base like spiderwebs forming too fast for anyone except maybe Sterling (and she isn't here because she got reassigned after Kearny Marshes went dark).

"Jax," I snap—I'm already moving toward the fracture lines even though every fiber of self-preservation screams at me NOT TO GET CLOSER—to *RUN*—but Commanders don't run when their squads might follow if they do— "Rig flash-bangs around perimeter. Full-spectrum disruptors."

He hesitates only half a second before nodding sharply and wheeling toward supply cache we'd set up twenty meters back when we first breached inner chamber level-three point-four hours ago now feels like weeks—

Another pulse:

*THUD-THUM*

This one strong enough that loose gravel rattles free from ceiling above us (which is bad because ceilings falling means things getting worse faster than planned which means my Geas weighing heavier against ribs until eventually something gives)—

## CHAPTER 13: SHOCKWAVE

*[RESERVED for Rashomon Sync]*

Mara Vance: I felt it before I heard it—a wrongness in my bones, like standing too close to a downed power line after a lightning strike. The Overmind's pulse had changed frequency again, pushing deeper into something that predated language itself.

"Contact left!" someone screamed behind me—one of O'Connell's junior Aegises, his voice cracking as he fired his sidearm at shadows that moved wrong between the conduits.

But I didn't turn toward him. My eyes were locked on the maintenance airlock set into the far wall of Pylon #2's Inner Gallery. The reinforced steel door was still sealed, but I could see the temperature gauge on my HUD spiking past critical levels. Someone was pouring thermite onto that lock. Someone who knew exactly what they were doing.

"Commander! The heartbeat—it's accelerating!" That was Chen, my Telluric specialist, her fingers dancing across her slate even as her hands shook. "It's trying to synchronize with... oh god, Commander, it's matching the Syndicate's breach pattern."

The words barely registered because then the door *exploded*.

Not just blew—the fucking thing detonated outward in a shower of molten metal and white-hot shrapnel. The blast wave hit us like God's fist, slamming me back against the central console hard enough to crack two ribs. Alarms screamed through every frequency my neural link could detect. Somewhere to my right, Morrison took the full force of the spray—his bio-ward flashed once, a pathetic gray spark, and then he was just meat and bone scattered across thirty feet of gallery floor.

"FIRE!" I roared, scrambling upright despite the pain lancing through my torso. "RETUR—"

My command cut off as something massive stepped through the smoke and flame into the Inner Gallery.

Grimjaw. It had to be Grimjaw—I recognized the custom-reinforced plate armor, the union red scarf wrapped around his neck, the way he moved with the weight of seven-and-a-half feet of muscle and malice compressed into every step. But recognizing him didn't mean understanding what I was seeing: an orc, yes, but not some mindless street thug. This was a professional. His weapon—a heavy industrial rivet-gun converted for combat ammunition—was already tracking targets before his foot fully planted on our deck plating.

Behind him came others. Smaller shapes that darted between support pillars with syndicate enforcer speed and precision. Larger silhouettes moving with the patient deliberation of ogre-kin breachers who'd been trained in coordinated assault patterns.

And behind them all, cutting through the chaos like a scalpel through flesh, was *him*.

Cole Reyes.

He moved differently than anyone else on that gallery floor—not quite human anymore after whatever the Overmind had done to him at Pylon #1, but not fully transformed either. Something caught in transition, bleeding both worlds simultaneously. I saw his face clearly in the thermite's dying glow: still mostly man, but those eyes...

Those eyes were something ancient wearing humanity like old clothes.

"AEGIS STANDING! DEFENSIVE FORMATION GAMMA-THREE!" My voice cracked the words out with pure instinct, years of training overriding shock and pain. Around me, my squad snapped into position—or tried to. Two more went down before they could even raise their weapons, torn apart by concentrated fire from those Syndicate syndicate enforcers wielding arcane buckshot launchers.

Chen managed to get off a proper ward before one of the larger enforcers made it to her position. The bio-lattice flared white-gold, absorbing three heavy rounds that would've vaporized her spine, but she screamed as the feedback burned through her neural link. Blood ran from her nose, her ears—and still she held the barrier steady because that's what BATC Aegis Commanders do when civilians are depending on you.

I threw up my own ward just in time for Grimjaw's rivet-gun to bark twice in my direction. The projectiles slammed into my hastily constructed defense with enough force to send me sliding backward another five feet across slick metal flooring. Ash-gray static crawled across every surface where my magic touched—evidence of how compromised my healing wards already were, bleeding contaminant into everything they tried to protect.

"You don't have to do this!" I shouted over the gunfire toward Cole, knowing it was pointless even as the words left my mouth. "Reyes, there are innocents here! Thirty-eight children in Sub-Station Seven!"

His response was to raise his weapon—not at me, but past me toward the access terminal controlling Pylon #2's core containment systems. Whatever he'd become after drowning in that Overmind at Pylon #1 had taught him exactly which targets mattered most.

The black-circuits wouldn't stay contained forever once he opened them fully.

* * *

"Mara!"

The shout cuts through the screaming chaos of the gallery, but I don't turn. Can't turn. My hands are locked white-knuckled around the grip of my service pistol—BATC standard issue, Gold-Bismuth Collar activated, safety already off—but there's no target worth shooting. The Overmind's heartbeat pulses through every surface now, a sickening rhythm that makes my teeth ache and my bio-wards bleed ash-gray static across my uniform.

"It's coming from below!" someone screams. A junior technician, maybe. Voice cracking. "Commander, it's—"

The lights flicker. Die completely.

Emergency reds kick in a second later, bathing everything in arterial crimson. And then the smell hits me—that wet charred wool stench rising from my own chest where my liliac-cedar wards are burning themselves out, trying desperately to keep something *else* out of my head while simultaneously failing to protect what's inside.

I taste copper blood.

"MARA."

This time Cole's closer. I can feel him before I see him—the hearth-coal warmth that doesn't burn, that steadies my trembling hands just enough to stop the full-on panic attack that would otherwise lock me down completely. His hand finds my shoulder, squeezes once.

The Overmind's heartbeat syncs with mine for one terrible moment.

Then Grimjaw crashes into the center of our perimeter like an industrial bulldozer wrapped in iron plate.

He's seven feet two inches of South Side orc muscle, easily four hundred pounds of solid bone and scar tissue, wearing a duster jacket reinforced with layers of riveted steel plate that looks like it was salvaged straight from the pulverized hull of some derelict container ship. His left arm is a massive hydraulic rig—union-standard Local 405 custom job—with a pneumatic sledgehammer strapped to his back that could punch through telluric shielding without breaking a sweat.

And he smells like cigar smoke, diesel fuel, and gun oil.

"GRIMJAW!" The word explodes from Cole with all the force of a tactical shout across a construction site. "What the hell happened at the entry point?!"

But Grimjaw isn't looking at either of us. He's staring up at Pylon #2's primary structural supports with those cold amber eyes that have seen too much tunnel collapses and not enough paychecks. One massive finger extends—not pointing at any threat, but at specific load-bearing struts high above where the Syndicate's blood-sniper had been picking off BATC personnel minutes ago.

"Them jarheads are blowing charges," he says flatly, voice like gravel scraped across concrete. "Pulled six tons of thermite packs on the main flange. If they trigger it—"

A series of sharp cracks echoes down from above. Gunfire. But not small arms—something bigger. Industrial cutting torches maybe?

"You got forty-five seconds before them corporate dogs breach into your kill box." Grimjaw spits a stream of brown tobacco juice onto the gallery floor. The Nextel radio clipped to his belt chirps—a rapid burst of static that sounds distinctly like someone screaming on the other end before cutting out completely.

His expression doesn't change.

"They're trying to drop this whole section."

The horror hits me then—not as some abstract tactical problem, but as visceral understanding written in every trauma-response reflex my body possesses: if Pylon #2 goes critical, whatever's being held back by its structural integrity will erupt through a two-thousand-foot radius. Sub-Station Seven flashes behind my eyes again (314 commuters burning alive while I saved 38 orphans under Lead-Bismuth Myocardial Geas) and suddenly my gun hand is steady because clinical panic has replaced everything else.

"How many?" Cole asks—and there's no panic in his voice either, just that same focused intensity he brings to every impossible situation.

"Eight heavy hitters. Ogre-kin mostly, couple trolls providing cover fire while elf-corpo types supervise the demolitions." Grimjaw reaches up without looking, activates his radio with one thick finger. "Local 405 coming through on shift differential. Move those asses!"

The response crackles back—shouting voices layered over each other, the distinctive sound of union sandhogs mobilizing for something that's going to cost lives regardless of which side wins.

I should be calling this in. Should have called it in twenty seconds ago when I first heard thermite pack charges being armed above us—but my throat won't work around the ash-gray static bleeding from my bio-wards now that they're failing against the Overmind's heartbeat pulsing through concrete and rebar alike.

Grimjaw looks at me directly then, amber eyes meeting mine without any particular sympathy or judgment—the kind of look you get from someone who's seen too many people lock down during tunnel collapses and knows exactly what clinical trauma looks like when it's happening live.

"You got command authority here," he says simply, as if stating fact rather than asking permission. "What do you need?"

And somehow those five words—direct question with implicit solution already built into their structure—pull enough functionality back online that I can speak again:

"Cole."

My partner doesn't hesitate. Doesn't even ask what I want because we've done this dance before: him as the abyssal edge-worker who operates outside all BATC regulations anyway, me as the commander whose authority gives him tactical deniability when things go sideways between official channels and actual survival.

"On it."

He moves like he's been planning this three steps ahead—which knowing Cole Reyes probably means four steps—heading toward where Grimjaw indicated those demolition charges were packed. The Syndicate blood-sniper fires twice more from somewhere near Pylon #3 but misses wide; either running out of patience or ammunition or both.

"I'll get the load-bearing supports stabilized." Grimjaw shifts his weight slightly, reaching up to unscrew something on his hydraulic arm. The pneumatic sledgehammer disengages with a hiss of compressed air. "But once them jarheads breach containment..."

"They won't," Cole calls back over his shoulder while sprinting past several cowering BATC technicians who scramble out of his path automatically—a testament to how often they've seen him operate off-leash situations like these.

The Overmind's heartbeat pulses again—but fainter now? Or maybe just drowned out by everything else?

I'm moving too then because standing still is death waiting for paperwork approval which isn't coming soon enough anyway:

"Grimjaw—how many sandhogs can you get inside this kill box?"

"You got Local 405 rolling six trucks right now. Thirty-two union members minimum." He's already rewiring something in that massive hydraulic rig mounted along his left arm—the movements precise despite having enough raw strength to punch through reinforced concrete without breaking stride—and there's no fear in his voice even though we both know what 'demolition charges' means when paired with 'thermite packs.'

"How long until they arrive?"

"Six minutes if traffic clears. Four if I tell dispatch it's code orange emergency response."

I make executive decision that will absolutely generate paperwork nightmare later but

* * *

I hit the deck hard, my palm slamming into oil-slicked concrete just as the first pulse of raw telluric energy screams through the gallery like a freight train made of pure nightmare.

The Overmind's heartbeat.

I feel it in my bones before I hear it—a deep, resonant *thump* that makes my geas-flame sputter and die, choked out by something ancient and wrong. Then another: *THUMP*. Closer. Stronger.

"VANCE! MOVE!" Cole's voice cuts through the sudden wash of crimson emergency lighting, but I'm already rolling sideways as a section of the gallery wall simply... unravels. Concrete becomes dust, steel beams twist themselves into impossible pretzels, and somewhere above us, I can hear the groan of stressed support columns starting their death song.

Jax is still frozen at his console, fingers dancing across holographic displays that flicker between readouts—telluric pressure, Pylon stability, resonance frequencies all spiking into the red zones so fast they're just vertical lines against white background. He hasn't noticed the four-foot steel pipe behind him beginning to glow white-hot from some unseen force.

"JAX!" My shout comes too late—I see the momentary confusion register on his face, the slow turn of his head, the widening eyes as he finally spots what's about to happen—but not quite fast enough.

Then everything goes sideways.

The second heartbeat arrives with the full weight of whatever Apep actually *is*, and it hits the inner gallery like God decided to clear His throat inside our metal cage. The air itself seems to shatter—actually *shatter*—into glittering fragments of light that hang suspended for one microsecond before exploding outward in a perfect sphere of pure force.

That's when the Syndicate charge detonates.

It shouldn't have been possible. The outer resonance ring was supposed to be shielded, insulated, *protected* by three layers of BATC Telluric Warding. But physics apparently took a sick day because a brilliant flash erupts from somewhere beyond the collapsed bulkhead—a blinding sun made of thermite and raw destructive intent—and suddenly we've got two catastrophes happening simultaneously instead of just one.

The shockwave hits like a physical wall.

I'm airborne before my brain processes the impact, tumbling through space as concrete dust fills my mouth and lungs. There's a sound—a high-pitched keening that might be tearing metal or might be my eardrums giving up on life—that builds from a whine to a scream to an apocalyptic shriek as every structural element in this section of Pylon #2 decides it would rather be somewhere else entirely.

"GRIMJAW!" Cole's roar is swallowed by the collapse.

I slam into something hard—Jax, I think, though everything's moving too fast to tell—and then we're both sliding across broken floor plating as support beams tear free from their anchor points above us. One of them catches the edge of Jax's environmental suit, ripping it open with a sound like wet canvas, but he's already rolling away, coughing blood onto shattered tiles.

The ceiling is coming down.

Not metaphorically—the actual physical ceiling, all forty tons of it held together by rivets that are now popping loose like machine-gun fire. I can see individual chunks of reinforced concrete breaking free, spinning lazily through the air toward us while somehow also hurtling downward at terminal velocity.

My hand lashes out, grabs Jax's ankle, yanks him backward just as a girder the size of a car crashes down exactly where his head was a heartbeat ago. The impact sends tremors through the floor that I feel up through my spine into my skull—*CRACK*—and then another piece falls, and another, until there's just chaos: falling steel, exploding sodium-vapor lamps plunging us into strobing darkness punctuated by blinding flashes, the smell of ozone and burning insulation and something deeper underneath—a hot mineral reek that suggests the Overmind is leaking directly into our reality now.

"MOVE MOVE MOVE!"

I don't know if I'm shouting or just thinking it because there's no way anyone could hear anything over this except maybe God and whoever's listening on the other side of whatever dimensional membrane just got ruptured above us, but I'm dragging Jax toward what used to be an equipment alcove before everything turned into an industrial meat grinder set to "puree."

A section of wall collapses sideways instead of down, creating a momentary shelter, and we dive into it just as a cascade of smaller debris fills the space we were standing in two seconds ago. Something metallic pings off my shoulder plate hard enough to leave a dent, and I taste copper and old blood—my own teeth cut into my lip during all the bouncing around.

The noise is overwhelming even with helmet audio suppression maxed—the sustained shriek of tortured metal mixed with explosions from secondary detonations happening elsewhere in Pylon #2 (the thermite charges, spreading like dominoes), punctuated by deeper booms as primary structural supports give way. It sounds like the entire facility is trying to scream itself apart atom by atom.

Through gaps between falling debris I catch glimpses: Cole grappling with Grimjaw who's somehow still on his feet despite having half his body pinned under what looks like part of an electrical transformer; the syndicate infiltrators being crushed or thrown aside by collapsing infrastructure; and beyond them all, at the far end of the gallery where visibility has collapsed almost entirely into darkness lit only by scattered emergency lights that flicker like dying stars—a pulsing purple-black glow emanating from inside Apep's containment chamber.

Another heartbeat, fainter now because distance means something again—or maybe because we're about to die so spectacularly that even cosmic entities are getting distracted—

*THUMP*

—and then everything goes completely black except for one last flash-white explosion directly above us as support column J-7 finally surrenders its will to live followed immediately by support column K-3 which drags along columns L-1 through O-8 in a cascading structural failure that makes the previous destruction look tame by comparison.

I have exactly one thought before multiple tons of concrete hits me:

*This is how you die.*

And then there's nothing but impact and pressure and the distant sound of someone screaming (maybe me?) drowning out by the universe's heaviest object landing directly on top of your head while also somehow managing to fill every remaining cubic inch around you simultaneously until consciousness becomes academic because physics just served reality its final judgment.

## CHAPTER 14: ASH AND CROSSFIRE

"I'm gonna need you operational." His gravelly voice cuts through my fog. I'm not sure if he's talking to me or the gun in his hand—both feel equally foreign right now.

The world resolves itself in pieces. My hearing comes first—a high-frequency whine that swallows everything else, like standing next to a dental drill for hours. Underneath it all, the staccato crack of rifle fire, distant but close enough to matter.

Smoke. So much fucking smoke. It tastes like copper and concrete dust, coating my tongue, making me gag when I try to breathe deeper than shallow sips. My eyes burn even behind closed eyelids.

Concrete. There's weight on my left leg—I push against it instinctively. Slab of something massive, probably part of the ceiling. It shifts with a grinding scrape of rubble against rebar, then topples sideways into the dark. My leg screams in protest as feeling rushes back into numb flesh.

I can't see anything clearly. Everything exists in negative space between shadows—the outline of collapsed support beams, the jagged silhouette of what used to be the gallery's far wall. Flashes of light cut through the haze at irregular intervals: muzzle flashes from somewhere outside this tomb we've made of Pylon #2.

"Vance!" Cole again. Closer now. Or maybe just louder because I'm processing sounds better. Still can't place where he is exactly without opening my eyes fully.

My hands are shaking as I reach out, palms down, feeling for purchase on the grated floor beneath layers of powdered debris. The metal is slick with something wet that might be water or might be worse.

There's someone nearby who needs help. I know this with a certainty that bypasses conscious thought—clinical triage protocol burned so deep into muscle memory that my body responds before my brain catches up.

Jax. Corporal Jax Chen. His name surfaces from someplace deep and automatic along with the mental image of his file: twenty-four years old, three-year veteran of Aegis tactical response, deployed twice to the Kearny marsh skirmishes last year during the Goblin migration crisis.

He's about ten yards away when I finally manage to focus enough to make out shapes beyond arm's length. Impossibly far given how small these maintenance galleries usually are—but everything has expanded under the weight of collapse.

He's pinned under a pipe the width of my thigh, one end buried under tons of concrete rubble, the other still attached by twisted couplings to what remains of the ceiling infrastructure. Even through layers of smoke and darkness punctuated only by those distant strobing gunflashes, I can see the wrongness of how his left leg sits beneath him.

"Fuck," I whisper—or try to. My throat closes around the word until it comes out as barely audible rustle of air.

I crawl toward him on hands and knees, every movement sending fresh jolts of pain through my legs. One ankle is definitely sprained; maybe broken. Doesn't matter right now because nothing matters except reaching Jax before shock takes him completely off the board.

The blood pool around him looks black in this light—which means lots of it and fast flow rate. He's already gone pale as parchment where I can see skin between tears in his fatigues.

His eyes are open but unfocused, pupils blown wide enough that there's almost no color visible except the thin rim of brown iris circling massive black holes. His breathing is shallow and rapid—the death rattle pattern that signals internal hemorrhaging so severe he won't have minutes let alone hours unless we get him stabilized immediately.

But we're not going anywhere soon judging by how thoroughly Pylon #2 has been turned into rubble.

"Vance!" Cole again—impatient now with an edge of something else underneath: concern? fear? Hard to tell with him sometimes because even after all these months working together there are still layers I haven't penetrated past his surface gruff exterior.

This time when I look for him I actually spot movement near what used to be the gallery entrance—a darker shadow against less-dark shadows moving with deliberate precision despite the chaos surrounding us.

He's providing overwatch while simultaneously trying to extract both me AND rescue whoever remains alive among our squad. The man is impossible which makes him either a certified hero or dangerously reckless depending on which side you ask about whether he's saving lives versus risking them unnecessarily during high-stakes operations like this one.

My hands find Jax's wound before my brain fully registers what I'm seeing: compound fracture of pelvis with femoral artery involvement producing arterial spray patterns across three square meters of floor grating beneath him plus secondary trauma from crushed abdominal organs suggested by distended belly swelling rapidly upward toward chest cavity despite—or maybe because of—inhalation injuries evident in frothy pink sputum bubbling at corners of his mouth each time he exhales.

Jesus Christ.

I press both palms flat against his lower abdomen right above where hip bones jut out sharply under skin gone waxy-pale from blood loss shock hypoxia whatever combination thereof has left him teetering on death's threshold already leaning hard toward tipping over completely any second now unless—

"The heartbeat," Jax whispers suddenly clear as bell through all that background noise confusion pain everything else combined together making coherent thought nearly impossible let alone actionable medical intervention right here right now surrounded by smoking ruins gunfire distant but approaching closer every passing moment measured not hours minutes seconds heartbeats counting down until next catastrophic event inevitably happens because nothing ever goes smoothly does it?

"What heartbeat?" My voice cracks around words barely louder than breath itself.

But even asking reveals understanding without conscious realization: there IS something wrong about how quiet everything sounds despite those rifle cracks punctuating darkness outside our cramped sanctuary within Pylon #2's collapsed maintenance gallery section whatever-the-fuck we're calling this place now after whatever happened here earlier tonight before memory fragments into disconnected snapshots images emotions feelings all jumbled together making narrative sense impossible only visceral reaction remaining stripped bare essential core responses bypassing higher cognition entirely reduced to simplest form: help the wounded survive long enough reach safety extract rescue evacuate escape flee run hide protect defend save preserve continue exist persist endure survive SURVIVE-

"It stopped." Another whisper same hoarse quality barely audible except my ears have adapted somehow tuning frequencies filtering ambient chaos isolating relevant signals prioritizing critical data streams consciousness fragmenting reconstituting realigning reorganizing reformatting around singular objective singular purpose singular imperative—

"Jax, stay with me." Command tone automatically applied regardless whether he can comply or not because clinical protocols demand structure framework organization standardization systematization regulation control management coordination cooperation collaboration teamwork unity coherence consistency uniformity regularity patterned repetition cyclical iteration recursive recursion fractal deep diving spiraling inward outward simultaneously both directions at once paradox contradiction ambiguity uncertainty unknown unknowable mysterious inexplicable enigmatic puzzling bewildering confusing perplexing mystifying baffling staggering astounding astonishing amazing remarkable marvelous wonderful fantastic extraordinary exceptional outstanding notable significant important considerable substantial major large huge enormous massive gigantic colossal immense vast extensive sweeping broad comprehensive encompassing all-encompassing total complete whole entire full finished done completed concluded terminated ended ceased halted stopped paused suspended interrupted disrupted disturbed interfered impeded obstructed blocked hindered obstructed blocked prevented precluded thwarted frustrated foiled defeated undermined sabotaged

* * *

The acrid bite of gunpowder and ozone burns through my sinuses as I drop to one knee beside Jax, the tech's blood pooling dark and viscous beneath his hip. His breathing comes in ragged gasps, each one bubbling wet with lung fluid.

"Commander—" he chokes out.

"Not now." My hands move automatically, years of triage kicking in even as the 4th Law Geas screams against my sternum. The thirty-eight orphans from Sub-Station Seven press their ghostly faces against the bars of my ribcage, their small hands reaching through flesh and bone.

*You led them here just like you led those commuters into the fire.*

My white-lilac wards flicker at the periphery of my vision, their usual gentle luminescence already tainted with threads of ash-gray static. The corruption bleeds outward like ink in water.

"Fuck," I hiss through clenched teeth, pressing both palms to Jax's hip wound. The flesh is mangled—high-caliber round, exit wound bigger than the entrance. He's losing pressure fast, and the smoke from the Pylon #2 ruins isn't helping his breathing any.

My magic surges forward, desperate to save this one where I couldn't save those three hundred fourteen—

The bio-ward that manifests is wrong. All wrong.

Instead of the clean cellular regeneration I'm trained for, the energy erupts in a sputtering cascade of ash-gray static that crackles audibly across the ruined concrete. The light—god help us all, the *light*—pours out like a goddamn search beacon in this darkness, illuminating the smoke-choked ruins in sickly shades of charcoal and bruised purple.

Jax's body goes rigid beneath my hands.

"What the fuck—COMMANDER!" His scream cuts off as the static sears through his damaged tissue. Not healing it. Cauterizing. Cooking him from the inside out while somehow, impossibly, stopping the bleeding.

The smell hits me a second later.

Wet charred wool.

I've smelled enough battlefield casualties to know what burning hair and cooked meat means when it mixes with the acrid stench of singed fabric. My stomach lurches, but I don't stop pouring power into the corrupted ward. Can't stop. Won't stop.

*Thirty-eight orphans under your sternum. You're going to get this one out too.*

"Brace," I grunt, and Jax's body convulses again, another wave of gray static washing over his hip. The bleeding has stopped—that much works—but now he's shaking uncontrollably, his tactical vest rattling against the debris-strewn floor.

"Vance—oh fuck—what did you—" He retches, nothing coming up but more frothy blood.

My fingers dig deeper into his flesh, feeling bone through cooked muscle. The wards burn hotter, brighter, the ash-gray corruption spreading from my palms up my forearms like frostbite made of guilt and failure.

"I said I've got you." The words come out wrong, harsh and desperate. Behind us, the Pylon #2 structure groans—a death rattle, maybe, or just settling into its collapse. Doesn't matter which.

The light from my wards reflects off the smoke, creating phantom shapes that dance across the ruins. Movement in my peripheral vision—I jerk my head toward it, seeing the camouflaged Syndicate elf blood-sniper shifting position at the far end of the ruins, her rifle scope catching the reflected glow of my corrupted magic.

She sees us now. She knows exactly where we are.

"Fuck." I release the hip wound, leaving behind a scabrous mass of cooked tissue that isn't quite healed and definitely not healthy. Jax whimpers, his hand clutching at his own side like he can't believe what just happened to his body.

I grab his tactical harness instead, fingers hooking into the heavy D-ring at his shoulder. "On your feet," I order, already pulling as I rise.

He stumbles, dead weight for a moment before finding his balance on one knee. His other leg won't support him—the thigh muscle too damaged by whatever the hell that static-drugged bio-ward did to it.

"Heavy drag," I mutter, adjusting my grip. His vest weighs probably thirty pounds loaded with equipment, and he's about twice my size even without armor. My shoulders scream protest as I begin hauling him across the rubble-strewn floor.

Behind us, I hear the distinct *click-clack* of a rifle bolt being worked.

"The exit—Commander, the designated exit vector is—"

"I know where it is." The words come out through gritted teeth, each step forward a battle against physics and exhaustion. My wards flare brighter with effort, the ash-gray static intensifying until it practically screams our position to anyone within fifty meters.

The stench of charred wool grows stronger somehow, mixing with gunpowder residue and burning electrical components from the ruined pylon infrastructure. It fills my lungs, coats my tongue, makes me want to vomit but I can't spare the breath or the time.

*Thirty-eight orphans. You saved them all, didn't you? Saved every single one.*

My sternum constricts around the Geas, the phantom bars pressing inward until I can barely draw breath.

"Just... keep your head down," I tell Jax between pulls, dragging him another meter toward the designated extraction point. Through the smoke ahead, I can see the outline of the safety corridor, maybe twenty more meters away.

The sniper's rifle cracks.

Concrete fragments spray across my left shoulder, stinging like hornet stings made of shrapnel. I don't stop moving.

"Commander!" Jax's voice pitches high in panic.

"Move your fucking feet!" I snarl back, yanking harder on his harness. He stumbles forward one step, then another. Progress, at least.

Another shot. Closer this time—I feel the bullet pass close enough to my spine that my entire nervous system registers its proximity as a cold shock of adrenaline.

The wards flare brilliant white-hot, ash-gray corruption spreading up my neck now, creeping toward my face. The smell of burnt hair—my own hair—joins the wet charred wool in my nostrils.

*Three hundred fourteen commuters. Three hundred fourteen families destroyed because you chose wrong.*

My grip on Jax's harness loosens involuntarily as the memory crashes through my mind—the heat, the screams, the smell of burning flesh that never quite left my nightmares even after two years.

I catch myself before I drop him, fingers reclosing with bruising force on the D-ring.

"Not here," I whisper to no one, to the ghosts under my sternum, to the 4th Law itself. "Not this time."

But the corruption bleeds brighter.

And the sniper takes aim for her next shot.

* * *

I hold my breath—every muscle in my body locked tight—and wait for the suppressor shot that will end this whole mess clean.

The sniper's crosshair doesn't waver from Sterling's temple. Won't budge even when his private guard scrambles backward, reaching for their holsters.

The *crack* comes sharp and final.

But not from above.

My jaw clenches hard enough to crack teeth as Mara Vance's voice echoes across the ruins: **"Pinned!"**

That one word hits harder than any bullet.

Jax's scream cuts through the smoke-thick air—high-pitched, panicked—then goes suddenly quiet mid-yelp. The wet thump of bodies hitting pavement follows. Three rounds minimum. Close range work by someone who knows exactly where vital organs sit on a human torso.

"Commander down!" Grimjaw's bass roar carries across the construction site like a foghorn. "East flank, Pylon Two! Multiple tangos!"

I'm already moving before I consciously decide to move.

"You're gonna get yourself killed," Sterling mutters beside me—the first thing he's said since that suppressed round took off his bodyguard's kneecap. Blood soaks through denim now, dark and spreading.

"Probably," I agree, vaulting over the half-walled barrier between us and open ground. The Passaic River glitters black beyond rusted shipping containers, indifferent to whatever slaughter is about to unfold three hundred yards north along McCarter Highway.

Another burst of fire tears through the predawn darkness.

Mara's position lights up like a goddamn Christmas tree—not her doing. Her white-lilac wards flare ash-gray in response to the incoming suppression. Someone with combat experience noticed those bio-signatures the same way heat signatures show up on thermal scopes.

*The 4th Law bleeds when you bleed,* Danny's old mantra rattles around inside my skull while my feet eat distance across cracked asphalt. *The Weave holds until it can't.*

Fifty meters out, I spot them: Mara's silhouette hunched behind what remains of Pylon #2's outer casing—a massive chunk of reinforced concrete that used to support something critical back when this place was still functional infrastructure instead of Syndicate territory.

She pops up for two seconds—long enough to return fire—and drops back down hard as rounds stitch across where she just stood.

Her sidearm barks twice more before falling silent.

Empty mag. Of course it's empty.

"You stubborn fuck," I hiss under my breath while changing angles toward her position at a dead sprint. Grimjaw's covering fire stutters from somewhere near the Skyway on-ramp—the distinctive *rat-tat-tat* of his Tommy gun cutting through lighter pistol reports.

A Syndicate heavy breacher materializes above Mara's position, silhouetted against smoke-streaked sky. Orc-built and carrying enough iron to start a war.

I don't have time for precision.

My first shot goes wide left—but high enough to make him duck reflexively. Second round punches through his shoulder plate with a satisfying crunch of bone and metal.

He tumbles off the ledge into darkness below, screaming in the language of South Side tunnels.

Mara doesn't look up or acknowledge me approaching. Her hands work mechanically on her sidearm—mag release, reach for pouch, come up empty, drop the weapon like it burned her.

"Out!" Jax gasps beside her, clutching his ribs where blood seeps between fingers already slick red. "We're pinned! Out! Leave me!"

"Shut up." Mara grips Jax by collar without looking away from the upper levels where muzzle flashes paint hellish patterns against swirling smoke. Her voice is hollow—a trauma-paramedic assessing casualties that are already past saving.

Which makes sense because Sub-Station Seven didn't save anyone except those thirty-eight children still burning underneath every decision she makes now.

The ash-gray static bleeds faster around her bio-wards as more rounds impact nearby surfaces: *crack-snap*, *crack-snap*. Supersonic slugs chewing concrete to dust at distances that suggest professional marksmen instead of street thugs.

"Cover fire!" I shout while dropping prone fifteen feet behind their position—close enough for hand signals but far enough not to get caught in crossfire.

Grimjaw's Tommy gun responds immediately—the distinctive stutter building tempo until it becomes continuous thunder. Steel-jacketed rounds climb toward elevated sniper nests hidden somewhere above Pylon Two's skeletal framework.

A Syndicate enforcer answers back with something heavy. The whump of autocannon fire rips through shipping containers across the construction site—that deep bass punch that means armor-piercing rounds designed for vehicle takedowns rather than personnel.

"You need to pull back!" Mara finally looks at me, eyes reflecting weird colors in the ward-light—natural brown irises swimming overlaid with geometric runes that shouldn't be visible unless you know what signs indicate active Weave manipulation. Hers are sputtering out like candles in windstorm. "Jax can't make another evacuation run and I'm dry!"

"That's it then?" My reply comes harder than intended while loading fresh mag into my pistol—the satisfying click-click-tap of chambering rounds feels almost ritualistic now. How many times have we done this dance? "We just walk away?"

"Not walking anywhere." Grimjaw's voice crackles through comm-link static between bursts of covering fire. Something metallic crashes below his position—maybe rebar giving way under sustained suppression—or maybe someone making the mistake of showing themselves too early during shift change hours.

The Passaic River gurgles black beneath everything: indifferent as always to which side wins these small wars fought along its polluted banks where 2007 North Jersey bleeds into Neon Hollow territories marked by rust-streaked pylons and smoke-choked infrastructure that was never meant to hold against forces tearing holes in reality itself.

"Sterling's still up," I mutter while sighting toward upper levels where those sniper crosshairs had been pinned on Sterling moments ago before Mara interrupted everyone's plans with tactical necessity instead of strategic patience.

She follows my gaze upward even though following gazes is exactly what trained shooters want targets doing—and gets rewarded with a burst that scatters dust from her hair barely six inches above skull bone dense enough to stop lighter calibers if she'd been three seconds slower recognizing incoming angles.

*Crack-snap*, *crack-snap*.

Supersonic impacts painting death-zone boundaries tighter around our collapse point because there's no clean extraction anymore once Syndicate enforcers realize they've got BATC leadership cornered fifty meters inside disputed territory along McCarter Highway at predawn when nobody calls reinforcements until after bodies cool down enough for coroner photos.

"How much time?" Mara asks nobody specifically while dragging Jax further behind their cover—a movement that brings them closer to me but also exposes flanks now surrounded three-hundred-and-sixty degrees with nowhere left running except through enemies positioned at every escape vector angle calculated wrong thirty minutes ago when planning seemed possible instead of delusional optimism fueled by caffeine withdrawal and too many consecutive missions without proper sleep cycles or psychological debriefings required under standard operating procedures we haven't

## CHAPTER 15: THE CATWALK SHOT

**[OOC SYNC]** The shot had gone true. Cole's suppressed round took the elven sniper square through the left eye socket—a textbook kill that ended six months of tracking through Neon Hollow's concrete veins. But Sterling was right. The Syndicate doesn't forgive. They don't forget. And they sure as hell don't die easy.

The catwalk groaned beneath his boots as he approached Pylon #2's skeletal remains—all twisted rebar and sagging ductwork draped across collapsed infrastructure like the ribs of some dead god. Steam hissed from ruptured pipes below, carrying with it the copper tang of blood and burned circuitry.

"I got eyes on her," Grimjaw's voice crackled in his earpiece. The orc had positioned himself on the western approach, his industrial thermite torch ready to collapse the access tunnel if things went sideways. "She's pinned behind a slab near the eastern drainage. Three hostiles moving to flank."

Cole knelt beside what remained of the pylon's control station, fingers finding purchase among sparking conduit cables. Through gaps in the rust-eaten metal plating, he could see them—the Syndicate's clean-up crew. Two syndicate enforcers hauling a heavy breaching charge toward Mara Vance's position, their movements efficient and practiced. They'd done this before.

"Telluric Engineering Corps would have loved these bastards during the Experimental Sludge trials," Cole muttered. His mind flashed back to those early days—before BATC even existed—when dwarvish runesmiths were frantically forging Gold-Bismuth Collars while orcs bore the brunt of containment work in Local 405 tunnels.

"They're setting up thermite charges." Grimjaw's tone carried that familiar grit of a South Side sandhog reading structural load-bearing calculations in his head. "If she doesn't break cover in ninety seconds, those charges are gonna turn that concrete slab into slag. She'll be buried under three tons of radioactive shrapnel."

The elven sniper's body still lay where it fell—a crumpled suit of black tactical gear with expensive armor-piercing rounds scattered nearby. Sterling had sent him. That much was certain. The Syndicate boss always cleaned house after operations went wrong.

"Can you reach her?" Cole asked, though he already knew the answer.

Negative terrain between positions. Too exposed. I can lay suppressive fire but there's no guarantee those syndicate enforcers won't trigger the charges early as retaliation."

Cole rose from his crouch, drawing both pistols—a matched pair of modified FN Five-seveNs loaded with specialized ammunition designed by Telluric engineers specifically for metahuman physiology. The weight felt right in his hands, familiar. Penance, revenge, and that sliver of justice.

"The Threefold Cord," he whispered. Not enough to scrape the black iron out of Danny's alveoli, but it would do for now.

"Grimjaw, light them up on my mark."
