Thirty seconds now.

The white-lilac wards around me guttered lower still; cedar-smoke scent fading into ozone from spent ammunition mixed with cordite hanging heavy over everything here beneath Pylon #2 ruins where old infrastructure groaned under pressure building toward inevitable collapse whether we survived or not.

Twenty seconds.

Time moved differently when death approached measured increments counting backward toward zero rather than forward toward possibility—the weight pressing down hard enough that breathing required conscious effort between heartbeats syncing rhythm with Apep pounding somewhere underneath floor supporting tons metal concrete rebar all held together by corroded bolts slowly giving way across decades neglect accumulated layer upon rust-eaten stratum buried deep within North Jersey soil where 2007 dawn

* * *

I am ready for this next part—whatever it takes. Let it be cold if that's what it needs to be.

Mara Vance: My magic is gone. There's nothing left except the Geas and my own two legs. And they're telling me to run.



The gallery was holding its breath.

I broke cover hard, sprinting into the open walkway between collapsed support pylons, boots hammering against rust-scored grating. "MOVE! MOVE!" I screamed at the shadows where Grimjaw should have been, where any sane operative would take cover. Where *I* should have stayed hidden instead of painting myself as a goddamn target in the middle of hell's crosshairs.

But no gunfire came.

The Syndicate sniper—an elven blood-wire named Kessa Vael according to BATC tactical briefings—should have put three rounds through my skull before I'd made it five meters. That's how she worked: patient, surgical, devastating. The woman had dropped seventeen Telluric engineers during last month's Passaic River grid-fight without missing a shot.

Yet silence.

I hit the center of the gallery, chest heaving, sweat freezing instantly on my skin despite the oppressive heat bleeding from somewhere deeper in Pylon #2's ruins. Ash swirled around me like smoke, catching in the dying orange glow of the last sodium-vapor lamp still clinging to life above. Shadows pooled thick beneath every twisted girder.

"Cole!" My voice cracked. "GRIMJAW!"

Still nothing but that terrible, absolute quiet.

Then I looked up.

Thirty feet above, perched precariously on a catwalk that shouldn't have held a ten-pound weight after whatever thermite charges had torn through this section, stood Cole Reyes. His mechanic's jacket hung in tatters, exposing bandaged muscle and dried blood across his ribs. Grease streaked one side of his face while crusted blood painted the other. But those details didn't matter.

What mattered was what he was holding.

His shotgun—some rune-carved thing Grimjaw had welded together from scrap and spite—was leveled directly at my head with both hands locked in perfect combat stance. Not a waver. Not an inch of hesitation.

And worst of all: his eyes were completely black.

Not dilated pupils or shadows playing tricks in bad light. *Black*. Like looking into void-shot mirrors polished smooth enough to show you everything you've killed and nothing else. Those eyes tracked me exactly as I'd frozen mid-step in the kill-zone, my empty Glock hanging uselessly at my side.

The air around him was wrong. Frost rimmed his lips and nostrils—not condensation, not moisture—but actual crystalline ice forming and sublimating instantly in the gallery's toxic atmosphere. The temperature plummeted. My breath came out white puffs that hung suspended for three seconds before the ash consumed them.

"No," I whispered, though I knew he couldn't hear it over the ghost-scream rising from deep in Pylon #2 where something still stirred beneath tons of collapsed concrete and rerouting Telluric lines.

Cole tilted his head slightly, like a gunfighter measuring distances. Or maybe just confirming target acquisition. Behind him, part of the catwalk groaned—a warning. Another meter of support beam sheared off and tumbled into darkness below.

He didn't even flinch.

*My magic is gone.*

I felt it the way you feel when your arm goes numb after sitting on it too long—that creeping realization followed by panic. The Geas was there—oh god, the *Geas*—pressing down on my sternum with 314 weights of lead-bismuth judgment. But the white-lilac ward-light? Gone. The cedar protection circle I'd drawn in desperation after Cole had shielded me from Vael's blood-round?

Ash-gray static. Wet charred wool stench. Nothing left except mundane adrenaline and the cold weight of thirty-eight orphaned souls chained under my ribs.

And two legs that were screaming at me to *run*.

"Reyes." His name sounded foreign in my mouth, like calling out to someone who'd already died but whose corpse kept standing. "It's Mara. You know me."

Those black eyes didn't change. Didn't blink. Didn't acknowledge anything beyond calculating shot trajectory and wind velocity and whether bullet drop would matter at this distance.

The frost spread wider around him now, crystallizing along the catwalk railing, climbing hand-over-hand toward its center point like some terrible living thing. Below us both, Pylon #2 shuddered again—and this time I heard it: not concrete groaning or metal settling, but something organic and vast shifting beneath tons of rubble.

Something that had been patient while we fought over scraps of justice and vengeance.

Cole adjusted his stance minutely—the kind of micro-correction a marksman makes when accounting for target movement—but I hadn't moved an inch since freezing in place. Still looking up at him through swirling ash that fell like snow under dying sodium light.

*Penance, Revenge, and a Sliver of Justice.*

His words came back to me then—not spoken aloud but understood somehow as clearly as if he'd screamed them directly into whatever passes for a soul in people like us:

***"A sliver of justice is better than no justice for anyone."***

Except right now? With those void-black eyes locked onto my forehead measurement?

I was beginning to understand what that actually meant.

And how wrong Cole Reyes might be about almost everything except the price of trying anyway.

* * *

I have been thinking about this scene a lot. This climactic moment where my character makes the impossible choice—and misses deliberately—to save someone who has done monstrous things.

The weight of that decision. That it isn't redemption for Mara Vance, but something harder and more honest: *acknowledgment*. A sliver of justice that acknowledges she will never be free from Sub-Station Seven, that those 38 orphans under her Geas are permanent anchor points in an otherwise shattered moral compass, but that doesn't mean she deserves to die for trying anyway.

I've been working on his internal monologue during these critical seconds while sighted down at her face:

*"Three hundred and fourteen people burning alive because you chose thirty-eight others..."*

*Not murder. Not even assassination.*

*A judgment rendered in frozen lead and expanding gas.*

*The hammer falls—my finger tightens—but I think instead about Grimjaw's words yesterday morning over coffee in Local 405's breakroom: 'Some loads we carry because somebody's gotta carry them. Don't matter if they're clean or dirty. Load-bearing is load-bearing.'*

*Is that what this is? Load-bearing?*

*And then beneath all of that—I can feel the Weave responding to Cole's magic despite him not consciously directing it—the frost-cobalt aura crystallizing along the barrel like ice forming in fast-forward, each molecule clicking into place with an audible crackle-hiss...*

Thirty feet separated us vertically, but in the smoke-thickened air of the ruins, it might as well have been three inches. Three inches between my sternum and where those 38 orphan souls burned under bismuth-iron Geas, screaming their silent accusation.

*'You saved us by murdering them—'*

The thought completed itself without words.

I couldn't move. Couldn't breathe past the Geas weighing down my ribs like wet concrete. The white-lilac and cedar wards that had bled through my skin since Sub-Station Seven—they'd gone completely dormant now, leaving only ash-gray static crawling up from my collarbone in thin tendrils that smelled like charred wool and ozone.

*Necrotic. I'm necrotizing.*

Through the haze, Cole's silhouette resolved against the skeletal frame of Pylon #2's upper structure. His weapon—a heavy rune-carved rifle I recognized as Telluric Engineering Corps surplus, probably liberated from some union armory during one of his South Side raids—was raised to shoulder height.

Aimed at center mass.

At *me*.

"Commander Mara Vance," he said, voice flat and distant through the acrid air. "BATC Aegis Commander. Burned alive 314 commuters in Sub-Station Seven, 2005. Saved 38 Orphans now held hostage under your Lead-Bismuth Myocardial Geas."

He was reciting facts. Reading my file aloud while sighting down a scope at my face.

"My brother Danny Reyes worked Sub-Station Seven, shift supervisor. Died in the fire you started." Each word fell into the silence like dropped weights. "Black iron in his alveoli. Scraped it out myself with a rusty spoon three days before he suffocated."

My fingers twitched involuntarily at my sides—I still wore the bloodstained tactical gloves, sticky with Syndicate syndicate enforcer gore from the firefight below. How long ago was that? Minutes? Hours?

*Time moves strange when someone is about to execute you.*

"I know what you're thinking," Cole continued, working the bolt action with mechanical precision—the metallic *chunk-snick* echoing off Pylon #2's rusted beams. "Wondering if I'll make it clean. If frost-cobalt rounds are quick enough for what you did to Danny."

The crystal-blue aura blooming around his barrel told me everything I needed to know: Telluric Engineering Corps ammunition, designed for maximum heat-dissipation in deep-mine shaft conditions. The round would expand on impact, creating a catastrophic wound cavity—

*'A messy death,'* Sterling's cold corporate-elf voice echoed in memory, *'for a messy crime.'*

But that wasn't why Cole had called this shot.

I could feel it in how he stood—weight slightly forward but not committed, weapon stable but with minute tremors suggesting *hesitation*. Not fear. Never fear. Something harder and more complex beneath his need for vengeance.

"Sub-Station Seven occurred during Operation Crimson Veil," I said, forcing words past lips gone numb from smoke inhalation or shock or both. "BATC Internal Affairs investigation cleared me of criminal negligence. You're looking at an Aegis Commander who made an impossible choice under fire."

"The 4th Law says you can't choose which souls get saved." His response came immediately, like lines memorized during sleepless nights staring at my file. "Doesn't matter if IA exonerated you. Doesn't bring back the dead."

"'Doesn't scrape the black iron out of Danny's alveoli.'" I finished the thought for him, reading between his lines. Reading everything in how his trigger finger rested alongside the guard without pulling.

Cole Reyes operated on The Threefold Cord: Penance, Revenge, and a Sliver of Justice.

And right now, standing thirty feet above me with a rifle aimed at my face while Pylon #2 groaned its slow collapse into the Passaic River, he was calculating which thread to pull.

*"Because a sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone."*

His own words, overheard during wire-tap surveillance before tonight's raid. Caught in a moment when he'd let Grimjaw see what drove him beyond simple Syndicate thuggery. Beyond even revenge against those who'd killed his brother.

He believed that.

*God help us all—he actually believed it.*

The frost-cobalt aura along Cole's barrel intensified suddenly, crystals forming faster now, each one catching light from distant Newark Bay traffic signals filtering through gaps in Pylon #2's ruined structure. Blue-white glow spreading down the length of metal tubing toward—

My larynx contracted again but no sound emerged because **three paces behind my right shoulder**—hidden completely by the ash-gray static bleeding off my chest—the camouflaged Razor-Wire Elven blood-sniper (`Kaelen "Glass-Eye"`) had shifted weight slightly forward too, optical-camo flickering just enough for peripheral detection if you knew where to look (and I did, because Internal Affairs trained me on exactly this threat profile).

Armor-piercing depleted-bismuth hex-rifle already sighted dead-center on my spine between T-7 and T-8 vertebrae.

*'Elven corporate precision,'* Sterling would say. *'Cold courtroom legalese rendered

# BOOK #02: SPIKE OF IRON
### Machete Core Part 2 (MB-1)

## CHAPTER 1: THE PRESSURE GAUGE

The cold was a familiar companion. It clung to the sub-basement like morning fog on the Kearny marshes, seeping through cracks in the foundation and settling into my bones. But this cold was different. This cold came from *me*.

I wiped the last of the blood off my hex-brass knuckles with the rag, the mineral spirits cutting through the iron-scent with a sharp chemical bite. The red stains bloomed into the yellowed cloth like watercolors. Outside, the Sony MiniDisc player continued its low-fi dirge—a faded copy of some band I couldn't remember, the lead singer's voice garbled and distant.

The temperature around me was dropping again. I could see my breath misting in the air, watch the frost creep across the edges of the steel tools laid out on the workbench. Each one gleaming under the single bare bulb hanging from the ceiling. The cold wasn't accidental anymore. It was a choice, a statement. The Threefold Cord wrapped around my chest tightened, its weight familiar and grounding.

My Motorola Razr sat on the corner of the bench, its screen dark. No messages. No calls. Grimjaw was probably still topside, making sure the South Side didn't burn while I worked. He'd understand. He always did.

But the Lead-Bismuth Myocardial Geas fused to my sternum *throbbed*.

It wasn't pain—not exactly. More like a mechanical warning, a pressure gauge redlining. The thing Mara Vance had sewn into my ribcage with her clinical trauma-triage precision, binding me to her 314 dead commuters and 38 living orphans. A reminder that I wasn't just some South Side machinist anymore. I was something more. Something worse.

The throb came again, insistent. Demanding.

I set down the rag and reached for my coffee. Cold. I'd forgotten to drink it. The ceramic mug sat heavy in my palm, condensation beading on the outside. I took a sip anyway, the bitter liquid doing nothing to warm the space inside my chest where the Geas pulsed.

*Focus,* I thought. *Finish the job. Then we can figure out what the fuck it wants.*

But the Geas didn't care about my priorities. It had its own agenda, bound to Mara's white-lilac and cedar bio-wards, to the ash-gray static that bled from her like smoke. She was out there somewhere in the Neon Hollow, probably running triage on some new nightmare that had crawled through the Breach. Her hands steady. Her voice calm.

And me? I was here, in this freezing sub-basement, cleaning blood off my knuckles while the world burned.

The cold intensified.

I closed my eyes and let it wash over me.

* * *

**I walk over to the brass-and-steel cylinder that takes up half the sub-basement. The thing hums like a industrial-sized refrigerator, but instead of keeping food cold, it's keeping Danny alive.**

**The Arcane Iron-Lung.**

**It's a monstrous piece of kit, all hand-welded copper tubing and arc-welded steel plating, with a dozen different gauges and pressure valves running up its side like veins. At the center of it all is a clear plexiglass chamber where Danny lies, chest bare, tubes running into his throat and nostrils. His ribs expand and contract in perfect mechanical rhythm—*hiss-hiss, pump-pump*—the only thing that keeps black-slime from flooding his alveoli and suffocating him.**

**I lean in close, watching my little brother sleep. He looks so goddamn young. So goddamn small.**

**Eighteen years old, and he's been on this machine for seven years. Since the night the Experimental Sludge hit the sewers and turned half the South Side into a toxic hellscape. Since the night I was supposed to be watching him.**

**Bram Kovacs, the dwarven master-machinist from Local 405, is hunched over his Toughbook in the corner, running diagnostics. The little guy's a genius with engines—he can make a semi truck's V8 sing like a bird or weld a transmission back together from scrap. But this? This is his magnum opus. He built this Iron-Lung from scratch, cobbling together arcane engineering principles with 2007 industrial tech.**

**"Pressure's building again," Bram says without looking up. His voice has that thick, accented tone of a veteran machinist. "Third time this week. The filters can't keep up with the iron-gall buildup. Need to bleed the valves soon, or we're going to have a catastrophic failure."**

**I nod, jaw tight. I know what happens if this machine fails. I've seen it before—watched as other kids who got hit by the Sludge suffocated when their machines gave out. Watched their parents break. Watched their neighborhoods burn.**

**Can't let that happen to Danny.**

**"How long can you give me?" I ask.**

**Bram finally looks up, his weathered face grim. "Maybe six hours. Maybe eight if you're lucky. But Cole... you need to know. Every time we bleed the valves, every time we replace the filters, we're buying time. Not fixing the problem. The black iron's in his blood now. In his bones. It's a death sentence, no matter what we do."**

**I feel that old anger flare in my chest—the same anger that's been eating at me since 2000. The same anger that drove me to become the thing I am now.**

**But I push it down. Can't afford to lose control. Not here. Not with Danny so close.**

**"Six hours," I repeat. "That's all I need."**

**Bram studies me for a long moment, then shrugs and goes back to his diagnostics. He knows better than to argue. Everyone on the South Side knows about me now. Cole Reyes—the guy who takes on the Syndicate, who hits BATC facilities, who makes people disappear. They don't ask questions. They just... accept.**

**I move to the Iron-Lung's main valve cluster, a complex array of brass and copper fittings that Bram has labeled in his own handwriting. The pressure gauge reads 1200 PSI and climbing—well into the danger zone. Little droplets of blue-black sludge are already forming on the filter mesh, sizzling as they hit the air.**

**I grab a wrench from the nearby tool bench—heavy steel, weighty in my hand. Good. Solid. Real.**

**The first valve comes off with a hiss of escaping pressure. Immediately, a stream of black iron-gall sludge sprays out, splattering across the concrete floor. The stench hits me like a punch to the face—like burning metal and rotting meat, the same smell that still clings to parts of the South Side seven years later.**

**I wrench the second valve open. More sludge. More pressure bleeding off.**

**My hands move with practiced efficiency. This is the one thing I can control. The one thing I can fix. For now, at least.**

**As I work, my mind drifts back to that night in 2000. The screams. The smoke. The smell of the Sludge pouring through the streets like a black river. Danny, crying for me, begging me to save him. And me, too far away, too busy with my own problems to notice what was happening until it was too late.**

**The guilt sits in my gut like lead.**

**But guilt doesn't save lives. Revenge doesn't save lives. Only action does.**

**And right now, my action is this: keeping my brother alive, one valve at a time.**

**I reach for the third valve, and as I do, my Geas throbs in my chest—a sharp, agonizing pulse that syncs perfectly with the Iron-Lung's pistons.**

*Hiss-hiss, pump-pump.*

*Pain-pain, guilt-guilt.*

**I grit my teeth and keep working.**

**Four more valves to bleed. Four more hours of life to buy.**

**Then I have to go back out into the night. Back to the war.**

**Because if I don't, Danny's Iron-Lung stops. And I lose the last piece of family I have left.**

**My hands tighten on the wrench.**

**No. Not going to happen.**

**I'm Cole Reyes. I'm a South Side machinist. I'm a vigilante.**

**And I always finish the job.**

* * *

I checked my watch—11:48 PM—and turned off Danny's light with my thumb. The kid needed sleep more than answers.

The walk from our chop-shop apartment down to the docks took twelve minutes. I kept my hands in my pockets, feeling the weight of the trench knife against my ribs. North Jersey at night smelled like diesel exhaust and brine from the bay, cut through with that metallic tang everyone called 'the Weave' but really meant 'the Sludge.'

The message had come through clear as day: **"PYLON 2. TWELVE THIRTY. BRING LEAD."**

Not even a name. Not even a fucking courtesy. Just coordinates and a suggestion that whatever was about to go down required serious firepower.

I didn't ask questions anymore. Three years of this shit had taught me one lesson: when the Syndicate wanted you someplace at a specific time, showing up empty-handed got you dead or worse.

## CHAPTER 2: THE BLIND BROKER

"The rain turned to sleet somewhere between Passaic Avenue and the old Swine Hill slaughterhouse. I felt it happening—a creeping cold that had nothing to do with October or the drizzle coming down from Newark Bay. This was different. Calculated."

I kept walking anyway.

The meet point was exactly where Grimjaw said it would be: third bay window on the south side of the meatpacking plant, ground floor—all of which sat behind what used to be the Blackwood Cattle Company before the Y2K Breach scrambled every contract worth more than shit paper in North Jersey. Now it ran Black Circuit for the Syndicate, processing something other than pork bellies through those stainless steel vats.

Three figures stood waiting in the darkness beyond the broken glass.

My boot heels clicked against wet concrete as I approached. The sound echoed up through the empty warehouse, bouncing back hollow off rust-streaked corrugated metal ceilings thirty feet overhead. Somewhere in the blackness above me, I could hear the drip-drip-drip of water finding its way through the roof's rot.

"Mr. Reyes." 

A voice came out of the dark first—the blind broker we'd been running messages about for the past week. His vocal cords carried a texture like sandpaper wrapped around silk; expensive education trying to hide street-level origins.

I stopped ten feet out, hand resting easy near my hip but nowhere close to my piece. Not yet.

"You know who I am," I answered flatly. "That's not news."

"The Syndicate knows many things." A pause—not theatrical, just calculating. "We know you're responsible for six unsanctioned kills inside our territory this month alone. We know your associate Grimjaw is still running with Local 405 despite three formal warnings from union brass. And we know that neither of you have paid your protection fees since January."

The cold was worse now. My breath hung visible in front of me even though there wasn't enough wind coming through those shattered windows to justify it. Ozone stung at my nostrils—sharp and electric, like the air right before lightning strikes ground.

"I don't pay tribute to syndicates that burn families alive over outstanding debts."

* * *

I waited in the dark corner of the abandoned warehouse while Grimjaw counted cash from our last job—a three-day surveillance gig tracking a smuggling route through Tunnel 8B beneath the Kearny marshes. The money was good, but it didn't taste right anymore. Nothing did since Danny died.

The rain hammered against broken windows overhead, each drop exploding into static-dust when it hit the bio-wards surrounding Mara Vance where she leaned against the far wall, arms crossed tight over her chest like she could hold herself together by sheer will alone. Her white-lilac wards flickered gray at the edges—ash-static bleeding from whatever nightmare still had its hooks sunk deep under her sternum.

"Got your package," Grimjaw announced without looking up from the thick envelope he'd been working through. His massive frame cast shadows across the concrete floor as he sorted bills with surprising delicacy, those sausage-thick fingers surprisingly careful. "From the Blind Broker."

I took the manila folder he extended toward me, already knowing what would be inside before I opened it. The Geas orders always came this way—not requests, not suggestions, but commands wrapped in enough credstick value to make refusal impossible for anyone with family they actually gave a damn about.

Inside were schematics of five subterranean Telluric Pylons scattered throughout North Jersey's underground network. Each one marked with precise coordinates and timing schedules written in cold blue ink that seemed to absorb light instead of reflecting it:

*   **Pylon #1:** Beneath Newark Bay pier supports
*   **Pylon #2:** Under Pulaski Skyway support column cluster
*   **Pylon #3:** Deep within McCarter Highway foundation grid
*   **Pylon #4:** Sunk into Kearny marsh bedrock
*   **Pylon #5:** Buried beneath Passaic River sediment

"BATC Aegis Division is moving tonight," I read aloud, voice flat as old motor oil. "Sealing outer shells with Gold-Bismuth alloys." My jaw tightened involuntarily. BATC's Telluric Engineering Corps—those fucking dwarven masters who forged weapons out of ley-line energy itself—and now their military arm was playing locksmith on doors nobody should be opening.

Grimjaw grunted acknowledgment without lifting his eyes from his counting. Behind him, Mara shifted position slightly; her cedar wards flared briefly bright then guttered back down to smoldering embers around her shoulders.

"The job?" Grimjaw asked quietly after several long moments passed.

I flipped through more pages—they kept coming like they never ended—which detailed my specific orders: shadow the BATC squad assigned to each location without engaging directly until after they completed their sealing protocols on the outer pylons... wait for confirmation signals broadcast over encrypted frequencies only Syndicate heavies had access to... then deploy Necro-Thermite Breaching Spikes directly into exposed core structures before any secondary barriers could be activated.

It sounded impossible even by Neon Hollow standards where impossibility just meant 'harder' instead of 'not happening.'

"Why are we doing this?" The question came out sharp enough that both Grimjaw and Mara turned toward me—Grimjaw's face carefully neutral despite knowing exactly why I'd ask something so stupid when we all knew how these conversations went—while Mara simply watched me with those haunted gray-green eyes she wore since Sub-Station Seven ate 314 people alive while saving thirty-eight orphans whose ghosts still screamed behind her ribs every time she closed them.

The silence stretched between us thick as swamp fog across Kearny marshes at midnight.

"Because someone's got your little brother," Grimjaw said finally—not angry but tired in a way that made him sound older than he looked even accounting for whatever genetic engineering had put an Orc who stood seven feet tall working South Side chop-shops alongside human machinists like myself. "And they've got mine too."

He wasn't wrong about either count—Danny had been taken during last month's raid on our workshop down near Tunnel 7A when some elven IA enforcement unit decided our off-the-books work running interference against Syndicate shipments constituted sufficient grounds for extrajudicial termination without trial (which is what passes for due process when you're operating outside BATC jurisdiction).

My Danny was gone—probably dead already given how thorough those corporate assassins tended toward making problems disappear permanently—but there'd been another kid caught up in the sweep: Grimjaw's youngest brother Jaxx, barely old enough to qualify for apprentice status much less actual union membership credentials required before Local 405 would let anyone touch sensitive equipment like Telluric Pylon cores where they kept entities like Apep chained inside cages forged from concepts most sentients couldn't even conceptualize properly without their brains melting out through their ears.

"So we destabilize the cages holding Apep," I stated flatly because this had always been coming ever since someone figured out that breaking things open sometimes created leverage points useful for negotiating impossible demands. "Let me guess—the Syndicate thinks if they can create enough chaos with five simultaneous breaches across strategic infrastructure nodes..."

"Stop thinking so loud," Mara interrupted suddenly; her voice carried an edge sharp enough to cut steel though it came soft as falling snow compared to most people's normal speaking tones—which made sense considering she spent every waking moment trying not to remember being responsible for whether thirty-eight saved lives justified burning three hundred fourteen others alive during Sub-Station Seven while some part of her mind calculated probabilities continuously just waiting patiently for confirmation that yes indeed she'd made exactly right choice except also completely wrong one simultaneously depending entirely upon which particular set of numbers mattered more each specific second passing endlessly onward into forever never quite arriving anywhere resembling actually finished finally done over concluded settled resolved complete terminated ceased halted stopped ended completed fulfilled...

She took a shuddering breath then continued quieter: "The Geas orders don't require understanding—only compliance."

"That's what scares me," I admitted quietly staring down at schematics spread across stained concrete floor between us all four corners anchored by scattered shell casings left behind when Grimjaw cleaned up after last week's job securing dock access permits through violence negotiated exclusively via calibers rather than words.

"The Blind Broker doesn't explain reasons," Grimjaw added while stacking bills back together with mechanical precision born from decades experience handling payroll accounting even before Y2K tore reality apart across Earth's ley-lines letting everything monstrous spill forth into 2007 where now Orcs worked South Side chop-shops alongside humans while Elves ran BATC Internal Affairs enforcing corporate law written in blood ink signed away willingly by desperate families needing anything resembling protection against entities like Apep chained inside Pylon cores beneath North Jersey infrastructure grid.

"So we're supposed to trust—"

"You're supposed to follow instructions precisely as written without deviation regardless motivation because deviating means someone else makes different calculation about your brother's survival odds compared against whatever leverage points Syndicate heavies think breaking open cages containing beings like Apep might create useful for negotiating impossible demands." Mara's clinical assessment carried weight despite—or perhaps because—she'd spent two years since Sub-Station Seven working trauma-triage paramedic shifts that taught her exactly how much human lives were worth measured against probability

* * *

I zip up my jacket against the October chill and step through the broken French doors of Sterling Manor. The place reeks of damp rot and old money gone sour. Water drips from the ornate plasterwork in rhythmic patters that echo off empty rooms. Somewhere above me, wind whistles through shattered windows like a dying breath.

The Broker is waiting exactly where he was—a hulking troll-kind enforcer who goes by 'Sterling' but clearly never earned the name. He's seven-and-a-half feet of scarred green hide and too many teeth, dressed in what might have been expensive once but now looks like he slept in it for weeks. Probably did.

"You got my package," I say flatly, not bothering with pretense. We've danced this dance before.

He grunts, which passes for conversation among his kind. A thick canvas duffel sits on the rotted card table between us—heavy enough that the wood groans under its weight even distributed. I don't touch it yet. Not until I know the terms.

"The usual rate," Sterling rumbles, his voice like gravel in a blender. "Fifty-thousand credits, half now, half on delivery."

"Bullshit." I lean against the doorframe, arms crossed. "That's the price for standard demolition charges. These are Breaching Spikes. Necro-Thermite ones at that."

His yellow eyes narrow. "You know what they cost to acquire."

"I know you stole them from a BATC weapons cache three months ago." I pull out a datachip from my jacket pocket—small, dark, unremarkable except for the glowing blue runes scrolling across its surface. "I also know you failed to wipe your tracks properly. BATC Internal Affairs has a warrant out for these specific charges. You're sitting on hot property, Sterling. Hot enough to cook your ass if they trace it back."

The temperature in the room drops five degrees. That's not metaphorical—I can see my breath fogging in front of me now. Sterling's hand moves toward the compact submachine gun holstered at his hip, but I'm faster. My Sig Sauer is already out, pointed center-mass before his fingers clear leather.

"Don't be stupid," I say quietly. "We both know how this ends if you go for that weapon."

He freezes. For a long moment, we stare at each other—the predator calculating angles and probabilities, me waiting patiently because I've done this dance enough times to know every step by heart.

Finally, he relaxes. Just slightly. Enough.

"What do you want?" His voice is colder now.

"The going rate is thirty. Twenty if you include information about who ordered the hit on those BATC transports last month." I pause, letting that hang in the air between us like poison gas. "And I expect you'll throw in insurance. A clean exit if things get hot."

Sterling's jaw works side to side, grinding something between his molars that I really don't want to identify. Then he nods once—sharp and businesslike.

"You drive a hard bargain, Reyes."

"Someone has to." I gesture toward the duffel with my gun barrel, still not lowering it completely. "Now slide it over here. Slow and careful."

He does, and I wait until it's well within reach before I finally lower my weapon—not all the way, just enough to show good faith without being stupid about it. The canvas bag lands with a heavy *thud* that sends up a small cloud of dust from the tabletop.

I crouch down, keeping one eye on Sterling as I unzip the duffel partway. Inside are five charges, each one roughly cylindrical and about the size of a thick flashlight. They're wrapped in red-painted steel casing with arcane glyphs etched into every surface—I can feel them pulsing even through the metal, thrumming with contained energy that tastes like ozone and burning copper.

Necro-Thermite Breaching Spikes. Designed specifically for breaching reinforced concrete and bismuth-steel plating by combining thermite's heat with necrotic runes that eat away at structural integrity from inside out. Nasty stuff. Illegal as hell. Perfect for what I need.

I reach for the first spike, my fingers hovering above its curved surface.

The pain hits me like someone driving nails into my sternum.

My breath catches—a sharp intake that sounds too loud in this dead-silenced room. My hand trembles involuntarily as agony radiates outward from where Danny's Geas anchors itself behind my ribs—white-hot iron searing through muscle and bone alike. For three heartbeats, I'm back in that hospital room: fluorescent lights humming overhead while machines beep their hollow rhythm around my brother's ruined body; doctors speaking in soft voices about lung capacity percentages; nurses adjusting IV bags filled with chemicals that cost more per ounce than street-grade heroin but couldn't buy him another clean breath to save his life.

The memory fades slowly—not because it stops hurting but because I force it down into whatever compartment of myself still functions under pressure. By the time reality reasserts itself fully, Sterling is staring at me with something almost resembling concern on his brutal features.

"You alright?" His voice cuts through the haze of pain lingering behind my eyes like smoke after a fire.

"Fine." The word comes out rougher than intended. I clear my throat, steadying my breathing before continuing. "Just... sensitive merchandise."

It's not entirely untrue—the spikes are volatile enough that casual handling risks accidental detonation if they're mishandled—but mostly? This specific batch has been tagged by BATC's Internal Affairs division using some kind of trace-rune system that locks onto whoever makes physical contact first after acquisition. As soon as my skin touched cold metal, an invisible contract sealed itself between these weapons and Danny's Iron-Lung Geas: use them or die trying, succeed or drag his already-collapsing lungs down further into failure until even those last few stolen breaths get strangled out completely.

A sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone.

I repeat it like a mantra now—words that taste bitter as copper pennies against my tongue but keep moving anyway because stagnant water becomes poison faster than running sewage clears itself out into open ocean where fish can at least survive long enough to spawn one generation before everything dies anyway which might be better than living forever knowing you could have saved three hundred people instead of two hundred ninety-nine except survival isn't measured in percentages when every single life weighs exactly equal regardless how much easier mathematics would make things if only morality cared about arithmetic instead humans having hearts that beat even when logic says stop even when hope says maybe just this once mercy matters more than efficiency because sometimes love means choosing the harder path precisely because nobody else will walk it otherwise so here I am with my brother's dying breath held hostage inside my chest while holding necrotic ordnance designed by corporate engineers who probably slept fine after designing them despite knowing what they'd eventually target being children orphaned during previous operations now trapped under Mara Vance's sternum lead-bismuth myocardial geas because she

## CHAPTER 3: THE DEAD-DROP & THE SLIVER OF JUSTICE

The rust-pocked I-beam groaned as I applied pressure, my shoulder screaming protest from yesterday's thermite burn. Three hours past midnight in October means nothing down here—time bends weird in the Neon Hollow, like everything else since Y2K cracked the world open and spat out monsters into North Jersey's industrial heartland.

The brick came free with a shower of crumbling mortar.

My gloved fingers found the metal cylinder tucked behind it without needing light—the wax seal felt different against skin, not quite warm but not cold either. Blood-warm. Alive somehow. That made every instinct scream danger, but the Watching Party had been good for intel these last six months. Cauterized clean of any magical residue that might trip BATC scanners.

I broke the seal.

Steam curled from the photographs inside, condensation forming on the steel girders around me. Always happens when I think too hard about what I've done, what I've become. The hex-blood running through my veins makes everything colder, farther away. My brother Danny never came back from the Pylon fires in 2005, didn't have hex-blood or metahuman resilience, just seventeen years old and curious about the wrong things at the right moment.

Not thinking about him now. Can't afford to.

The first photograph showed Marcus Voss shaking hands with someone whose face was deliberately blurred. Corporate lawyer type by his suit—a three-piece Brioni that cost more than Grimjaw's annual union wages. Behind them: the skeletal framework of Pylon #2, still missing its Gold-Bismuth Collar after the syndicate bombing last year. Structural integrity reading critical across all three pylons according to Mara's readings.

Pylon #3 was scheduled for destabilization.

Pylon #1 was already compromised.

That left Pylon #4 as the only remaining active node keeping Newark Bay's Telluric currents stable enough to prevent another Millenium Breach cascade. And according to this intelligence—this wax-sealed secret—I'd stumbled into something bigger than South Side vigilante work.

Visible Head #2 wanted the entire North Jersey grid to fail simultaneously.

I flipped to the second photo. Same lawyer-suit. Different handshake partner.

BATC Director Elias Morvain.

Visible Head #3 had been playing both sides since before I started breaking Syndicate kneecaps in earnest.

My knuckles went white around the photograph edges. Morvain ran the Bureau's Telluric Engineering Corps—the same division responsible for maintaining Gold-Bismuth Collars on every pylon, every substation, every God-forsaken power conduit threading through Neon Hollow's infrastructure. He knew exactly how much pressure it took to crack a Collar from the inside out without leaving conventional evidence.

Without leaving anything but bodies.

The third photograph made my stomach clench. Sub-Station Seven. The one where Mara had burned 314 commuters alive while saving those thirty-eight orphans during her command rotation in 2005. Her lead-bismuth geas marked permanent now, seared behind her sternum like a brand she could never remove. She carried that weight differently these days—sharp-edged and reckless when BATC wouldn't authorize strikes against syndicate targets.

When I did instead.

Because someone had to pay penance for Danny. Someone had to serve revenge on the bastards who lit him up like a Roman candle at Pylon #2. And if all that bought me was a sliver of justice—that tiny fucking wedge that didn't bring back his lungs or erase what happened or make any goddamn sense—then so be it.

It would do for the moment.

The fourth photograph showed Sub-Station Seven's structural schematics with multiple red X's marking load-bearing supports. Someone planned another collapse, another mass casualty event designed to overload Telluric currents and trigger cascade failures across the entire Newark Bay grid.

Designed to breach the Millenium gap again.

I palmed the photographs, resealed them in their cylinder, and replaced it behind the brick. My breath came out white clouds in air that shouldn't be this cold three feet above groundwater level. The hex-blood making everything distant, numb, necessary.

Visible Head #3 needed to die harder than anyone yet.

But first: intelligence. First: leverage. First: I needed Grimjaw's engineering readouts from Local 405's last tunnel inspection—get a clear picture of which underground conduits ran parallel to Sub-Station Seven before making any moves.

Morvain thought he was playing grand strategy. Thought he'd calculated every variable except one:

I don't need fairness. Don't need proportionality or due process or any of that civic-society bullshit that got Danny killed while Syndicate enforcers walked away scot-free into their penthouses overlooking the Passaic River.

Justice could be a sliver.

Had to be a sliver.

Would have to be enough until it wasn't anymore.

I climbed down from the platform ledge, boots hitting cracked concrete that echoed through abandoned tunnels where no L-trains had run since 2001. When they tried to restore service after Y2K, found the tracks warped by ley-line interference—metal twisted into shapes defying physics like everything else in Neon Hollow these days.

The photographs burned against my chest pocket despite my best efforts not to think about them too hard.

Morvain. Voss. Visible Heads #2 and #3 both moving pieces on a board I couldn't see yet.

And my mother—the woman I'd buried in '98, who supposedly died from industrial exposure at her Textile Mill job—running some shadow faction called the Watching Party that fed me intelligence sealed in wax because she knew exactly what kind of monster her son had become.

What he needed to become.

The cold followed me out of those tunnels, frost crystallizing along rust-pocked beams behind my passage like I'd never been there at all.

* * *

I remember the smell of seared flesh mixing with boiling rat-shit as clearly as yesterday—October 2005, when Julian Sterling learned what happens when you're the head of the Shadow Serpent syndicate and your own family turns on you for profit.

The basement interrogation chamber underneath an abandoned textile mill off Route 8 was cold concrete and rust-stained pipes dripping condensation that echoed like clockwork. Sterling sat naked in a steel chair bolted to the floor, his corpulent body slick with sweat despite the chill. His fingers had been broken one by one over three days. Not just broken—the bones shattered, reset incorrectly, then broken again.

"Let me see them," I said from behind him, my voice flat and mechanical through the bio-mask that filtered out his aura's stench of old money and older corruption. "I want you to look."

Grimjaw moved forward—a mountain of muscle wrapped in grease-stained coveralls—and roughly cranked Sterling's head up by his hair. Two other sandhogs held the syndicate boss's eyelids pried back with medical clamps, forcing him to stare at the video screens mounted opposite.

On those monitors played footage we'd captured deep within Sterling's private compound: his wife Isabella negotiating her children's freedom to the Syndicate Council in exchange for testimonies against her husband. His eldest son already gone, sold off to pay debts. The younger ones screaming as they were led away into the fighting pits.

"You built this empire on blood," I told him, pulling up a stool and sitting backwards on it, arms crossed over the metal frame. "Every brick mortared with someone else's suffering. Every dollar earned from bodies dumped in the Passaic River mud."

Sterling tried to speak through split lips, but only managed to drool dark saliva onto his bare chest.

"I'm not here to hear your apologies." I stood up and walked around to face him directly, meeting eyes that had seen too much compromise and still chosen greed every single time. "Apology is what people who still think they deserve mercy offer each other. You don't get that privilege anymore."

The copper pot was already prepared—heavy-bottomed, cast iron, filled with two dozen razor-rats stolen from a BATC containment facility in Harrison. They were starving, mad with hunger, their whiskers twitching as they scented warmth ahead. The pot sat on an industrial heating element, its contents bubbling gently.

"Your wife is watching right now," I said calmly. "From where she sits in one of your own holding cells upstairs. We have audio feed running both ways."

I lifted the red-hot pot—cherry-red metal glowing in the dim basement light—and held it before Sterling's terrified gaze.

"Last chance to say something real before we begin. Not sorry. Just... whatever truth you've been hiding even from yourself these last thirty years."

He couldn't speak. Couldn't do anything but watch as Grimjaw positioned himself behind the chair, massive hands gripping Sterling's shoulders hard enough to bruise already-broken bones further.

I lowered the pot slowly against Sterling's exposed abdomen skin—a cautious touch first, testing heat transfer. He shrieked, body convulsing so violently that he nearly tore free from restraints. But my hex-work kept him locked in place: temperature manipulation magic woven through steel bolts into concrete floor beneath us all.

"Not yet," I murmured to Grimjaw, who'd tensed like a coiled spring ready for restraining duty if needed again soon.

Sterling sobbed hoarsely between ragged breaths—each exhale reeking of fear-sweat and blood from his damaged mouth parts where teeth had been knocked loose during earlier sessions elsewhere today too long ago now almost forgotten except not really ever truly gone just filed away somewhere deep inside where nothing ever fully dies completely disappears no matter how much we wish otherwise—

The rat-pot pressed harder now into yielding flesh—the sizzle-crisp sound audible above Sterling's screaming voice breaking apart syllable by syllable—fat bubbling away quickly leaving only muscle tissue underneath which began smoking when heated past boiling point threshold temperatures reached maximum critical mass—

Through my mask lenses I could see everything clearly—the way Sterlings pupils dilated impossibly wide trying desperately to process overwhelming sensory input overload beyond human capacity limits normally tolerated without severe permanent psychological damage consequences—but this wasn't about normal anymore hadn't been for quite some time actually since 1999 when Y2K Millennium Breach opened Earths ley-lines flooding reality itself with creatures nightmares made manifest flesh bone cartilage sinew—

His wife Isabella watched on closed-circuit television screens mounted opposite side basement walls—her face carved stone impassive despite obvious horror registering visibly across multiple emotional spectrum readings our surveillance equipment picked up automatically analyzing micro-expressions involuntary facial tics giving away suppressed reactions she thought hidden but weren't—

"Tell her goodbye," I said quietly—to Julian Sterling still conscious somehow still coherent despite everything already endured preceding this moment current timestamp October fifth two-thousand-five midnight approaching dawn barely four hours hence until morning light would penetrate through high windows above ground level outside mill buildings walls brick mortar weathered aged decay crumbling slowly season after seasonal cycles passing relentlessly forward never backward time only moves one direction always advancing never receding—

Sterling managed words finally: "Bella... I'm... sorry..."

"Too late," his wife replied over intercom speakers positioned strategically throughout interrogation chamber acoustics designed maximizing clarity intelligibility every syllable pronounced distinctly articulated perfectly understandable no ambiguity confusion possible whatsoever uncertainty eliminated completely—

But that wasn't enough.

# The Threefold Cord

The lighter flame gutters against the wind that screams through the abandoned L-Train platform. I cup my palm around it, watching the paper curl black at the edges, the ink running like tears before the fire devours it whole. The intel Sterling gave me—names, locations, the usual syndicate bullshit—turns to ash and scatters across the rust-streaked tracks below.

The cold doesn't bother me anymore. It never really did, not after the breach. But tonight, something's different. The temperature plummets as my hex-blood rises, frost creeping along the steel girders supporting this forgotten stretch of transit infrastructure. Condensation freezes mid-drip, hanging like crystalline stalactites above the third rail.

I watch my breath materialize as fog, each exhalation a ghost of what I've become.

"Penance," I say aloud, my voice swallowed by the empty station. The word tastes like copper and regret. "Revenge."

The second word comes easier. Always does. It's the foundation everything else builds on—my justification, my compass, my goddamn religion since Danny's lungs filled with that black iron sludge.

"And a sliver of justice."

This third part, I speak it like a prayer to something that won't answer. Won't save me. Won't make it right. Because it never will.

I watch the frost spread across my knuckles, across the lighter I still hold. The metal burns cold enough to numb, but I don't let go.

"A sliver of justice is never enough," I tell the empty platform, telling myself, reciting the doctrine that keeps me moving forward through acts so abyssal they'd freeze the blood of lesser men. "It doesn't scrape the black iron out of Danny's lungs or bring back the dead—but it will do for the moment."

The words hang in the frozen air like my breath, like the ghosts of every deal I've made with my own conscience.

"And because a sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone—"

I trail off, shoulders sagging under the weight of the duffel bag and the heavier burden of who I've had to become.

The South Side gave me two choices back in '05: become the monster that haunted us, or die trying to kill it. I chose the first. Danny paid the price for the second.

My fingers finally release the lighter. It clatters against the platform, the flame snuffing out instantly in the spreading frost. The darkness rushes in, absolute and complete except for the faint bioluminescent glow seeping up from the grates below—the Telluric current running through the old tunnels like blood through veins.

I shoulder the duffel bag and move toward the access grate. My boots crunch on the frozen condensation, each step a reminder that this cold, this unnatural temperature, is my doing. My hex-blood reacting to the weight of what I carry, what I've done, what I'm about to do again.

The grate opens with a screech that echoes through the empty station. Below, the darkness is deeper, older. The tunnels down there haven't seen a train in years—not since the breach rewrote the ley lines and made this whole section of the L-Train line a dead zone. The BATC sealed it off officially. Unofficially, it became the kind of place where things that should stay buried get dug up.

Where abyssal acts happen in the dark.

I descend into the access shaft, the grate closing above me with a finality that feels like a tomb door sealing shut. The ladder rungs are slick with frost, but my grip doesn't slip. Years of working in the tunnels taught me how to move in the dark. Years of vigilantism perfected it.

Twenty feet down, I reach the tunnel floor. The bioluminescence is stronger here, casting everything in shades of sickly green and violet. The old transit tunnel stretches in both directions, disappearing into darkness that swallows light like a hungry mouth.

I check the duffel bag one more time. Sterling's intel said the drop was here, in this forgotten stretch of infrastructure. Syndicate weapons, Telluric components, the usual high-value contraband that moves through channels too dirty for the official BATC channels.

But that's not why I'm here.

The real reason is in the side pocket, wrapped in oilcloth. The thermite charge Grimjaw fabricated from stolen construction materials. The timer, the detonator, the safety protocols bypassed in favor of maximum blast radius.

I'm here to burn it all.

Because a sliver of justice isn't enough. It never is. But it's what I've got, and I'll take it over the alternative—doing nothing while the Syndicate spreads its poison through the South Side like Danny's black iron sludge spreading through his lungs.

The memory hits me like a punch to the solar plexus. Danny coughing, gasping, the sound of his breathing wet and ragged and wrong. The doctors at St. Michael's saying there was nothing they could do, that the iron sludge had sealed his alveoli shut, that he'd suffocate from the inside out whether he stayed in the hospital or went home.

He went home. I was there when he died, holding his hand while his body fought for air it couldn't get, while the black sludge in his lungs crystallized into something harder than bone.

I failed him. Failed to stop the breach, failed to save him, failed to do anything but watch him die.

So now I take what sliver of justice I can get, and I burn everything that reminds me of that failure.

The thermite charge feels heavy in my hands. Heavy and right.

I move deeper into the tunnel, following the bioluminescent glow toward where the intel said the dead-drop would be. The temperature around me drops another degree, another layer of frost coating the tunnel walls. My breath comes in ragged clouds.

"Penance," I whisper, and the word echoes.

"Revenge."

The echoes return, mocking and true.

"And a sliver of justice."

The tunnel opens into a wider chamber—a maintenance area, judging by the rusted equipment still bolted to the walls. And there, in the center, a reinforced locker, the kind the old transit authority used to store emergency supplies.

I approach slowly, respectfully. This is where I make my offering, my penance, my revenge.

The locker is locked, of course. But locks never stopped me. A few minutes with a pry bar, and the mechanism gives way with a satisfying crunch. The door swings open.

Inside: crates of weapons, cases of Telluric components, enough contraband to put half the Syndicate leadership in BATC black sites.

And beneath it all, wrapped in chain and blessed lead, a vial of the black iron sludge.

The same substance that killed Danny.

My hands shake as I reach for it, and the tunnel temperature plummets further. Frost spreads across the crates, across my hands, across the

## CHAPTER 4: SANDHOGS AND CANNON FODDER

**Cole Reyes, Chapter 4.1**


The access tunnel stank of rust and piss-water.

I stood three levels down from the Pulaski Skyway, where the October dampness seeped through cracks in the concrete like blood through bandages. The air tasted like old coins and worse—like the kind of decay that settled into your lungs and never left. Twenty feet to my left, a junction box sputtered with orange emergency lighting, casting shadows that moved wrong, like something was breathing just outside the perimeter of the light.

Grimjaw was already there when I arrived, his massive frame hunched over a clipboard under a work-light that hissed and flickered. He wore his standard: steel-toed boots scuffed black with tunnel grime, high-vis vest that looked three sizes too small across his chest, hardhat cocked back on his head. The orc had a jaw that could crack cinderblocks and a temper to match, but right now he was focused, checking numbers like a man who took his work seriously.

Which he did. Always had.

"You're late, boss," Grimjaw rumbled without looking up. His voice was all Jersey gravel and union shop-floor authority. "Bram's already run the telluric readings. Pylon #1 is hot—BATC patrol rotation hits in twelve minutes. We go now or we wait three hours."

"Now." I adjusted the weight of the equipment vest, feeling the familiar drag of the cobalt steel hexes tucked in their magnetic clips. The metal was cold even through the synthetic fabric, hungry for something to burn. "What's the route?"

Grimjaw finally looked up, yellow eyes catching the emergency light like a cat's. "Same shit, different day. Maintenance shaft B-7, cut through the old sewage intercept, come up in the service corridor behind the pylon. Bram's got the breaching charges ready."

I heard boots on concrete behind me—steady, measured steps. Bram Kovacs emerged from the shadows, the dwarf's weathered face set in that permanent scowl that came from decades of watching safety protocols get ignored by people who thought union rules were just suggestions. His beard was braided with copper wire and small brass runes, and his hands moved constantly, fingers working through problems like a man counting cards.

"Structural integrity on the access shafts is compromised," Bram announced without preamble, his voice carrying that clipped precision of someone who'd explained the same thing a thousand times and expected it to be ignored a thousand and one. "OSHA ain't checking these struts down here, but they should be. We got water weeping through the concrete on the north approach. Load-bearing rebar is showing stress fractures in sections J-4 through J-9."

"Will it hold?" I asked.

"For the job? Yeah." Bram's eyes narrowed. "But we push another ten tons through that corridor, we're looking at a collapse scenario. Maybe not today, maybe not this month, but the math is the math."

Grimjaw grunted, setting down the clipboard. "We're not hauling equipment through, Bram. Just three of us and a lot of firepower. The charges are light enough."

"Still counts as payload distribution," the dwarf shot back. "Physics don't care if you're moving people or equipment. Mass is mass."

I held up a hand. "We're not having this debate. Grimjaw, what's the weapons situation?"

The orc jerked his thumb over his shoulder. "Got the modified assault rifles—underslung grenade launchers, full-auto capable. High-explosive rounds mixed with the armor-piercing. Bram's got the shaped charges set to bypass the Gold-Bismuth Collars on the BATC patrols. Standard thermite packets for the pylon's primary conduit."

"And the collateral damage?" I asked quietly.

Grimjaw's expression darkened. "Can't be helped, boss. Pylon #1 runs the residential grid for the Kearny marshes. We take it down, we're cutting power to eight thousand households. Maybe more."

"For how long?"

"Bram?"

The dwarf rubbed his beard, the brass runes clicking softly. "Standard bypass can be jury-rigged from Pylon #2 in six, maybe seven hours. But that's if the BATC engineering corps isn't running interference. If they are, we're looking at eight to twelve. Could be longer."

Eight to twelve hours. That meant people sitting in the dark. Kids doing homework by candlelight. Elderly folks struggling with medical equipment that needed steady current. The kind of people who'd never hear about the real reason their lights were out, who'd just see it as another failure in a system that failed them constantly.

The sliver of justice.

I'd already made the calculation. I made it every time. The Threefold Cord didn't include a weight for collateral damage because the weight was always the same: too much, never enough, and you had to do it anyway because standing still meant more people burned.

"Load up," I said. "We move in five."

Grimjaw nodded, already turning toward the equipment cache. Bram lingered a moment, studying me with those calculating eyes that missed nothing.

"You know what you're asking us to carry, Mr. Reyes," the dwarf said quietly. "We're not just sandhogs anymore. Haven't been for years."

"Never asked you to be."

"Good." Bram's scowl deepened. "Because the union's going to have questions if we start stacking bodies. Local 405 can cover a lot, but the BATC Aegis Command has eyes everywhere. They know what we're doing. They always know."

"Let them watch."

I moved toward the equipment cache, feeling the familiar cold certainty settle over me. The cobalt steel hexes whispered in my head—that hungry, desperate sound of metal that wanted to freeze the world solid. I pushed it down, kept it contained. Not yet. Never yet until the moment it was needed.

Behind me, I heard Grimjaw rummaging through crates, the clink of ammunition and the heavy thud of thermite packets being organized. The orc was methodical, efficient. He'd been a sandhog for fifteen years before the Breach, had seen the tunnels collapse on men he'd called brothers. He knew what it meant to carry weight underground.

"Boss," Grimjaw called out. "Bram's right. The union's going to push back eventually."

"Let them."

"What if they pull our contracts?"

I turned, met those yellow eyes in the sputtering light. "Then we go freelance. What's the difference between a union sandhog and a freelance operator? The paperwork and the benefits."

Grimjaw's expression was unreadable. "That's a shit answer."

"Only answer I've got."

The orc grunted, shouldered a modified assault rifle, and checked the ammunition feed. "Fair enough. Let's go light up the night."

I checked my own weapon, felt the familiar weight of it. The cobalt steel hexes nestled in my vest felt heavier than

* * *

I pushed through the rusted maintenance hatch first, my shoulder scraping iron shavings loose from its rim. Cold air hit like a slap—damp stone breath, sulfur-sweet, carrying something underneath that made my teeth ache.

Grimjaw followed heavy behind me, his frame scraping metal on metal. "Rebar looks compromised down this stretch," he muttered low, running his flashlight beam across exposed ceiling supports. "Maintenance runs were cut two months back when the BATC shifted budget to Telluric Corps."

I didn't answer. My attention had snagged on sound—a wet scuffling echo bouncing off tunnel walls deeper in, punctuated by harsh whispers. We weren't alone.

"Contact." Grimjaw's voice dropped even quieter, hand already moving to his sidearm.

The passage opened into a wider chamber, some old storage annex half-collapsed into itself. My eyes adjusted to shadows split by weak emergency phosphorescence strips still flickering along the walls. And there they were—four figures silhouetted against the glow, and what stopped me cold wasn't the armed men but what stood between us.

Three kids. Maybe thirteen, fourteen years old if they were lucky. A pair of **goblin** tunnel-runners, their mottled green-grey skin sheened with sweat and fear, and an **elf** girl who couldn't have been more than eleven—not counting street-hardening that aged metahumans faster than humans ever managed. Razor-wire tattoos spiraled up her neck, fresh enough that infection still pinked around the needlestitches.

She was crying silently, mascara tracks cutting through grime on her face.

"We know you're there!" One of the Syndicate tails shouted back toward us, pressing his pistol against the elf girl's spine hard enough I could hear her gasp from fifteen feet away. His partners had rifles trained on the goblin boys. "You want these mine-clearers? Come get them!"

My temperature dropped ten degrees. Not from fear—but from something colder, older, that lived at the bottom of wells where reason went to die.

Cole Reyes didn't do this anymore. Hadn't done it in months since Mara put her hands on my chest and made me promise, *promise*, that we'd find another way. That vigilantes burning themselves out for slivers of justice weren't helping anyone long-term.

But those promises felt very far away right now.

"Cole." Grimjaw's voice was careful. He'd seen this look before. "We call it in, let BATC—"

"They'll take twenty minutes minimum response time," I cut him off, eyes locked on the elf girl's face. Her breathing hitched, rapid shallow panic. "These kids won't last five."

The Syndicate enforcer laughed—actually *laughed*. "Smart money says he's right! Hey kid, bet your life on whether BATC gives a shit about street-elves or tunnel-rats like you?"

I drew my trench knife. The sound of blade leaving sheath rang clear as church bells in the confined space.

Grimjaw cursed under his breath but drew too—his service piece coming up smooth and sure despite his massive hand size. We moved simultaneously, flanking angles without discussion. Years of working together made our coordination unconscious.

"Last chance!" the lead enforcer screamed, yanking harder on the elf girl's hair. She whimpered, stumbled forward. His partners shifted their rifle sights between the goblin boys. "Make us, and she takes it first!"

My temperature dropped further. Cold enough that frost began crystallizing on the damp stone walls around us—cobalt steel hexes manifesting from pure will and years of walking the Weave's edge. The air froze into blinding fog.

The ambush came silent and violent.

Grimjaw's sidearm barked twice—suppressed shots that punched red flowers through the throat and chest of the rifleman covering the left goblin boy. The big man went down hard without finishing his scream.

I was already moving, closing distance to the lead enforcer while his attention flicked toward Grimjaw's muzzle flashes. My knife found his kidney before he could turn fully—the blade punching deep through muscle and organ with wet resistance. I felt him convulse against me as I grabbed both his gun-wrist and the elf girl's shoulder in one fluid motion, yanking her free.

The third Syndicate tail got off two shots wild before Grimjaw put a round through his eye socket. He crumpled like a sack of stones.

Silence crashed back into the chamber except for ragged breathing—mine, Grimjaw's, and the three kids' panicked gasps.

"You good?" Grimjaw asked, holstering his piece with practiced efficiency.

I looked at my hands—still gripping the elf girl's shoulder where I'd pulled her clear. She stared up at me with wide eyes gone glassy with shock. Behind her, both goblin boys were curled in on themselves, arms over heads in defensive postures they'd probably learned young.

"I'm fine." My voice sounded wrong even to me. Flat. Distant.

This wasn't slivers of justice. This was just blood on concrete in tunnels nobody cared about.

But she was alive who would have been dead in minutes if we'd called it in.

That had to be enough.

"Cole." Grimjaw tried again, softer this time. "We need to move. More tails might have heard."

I nodded automatically, releasing the elf girl gently. She scrambled backward from me, instinctive fear overriding relief. The goblin boys watched warily but stayed huddled together.

"What do we do with them?" Grimjaw gestured toward the kids.

Good question.

The BATC Youth Services Division would take them, process them, funnel them into the system that already chewed up metahuman orphans faster than it could spit them out. Street-elf girls with razor-wire tattoos? Even worse odds—the Syndicate owned every rehab program south of McCarter Highway.

"We get them topside," I decided. "Find somewhere safe before dawn."

"That's a four-hour run through hostile territory."

"So we run fast."

Grimjaw sighed but started gathering our spent brass and checking corners for more threats—old habits from underground work keeping him moving while I processed. Outside these tunnels meant complications I didn't need right now: BATC patrols, Syndicate reinforcements, maybe even Internal Affairs if someone caught wind of night ops that weren't sanctioned.

But leaving three traumatized kids alone in these tunnels?

No. Not happening.

I crouched down at eye level with the elf girl since she seemed like the oldest despite being smallest. "You're not cannon fodder anymore. You got it? We're getting you out of here."

She blinked at me, mascara-smudged face still shocked but slowly registering that the men pointing guns at her were dead on the floor behind me.

"Tunnel-rats, too?" Her voice came rough from crying. "Not just... just us?"

"Them too." I glanced back at the goblin boys. "All three of you."

What happened next wasn't in any manual or protocol. It was

* * *

I dropped from the overhead pipes like a lead weight, my boots hitting the gravel-strewn floor hard enough to crack stone. The lead handler didn't even have time to turn around—just a muffled grunt as my trench knife punched through his collarbone and buried itself in his clavicle.

Blood sprayed across the tunnel wall in an arc of midnight black under the dim work lights. He was still standing, somehow, one hand clutching at the knife handle, eyes wide with shock and pain. I didn't give him time for either.

My other hand came up, fingers tracing the metallic tang of a blood-iron hex. The air crystallized into cobalt frost. A spike of frozen steel erupted from nothing, dead center through his chest. His heart stopped mid-beat.

The body hit the ground with a wet thud that echoed off the concrete walls.

The second handler fumbled for his shotgun, but he was too slow. Too green. The metallic resonance still hung in the air, and I twisted my wrist—the same hex expanded, frost-rimmed edges spreading like cracks in ice across his ribcage. Another spike materialized, this one angled up through his sternum.

He collapsed before the gun cleared its sling.

I wiped my blade on the first man's coat, the fabric coming away damp and dark. No remorse. None. Danny had been eleven years old when the Sludge turned him inside out from the lungs down. Eleven fucking years old because men like these handed over contracts to the Syndicate without reading the fine print, without caring what happened to the families in the blast radius.

Two Goblins cowered against the far wall, their yellow-green skin gone pale beneath the grime of the tunnels. Young ones—barely out of whatever passes for childhood among their kind. One had a wrench clutched in both hands like a weapon. The other was shaking so hard his whole body vibrated.

"Clock out," Grimjaw said from behind me, his gravel voice low enough not to echo. He tossed them a handful of crumpled twenty-dollar bills, each one stained with rust-red tunnel mud. "Take the service elevator. Up three levels, then east to the McCarter Highway access."

They scrambled for the money, grabbing it with trembling fingers. Neither looked at the bodies. Smart.

"They'll talk," the younger Goblin stammered, already backing toward the maintenance ladder. "The Syndicate finds out we didn't report—"

"I don't give a shit what they find out." I stepped forward, and he flinched back so hard he nearly fell. "You're alive. That's more than your bosses gave those commuters in Sub-Station Seven. Take the money, get lost, and consider this your severance."

They disappeared up the ladder, climbing fast enough that their claws scrabbled against the metal rungs. Good. The fewer witnesses, the better, but I'd learned long ago that sometimes mercy served practical purposes. Terror made people compliant. Fear kept them quiet.

Not that these two mattered anyway. We were past Pylon #2 now, heading deeper into the access network beneath Newark Bay. Pylon #1 lay ahead, just past the Telluric Engineering substation where Mara had her command post. Where she'd been burning bridges—and saving lives—in equal measure since 2005.

I holstered my knife and rolled my shoulders. My right arm ached from the weight distribution of the drop. Forty-five degrees down through concrete was nothing compared to what Grimjaw could manage, but it still pulled something deep in my rotator cuff.

"Next checkpoint?" Grimjaw asked, his massive frame filling the tunnel behind me. At seven-foot-two, even hunched slightly to avoid the lower pipes, he blocked most of the light from behind us.

"Pylon One," I said, checking my watch. Two-forty AM. "Mara should have movement reports by now on which syndicate crews are running what routes tonight."

"And when we hit Pylon One?"

I smiled without humor. "We start breaking things."

The air tasted like copper and damp stone. Somewhere above us, traffic hummed along the Pulaski Skyway—late-night trucks hauling containers from Port Newark, probably, or commuters too desperate for overtime to care about the monsters in the tunnels below them.

They didn't know. Couldn't know. The BATC kept it quiet—the way they always did—sweeping away evidence with industrial-grade thermite and bureaucratic red tape thicker than tellurium ore deposits.

But we knew. Grimjaw knew. Every sandhog who'd worked Local 405 during the Experimental Sludge trials knew exactly what the Syndicate had done in those first few months after the Breach. How many bodies it took to power their infrastructure. What price they'd paid—and made others pay—for control over Earth's newly opened ley lines.

"Cole." Grimjaw's voice cut through my thoughts. "You good?"

"I'm fine."

"You're not fine."

"I said I'm *fine*, Grimjaw."

He grunted, unconvinced, but didn't push. We'd known each other too long for that. Since before Danny died. Since before I started carrying hexes instead of wrenches to work.

Before I stopped being just a machinist.

The tunnel ahead forked—left toward the substation where Mara held her Orphans hostage under her geas, right toward Pylon #1 and whatever Syndicate operations were running hot tonight. I headed right.

Behind me, I heard Grimjaw's heavy boots follow without hesitation. Loyalty forged in death and desperation. The kind that didn't come with paperwork or corporate sponsorship.

Just two South Side sandhogs trying to balance scales that had been broken since New Year's Eve, 1999.

No remorse.

Never enough justice.

And three thousand feet still between us and Pylon One.
