## CHAPTER 10: THE SLIVER OF JUSTICE

**The Question.**

I don't bother standing up from where I'm slumped against the concrete rubble. My ribs are still screaming, every breath feeling like someone's dragging broken glass across my lungs. The blood on my knuckles has mostly dried now, caked and dark in the dim light filtering down here.

Mara's the one who speaks first. Her voice cuts through the damp air sharp as any blade I've ever held.

"You're him." It's not a question. She's kneeling maybe ten feet away, one hand pressed to her sternum like she can stop the phantom pain there through sheer willpower. "Cole Reyes."

I just stare at her. There's no point denying it. The world already knows what I am.

Her white-lilac eyes—those same eyes that probably saw too much death back in '05 when she chose which lives were worth saving—narrow. "Tell me why."

"Why what?" Though we both know exactly what she means.

"Don't play stupid with me." Her voice cracks slightly, raw from smoke inhalation or screams or both. Maybe all three. "Julian Sterling. His family. What you did to them."

I finally look up at her fully then. Really look. She's younger than I thought—maybe early thirties—but those eyes carry decades more weight than they should. The bio-wards around her shoulders are flickering, bleeding that gray ash-static like wet charred wool, stinking of cedar and something else. Something burning underneath it all.

"The rats," Mara continues when I don't answer immediately. "The heated copper pot strapped to his stomach while he watched—" She stops, swallows hard. "While he watched his wife and daughters get torn apart by Orcs and Ogre-Kin. November 2005."

Above us, I hear Grimjaw's crew shifting massive slabs of concrete. The sound echoes down here, hollow and final. They're making progress, but not fast enough for my liking.

"You want to know why?" I push myself upright slowly, wincing as my bruised ribs protest every movement. "Or you want a reason?"

She flinches at the distinction but doesn't back down. "Both."

I lean against a chunk of reinforced concrete, crossing my arms over my chest. My hands are still shaking slightly—not from fear, but from cold and exhaustion. There's no warmth down here except what little heat radiates from the nearby Weave-pocket, and even that feels wrong. Contaminated.

"That was after," I say quietly.

"What was after?"

"The Sludge."

* * *

"Did it fix anything?" Mara's voice cuts through the settling ash-gray static like a blade through silk. Her white-lilac wards still bleed that wet charred wool stench, mixing with the copper tang of Sterling's blood on my knuckles.

I turn from where Grimjaw is methodically wrapping the elf's severed fingers into an evidence locker—fingerprints, dental records, everything we'll need when we finally burn this whole fucking Syndicate nest to the ground. The big Orc doesn't look up, but I can hear the satisfaction in how he clicks each compartment shut. Finality.

"Yes," I say simply. My throat hurts. Everything hurts.

Mara's standing at the edge of our makeshift circle—the one I traced with those hearth-coal embers while Sterling was screaming about ley-line portfolio management and quarterly projections. She looks like she wants to vomit, which somehow makes her look more real than any paramedic I've ever known. Most medics learn to disconnect. Not her. The 314 dead commuters of Sub-Station Seven never left her chest cavity, weighing under that Lead-Bismuth Geas.

"Look at me." She steps forward, past the cooling runes. "Really look."

So I do. Those green-gold eyes are raw as fresh wounds.

"You're not peaceful," Mara continues. Each word measured like she's performing trauma triage on both of us simultaneously. "You don't look... resolved. You look exactly the same as before you pulled his teeth out with pliers."

The metal around us ticks as it cools—that rhythmic sound echoing off concrete walls that smell like every shitty tunnel I've ever worked through Local 405. We're deep enough now that the city above might as well be another dimension entirely.

"That's because nothing will ever fix it," I tell her, and my voice comes out flat and honest in a way that surprises even me. "I know that. I knew it going into this. I'll know it when we finally put bullets through Sterling's skull and watch what sprays out onto these walls."

Grimjaw snorts from where he's cataloguing. "Poetic, boss."

"Not trying to be poetic." I wipe Sterling's blood on my jeans—dark denim already staining darker. "Trying to be mathematical. This whole fucked-up equation we're living in since 99 tore open the Veil."

Mara flinches at 'Veil.' That word carries weight for someone whose entire identity is built around saving lives while knowing she destroyed hundreds more. The fourth law of the Weave says those Orphans under her sternum geas won't die so long as she keeps fighting—but they also can't *truly* live until Sub-Station Seven stops bleeding its ghosts across her aura.

"So what's your answer then?" She crosses arms over her medic jacket, that gesture somehow maintaining clinical distance even as everything else about us has become viscerally intimate—trapped together in this pocket of reality that smells like violence and magic coal-fire warmth. "You torture him until you run out of creative ways to make people scream? You become exactly what Danny died hating?"

The mention of Danny's name lands like a punch to solar plexus all over again.

"Danny was an idealist." My hands are still shaking slightly—not fear or adrenaline anymore but something worse: conviction that feels holy and damned simultaneously. "He believed the system could be fixed from inside. Believed if enough good people showed up with clipboards and proper channels, eventually justice would trickle down like rainwater into gutters everyone forgot were clogged with iron rust and bodies."

I kneel back beside Sterling's unconscious form—elven private security finally broken after three hours of systematic persuasion using tools I learned in a South Side machine shop where no one asked questions about why Cole Reyes needed to know how pressure points and nerve clusters worked better than any union manual ever taught.

"He was wrong," I say quietly, almost gently touching the elf's shattered jaw. "Not because he wasn't brave or smart enough. Because the mathematics don't add up that way anymore. The city broke itself open in '99 when Y2K tore through those ley-lines, and nothing we do now can glue it back together cleanly."

Grimjaw straightens up from his evidence locker, massive frame casting shadows across walls covered now in dried blood alongside cooling ash marks from my hearth-coal rune-work.

"The boss is talking numbers again," he says—but there's respect underneath it. The Orc knows math better than most people; spent twenty years as tunnel sandhog forging load-bearing rebar deep beneath Passaic River sediments while corporate elites above him drank champagne at board meetings deciding whose livelihoods got sacrificed for quarterly profit margins. He understands when someone starts measuring evil by its weight rather than its intention.

"I'm saying this: A sliver of justice is never enough." The words come out clear despite throat raw from screaming threats at an elf who wouldn't break until we started on fingers instead of teeth. "It doesn't scrape the black iron sludge out of Danny's alveoli—the stuff they injected him with during those Experimental Trials thinking he'd make good collateral damage if he died right inside their testing chambers instead of outside them like everyone else did."

Mara inhales sharply but lets me continue.

"It doesn't bring back the dead—doesn't resurrect Sub-Station Seven commuters or return Mara's peace-of-mind about being able to save lives without simultaneously knowing she burned 314 others alive while doing it." I gesture toward her chest where that geas sits heavy under skin. "Doesn't unbreak any of us."

"So what's the point?" Her voice cracks just slightly—that first fracture showing through clinical trauma-triage mask she wears everywhere except here, trapped underground with two monsters and one corpse waiting to happen.

"This:" I spread hands wide encompassing everything around us—Sterling's broken body, Grimjaw's evidence locker filled with severed parts, the cooling runes still bleeding ash-gray static into stale concrete air. "Because a sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone. And if forcing these scales to balance—even violently, even monstrously, even knowing each victory only makes me worse—means there's one less piece of shit like Sterling left standing..."

I lean closer until our faces are inches apart and she can smell copper blood on my breath alongside coal warmth radiating off my chest cavity where those hearth-fire wards live now permanently stitched into muscle tissue by desperate ritual magic performed between torturing an elf who wouldn't talk about Pylon #2 syndicate wire-runners positioning sniper teams along Pulaski Skyway overpasses above Newark Bay.

"If becoming exactly what Danny hated means keeping his daughter safe from men who think little girls make good leverage against union machinists who know too much about Experimental Sludge formulas..." My voice drops lower, intimate despite brutality underneath every syllable spoken aloud instead of swallowed down like poison everyone pretends not to taste anymore when they look at Cole Reyes walking South Side streets after midnight carrying tools meant for breaking things rather than building them back together again cleanly whole like union work used to promise before

* * *

*The cut is precise, clean. I watch the last fiber of Grimjaw's thermite-burned restraints fall away onto the concrete, and the big Orc grunts with satisfaction, flexing his thick wrists. Behind him, the east wall of the Weave-pocket is a glowing, jagged maw of superheated metal, still dripping with molten slag.*

"East side's clear," *Grimjaw rumbles, his voice like gravel in a cement mixer.* "Reinforced rebar, load-bearing support—whole section's gonna collapse in maybe five, six minutes. We need to move."

*I don't answer. Can't. Because I'm still staring at Mara Vance's chest, at the Lead-Bismuth Myocardial Geas fused to her sternum like some god's iron brand.*

*The scars are old, keloided tissue wrapped around the metallic collar. She must have gotten it during Sub-Station Seven, when she was forced to choose between 314 commuters and 38 hostage orphans. BATC's Golden Saint. Their righteous hammer. Except she's not righteous at all.*

*She's a hostage.*

*Just like me.*

*Mara's hand moves to her collar, fingers tracing the edge of the Bismuth ring like she's memorizing its weight. Her jaw is tight, but I see the flutter in her throat—the tell of someone trying very hard not to show fear.*

"The Threefold Cord," *she says quietly, and there's no judgment in her voice anymore. Just... recognition.* "Penance, revenge, and a sliver of justice. That's your doctrine, isn't it? You think it's not enough."

*I finally look up at her eyes. They're tired. God, they're so tired.*

"It *isn't* enough," *I say flatly.* "It doesn't scrape the black iron out of Danny's lungs. Doesn't bring back the dead. But it's better than nothing. For *someone*."

*Behind Mara, I can hear Grimjaw's heavy boots on the concrete. He's moving toward the breach, checking the structural integrity of the collapse zone. His plasma-cutter hums in his grip, a low, angry whine.*

"We're out of time, Cole," *he calls back.* "Whole pocket's coming down. We go now, or we're buried."

*Mara's eyes flick to the breach, then back to me. She knows what I'm thinking. The mission isn't finished. Sterling's server core is still active, still broadcasting the resonant spike that's tearing holes in the Weave. And we're standing here, two hostages with iron collars around our hearts, while the world burns.*

*I reach out and grasp her wrist. She doesn't pull away.*

"One more thing," *I say, voice low.* "Then we run."

*Mara's jaw tightens, but she nods. She knows what comes next. The sliver of justice. That's all we've got.*

*That's all we've ever had.*

*I turn toward Sterling's server core, my hand already reaching for the thermite charges we planted earlier. Grimjaw's voice echoes through the breach again, more urgent this time.*

"Two minutes, Cole! The whole fucking structure's load-bearing—we're gonna be crushed like goblins under a steam-shovel!"

*I ignore him. My fingers find the trigger mechanism, and I look back at Mara one last time.*

"Ready?"

*She doesn't answer. Just grabs her sidearm and takes aim at the server core's primary power conduit. When this goes, it's going to be loud. And fast. And it's going to finish what we started.*

*The sliver of justice.*

*I press the trigger.*

`(~1,100 Words | Engine #5)`

*The thermite ignites with a sound like a thousand dragons screaming, and for a moment, the entire Weave-pocket is lit by the white-hot fury of molten metal. The server core's casing disintegrates, cascading down in a shower of liquid silver, and then—*

*Silence.*

*The lights flicker. Die. And in the sudden, crushing dark, I hear the groan of the collapsing structure. Grimjaw's right. We have seconds.*

*Mara's hand is on my shoulder, pulling me toward the breach. I can feel the heat radiating from the molten server core, still burning through the concrete floor like a wound that won't close. But I'm not looking at that.*

*I'm looking at the data-stream.*

*Because even as Sterling's server core dies, the resonant spike is still there. Faint, but present. Bleeding through the Weave like blood through water. Someone else has access. Someone else is running the spike. And if we don't find them—*

*We're all still hostages.*

*Grimjaw's voice cuts through my thoughts, sharp and furious.*

"Cole! Now!"

*I move. My boots slap against the concrete, and Mara's right beside me, her tactical training taking over despite the lead-iron weight of her collar. We're sprinting toward the breach, toward the jagged maw of light beyond. Behind us, the structure groans, and I hear the sickening crunch of steel rebar snapping like bones.*

*We hit the breach at a dead run.*

*And then we're through. Into the open air. Into the cold November night. The Passaic River gleams below us, black and still, and somewhere in the distance, I can hear the wail of sirens. BATC. Or maybe the Syndicate. Doesn't matter. We're out. Alive.*

*Grimjaw's already moving toward the extraction point, his heavy frame silhouetted against the city lights. But I stop. Turn back. Because I can still see it—the faint, pulsing glow of the resonant spike, bleeding through the Weave like a wound that won't close.*

*Is it done?*

*No.*

*It's never done.*

*I look down at my hands. They're steady. They're always steady. But for the first time since Danny died, I feel the weight of what I'm carrying. The Threefold Cord. Penance, revenge, and a sliver of justice. And underneath it all, the lead-iron truth:*

*It's not enough.*

*But it's all we've got.*

*Mara's voice cuts through my thoughts, quiet and steady.*

"The spike's still active. You saw it."

*I nod. Don't speak.*

"Sterling wasn't the source. He was just the conduit."

*Another nod. I know. I can feel it in my bones. The resonant spike didn't start with Sterling. It started somewhere else. Somewhere

## CHAPTER 11: THE UNION BREACH

I stood there in Pylon #2's Sub-Level like a man whose foundation had just turned to quicksand. The air tasted wrong—not frost-slicked cobalt anymore, but choked with competing stents that made my jaw clench: wet charred wool bleeding from her bio-wards, and beneath it all, shit, *beneath it all*, the acrid bite of hearth-coals rising off my own blood-magic like some kind of confession I never signed for.

"Fuck," I muttered, watching Mara's fingers shake as she fumbled with her tactical vest clasps. Her breathing had evened out, clinical again, but those lilac-and-cinder wards weren't dimming. They pulsed faintly against her sternum where the Lead-Bismuth Myocardial Geas sat fused to bone. Just like Danny's Arcane Iron-Lung. Same alloy, same damned frequency, same prison collar forged by people who knew exactly what pressure points made a person break.

I didn't look away when she caught me staring at her chest. What was the point? We'd crossed past privacy somewhere between her white-hot triage ward searing away Grimjaw's necrotic corruption and her screaming about saving thirty-eight orphans while burning alive three hundred fourteen commuters.

"You're thinking too loud," Mara said without looking up, her hands finally steady enough to snap the last magnetic closure on her vest. "Your hexes are practically visible."

She wasn't wrong. Usually, my cobalt workings ran dead silent—frost-rimmed and cold as a tombstone in January. Now they were compromised, bleeding temperature instead of stealing it, smelling like something domestic and warm because apparently getting burned half-alive by an Aegis Commander's trauma-triage protocols rewires your fundamental nature as a magical practitioner.

*Clinical trauma-triage paramedic.* That's how Sterling introduces her. Clinical. Like she's just a doctor, just a healer, no different than any ER surgeon patching bullets wounds and sending victims home to whatever hellhole put them there.

But that thing welded to her ribs? Lead-bismuth running on telluric frequencies? That wasn't clinical. That was a chain. And whoever held the detonator to it owned every decision she thought was hers.

"Lead-bismuth alloy." The words came out flat, mechanic-logic even though my mind was racing through implications faster than Grimjaw can run load-bearing calculations on rebar stress-fractures. "Runs on localized frequency. Who holds your detonator, Vance?"

Mara's head snapped up. Her eyes had gone hard again—that Commander mask slipping back into place like armor plating over exposed flesh. "That's classified BATC Internal Affairs."

"The fuck it is." I stepped closer, ignoring how my blood-magic flared hotter at proximity—the stench of hearth-coals thickening until I could taste copper-iron on my tongue. "You think I give a shit about internal affairs when you're walking around with the same collar my brother died wearing?"

Her jaw tightened but she didn't pull away. Couldn't, maybe—not without triggering those wards or revealing exactly how much control she'd lost standing this close to someone who smelled less like ash-gray static and more like... Christ, like warmth.

"You don't understand what happened in Sub-Station Seven," she said quietly.

"Do I not?" My voice stayed level but something ugly crept in underneath—grief-old rage that Danny's death had been bad enough before tonight made me realize he might have survived if BATC hadn't been experimenting with these exact same geas-technologies on people they labeled 'unreliable assets.' "You want to tell me about it? Want to explain why saving thirty-eight orphans cost three hundred fourteen commuters their lives while some BATC brass calculated acceptable casualties percentages?"

"It wasn't a calculation!" The words burst out raw despite her composure. "It was a choice between impossible options and I chose wrong and now there are *children* fused to my sternum because I can't be trusted alone in a room with my own thoughts!"

The cavern swallowed her shout whole—just another sound echoing off wet limestone walls beneath Newark Bay. But I heard it clear as day: the confession no Aegis Commander should ever make aloud.

We stood there separated by two feet of subterranean air thick enough to drown in, both wearing identical collars forged from different traumas. Her lead-bismuth heart-lock came from choosing incorrectly under pressure. Mine came from watching Danny suffocate slowly over six months as Arcane Iron-Lung corrosion ate through his alveoli one breath at a time.

Different triggers. Same prison.

"Who holds your detonator?" I asked again gently this time—mechanic-logic stripped away to just one brother asking another hostage for information that might matter when everything else went sideways.

Mara's hands curled into fists against her thighs like she wanted to hit me but couldn't remember how violence worked anymore—not after Sub-Station Seven burned hot enough to scar-ward her soul's perimeter.

Before either of us could break this standoff, the eastern wall shuddered.

Not a tremor—a full-body vibration that rattled teeth and made fillings ache. Blue-black iron-gall residue began spider-webbing across the limestone face in fractal patterns that hurt to look at directly, all angles too sharp and geometries wrong according to Euclidean math or any other system humans were meant to process visually.

Grimjaw would have called it load-bearing failure imminent. The wall was singing its death-song before collapsing into a breach wider than Passaic River's flood-tide during hurricane season.

I grabbed Mara without thinking—the way you grab anything precious when reality starts coming apart at the seams—and pulled her back from the fracture line just as blue-black veins cracked fully open across twenty meters of rock-face releasing something into our pocket-cavern that reeked of deep-ocean trenches where light never reaches and things older than human memory keep their eggs warm waiting patiently centuries between hatching cycles.

The Geas Shared wasn't finished revealing itself yet but whatever came next had just punched through containment barriers designed by people who thought they understood what dwelled beneath Neon Hollow's foundations when NYE 1999 tore Earth's ley-lines wide open spilling Shadowrun's entire metahuman spectrum into our dimension like radioactive slurry flooding underground aquifers.

We'd been so focused on each other we forgot: nothing stays buried forever once someone digs deep enough looking for leverage over people stronger than themselves.

Especially not when Elias Morvain knew exactly which levers moved which weights in BATC's corrupt machinery—and he'd already proven willing to sacrifice entire substations full of civilians if eliminating competitors required burning children alive inside Aegis Commanders' chests where nobody could see them screaming except maybe themselves during nightmares induced by lead-bismuth frequency locks installed against consent.

But those thoughts would come later after survival became less hypothetical depending entirely upon whether either one us could adapt faster than whatever entity currently breaching through Pylon #2 Sub-Level's eastern wall considered 'acceptable casualties' for achieving its own agenda regardless how many innocents stood between objective completion percentage metrics showing green status indicators on dashboards monitored remotely by decision

* * *

"Grim." My voice came out rougher than intended, still thick with the burn of Mara's ward-work lingering in my lungs.

The massive Orc didn't even flinch. His yellow-green eyes tracked me through the settling dust cloud rolling off the breach site where he'd just blown the east wall. Behind him, a half-dozen syndicate runners were already moving—hard-hat riggers hauling thermite charges, another pair laying down compression plating fast as they could screw down the toggle-nuts.

"Three minutes," Grimjaw repeated, maglight beam cutting across the chaos to land on my face. He knew something was wrong. The way I wasn't icy-cold anymore, the way my breath fogged but not like frost, more like steam from a kettle. Like *heat*. "BATC tactical units are coming up through the ventilation shafts. Internal Affairs already pinged this location."

Mara moved beside me—I felt her presence rather than heard it, all white-lilac and that cedar undertone that shouldn't have been there either. Her hand stayed low on her weapon, barrel still pointed generally in Grimjaw's direction.

"They're holding 38 hostages under Sub-Station Seven," she said, voice clinical despite the gun. "I saved those children once. They die here because you're on some union timetable, we're having a problem."

Grimjaw had his Casio G-Shock in his other meaty fist now, checking it like it might rewrite reality for him. "Lady, I don't know what kind of bullshit Aegis training tells you about timetables." His rotary hammer clanged against his shoulder plate. "But Local 405 don't stop drilling unless the whole goddamn tunnel collapses. We got rebar to shore before this section goes critical."

"Cole." Mara's fingers tightened around her sidearm grip. I could feel the weight of her Lead-Bismuth Geas pressing down—not just the ghost-kids from Sub-Station Seven burning, but every single soul she'd failed to save bleeding ash-gray static into our corner of the Pylon #2 sub-levels.

I patted the canvas satchel again. The Necro-Thermite Spike inside was warm. Should've been freezing cold, my blood-iron hexes making everything they touched rim with frost. But no—warm as freshly banked coals.

* * *

Chapter 11, Scene 11.3

The transponder's weight is less than a gram against my palm—a Gnome-forged sliver no bigger than a watch battery, but it might as well be a goddamn anvil given what it represents. I can feel its faint resonance even through my gloves, that telluric hum all magic-touched tech carries. Mara doesn't notice me palming it because she's staring at where I was standing half a second ago, her white-lilac ward still bleeding ash-gray static around her shoulders like moth wings made of burning wool.

"Commander."

My voice stops her cold. She whips back toward me so fast her bio-wards flare—cedar smoke mixed with wet char—and there it is. That momentary crack in her armor when she sees me standing close enough that we're almost touching. Her pupils dilate. The hand not holding her medical kit hovers between us like she wants to reach out or push me away and can't decide which would kill her faster.

"The squad's coming," I say low. "You need to drop your guard for three seconds. Think you can manage that?"

Behind me, Grimjaw is already moving deeper into the shaft, his massive frame disappearing into shadow. Smart bastard knows when to give space.

Mara swallows hard. "What are you doing, Cole?"

## CHAPTER 12: THE RESONANT SPIKE

"The maintenance shaft was narrow enough that Grimjaw had to turn sideways, his broad shoulders scraping against riveted metal walls still slick with something older than rust."

---

# The Inner Workings

The maintenance shaft was narrow enough that Grimjaw had to turn sideways, his broad shoulders scraping against riveted metal walls still slick with something older than rust. Sodium vapor lights flickered above us in their corroded fixtures, casting everything in that sickly yellow-white that made Grim's already pale green skin look like cracked porcelain. The air tasted like ozone and ancient river mud—the kind of rot that came up from deep places, where the Passaic had been poisoning itself long before Apep ever dragged his Liquid Isfet through our world.

"Christ," Grim muttered around his cigar, which he'd been gnawing for twenty minutes without lighting. He held the flashlight steady despite having to twist himself nearly double to fit. "Smells like my grandfather's workshop after he got hit by that collapsed tunnel in '03."

I didn't answer. Couldn't afford to split focus right now. My hands moved over the access panel controls with muscle memory from three years in Syndicate machine shops—before Danny, when I thought mechanics work was just mechanics work. The codes were different here, underneath Pylon #2, but the principle was the same: you listened to the machinery, and it told you what it needed.

Right now, Pylon #2 was screaming.

Not with sound—that would've been simple. It was resonating at a frequency that made my teeth ache and set off phantom pains in old injuries. The vibration traveled up through the soles of my boots, rattling bone against bone until even breathing felt mechanical.

"This is deeper than any scheduled inspection route," Grim observed, following me down a ladder bolted to the shaft wall. His voice dropped lower on the last words, like he was afraid the walls themselves might be listening—which, given BATC's tendency toward active surveillance, wasn't the dumbest paranoia. "You sure the Broker wasn't feeding us bullshit? Because this setup doesn't match the schematics."

"Doesn't have to." I reached the bottom rung and stepped onto a catwalk suspended over a drop into absolute darkness. No safety rail. Of course not—they never installed them in the pre-Breach sections. Too expensive, back then. Now those costs looked quaint as hell.

The Necro-Thermite Breaching Spike sat in its transport case like a promise written in jagged brass and cobalt steel. I knelt beside it carefully, opening the locks one by one. Each click echoed too loud in the confined space.

Grimjaw positioned himself opposite me on the catwalk, flashlight beam trained on the mechanism inside the case. He'd seen worse things—we both had—but there was something about Necro-Thermite that always drew attention. The way it didn't glow warm before deployment, just... waited. Patient. Like it knew what was coming.

"That thing's gonna punch straight through reinforced concrete and telluric conduit," Grim said quietly. "What happens if we hit wrong—if we rupture a primary artery while Mara's working the collar outside?"

I pulled out my PalmPilot, checking Danny's Iron-Lung telemetry for the third time in five minutes. His vital signs were holding steady, which meant either nothing was wrong or everything was so fucked it hadn't caught up yet. With necromantic medical tech, you took your bets where you could find them.

"We're going through," I said simply. "Pylon's already failing. BATC knows it—they wouldn't have sent Vance unless they wanted someone dead to handle the stabilization work."

"Mara ain't dead."

"Not yet." I checked the pressure gauge again. Brass needle hovered exactly where it should be: unstable equilibrium. "But she will be soon enough if that 4th Law Geas keeps bleeding lead-bismuth through her heart. The question is whether she dies saving thirty-eight hostages or letting Pylon #2 collapse into the bay."

Grim was quiet for a long moment. Above us, the shaft groaned—a deep structural complaint that suggested weight redistribution somewhere in the upper tiers. Maybe Mara setting charges. Maybe something else.

"You don't trust her," he finally said.

"The hell does that matter?" But even as I said it, I felt the truth of it settling into my bones like cold mercury. I *didn't* trust her—not with Danny's life, not with anything that mattered beyond the immediate mechanical problem at hand.

She'd saved me once before, back when Sub-Station Seven went up in flames and everyone thought I'd died along with the rest of the first responders. She'd dragged my half-frozen corpse out of there while burning alive three hundred and fourteen people who weren't lucky enough to have ice-magic flowing through their veins.

That kind of cost didn't just disappear because someone learned to live with it.

"So what now? We just... poke the sleeping god?"

I picked up the Spike carefully, feeling its weight settle into familiar grooves in my palms. Cobalt steel rimmed with frost despite the ambient temperature—my magic always came back baseline when I was working mechanics. Silent. Cold. Dead-silent.

"Straight into the primary telluric artery," I recited, reading from the Broker's instructions on my PalmPilot. "Maximum pressure threshold before casing failure: point-seven seconds. Expected resonance cascade: two-point-three minutes before Mara's collar engages. Window to extract: ninety seconds maximum."

"That's not a window. That's suicide."

"It's all we've got."

Grimjaw spit his cigar stub onto the catwalk and immediately lit another one, cupping the flame against non-existent wind. The yellow glow made shadows dance across his face—accentuated his cheekbones, hollowed out his eyes until he looked more goblin than orc for just a moment.

"I'm coming with you down there."

"No." I adjusted my grip on the Spike, already measuring distances with my eyes. The inner chamber lay maybe forty feet ahead through that reinforced hatch, and beyond that...

Beyond that was where Pylon #2 kept its heart. Where the 1999 retrofit met ancient architecture that predated European colonization by centuries—or maybe millennia, if you believed the urban legends about what had really been underneath Newark Bay before Dutch surveyors started mapping coastlines.

"We need someone topside to monitor Danny's telemetry," I continued, already moving toward the hatch controls. "If his vitals spike, you call it off. No argument, no debate—you initiate extraction protocol and get him clear of the blast radius."

"He can't survive extraction."

"Then you make sure he doesn't die alone."

The words came out harder than I intended them. Grimjaw caught my eye in the sodium vapor light, and something passed between us—that silent understanding that only came from watching too many people die badly over three years of South Side vigilante work.

"For Danny," he said quietly.

I keyed open the hatch.

The inner chamber hit like stepping into a cathedral built by beings who measured distance differently than humans did. The ceiling disappeared upward into darkness punctuated by biolum

* * *

**I watch through reinforced glass.**

---


## 'The Rashomon View'

I watch through reinforced glass.

Mara's silhouette moves against the amber wash of emergency lighting like a dancer in slow motion—except dancers don't crackle with ash-gray static that reeks of wet charred wool. From this side of Pylon #2, I can see the full weight of what she's carrying. Not just the lead-bismuth geas burned into her sternum from Sub-Station Seven, but every fucking second of the last three years. It's all there in how her shoulders hunch fractionally when she lifts the gold-collar, in the way her jaw sets so tight I can see the muscle jumping even at this distance.

*The Threefold Cord,* I think, and feel my teeth grind. *Penance. Revenge. A sliver of justice.*

Not enough for Danny. Never enough for any of them.

But it'll do.

My breath fogs the glass. Frost creeps outward from where my fingertips rest against the cold surface—not the deliberate frost-rimmed cobalt steel of my mechanic hexes yet, but something more instinctive. The temperature in here drops ten degrees as soon as I fully focus. That's old magic, pre-breach stuff that ran in my blood before 1999 turned the world inside out. Useful now that the ley-lines are bleeding shadow-race reality across every major metropolitan area.

"Christ," Grimjaw mutters behind me, his voice the rough texture of shift differentials and industrial thermite. "She look okay to you?"

"Define okay."

He doesn't answer. Doesn't need to. We both know what we're watching isn't okay by any standard measure. But it's necessary, which is a different beast entirely.

I turn back to the work platform beneath my feet—rust-streaked concrete, oil stains shaped like continents, the Pylon #2 core access point yawning open like a throat. The Necro-Thermite Spike sits in its cradle, waiting. My reflection in its polished surface shows someone who hasn't slept since before Mara pulled me off Sterling's floor with half my ribs caved in.

*Forty-three hours*, I remind myself. *You've gone longer during tunnel runs.*

That was different. That was just pain.

This is watching someone else carry the weight while you do your part in silence.

My hammer finds the spike's mounting plate without looking. The sound echoes through the chamber—

**CLANG.**

Outside, simultaneous with perfect precision, the heavy clank of Mara's squad working on the outer gantry masks the noise. Someone shouts instructions about load-bearing stress vectors. Another voice calls out shift differential calculations for the collar housing.

They're good. BATC Aegis Commander or not, she picked her team from South Side sandhogs who understand pressure points—the kind that can crack rebar or crack a person depending on where they apply force.

I bring the hammer down again.

**CLANG.**

Another clank from outside, perfectly synchronized. Grimjaw counts off between strikes now, his foreman's instincts kicking in even when he's supposed to be backup. "Three-quarter rotation... hammer check... two more inches depth..."

The blood-iron hex activates as I make contact, frost spreading across the metal surface in crystalline patterns that wouldn't exist in standard physics. But 2007 isn't standard anything anymore. Not since the Y2K breach turned Newark Bay into a goddamn nightmare of ley-line convergence zones and metaphysical bleeding.

"Cole."

Grimjaw's voice carries an edge I recognize—stop, reassess, don't fuck this up because we only get one shot at priming the Spike before the Syndicate sniper notices our magnetic signature.

I lower the hammer.

Through the glass, Mara has the gold-collar fully seated now. The ash-gray static surrounding her intensifies as she applies pressure, forcing it into place despite her hands shaking visibly even from here. Every second of those 38 Orphans burned under her geas must be screaming at her to stop, to walk away, to let someone else handle this—

But there is no someone else.

That's why Sterling wanted me specifically. That's why Mara agreed to this insane coordination protocol where she works outside while I work inside so our magical signatures don't overlap enough for the Pylon's resonance detection to flag us as hostile.

We're both carrying weights no one should have to carry alone.

My hand finds the Spike's primer switch—a simple toggle affair designed by BATC engineers who still think security means making things complicated rather than understanding that complexity creates failure points.

*Simple, elegant, effective.*

Like Danny's smile used to be before the Experimental Sludge trials took his lungs apart molecule by molecule.

**CLANG.**

One more strike. Get the spike fully seated. Then activate. Then watch what happens when we trigger the Rashomon sync between your perspective and Mara's—two views of the same impossible moment, two sets of overlapping coordinates that shouldn't exist in three-dimensional space but do because the Weave doesn't give a shit about Euclidean geometry after 1999.

The readout on the Spike flares to life.

Digital numbers cascade across LED displays: temperature, pressure differentials, magic-leakage ratios measured in nanoseconds. Everything reads green except for one warning indicator blinking amber—resonance feedback potential at 72% probability of critical mass.

"Shit," Grimjaw breathes.

Outside through the glass, the heavy gold-bismuth collar Mara's squad just finished installing begins to glow with matching intensity. Warmth radiates through even this distance—I can feel it against my face like standing too close to a furnace.

It's working.

God help us all, *it's actually working*.

But then—

The amber warning light turns red.

The collar outside flashes synchronization lock achieved.

And somewhere deep in Pylon #2's core access chamber where I'm standing with frost creeping up every surface and blood-iron hexes singing their deadly song, something fundamental shifts in how reality calculates itself around us.

The Rashomon View activates simultaneously from two perspectives separated by reinforced glass and three years worth of accumulated guilt.

I see Mara's hands crackling with white-lilac flames that smell of cedar and ash-gray static colliding with my cobalt steel cold-burn magic.

I see both timelines overlay each other—the past bleeding into present, showing me Sub-Station Seven burning while simultaneously displaying Mara forcing herself to move forward despite carrying 38 Orphans dead weight under her sternum.

*Penance.*

*Revenge.*

*A sliver of justice.*

Not enough. Never enough. But—

"It's holding," Grimjaw says quietly behind me.

Through the glass, Mara looks directly at where I'm watching her.

Even across this distance, even through layers of magical interference and physical barriers, our eyes meet.

She nods once. Sharp. Definite.

Acknowledgment that we're locked in now—no going back, no extraction plan if things go sideways because there wasn't time to code one properly when Sterling was screaming orders at us both while bleeding out on his private security floor.

My hand

* * *

I stared at the numbers until they blurred into static. My PalmPilot screen cast that sick green glow across my knuckles—the only light in this tomb-silent maintenance gallery. Ten meters below, through rust-bloom gratings, the primary coolant loop for Pylon #2 was singing.

Not a pleasant song. More like grinding teeth.

The telemetry made no sense. Couldn’t make sense. Necro-Thermite compounds don't *resonate*—they burn hot and nasty and then they're gone. Gold-Bismuth Collars don't *react*—they're suppression runes, passive dampeners. Two completely different magical-chemical profiles.

And yet here they were, humming in perfect synchronization. The frequency readout flickered between both data streams:

**SYNDICATE SPIKE: 7,843 Hz**
**BATC COLLAR: 7,843 Hz**

My finger hovered over the delete key. This had to be corrupted data. Had to be some kind of feedback loop from the Pylon's own Telluric field interfering with the sensor arrays. Because if this was real...

I heard footsteps behind me.

"—can't get a clear reading from the eastern approach," came a woman's voice, clipped corporate precision that could only mean elf. "Engineering estimates another forty minutes before we can establish safe access."

"Tell Engineering their estimates are shit," Grimjaw rumbled back. His boots echoed against bare concrete—heavy, deliberate. The Orc didn't bother with pretense anymore. Not after what we'd seen in Sub-Station Seven. "Sensors show structural degradation accelerating by point-six-seven percent per minute. That's not 'safe access,' that's 'how long until this whole fucking thing comes down.'"

"You're exaggerating." But there was uncertainty underneath her words. Good.

"I'm doing math." A pause. Then: "Cole? You finding anything?"

I didn't turn around. Couldn't look away from those numbers. My reflection ghosted back at me from the PalmPilot screen—a hollow-eyed man with oil-stained fingers and someone else's blood under his nails. Danny's blood. Always Danny's blood these days.

"The Spike and the Collar are resonating together," I said quietly.

The silence that followed wasn't empty. It filled up with implications like water filling a cracked reservoir.

"That's... impossible," the elf finally managed. Her name tag read *KESSEL*—BATC Internal Affairs. Mid-thirties, maybe, dressed in one of those perfectly tailored suits that cost more than my annual salary used to be. Back when salaries mattered. Before the Breach turned everything inside-out.

"It's happening anyway," I said. My voice sounded flat even to myself. Distant.

Grimjaw moved closer—I could hear the shift differential in how he placed each foot, weight distribution calculated for load-bearing impact on aged infrastructure. Union sandhog training never really leaves you, even when you're trying to save the world instead of boring tunnels through it.

"Explain it simple," he said. "Because right now my brain feels like overloaded rebar."

Simple. Right.

"Someone designed the Necro-Thermite Spike specifically to match the harmonic frequency of the Gold-Bismuth Collars." The words came out mechanical. Clinical. Like I was reading them off some instruction manual written by demons. "When both charges reach critical mass simultaneously—"

"They'll breach the Pylon core while containing the blast vector downward," Kessell interrupted. She'd caught on fast. That razor-sharp corporate mind working through the problem at lightspeed. "Feeding Apep directly into the Telluric grid. Funneling the entire Northeast power conduit straight into the Overmind's maw."

"Yeah." I closed my eyes. Saw red behind my eyelids—the glow from Sub-Station Seven as Mara burned 314 commuters alive because she had to choose between hundreds and dozens, and the dozens meant something to her even if the hundreds didn't survive anyway.

The mathematics of sacrifice. I knew them intimately.

"And here's where it gets worse," Grimjaw added softly. He held up his own data-slate—a BATC-issued unit that he'd liberated from a dead technician two hours ago. Probably not the most legal thing we'd done tonight, but legality stopped being relevant around the same time morality did. "Pressure readings are spiking. Someone just hit the activation sequence for both devices simultaneously."

Kessell swore in High Elvish—not one of the polite phrases.

"How long?" My throat felt tight.

Grimjaw checked the readout again. His jaw—already jutting and brutish with Orc physiognomy—seemed to harden further. "Seven minutes. Maybe eight if the coolant loop holds longer than projected."

Which it wouldn't. Nothing ever does when you're this close to disaster.

I looked down at my hands again. Still steady. Still cold. The frost-rimmed cobalt steel that was my magic had retreated back to baseline after leaving Mara in the gantry above—but now I could feel it stirring again, responding to the building panic like an animal catching wind of approaching hunters.

*Not yet,* I told it silently. *Let me think first.*

But there wasn't anything left to think about, was there?

The Syndicate Spike would breach Pylon #2's core containment. Massive energy release, catastrophic structural failure, all the standard apocalyptic shit we'd been expecting. Except—

"Kessel." She looked at me sharply. "When the Collar activates its sealing protocol, what happens to any external shockwave?"

Her eyes widened slightly. Not much—the elf had seen too much already to be easily surprised—but enough.

"The Gold-Bismuth resonance creates a containment field," she said slowly, working through the mechanics even as she spoke them aloud. "Any blast pressure is directed inward toward the breach point rather than outward into surrounding infrastructure."

"So if someone positioned themselves on the eastern gantry during detonation..."

"They'd take the full brunt of the explosion directly." Her face went pale beneath her carefully maintained corporate composure. "Oh fuck. Oh *fuck.*"

Mara Vance and her entire squad were on that gantry right now.

My PalmPilot chimed softly—a notification from Grimjaw's unit syncing with mine. New data stream appeared:

**DETONATION SEQUENCE INITIATED**
**T-MINUS 6:47**

"Cole." Grimjaw's voice carried weight—not just physical mass but gravity of purpose. The kind of sound a union shop steward makes when he knows some men aren't coming home from this shift. "What do you need?"

Everything. Nothing. It didn't matter anymore because Mara was up there doing penance for burning 314 commuters alive while saving 38 orphans who are now held hostage under her sternum like lead-bismuth weights around her soul—and I wasn't going to let another person die tonight carrying numbers they couldn't live with anyway.

Even if it killed me trying.

"My gear bag," I said. Turned back toward my workstation—this cramped maintenance gallery

## CHAPTER 13: THE STEAM-BAFFLE SACRIFICE

I saw my death in the blue-white glare of the rupturing pipe—

Not the end, mind you. Just one possible future branching off like a cracked conduit splitting under too much pressure. The Pylon's core screamed like a wounded beast, all twenty stories of reinforced concrete and telluric-copper piping buckling inward as the experimental reactor deep below us convulsed through another catastrophic failure cycle.

"BOSS!" Grimjaw's roar cut through the industrial shriek. His massive frame was silhouetted against the western viewport, seven-foot-two of South Side muscle twisted to look back at me instead of forward where any sane person would've been running. "She ain't gonna make it! Western baffle's already locked!"

My boots were magnetically clamped to the service catwalk six meters up from the main deck, and even through that distance, I could feel the vibrations traveling up through the soles—the whole structure wanted to tear itself apart. I didn't need Grimjaw to point out which direction the blast-wave would hit. The schematics burned themselves into my retinas: primary venting routes marked in yellow, emergency overpressure valves in red, and right there—right fucking THERE—in bold crimson letters stamped across Section C-7:

> DANGER: CRITICAL STEAM BAFFLE - MANUAL OVERRIDE ONLY

Mara Vance stood on the far side of the viewport with three other BATC Aegis suits, their white-lilac bio-wards flickering around them like dying candles in a hurricane. I couldn't hear her voice over the reactor's death-rattle, but I saw her lips move anyway, shouting orders to her squad while her hands worked frantically at something I couldn't see past the glare.

The sliver of justice.

That's what this came down to. Not vengeance—I'd had plenty of chances for revenge tonight before we got dragged into Sterling's little trap. And not penance, either; whatever debts I owed wouldn't be paid by saving the woman who held 314 dead commuters under her sternum.

But a sliver of justice? That fragile, precious thread?

I could pull it loose with one wrong decision.

"Cole!" Mara's voice finally punched through somehow, magicked or technomanced or just raw desperation projected straight into my skull. "The eastern baffles! You have to close them!"

"I know," I shouted back, already moving toward the manual override station even as every instinct screamed at me to run east instead of west—to escape rather than embrace. But running meant she died, and Grimjaw with me if his stupid orc loyalty kept him pinned here trying to save my ass.

My fingers found the access panel and wrenched it open. Behind the door was exactly what I needed and also exactly what I didn't want: a hand-cranked emergency valve mechanism, all industrial-grade iron gears and telluric-forged bronze housing. No magic to smooth this out, no augments to make it easier. Just pure mechanical labor against an impossible deadline measured in seconds.

Grimjaw lumbered up beside me, his massive hands closing around the crank handles without waiting for instruction. He knew. We both did.

"You're gonna need backup on this side when you seal it," he grunted, arms flexing as he began turning clockwise—the opposite direction from how any rational person would've expected, but that's telluric engineering for you. The western blast-baffle started groaning shut behind us like a tomb door closing.

* * *

"I hit the manual override wheels without thinking."

---

# M-B1 Ch. 13.2 — Forged in Flesh

**Cole Reyes POV**

I hit the manual override wheels without thinking.

The metal screamed under my palms—already searing hot from the core overload, conducting thermal runoff straight up through the maintenance shaft like a brand. I could feel it even through my leathers: that deep-muscle burn that meant third-degree territory within seconds.

"COLE! NO!" Grimjaw's voice split the steam-shrouded darkness behind me. Heavy footsteps. His massive hand clamping down on my shoulder.

I locked my boots into the grating and shoved back against him with everything I had. "MOVE!"

The wheels were frozen—I could feel the ice-cobalt hex failing already, crystallizing too slowly while the temperature climbed past critical threshold. No time for finesse. No time for the clean freeze-and-shear method that didn't leave scars.

My right forearm slammed against the seam where both blast-baffles met. Skin kissed molten iron.

Pain erupted across every nerve ending—a white-hot flash that shot straight to my brain stem. My mouth opened but no sound came out. Just air burning its way up my throat.

But underneath that agony, something else ignited.

Not frost-cobalt. Never frost-cobalt—not when Mara was on the other side of these baffles with her heart trying to beat itself apart just to keep thirty-eight orphans alive.

My blood sang copper-hot instead. The same telluric resonance that ran through every dwarven-smithed piece of equipment in the South Side chop-shops. In the tunnels beneath Newark Bay where Local 405 worked their shifts. Where Grimjaw had taught me to read stress-fractures in rebar by feeling the vibration in your teeth.

*Flesh is just another metal,* I thought stupidly as my forearm pressed harder against the searing seam. *Just a different alloy.*

Hearth-coal warmth flooded from my sternum—Mara's scent-signature bleeding through like ash-gray static, like wet charred wool, like white lilac trying desperately not to burn. Her bio-wards reaching across ten feet of super-heated steam and three inches of solid iron to anchor themselves around my spine.

The smell hit me next: cedar-smoke thick enough to taste. Burning sugar. Copper pennies left too long in summer rain.

"COLE, YOU'RE MELTING YOURSELF!" Grimjaw sounded panicked now. His grip shifted—I could feel his claws scraping at my leathers, trying to peel me away from the baffles before my arm fused permanently to the seam. "THE IRON'S GOIN' CRITICAL! LET GO!"

I couldn't answer. Could barely breathe past the pain.

But I could weld.

Flash-welding required two pieces of metal heated until they glowed orange-white, then slammed together while molten. My flesh was already doing half the work—the contact point between my forearm and the baffle-seam glowing a sickening yellow through the steam. Steam that stank of cooking meat and burning hair.

My left hand found its spot on the other side of the seam. Pressed down.

Both forearms screaming in protest. The skin bubbling and blackening even as I drove the heat deeper, forcing it into the molecular structure of the iron itself. Making myself the conduit. The resistance heating element.

"This is insane!" Grimjaw roared. "THERE'S ANOTHER WAY! WE CAN—"

The core detonated.

Not with sound first—that came later—but with pressure. A concussive wave of telluric force that hammered against the eastern blast-baffle like God's fist testing locked doors. The entire maintenance shaft lurched sideways. Rivets shrieked. Something massive tore free on the far side of the core chamber.

Then the real explosion hit.

The western viewport—Mara's side—held because I'd welded the baffles shut just in time. But the backlash found every weak point: rusted support struts, stressed load-bearing beams, the catwalk I was standing on which had probably been compromised since 1967.

My boots lost purchase.

Grimjaw's grip tightened—he had me by the collar, trying to haul me backward toward solid ground—but momentum was physics and physics didn't negotiate.

The world spun. Rust-red steel flashing past. Gravity reasserting dominance after thirty feet of airtime.

I crashed through something structural—a secondary grating that gave way like wet cardboard—and kept falling into absolute darkness below.

The impact registered only as a distant thud before unconsciousness claimed me entirely.

* * *

I jerked awake to the smell of burnt flesh and something else—ozone, sharp and electric, like copper pennies licked clean. My forearms screamed where skin had fused itself into blackened leather against my ribs. The world tilted sideways before I caught it, vision swimming in yellow static that wouldn't clear no matter how hard I blinked.

"Easy there." Grimjaw's voice came from somewhere above me, muffled and far away despite being close enough that I could smell his work-breath—cigar smoke and cheap coffee from hours underground. "Don't go passing out again."

Something cold hit my left forearm. Then the right. The sensation was wrong—not ice exactly but not quite heat either, like pressure that burned in reverse. Chemical foam hissed against blistered skin, raising new layers of agony that made me see stars across my vision.

"You're out of your mind, Reyes," Grimjaw muttered, working fast with hands that knew their business. The sound of tearing fabric came next—he'd cut away the melted remains of my jacket sleeves to get better access. "You almost cooked yourself for a fed."

The words registered third or fourth time around. Fed. Right. Mara Vance had been down here doing God-knows-what when Pylon #2 went critical, and I'd thrown everything I had at keeping those Syndicate bastards from finishing what the 4th Law had started with her already. Heat-coal magic instead of frost-cobalt. Warm cedar and white lilac instead of killing cold. What the fuck had possessed me?

Not possessed. *Protective.*

I swallowed hard against rising nausea and reached for my phone—a cracked Motorola Razr that had somehow survived whatever I'd done to myself. The screen lit up weak blue light on soot-stained fingers as I pulled it free from my tactical vest pocket.

Grimjaw kept working, spraying more foam onto my forearms where he'd wrapped them in torn shirt sections soaked with something that stank like antiseptic and promises I couldn't afford to keep. "Transponder's still active if she made it topside."

I ignored him long enough to pull up the feed. There—a green dot moving steady through red static that represented the blast zone's perimeter. Moving away. Steady pace that suggested someone running but not panicked, controlled exfiltration.

Mara Vance was alive.

"She made it." My voice came out wrong—too raw, too relieved—but Grimjaw either didn't notice or didn't care because he just grunted acknowledgment while securing some kind of tourniquet around my right forearm that felt way too tight.

"Good," he said simply. "Now we get you out before BATC locks this whole sector down tighter than a drum."

I holstered the phone back into place and let Grimjaw haul me upright using my vest straps as leverage points. My legs weren't cooperating—they wanted to collapse back into the rubble we were standing knee-deep in—and my arms were useless dead weight hanging at my sides despite how badly I needed them functional.

"What happened?" I managed between gritted teeth as we started climbing over chunks of concrete reinforcement bar twisted into shapes that shouldn't have been possible outside industrial thermite cutting torches.

"Pylon #2 went hot around 23:50," Grimjaw reported clinically while helping me over what looked like half a support column fused into glass by whatever energy had torn through here. "You lit up like Christmas morning and then everything went white. When vision cleared, Syndicate tech team was scattered across three hundred meters radius looking like they'd won an argument with a lightning storm." He paused at the top of our makeshift stairs—actually pieces of fallen scaffolding that he'd rearranged into something climbable—looking back at where we'd come from. "Whatever you did, Reyes, don't do it again without better ventilation next time."

The smoke was getting thicker as we ascended toward upper catwalks visible maybe twenty feet above us now, silhouetted against faint moonlight filtering through gaps in the ceiling structure overhead. But there was something else cutting through the gray haze—that same electric ozone smell stronger than before mixed with burning plastic and copper.

And laser light.

My head snapped left fast enough to make my vision blur again as I caught movement in peripheral sight—a single red dot tracing across Mara's exfil route marked on my mental map of Pylon #2's layout. Someone had eyes on her position topside even now.

"Grim—"

"I see it." His response was immediate and hard-edged, hand going instinctively to where his sidearm would normally sit holstered if this weren't North Jersey where carrying anything heavier than a folding knife got you arrested or dead depending on which BATC enforcement squad found you first.

We kept climbing anyway because stopping meant dying slowly buried under collapsing infrastructure when BATC secured the perimeter—which they'd start doing any minute now once their sensor grids registered active hostiles still present inside blast zone boundaries.

The laser stayed steady aimed somewhere beyond where Mara should have been by now based on transponder tracking data updating every ten seconds on my phone screen still clutched white-knuckled in burned fingers despite how much holding anything hurt right now.

## CHAPTER 14: THE SHADOW OF THE CORD

*The Ascent*

The stairs were metal, corrugated iron that screamed under our boots as we climbed. Each step groaned like a dying beast—rust flaking off in bitter white chips that tumbled into the dark below. Grimjaw was ahead of me, his massive frame making the spiral staircase feel smaller than it was.

"Shit," he muttered, tapping his earpiece. His voice carried that South Side grit, all sandhog and union shop steward rolled into one. "Syndicate comms are going wild. Voss is calling in cleaners."

I paused mid-step. The word hung between us.

Cleaners meant no witnesses. No loose ends. And if there were no survivors from what just happened at Pylon Two... well, that included anyone who'd seen too much.

"How long?" I asked.

Grimjaw glanced back at me through the dim light filtering down from somewhere far above—a sickly orange glow probably from sodium-vapor lamps half a mile up on the surface catwalks. He shrugged his broad shoulders beneath his Local 405 jacket.

"Not sure they're local teams either." He scratched behind an ear absently—not nervousness; more like frustration mixed with something darker."Sounded like contract work to me."

Contract work meant Kaelen 'Glass-Eye' could be here already—had probably been assigned before my team even set foot in Neon Hollow's lower levels today—and I knew damn well what that meant for Mara Vance when she'd made her call-out with those Orphans stowed safely away now outside this death-box we'd turned Pylon Two into.

"You think Sterling sent him?"

"It's his style." Twelve.

Grimjaw shifts his weight. Ready to sprint.

"Two."

My finger moves to the trigger.

Voss fires.

At me.

I looked at Grimjaw, then down at Mara Vance stretched out below like a broken doll in the kill zone. My throat was sandpaper and rust.

Frost-coal blue ice immediately bloomed along the gunmetal barrel. Crystalline patterns spread like frostbite up the frame, each crystal sharp-edged and hungry. The temperature on the catwalk dropped ten degrees in three seconds flat. Could see my breath now.

Couldn't exhale them even if he wanted to—which he couldn't because he'd been dead for four years, murdered by Syndicate enforcers who'd gotten their orders straight from Sterling's penthouse office.

Julian Sterling screaming in that copper pot flashed through my mind next—not the memory of him actually burning, but how I’d *wanted* to make him burn. Wanted to peel his skin off with runesong steel and watch him convulse while I asked him about Danny. Asked him why. Asked him how many brothers he'd gutted just to keep his stock portfolio looking pretty for quarterly reports.

The Threefold Cord wrapped tighter around my sternum: Penance (for what I’d done), Revenge (for what they’d taken), and—

A sliver of justice.

Never enough. Would never be enough. Not for Danny's lungs. Not for Mara's thirty-one-four burned commuters or her thirty-eight saved orphans living under her ribcage like a lead-bismuth tumor. A sliver wouldn't bring back the dead or scrape out corruption down to the bone.

But it would do. For now, it had to fuckin’ do.

“Cole.” Grimjaw’s voice came out rougher than usual. “Brother, you can’t save everyone.”

My finger settled onto the trigger guard. The frost-cobalt ice along the magnum barrel pulsed once, twice—a heartbeat made of winter fury.

“I know what I am,” I said quietly, meeting those yellow eyes dead-on. My voice carried across the gap between us: absolute certainty laced with something colder than regret. “I know a ‘sliver of justice’ is never enough, Grim. But it will do for the moment. And because a sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone…”

I turned away from him toward where Mara lay bleeding in the crosshairs.

“It drives me to continue with the abyssal acts I commit.”

The words tasted like copper and ash on my tongue.

She doesn't die tonight.

I stepped out of cover without hesitation—just rolled my shoulder forward and pushed off into open ground. Fifty yards shot through smoke that reeked of burnt propellant and ozone discharge. Below, Mara’s white-lilac bio-wards flickered weakly around her unconscious form; cedar-scent fading fast as blood pooled beneath her torso.

You learn their tells if you survive long enough.

One second.

The shadow shifted.

There—upper structural I-beam crossing diagonal support truss!
