## CHAPTER 15: THE SECRET SHOT

I stood on the upper catwalk, three stories above the Sub-Station Seven wreckage, and watched death aim its crosshairs at Mara Vance while she knelt unconscious among the bodies. My arms were burning—chemical burns from the Syndicate thermite charges that had torn apart the maintenance shaft two minutes ago—and I could smell my own flesh cooking under the coating of industrial solvents still clinging to my coveralls.

But pain was just data. And the only data that mattered right now was the shadow-sniper crouched in the ventilation duct behind Mara's prone form, the one whose camouflaged elf-pattern skin rendered him invisible unless you knew exactly where to look. Unless you'd spent enough time tracking Syndicate assassins through these tunnels to recognize the way light bent wrong around their positions.

I raised my .45 AutoMag—heavy as hell, kicking like a mule even when your hands weren't shaking from adrenaline—and settled into the stance Grimjaw had drilled into me during our range sessions down in Local 405's training cellar. Breathe in slow. Hold it. Let half out.

The crosshair fell on Mara's forehead.

She stirred then, groaning softly, one hand lifting toward her temple. The movement made her head tilt slightly left—exactly the angle I needed. Through the red dot superimposed on my scope overlay, I could see past her, into the shadows beyond. There—a glint of brass casing. A fraction of an inch of exposed barrel.

My finger touched the trigger.

Time did something strange up here on the catwalks. Maybe it was the Y2K residue still bleeding through the reality cracks in this part of Newark Bay—residual temporal distortion from when the Millennium Breach first tore open across Earth's ley-lines back in '99. Or maybe it was just the hyper-focus that comes when every muscle in your body knows you have one shot and no margin for error.

Either way, everything crystallized into perfect clarity.

I could smell the ozone from the live conduits below, mixed with wet copper from all the blood pooled on the grated floor. Could feel each individual blister forming on my forearms where hot shrapnel had kissed skin. Heard the distant rumble of traffic on the Pulaski Skyway cutting through the chemical fog bank rolling off the Passaic River.

And underneath it all: the faint scent of white lilac and cedar warding-salts that always clung to Mara Vance even after she'd been awake for forty-eight hours straight triaging casualties at disaster sites like Sub-Station Seven.

That smell shouldn't have been there anymore—not after what happened in 2005, not after the Geas that burned through her chest and turned those 314 commuters into ash while saving 38 orphans from a goblin war-band. Shouldn't have survived the BATC Internal Affairs investigation or the court-martial proceedings or whatever dark ritualistic binding they used to make sure she never forgot burning people alive because thirty-eight kids lived instead.

But it *was* there. And that meant something I didn't have time to process right now.

The sniper moved—just slightly—in the shadows behind Mara. His rifle shifted position, tracking her groaning form as she tried to push herself up onto her elbows. The barrel swung toward her head, following instinctively where his target's body led him.

I held my breath completely this time. Let my shoulders relax by millimeters until the weight settled perfectly into my stance.

My finger tightened around the trigger.

Mara looked up then—as if sensing eyes upon her—and our gazes locked across the distance between us. Her brown irises were wide with confusion, pain, maybe recognition of me standing three stories above her holding a gun aimed directly at her face.

She had every reason to believe I was about to execute her.

Every reason except the one that mattered: I wasn't aiming at her at all.

The Syndicate elf-sniper's finger touched down on his trigger guard. The movement was subtle—a microsecond shift—but I saw it reflected in the way light caught along his jawline for just an instant before he disappeared back into full camouflage mode.

Two seconds to decision. Maybe less.

Cole Reyes operates on The Threefold Cord: Penance, Revenge, and a Sliver of Justice. Crucial Canon Rule: Cole explicitly admits that the 'sliver of justice' is NEVER enough—it does not scrape the black iron out of Danny's alveoli or bring back the dead—but it will do for the moment. That exact truth is what motivates him and drives him to continue with the abyssal acts he commits: because a sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone.

Penance first: My little brother Danny died screaming in a hospital bed after inhaling Experimental Sludge fumes during the 2000 trials. His lungs collapsed like wet paper bags, drowning him in fluids while doctors watched helplessly through Plexiglas walls because nobody could get close enough without their own organs liquefying from the radiation signature embedded deep in his alveolar tissue.

Revenge second: I've spent seven years since then doing things that would make Satan himself think twice about hiring me as contract labor. Things that would strip away whatever humanity might have been salvageable if I'd just let go instead of tightening my grip around every night's descent into whatever comes after conscience dies completely under weight repeated trauma.

Justice third—or rather, that sliver thereof—which Mara Vance represents even though she doesn't know it yet beyond some gut-level instinct that keeps her from trusting anyone completely anymore either except maybe Grimjaw when he shows up with union coffee and thermite charges disguised inside hollowed-out donuts (a trick those South Side sandhogs perfected during tunnel operations).

But here's what people miss about The Threefold Cord: It doesn't rank-order anything neatly into priorities or moral hierarchies or any other tidy framework you can use to justify why sometimes you have to be monster-to-others so long as your intentions remain pure underneath all that bloodstain accumulation.

Sometimes all three strands bind together simultaneously and there's no separating which thread drives each action individually—only knowing that cutting one means unraveling everything else too including yourself which isn't acceptable because someone has to stand between monsters and victims even if standing means becoming something worse than both occasionally along way forward through darkness only broken occasionally by moments like white lilac scent hanging around paramedic who burned 314 people alive saving thirty-eight kids different calculation entirely whether numbers balance morally but they're all that matters practically speaking when choosing who lives versus who becomes ash gray static bleeding 4th Law wounds across chest cavities larger than should fit inside ribcages anatomically speaking clinically triaged by woman haunted equally blessed cursed depending perspective taken towards outcomes achieved versus costs paid achieving them...

My finger tightened fully on the trigger.

* * *

I never bothered asking Grimjaw if he knew Kaelen Glass-Eye by name or reputation. Didn't need to. When that elf squeezed his trigger finger behind Mara's head—a three-inch spread shot designed for maximum organ damage at that range—I'd already calculated the thermal bloom off his rifle scope, traced the microsecond heat signature through my hearth-coalsight.

The magnum was up before consciousness caught up with muscle memory. Weight forward, sight picture acquired, breath held. My left hand pressed flat against Mara's sternum—not pushing, just there, a point of contact in the darkness where the South Side tunnels ran black as a closed coffin and smelled like rust and wet stone.

Boom.

The sound hit harder than the recoil. That magnum roared like a diesel engine firing on all cylinders inside an echo chamber, the muzzle blast painting our side of the catwalk orange-white-blue and back again while my ears rang so hard I could feel it in my teeth. But I saw what mattered:

That cobalt slug sang through the air exactly two inches past Mara's right ear.

Close enough to part her hair. Close enough that when she finally processes this moment—probably won't be tonight; trauma does funny things to temporal perception—that strand will still be hanging loose along her jawline tomorrow morning. A ghost-thread reminder that someone wanted her dead.

The slug didn't slow down after bisecting empty space where Mara's skull had been one-tenth-of-a-second prior. It kept flying, supersonic and hungry, straight into the active optical camouflage field that made Kaelen "Glass-Eye" invisible to everything except the electromagnetic spectrum heat signatures visible to me through my coal-burning eyes.

Impact. Detonation.

Depleted-uranium bismuth hex-round hitting depleted-bismuth hex-rifle scope at 180 degrees angle produces results you can't unsee even if you tried. The elf's head simply exploded—instantaneous overpressure rupture. Brain matter painted the concrete wall behind him in gray-red-black paste. Bone fragments scattered across twenty feet of gantry floor like thrown dice showing snake-eyes death itself. His body dropped before his rifle did, both items making almost simultaneous impacts that echoed off wet stone.

"Contact!" Grimjaw's voice cut through smoke and ringing ears, though he was already moving—seven-foot-two frame hauling ass toward our six o'clock position because he'd spotted the thermal bloom too. Maybe not as fast as me with coal-sight, but close enough on a good day.

Mara went down hard—a knee-first drop I felt more than saw since I couldn't look away from where Glass-Eye had been standing until three seconds ago. Her left hand came up instinctively covering where she probably thought blood should be dripping from a hole that wasn't there.

Smart girl. Trauma-trained reflexes kicking in before conscious thought could short-circuit them out.

I didn't watch her process it. Didn't need to. Already reloading—the magnum clicked home fresh rounds while my other hand kept steady pressure against Mara's sternum because some part of me needed to know she stayed solid and real and breathing despite all evidence suggesting otherwise about tonight.

"The fuck," Grimjaw muttered low beside me now, staring at what remained of Kaelen "Glass-Eye"—which is to say nothing recognizable except torso and legs connected by spine column ending in separated cranial base still attached to severed cervical vertebrae spilling yellow-white cerebrospinal fluid onto concrete like broken eggs leaking down drains created by bone fragments digging divots into surface material upon impact release velocity calculations that made you glad you weren't standing anywhere near--

"Razor-Wire Syndicate work," I said flatly even though we both knew this already without needing words for confirmation between us after eight years running Local 405 together through every shitstorm North Jersey had thrown at South Side union workers since Y2K tore open whatever goddamn seam reality used when someone forgot to back-up their source code correctly during millennial rollover protocols designed by lawyers who thought 'glitch' meant something cute instead of catastrophic failure mode cascading across dimensional membranes separating possible worlds from actual ones where people tried living paycheck-to-paycheck while corporate magic-users played their hex-games with worker lives as acceptable losses written off quarterly earnings reports submitted to shareholders too rich to give half-a-fuck about anyone below executive suite level compensation packages including stock options vesting schedules calculated precisely enough so nobody important ever felt responsible when things went sideways bad wrong terrible horrible fucked beyond repair damnation eternal level bad which basically described most days working underground maintenance codes inspecting structural integrity load-bearing rebar tension stresses—

I stopped counting syllables somewhere around 'stock options'.

Point being: We knew exactly whose playbook this came out of. Razor-Wire operated with precision that bordered clinical—every shot counted, every casualty justified by cold actuarial tables measuring expected outcomes against projected benefits margins calculating risk versus reward ratios optimized toward maximum profit extraction minimum liability exposure scenarios where human beings got reduced down into variables labeled 'acceptable attrition percentages' in spreadsheets maintained by accountants who'd never actually seen what happens when depleted-uranium bismuth hex-rounds hit bone density concentrations exceeding safety threshold limits established by Occupational Safety Health Administration regulations governing workplace environmental hazard exposures under normal operating conditions which these definitely weren't--

"Cole." Grimjaw's hand clamped down heavy on my shoulder—not rough but firm enough pulling me back from wherever my thoughts had wandered toward mathematical calculations concerning optimal trajectory vectors for projectile munitions fired at high velocity through dense medium atmospheric pressures measured in PSI units standardizing measurements—

Right.

Focus.

Mara was still kneeling three feet away, one knee pressed into concrete wet-sticky from brain matter splatter radius extending outward from where Glass-Eye used to be whole-enough-for-medical-examiner-certification alive enough breathing independently without mechanical assistance devices sustaining cardiovascular function across time gradients measured continuous seconds minutes hours years decades centuries millennia epochs eras periods ages eons—

She looked up at me.

Not scared yet—still processing whether she should be or not depending entirely upon how her trauma-triage training interfaced with whatever religious/spiritual framework governed her personal cosmology regarding divine providence intervention miracles coincidence probability distributions calculated against baseline expectations derived from empirical observation accumulated across lifetime experience sampling population subsets stratified demographic categories sorted hierarchical taxonomies classifying entities according to shared characteristics traits attributes properties features qualities aspects dimensions parameters variables constants coefficients factors terms expressions formulas equations theorems axioms postulates principles laws rules doctrines dogmas creeds tenets beliefs convictions certainties uncertainties doubts questions queries inquiries investigations examinations analyses studies researches explorations discoveries findings revelations enlightenments awakenings satori kensho nirvana samadhi ecstasy rapture bliss joy peace harmony balance equilibrium stability steadiness consistency reliability dependability trustworthiness credibility veracity authenticity genuineness sincerity honesty integrity honor dignity nobility virtue righteousness justice fairness equity impartiality objectivity neutrality detachment transcendence liberation freedom autonomy independence self-determination agency volition choice decision making authority power control mastery command domination subjugation enslavement bondage captivity imprisonment incarceration detention custody restraint confinement limitation restriction constraint inhibition obstruction hindrance impedance resistance opposition counteraction adversarial confrontation antagonism hostility aggression violence brutality cruelty mercil

* * *

I don't hear the shot.

Not really. There's this strange moment where my world narrows down to the front sight of the Custom '87 and the elf sniper's head. Time does that thing it does when adrenaline hits your nervous system like a freight train—the whole universe compresses around two points: the bead and the target.

The hammer falls.

I feel the kick through my palm, up through my forearm, into my shoulder. The slide cycles smooth as glass. Brass tumbles end-over-end through the smoky air, glinting copper in the sodium lights.

But the sound comes *after*. A thunderclap that rolls through the metal catwalks and echoes back at me from a dozen different angles. For one microsecond before that, there was only silence. Perfect, crystalline silence while physics did its work.

The elf twitcher jerks backward like she's been yanked by an invisible wire. Her body goes rigid, arms splayed wide against the pylon's support struts. Then gravity remembers her and she crumples sideways off the maintenance platform.

She doesn't make a sound. Not even a gasp. Just... stops being a living thing and becomes a falling weight.

Grimjaw curses low in his throat. "Fuck—you missed?"

I'm already moving toward the edge of our position, keeping low behind the ventilation ducts. "Check the scope."

He fumbles with the Mark One Mod Zero thermal spotter we liberated from Pylon #3. His big fingers work surprisingly delicate on the focus ring. "Uh... no shit. She's down. Hard." He looks up at me, his yellow eyes catching the light weird. "Christ, Cole. Where'd you learn to shoot like that? That was two hundred yards in this shit wind."

I don't answer. I'm watching where she fell. There's a darker shadow now on the concrete below—a spreading stain that wasn't there before. The blood runs black in the shadows.

"You see that?" Grimjaw asks quietly. "Shit. That's gonna draw attention."

"We're already drawing attention," I mutter back. I flip open my Razr—the screen lights up green and shows me Danny's vitals still ticking along stable inside his iron-lung. Good. Very good. But we can't stay here. This section is going hot any second now.

Through the smoke drifting across our firing line, I catch one last glimpse of Mara Vance. She's running now, really *running* toward the emergency ladder. Her white paramedic coat flares out behind her like wings. Behind her, the hostages are being shuffled by Syndicate goons toward the secondary containment zone.

She made it. She actually made it out.

I feel something loosen in my chest. Not relief exactly. More like... tension finding a different configuration. The kind of tension you get when you've been holding your breath underwater too long and finally surface.

"Move," I say to Grimjaw. "Eastern maintenance tunnel. We need to be gone before BATC security sweeps this sector."

He doesn't argue. Just turns and heads into the darkness ahead of me, his massive frame somehow managing to move quiet as a ghost despite his size. Years of sandhog work doing deep tunnel excavation—learning how to walk without making noise so you don't disturb the structure. It comes in handy more often than you'd think.

As we move through the catwalks, I'm already cycling problems in my head:

One: Voss lost an elite sniper tonight. He's not going to let that slide.
Two: We just breached Pylon #2. That means three left standing between us and closing the Breach for good.
Three: Mara Vance is carrying a Lead-Bismuth Geas under her sternum—the weight of 314 dead commuters from Sub-Station Seven. She thinks she failed them all. Tonight proved otherwise, but will she believe it?

"Voss is gonna find out you flatlined his shooter, Cole," Grimjaw says quietly as we descend a service ladder into the deeper tunnels. His voice echoes strangely off the corrugated metal. "We just put targets on our own backs."

I step down onto solid concrete, landing soft. My boots barely make a sound. "Let them come."

The words taste like copper and old blood in my mouth. But they're true enough.

I touch the motorola again. Check Danny's iron-lung telemetry. Still stable. Check Mara's transponder—the little green dot is climbing steadily toward the surface, away from the Pylons, back into the world above where sunlight still exists and people live normal lives untouched by the Breach.

"We have three more Pylons to breach," I say, pocketing the phone. The concrete under my feet smells like industrial solvent and years-old oil. Familiar. "And now we know exactly who we're hunting."

That's the thing about revenge. It's never satisfying when you achieve it. There's no warm glow of justice, no moment where everything suddenly makes sense. You just feel... hollow. Like you carved something important out of yourself and realized too late that it was something you actually needed.

But a sliver of justice is better than none at all.

I snap the flip-phone shut with my thumb. The click sounds loud in the darkness around us. Final. Done.

Above, through the grating, rain starts to leak through—Neon Hollow rain that smells like exhaust fumes and ozone. It patters against the metal, steady and cold.

Book 2 ends here.

**End Chapter 15**

***
`[SIGNAL ENDING: M-B1 CH15 Scene 3 - Fade to Neon Hollow]`

# BOOK #03: THE GLASS REGISTRY
### Prequel Duology Part 1 (MA-2)

---

## CHAPTER 1: THE DEAD ELVEN SNIPER

The crack was deafening—a thunderclap that ripped through my ribcage and left my ears screaming with white noise.

I flinched hard, my Aegis shields snapping up in a burst of white-lilac light, bracing for the impact, for the hot lead to tear through flesh and bone. My heart hammered against my sternum. One second. Two seconds. Nothing.

The silence that followed was worse than the gunshot.

My breath fogged in the freezing air as I turned slowly, the Motorola Razr clutched tight in my palm. Its flashlight beam swept across rust-streaked concrete, over tangled conduit cables dripping with condensation, up toward the gantry thirty feet behind me where Kaelen "Glass-Eye" had been perched like some Gothic gargoyle, his rifle trained on my spine.

He wasn't there anymore.

What remained slumped against the metal railing was something else entirely—the shell of what had been an Elven sniper. Half his skull was gone, collapsed inward into a crater of pulped tissue and bone fragments. The exit wound was massive, fist-sized, the edges cauterized black around a dark crater. Behind him, the concrete wall wept gray dust from where the round had punched straight through reinforced barrier.

My stomach lurched.

Not from the gore—though God knows there was enough to make even seasoned Aegis grimace—but from the implications tearing through my mind like shrapnel. That shot hadn't come from Kaelen's position. It had come from somewhere *behind* that concrete pillar. From where the Butcher of Sterling Manor was supposed to be hiding in the shadows, watching, waiting.

Cole Reyes just saved my life.

I moved closer, boots crunching on shattered glass and grit. The stench hit me next—wet charred wool mixed with iron-gall residue sizzling from the Elf's optical-camo suit, leaking blue-black fluid onto the floor below. My white-lilac ward flickered, fighting against an ash-gray static that made my teeth ache.

The dead Elf's modifications were all wrong for High-Spire work. Sub-dermal wire-jacks at his temples, cheap optical camo stitched into what looked like a 2004 North Face jacket, probably stolen from some dead backpacker up in the Passaic River woods. No elegance. No refinement. Just desperate Razor-Wire street-magic cobled together by someone who'd never seen real Aegis work.

He'd been cold-blooded about it too—no hesitation when he drew down on me. The kind of merc who'd put two rounds in your head without a second thought.

And Cole had stopped him anyway.

I crouched beside the corpse, ignoring how the temperature kept dropping around me—that telltale frost-cobalt signature Cole left behind when he worked up close. My fingers found something embedded in the steel grating near the wall: a slug, still humming with residual energy. I pried it loose carefully, holding it up to the sodium-vapor glare.

It was huge—not standard BATC issue. Some kind of hand-loaded round, the metal frosted white with that same unnatural cold radiating off it. Depleted bismuth maybe, or something worse. Something that could punch through concrete and bone alike without slowing down.

In the distance, sirens began wailing.

BATC response teams, finally getting their shit together enough to follow my trail into the sub-basements. They'd find this mess soon enough—the dead sniper, the exit wound through solid concrete, the slug that shouldn't exist according to any ordnance database.

They'd ask questions I couldn't answer.

I pocketed the round anyway, standing slowly as my joints protested the cold seeping into my bones. The tinnitus in my ears was fading, replaced by the rhythmic thump-thump of blood rushing back to my head. Alive. Somehow still alive.

Cole Reyes saved you.

The thought sat bitter on my tongue as I moved toward the far end of the corridor, leaving Glass-Eye's body slumping against his gantry like discarded meat. Behind me, the sirens grew louder, echoing through the transit tunnels like hunting dogs closing in for the kill.

I needed to move faster.

Needed to figure out what the hell had just happened before someone decided I was worth more dead than alive—which, given my current track record, wouldn't take long at all.

* * *

The ash-gray static recedes like fog burned away by noon sun, though it leaves its signature—a bitter taste of copper behind my teeth, the phantom stench of wet charred wool clinging to the back of my throat from November 2005. I force my breath to slow. Four counts in. Hold. Four counts out. The tactical training kicks in before the trauma can fully manifest.

My hands stop shaking.

I crouch beside what remains of Kaelen—or whoever he was pretending to be. The corpse slumps against the reinforced concrete pillar, dark ichor pooling beneath his skull where Cole Reyes' slug punched through three feet of engineered stone and bone alike. The entry wound is small, nearly surgical despite the violence of impact. Exit wound... well, there isn't one. Not anymore. What came out the other side vaporized into copper-tinged mist that still hangs in the air like morning fog over the Passaic River.

The Panasonic Toughbook boots up in my lap, its heavy plastic casing familiar, grounding. My laser-mapping peripheral deploys automatically—green geometric patterns sweep across the corridor, mapping trajectories, measuring angles, calculating physics that should be impossible. The math scrolls across my vision:

*   Distance: 87 meters
*   Obstruction: 3'4" reinforced concrete (Class 6)
*   Target velocity: Stationary
*   Projectile mass: 19.45 grains depleted-uranium slug
*   Probability of penetration: 0.0003%
*   Probability of lethality given penetration: 89%

I watch it again. And again. The numbers don't change just because they're wrong.

"Commander Vance, we got a breach-alert on Pylon Two. You still breathing down there?"

Lieutenant Thorne's voice crackles through the Nextel clipped to my tactical vest. Dwarven. Efficient. Probably already has the meat-wagon dispatched before I can confirm the casualty.

"I'm breathing, Lieutenant." My voice sounds steady even as my fingers trace the frost-cobalt residue on the concrete pillar. "Call the meat-wagon. We've got a dead wire-runner on the gantry."

"And the threat? Reyes?"

"He's gone." I swallow the bitter taste. "But he didn't kill me."

There's a pause. Then: "Copy that, Commander. Team's en route to your position. Estimated three minutes."

I end the transmission and return my attention to Kaelen. Or his body, anyway. The corpse wears military-grade optical camouflage—expensive tech, the kind that runs off portable battery packs and leaves distinctive thermal signatures when it fails. This one is failing. Crackling static distorts the edges where the cloaking field meets reality, like heat shimmer over summer asphalt.

The rifle beside him tells its own story. MP5SD submachine gun, but someone's customized it with rune-etched modifications. Illegal modifications. The suppressor isn't standard-issue polymer; it's machined from depleted-uranium alloy, which explains the vaporized exit wound. Explains why the slug burned cold instead of hot when Cole's shot punched through.

I photograph everything with the Toughbook's integrated camera. Click. Flash. Click. Flash. Document the scene while my pulse hammers in my ears.

Why did you spare me, Cole?

My gloved hand reaches out, touches the frost-coating on Kaelen's weapon. The metal burns ice-cold despite the ambient temperature of the sub-basement corridor. Hex-work metallurgy—someone paid serious credits for this setup. The kind of money that doesn't come from standard Syndicate operations.

I trace the rune workings etched into the suppressor housing. Standard activation glyphs, but there's something else underneath. A serial number, partially obscured by scoring from repeated firing cycles. I lean closer, squinting against the Toughbook's backlight as I enhance the image.

The serial resolves:

*   BATC-IA-7349

Internal Affairs.

My stomach drops into my boots.

"Fuck."

The word escapes before I can stop it, echoing off concrete and rebar. Internal Affairs. Which means either Kaelen was one of ours—corrupted, working both sides—or someone wanted us to think he was, creating a trail designed to burn the Bureau from the inside out.

Or maybe both.

The optical camouflage battery pack sparks once, twice, then dies completely. Reality snaps back like a rubber band released. Kaelen's corpse sits fully visible now, no longer obscured by military-grade stealth tech. He wears dark tactical gear over what looks like civilian clothes underneath—jeans, leather jacket, nothing that identifies him beyond the BATC-issued radio clipping to his collar.

I pull up the Bureau database on my Toughbook. Cross-reference the serial number with active personnel files. The search engine whirs.

No results found matching query: BATC-IA-7349

Which means either it's a fake—elaborately constructed to look legitimate—or someone has scrubbed the records already. Cover-up in progress.

I photograph the serial anyway. Evidence is evidence, even if it leads nowhere obvious.

Movement catches my peripheral vision. There—partially concealed behind an exposed water pipe near the gantry access ladder. A secondary modification on Kaelen's rifle. Some kind of transmitter unit, still blinking its status light red.

Active transmission.

My heart rate spikes as I lean closer, careful not to disturb the body. The device is embedded in the weapon's stock, custom-fitted. Professional work. Not something you slap together in a garage between shifts at the McCarter Highway dockyards.

I snap another photo. Then another. Multiple angles because this—this is important somehow. I can feel it in my bones.

The Panasonic Toughbook saves each image automatically, timestamped and geo-tagged to Pylon Two sub-basement coordinates. Chain-of-custody protocols engage. Digital signatures lock into place.

"Commander Vance, team is approaching your position. ETA thirty seconds."

Thorne again. Closer now. They're taking the stairs instead of waiting for the transit car.

"Copy." I stand slowly, knees protesting from crouching beside a corpse that shouldn't exist. From surviving what should have been fatal.

Kaelen's eyes are open. Still open. Staring at nothing. Waiting for answers that won't come from a dead man.

Why did Cole spare me?

The question gnaws at me like rats in the walls of some abandoned warehouse along the Newark Bay shoreline. He had the shot. Had already killed once tonight—the sniper who'd been targeting me through the reinforced concrete pillar. Could have added me to his scorecard without breaking stride.

But he didn't.

Which means either: one, he needs me alive for something; two, there's a line even someone like him won't cross; or three, I'm useful to him in ways I haven't figured out yet.

Or maybe all three.

The footsteps grow louder. My Dwarven lieutenant will arrive any second with her

* * *

The flashing red-and-blue lights paint everything in strobing crimson and ice-white. I can hear them now—the distant squeal of tires on wet asphalt above ground, the rhythmic thump-thump-thump of helicopter rotors cutting through the November rain. They're closing in.

Sixty seconds. Maybe less.

My white-lilac ward flares weakly around my fingertips, casting sickly purple shadows across the concrete. It tastes like copper pennies and fresh-cut cedar, but underneath—that phantom stench rises again. Wet charred wool. 2005. The Pylon incident that shouldn't still haunt me but does, always when I'm about to do something stupid.

Like this.

The slug sits in my palm, frost-cobalt gleaming even under the emergency lighting. Depleted-bismuth core, IA-linked scope mounting, military-grade kinetic dampeners worn smooth from use. This isn't just ammunition. This is Cole Reyes's signature, his ghost-mark burned into every molecule. If BATC finds it here, if they run the trace...

He'll never make it to Pylon #3.

I don't know why I care. The Butcher killed seventeen agents last month—including Orcish heavies twice my size who actually knew what they were doing. He's responsible for three breaches in as many weeks. By protocol, by duty, by the oath I took when they pinned these bars on my collar, I should be bagging this evidence right now, calling it in.

But I'm standing here instead, staring at my reflection in the polished metal.

My nose starts bleeding first. The white-lilac weave protests violently as I force it open wider than recommended, pushing bio-light through my circulatory system until my veins glow faintly beneath my skin. The feedback hits like an ice-pick behind my eyes. My knees want to buckle, but I lock them straight.

*Just scrub. Just clean. Just erase.*

The light pours into the slug, and I feel Cole's signature fighting back—frost-cobalt resistance burning against my palms. There's intention in this ammunition. Purpose. Someone loaded this round expecting to kill someone important, and they didn't give a shit about leaving tracks.

I push harder.

Blood drips onto the concrete. My vision tunnels, the strobing lights becoming a single nauseating pulse of red-white-red-white. The metallic taste floods my mouth—copper and something worse, like licking an old battery. My fingers cramp around the slug.

And then it gives.

The frost-cobalt goes sterile. Ash-gray. Unlinked. Untraceable. Just another piece of metal that happened to be lying around Pylon #2 sub-basement where someone fired it through a concrete pillar during a breach situation which is frankly not even that unusual given current conditions and—

I stuff it in my pocket.

The rifle scope comes off next, IA-chip still embedded in the mount. I can feel its ghost-marks too—the way Cole looked through it, the targets he acquired, the breath he held before squeezing down on the trigger. All of it washing over me in waves that make my stomach turn.

But I take it anyway.

My white-lilac ward flares once, brilliant and desperate, as I wrap the scope in bio-light and tuck it against the small of my back. It burns cold against my spine, and I know I should feel guilty but mostly I just feel tired.

The doors explode inward.

"BATC! Clear! Weapons down!" The Orcish heavy doesn't wait for compliance—his flashlight beam sweeps across my face, blinding me momentarily, and I hear the rack-chamber of three shotguns at least. Human tacticals behind him, younger agents with wide eyes and tight lips who've probably never seen an actual combat scene up close.

I raise my hands slowly, blood dripping from my nose onto my uniform.

"Stand down, breach-team," I say, keeping my voice level even as my knees threaten to give out. "Threat is neutralized."

"Commander Vance?" The lead tactical steps forward, his Maglite still trained on my face like I'm the enemy here. Which, technically, I guess I am now.

"Confirmed dead," I tell them, gesturing toward the body without looking at it again. Can't afford the hesitation, not when they're watching me this closely. "Single sniper, frost-cobalt ammunition. Caught a round through the throat. He's been neutralized."

"Where's your backup?"

"En route." Not strictly true, but they won't question it. I'm Aegis Commander. My word carries weight even when it's technically a lie.

They're going to search anyway. They always do. Protocol demands it. But they'll find nothing—just concrete dust and blood spatter and the faint smell of burnt cedar that means someone used heavy weave here and didn't bother cleaning up after themselves which frankly is sloppy workmanship but whatever.

My hand brushes against something hard and metallic sliding down the inside of my tactical belt.

I don't react. Don't flinch. Just keep my hands raised as the tacticals spread out, their boots crunching over broken glass, weapons sweeping across corners and shadows and every goddamn hiding spot in this sub-basement corridor.

Someone just planted evidence on me.

And I have absolutely no idea if it's Cole trying to frame me or BATC already knowing what I did or something worse entirely.

The Orcish heavy approaches, sniffing the air with his nostrils flared. They can smell weave-use better than humans. He'll know I just scrubbed something. He has to know.

But he just grunts and waves his team forward.

"Clear!"

"All clear!"

"Moving to perimeter sweep!"

As they turn away, still searching, I feel the weight at my spine. The scope. The evidence. The proof that I chose to protect the Butcher over protocol, duty, everything I swore to uphold.

And beneath all that, pressing cold against my lower back: whatever the hell just got dropped onto me while I wasn't looking.

I wipe the blood from my lip with the back of my hand and force myself to stand straighter.

"Secure the area," I say. "I'm calling this in."

My hand moves to my comm-piece, and I wonder if I should be scared right now.

Wonder when exactly I became someone who makes choices like this.

Wonder if there's any going back from here.

## CHAPTER 2: THE INQUISITOR & THE TRANSPONDER

The November rain tastes like rust and diesel fuel.

I'm sitting on the bumper of an ambulance, watching my breath fog into the freezing night air while some EMT checks my vitals with practiced indifference. Her name tag says RODRIGUEZ in block letters. She's human, which means she doesn't give a damn about the faint purple burn-scorch on my left forearm where the sniper's round clipped me.

Pylon #2 is still smoking three hundred yards behind us, a skeletal tombstone for two dead men and whatever secrets they were carrying.

"Blood pressure's elevated," Rodriguez mutters, wrapping the cuff around my bicep. "You want to talk about it?"

What I want to do is scream that something is wrong—that I can feel it crawling up my spine like ice and static—but instead I watch the sodium-vapor lights flicker across the Passaic River. Somewhere past those chemical-plant smokestacks, Newark Bay churns black against the horizon.

A set of headlights cuts through the curtain of rain.

Black. Pristine. A Lincoln Town Car that costs more than Rodriguez makes in three years.

The car stops. The door opens.

Vane Thorne steps out wearing a charcoal suit that somehow looks pressed despite the weather, despite the hour, despite the fact that we're standing in a crime zone that smells like charred electronics and gunpowder. He closes the door with a soft *thunk* and stands there for a moment, letting the rain decide whether it wants to touch him or not.

It doesn't.

"Rodriguez." His voice has that smooth quality that comes from expensive vocal coaching—no regional accent, no emotional inflection, just pure corporate precision. "Step away from Commander Vance."

She looks at me. I give her a slight shake of my head. She knows what Thorne is: BATC Internal Affairs. High-Spire. Elf. The kind of metahuman who eats field commanders for breakfast and uses their bones as dental floss.

Rodriguez unbuckles the blood pressure cuff wordlessly and retreats into the ambulance, pulling the doors shut behind her with a sound like finality.

Thorne approaches slowly, his feline tapetum lucidum eyes catching the yellow streetlight in a way that makes them glow faintly, hypnotically. It's a predator's adaptation—the kind of genetic tweak that screams *I see better than you in the dark*.

"I have questions about the sniper," he says when he's close enough that I can smell his cologne cutting through the industrial smog. Something expensive. Italian. Masculine without trying too hard.

"A lot of dead people tonight." I slide off the bumper, feeling the cold seep through my tactical boots. "What's your angle?"

His smile doesn't reach those glowing eyes. "The angle is logistics, Commander. Specifically: how a Razor-Wire junkie manages to drop dead from a trajectory my forensic-mages can't even triangulate."

My hand moves automatically toward where my sidearm should be before I remember—it's in evidence. All our weapons are. Standard protocol after an officer-involved shooting.

"Sloppy work," Thorne continues, circling me like a shark testing water. "*Thwack-thwack* goes the windshield wipers. *Bang* goes the sniper. But here's what bothers me: no weave-signature on the fatal slug. None. That takes Aegis-level bio-wards. That takes resources. That takes intent."

I meet his gaze levelly, fighting the urge to touch my chest where Cole slipped that transponder during the chaos. The device feels like a living thing against my ribcage—a promise and a threat rolled into one.

"Maybe the junkie bought a defective hex-round on the South Side," I say evenly. "I don't micromanage Syndicate suicide runs."

"And maybe," Thorne counters smoothly, producing a silver warrant-stylus from his inner jacket pocket, "you're lying to a BATC Inquisitor. Level-3 IA Audit, Commander Vance. Effective immediately. Your unit's armories are restricted pending review."

He holds up the stylus. It glows faintly with corporate magic—legal paperwork woven into reality itself.

"The warrant's already filed," he adds conversationally. "Your access codes will deactivate at 0400 hours. You have approximately fifty-five minutes to brief your replacement."

Behind him, Pylon #2 groans as emergency crews begin their work, the sound echoing across the Kearny Marshes like something dying.

I want to reach for my sidearm. I want to tell him about the runner in the warehouse, about Cole, about the things I'm starting to remember that I shouldn't be able to remember because they haven't happened yet—but all I can do is stand there in the rain while Internal Affairs dismantles my command structure piece by piece.

"Anything else?" My voice comes out harder than intended.

Thorne's smile widens fractionally. "No, Commander. That covers it." He pockets the warrant-stylus with a gesture that looks almost casual but isn't. "Oh—and Vance?"

"Yes?"

His eyes catch the light again, that feline glow intensifying just slightly. "You smell like charred wool. Interesting choice for cover scent on a night like this."

Then he turns and walks back to his Town Car without waiting for an answer, sliding into the passenger seat with fluid grace while some driver I never even noticed pulls away into the darkness toward McCarter Highway.

I watch the taillights disappear around a bend in the road before allowing myself to breathe properly again.

My chest feels tight where the transponder pulses against bone.

Fifty-five minutes until my armories lock down. Fifty-five minutes until Thorne starts digging through every log file, every expenditure report, every goddamn coffee cup left on my desk.

And somewhere in this nightmare, Cole is still out there with whatever the hell he stole from Pylon #2 while I was bleeding on concrete and Vane Thorne was writing my termination papers in corporate heaven.

The EMT—Rodriguez—cracks open her door again. "You need transport?"

"Not yet," I say quietly, pulling out my burner phone from my tactical vest. The screen lights up: 0317 AM. Forty-three minutes now.

Someone needs to warn the others. Someone needs to figure out what Cole actually took and whether it's worth dying for.

But first, I pull up my contacts list and scroll past names that mean nothing anymore.

Forty-three minutes until IA locks everything down.

Forty-three minutes to save what remains of Aegis Command.

I press dial on the only number that matters right now—the one that leads deeper into whatever conspiracy just tried to kill me twice in one night—and listen to the phone ring once, twice, three times while rain runs cold down my collar and the ghost of Thorne's yellow eyes watches me from everywhere and nowhere at once.

The line clicks open.

"Vance." I keep my voice low. Urgent. "Cole made contact. We have problems."

A pause on the other end long enough for doubt to creep

* * *

The rain hammers down harder now, each drop striking my tactical vest like tiny needles. I can feel the weight of the transponder against my ribs where it nestles in the hollow beneath my sternum—a foreign object embedded in flesh, a ghost Cole left behind without me ever feeling its insertion.

Thorne stands between me and the Crown Vic, water streaming off his black Inquisitor's coat. He holds out one gloved hand, palm up. "Your laptop, Commander."

I don't move immediately. The Panasonic Toughbook sits in the passenger seat, its screen dark, its hard drive holding secrets that would burn Cole and the entire rogue operation to ash if discovered. My fingerprints are on every key. My suit's telemetry logs everything—biometrics, tactical positioning, weapon discharge patterns. And buried in there, compressed and hidden in what should be innocuous maintenance files, is the laser-mapping reconstruction of that impossible shot from Pylon #2.

"Commander." Thorne's voice cuts through the rain's percussion. His silver stylus taps against his other palm, waiting.

My weave tastes of charred wool as I reach into the car. The suppression is working—barely. My corrupted bio-ward spirals around my neural pathways like smoke seeking ventilation, but it's enough. Enough to keep my heart rate steady, my microexpressions locked down tight.

I lift the Toughbook carefully, hands visible, no sudden movements. As I pass it over, our fingers don't touch. His eyes never leave mine.

The moment the laptop leaves my possession, I channel the pulse.

It's subtle—I've practiced this exact maneuver in the simulations after 2005. A concentrated burst of ash-gray static, localized, precise. My corrupted weave makes the signature untraceable; even I'm not entirely sure how I'm doing it anymore, just that I can. The pulse lances through the motherboard's sensitive components.

Thorne's expression flickers—just for a fraction of a second—when he tries to connect his stylus to the USB port. There's a sharp crackle of electricity, a blue spark jumping between metal and plastic. The Toughbook's power indicator blinks once, then dies completely.

"Damn." He turns the dead machine over in his hands, examining it with narrowed eyes. "What did you do?"

"Nothing," I say flatly. "Equipment failure. You see what happens out here—the moisture, the proximity to the Pylon collapse. Electrical interference." The lie rolls off my tongue, smooth and cold. My weave burns with the effort of maintaining it, but I don't break eye contact.

He sets the Toughbook on the hood of his own vehicle—a black Crown Vic identical to mine—and taps it with one finger. "Convenient hardware failure, Vance."

"File a requisition form for a new one." I turn toward my mobile command post. "I'm going back to my vehicle. I have orphans to check on."

His hand shoots out, grabbing my arm above the elbow. Not hard enough to hurt, but firm enough to stop me. "You're not done talking yet."

I look down at where he touches me, then slowly raise my eyes to meet his gaze. When I speak, there's no inflection, no emotion—just dead air. "Remove your hand."

For a moment, tension crackles between us sharper than any static discharge. His jaw works. Then he lets go.

"I'll be monitoring your movements closely, Commander." He pulls out a Nextel, thumbnails already flying across its screen. "Thorne here. Put a tail on Vance. She's hiding something from the Pylon."

I don't wait to hear more. The rain soaks through my vest as I walk to my Crown Vic, each step deliberate, controlled. Behind me, I can feel Thorne's eyes boring into my back like drill bits seeking purchase in bone.

Inside the vehicle, I slam the door hard enough to rattle the frame. My hands are shaking—not from fear, but from the adrenaline dump of holding that lie together while my corrupted weave screamed warnings at every level of my nervous system.

The transponder pulses once against my ribs.

*He knows something is wrong,* I think, gripping the steering wheel. *He just doesn't know what.*

And if Cole's still alive somewhere in this soaked, corrupt landscape, Thorne hunting for evidence means we're running out of time to bury whatever secrets that damaged Pylon was meant to protect.

* * *

I lock the Crown Victoria's doors behind me, watching through the side mirror as IA Inquisitor Chen's black Suburban pulls away, its taillights bleeding crimson across the wet asphalt of the McCarter Highway service road. The interior of my mobile command post smells like stale coffee and damp upholstery—a familiar scent that should be comforting but only makes my stomach turn harder.

Three hours. That's how long I sat in that interrogation room while Chen picked through my report with surgical precision, his questions cutting deeper than any blade. Where were you when Pylon Two went down? Can anyone verify your position? Why did your tactical weave spike so aggressively at 0247 hours?

I'd lied through my teeth, each word tasting like ash. Said I was coordinating evacuations. Managing containment protocols. Never mentioned Cole Blackwood. Never breathed a word about the shadow-man who'd appeared out of nowhere to drag me from certain death.

My hand trembles as I reach into my tactical belt, fingers closing around something solid and heavy that definitely wasn't there before. The object is warm against my palm, wrapped in layers of electrical tape that feel oddly deliberate—protective even. Carefully, I pull it free into the dim glow of the dashboard lights.

A transponder. No—not just any transponder. This is Gnome-forged, unmistakably Undercity tech. The soldering work is crude but brilliant, wires wound around a 2005 watch battery in a pattern that would make standard BATC engineers weep. Green insulation tape, copper wiring that catches the light like veins of gold. Someone assembled this by hand, probably in some sweatbox workshop beneath Newark's industrial sector.

*Cole.*

The realization hits me like a physical blow. He'd been there. At Pylon Two. In the chaos of the collapse, during those few seconds I thought I was dead—he must have slipped this onto me. A breadcrumb trail. An escape route.

I look down at the device, turning it over in my hands. There's no visible power indicator, but I can feel it—minute vibrations pulsing through the metal casing. Active signal.

My Sony MiniDisc player sits on the passenger seat where I left it, its green LCD screen glowing softly. I yank out the optical cable, my fingers working faster than my conscious thoughts. The port matches perfectly with the transponder's output jack. As soon as I plug them together, the player's display flashes: *SIGNAL DETECTED - ENCRYPTED FREQUENCY*.

Of course it's encrypted. Gnomes don't believe in making anything easy.

But I know their style. South Side frequency brokers use raw radio-telemetry to bypass BATC wards—they're too cheap for proper magical encryption, so they rely on complexity and obfuscation instead. It takes twelve minutes of manual key sequencing before the player cracks enough header information to spit out plaintext:

*PULSING SIGNAL: GPS COORDINATES [30.267N 97.743W] NEON HOLLOW SHIPYARDS PYLON THREE*

Pylon Three.

The words burn themselves into my retinas. That's not just any location—that's where this whole nightmare started. Where we first detected the breach in the Millennium Seal. Where Cole had been investigating before Pylon Two went dark.

I grab my Motorola Razr from the dashboard mount, thumb already moving across the keypad to check for active jammers. Clear. But that doesn't mean anything. Cole could be anywhere by now—or nowhere at all.

The Crown Vic's heater kicks on with a soft rumble, fogging the windows until the outside world dissolves into gray silence. Just me, this impossible device, and a set of coordinates pointing straight into the heart of what remains of our operation.

I think about Inquisitor Chen, about his questions, about how long before IA realizes I'm lying. How long before they notice inconsistencies in my report. The weave spike he'd mentioned—he knew something was wrong even if he couldn't prove it yet.

My tactical belt feels heavy around my waist. Standard gear: sidearm, spare magazines, flash-bang rounds, one canister each of iron dust and silver solution. Nothing special. Nothing that would explain why my weave is still reeking like charred wool despite two hours of meditation attempts.

*Because you're suppressing it,* whispers a voice in the back of my mind. *You've been suppressing it since you felt Cole touch your arm.*

I didn't want to believe it then. Don't want to believe it now. That kind of connection—it goes both ways. If Cole planted this transponder on me, if he's using Gnome tech to ping my position...

He knows exactly where I am too.

The MiniDisc player pulses another signal. Different frequency this time—not coordinates but text:

*MOVE NOW*

No explanation. No context. Just two words and an imperative that makes every instinct in my body scream *run*.

Through the fogged windshield, I can barely make out Pylon Two's location across Kearny Marshes—a dark silhouette against the pre-dawn sky where there used to be lights and life. Where forty-three agents lost their lives because we didn't know enough fast enough.

Pylon Three is waiting.

Cole is waiting.

And somewhere between here and there, answers—or death—are inevitable.

I start the Crown Victoria's engine.

---

## CHAPTER 3: THE VAULT & THE NOSEBLEED

The blast doors groan open like a throat clearing phlegm. I step into the belly of Sub-Station Seven and the air hits me first—a cocktail of industrial recirculation and something else, something my brain tries to process as "clean" but smells like wet charcoal soaked in ammonia. The fluorescent tubes overhead cast everything in that sickly green-yellow glow that makes everyone look dead already.

My white-lilac weave sputters the moment I cross the threshold.

I feel it in my teeth first—that metallic tang of static discharge as the bio-wards flicker, bleeding ash-gray through the purple-pink cascade. The Vault shouldn't be this hostile. Shouldn't be *reaching* at me like a dying thing with too many fingers. But then again, nothing about Sub-Station Seven has been normal since November 19th, 2005, when three hundred and fourteen commuters burned alive trying to escape the Passaic River breach.

I see their shadows on the walls even though they've been scrubbed clean seventeen times since then. Phantom scorch marks dancing along the reinforced concrete, shimmering at the edges of my peripheral vision before dissolving into nothing. The HVAC units hum their eternal monotone prayer to gods who stopped listening after the Millennium Breach split reality open like a ripe fruit.

"Commander."

Rix emerges from behind the nurse's station, her Goblin features twisted into an expression somewhere between exhaustion and resignation. Her splice-runners are supposed to make her faster, stronger, better at triage—but right now she just looks tired. We all look tired.

"They're restless tonight," she says, and there's something wrong in how she says it. Like she's reporting enemy movements instead of patient statuses. "The leylines are buzzing like a kicked hornet's nest."

I nod, feeling the truth of it in my bones. The whole grid is singing off-key tonight. What Cole's doing up there at the pylons—the secondary seal crack, the harmonic resonance test—it's rippling down through the infrastructure like shockwaves through water. These kids feel every vibration.

"The children?" I ask, because someone has to.

"They're sedated. Heavy cycle." Rix rubs her eyes with the back of her hand, leaving smudges on her gray skin. "We had two episodes of temporal displacement around 0300 hours. One of the girls woke up speaking fluent Yiddish from 1947. Took us forty minutes to bring her back."

The Orphans. Thirty-eight of them, rescued from the ruins of the Port Authority Bus Terminal collapse, pulled screaming from the wreckage when they were six years old. Twelve now. Old enough to remember what happened but young enough that their minds rewrote it into nightmares instead of memories.

I walk past the rows of cots, each one with its little monitor beeping out a steady rhythm—*bip-bip-bip*—like tiny hearts keeping time. Some of the children stir in their sleep, faces peaceful, innocent. Others twitch and mumble things that make my stomach clench.

I'm looking for something here. A reason, maybe. Justification. Something to balance what I did an hour ago—turned over the sector codes to the Butcher, handed him the keys to half the tri-state defense grid. Treason by any other name still smells like blood and desperation.

But these kids don't know about treason. They just know sleep and sedation and the ghost-smell of charred wool that seeps up from the old foundation stones, from the bones of Sub-Station Seven's first victims, ground into the concrete like martyrdom and bad decisions.

My weave stutters again, static crawling up my spine like ice-cold fingers. The Vault is bleeding psychic residue tonight, all that accumulated death and trauma leaking through the cracks where reality got broken.

"Keep them sedated if you have to," I tell Rix, and my voice comes out wrong—hollow, distant, like it's echoing up from the bottom of a well. "The grid is unstable."

She looks at me with eyes that have seen too much, understood too much.

"Yes, Commander."

Another cot. Another sleeping child. Another biometric readout telling me everything is normal even though nothing has been normal since the day the world split open and decided to eat itself alive.

Behind me, something shifts in the darkness at the back of the ward.

I should turn around. Should check it out. That's what an Aegis Commander does—protects, defends, stands between the innocent and whatever horrors crawl out of the dark places between dimensions.

Instead, I keep walking toward the far end, counting cots, counting breaths, counting down to when this nightmare ends or kills us all, whichever comes first.

A soft sound echoes behind me. Almost human. Almost.

Then silence.

And from somewhere deep in the Vault—a scream. Piercing. Pure terror distilled into a single syllable of sound that makes every hair on my body stand up and beg for mercy.

* * *

The screaming starts before I see it.

My boots are still wet with marsh water when I hear the high-pitched wail cutting through the Vault's subterranean hum. Not pain exactly—not yet—but the sound of something breaking wrong on the inside. I'm already moving, my weave flaring bright white against the ash-gray static that's been clinging to my consciousness since Pulaski.

The back cot is chaos.

Jax—eight years old, Orcish, one of the Orphanage kids we pulled from the Passaic flood three weeks ago—is convulsing like he's being electrocuted. His small body arches off the thin mattress, muscles locking, unlocking, locking again in violent sequence. The smell hits me next: wet charred wool mixed with copper and something else, something metallic that makes my throat constrict.

Iron-gall residue.

It's pouring from him. Not bleeding, but *flowing*—thick sizzling rivulets of blue-black ichor streaming from his nostrils, from the corners of his clenched eyes, smoking where they hit the cotton sheets below. The fabric blackens instantly, eating through, revealing the springs beneath. Steam rises in acidic wisps.

"COMMANDER!" Rix slams a tray down on the medical table hard enough to make instruments jump. Her yellow-green goblin skin has gone gray with panic. "He just—he was sleeping! Then this!"

I don't answer. I'm already there, throwing myself over Jax's thrashing form, pressing both palms flat against his chest where his heart hammers frantically beneath ribs too small for what they're being asked to do. My fingers sink slightly into flesh that feels wrong—too hot, fever-burning hot, but textured strange, like touching someone filled with sand instead of blood.

My weave responds automatically, white-lilac light erupting between us, warding protocols engaging. But the ash-gray static is *strong* here in the Vault, triggered by the smell, by the closeness of walls, by the memory of what happened to Sub-Station Five. It fights me. My bio-wards flicker, strain across his chest in a desperate net of protective geometry.

"Temperature spike!" Rix is shoving syringes onto the tray, her clawed fingers fumbling. "Core temp spiking! He's cooking himself, Mara, he's—"

"I see it!" The words come out gritted teeth. Jax's heart rate is 210 beats per minute and climbing. His lungs are filling with toxic residue, each breath producing wet crackles audible even over his whimpering screams. I can feel it—the iron-gall eating at his bronchial tissue, corroding, dissolving from the inside out.

My hands burn where they touch him. The residue is acidic enough to eat through cotton, and skin isn't much thicker. I push harder, forcing my weave deeper, feeling for his cardiac node. There—a fluttering rhythm, arrhythmic, failing.

I grab it.

The sensation is like grasping a live wire wrapped in silk. Pain lances up my arms as I manually regulate, slowing, slowing, forcing his heartbeat down to something survivable while simultaneously pushing raw arcane energy through his lungs. The effort makes me scream silently into the back of my throat. Every muscle in my body locks as I pour myself into him, fighting the poison, fighting the static, fighting gravity itself.

"Twenty CCs bismuth-saline! NOW!"

Rix doesn't hesitate. The needle slides into Jax's thigh, the thick coagulant mixture hissing as it hits muscle. The monitors behind us—crude things scavenged from who-knows-where—start flatlining, then recover, then flatline again in stuttering rhythm that matches Jax's struggling pulse.

His body goes rigid beneath me.

Time stops.

Then his chest heaves once, twice, and the convulsions ease. The iron-gall flow slows, becomes trickle, stops. The sizzling sound dies away, leaving only our ragged breathing and the frantic chirping of medical equipment returning to normal ranges.

I collapse forward over him, sweat pouring down my face, dripping onto his still-warm skin.

"Mara?" Rix's voice comes from very far away. "Commander, you need to see this."

I lift my head, blinking bloodshot eyes at her gesture toward Jax's chest. The white-lilac afterglow of my weave still illuminates his torso, but underneath—that's not bruising. That's light. A rune-like brand glowing faintly under the skin of his sternum, pulsing in time with his now-stabilized heartbeat.

BATC telluric seal.

Impossible. We checked these kids three times. No seals, no implants, nothing. They were clean.

Jax's eyes flutter open, dark and confused and completely human. He doesn't see the brand glowing beneath his own flesh. But I do.

And that changes *everything*.

* * *

The water runs hot over my hands, turning black at first where the iron-gall ink clings to my skin like some dead thing refusing burial. I scrub harder, watching the dirty water spiral down the drain—a miniature vortex of filth and exhaustion. The mirror above the sink shows me what I look like after hours in that vault with Jax convulsing on the concrete floor while his blood pooled around him in patterns that looked almost deliberate, almost like someone had painted it there.

My reflection stares back pale and haunted beneath the harsh fluorescents. There are smudges of ash-gray across my left temple where my white-lilac weave has been corrupted by whatever the hell is happening inside Sub-Station Seven. The smell hits me again—that wet charred wool stench—and suddenly I'm not standing in this washroom anymore.

I'm back in the orphanage basement during the raid. Twenty-oh-five. Fire and screaming and the way the air itself seemed to crack when they detonated those charges outside. The smell was different then but somehow the same—burnt fabric, burnt flesh, burnt hope. I'd found three children hiding behind a boiler, their faces blank with shock as the building groaned around us. I got two out before the ceiling came down.

One stayed behind.

I blink hard and I'm back in the present. My hands are clean now, or cleaner anyway. The MiniDisc sits in its cradle on the counter beside me, its little screen glowing green in the dim light. I pulled it from my jacket pocket without thinking, fingers moving through muscle memory to plug it into the port built into the wall. Standard procedure. Log everything.

The data scrolls past: timestamp, coordinates, harmonic readings. November twelfth, zero-four-hundred-twelve. Pylon Two. And there it is—a spike so sharp and violent it makes my jaw clench just looking at it. Zero-four-hundred-thirteen.

Jax's seizure started at zero-four-hundred-fifteen.

Three minutes. It took three minutes for the backlash to travel through whatever sick circuit connects that pylon to the vault where I've been keeping watch over these children like some broken guardian angel who can't even tell what she's supposed to be protecting them *from*.

I pull up the schematic Thorne made me download before he wiped my laptop. Before he tried to make sure I wouldn't have evidence of what we'd actually been doing here. The file loads slowly—the infrastructure's barely holding together—and there it is in clinical blue lines and mathematical precision:

Pylon Two. Secondary seal. Harmonic frequency: 7.83 Hz.

I know that number. Everyone in BATC Aegis knows it. Seven-point-eight-three Hertz is the Schumann resonance—the fundamental frequency of Earth's electromagnetic field. It's what keeps reality stable, keeps the veil between worlds from tearing wide open.

It's also the frequency that resonates with human consciousness.

My thumb hovers over the trackpad. I don't want to do this calculation but I'm already doing it, pulling up Jax's medical records from the orphanage files—another thing Thorne didn't bother scrubbing because he never thought anyone would look close enough. Brain activity during crisis event: peak frequency detected at...

Seven-point-eight-three Hertz.

The porcelain sink feels ice-cold beneath my palms as I lean forward, staring at the numbers like they might rearrange themselves into something less monstrous than what they're clearly spelling out. But mathematics doesn't lie. Physics doesn't care about morality or compassion or the hollow ache that's spreading through my chest right now.

They're using the children as anchors.

The Pylons aren't just seals on some dimensional breach. They're batteries powered by living human neurons firing in rhythm with the planet's own electromagnetic heartbeat. Each one of these orphans has had their life force woven directly into the Doomsday Lock—converted into raw energy to hold back whatever horror is pressing against the other side.

And when Cole Reyes cracks those secondary seals, the harmonic feedback hits the children first. Hits them so hard it makes their brains hemorrhage and their bodies convulse and their hearts stop beating in sync with the world around them.

He's not trying to destroy New Jersey.

He's trying to save these kids by breaking the circuit before BATC can drain every last drop of life from them.

My Nextel chirps sharp and insistent on the counter beside the sink. The screen lights up with a deployment order:

**ALL AEGIS UNITS PROCEED TO NEON HOLLOW SHIPYARDS IMMEDIATELY. PYLON THREE UNDER THREAT.**

I stare at it. My hand moves toward the device but stops halfway. Around me, somewhere deep in Sub-Station Seven, I can hear the distant hum of machinery—that constant vibration that's been my companion for weeks now. It sounds different today. Hungry.

They want me to defend Pylon Three.

They want me to stand between Cole Reyes and the machine that's slowly killing innocent children because he knows what we've done here and he's finally moved beyond protest into action. Because someone has to pay attention long enough to realize that BATC isn't protecting this city.

We're powering something with souls.

The washroom feels smaller now, walls closing in as comprehension settles over me like a shroud. Julian Sterling. Marcus Voss. All those High-Spire executives who smile during press conferences about safety and security while they engineer tragedies to create batteries out of orphans.

And I've been guarding the vault.

I've been making sure none of them escaped so their energy would stay pure and stable for whatever doomsday scenario requires such desperate measures.

My reflection in the mirror looks back at me—pale and hollow-eyed and broken—and I wonder if there's any coming back from this realization. If I can still be Mara Vance after knowing what Commander Mara Vance actually does for a living.

The Nextel chirps again. Insistent.

*All Aegis units to Neon Hollow Shipyards.*

Yes, I think. But not to protect the machine.

To see exactly how far they'll go when someone finally comes to break it.

---

## CHAPTER 4: PYLON #3 & THE CORPORATE ELVES

The convoy rolled through pre-dawn darkness, headlights cutting through sheets of freezing rain that hammered the windshield like thrown gravel. I sat up front in the lead Humvee, knuckles white on my service weapon, jaw clenched so tight my molars ached.

"Two minutes out," barked Sergeant Reyes from the driver's seat. His breath fogged the cabin despite the heater running full blast.

Through the rain-smeared windows, the Neon Hollow Shipyards materialized like something dragged up from the bottom of Newark Bay—all corroded steel, rust-streaked shipping containers stacked like tombstones, and skeletal gantry cranes frozen mid-motion against the bruised November sky. The place reeked before we even opened the doors. Diesel fuel and iron rot, undercut by something worse. Rotting fish. Death.

We piled out into the storm.

Rain needled through my BATC tactical jacket immediately, sharp as glass shards against my face. Around me, my twelve-strong tactical team fanned out, boots clunking heavy on wet steel plating. The cold bit through everything. Behind us, three more armored vehicles idled, engines growling, exhaust misting in the gray light.

"Perimeter sweep!" I shouted over the rain. "Sector-by-sector! Watch those shadows!"

The shipyards sprawled before us—a maze of containers, half-demolished warehouses, and flooded drydocks reflecting nothing but storm clouds. Somewhere in this industrial graveyard was Pylon #3, the third anchor point in the Butcher's containment field. And according to Command, it was being fortified.

By who, exactly, they didn't specify.

I advanced toward what looked like command central—an open area between two massive container stacks where several figures huddled under an enormous umbrella. As we approached, the figure in the center became clearer: a man in his late forties, maybe early fifties, dressed in a camel-hair coat so pristine it seemed to mock the surrounding decay. Beside him stood something that made my tactical assessment skills kick into high gear: Ogre-Kin bodyguard, eight feet tall minimum, arms like tree trunks, hands wrapped around an umbrella pole thick enough to be a crowbar.

But it was the other figures that made my stomach drop.

They weren't standard security. Dozens of them, moving with that unnatural grace that marked High-Spire Elves, all dressed in expensive suits despite the weather. They carried briefcases in one hand and assault rifles in the other—the weapons etched with runes that even from here gave off the telltale shimmer of arcano-enchantment.

Corporate lawyers. Armed corporate lawyers.

"Sir." My voice cut through the rain as I approached within ten meters, weapon still holstered but ready. Professional. Controlled. "Aegis Command sent my unit to secure the perimeter."

The man didn't look up. His fingers danced across a PalmPilot that glowed blue-green in the pre-dawn gloom. Behind him, six more elves materialized from behind containers, their rifles tracking us with that unsettling precision that came from centuries of perfect muscle memory.

"My name is Marcus Voss," he said without looking up, voice smooth as river stones rolling in oil. "Head #2, Corporate Compliance Division. Your unit is relegated to the outer barricades, Commander Vance. My private contractors have the core. Do not cross the yellow tape."

I followed his gesture. There—yellow police tape strung between containers about thirty meters away, beyond which lay what looked like the entrance to a flooded drydock. And beyond that...

Something cold ran down my spine that had nothing to do with the rain.

"You're fortifying Pylon #3," I said, watching those High-Spire Elves. Watching how they moved, weapons held with casual deadliness. "Against the Butcher."

"Not just against the Butcher." Finally, Voss looked at me. His eyes were gray as storm clouds over Newark Bay. "Against anyone who might try to interfere with BATC operations. Internal oversight included."

My weave tightened inside me, white-lilac energy coiling like a spring wound too far. The cedar smell sharpened, cutting through diesel and death-stink.

"You're bypassing Aegis command structure entirely."

"Commander." His smile was thin as a razor. "We're *reorganizing* it. There's a difference."

Behind him, one of the Elven contractors opened his briefcase. Inside: not documents, but glowing crystalline matrices pulsing with arcano-energy. Rune-work so complex it hurt to look at directly.

"What the fuck are you preparing for?"

* * *

The smell hit me first—that goddamn cedar, sharp and acidic where it shouldn't be, cutting through the chemical soup of industrial decay. My weave coiled tighter around my spine as I stepped into the corridor leading to Pylon #3's primary access hatch, the white-lilac flickering at the edges of my vision like angry fireflies trapped under glass.

Then I saw them.

Three High-Spire Elven attorneys, standing in perfect formation between me and the reinforced door. Their tactical suits were immaculate—water-repellent black with silver accents that caught the sickly yellow light from the failing shipyard fluorescents. The fabric had that otherworldly shimmer that marked corporate enchantments, probably cost more than my annual salary.

The lead one smiled when he saw me. Too many teeth, too white, the kind of smile that meant trouble.

"Commander Vance," he said, his voice smooth as silk over broken glass. He held up a PalmPilot, its screen glowing with that distinctive azure-cyan glow of active arcano-compliance protocols. "I'm Sylas. My associates are Fennrick and Kaelen. We represent Pylon #3's corporate interests under the auspices of—"

"I know what you are," I cut him off, keeping my hands visible but ready. The cedar smell was getting worse, making my eyes water. "Arcano-compliance lawyers. You're here because someone signed away the rights to this entire sector."

Sylas's smile never wavered. "Class-4 Proprietary Leyline Sequestration, effective 04:00 hours this morning. All municipal Aegis personnel lack requisite telluric-grade clearance." His thumb swiped across the PalmPilot. The air in front of him rippled, and suddenly there was text—actual hard-light words suspended in mid-air, burning themselves into my retinas like laser-etched tattoos.

*...BATC MUNICIPAL FORCES HEREBY DENIED ACCESS TO PYLON #3 CORE FACILITIES PER SECTION 4A OF THE 2007 CORPORATE LEYLINE ACT...*

The text pulsed, each flash sending needles through my skull. Behind it, I could see the three Elves' hands resting on their suppressed MP5s, casual but ready.

"Read carefully, Commander," Sylas continued, his tone dripping with condescension. "Subsection 4A specifically states that any unauthorized breach will result in immediate termination—of employment, citizenship records, and life." He tilted his head. "We'd prefer not to invoke those provisions. Return to your perimeter. Let our certified technicians handle the situation."

My jaw ached from clenching. The white-lilac surged again, hotter now, fed by my anger. Those corporate vultures had sequestered an active Pylon, and these smiling predators were supposed to stop me?

* * *

I pressed myself against the rusted corrugation of a shipping container, feeling its cold bite even through my tactical vest. The wet metal stank of decades-old brine and oxidation—an smell that clawed up from the flooded concrete below where Pylon #3 squatted like a sleeping leviathan.

The micro-transponder sat in my palm, no bigger than my thumbnail. Cole had placed it during our last raid, before everything went sideways. Before the Elves sealed this place tighter than a banker's wallet. I could feel the faint vibration of Gnomish engineering humming through it—a frequency just outside normal perception, dancing along wavelengths the corporate magi never bothered to monitor because they didn't think anyone *could*.

"Commander." Jensen's voice crackled in my earpiece. Static and distance made him sound farther away than he was. "Perimeter holding. Three Elf patrols rotated north. You've got maybe five minutes."

I didn't respond verbally. Instead, I pulled the Sony MiniDisc player from my belt pouch—the one piece of retro tech that still worked better than anything new-money could buy. The copper wiring was delicate work, each strand thinner than spider silk. My fingers moved with the muscle memory of a thousand field repairs, splicing the transponder's output into the player's amplifier circuit.

The cedar scent sharpened as my weave coiled tighter. White-lilac suppression felt like swallowing broken glass, but I couldn't risk them detecting my bio-wards. Not yet.

"Three... two... one," I whispered, activating the modified MiniDisc.

The Gnomish frequency bloomed through the speaker—barely audible, more felt than heard. It was beautiful in its crude efficiency: no aesthetic flourishes, no Elven elegance. Just raw harmonic resonance tuned to slip through the cracks in reality's infrastructure. I synced my own weave to match, feeling the white-lilac burn as I forced it into phase with that alien oscillation.

Behind me, I could hear the squad settling into overwatch positions. Smart kids. They knew not to ask questions when their commander started playing with tech that looked like it belonged in a junkyard.

The hard-light injunction wall shimmered ahead—a barrier of compressed photons and corporate law given physical form. Walking into it would feel like trying to push through solid diamond while standing in an electric storm.

I took a breath and stepped forward.
