## CHAPTER 15: THE ROOFTOP REVELATION

The wind screams across the rooftop like something alive, tearing at my soaked uniform jacket and sending sheets of rain horizontal across the concrete expanse. I crouch behind the HVAC unit, fingers working frantically over the stolen Nextel repeater, its plastic casing slick beneath my blood-freezing grip.

"Come on... come on..."

My white-lilac wards flare bright enough to cut through the storm's darkness—swirling halos that deflect the rain in sizzling steam clouds around me. The wards scream against my consciousness, a constant pressure like someone pressing their thumbs into my temples while whispering warnings in a language older than names. They're reacting to everything: the electromagnetic chaos of the storm, the telluric currents running wild through Newark Bay, the *wrongness* that's been bleeding through reality's seams since this whole goddamn nightmare started.

But right now? They're just making it harder to concentrate.

I slap the repeater against my thigh, wincing as pain shoots up from my knee—the one I busted during last week's raid on the Kearny Marshes drug lab. The one that still aches when the barometric pressure drops. Like now. Of course.

Below, red lights sweep across wet asphalt. The Elven security teams are doing grid searches, their forms too graceful even for the shadows they move through. Corporate mercs. Excessively expensive. Which means someone's paying serious cred for information about BATC operations.

Someone who knows exactly where we are.

The scent hits me then—cedar and pine resin, sharp and clean from my wards mixing with ozone from the lightning strikes illuminating the Newark skyline every few seconds. But underneath it all, clinging like smoke to fabric, comes something else entirely: warm hearth-coals. Ash and embers. The smell of endings.

My chest tightens.

"Cole." His name tastes bitter on my tongue.

I key the Nextel again, forcing the repeater to cycle through frequencies. My other hand traces sigils in the air—not really casting anything, just keeping the wards primed and focused. Keeping them from burning out completely. They've already consumed more stamina than they should tonight. I can feel it in my bones, that particular emptiness that comes from pushing metaphysical hardware past its design specs.

A glow catches my peripheral vision. Yellow. Predatory.

On the fire escape of the adjacent building, maybe twenty feet away through the rain-shrouded darkness, a Goblin splice-runner sits perched like some kind of gargoyle. His eyes catch what little light there is and throw it back, twin yellow disks set in a face that's too wide, grin too many teeth.

We make eye contact.

He could be here for any number of reasons. Could want to sell my position to the highest bidder. Could want to gut me for whatever tech I'm carrying. Could just be passing through and decided I was worth his attention.

I reach into my pocket with deliberate slowness, pulling out a silver cred-stick—the good stuff, government issued, traceable only if someone knows where to look. I hold it up between two fingers, making sure the reflectivity catches what little light exists.

The Goblin tilts his head, considering.

Then he holds out one clawed hand, palm up.

I toss it underhanded, an easy arc that even the wind doesn't manage to screw up completely. He snatches it from the air without taking his eyes off me, examines it for exactly one second, then pops it into his mouth like candy.

"Mmph," he says around the metal, "Vance."

My blood runs cold despite the warmth radiating from my chest. Despite knowing I should have expected this. Splice-runners don't just appear by accident. Someone sent him. Someone who knew I'd be here.

"Who?" My voice comes out sharper than I intend.

He grins wider, showing more teeth than should fit in any mouth. "Pretty please with sugar on top?"

Before I can respond—or decide whether responding is even smart—he drops backward off the fire escape and vanishes into the smog-choked alley below. Just... gone. Like he was never there at all.

Except now I know someone's watching. Someone close enough to track my movements through the storm.

The Nextel repeater crackles in my hands. Static. Then something else—a signal trying to break through the telluric interference that's been making comms a nightmare since midnight.

Green light blinks once. Twice.

Encrypted Black-Circuit frequency.

And then it goes solid.

Not yellow. Not red.

Solid green.

My heart hammers against my ribs hard enough to hurt as my wards spike bright enough to make everything around me glow white for just a second—the concrete, the rain droplets suspended mid-air, the blinking aviation beacon on its tower that suddenly seems much closer than it should be.

Cole's frequency.

It's Cole.

I press the receive button so hard my knuckle goes white.

* * *

The Nextel chirps—a harsh, digital intruder in the symphony of rain hammering against the rooftop. My hand fumbles for the device in my jacket pocket, fingers already slick with moisture and adrenaline. The plastic case is cold against my palm, the screen lit by that familiar sickly green glow.

"Vance."

Cole's voice cuts through the static like a razor blade through silk. Distorted. Compressed. Each word arrives wrapped in layers of interference—the lead shielding of the Old Mint below us, the telluric radiation bleeding from Pylon #4, the atmospheric conditions turning this into a nightmare of signal degradation.

"Commander." He corrects himself, and I can hear blood in his voice. Literal blood. The wet rasp of breath fighting past ruptured lung tissue.

I press myself harder against the HQ's access panel, my white-lilac wards flaring bright enough to cast dancing shadows across the concrete. They're screaming warnings now—urgent pulses of protection magic that taste like copper and ozone. But I ignore them. Need to hear this.

"The vault," Cole continues, another wet cough interrupting mid-sentence. "Under Pylon four. You were right about the—"

A heavy metallic thud echoes through the connection. Something large hitting something metal. Then hissing. Steam? No—it's him again, breathing through what sounds like a throat full of broken glass.

"Bring your MiniDisc. There aren't three of them, Little Halo."

My stomach drops. The Nextel nearly slips from my grip as my white-knuckled fingers lose their purchase on the casing. Rain runs down the screen in rivulets, distorting the display but not enough to hide the call status: ACTIVE - 2:37 REMAINING.

"There aren't three?" My thumb jabs at the push-to-talk button with enough force to crack plastic. "Cole, what do you mean there aren't three? Who is the third signature?"

The static swells. For one terrible moment I think he's gone, that the interference has swallowed him whole, dragged him down into that dead space between transmission and reception where signals go to die. My heart hammers against my ribs hard enough to hurt.

Then: "Not... person." His voice fragments across multiple frequencies, reassembling itself like shattered glass being pieced together by an amateur surgeon. "Corporate... entity."

I'm already moving before the words fully register, my boots slipping on the wet rooftop surface as I lunge for the access ladder. "Cole, stay with me! What corporate entity? Morvain Estate—"

Another sound. This one final. The distinctive click-clack of a handgun's slide releasing. The hollow echo of metal against stone. Then silence.

Complete silence except for the hiss of static.

"No no no NO—" My free hand slams against the Nextel's housing, as if brute force could resurrect a dead connection. The wards around me spike, flaring so bright they cast everything in harsh ultraviolet. The rain sizzles where it touches the magical field, turning to steam.

But Cole is gone.

I stare at the phone's display until my eyes burn. Until the rain has thoroughly soaked through every layer of clothing I'm wearing. Until my white-lilac wards have burned themselves out, fading to barely-there whispers of protection magic that smell like scorched lavender.

There aren't three signatures because the third wasn't a person.

The Morvain Estate isn't a house.

It never was.

Slowly, mechanically, I unfold the torn authorization document from 1999—the one we'd found in the Lincoln Tunnel maintenance shaft. The one with two clear signatures and one illegible smear of ink. Rainwater runs across its surface, smearing what little text remains visible.

The third signature wasn't a name.

It was a seal.

A corporate seal.

And underneath it, partially obscured by water damage and time: THE MORVAIN ESTATE HOLDING COMPANY - PROPERTY DEVELOPMENT DIVISION.

My hands are shaking now—not from cold or fear, but from the weight of revelation. Twenty-eight years. Twenty-eight years of hunting ghosts when we should have been hunting...

*Shit.*

The MiniDisc in my other pocket suddenly feels like a lead weight. All those signatures. Every single one we've collected since 1980. Cross-referenced against known syndicate operatives, confirmed metahuman assets, vetted contacts.

What if none of them were people?

What if they were all shells? Corporate entities designed to obscure ownership, to create plausible deniability, to wash money through layers of bureaucratic red tape so thick you couldn't tell where one organization ended and another began?

"Commander Vance." The voice makes me jump—Lieutenant Kowalski's face appears at the top of the access ladder, rain plastering his dark hair to his skull. "We have movement below. Multiple contacts approaching the Old Mint perimeter."

I look down at the Nextel still clutched in my hand. At the authorization document. At my reflection in the phone's dark screen—a ghost of myself standing in a storm that just got infinitely worse.

"There aren't three," I whisper to no one. To Cole, wherever he is. To the Syndicate, to the Morvain Estate, to whatever fresh hell is waiting for us inside that vault.

Then louder, speaking into the rain itself: "There never were."

I pocket both documents—the paper and the phone—and descend into BATC Headquarters. Behind me, the wards finally collapse entirely, their scent fading to nothing as the rooftop returns to ordinary darkness.

But I know better than that.

Nothing about tonight is ordinary anymore.

* * *

The door explodes inward with the crackle of police-grade breaching rounds.

I don't turn around. Don't break my lock on Pylon #4, where Cole's signature pulses like a dying heart—faint, erratic, bleeding out inside that godforsaken vault.

"BATC Security! Freeze!"

The voice is dwarf-timbered, used to being obeyed. I can hear the weight of their gear clanking—ceramic plates under tactical vests, sidearms unsnapping from holsters, combat boots crunching across wet gravel.

My white-lilac wards flare hotter, casting everything in that sickly lavender glow. The rain hammers down harder now, each droplet striking my skin like ice needles. But underneath it all, threaded through the tempest, I smell hearth-coals. *Warm*. *Desperate*.

Cole's fear.

"Commander Vance! Stand down!" The second guard, different voice—elf maybe, from the way they modulate frequency for maximum carry. "You are in violation of Section 7-A of the Aegis Protocol. Surrender your weapons and comply!"

I'm already running.

Not toward them. Away from everything—the safety rails, the proper exits, the goddamn rules that got us here in the first place. My boots slip once on the wet rooftop, gravel scattering, but I catch myself and push harder, legs burning as I sprint across forty stories of exposed concrete and neon-slicked danger.

Behind me, heavy footsteps give chase. Radios crackle. Someone's shouting into their comms: *"She's moving! Armed suspect—wait, she's not armed, she's—where the fuck is she going?!"*

The edge approaches fast. Too fast. Forty stories drops away into blackness punctuated by sodium-orange streetlamps and the occasional red flash of a traffic signal. Below, the Pulaski Skyway cuts through rain-soaked darkness, trucks rolling like slow-moving metal beetles along the elevated highway.

I don't stop.

"VANCE!" That dwarf again, closer now. Desperation creeping into his voice. "DON'T DO THIS!"

My wards detonate around me—a supernova of white-lilac light that sends the security team stumbling backward, hands raised against the glare. In that moment of blindness, I reach deep. Deeper than I've ever reached before. Every ounce of my weave, every thread of kinetic dampening I can spin, pouring it all into a cocoon around my body.

The Myocardial Geas throbs against my sternum—not pain exactly, more like pressure, a living thing beating in time with the telluric grid that runs beneath this whole rotten city.

And then there's nothing but air.

Wind screams past my ears, a physical force that tries to tear the breath from my lungs. The building falls away. Newark Bay spreads out below me, a sprawling dark mirror reflecting neon signs that blur into streaking ribbons—red, blue, orange, all bleeding together as terminal velocity kicks in.

My wards burn so bright they hurt to look at even for me. The mathematics cascade through my mind: trajectory angles, deceleration curves, impact vectors. It's beautiful and terrible all at once.

*"She's gone over! She actually jumped—the Commander just went over the edge!"* 

That elf's voice fades behind me as I fall, tumbling end-over-end through sheets of rain. Below, something moves. Something *fast*.

The freight train on the elevated tracks.

It emerges from beneath a bridge like a steel serpent cutting through black water, its boxcars stacked high, moving north toward Kearny. North toward the Old Mint where Cole is dying in darkness.

I adjust my vector—just slightly—but in freefall, slight means everything. The train rushes up to meet me, growing larger by the second. Boxcar. Bridge support. Another boxcar. A maintenance ladder.

"Please," I whisper to whatever gods might be listening. "Just this once."

My kinetic field flares impossibly bright.

Impact.

The world becomes white noise and violence. My bones scream. The kinetic dampening absorbs what it can—a shockwave that tears across the rooftop with enough force to shatter three streetlamps in a row—but physics is unforgiving. Even with magic, forty stories has weight. Has consequence.

When the light fades and I can see again, I'm lying across rusted metal, rain pelting down, train wheels clacking beneath me. Inside my mouth, copper. Taste of blood. But alive.

Alive and moving north.

I push myself upright, legs shaking, ribs definitely cracked somewhere under the left side. But my wards still burn steady, and Cole's signal—that desperate coal-scent of his fear—pulls me forward like gravity itself.

The Old Mint appears ahead, squatting against the night sky like a tombstone made of brick and despair. As the train carries me closer, I see the breach point. See the way the vault walls have been peeled open like an orange, raw concrete edges glowing faintly with residual weave.

And there, deep inside, barely perceptible but *there*:

Cole.

I don't wait for the next bridge. Don't wait for anything except momentum and rage and the bone-deep certainty that if I don't reach him right now, in this moment, I'll fail at the one thing that matters.

At 1:25 AM on November 16th, Commander Mara Vance leaps from a moving freight train into the heart of the Old Mint.

Ready to tear reality apart to save her partner.

# BOOK #04: RUST AND BONE
### Prequel Duology Part 2 (MB-2)

---

## CHAPTER 1: THE IRON-LUNG & THE GNOME-FORGED FREQUENCY

The stairs down are always colder than they should be. I feel it first in my forearms—that bone-deep chill that isn't quite natural, like walking through a meat locker that someone forgot to plug in. The gauze wrapped around my wrists has gone stiff with dried blood-iron residue, black against the gray concrete.

I'm dripping something onto the steps. Each footfall leaves a dark smear behind me, metallic and wrong-smelling. The burns from the catwalk haven't stopped weeping their frost-cobalt shit yet.

The sub-basement door hangs open at the bottom landing. Light spills out—not electric, but the warm orange glow of brass fixtures burning kerosene. I can hear him before I see him. Bram's been working on the manifold since before sunrise, probably won't stop until he passes out face-first in his coffee.

"Christ's machine-guns, Cole!" His voice echoes up the stairwell, gravelly as crushed asphalt. "You look like you went swimming in a goddamn foundry."

I push through the door. The chop-shop spreads out below—a warren of workbenches cluttered with disassembled engines, brass tubing stacked like cordwood, and the massive silhouette of the Arcane Iron-Lung taking up most of the center space. It's all glass bells and copper piping, Victorian mad science married to union-grade hydraulics. Danny's inside, visible through the reinforced panes, his chest rising and falling to the rhythm of those massive bellows.

Bram doesn't look up from where he's hunched over the pneumatic manifold, one arm deep in the machinery's guts. He's got his torque wrench in his free hand, turning it with the practiced ease of someone who's made this adjustment a thousand times. His apron is stained with oil that's been there so long it's started to crack like leather.

"Hand me that three-eighths socket," he says around the cigarette dangling from his lips. "This pressure-valve is tighter than a corporate auditor's ass."

I grab the socket from his tool tray—still hot to the touch—and pass it down without a word. My breath comes out in clouds. The temperature in here has dropped at least ten degrees since I walked in.

Bram catches sight of my forearms, eyes narrowing. "Jesus, Mary, and Joseph. What happened up there?"

* * *

The Toughbook's harsh LED glow throws Danny's pale face into sharp relief against the chop-shop's darkness. My brother's fingers dance across the mechanical keyboard inside the Iron-Lung's pressurized gauntlets, each keystroke precise despite the bulky rig. The decrypt program emits a high-pitched digital whine that grates against my teeth.

"These Gnome hardware-smiths are paranoid, Cole," Danny's synthesized voice crackles through the speakers. "It's a rolling 256-bit hex-cipher wrapped in a telluric feedback loop."

I lean over his shoulder, watching the cascade of code scroll down the screen. Bram hovers nearby, muttering about cipher-keys and overengineered security protocols. The old man's right—Gnomes always complicate things. But I slipped that transponder into Mara Vance's belt during our close-quarters clash at Pylon #2 for a reason.

My frost-cobalt blood-iron begins to hum beneath my skin, a familiar cold that drops the ambient temperature ten degrees. I channel the energy toward the laptop's overheating motherboard, feeling the machine's heat dissipate under my hex-work. The cooling fan kicks into overdrive with a mechanical shriek.

"Keep pushing, Danny. Stabilize the thermal spread."

Danny's fingers don't falter. "Already on it, hermano. Just need another thirty seconds before the frequency sync locks."

Bram shifts his weight, the floorboards creaking. "If this thing was planted by Syndicate tech, we're looking at military-grade encryption. Could take hours to crack."

"Not hours," I rumble, my voice dead-silent and low. "Minutes. These Gnomes work for both sides—they cut corners where it matters."

The PalmPilot in my hand displays the transponder's weak ping, tethered to the Toughbook's input port. Mara's signal flickers across the screen, moving through what looks like the Kearny Marshes. But there's something else—a secondary data stream bleeding into the primary channel.

My blood runs cold for reasons unrelated to the hex-work.

"Danny, switch the audio feed to full spectrum. Now."

The decrypt finishes with a sharp chime. The Toughbook's speakers erupt with static before clarifying into a live audio broadcast. My eyes narrow as two distinct conversations overlap:

"...should have moved the shipment off McCarter Highway by now..."

"...watching Pylon #2, but nothing on the catwalks..."

Syndicate. And BATC. On the same encrypted trunk line.

"You seeing this?" Bram's voice cuts through the revelation.

I am. And suddenly everything makes terrible sense. Mara Vance wasn't just Syndicate muscle working alone. She was a node in something larger—something that bridged rival factions through Gnome-brokered technology.

Danny's gauntleted hands freeze over the keyboard. "Cole... the cross-channel communication is active. They're coordinating."

Through me. Through the transponder I'd planted thinking I was tracking one woman.

* * *

The screen glows like a sickly sun in that basement, bathing our faces in that pale blue light. My knuckles ache from gripping the edge of the workbench. Three organizations. Three. Sharing infrastructure. Sharing tech. Sharing secrets while we're down here playing grab-ass with scrap metal and hex-work.

"Jesus fucking Christ," Danny breathes. His voice cracks. Kid's seen some shit in his short time working for me, but this? This is different. This is the kind of conspiracy that gets you disappeared, that makes you wake up in a puddle of your own blood somewhere near the Passaic River with no memory of how you got there.

Bram's already moving before I can process it. The *clack-clack* of him racking his MP5 echoes off the concrete walls like a church bell announcing the apocalypse. He drops his wrench—*clatter*—and brings the weapon up, muzzle pointed at nothing yet ready for everything. That rune-etched slide catches what little light there is, glowing faint blue-green.

Then it happens.

A sound from above. Not footsteps—not yet. Something heavier. The entire shop floor vibrates through my boots, rattling loose tools across every surface. Metal on metal. The reinforced garage door—that three-inch steel slab that's stopped more than one angry husband looking for his wife's boyfriend—shudders again. Harder this time.

*Thud-thud-thud.*

Someone's testing it. Testing the locks. Trying to see if they'll give.

Bram's already got the bolt thrown on the basement door behind us, backing toward Danny with that MP5 trained on the stairs. Smart kid. Getting between the threat and the asset.

"That ain't the cops, Reyes." Bram's whisper cuts through the ozone-thick air. "Cops knock with a warrant, not a battering ram."

My eyes find his. Hold. Then drift past him to where Danny stands white-faced against the Iron-Lung's main housing unit, hands raised like he's surrendering even though nobody's pointed a gun at him yet. Good. Should be scared. Everyone should be scared right now.

I reach down to my ankle holster without thinking, pulling out the sawed-off. The weight settles into my palm familiar as an old lover. Four rounds. Depleted-bismuth slugs. Each one costs more than most people make in a week, but money doesn't mean shit when you're facing something that can shrug off regular lead like it's paper.

The shells slide home with that perfect *snick-snick* sound. Cold. Heavy. Final.

Frost-cobalt blood-iron hexes flare through my veins—not from anger, not from fear, but from pure cold calculation. My breath fogs in front of me. Ten degrees colder, easy. The concrete floor might start weeping frost if I let it go much longer.

"Keep the lung running, Bram." My voice sounds wrong. Flat. Dead. Like someone else is speaking through my mouth. "I'll take out the trash."

I don't wait for acknowledgment. Already moving toward the stairs, boots silent on the grimy concrete. Each step up feels like wading through ice water. The sodium-vapor lights above bleed through the grate at street level, casting everything in that sick yellow glow that makes everyone look like corpses waiting to happen.

*Thud-thud-thud.*

They're working the door harder now. Impatient.

My hand finds the release latch. Rests there. Waiting.

Three seconds pass. Five. Ten.

Then I kick it hard and fast.

The garage door groans as it rolls upward—metal screaming against metal—and suddenly I'm staring into two massive silhouettes blocking out what little light bleeds down the alley. Sodium-vapor throws them into sharp relief: broad shoulders, heavy coats, faces lost in shadow.

Neither one moves yet.

Just stands there. Watching. Waiting to see what I'll do.

My finger rests alongside the trigger guard. Not on the trigger. Not yet.

"You boys lost?" My voice carries across the empty lot behind my shop. Echoes off brick walls. Comes back hollow-sounding, like a ghost asking the question instead of me.

They don't answer.

Instead, the bigger one reaches up and flips back his collar.

And that's when I see it—the glint of something metallic pinned there. Catches the sodium light just right.

A badge.

Fuck.

---

## CHAPTER 2: THE BROKER'S INQUISITORS

The sodium lights make everything look like it's rotting from the inside out—yellow-orange and sickly, casting long shadows that twist around the dumpsters like dying things trying to reach up from their graves.

I step into Chop-Shop Alley and I know immediately something's wrong.

The air tastes different. Metal. Sharp. Like blood on cold steel.

Two figures block the far end, massive even in the dim light. Ogre-Kin. Their breath comes out in clouds of vapor, each exhalation thick enough to see in the November night. The bigger one shifts his weight, leather creaking against armor underneath. His face is a ruin of old scars, jaw jutting out like he's chewing on concrete.

"Cole Reyes," the scarred one says, voice like gravel in a cement mixer. "We got business."

My boots touch the puddle near the alley entrance and it doesn't just reflect the streetlight—it *freezes*. Thin ice spreading outward in spider-web patterns, frost-cobalt bleeding through my blood-iron where I'm standing.

Sledge—because I know that name even before he speaks it—watches the ice but doesn't flinch. Professional. "Broker sent us. Says your aim was a little wide at Pylon #2. Says maybe you're going soft on the badge." He takes another step forward, the second Ogre-Kin moving to cut off any retreat toward the street. "Get in the trunk. Downtown for an audit."

The Crown Vic behind them is a '99, black, parked crooked across the curb. Trunk already popped. They planned this.

"I don't go anywhere with anyone unless they earned the right," I say, voice flat. Calm. "Tell the Broker my aim is exactly what it needs to be."

Sledge's smile shows too many teeth. "That ain't how this works, machinist. You work for the Syndicate now. That means you answer when we call."

I count the angles while we talk. The fire escape ladders bolted to the brick walls, third rung from the top rusted loose—I remember that from last spring. The blind spot between dumpster three and four. The way the sodium light leaves a darkness pool under the Crown Vic's chassis.

"Last chance," Sledge says, hand disappearing into his duster. When it comes out again, it's holding something heavy, rune-etched iron that gleams wet in the sickly orange light.

But I'm already weaving frost-cobalt through the iron of the fire escape above them, feeling the cold bite deep into the metal structure.

* * *

The air cracks like a whip.

I don't think—I *pull*. Blood-iron lances from my palms, invisible chains of frozen force that wrap around the bolted fire-escape above. The rusted iron groans, metal screaming against stone as I wrench it downward with everything I've got.

The second Ogre-Kin—twin to the one bleeding out behind the Crown Vic—has just enough time for eyes to go wide before three tons of industrial scrap crashes down on his skull. The impact is wet and final, bone crunching inside the cage of his helmet as the metal settles with a mechanical sigh.

No mercy. Not here. Not now.

"Cole!" Mara's voice carries from somewhere distant, muffled through concrete walls. She's still alive in there. Still fighting. That's all that matters.

Sledge breaks cover from behind the sedan's engine block, and he's faster than his brother was. His telluric armor—a swirling aura of brown earth-magic—crackles to life across his massive frame. He brings up some kind of compact submachine gun, spitting 9mm rounds in controlled bursts.

I slide left on asphalt slick with rain and blood, frost-cobalt spreading from my fingertips across the ground where I touch. Each bullet screams past, so close I can feel the heat of their passage even through my aura. One grazes my shoulder—doesn't even break skin, the kinetic energy deflected into ice crystals that shatter mid-air.

Then I'm up, shotgun coming around in a smooth arc. Time dilates. I see the rounds leaving his weapon, spinning lazily through space. See the sweat beading on Sledge's jaw beneath his helmet. See the pulse in his neck, frantic and animal.

He's aiming center mass when I fire.

The depleted-bismuth slug—loaded specially for occasions like this—roars from the barrel at hypersonic velocity. No sound, just the physical *impact* as it punches through his telluric shielding like paper. The magic disintegrates in a shower of dead sparks, and the slug continues straight through his chin, under the tongue, and out the back of his skull in a spray of grey matter and bone fragments.

Sledge drops his weapon. It clatters against wet pavement. He takes two steps forward before his legs give out, falling face-first into a spreading puddle of his own brains.

I don't wait. Can't wait. Already moving forward, boot planted against his spine as I drive him harder into the gutter. Once. Twice. Three times until something breaks wetly inside his chest cavity.

"Stay down," I snarl.

He's already gone, eyes glassy and fixed on nothing. His lips move once, twice, forming words in some guttural Orcish dialect that sounds like grinding machinery. Blood bubbles from his mouth. Then he goes still.

Behind me, the fire-escape groans again. I glance back—the section I ripped down has settled fully now, completely crushing what's left of his brother into the alley floor. Good enough.

My burner Motorola Razr starts vibrating in my jacket pocket. Insistent. Restricted caller ID flashing across the cracked screen: UNKNOWN NUMBER.

I ignore it.

The shotgun clicks empty as I rack another round—a standard 00 buck load this time, no exotic metals. Just raw stopping power. "Mara!" I shout toward the warehouse door. "How many more you got in there?"

No answer. Just silence, broken by distant sirens growing closer from the direction of McCarter Highway.

I check Sledge's body for weapons, find a belt knife—some kind of ceremonial blade with runes carved along the fuller—and pocket it. The submachine gun is too bulky, probably untraceable anyway. I leave it where it fell.

The phone vibrates again.

"This ain't over," I mutter, staring at the corpse. Someone sent these freaks after us. Someone who knows Mara's face, knows where we were headed. That means our position is compromised. Hard.

I need to get her out of here before backup arrives. Need to find out what Vane Thorne wanted bad enough to send two Ogre-Kin assassins. Need to—

The Razr buzzes a third time.

"Fuck it."

I pull it out, thumb hovering over the accept button. The display reads: URGENT CONTACT. Below that, a single line of text appears:

*WE KNOW WHAT YOU ARE, COLE REYES.*

The sirens are closer now. Red and blue lights beginning to flash across the far end of the alleyway.

My finger hovers.

Then presses.

The connection clicks live, and a voice—synthetic, distorted through some kind of digital scrambler—fills my ear:

"You've been selected for an evaluation. Your performance will determine your continued... existence."

I grip the phone tighter. "Who is this?"

But the line has already gone dead.

Behind me, something moves inside the warehouse. Not footfalls—too light for that. More like... breathing? No, not quite. Like metal shifting against metal.

I spin toward the sound, shotgun raised.

The door hangs open slightly now. A crack of darkness visible beyond it.

And from within that darkness comes another sound—the wet slap of flesh on concrete.

Multiple sets of footsteps.

"We got company," I whisper into the dead phone, then pocket it without waiting for response. "Mara, if you can hear me—stay back from the door."

* * *

The air tastes like ozone and dying stars.

I stand over what's left of Sledge, my breath misting in clouds that shouldn't exist in November heat. My body does this sometimes—drops everything around me to freezing when the iron gets thick in my veins. Frost spreads across the pavement like cancer spreading through lungs. Like the black tar Danny breathed into his before he was old enough to vote.

The chop-shop reeks of motor oil and rust, but underneath that is something worse. The copper smell of fresh blood mixing with the acrid bite of diesel exhaust. My knuckles are split open, embedded with fragments of teeth. Someone's teeth. Sledge's teeth. I don't remember hitting him that hard.

I crouch down, ignoring how my knee cracks—a sound like ice breaking on the Passaic River—and start patting down the corpse. Professional. Methodical. This is work now. Was work two minutes ago. The line blurs in ways that would make a priest weep.

No wallet. No ID. Smart. There's always a burner phone though. There's always one.

My fingers close around cold plastic in Sledge's jacket pocket. A Motorola Razr, matte black, probably paid for with cash from whatever job the Broker had him running. I flip it open. The screen glows sickly blue against the darkness of the alleyway, illuminating the frost creeping up the brick walls.

Three text messages. All from an unknown number.

*"Package delivered."*

*"Target acquired."*

*"The Watching Party thanks you."*

Well. Fuck.

I shove the phone in my own jacket and grab Sledge under the arms. He's dead weight in more than one sense of the word. Heavy. Warm blood soaking through my gloves as I drag him across the pavement toward the disposal chute—an industrial-sized vat of hydrofluoric acid that the chop-shop uses for "disposal." Efficient. Quiet. Permanent.

The bodies hit the ground with wet thuds. One, then two. Sledge and his partner, whose name I never bothered learning because names matter less when people choose to operate outside of them.

"Sorry," I mutter to no one. To myself. To Danny's ghost haunting my lungs along with everyone else's.

The hiss of the acid welcomes them like a lover. Chemical dissolution. Nothing left but stories and teeth fragments in my knuckles.

I stand there for a long moment after they've disappeared into the greenish foam, watching nothing. My breath plumes white in air that shouldn't be cold enough to do this. The Neon Hollow skyline presses down on me—a weight of glass and steel and too many secrets buried beneath asphalt and concrete.

The sliver of justice doctrine.

I call it that in my head sometimes when I need to sleep without screaming. Threefold cord: Penance, Revenge, and that third strand—frayed, thin, barely holding anything together—that I label Justice even though we both know it's a lie.

Penance is easy. Every punch I throw at someone who hurt someone else is penance for the times I didn't. For the nights I stayed home while monsters walked free. Revenge is honest work at least. Eye for an eye leaves everybody blind, sure, but blindness beats being food.

Justice? That's the sliver.

Never enough. It doesn't scrape the black iron out of Danny's lungs. Doesn't bring back the dead or un-break the broken or make anything right except for one small equation: someone who deserved pain felt pain instead of causing more pain somewhere else.

One sliver in a mountain of rot.

But here's what I tell myself in the freezing darkness of my own aura:

A sliver of justice for someone is infinitely better than no justice for anyone.

And tonight, Sledge had justice. Rough. Bloody. Final. The kind that makes frost spread across alleyways like death spreading through the city.

It will do for now.

Because what else am I going to do?

I pull out his burner phone again, scroll through contacts. Nothing useful—not even names, just numbers. But there's another text notification waiting:

*"The Broker is blind. The Watching Party sees. Check locker 402 at Blue Line transit hub."*

My jaw clenches so hard something pops in my skull.

The Broker. Blind.

That changes everything.

Or maybe nothing.

Either way—I've got a locker to check and a city full of people who need their slivers before they starve on empty scales.

I start walking toward McCarter Highway, leaving frost melting into bloodstains behind me like evidence dissolving with morning light.

---

## CHAPTER 3: THE WATCHING PARTY DEAD-DROP

The Crown Vic's engine dies with a final wheeze that echoes off the brick warehouses lining the South Side streets. I kill the headlights and sit there in the darkness, listening to rain drum against the roof. The sodium-vapor lamps outside paint everything in that sickly orange glow—the color of infection, the color of this whole damn city bleeding out into 2007.

My breath fogs the windshield. Not from cold. Never from cold anymore.

I slide out of the driver's seat, boots hitting pavement wet enough to mirror the neon sign of some all-night bodega three blocks down. The smell hits me immediately—ozone and motor oil and something darker underneath it all. Decay. Magic leaves a residue like roadkill leaves a stain.

Two blocks. That's what I give myself before someone notices I don't belong here, even if they can't put their finger on why. The kind of wrongness that makes your teeth ache.

The Blue Line Transit Hub rises up ahead like a tombstone made of concrete and bad architectural decisions. Some modernist fuck thought stacking slabs of gray misery would be beautiful once upon a time. He was wrong. The place looks like a bombed-out cathedral now, its arches spilling shadows thick as tar across the concourse.

A figure detaches itself from beneath one of those arches—a Goblin by the look of him, all twitchy limbs and eyes too big for his skull. Street-slang pours out of him like vomit: *"Spare a cred-chip, heavy? Just need a bump for the rail. My splice is screaming, man. Fucking screaming."*

I toss him a five without making eye contact. Don't want to know what he means by 'splice.' Don't want to know half the shit that goes down in this city anymore. The bill catches the light and he snatches it with fingers that shake like he's plugging into an electrical socket.

"Take a walk," I tell him, voice low. "This sector's about to get cold."

He's already backing away, muttering about how he didn't see nothing, hear nothing, but his feet are moving and that's what matters.

Locker 402 sits in the bank near the defunct ticketing booths. Rust has eaten through the metal like cancer, leaving weeping orange stains down the doors. I feed quarters into the mechanism—heavy clink, mechanical groan—and the door pops open with a hiss of displaced air.

Inside: black wax sealed tight around an envelope, resting on iron shavings that smell sharp enough to make my nose wrinkle. Warded, probably. Trapped maybe.

I pull out my PalmPilot, thumb scrolling through the detection protocols Mara insisted I learn. The screen glows blue-white in the darkness:

**NO ACTIVE MAGICAL TRAPS DETECTED**
**WARNING: RESIDUAL COLD-SOURCE SIGNATURE**

Of course there's frost-cobalt residue. Everything I touch these days gets coated in it eventually. I'm surprised it doesn't snow every time I take a piss at this point.

My fingers break the wax seal.

The envelope opens.

* * *

The envelope sits on my lap like a loaded weapon wrapped in wax paper. I'm parked under the skeletal canopy of the Blue Line overpass—rusted steel girders dripping condensation that freezes mid-air before shattering against the Crown Vic's hood. The heating system wheezes its last breath before dying completely, but I don't care. My hands are already numb from gripping the steering wheel.

I slide the knife under the wax seal.

It doesn't break clean. The blade catches, then the whole thing gives way with a wet crack that sounds too loud in the confined space. Black wax smears across my thumb as I peel back the flap. Inside: heavy parchment, the kind that costs more than most people make in a week, and a stack of glossy eight-by-tens held together by a rubber band.

The note first.

My fingers uncurl it slowly, and even in the dim dashboard light, I can read the handwriting—crisp, precise, with an old-fashioned flourish that makes my teeth ache:

*"Cole Reyes. Your vigilance has not gone unnoticed. We watch you watching them. Marcus Voss. High-spire corporate Elf. Shareholder in the grid that failed at Sub-Station Seven. He knows why those transformers blew. Why the union men died screaming. Why the air still smells like burnt copper three weeks later."*

I read it again. Then once more.

"Marcus fucking Voss," I say to the empty car, voice low and gravelly. The name tastes like rust in my mouth. Every South Sider knows Voss—a high-rise bloodsucker who buys up property while the neighborhoods rot around him. Owns half the Passaic River waterfront through shell companies and political bribes.

The photos spill into my lap.

Grainy night shots, probably taken with a long lens from across the shipyards. The drydock at Pylon #3—abandoned Union machinery, broken cranes hanging like nooses against the sky. But there's movement in these images. Men in tactical gear moving crates. Heavy stuff, the way they're grunting and straining under the weight. And beyond them, partially obscured but unmistakable: Marcus Voss himself, silk suit pristine despite the industrial filth, directing operations with hand signals.

Undocumented cargo. In the dead of night. While the union tries to figure out how their members ended up as grease stains on concrete walls.

My jaw clenches so hard something pops in my neck.

Mara's down in the BATC archives right now, digging through digital corpses for answers about Sub-Station Seven. If she finds what I think she'll find—the transaction records, the maintenance logs showing deliberate sabotage—that trail leads straight to Voss. Which means if he's moving tonight...

I grab the Nextel walkie-talkie from the passenger seat, thumb hovering over the push-to-talk button. Grimjaw's number is already pre-programmed. My Orcish second-in-command, currently running surveillance on the Kearny Marshes for any sign of those fucking Weavers.

*Thwack-thwack-thwack.* The windshield wipers beat an impatient rhythm as freezing rain streaks across the glass, distorting the skeletal cityscape beyond. Newark Bay lies somewhere out there in the darkness, its waters black as oil, reflecting nothing.

I hit talk.

"Grim," I say when his gruff voice crackles through, "we've got a situation at Pylon #3 Shipyards. Voss is making a move—tonight. Need you to pull back from the marsh and—"

Static cuts me off mid-sentence.

Not just static. A high-pitched whine that makes my ears ring and sets every nerve ending on fire. The photos scatter across the passenger seat, and for one horrifying moment, I swear I can see them *moving*, the figures in the grainy images turning their heads toward me despite the frozen shutter speed.

The frost-cobalt chill that never leaves me suddenly spikes like I've been dunked in dry ice. My breath comes out in clouds so thick they fog the inside of the windshield.

Something's here. Watching me watch them.

I slam my fist against the steering wheel, killing the radio with the impact. The dash lights flicker once, twice, then stabilize. When I look down at the scattered photos, they're just photos again. Dead paper. Motionless.

But the feeling remains—that crawling sensation between my shoulder blades that means eyes are on me.

*"We watch you watching them."*

Fucking right you do.

I scoop up the photographs with shaking fingers, stuffing them into my jacket pocket alongside the note. Marcus Voss thinks he's invisible up there in his glass tower, pulling strings while men die in the dark. Thinks his money buys him invisibility.

He's wrong.

And tonight, I'm going to make damn sure he understands what happens when the South Side finds you.

Even if it costs me this fucking chill running through my veins like liquid nitrogen.

Even if it means walking into whatever trap he's laid for anyone stupid enough to come looking.

The Crown Vic's engine turns over with a reluctant cough. Once. Twice. Then it roars to life, spewing black exhaust into the freezing rain-soaked night as I peel out from under the Blue Line overpass, heading south toward Passaic River.

Toward Pylon #3.

Toward Marcus Voss and whatever the hell he's hiding in those drydocks.

The windshield wipers keep time: *thwack-thwack-thwack.*

Like a countdown.

Like a heartbeat before violence.

* * *

The Nextel chirped twice at 2:47 AM—a harsh digital bark that cut through the dead air of the South Side streets. I was hunched behind the wheel of my Charger, parked under the skeletal shadow of the Pulaski Skyway's support columns, watching steam rise from the cracked pavement like ghosts from New Jersey's industrial past.

"Cole." Grimjaw's voice came through crackling and distorted, his usual rumble compressed by the cheap radio equipment. "What the fuck are you thinking?"

I keyed the mic without responding immediately. My breath hung in the air—frost-cobalt chill rolling off me in visible waves, condensing on the windshield. The temperature had dropped below freezing two hours ago, and the whole city felt like it was holding its breath.

"You awake?" Grimjaw tried again, and I could hear the edge of irritation underneath. Good. He needed to understand this wasn't a negotiation.

"Always awake," I said finally, keeping my voice low enough that it wouldn't carry beyond the car's interior. "Tunnel four. Get me access."

A long pause. In the distance, beyond the Newark Bay shoreline, I could see the navigation lights of container ships moving through the black water like luminescent insects. The Pylon #3 drydock sat dark against the horizon—a massive concrete monolith where Voss Maritime kept their decommissioned vessels rotting in saltwater graves.

"Boss, we're talking about corporate security. Voss has mercenary teams crawling all over that sector since Sub-Station Seven went tits-up." Grimjaw's accent was pure North Jersey—no fantasy affectations, no pretend medieval speech. Just an Orc who'd worked the docks for twenty years and knew how to swear in three languages, none of them Elvish. "You want me to get my guys killed over some hunch?"

"Not a hunch." I reached across to the passenger seat, fingers closing around cold steel. The shotgun magazines made satisfying metallic *clacks* as I slammed home fresh rounds—the sound of preparation, of purpose. "Just keep the perimeter clear. Four guys maximum. Eyes and ears only."

The smell inside the Charger was stale cigarette smoke and old coffee. My hex-reserves—blood-iron containers filled with concentrated magical energy, hidden under the floor mat—felt warm against my palm when I checked them. Three full vials. Enough for what I had planned.

"You're pulling my guys off third shift for a ghost hunt," Grimjaw rumbled back, his patience wearing thin. "Voss's corporate suits have that drydock locked up tighter than a drum. We'll pop the grating on tunnel four, but you're on your own once you're inside."

"That's all I need." I released the mic button and watched my breath crystallize in the air. The frost-cobalt chill wasn't just magic anymore—it was part of me now, seeping into everything I touched. The door handle felt like ice when I grabbed it, though I hadn't breathed on it.

I stepped out into the November darkness. The industrial seawall stretched before me—a cracked concrete barrier covered in graffiti tags and rust-streaked chain-link fencing. Beyond that, the entrance to the maintenance tunnels, half-hidden by fog rolling in from the bay.

My boots crunched on broken glass as I approached the water's edge. The smell hit me immediately—that distinctive combination of brine, diesel fuel, and chemical runoff that meant New Jersey waterways. Oil-slicked and freezing, probably contaminated with who knew what chemicals from decades of industrial abuse.

The Nextel chirped again.

"Tunnel four is open," Grimjaw said simply. "Thirty seconds window. Make it count."

I dropped the radio into my jacket pocket without responding. Thirty seconds was all I needed.

The water lapped at my ankles as I waded in, feeling the shock of cold bite through denim. Above me, the massive silhouette of a drydocked freighter loomed against the night sky—the rusted hull rising hundreds of feet, its weight making the whole structure groan audibly in the wind.

Somewhere beneath those tons of rotting steel, something had survived Sub-Station Seven. Something Voss Maritime didn't want anyone to find.

And I intended to make damn sure they couldn't hide it any longer.

## CHAPTER 4: THE PYLON #3 DRYDOCK RASHOMON SYNC

The rust tastes like copper on my tongue as I drop into the drydock floor. Concrete crumbles beneath my boots—someone was here recently, someone heavy enough to crack the decades-old surface. The November air bites through my leather jacket, carrying that familiar Port Newark stench: stagnant seawater, diesel fuel, and underneath it all, the sweet rot of metal eating itself alive.

I move between the containers like a ghost. Forty-foot steel behemoths stacked three high, their sides streaked with orange-brown rust that weeps down to the ground. My breath clouds in front of my face, but the frost-cobalt humming just under my skin keeps my core temperature steady. The cold doesn't touch me anymore—not since the Breach changed what I am.

That's when I catch it. A signature. Faint, but distinct.

White lilac.

My jaw clenches so hard my teeth ache. *Mara.* What the hell is she doing here? This is Voss territory, and even the Bureau knows to stay clear after dark. Unless... unless she's gone rogue completely.

I track the signature around a container marked *"FRAGILE - GLASS."* Someone's already pried open one end of the beast—the lock dangling by twisted bolts, the door hanging at a drunk angle. Inside, dim light from a work lamp spills across puddles of something I don't want to identify. Diesel maybe. Maybe worse.

I slip inside. My shotgun comes up instinctively, the weight familiar and comforting against my shoulder. The container reeks of rust and unwashed bodies. There's a cheap folding table, some crates stacked as makeshift furniture. And movement—

A shadow detaches from the corner, and suddenly I'm staring into the barrel of a rune-etched service pistol. The blue-white glow from the engraved runes catches on the chamber, and I can see the tiny copper jacket of the round already seated.

"Give me one reason not to put a hollow-point through your chest, Reyes."

Mara's voice. Rougher than I remember. Harder.

My finger stays firm on the trigger guard. Frost-cobalt crawls up my forearm, responding to the adrenaline spike. The temperature in the container drops ten degrees in three seconds. Condensation explodes across every surface—not water droplets, but frost forming in crystalline patterns that spread like neural pathways across the corrugated steel walls.

"I could say the same thing about you, Commander," I say, keeping my voice level. "Only difference is I've seen what happens when Bureau operatives get sloppy with their weapons."

Her eyes are darker than I remember. Not just the physical color—something deeper. Burnt-out. She's been running harder than I thought.

"If you know what's good for you, lower that cannon."

We're locked now. Two guns, two breathing spaces apart. Her white-lilac wards flare around her wrist—they're corrupted though, threaded through with ash-gray static that wasn't there before the Breach. That static makes my teeth ache. Makes my stomach turn.

I can feel her magic pressing against mine. The air between us starts to crackle. My frost-cobalt wants to expand, to freeze everything solid. Her lilac-ash wants to burn, to consume. Neither of us moves.

"So we're doing this dance again," she whispers. There's something beneath the menace now. Something raw. "Last time you got lucky. Don't think it'll happen twice."

"Lucky?" I let out a short, humorless laugh. It comes out as vapor in the freezing air. "Is that what they tell themselves at Quantico? That I got lucky?"

The shotgun doesn't waver. Neither does her pistol.

We stand there in the rusted container, surrounded by the stink of decay and diesel fuel, while somewhere outside the drydock gates, Newark sleeps on. But sleep doesn't come easy on the South Side anymore. Not since 2001. Not since the sky tore open and god-knows-what started bleeding through.

Mara's hand tightens on her weapon. I can see it in the way her knuckles whiten, the way the runes on the barrel flare brighter.

"You son of a—"

"Wait." I cut her off, slowly lowering the shotgun until the muzzle points at the floor. The movement costs me something—makes me vulnerable—but if we keep this up, one of us is going down regardless of who shoots first.

My left hand reaches into my jacket. Slowly. Deliberately. Mara tracks every millimeter of motion with those dark eyes.

I pull out my PalmPilot. The screen glows blue in the dim light from the work lamp, casting shadows across her face that make her look like death itself wearing a Bureau uniform.

"What the hell are you—"

"Just look at it," I say quietly. My thumb hovers over the power button. "Look at the date on the last log entry. November third. Two days before your supposed mission to secure the Passaic River bridges."

She doesn't take her eyes off mine. "Reyes..."

"Trust me for thirty seconds, Commander. That's all I'm asking."

The frost-cobalt pulses around me like a heartbeat. Her lilac-ash crackles back. The air tastes like ozone and rust and something electric that makes my hair stand on end.

Mara's jaw works. Once. Twice. Then she glances down at the PalmPilot.

And freezes.

"This... this isn't possible."

* * *

The rust smell hit me first—that metallic tang of iron eating itself alive. It coated my throat, mixed with stagnant seawater and diesel fumes that made my eyes water. I'd been holding my breath without realizing it when I slipped into the drydock container, and now my lungs burned as I exhaled.

My PalmPilot felt like a brick in my pocket, its ruggedized casing warm against my hip. Danny's last gift to me before he went dark. The decrypted audio file still playing on loop in my head from the transponder data he'd pulled—those fragments of conversation that didn't make sense until they did, like puzzle pieces slotting into place at the worst possible moment.

I set the device down on a rusted oil drum, its surface pitted with decades of corrosion. The green pixelated glow of the screen seemed unnaturally bright in the darkness of the container. My frost-cobalt static crackled around my fingers involuntarily, responding to the adrenaline surge. I could taste ozone on my tongue.

The container was barely twenty feet long, metal walls pressing in on all sides. A metal box within a larger metal box—the shipyard drydock surrounding us like a tomb. I heard her footsteps before I saw her.

Mara.

She froze in the doorway, pistol raised, those white-lilac and ash-gray trails of static already beginning to coalesce around her hands. Her trauma bleed smelled like charred wool and burnt coffee beans—those Elven scars she couldn't hide any more than I could hide mine.

"Cole," she said. Not a question. Recognition sharp and immediate.

I didn't move toward my own weapon. Instead, I tapped the PalmPilot screen, bringing up the audio interface. "We need to listen to this together."

Her eyes narrowed, but something in my voice must have registered because she lowered the pistol incrementally, slowly enough that she could raise it again if needed. She reached into her jacket with her free hand and pulled out what looked like an antique—a Sony MiniDisc player, all silver plastic and buttons that required actual finger pressure instead of touch sensitivity.

"The fuck are you doing with a MiniDisc?" I asked before I could stop myself.

"It holds three hours of uncompressed audio." Her tone was flat, professional. "And it's untraceable by most modern scanners. Pre-digital infrastructure."

She plugged a patch cable between the MiniDisc player and my PalmPilot. The mechanical whir as the disc began spinning up seemed obscenely loud in the confined space. My frost-cobalt static intensified, tiny ice crystals forming at the edges of the container where the temperature dropped. Her white-lilac energy responded, creating a crackling tension in the air that made every hair on my body stand up.

The sync completed. Audio streamed from both devices simultaneously, overlapping perfectly.

*"...the container ship manifest matches, Voss will have his payment..."*

A high-spire Elf, his accent clipped and corporate-smooth. One of those lawyers who wore suits worth more than a machinist's annual salary.

*"...union contracts signed through December, no problems on our end. The Syndicate understands the arrangement..."* 

An Ogre-Kin, voice like gravel grinding underfoot. An enforcer. Someone used to breaking things that couldn't be fixed.

They were talking about payoffs. Coordination. But not between enemies.

Between business partners.

Mara's face went pale beneath her tan. I watched her expression shift through disbelief, anger, and something worse—betrayal so complete it hollowed out your insides. That look I'd seen in the mirror after Danny first showed me the transponder data.

"They're owned by the same puppeteer," I said, leaning over the oil drum, keeping my voice low and rumbling. "Your BATC bosses and my Syndicate handlers. They aren't fighting a turf war, Mara. They're putting on a show."

She stared at the screen, at the audio waveform displaying two voices in perfect synchronization. Her Elven corporate conditioning warring with the undeniable truth playing out in real-time before us.

"It's why the violence escalated right when the union negotiations started." My words came faster now, pieces connecting. "It's why they hit our dockworkers hard enough to draw attention but never hard enough to actually stop operations. It's why the BATC raids always happen just after a syndicate shipment moves through."

"Exploiting the divide," Mara whispered. She looked up at me, and for the first time since I'd known her, she looked uncertain. Vulnerable. "Keeping the Elves and Dwarves at each other's throats while they bleed the city dry."

The realization hit us both like a physical blow—the weight of the conspiracy, the scale of it, how deep the rot ran through every layer of authority we'd trusted or opposed or simply existed under.

Before we could process the magnitude of it, before we could even begin to strategize what came next, the sound hit us.

*Thwump-thwump-thwump.*

Military-grade helicopter rotors, so close that the entire corrugated roof of the container vibrated with each beat. The metal walls rattled, dust cascading from above. Searchlights swept across the exterior, painting moving shadows that flickered across Mara's face like a death sentence being written in light.

Someone knew we were here. Someone with air support.

Mara grabbed my arm, pulling me toward the opposite side of the container as the searchlight beams intensified, converging on this specific box among thousands scattered throughout the shipyard drydock. Through gaps in the corrugation, I caught glimpses of dark shapes descending on cables. Tactical teams.

"The PalmPilot," Mara said sharply. "Can you wipe it clean?"

I was already trying, fingers flying across the screen even as my frost-cobalt static began responding defensively to the threat outside. But the device was stubborn, fighting my commands, and I realized—

"—it's networked to their systems," I finished grimly. "They're watching everything we do. It's not just a data retrieval device. It's a tracker."

The searchlight beam slammed directly through a gap above us, blinding white that painted everything in harsh relief. And in that moment of illumination, I saw her face clearly—the same fear and determination I felt reflected back at me.

We'd found the truth.

Now they were coming to make sure we took it to our graves.

* * *

The smell hits me first—that cloying mixture of iron oxide and stagnant seawater mixed with diesel fumes thick enough to chew. My boots squelch against wet concrete as I haul myself up into the drydock container, the corrugated steel walls still dripping from when they drained this section last week. 

Something's wrong.

The air feels electric—not my kind of electric, not telluric current singing through my bones—but something else. Something sharper. Chemical. Wrong.

"Grimjaw, you seeing what I'm seeing?" I mutter into the Nextel clipped to my vest collar, keeping low as I move deeper into the container. Stacked shipping containers loom like metal tombstones in the darkness ahead.

Static crackles in response. Then: "Negative on visuals, Boss. Thermal shows three heat signatures in your sector. Could be hostiles, could be—"

The rotors cut him off.

Not one set. Two. Maybe more, echoing off the drydock walls. The sound builds from a distant thrum to an earth-shaking roar that rattles loose bolts from the container walls. Metal screams. My teeth rattle in my skull.

"Contact! Air!" Grimjaw's voice erupts over the comm, all gravel and panic. "Boss, they're corporate gunships but no markings! No fucking transponders!"

I drop low behind a stack of rusted barrels, heart hammering against my ribs. The spotlight hits first—a blinding white spear that lances through gaps in the container walls, painting everything in harsh, unforgiving light. Dust motes dance in the beam like deadly snow.

Then I see her.

White-blonde hair. Tactical gear that looks custom-sewn. And those eyes—violet, glowing faintly in the reflected light. Mara. Of course it's fucking Mara.

She's at the far end of the container, crouched by another stack of containers, frozen like she's seen a ghost. Our eyes lock for half a second before the spotlight sweeps again, and we're both plunged back into relative darkness.

*"We got company,"* I hiss over the Nextel, knowing she'll hear it too if Grimjaw patches me through. *"Hostile air assets. Gunships."*

Mara doesn't respond with words. Instead, her hands come up, pale static crackling between her fingers—not frost-cobalt like mine, but something colder. Whiter. Ash-gray with veins of sickly violet that make my skin crawl.

The spotlight finds us again.

This time it stays.

*"GRJAW!"* I bark into the comm. *"What do you have on those birds?"*

The rotors are deafening now, so close the entire container shakes. Something metal clangs against the exterior wall. Then another sound—that distinctive, bone-chilling shriek of rocket propulsion building to full burn.

*"Willie-Pete! Boss, they're loaded with white phosphorus!"* Grimjaw's voice is raw panic. *"Get clear! GET CLEAR NOW!"*

I don't think. Can't think. My veins bulge black as the telluric current floods my system—I can feel it singing through every capillary, every artery, pooling in my chest cavity until breathing becomes an effort.

Mara's already moving toward me, hand outstretched—

The rockets ignite fully.

Three streams of fire—bright white, chemical-bright, beautiful and terrible—curve through the night air and slam into the container above us.

The explosion is biblical.

Steel screams. Metal vaporizes. The container erupts outward in a shower of molten fragments and superheated gas. White light floods everything, bleaching color from the world. Heat hits me like a solid wall—my skin tightens across my skull, my eyes water from the thermal wash.

I grab Mara by the tactical vest, yanking her away from the container doors just as the first wave of fire rolls over our position. Her scream gets lost in the roar. My frost-cobalt flares instinctively, creating a bubble of relativistic cold around us—but it's not enough, won't be enough, the heat is too much, too fast—

Another impact.

Then another.

The drydock becomes a kill-box. Rounds punch through steel walls like tissue paper. Machine gun fire—that distinctive *thwack-thwack-thwack*—joins the chaos. The helicopter searchlights paint us in their beams, relentless, hunting.

*"We aren't running,"* I snarl through clenched teeth, veins standing out on my neck as I pour more current into the shield. My fingers find Mara's arm—she's trembling, or maybe that's just the vibration from the rotors shaking reality itself—and I pull her behind the relative cover of a support pillar just as the next volley tears through where we were standing half a second ago.

Her violet eyes meet mine again.

*"We can't outrun white phosphorus,"* she shouts over the noise, her voice barely audible even this close.

The rockets are reloading. I can hear it—the mechanical whine of the launcher systems, the hiss of fuel cells charging for another burst. We have seconds. Maybe three. Maybe two.

My eyes go completely black.

Blood-iron shield. Heaviest one I've ever woven. It costs me—I can feel the price already, organs straining, something wet and warm trickling from my nose—but there's no other choice now.

The next salvo comes in.

Everything goes red.

---

## CHAPTER 5: WHITE PHOSPHORUS & HEARTH-COALS

The first rocket screams in from the north, trailing smoke like a dying prayer against the pre-dawn darkness. I see it in my peripheral vision—a streak of orange against black—and my brain does the math in nanoseconds. Thermal targeting. They've got the containers painted already.

"COLE!" Mara's voice cuts through everything but it's too late, always too fucking late when you're dancing this close to oblivion.

The missile hits Pylon #3 and the world goes white.

Not metaphorical white. Not cinematic flash-bang white. This is *white*—a nuclear sun born from solid fuel oxidizer and thermite, a star collapsing into existence at ground zero. My retinas burn even through closed eyelids. The shockwave hits like God's fist slamming into the earth, lifting the entire drydock section six inches before gravity remembers its job and drops us back down with teeth-rattling finality.

I don't think. Thinking is for men who have time.

My body moves before my mind catches up, muscle memory from a thousand fights in a dozen lifetimes. I'm already moving toward Mara when the second rocket impacts, closer this time—I can feel the heat on my skin, taste copper and ozone as my blood boils just under the surface.

*No.*

Third rocket. Fourth. The sky opens up and pisses fire down on the shipyards, transforming the rusted graveyard of steel into an inferno. White phosphorus rounds start raining down like meteorites, each one bursting on impact into liquid hell—1,500 degrees Fahrenheit, burning hotter than the surface of the sun, impossible to extinguish, feeding on oxygen and flesh alike.

I grab Mara with hands that aren't entirely human anymore, fingers elongating into claws as my baseline magic kicks into overdrive. The frost-cobalt is there, always cold, always dead-silent at the base of my spine—but underneath it now, something else. Something *warm*.

The shipping container we've been using for cover explodes inward, shrapnel screaming past my head close enough to kiss. A chunk of metal the size of my forearm punches through where my heart was half a second ago. I twist, taking the impact on my shoulder, feeling bone crack and reform in microseconds.

"Stay down!" The words tear out of my throat raw and animal.

But she's already down. I slam her onto the steel floor of the adjacent container, my weight pinning her completely. My back takes the worst of the heat as the white phosphorus starts eating through the roof above us, droplets of molten death hissing as they splash onto the corrugated iron.

This is it. This is how you die in 2007 North Jersey—burned alive in a drydock while men who sold their souls to demons watch from beyond the perimeter fence.

*Fuck. That.*

My left hand drives into the container wall. Iron screams as my fingers punch through three inches of reinforced steel like paper. Blood flows—not mine—and the metal obeys. It *bends*. It ripples upward under my palm, responding to will that predates language, older than fear, older than hope.

I pull. The walls groan. My right hand joins in, both palms pressed flat against rust and decay, and I'm drawing metal up around us like a cocoon, like a tomb, like a shield forged in desperation and blood.

The phosphorus rained down faster now, dozens of impacts per second, each one detonating with sound like cracking bones and splitting skulls. The liquid fire runs down the exterior of our dome, pooling at the base, consuming everything. The smell hits me—melting steel, burning chemical accelerant, vaporized seawater, and underneath it all, something sweet and wrong.

*Lilac.*

Mara's scent. Her perfume. Her soul made odor.

My frost-cobalt snaps.

Not gradually, not over time, but like a wire pulled too tight finally breaking—the cold that has been my constant companion since 1997, the dead-silent weight that let me kill without hesitation or remorse, just... *shatters*.

And where it breaks, heat floods in.

Not just warmth. Not just the fire burning outside our makeshift fortress. This is *heat*—a furnace built in my chest, fed by rage and terror and something else I don't have words for because words are for men who aren't currently being immolated alive while protecting the only woman who ever mattered.

The iron beneath my hands glows red. Then orange. Then yellow-white.

My vision tunnels, expands, fractures into prismatic shards. I can see the individual molecules of steel, can feel the quantum spin of every atom responding to the pressure building inside me. This isn't baseline magic. This isn't the frost-cobalt or whatever new fucked-up thing is trying to bloom in its place.

This is raw *power*, undifferentiated and dangerous as a loaded gun pointed at your own head.

"Cole!" Mara's voice cuts through the expanding roar in my ears. "COLE!"

I feel her hands on my face. Warm. Alive. Real.

The iron dome cracks.

A fissure runs from top to bottom, white phosphorus pouring through the gap like liquid stars. The smell hits me again—lilac and hearth-coals and something ancient and hungry waking up after a very long sleep.

*Oh God.*

*What have you done?*

* * *

The pressure builds like a scream trapped behind teeth.

My hands are bleeding on her tactical vest—not from the frost that should be there, but from something else entirely. Something warm. My fingers dig into the fabric, knuckles white against the black material, and I feel it then: the first crack in my foundation.

The dead-silent cold that's lived in my chest since Sub-Station Seven shatters.

It doesn't melt gradually. It *explodes*.

One moment I'm holding back white phosphorus with the zero-remorse void that made me the Butcher of South Side. The next, my entire body erupts like a goddamn supernova of warmth. Frost-cobalt energy—my signature, my shield, my identity for ten years—flashes once, twice, then ignites into something I've never felt before.

*The hearth.*

Heat floods through my veins. Not chemical heat. Not the sickly burn of phosphorus. This is different. This is home-fire warmth, the kind that remembers when you were small and scared and needed protection. It radiates outward from where our bodies press together, expanding until the entire cramped space beneath the dome glows with it.

The scent hits me next.

Ozone and burning iron-gall vanish instantly, replaced by something that makes my knees want to buckle. Warm hearth-coals. Rich, earthy, comforting. And underneath it all—the ghost of white lilac. Mara's scent. Her *ward*. Her essence, somehow intertwined with mine now.

*"No,"* I breathe out, but it sounds wrong. Desperate. Stripped of all my noir armor.

My heart hammers against my ribs—a sensation I haven't felt in a decade. Each beat is agony and ecstasy combined. Blood rushes in my ears. The frost-cobalt sparks dancing in Mara's eyes catch the light from my own aura, and they're not cold anymore. They're warm. Alive. *Connected*.

"Reyes..." Her voice catches as she inhales deeply. "Your wards... they're *burning*."

I know.

God help me, I know exactly what this means.

The 4th-Law paradigm shift slams into me like a freight train. My Weave, carefully constructed over years of vigilante work, of killing, of maintaining that perfect dead-silent cold—it's unraveling. Rewriting itself around her. Tethering to her life-force like vine tendrils seeking sunlight.

"I know," I rasp, the words torn from somewhere deep in my chest. Somewhere I thought was hollow. "I know."

The irony isn't lost on me. Ten years of being a machine, a weapon, a ghost who couldn't feel his own heartbeat. All to keep people safe. To protect the South Side from things that go bump in the night. And here I am, finally feeling *something real*, while the iron dome above us groans under the sustained barrage of those gunships.

Metal shrieks. Structural supports buckle with a sound like tearing flesh.

We have maybe seconds before the whole damn thing collapses.

But right now, pressed together in this moment, surrounded by warmth and hearth-coals and white lilac, I'm more terrified than I've ever been. Because I understand now what the old-timers meant when they talked about the cost of true connection. The price of letting someone else inside your walls.

My hands are still gripping her vest, but I can feel her breath against my neck. Fast. Scared. Alive.

And for the first time since Danny went into the iron-lung, so am I.

The dome shudders violently overhead, chunks of rusted metal raining down around us.

* * *

The world exploded in white noise and blue static as my frost-cobalt died, the dome shattering like a mirror struck by a hammer. For one impossible moment, I felt the heat—the actual *heat*—of something burning in my chest, not cold, not empty, but *warm*, like standing too close to an oven door that had been baking bread for hours.

Then gravity remembered me.

My hands were on Mara's shoulders—when did I grab her?—and we were falling through rusted steel that screamed as it gave way beneath us. The container loomed above, already wreathed in the first licks of blue-white flame from whatever payload the Serpent had stashed inside. I saw it all in a flash: the thermite charge, Grimjaw's work, the only reason we weren't already vaporized.

The water hit like a freight train made of ice.

We plunged into blackness that tasted of oil and decades of chemical runoff. The shock stole my breath, then the freezing temperature drove it out of my lungs in bubbles that raced toward a surface I couldn't see. My leather jacket, soaked through, dragged at my arms. Mara was a struggling weight beside me—or maybe I was dead weight, and she was the one fighting—but our hands stayed locked together even as the current tried to tear us apart.

I kicked toward where I thought light might be.

My vision swam with afterimages: the collapsing dome, Mara's face in the amber light, the scent of *hearth-coals* that should have been impossible, that should have meant I'd finally lost my mind completely. But the cold was real. The pain was real. The warmth still glowing somewhere deep behind my ribs? Also real, and that terrified me more than anything else ever had.

My head broke surface in absolute darkness punctuated by a distant, thudding rhythm—secondary explosions, the drydock tearing itself apart from the inside out. I gasped, choking on seawater, and felt Mara's hand clamp onto my wrist with desperate strength.

"Tunnel," I sputtered, trying to orient myself. "Grimjaw... extraction point..."

The current pushed us through a submerged corridor barely wide enough for my shoulders. Something brushed against my leg—I didn't look down—and the walls were slick with something that wasn't quite algae but wasn't exactly biological either. This far beneath the docks, the Kill-Boxes bled into older infrastructure, pre-war maintenance tunnels that predated the whole industrial sprawl above them.

We hit concrete hard enough to knock what little air remained from my lungs again. My forearms burned—not frost-cobalt burn, but something worse, like touching a live wire. I collapsed onto an embankment slick with God-knows-what, coughing up water that tasted like it had dissolved half the Passaic River bottom.

Mara lay beside me, her breath coming in ragged gasps, her white hair plastered dark against her skull. In the weak moonlight filtering through a grate somewhere above, I could see the glow clinging to her skin—the same impossible lilac luminescence that coated my hands, that made the air around us smell of *home* and *firelight* and things I'd never experienced because I was raised in a machine shop smelling of cutting oil and despair.

"You're glowing," she whispered, her voice raw. Not afraid, just... observant. Like she'd just seen a theorem prove itself backwards and was trying to understand the mathematics of it.

I held up my hands, watching the residue pulse faintly with each heartbeat. The scent intensified—warmth and coal smoke and that white lilac that shouldn't exist outside a funeral parlor but somehow smelled like salvation instead of death.

"What did you do?" Mara asked, sitting up slowly, her eyes fixed on mine. "What did you *give* away?"

The question hung between us as a flashlight beam cut through the darkness at the far end of the tunnel. Heavy footsteps—Grimjaw's distinctive gait, too measured for panic, too purposeful for anything but retrieval.

"Boss! You alive down there?" His voice echoed off the concrete walls, but beneath it ran an undertone I recognized from years of working alongside him: concern. Fear, even. Grimjaw didn't frighten easy.

"We're alive, Grimjaw," I called back, my voice steady despite my heart hammering against my ribs like it wanted out. Despite the way my forearms still smoked with heat I couldn't explain. "Get the truck."

I looked back at Mara, saw her staring at me with an expression I'd never expected to see directed at Cole Reyes, South Side Machinist and Vigilante. Not respect—she'd had that before. Not desire—I wasn't sure what that looked like anymore. Something else entirely.

My doctrine—the sliver of justice I'd carried since I was twelve years old, sharpened in the machine shop while my father bled out on the floor above—had just been rewritten by something fundamental. By someone who smelled of white lilac and made my frost-cobalt burn warm instead of cold.

*She* was my sliver now.

The thought should have horrified me.

Instead, as Grimjaw's silhouette grew larger in the flashlight beam, as he stopped dead in his tracks and his yellow eyes narrowed with recognition of what he could smell on the air—that impossible mixture of iron and lilac, of the Butcher's work and warmth—I realized I was smiling through split lips and blood and seawater.

"Boss..." Grimjaw rumbled, taking another step closer, his nostrils flaring as he processed the scent wafting off my soaked jacket. The hearth-coals. The goddamn *hearth-coals*. "What did you do?"
