I stood slowly, helping Mara to her feet. My leather creaked wetly, and I could feel the residue coating my palms starting to seep into my skin, becoming part of whatever had been broken and remade inside Pylon #3.

"I found my way home," I told him, and meant it more than any words I'd ever spoken in my entire miserable life. "Now let's get moving."

---

## CHAPTER 6: THE TORCH BURNS BOTH WAYS

The gunship's white-phosphorus payload turned the night into day—a blinding magnesium flare that painted everything in shades of hellfire orange and bone-white. I shoved Mara hard toward the extraction point, watched her stumble and catch herself against twisted metal, already moving without thinking.

"GO!"

My voice barely cut through the screaming wind and the *whoosh-WHOOSH-WHOOSH* of rotary-wing downwash. The drydock floor beneath us was slick with phosphorescent oil, burning pools of it reflecting the hell-light like gates to somewhere worse than here.

I didn't wait to see if she made it. Couldn't afford to.

Behind us—no, around us now—they were coming fast-roped from above. Corporate Elves in black tactical gear, their tapetum lucidum eyes catching the firelight like demonic headlamps. Military-grade hardware clutched to chests protected by Kevlar and hex-sigils I couldn't read past the glare.

My shotgun came up instinctively. Pump-action. Depleted-bismuth slugs already chambered.

*CLACK-CLACK-CLACK.*

The first two went down before they could properly acquire targets. Bismuth shredded through their protective wards like tissue paper, the slugs' anti-metahuman composition doing exactly what it said on the tin. No freezing effect though—I noticed that immediately. My blood-hexes weren't dropping the ambient temperature anymore. Instead, something else entirely was happening.

Heat bloomed in my chest, radiating outward. The iron-gall residue on my hands and forearms glowed with a warm, ember-like luminescence. Warmth spread across the concrete where my shields manifested, actually *melting* the puddles rather than flash-freezing them into slippery hazards. The smell hit me next: hearth-coals, burning wood, smoke thick enough to taste mixed with an undertone of white-lilac so sharp and sweet it shouldn't have existed in this chemical warfare nightmare.

"Fuck," I breathed, racking another shell as three more operatives dropped into position.

They moved with that trained precision corporate money buys. Flanking maneuvers, crossfire positions, overlapping fields of fire. One raised an RPG toward Mara's escape vector—

I slammed both palms down against the concrete.

Blood-iron barricade.

The shield erupted upward, a wall of crystalline red that caught the RPG's payload square-on. The explosion walked the perimeter of my barrier, rolling heat-waves across its surface, but it held. For maybe half a second.

Then the sheer kinetic force of the warhead shattered it.

Shrapnel screamed past my head close enough to feel individual bits kiss my hair. But I was already moving, momentum carrying me into CQC range before they could react. Elbow strike to one throat—cartilage crunched wetly. Spin, bring the shotgun's stock around—the other operator's knee bent wrong, capslock of femur snapping audible even over the wind.

The third tried to bring his sidearm up. My hand closed around his wrist mid-motion. The iron-gall residue on my fingers seared through his glove like acid, skin bubbling beneath synthetic leather as I yanked him forward and *shoved* a localized spike through his sternum. He gurgled something in corporate-speak about sector leases and Voss holding paper, eyes going wide and bright with recognition before his lights went out completely.

I dropped him.

My jaw stung where a grazing round had kissed bone. Warm blood trickled down my neck, mixing with the sweat on my collar. When I touched the wound, my fingertips came away smoking—not from frost, but from that same ember-heat radiating from my core now.

Gone. All gone. The frost-cobalt cold that'd been my signature since first making blood was just... gone. Replaced by this terrifying warmth that smelled like her. Mara. White-lilac and woodsmoke and something deeper underneath that made my teeth ache.

"Cole!"

Her voice carried across the burning drydock, desperate and distant. The extraction point was clear now—she'd made it. Good. That was good.

More fast-ropes were descending though. Maybe six or seven operatives still coming down into hell while the gunship circled overhead, its white-phosphorus pods already reloaded and seeking fresh targets.

Time to vanish.

I ran for the storm drains, boots splashing through burning oil, heat rising in waves that should have been killing me but instead felt almost pleasant against my fevered skin. Behind me, automatic fire chewed up concrete where I'd been half a second ago. A rocket-propelled grenade whistled past close enough to buffet me with pressure alone.

The grate was ahead. Steel reinforced, heavy-duty drainage for when the Passaic flooded worse than usual. I hit it at full sprint, grabbed with both hands, and *wrenched*.

Bolts screamed. Metal shrieked.

It came free in my hands as another RPG impact sent shockwaves across the entire structure. I dropped through without hesitation, falling into darkness thick enough to swallow light whole.

My body hit water below with a splash that sent spray everywhere. Cold. Actually cold—real cold unlike anything I'd felt in days now. The underground channels here ran deep beneath Newark Bay, ancient infrastructure from when this whole area was still passable marshland rather than industrial wasteland.

I surfaced gasping, treading in pitch blackness broken only by emergency lights spaced too far apart.

My jaw still bled. My hands still smoked with ember-light.

And I could still smell her on my skin like a brand I couldn't shake loose.

* * *

The sub-basement reeks of ozone and burnt copper. My boots scrape against concrete littered with socket wrenches and spent plasma cartridges. Every step sends a fresh spike of pain through my left knee—the kind of deep-joint agony that makes you wonder if you'll even make it to morning without surgery.

Bram Kovacs hunches over the workbench, dwarf hands moving with impossible precision as he traces an arcano-plasma cutter around a Panasonic Toughbook's magnesium chassis. The blue-white flame casts dancing shadows across his scarred face. He doesn't look up when I enter, but then again, he never does. The old bull can hear a rat pissing on cotton from three floors down.

"Got your order," he grunts, gesturing toward the corner with his welding goggles still clamped to his forehead. "Depleted-bismuth bits came in from the Hoboken supplier. Cost us extra."

Behind me, I hear the deliberate thud of heavy boots. Grimjaw.

My foreman materializes from the darkness between shipping crates, seven-foot-two of compact muscle and jutting tusks. His yellow eyes track me like a predator watching wounded prey. For a guy built like a brick shithouse, he moves quiet—too quiet.

"You're bleeding," he states flatly. Not a question.

He tosses a rag at my chest. I catch it one-handed, press it to the cut above my eyebrow. Warm. Too warm. The blood shouldn't be this hot.

"You were supposed to be back by midnight," Grimjaw continues, circling me like a shark. "It's three-fifteen. Something happen at that drydock?"

The radio crackles something about the Devils game, but Grimjaw reaches out and kills it with one meaty finger. Silence crashes down like a tomb lid.

I start wiping my face, trying to buy time. The rag comes away dark red, streaked with something that glints metallic under the fluorescents.

"Job went sideways," I mutter. "Had to extract early."

"That ain't job-related." Grimjaw leans in, nostrils flaring wide. His broad snout twitches. "Christ, Cole. What is that smell?"

Bram finally looks up from his work, those ancient dwarf eyes narrowing. He sets down his torch carefully, the plasma sizzling as it cuts off.

"It smells like... flowers?" Bram's voice carries genuine confusion. "Lilac? In *here*?"

Grimjaw's hand shoots out, clamping onto my pauldron hard enough to dent steel. He yanks me close, bringing me nose-to-nose with his scarred muzzle.

"Not just lilac," he growls. "I know that stink. Been around enough badge-magic types to recognize high-spire signature residue when I'm standing knee-deep in it." His eyes bore into mine. "That's Aegis-grade protective enchantment leaking off you like cheap perfume. Which means either you got yourself drafted against your will, or—"

"Or what?" I ask quietly.

His jaw clenches, tusks grinding audibly. "Or you're sleeping with someone who wears a Federal Protectives sigil on her collar."

The sub-basement goes dead silent except for the dripping of an old radiator somewhere in the walls. My hand moves instinctively toward my sidearm—a habit I can never break—but Grimjaw's grip doesn't loosen.

"The Butcher of Sterling Manor doesn't get involved with Federal Protectives," he says slowly, like he's explaining basic arithmetic to a child. "It's suicide by bureaucracy, and we both know it." He shakes his head, disgust twisting his features. "Weld your heart to a brass-badge, boss, and the torch burns both ways. She goes down, she's taking your whole damn ribcage with her. The Feds don't play nice with freelancers once they've claimed ownership."

"I'm not owned by anyone."

"Not yet." Grimjaw releases my pauldron and steps back, but his yellow eyes don't leave mine. "But you're tagged now. I can smell it. That white-lilac and hearth-coals combo? That's permanent marker in the magical bloodstream. You're carrying her wards, her protection, maybe even some of her combat hexes as residual contamination."

He runs his hand over his shaved skull, clearly troubled. "This is bad, Cole. Really fucking bad. What'd you do—pull some civilian out of a situation that should've been a clean extraction?"

I don't answer. Can't answer.

Grimjaw reads my silence perfectly. His massive frame slumps slightly.

"Fuck," he whispers. Then louder: "FUCK!"

Bram clears his throat. "The depleted-bismuth drills are calibrated for tomorrow's job on the Passaic docks. We can proceed as planned if needed."

I appreciate Bram trying to normalize things, but Grimjaw isn't having it.

"Planned?" My foreman laughs bitterly. "There ain't no plan when the Federal Protectives have their hooks in you! You know what happens next, right? They'll test you at every checkpoint. Your blood-iron signature will be compromised with Aegis magic. You'll fail certification for half the contracts we run. Insurance premiums triple overnight because technically you're 'contaminated' with federal-grade enchantment."

He grabs my shoulders, forcing me to look at him. "And worst of all? She knows where you live now. Not your apartment—your *heart*. That protective dome she dropped around you? It's got an anchor point. Probably your sternum or behind your left ear where the bone's thin. And now she can track you through that connection whether you want her to or not."

"I didn't ask for her protection."

"You didn't refuse it either!" Grimjaw releases me and steps back. "That's the whole goddamn problem, Cole. In this world, you don't get to opt out once someone plants high-level wards inside your circulatory system. The magic decides for both of you."

He paces between the workbenches, clearly agitated. "Three years I've worked for you. Three years of clean operations, no federal interference, no brass-badge bullshit. And one night, you pull some do-gooder nonsense at a drydock, and suddenly we're playing Russian roulette with the entire South Side network."

I finally find my voice: "Bram, are those drills ready or not?"

The dwarf glances between us before nodding. "Yes. All twelve units, bismuth-depleted and magnetic-aligned per specifications."

Grimjaw stops pacing. His eyes lock onto mine, and I see something I've never seen in them before: fear.

"You're really going to pretend this isn't happening," he says quietly. "Aren't you."

It's not a question.

I meet his gaze without flinching. "The job's still green. Passaic docks, tomorrow morning, seven AM sharp. Bring the drills." I adjust my pauldron, feeling the dent Grimjaw left in the metal. "If

* * *

The sub-basement reeks of coal and copper, an iron-smoke perfume that wraps around my ribs like the ghost of every promise I've ever made. My tactical rig hits the concrete floor with a sound like breaking teeth—velcro ripping free, polymer plates scattering across oil-stained pavement. The air tastes thick enough to chew.

I'm standing naked except for blood-soaked boxers in front of the Iron-Lung, and I can feel every bruise singing its own dull ache beneath skin that's still humming with Voss's poison-iron residue. That warmth. That *terrible* warmth that smells like home fires burning while everything else burns too.

Through the brass-and-glass chamber walls, Danny floats.

Eighteen years old, preserved in gold-bismuth light, sustained by stabilizer collars that glow like halos around his neck and shoulders. His chest rises and falls with mechanical precision—the rhythmic *hiss-thump* of pneumatic valves keeping him alive in suspended animation. Condensation drips down the brass fixtures above him, each droplet catching the sodium-vapor streetlight filtering through the grating overhead, turning into tiny prisms before they fall.

I press my forehead against the cold glass.

The chill should shock me. Should ground me. Instead it just makes me aware of how hot my blood runs now, how the hex pollution has twisted my gift from ice-forged protection into something warm and suffocatingly close to the feeling of being held. Of being home.

"Fuck," I whisper, watching my breath fog the glass between us.

Danny's voice comes through the synthesized comm-speaker mounted on the Iron-Lung's control panel. Weak. Sharp as broken glass.

"You're bleeding," he says. "Your heart-rate monitor spiked, Cole. You met with her."

My hand flattens against the glass, palm wide, fingers spread. I can see him clearly through here—dark hair floating around his head like a corona, eyes closed in medicated sleep, the slow pulse visible at his throat. The black iron deposits in his lungs show up as shadow-mottling on the X-ray overlay displayed on the nearby monitor.

"I did," I say.

A pause. The *hiss-thump* continues its metronome rhythm.

"And?" Danny asks. "Does she change the math?"

I want to lie. Want to tell him yes, that Mara Voss is some kind of solution, some kind of answer to the equation of our lives gone sideways. But the smell of coal and copper in this room won't let me. The warmth radiating from my own corrupted blood won't let me.

"No," I say quietly. "No, Danny. She doesn't change anything."

Another pause. Then: "That's what I thought."

I slide down until I'm sitting on the concrete floor, still pressed against the glass. The cold seeping into my bare shoulders does nothing to kill the warmth beneath my skin. If anything, it makes it worse—a feverish heat that smells wrong and right all at once.

"The Threefold Cord," I hear myself saying, the words coming out automatic, rote doctrine learned from my father's father. "First strand: Justice for those who cannot seek it themselves. Second strand: Protection for those too weak to defend themselves. Third strand: Mercy for those who've lost everything but their names."

The words taste like ash now.

"Did you know," Danny says, and there's something different in his synthesized voice—a crack beneath the artificial perfection—"that you say that when you're scared? When you need grounding, you recite your grandfather's creed like a prayer."

"I am scared." The admission comes easy because it's true enough to cut through bone. "Danny, I'm so fucking terrified."

"Of dying?"

"Of failing."

I close my eyes and see her again—Mara Voss standing in that warehouse office, rain-soaked and breathing hard, blood on her face and fury in her eyes. See the protective hex I threw up around her without thinking, how it cost me, how it weakened my already-fractured defenses against Voss's counterattack.

See Danny floating in his brass-and-glass prison while I play vigilante games with people who can actually fight back.

"A sliver of justice for someone is better than no justice for anyone, Danny." My voice cracks on the words. "We keep moving. That's the only math that matters. We just... we keep moving forward until we either fix this or die trying."

"That's not math, Cole. That's faith."

"It's all I have left."

The warmth spreading through my chest intensifies, and suddenly I understand why Mara smelled like lilacs and smoke when she was close—the hex pollution has been building for weeks now, and what started as frost-cobalt protection has transmuted into something else entirely. Something that wants to burn everything down just to feel warm for five minutes first.

My Motorola Razr buzzes where it's clipped to my discarded tactical rig.

Burner text from an unknown number: *Safe-house. Boiler room. One hour. You need stitches.*

I know that number. Know it by the weight of unsent texts and unmade calls.

Standing slowly, joints protesting, I grab my leather coat off the workbench. The smell of coal follows me as I pull it on over my bare torso, the familiar weight settling across my shoulders like armor made of bad decisions and worse choices.

"Cole?" Danny's voice stops me at the stairs.

"I'm here."

"Are you really going to keep doing this? Even knowing it won't fix anything?"

I look back at him—at the boy who should be twenty-one years old by now instead of frozen at eighteen—and make myself answer honestly.

"Yes," I say. "Because a sliver of justice is still justice. And someone has to pay for what they did to you."

The words ring hollow in the sub-basement, echoing around brass valves and glass chambers and the shadows between them. But they're all I've got, so I take them with me up the stairs, leaving Danny floating in gold-bismuth light while I go meet another monster wearing human skin.

One hour.

Time enough to bleed out or get stitched up—doesn't much matter which comes first anymore.

---

## CHAPTER 7: THE BOILER ROOM STITCH (RASHOMON SYNC)

The November air tastes like rust and river water when I roll through East End at four-forty-five. My Honda's headlights catch nothing but the skeletal outline of the 1930s tenement, third building past the abandoned shipyard. No lights. No movement. Just the way I like it—or the way I've trained myself not to fear.

I kill the engine two blocks out.

The cold hits different this time of year. Bites through leather and denim like it's got teeth. I check my watch—Marisol's watch, actually, the one she left behind with the apartment keys—and do the perimeter sweep. Old habit from my machinist days, moving quiet as grease, checking sightlines and shadows for anything that doesn't belong.

East Newark stinks of diesel and decay. The Passaic River runs black in the distance, catching streetlight like oil on water. Somewhere in Kearny, a train screams across the Pulaski Skyway. Normal sounds. Safe sounds.

Except they're not.

My wards prickle up my spine—that same frost-cobalt feeling I've carried since Newark Bay decided to reclaim its dead. Blood-iron humming just beneath my skin, ready to ignite if Voss's trigger-pullers get ambitious tonight.

They won't. They're sloppy now, desperate. Using standard corporate Elven hitters instead of Syndicate muscle. Rookie mistake.

I circle the tenement twice before approaching the basement entrance. Concrete steps worn smooth by decades of feet I'll never know. The door hangs open on broken hinges—I don't touch it, just slip inside where the darkness waits thick as syrup.

Descending.

The boiler room sprawls below ground level, lit by a single swinging bulb in a wire cage. Sixty watts of sickly yellow light barely pushing back the shadows. The ancient heater clanks rhythmically—a mechanical heartbeat counting down to something I can't name.

And there she is.

Mara stands beside a rusted metal table, already setting out her med-kit with those precise movements that tell me she's been waiting longer than necessary. Her BATC uniform has vanished somewhere between here and the Bronx office. Now she wears a plain black tank top and cargo pants, hair pulled back tight enough to make her face look carved from stone.

She doesn't turn when I enter.

"I'm alive, Mara," I say, letting iron creep into my voice. "In case you were worried."

"Voss's people made another run at your apartment." She pulls out surgical gloves, snaps them on without looking. "Missed by three minutes. They used thermobarics this time."

"So they're learning." I stay by the stairs, one hand near the SIG Sauer holstered at my hip. Old reflex. Can't trust anyone completely, not even someone who saved my life twice over. Especially not someone who looks at me like I'm simultaneously a problem and a solution.

"You're bleeding." Her eyes finally find mine, dark and unreadable in the cage-light. "Left shoulder. Smeared across your jacket."

I glance down. Right. The drive-by outside the Ironbound district. Forgot about that. Doesn't hurt yet—shock does that to you, turns pain into background noise until it can't be ignored anymore.

"Sit down, Reyes." Not a request. Never really is with Mara. She gestures to an ancient wooden chair positioned between the boiler and the table. "You're losing volume I don't have time to replace properly."

My wards flare without warning—that blue-black static electricity crackling up my arms, responding to whatever fucking frequency she's putting out just by existing in proximity. But there's something different tonight. The sparks shift mid-air, turning orange-gold before hitting the concrete floor like dying embers.

The smell hits me then. White-lilac.

Jesus Christ, where did white-lilac come from?

"I need to stitch you up," Mara says quietly, and now she's closer—I didn't see her move—but she's standing between my knees before I realize she's crossed the room. Her hands are steady when she reaches for the needle and thread on the table behind me. "This is going to hurt."

"The bleeding already hurts."

"Not like this."

* * *

The needle slides through my skin like a lover's whisper, hot and sharp and utterly necessary. I don't flinch—not because I'm tough, but because every nerve ending has surrendered itself to something far more primal than pain.

Mara leans over me, her face inches from mine, close enough that I can count the individual lashes framing those storm-gray eyes. Her fingers work with surgeon's precision against the jagged tear in my jaw, pulling flesh together one careful stitch at a time. But it's not her skill that makes my blood sing—it's what bleeds from her as she works.

White-lilac.

The scent hits me first, flooding my lungs with something warm and impossibly soft. My chest tightens, but not with the familiar frost-cobalt constriction I've worn like armor for the last decade. This is different. This is *heat*.

"Stay still," Mara murmurs, her voice barely audible above the rhythmic thump of my heart. "This one's deep."

Her left hand presses against my cheekbone, anchoring my head while her right guides the curved needle through another pass. The pressure sends sparks cascading across my vision—but not the cold blue static I'd expect. These burn orange. Amber. Like coals banking in some forgotten hearth.

I should be pushing her wards out of my mind right now. Should be sealing myself behind walls of rust-red iron, keeping her trauma and mine separate, controlled, safe. That's what Cole Reyes does. That's how I survived the South Side when everyone else fell.

But standing here, bleeding onto this concrete floor, I realize something that terrifies and exhilarates me in equal measure: I don't want to be safe anymore.

Mara's breath catches. She feels it too—the shift in my aura, the way my defenses have morphed from crystalline ice into something molten and responsive. Her gray eyes flick up to meet mine, wide with recognition.

"My wards..." she whispers, watching her white-lilac light dance across my skin where we touch. "...they're not cold anymore."

They haven't been since the drydock.

The thought arrives unbidden, undeniable. Not since I felt her panic through the water, not since I dragged her back from drowning in those oily depths, not since our blood mingled in the dark—mine hot with adrenaline, hers cold with whatever hell she carries from Sub-Station Seven.

"Cole?" Mara's voice trembles. "What are you doing?"

But I can't answer her because I'm barely aware of my own hands anymore. They've moved without conscious thought, settling on her hips as she kneels beside me. The contact sends another wave of warmth through both of us—and suddenly our auras aren't just touching, they're *weaving*.

Fourth Law of the Weave: all things bound by proximity must eventually merge.

The boiler room disappears. There's only this: the smell of burning coal mixing with white lilacs until the air itself tastes like honey-black smoke; the metallic tang of my blood pooling between us; the electric hum building in our combined frequencies until every loose tool on the nearby workbench begins to vibrate sympathetically.

Mara doesn't pull away. Instead, she leans closer, her free hand coming up to press flat against my chest, right over my heart. She can feel it—the frost-cobalt finally cracking open, releasing a decade of winter into something that feels dangerously like hope.

"You did this," she breathes, wonder coloring her voice. "You're letting them warm."

I swallow hard against the sudden tightness in my throat. "They haven't been cold. Not since the drydock."

Her eyes search mine for something—I don't know what—and find it. Her lips part slightly, and I catch the faintest glimpse of teeth before she closes the distance between us.

The kiss is everything the last ten years weren't: unguarded, desperate, real. Her mouth tastes like white lilac and desperation, like thirty-seven commuters screaming in the dark and the stubborn refusal to let go. My hands tighten on her hips, pulling her flush against me despite the angle, despite the blood, despite the fact that we should be thinking about BATC Dwarves and Syndicate Elves and every other complication waiting outside this concrete box.

But right now? In this moment?

There is no outside. There is only heat.

Mara breaks the kiss slowly, her forehead resting against mine as both our chests heave with effort. Her fingers are trembling as she ties off another stitch—sloppy work, far from her usual clinical precision—but I can't bring myself to care.

"Cole." His name sounds like prayer and warning all at once.

I don't answer with words. Instead, I tilt my head just enough to press my lips against hers again, gentler this time, reverent. The boiler's furnace rumbles behind us, feeding those hungry flames, and somewhere in the back of my mind I recognize the irony: I'm finally warm, finally burning bright instead of frozen and small, and it's happening in a place built entirely around contained destruction.

When Mara pulls back this time, she doesn't look away. Her gray eyes hold mine steady, and I can see the ash-gray static of her trauma swirling there alongside something else—something warm and alive and terrifyingly vulnerable.

"My turn," she whispers. "Let me see."

She releases my jaw—eight stitches done, maybe two more to go—and presses both palms flat against my chest again. But this time it's not about anchoring or healing; it's about feeling. Really *feeling* what I've been carrying since the day I watched my crew get slaughtered on the South Side.

The contact sends electricity racing through my nervous system. My wards flare outward instinctively, but they're not cold anymore—they're responsive, reactive, wrapping around hers in spiraling patterns that make the air shimmer between us.

Mara gasps softly as the connection deepens, as decades of frost-cobalt trauma floods into shared space where we can both feel it: the crushing weight of survival guilt; the hollow ache of every friend buried too young; the bone-deep exhaustion of being strong for everyone else while bleeding out inside.

"Oh, Cole." Her voice breaks. "You've been so alone."

"Still am," I lie automatically, even as my hands tighten possessively on her hips. Even as I pull her closer until there's no possibility of misunderstanding what I want from this moment.

Her laugh is bitter-sweet as she leans down again, her lips brushing against mine with each word. "You. Are. Terrible. At. This."

Then she kisses me properly—no hesitation now, just raw need meeting desperate hope—and I realize I'm kissing back with equal abandon, all my carefully constructed walls reduced to ash-coal warmth at our feet.

The boiler room dissolves into background noise: the steady drip of radiator pipes, the distant wail of sirens cutting across Newark Bay, the muffled argument somewhere above our heads as the rest of the world continues its grim business without us.

But here? In this concrete prison that smells like smoke and lilacs and

* * *

The air crackles between us like live wire meeting copper.

I can't remember deciding to close the distance. One moment I'm staring at the raw red wound on her forearm where the stitching ended, watching that impossible laceration knit itself closed with threads made of distilled moonlight. The next moment my hand is braced against the cinderblock wall beside her head and my mouth is on hers.

It's not gentle. Nothing about this has ever been gentle. My lips taste blood—mine or hers, it doesn't matter—and beneath that metallic tang there's something else. White lilac. That same suffocating perfume that rose from the hearth-coals when she pulled my soul back from whatever hellscape I'd wandered into during the stitching.

Her hands are in my hair, pulling, and I feel the points where her nails break skin register as distant information. More important is the way her body moves against mine, desperate and searching. The boiler room suddenly feels too small, too hot, the roaring furnace in the corner matching the heat blooming across my chest where our magics collide.

Cobalt and white lilac.

Frost and flame.

My blood-iron screams in protest even as every cell in my body surrenders to the warmth spreading through my veins. A decade of ice-cold doctrine melting in the space of a heartbeat. The Geas around her neck—the binding Voss placed on his own daughter like she was livestock marked for slaughter—I can *feel* it now, pulsing in time with her pulse. Can feel how it constricts whenever she breathes, the way it burns when she defies him, which is apparently fucking constantly.

I make a vow then, silent and terrible:

*I will unmake you,* I think at the binding. *I don't care what it costs. I don't care if it kills me.*

The thought arrives clear as crystal despite the chaos of kissing her, despite the way her tongue meets mine and I'm drowning in white lilacs and the smell of burning concrete as sparks cascade off our shoulders—my frost and her fire creating new colors that have no names in any language I know.

When we finally break apart, foreheads resting together, I'm gasping like I've run the length of the Pulaski Skyway. My hand is still braced against the wall. Her fingers are tangled in my hair.

"My father," Mara says, her voice rough, "is going to use you to get to me."

"Let him try." The words come out wrong, all gravel and damage. I clear my throat but don't move away from her. Can't seem to convince my body that distance would be the smart play here.

Her eyes—those same green-gold eyes as Voss, though infinitely less cruel—search my face. "Cole—"

My Nextel cuts through whatever she was about to say, shrill and insistent.

I snatch it up without looking away from her. "Reyes."

"Cole. It's Danny." His voice has that tight quality he gets when he's trying not to freak out completely. "The Gnome brokers found it. Found the trunk line beneath the Old Mint."

"Found *what*, Danny?" I ask, even though I already know. Already feel it in my bones like an incoming winter storm.

"The thing Voss is hiding. Under the whole fucking district, Cole. It's massive. And it's waking up."

Behind me, I hear the boiler kick into overdrive with a mechanical groan that rattles the pipes along the ceiling. Steam hisses through valves. The temperature in the room spikes another ten degrees, making sweat bead along my spine.

"You're sure?" I ask, though confirming the obvious is stupid.

"I'm sure. We need you back at headquarters. Now."

I should go. Every instinct screaming at me to peel myself off this wall, grab Mara by the arm, and haul us both back to Ironwood where we can hole up behind warded doors while Danny and his team figure out what fresh hell Voss has been brewing under Newark's financial district.

But I don't move.

Mara watches me with those predatory eyes, waiting to see which way I'll jump. Her breathing has mostly returned to normal, but there's still color high on her cheeks and her lips are swollen. The stitching on her arm has finished its work—smooth skin now where there was raw wound before, though if you know where to look you can see faint scars shaped like sigils.

"We should go," she says quietly. Not moving either.

"Yeah." My thumb traces the line of her jaw, feeling her swallow against my palm. "We probably should."

The Nextel crackles in my hand. "Cole? You copying?"

I key the mic but keep my eyes locked on hers. "Copy, Danny. Give me twenty minutes."

"Make it fifteen. Whatever's down there just punched through another two feet of concrete. Things are getting unstable."

I click off without responding.

Mara finally shifts away from the wall, putting maybe an inch between us. It feels like a mile. She reaches for the oversized hoodie she'd discarded earlier, pulls it on over her tank top with movements that seem deliberately slow, like she's trying to memorize how my face looks in this light—the dim yellow glow of the boiler room's work lamps making everything feel like we're underwater, suspended in amber.

"The Old Mint," she says, half to herself. "Of course. It's where he started, back when the BATC was just him and a handful of other degenerates playing at being gods." She meets my eyes again. "What do you think is down there, machinist? What could possibly be worth hiding beneath half of Newark's financial core?"

I want to say I don't know. Want to pretend I'm not already running calculations based on the residual magic signatures Mara pulled from Voss during their last confrontation. But lying to her—lying to myself—seems pointless now.

"A heart-stone." The words taste wrong even as I speak them. "Big enough to power something massive. Something that runs on fear instead of blood-iron or will-spark."

Her expression goes carefully neutral, which means I've hit closer to the truth than either of us wants to admit.

"My father," she says quietly, "has been planning his endgame since before I was born. This isn't about controlling the South Side or consolidating power among the Gnome cartels. He's building something. A final weapon."

The boiler kicks again, louder this time, and dust shakes loose from the ceiling beams. Somewhere in the distance—a few blocks maybe—I can hear sirens starting up. Police or paramedics, it doesn't matter. They'll never make it here in time for whatever's coming.

"Then we stop it." Simple statement. Uselessly simple given what stopping something like that would actually require.

She smiles then, sharp and sad. "Is that your doctrine speaking, Cole Reyes? Or are you finally admitting what you've known since you dragged me out of Voss's mansion?"

I should lie. Should tell her it's about duty and the machine-gun philosophy I've been running on

---

## CHAPTER 8: THE TELEMETRY BROKERS

The descent is always worse than memory suggests.

I take the maintenance ladder three levels down, my boots finding rusted rungs slick with condensation that drips from the Passaic River's underground runoff. The air grows thick, metallic—a taste like licking battery terminals mixed with the sweet rot of decades-old sewage. My wards hum their steady warmth against my spine, a coil of hearth-coals waiting to become an inferno if needed.

Level Minus Four smells like ozone and desperation.

The tunnel opens into chaos.

What should be a sterile server facility has been transformed into something between a mad scientist's laboratory and a crack house. Towering racks of ancient Compaq servers stack six feet high, their cooling fans creating a deafening white noise that vibrates through bone. Between them, Gnome telemetry brokers have woven a web of copper wiring that would make a spider jealous—runic symbols etched onto conduits, glowing faintly green where they intersect with fiber-optic cables thicker than my wrist.

Neon tubes overhead flicker in sickly pinks and electric blues, casting everything in a light that makes reality feel negotiable.

"Shit."

A voice cuts through the mechanical roar. I spot him hunched over a workbench littered with desoldered components: a Gnome, maybe four feet tall even in his heavy steel-toed boots. His soldering visor casts amber light across eyes that reflect the CRT monitors around him like a cat's. The hoodie he wears looks like it hasn't seen a washing machine since 2003, stained with flux and what might be motor oil.

"Tell me you got clearance from the Brokerage, or I'm gonna have to ask you to fuck off back upstairs." He doesn't look up from whatever circuit board he's murdering with a soldering iron. "This is a restricted grid. BATC telluric-sweepers pinged us three times this morning already. We're running hot enough to melt through to Level Minus Six."

I pull out the ruggedized Panasonic Toughbook, its screen still displaying Danny's last message before we lost connection. "I need network access. Your mainframe, not some sub-sub level garbage."

That gets his attention. Those amber eyes lock on me with sudden intensity.

"You're bringing heavy heat down here, Reyes." How the hell does he know my name? "And you're carrying more than just hardware in that bag. I can smell the wards from here—like someone bottled November rain and poured it into your bones."

The Gnome straightens up, setting down his iron. His fingers are steady despite their size—they move with the precision of someone who's spent twenty years working with components smaller than rice grains.

"Name's Jax. I run hardware for Sector Seven. And if you want into my grid, you better come correct with credentials, because I don't do freelancers, and I sure as hell don't do vigilantes looking for information they ain't ready to process."

My wards pulse once, a warning growl. But I keep my voice even.

"I'm not here to play games. Someone killed three people at the Iron-Lung drydock yesterday. The evidence trail leads through your servers or the ones connected to them. So either you help me follow it, or I find another way. Either option works for me."

Jax stares at me for a long moment, those reflective eyes calculating angles I can't see. Then he laughs—a sound like grinding gears.

"Fuck it. You got balls coming down here alone." He gestures to an open port on his main console, a tangle of Cat5 cables sprouting from it like wires from a severed spine. "Plug in. But fair warning: this network is hostile. We're running off the city bedrock power grid, which means any corporate ICE that finds us gets fed directly through the foundation stone itself. You'll cook your laptop in about six seconds flat if you can't keep it cool."

I set the Toughbook on the edge of his workbench, already opening the network port. My fingers move by memory—I've done this enough times to know which protocols need hardening before hitting anything this deep in the Undercity.

*The machine boots up. Danny's synthesized voice crackles to life:*

"Status?"

"Inside," I say aloud. "Level Minus Four server farm. Gnome operator calling himself Jax."

"Tell the wire-head to bypass the secondary firewall. I have Voss’s MAC address from the drydock."

Jax's eye twitches. "Wire-head? Listen here, spark-plug, I was routing fiber-optics before you were a glint in your daddy's eye. This ain't some hacker setup—this is hardware engineering. You want my help, you show some fucking respect."

"Danny isn't being disrespectful," I cut in, keeping my tone neutral. "He just needs what he needs. The MAC address is priority one."

Those amber eyes narrow at me, then at the screen where Danny's text appears in green monospace font.

"...Fine. Fuck." Jax turns back to his console, fingers flying across keys with supernatural speed. "Bypassing secondary firewall now. But if this blows back on me, we're gonna have problems, Reyes."

The cooling fans seem to whine louder as power surges through the system. Every monitor in the facility flashes red for exactly three seconds.

*Uh, Reyes?*

This ain't a standard corporate trunk line. This is a black-circuit fiber-optic cable, and it's drawing power from the city's bedrock.

I feel it then—the wards tightening against my spine, their comfortable heat suddenly spiked with warning ice. Something about this connection is wrong. Not just deep, but *wrong*.

"What did you just tap into?"

* * *

I can feel the heat radiating from my palm where I'm gripping the Nextel ward-cracker. It's a ugly thing—all duct tape and exposed wires, like something Jax assembled in his bathtub at three in the morning—and it's screaming at me in a way that makes my teeth ache. That high-pitched whine cuts through the hum of the server farm, making the hair on my arms stand up.

"Hold the feed, Cole!" Danny's voice crackles through my earpiece, sharp with panic. "The Elven ICE is trying to back-trace the blood-signature!"

I don't loosen my grip. Can't. My fingers are wrapped so tight around the device that I can feel the vibration of its failing components rattling up my forearm. The smell hits me next—that acrid stench of electronics about to give up the ghost, plastic starting to melt from the inside out.

But underneath all that, there's warmth. That steady, coals-in-the-hearth glow that's been radiating from my wards ever since I made that vow to Mara. The heat spreads from my chest down my arm, pooling in my hand where it meets the copper leads.

"Let them choke on it," I say, voice low and steady despite the chaos. "Burn through, Danny."

Jax shifts beside me, his bulk casting shadows across the rows of servers. His eyes are wide as he watches what I'm doing—or rather, what my magic is doing. He built this thing to handle maybe five minutes of continuous feed before it cooked itself into slag. But my wards aren't just feeding power; they're *transforming* it, translating that arcane heat into something the ward-cracker can use without burning out.

The Nextel shrieks louder, metal groaning, and then—

"Shit! They're coming through fast!" Danny yells. "Three... no four ice-breakers, they look like—fuck, Cole, these things are Elven architecture. They're learning from our attacks!"

On the Panasonic Toughbook propped against a server rack, a wireframe map of North Jersey's Undercity flickers to life. Green lines representing our digital footprint scatter like frightened birds as purple constructs—the Elven ICE—converge on our position. They move with that eerie grace that only metaphysical programming can manage, anticipating our movements before we make them.

My blood drips onto the copper leads.

I didn't cut myself on purpose—didn't need to—but the wards know what's required. A bead of crimson swells at the tip of my index finger and falls, landing with an audible sizzle against the heated metal. The smell changes. Copper and ozone now, mixing with that burnt plastic. Steam rises in thin wisps.

"Cole, your signature's too bright," Jax warns. "They'll track us back to you in seconds."

"He's right," Danny adds urgently. "The ICE is clustering around the blood-magic frequency. If you don't pull back—"

"I'm not pulling back." I lean forward, pressing my forehead almost against the crackling device. The hearth-coal magic pulses stronger, responding to my will. "Push harder, Danny. Give me everything you've got."

"You want me to feed more power into a system already overheating?"

"Damn straight."

There's a long pause. Then: "You're insane."

"Mara trusted you could do this," I say quietly. "So let's prove her right."

Another drop of blood. Then another. Each one hisses and evaporates instantly, but the magic they carry doesn't just burn away—it *charges*. The Nextel ward-cracker starts humming beneath all that screaming static, a deep resonant tone that I feel in my bones. The overheat warnings on its cracked LCD display flicker out, replaced by something impossible: full operational capacity.

Jax stares. "No way. It should be melting."

"It's running on iron-blood," I tell him, voice strained as I pour more heat into the wards. Sweat beads on my forehead, drips down my temples. My whole arm is shaking from the effort of maintaining the channel. "Old-school magic doesn't play by the same rules as corporate tech."

"Then hurry up before your arm falls off!"

Danny's fingers fly across his keyboard somewhere in the darkness above us. "Alright, new plan! I'm routing us through three redundant ghost-nodes. Should give us enough cover for a sustained assault. But Cole, once we breach, we have maybe thirty seconds before Voss's security realizes what hit them."

"Thirty seconds is all I need."

The wireframe map shifts, zooms. The purple ice-breakers swarm our position but can't quite close the distance—pushed back by whatever alchemical bullshit my wards are conjuring now. The code Danny's feeding into the system translates to raw force in ways that shouldn't work according to any programming manual I've ever seen.

"Twenty seconds!"

The firewall looms ahead in the digital space—a massive construct of interlocking wards so dense and complex that looking at it makes my eyes hurt even through the Toughbook's screen. This isn't some off-the-shelf defense package. This was built by someone who understood both magic and machinery, who knew how to blend arcane architecture with digital protocols until you couldn't tell where one ended and the other began.

"This thing's huge," Jax breathes. "How much power would it take to crack something like this?"

I don't answer. Instead, I squeeze harder around the Nextel ward-cracker and let go of every restraint I've been holding back. The hearth-coal heat explodes outward from my chest like a physical force, flooding down my arm, pouring into the device, surging through copper leads and resistors and capacitors that weren't designed to handle this kind of metaphysical voltage.

My blood boils before it hits the metal. Steam hisses. Plastic cracks. And beneath it all—that deep resonant hum grows stronger, building toward something critical.

"Ten seconds! Cole, for fuck's sake, pull back or you'll—"

*CRACK.*

Something gives way inside the ward-cracker. For one terrible moment I think we've lost it, burned out the whole operation just as we were about to breach.

Then the firewall *screams*.

It's not an audio sound—the Toughbook doesn't have speakers—but I hear it anyway, resonating directly in my skull. That same high-pitched agony as the Nextel screaming, but multiplied a thousandfold. The wireframe map flashes white, then red, then fractures like glass. Pieces scatter into nothingness.

And when the light fades, there's a line.

Thick. Pulsing. Crimson.

It starts at Pylon #3, cuts through the Undercity's digital infrastructure like a hot knife through butter, weaving between server clusters and data nodes with impossible precision. And it ends—

"The Old Ironworks," Danny says quietly, his voice stripped of all its earlier urgency. "Jesus Christ, Cole. It's terminating deep beneath the Old Ironworks."

I release my grip on

* * *

The trace resolves at 09:17 AM exactly, bleeding across the Toughbook's cracked screen in a cascade of green phosphorescence. My fingers hover over the keyboard, watching the data packets cluster like iron filings around a magnet's pole. There—a definitive spike in power draw, concentrated and sustained.

Pylon #4.

"Fuck me sideways," I mutter, leaning back hard enough that the chair groans beneath my weight. The server farm air tastes like ozone and old sweat, recycled through filters that haven't been changed since before the Fracture. Above us, somewhere four stories of concrete and rebar above our heads, the number 6 train shudders past, rattling the floor plates.

I pull up the architectural schematics—corrupted, half-erased files salvaged from the city's dead network archives. The Old Mint looms on-screen, its pre-flood foundations marked out in faded amber lines. But what catches my attention isn't the building itself; it's what's underneath. Pylon #4 extends another two hundred feet down into the earth—or what used to be earth before they poured the foundation beds for Newark's first skyscrapers.

Deeper than that. Deeper than any construction record shows.

My wards pulse warm against my sternum, a steady thrumming that feels almost alive. Different from the cold dread that usually coils there. This is something else. Purposeful. Focused. Mara's face flashes behind my eyes—not her corpse, not the horror of what Voss did to her, but how she looked that last night at the waterfront. Hopeful. Terrified. Trusting me to finish this.

I slam the Toughbook shut, the latch clicking with finality. The green glow dies immediately, leaving me in near-darkness punctuated only by the blinking status lights on the thousand other servers surrounding us. Their hum fills the silence, a mechanical mantra.

"Jax," I call out toward where the ganger's supposed to be guarding the stairwell. "You still breathing over there?"

A grunt. A shift of weight against metal. "Still here, Reyes. You done playing with your toy?"

I stand, pocketing the Toughbook, and cross to his position. Jax sits on an overturned ammunition crate, some kind of half-smoked stim stick burning between his fingers. He looks haggard—dark circles under both eyes, the kind you get from too many nights running interference through the Undercity's worst neighborhoods.

On the desk beside him, I dump three uncut bismuth coins. They hit with heavy metallic clinks, rolling slightly before settling into place. Pure, dense, worth more per ounce than gold in the right markets.

"That's for your trouble and discretion," I say. "Mouth stays shut about what you saw here."

Jax's eyes widen fractionally before he schools his expression back to its usual cynical mask. He scoops up the coins, biting one experimentally—the bismuth resists his teeth, impervious even to the enhanced strength most metas run. "Shit, Cole. This is—"

"It's payment. Take it or don't." I pull out my Razr, thumbing through the contacts until Grimjaw's number pops up. My jaw tightens as the phone rings once, twice, three times.

Four rings. Five. Then—

"Boss?" Grimjaw's voice cracks through, gravelly and thick with sleep—or whatever passes for sleep when you're built like a refrigerator and twice as mean. "What time is it? Jesus fucking Christ, you know what hour it is?"

"It's time to work," I cut him off. "Wake up Bram and the sandhogs. Load the heavy depleted-bismuth drills."

A pause. I can hear him shifting position, probably sitting up in bed with his characteristic groan of old machinery protesting movement.

"What's the target?" he asks finally, all business now that the surprise has worn off.

"The Old Mint. Pylon number four." The words taste wrong in my mouth, tainted by how deeply we're going to have to dig. "We're going through the foundation."

Grimjaw laughs—that deep, brutal Orcish sound that I've heard precede both celebrations and executions over the years. "Union standard, Cole. You know what kind of heat that's gonna draw? Old Mint security runs twenty-four/seven, and that's just the surface layer."

"Not our problem." I keep my voice flat, emotionless. "The job's the job. We'll bring the big toys if we need them."

"You got authorization from the Contractors Guild? Because last I checked, breaching pre-flood infrastructure without clearance is—"

"I don't give a shit about the Guild," I interrupt again. "Voss is digging toward something ancient, Grim. Deeper than any records show. If I'm right, this goes beyond territorial disputes between rival telemetry brokers."

Silence on the other end. Long enough that I check the screen to make sure we haven't dropped the connection.

"Alright," Grimjaw says quietly. "Sandhogs assemble in one hour. Bring the thermite lances and the bismuth drills. If we're breaking into foundations that old, we're bringing serious firepower."

"Good man." I flip the Razr shut, pocket it again.

Jax's watching me with narrowed eyes, the coins still clutched in his fist. "You planning something stupid, Reyes?"

I meet his gaze levelly. "Always am."

---

## CHAPTER 9: BREACHING PYLON #4

The stench hit me first—that thick cocktail of wet earth, machine oil, and something else. Something older. Like digging too deep and hitting graveyard soil.

I descended the rusted iron ladder into darkness that swallowed sound whole. My boot hit bottom and the beam from my headlamp cut through the black, illuminating a tunnel that hadn't seen a subway car in forty years. Graffiti tags faded to ghosts on the curved brick walls. Water dripped somewhere in the distance, each drop echoing like a heartbeat.

"About fuckin' time."

Grimjaw's voice rolled out of the gloom, and there he was—a mountain of green-skinned muscle and scarring, his yellow eyes catching the light like a cat's. Behind him, four Ogre-Kin were making the tunnel feel small. Each one stood seven feet easy, their shoulders broader than most doorways, muscles cording beneath patches of crude body armor bolted together with mismatched plating.

"The boss said you'd be late," Grimjaw continued, working the charging handle on some kind of heavy bolter that looked more artillery piece than personal weapon. "Something about a detour through Ironbound."

I didn't answer. Instead, I moved past him toward where the real work was happening.

Bram Kovacs crouched before what had to be eight tons of machinery—some kind of tripod-mounted arcano-drill that whined softly as it cycled through startup sequences. The Dwarf was a study in contrasts: one side of his face bore the refined features of someone who'd spent decades in academic circles, but the other had been smashed flat by an industrial accident years back, leaving a landscape of scar tissue and metal implants. He was spit-chewing tobacco again—the dark stain at the corner of his mouth already forming.

"This concrete is reinforced with telluric-steel, Cole." Bram's good eye fixed on me while his scarred side remained blank, emotionless. "The drill's gonna scream like a banshee in a blender when we hit it."

I knelt beside the machine, running my gloved hand along its housing. Cool metal, humming with barely-contained power. The bismuth tip gleamed dull gray in the work lights someone had strung up—a constellation of halogens that cast everything in harsh relief, turning shadows into monsters on the tunnel walls.

"Let it scream." Grimjaw's voice cut across the space. His boys had spread out now, two of them hauling crates marked ACOUSTIC DAMPENERS across the wet floor. The third was testing something that looked like a portable sound cannon. "If Voss's corporate suits come down here, my boys will turn 'em into paste."

I tapped the drill housing with my knuckles, feeling the vibration travel through my bones. "Just get me through the wall, Bram. I'll handle what's on the other side."

The Old Mint loomed beyond—its foundations spreading like a web beneath downtown Newark. We were underneath it now, maybe thirty feet down, close enough to feel the weight of history pressing from above. That building had stood since the Civil War. Had survived riots, fires, the slow rot of economic decay. Now it housed something worse than any of those things.

Something that wanted out.

"The dampeners are live," one of the Ogre-Kin grunted. He had a voice like grinding gears, and I could see the words forming around tusk-like protrusions jutting from his lower jaw. "Street level won't hear shit."

Bram spat a stream of black tobacco juice onto the ground. It hissed where it landed in a puddle. "Drill's ready. But once we punch through, Cole, you're on your own for about thirty seconds before my boys can follow. The passage is narrow—single file only."

"Thirty seconds is all I need."

That wasn't entirely true, but they didn't need to know that. My shotgun felt right in my hands as I checked it over—slotting specialized shield-breaker rounds into the tube magazine. Each round carried a payload of crystallized iron shards wrapped in binding runes that would tear through arcane defenses like paper. Expensive ammunition. The kind you bought on the black market because the city's legal arms dealers wouldn't sell to someone with my... reputation.

My blood-iron hummed low in my veins—that familiar warmth beneath my ribs that meant the magic was awake and hungry. It wanted violence. Wanted release.

The hearth-coal scent helped anchor me. I'd rubbed some under my nose before coming down here—a trick an old mentor taught me years ago. Coal smoke meant home meant safety meant *human*. Without it, without that smell reminding me of warm kitchens and Sunday dinners instead of corpses and blood-magic, I'd slip too easily into that place inside myself. That sociopathic void where killing became art and mercy became weakness.

Couldn't afford that tonight. Not when Mara was counting on me.

I checked my watch: 11:37 PM. She should be in position by now, somewhere above us on the street level, watching for any sign of what we'd breach. Her job was eyes-on. My job was making sure nothing escaped those foundations that shouldn't see daylight.

Grimjaw's crew had finished setting up their positions. Two of them manned heavy weapons near the tunnel entrance—just in case something tried to come at us from behind. The other two flanked Bram's drill position, ready to pour fire into whatever emerged from the breach once we cut through.

"The wall ahead is two feet thick," Bram said, his fingers dancing across a control panel that looked too complex for machinery this crude. "Maybe three. But that telluric reinforcement means we're looking at forty-five seconds minimum to cut through. Could be longer if the ward-mages who set this up knew what they were doing."

"Just start drilling."

Bram looked at me, then at Grimjaw, then back at me again. Something passed between us—an unspoken acknowledgment that this could go sideways in a dozen different ways. That we might be walking into more than just reinforced concrete and arcane wards.

He engaged the drill.

The bismuth tip hit the warded concrete of The Old Mint's foundation with a sound like God's own hammer striking an anvil. Blue sparks exploded outward in a shower so bright it burned white through my headlamp filters. The shockwave rattled my teeth, made my bones ache, sent ripples through the puddles around our feet that sloshed against the walls.

The drill screamed.

And beneath that screaming metal, I heard something else—a deep, resonant humming that vibrated up from below. From deeper in the earth than these tunnels should reach.

Whatever was down there didn't want company.

I checked my shotgun one last time and moved toward the breach point as Bram's machine chewed through ancient concrete like tissue paper.

* * *

The drill screams as it punches through the final barrier—a sound like God's own bone saw tearing through reality itself. Then everything goes sideways.

Iron-gall detonates in our faces.

I see it coming a half-second too late—the telltale shimmer in the air, like heat waves rising off summer asphalt but wrong, *wrong*, because it's cold and tastes like rust and old blood. My instincts scream danger but my body's already moving, blood surging up my arms in hot rivulets that smell like the machine shop floor after a long day's work.

"SHIELD—!"

The word tears from my throat as I slam both palms forward. Blood-iron erupts around us in a hemisphere of crimson light, the hearth-coal scent hitting me hard enough to make my eyes water. Good. The anchor. I need the goddamn anchor right now or I'm going to lose myself in this.

The blowback hits my shield like a freight train made of angry physics.

Concrete dust fills the tunnel in a choking cloud. Behind the shield, Grimjaw and Bram become silhouettes, their shadows writhing under the pulsing red glow. I hear the Ogre-Kin—those hulking bastards we brought along for heavy lifting—hit the far wall with impacts that would've killed normal men. Armor buckles with sounds like car doors getting crushed in a compactor. Bones crack. Someone screams.

"Push through!" Grimjaw's voice cuts through the chaos, his massive frame hauling one of the stunned Ogre-Kin upright by his collar. "Boss! Push through or we're dead!"

The drill behind us is melting. I can hear the metal screaming, the electric whine turning into something organic and furious. Bram's face is visible through gaps in the shield—a grim mask of concentration as he pours more power into keeping the bit spinning, grinding through whatever hellish geometry the ward-masters have woven down here.

"*KEEP IT RUNNING!*" I roar back at him, and the words come out wrong somehow, tinged with copper and the metallic tang of my own blood dripping from my nose, my ears, somewhere deep in my sinuses where it shouldn't be able to reach.

My shotgun comes up instinctively—the Remington feels like an extension of my arm, like it grew there instead of me buying it secondhand from a pawn shop on South Orange Avenue. The front sight glows sickly green where it overlaps with the gravity ward embedded in the rebar. Those bastard runes are everywhere now, glowing like infected wounds in the steel skeleton of the tunnel.

I fire point-blank.

The buckshot hits the rune dead center. For a moment nothing happens—then the symbol *shrieks*, a sound I feel in my teeth rather than hear, and the iron-gall coating it flash-boils into toxic steam that makes my eyes burn and run.

The rune shatters.

The gravity ward collapses with a concussive *pop* that slams against my eardrums hard enough to make me stumble. My shield flickers but holds, the hearth-coal heat intensifying until sweat beads on my forehead and runs down the small of my back. I can smell my own hair starting to singe.

Then the drill punches through.

The final layer of rock gives way with a sound like breaking glass—though thicker, older, like the last barrier between this world and something that was never meant to be found. A rush of air blows back through the hole, stale and foul and so ancient it tastes like time itself has turned sour.

Behind that wind is darkness. Not the absence of light, but something darker—a void that drinks photons and spits out despair.

"*By God,*" Grimjaw breathes, his usual bravado stripped away. "Boss... what the hell did we just open?"

* * *

The chains bite deep into weakened concrete, and the whole section of floor groans like something dying. Then it gives way.

I'm already moving when Grimjaw's heavy bolter coughs its first round. The concrete fragment tumbles down into absolute darkness—a void so complete my halogen cuts through it like a blade through wet paper. Dust erupts upward, tasting of rust and decades-old mortar, coating my throat as I drop through.

My boots hit solid ground three meters down. The impact jolts up through my knees, and I have to catch myself against the rough-hewn edge of the breach. Behind me, I hear Bram's muttered curses and the clang of metal boots on concrete as the others follow.

But none of that matters because my light has found purchase now, sweeping across surfaces that make my stomach clench.

Stone.

Not poured concrete. Not brick. Stone.

Massive fucking blocks, each one bigger than my pickup truck, fitted together so tight you couldn't slide a credit card between them. The walls recede into shadows my light can't penetrate, but what I see in this cone of illumination makes no goddamn sense. Carved glyphs spiral up the pillars—some kind of hybrid nightmare blending Egyptian cartouches with Mayan step-pyramids, all rendered in a style so archaic it hurts to look at it.

"This ain't Syndicate," Grimjaw breathes from behind me. His voice is wrong—the usual union swagger stripped away, leaving something closer to awe. Or fear. Maybe both. "Cole, this ain't no fucking Syndicate vault."

The Ogre-Kin's massive frame hunkers beside me, his boltgun lowered and forgotten. He runs one thick finger along the nearest pillar, stopping short of actual contact like he's afraid the stone might bite him.

Bram crowds in close, those Dwarven eyes of his narrowing as they adjust to the dark. "This stone..." His voice drops lower, almost reverent. "It ain't been cut with any machine. Look at the edges, Cole. Look at how the blocks fit." He looks up at me, and there's something ancient in his expression that doesn't belong on his weathered face. "This is older than the city. Older than the continent."

I don't answer because I'm already moving deeper, the beam of my flashlight cutting through air that tastes wrong—dry rot and ancient dust, sure, but underneath that is something else. Something sweet and sickening that turns my stomach even as it pulls me forward. The Sludge smell.

My hearth-coal scent burns brighter in response, anchoring me against whatever psychic shit is trying to seep out of these walls.

The chamber opens up ahead, expanding into something vast enough to swallow whole buildings. My light catches more pillars, dozens of them, arranged in a pattern that makes my eyes water when I try to follow it. Between them: darkness so thick it feels solid.

Then I see it.

At the far end, maybe twenty meters out, rising from a floor that disappears into blackness: an altar. Raised platform of black basalt, polished smooth by hands that worked before the first European ship ever smelled New Jersey shore.

And on that altar sits a tablet.

Obsidian. Black as midnight, big around as one of Bram's beer kegs, covered in glyphs that seem to shift when I look directly at them. But that's not what makes me freeze mid-step, my hand instinctively reaching for my hammer.

The fiber-optic cables.

Modern ones, sleek and bright blue, snaking across three-thousand-year-old stone like some kind of technological parasite. They're plugged directly into the tablet, disappearing into ports carved or drilled—I can't tell which—into the obsidian surface itself.

Voss.

This has to be Voss.

"Jesus Christ," Grimjaw whispers. "What the fuck did we just find?"

I don't answer him because I'm already moving toward the altar, boots crunching on debris I can't identify, my light beam locked on that impossible fusion of ancient evil and modern technology. The sweet-sickness grows stronger with each step, making my teeth ache and my blood-iron sing against my ribs.

But underneath all that horror, all that wrongness:

There's power here.

Raw, untapped, older than anything the Syndicate ever dreamed up in their labs. Power that predates electricity, predates steel, probably predates humanity's ability to even *conceive* of magic.

And someone—Voss, had to be Voss—found it.

Found it and tried to plug it into the grid like it was just another damn transformer station.

---

## CHAPTER 10: THE TABLET OF THE FOUR HEADS

The chamber breathes.

I feel it against my sternum—that low, rhythmic thud that isn't quite sound but presses into bone anyway. Grimjaw and Bram have fallen back to the breach entrance, their silhouettes barely visible through the shifting darkness. The air tastes like rust and something older, something that predates concrete and steel.

My shotgun rests against my shoulder, the weight familiar even as my hands tremble slightly. Not from fear. From the pressure. Everything here feels compressed, dense with centuries of accumulated wrongness.

"Hold the line," I call back, my voice swallowed by the obsidian pillars. "Don't let anything through."

The altar dominates the center of the space—a slab of black stone that seems to drink the ambient glow from my wards. Those cobalt flames are working overtime tonight, casting everything in that sickly blue-white radiance while pushing back an encroaching dark that moves with purpose.

Then I hear them.

Footsteps. Crisp. Deliberate. Echoing from a stairwell I hadn't noticed before, tucked behind one of those goddamn pillars on the far side. My finger tightens on the trigger. The wards spike, and suddenly—

White-lilac.

Mara emerges from the shadows like a ghost wearing tactical gear, her BATC Aegis uniform caked in dust and cobwebs. She's holding her service pistol at low ready, those sharp eyes scanning the room until they lock onto me. Her weapon doesn't waver for three full seconds before she lowers it slowly.

"You're hard to find when you want to be," she says, breathing hard. Her gaze darts around the chamber, taking in the impossible architecture, the pulsing fiber-optic cables snaking along the walls like veins. "I tracked Voss's encrypted signals down here. What the hell is this place, Cole?"

I keep my shotgun trained on the darkness surrounding us rather than her. My wards flare brighter, responding to her presence, and something shifts in the oppressive weight of the room. Where there was only crushing pressure, now there's... resistance. Like two magnetic fields colliding instead of merging.

"I think it's the reason Neon Hollow was built in the first place." My words come out rougher than intended. I clear my throat. "The Pylons aren't power generators, Mara. They're nails."

"What?"

* * *

The air in the chamber tastes like copper and ancient dust. I can feel the weight of centuries pressing down on my skull, trying to crush my thoughts into primordial paste. The stone walls weep moisture that smells wrong—like something that's been dead longer than memory.

Mara's presence cuts through it. When she descended from the surface level, syncing with her counterpart who'd breached the Mint above, something shifted in the fabric of this place. Our Weaves—my hearth-coals and her white-lilac—intertwined in the oppressive dark, creating a psychogenic anchor that pushes back against whatever malevolent consciousness festers here.

She stands beside me now, her tactical vest still damp with sweat and river water from her descent. Her fingers trace along the edge of the obsidian tablet that dominates the far wall—a massive thing, easily eight feet tall and four wide, its surface so polished it reflects our distorted shapes like a funhouse mirror.

"Voss was here," I mutter, eyeing the crude setup his team left behind. A Panasonic Toughbook balanced on a stack of rusted crates, wires snaking across the floor and plugging into some kind of arcano-scanner clamped around the base of the tablet. The screen glows sickly green in the darkness, casting shadows that make Mara's face look carved from bone.

I crouch by the rig, pulling cables with practiced ease. My Nextel comes out, already paired with my comm-link. The secure handshake chirps harshly—the sound echoing off the vaulted ceiling like an accusation.

"You're sure about this?" Mara asks. Her voice is steady, but I can see the way her hand hovers near her sidearm.

"Danny needs to see what we're looking at." I plug my rig into the scanner's auxiliary port, routing the raw image data directly through my connection. The tablet pulses faintly under the scanner's probe, glyphs upon glyphs etched into its surface in a chaotic blend that shouldn't exist. Canaanite-Egyptian symbols bleed into Mayan script, each set of markings warring with the others for dominance.

Static crackles in my earpiece. Once. Twice. Then Danny's voice cuts through, layered with something I've never heard before—pure terror wrapped in academic awe.

"I'm getting it. Holy fuck, Cole, I'm getting it."

The Toughbook screen flickers as he remotely activates the translation software. Data streams across the bottom of the display—a cascade of failed algorithms and syntax errors. The scanner whines higher in pitch, that buzzing sound making my teeth ache.

"Cross-referencing the glyphs with the Undercity databanks," Danny continues, his voice dropping lower. "Cole... this syntax is pre-cataclysm. It's older than anything in our archives. This isn't just a warning. It's a containment protocol."

Mara steps closer to the tablet, her gloved finger hovering over one of the carvings. A massive serpent, coiled around itself in impossible geometry, its four heads reaching toward different points on the compass rose carved below them. Each head has a different expression—rage, sorrow, hunger, and something that looks like cosmic indifference.

"Containment for what?" she asks quietly.

Before Danny can answer, the screen flashes. The translation software spits out text in bold, red letters that burn themselves into my retinas:

**THE TABLET OF THE FOUR HEADS OF THE SHADOW SERPENT.**

My stomach drops. Behind me, I hear Mara's sharp intake of breath.

"That's not possible," Danny whispers from the Iron-Lung. "That entity was sealed during the First Breach. It's supposed to be dead."

The obsidian surface ripples.

* * *

The air in the chamber tastes like copper and ancient stone. My hearth-coal ward flickers against the oppressive weight pressing down from above, from below, from everywhere at once. The temperature dropped the moment we entered this room—this vault carved out of bedrock beneath Pylon #4 where no construction crew ever set foot.

Mara stands beside me, her white-lilac aura burning steady despite the psychic pressure that's making my teeth ache. The ruggedized monitor Danny rigged sits on a pedestal of weathered limestone, its screen scrolling through fragmented Coptic glyphs as the translation software chews through centuries of linguistic decay.

"Almost there," Danny's voice crackles through my comm. "Give me thirty seconds."

Thirty seconds feels like forever in a place like this.

I sweep my flashlight across the walls. More carvings. More warnings written in languages that died before Christ walked Galilee. Somewhere deep below us, something shifts. Stone grinding against stone. The sound travels through my boots, up my spine, settles behind my eyes like pressure building before a storm.

"The Experimental Sludge," Mara says quietly, reading my mind—or maybe just knowing what I'm thinking because we're both staring at the same damn problem. "If this tablet says it's not what we think..."

"It never is." I keep my voice flat. Mechanic-noir pragmatism. What else can you do when reality keeps proving itself more fucked than your worst nightmare? "Danny, how much longer?"

"Twenty seconds. Fuck, Cole, the encryption layers on this thing are—"

The monitor flickers. Text floods the screen.

I lean closer. Mara's shoulder brushes mine as we read together:

*The black venom of Apep flows from the Overmind's fangs, not waste but weapon, not byproduct but dominion. Four Heads stand above the serpent's coiling form, each believing themselves master while serving the same cage. One Head wears the mask of commerce, another the uniform of order, the third the robes of knowledge. But the fourth...*

My stomach drops.

"The Syndicate Broker," I say, the words coming out dead even though my pulse is hammering. "Marcus Voss. And whoever runs the BATC." Three visible heads. Three factions tearing the city apart while playing the same song from different sheet music.

"And a fourth," Mara whispers, her hand finding my wrist. Her fingers are ice cold despite her ward burning bright. "A Shadow Head."

The chamber grows colder. My hearth-coal ward gutters for a second before flaring back to life, and that momentary dip sends a spike of primal terror straight through my chest. Something down here doesn't want us reading this. Something knows we're close to understanding.

*They've been playing us against each other,* Mara says without saying it, because we both get it now. Years of violence between Syndicate cells and BATC task forces, between cops and criminals, all of it carefully orchestrated distraction while they bled their true source of power: an ancient god locked beneath our feet, pumping Experimental Sludge into the Passaic like poisoned wine.

"Cole." Danny's voice cuts through the comms. Panicked edge I rarely hear in his tone. "Mara. Look at the bottom of the tablet. The translation just finished the prophecy section. It names you both."

I shine my flashlight downward where older carvings overlap newer ones, a palimpsest of desperation spanning millennia. The glyphs glow faintly under the beam—residual energy or maybe just my imagination after staring too long into the void.

Danny feeds the translation through:

*The Daughter of the White Ash and the Threefold Iron Blade shall break the Nails.*

Mara and I stare at each other across two inches of stone-laden air. No words. Just recognition hitting like a freight train at 80 mph.

White ash. That's her. Has to be. The signature scent of her bloodline, the hearth-fire that burns clean and hot enough to forge wards that last centuries.

Threefold iron blade. My father's trinity knife, the one I carry even now, its three separate edges bound into one weapon that cuts deeper than steel should.

We are the catalysts.

The Four Heads need someone exactly like us to trigger whatever the fuck comes next.

---

## CHAPTER 11: THE NAILS OF APOPHIS

The air down here tastes like copper pennies left too long in someone's pocket—ancient metal, oxidized and bitter on my tongue. I set the Panasonic Toughbook down on what used to be an altar, or maybe just a fancy table for some Egyptian bureaucrat who thought he'd conquered New Jersey three thousand years ago. The limestone crumbles under the machine's weight, little puffs of dust that smell like nothing so much as the graveside at St. Lucy's where we buried our mother.

"Got you set up," I tell Mara without looking at her. My hands know the drill—they always do. Thick fiber-optic cable, heavy-gauge, military surplus from some warehouse in Bayonne that probably had better security than Fort Knox. Grimjaw's crew did the hard part already, but I check every connection anyway because dead man's switches don't care how tough you are when your lungs fill with Passaic River sediment.

The tap slides into place with a satisfying click. Green LEDs start blinking their little morse code lies about stability and connectivity.

Mara moves to the obsidian tablet like she's being pulled by gravity instead of choice. The sodium-vapor flare in her hand throws everything into harsh yellow relief—all sharp angles and deep blacks, no gray areas down here where they belong. The shadows it casts are wrong somehow, stretching out longer than physics says they should, reaching toward the walls where hieroglyphs crawl like insects over black glass polished smooth by hands that died before Christ was even a rumor.

"Light this up," I say. "Need to see what we're dealing with."
