I strap the last magazine into my vest pouch, feeling the familiar weight settle against my ribs like a second heartbeat. Silver-jacketed hollow points—standard issue for what we're dealing with now. Not that standards mean much anymore.

The harmonic dampener clicks into place on my belt, its low vibration thrumming through the fabric of my cargo pants. Good. The tech's holding. For now.

Chalk dust coats my palms, white and fine as bone powder. I wipe it across my tactical pants, watching the residue fall away in lazy spirals. The air around me shimmers with white-lilac light, steady and clean—not the corrupted mess it was an hour ago. Though if I let my guard down, even for a second, I can still smell that ash-gray static. Wet charcoal. Burnt wool.

*Sub-Station Seven.*

Three hundred fourteen commuters, turned to cinders by something that shouldn't exist outside of nightmare fuel.

I shake my head hard, dispersing the thought before it can take root. The frost-cobalt pulse comes automatically—that stabilizing warmth Cole's presence leaves behind, even when he's not here. Even when we're both about to walk into separate versions of hell tonight.

My keys jingle as I snag them from the table. Crown Vic's waiting downstairs, full tank, ammo cached in the trunk. Standard prep. Professional.

The Nextel chirps.

I freeze mid-turn, hand hovering over the walkie-talkie clipped to my belt. That harsh, electronic *chirp-chirp* cuts through the safehouse silence like a car alarm in a graveyard.

"Vance, you on the channel?"

Torin Kaelen. Torque. His voice rumbles through the speaker—gravel and gravelly machinery, the way it always does when he's working the deep excavations beneath Newark Bay. I can hear it in his tone: the whine of drills, the groan of earth-moving equipment, the metallic scrape of gold-bismuth ore being sorted and shaped into collars for the really nasty things we've been pulling out of the Passaic River lately.

"Yeah, Torque. Talk to me."

I press the push-to-talk button, thumb holding it down with practiced ease. The Nextel crackles with interference, shadows of conversations bleeding through from other channels—the BATC grid alive and buzzing even at this hour.

"The kids are awake," Torque says. His voice softens, just barely. Enough that I notice it. He's a dwarf who spends twelve-hour shifts in the dark, shaping metal with his bare hands, but something about those words makes him sound almost... gentle.

"They know you're going off-grid tonight." A pause. Machinery hums louder in the background. "You better get down here."

My chest tightens. Not from fear—from something worse. Responsibility. The weight of promises made to children who've already seen too much. Who've lost too much.

The Nextel clicks back into sleep mode. I unclip it slowly, running my thumb over the rubberized surface. Downstairs, past the industrial grime of the South Side, past the rusted girders and abandoned warehouses, Torque is waiting with the only thing keeping us human right now.

I kill the safehouse lights.

Darkness floods the room, absolute except for one detail—the faint blue-black sizzle still clinging to the concrete pillar where my mother's sector code burned itself into existence. That glowing script, counting down. Always counting.

To what? To when? To whether any of us make it through what's coming.

The safehouse door groans as I pull it open.

---

## CHAPTER 2: CHAPTER 2

The staircase groans beneath my boots, each step down another descent into the earth's dark memory. Rust flakes like orange snow, catching what little light bleeds from the surface world above. My hand never leaves the rail.

"Watch your footing on the lower landing, Commander," Ramos warned from three steps above me, his heavy tactical flashlight throwing a jaundiced yellow beam through the falling rust. "The salt damp has eaten right through the stringers. One wrong step and you're taking a thirty-foot bath in raw drainage."

"I've swum in worse than Passaic runoff, Sergeant," I said without looking back, keeping one hand braced against the cold brick wall. "Check the telluric meter on your chest harness. What's the ambient reading?"

"Forty-two millivolts and climbing," Ramos answered, the faint ticking of the needle audible over the drip of condensation. "Whatever Morvain's running down here, it's drawing off the main grid. The whole foundation is vibrating."

"It's not drawing from the grid," Cole muttered from the top of the stairwell, his silhouette dark against the drizzle outside. "It's feeding into it. The bastard's running an illegal siphon. Keep moving before their maintenance crew does their midnight rounds."—forty-three steps total, I've counted them before, though counting doesn't make returning here any easier.

The air hits me first. Always does. Ozone sharp enough to taste, mixing with decades of accumulated dust and that particular smell of desperate human habitation. Someone's cooking something in a hotplate—cabbage maybe, or worse—and underneath it all runs the metallic tang of the Vault itself. Concrete and rebar and fear, old fear baked into the walls like sedimentary rock.

I pause halfway down. Let my lungs adjust. The white-lilac begins its slow crawl up my spine, that familiar warmth spreading through my shoulders and chest. It wants to bloom, wants to push outward with full strength, but I rein it in. Not yet. Never scare them with power when they need safety most.

Thirty-eight souls down there. Thirty-eight ghosts walking in children's bodies.

I take the last seven steps slower now, deliberately softening my footsteps, altering my posture even before I clear the stairwell. Shoulders relaxed instead of squared. Hands visible and open at my sides instead of ready at belt level. The tactical mind stays sharp—it always does—but the armor goes away. Can't protect these kids if they can't see past the uniform to the person underneath.

They're clustered mostly on the far side, near the makeshift sleeping quarters someone's cobbled together from salvaged couches and military-issue cots. The sodium lighting casts everything in that sickly yellow-gold, making shadows pool too deep beneath their eyes, in the hollows of their cheeks. I count faces as I move forward: twelve humans, eight Elves, nine Dwarves, nine Orcs. All different. All the same now.

A young Dwarven girl—Maya, her name tag says, though she's outgrown it twice over—peels away from the group. Her braids have come loose, dark hair hanging wild around a face still streaked with dust from this morning's evacuation. She tugs at my cargo pants, fingers small enough that I feel the trembling through the fabric.

"Are the suits coming back, Commander?" Her voice cracks on the question, barely more than a whisper against the drip-drip-drip of condensation from the exposed pipes overhead.

"No," I say immediately, kneeling until we're eye-to-eye. "Not tonight."

My hand settles gently on her shoulder—not grabbing, not controlling, just there. Present. Real. "Tonight, I'm going to them."

Her dark eyes search mine, looking for lies or reassurance or maybe both. "Promise?"

I should lie. Should tell her something soothing about how everything will be fine, how the adults will handle it all. But I'm done lying to children who've already seen too much truth.

"I can't promise forever," I tell her instead, my voice low, grounded, no mystical inflection whatsoever—just one cop talking straight to a scared kid on what used to be the South Side before the Breach redrew every map. "But I promise tonight. And tomorrow night, if you need me here again, I'll be here. That's what I do."

She considers this with the seriousness of someone too old for their years. Then nods once, sharp and certain, and returns to her corner where three other Dwarven kids wait. They huddle together like birds making themselves smaller in the face of something vast and hungry.

The white-lilac aura pulses outward now, gentle as breath, washing over the entire Vault in waves of cedar warmth and hearth-coal comfort. It finds the terrified Elven boy hiding behind an overturned milk crate—the one whose parents didn't make it out, whose screams I'd heard through three city blocks—and wraps around him like a blanket. His bio-wards are gray-trauma saturated, ash-colored and brittle, but my aura moves through his defenses softly, giving his exhausted systems permission to rest without letting go of vigilance entirely.

Someone has a Sony MiniDisc player going in the corner—tinny hip-hop from 2003 bleeding through the speakers, some artist I vaguely recognize but can't name. The bass is completely absent, just mids and highs fighting against the ambient noise of the Vault. A teenager with headphones around his neck keeps the volume low, considerate despite everything. Respectable.

I move deeper into the space, acknowledging each cluster with a nod or brief eye contact, letting them know they're seen without overwhelming anyone. The humans gather near the makeshift kitchen area, two mothers sharing a thermos of something that smells more like coffee than it probably is. An older Orc woman sitting alone on the edge of a cot, rocking slightly, staring at nothing. Her son died in Sub-Station Seven. I remember her testimony from the investigation, remember the precise way she described watching him burn.

"Mrs. Kesh," I say quietly as I approach. "Can I sit?"

She blinks up at me, recognition slow to surface. When I lower myself beside her, she rocks faster for a moment before settling back into rhythm. "They said you found him."

"My team did." Not me personally—I was three blocks away coordinating air support—but close enough that the distinction matters less than what she needs to hear. "He didn't suffer long."

A lie. Maybe. The forensic data suggested minutes but felt like hours even compressed. But I'm learning that grief doesn't need accuracy, only shape. Something to hold onto when everything else dissolves.

Above us, a fluorescent tube flickers once, twice, then dies completely. Someone should replace it—the dying light casts worse shadows than steady dimness would—but no one moves. We've all gotten used to the decay. The Vault was never meant to be permanent, just survival until better options emerged. Three years later, it's still here, still necessary, and there are nights I wonder if we'll ever truly escape its gravity.

The white-lilac aura pulses brighter now, pushing harder against the accumulated trauma weighing down this space. Cedar scent mixing with ozone. Hearth-coal warmth fighting dust and fear. It won't fix anything—can't bring back the dead or unbreak broken children—but it gives them temporary shelter from the worst of it.

Tomorrow I'll go back above ground. Tomorrow I'll face the Syndicate suits who let Sub-Station Seven happen, who prioritized profit margins over safety protocols, whose negligence turned a Tuesday morning shift change into an inferno that consumed forty-seven souls including thirty-eight children's parents.

But tonight is for the ghosts. Tonight is for bearing witness to their survival.

* * *

I kneel beside them on the cold concrete floor, my knee joints protesting slightly as they always do after too many hours in tactical stance. The bunker reeks of damp earth and old fear—something you get used to when you run black-site operations beneath union halls in the Kearny Marshes.

Jax is maybe seventeen, if that. Hard to tell with Orcs sometimes—they mature fast or they don't make it past fourteen. His skin has that characteristic leathery texture, rough as sanded oak, and I can see where the Syndicate's runners got careless with their brand. The faint green glow of the Geas mark pulses just below his wrist, a sickly luminescence that makes my teeth ache.

"Burns less when you do that," he grunts through his lower tusks. His voice carries the flat affect of someone who's learned pain is temporary but debt is forever. South Side accent, probably from over near Newark Bay where the waterfront docks still operate under pre-Concordance rules.

Beside him, the Razor-Wire elf can't be more than twelve. Her ears are decorated with safety-pins—cheap street jewelry that catches the dim red emergency lighting strung across the ceiling beams. Her tapetum lucidum eyes reflect the light back at me like a cat's, yellow-gold and wary.

I'm already pulling off my tactical gloves, fingers working the Velcro releases without looking. The fabric peels away revealing my bare hands, and immediately the white-lilac aura flares to life around my fingertips—not from intent but from necessity. The children need calm right now more than anything else.

Fresh cedar floods the space. Warm hearth-coals.

It's all I can do to keep the ash-gray trauma from bleeding through because god help me, I remember what this feels like. Remember standing in a basement somewhere down near the Passaic River watching my own sister's brand pulse while some Syndicate runner explained how much she was worth on the arcane black market.

My hand hovers above Jax's forearm. "This will hurt worse before it gets better."

"Lady, everything hurts worse before it gets better." He doesn't pull away though. Just stares past me at the far wall like there might be something interesting painted on the concrete blocks.

I place my palm against his skin.

The moment contact makes, frost-cobalt warmth floods out—not mine, not from any magic I've trained with at Aegis Command. That's Cole's imprint, lingering psychic residue from when he touched these kids earlier. The Butcher has... peculiar talents when it comes to pain transference. Nasty business usually, but right now it means temporary relief for two terrified metahuman teenagers who've been property since they could walk.

Jax's breath hisses between his tusks. The green glow of his brand flickers, dimming slightly as my aura pushes against it—white-lilac suppression protocols kicking into high gear. Not enough to break the tether. Never enough for that without hitting the master console itself.

But enough to give him a few hours' respite from whatever hell the Syndicate's coding inflicts on its bonded assets.

"You're going to cut it," the elf girl says. Statement, not question. Her voice is surprisingly steady for someone so young. "Going to the Morvain Estate tonight. My cousin works security there—before they slot her last week. Said you were coming."

"I'm going to shatter their master console," I tell her, meeting those yellow-gold eyes dead-on because children need truth even when adults can't handle it. "Cole and I are making the approach through the Pulaski Skyway tunnels around midnight. By dawn, every Geas mark in this district goes dark permanently."

"By dawn." Jax repeats it like he's testing how the words feel in his mouth. Testing whether promises mean anything anymore.

"They better not miss, Vance." The elf's name tag reads 'Kira' in faded permanent marker scrawled by someone with terrible handwriting. Her ears twitch toward the sound of distant sirens—police or something else, hard to say from down here. "They'll slot us all if you do. Everyone in Local 405. Everyone at the Union Hall. Whole building gets red-flagged."

I don't flinch at the threat. Don't show fear because children learn what adults tolerate.

My hand moves from Jax's arm to Kira's wrist where an identical brand pulses sickly green against her pale skin. Same rough treatment as the boy's—a syndicate runner who didn't care about collateral damage while applying corporate property marks.

The moment my fingers touch her forearm, ozone sharpness explodes across my senses. That unique smell of electricity and magic fighting each other like rival gangs over territory rights.

"Then we'd better not fucking miss," I say quietly.

And make a vow to these kids that I'll be breaking before sunrise comes to North Jersey: I am going into hell itself if that's what it takes.

* * *

I stand up slowly, my knees protesting after too long kneeling beside those terrified children. The white-lilac of my aura hangs in the air like morning fog, still clinging to them, still whispering promises that everything will be alright even though I know better than to make such promises.

The vault's interior lights cast harsh shadows across the assembled families—twenty-seven souls total, crammed into a space meant for emergency supplies and union archives. Some have pulled blankets over their heads. Others stare at nothing, eyes hollow. A toddler begins to cry somewhere in the darkness, quickly shushed by a parent whose hands are probably shaking.

I ignore the pull to comfort them again. Every minute I linger here weakens what needs doing tonight.

Fidget sits hunched on an overturned crate near the vault entrance, his gnarled fingers dancing across a modified PalmPilot, stylus clicking against plastic in rapid-fire succession. The Gnome barely reaches four feet tall, his coat patched and re-patched until it's more duct tape than fabric. Years of tinkering in cramped server rooms have left him perpetually stooped, shoulders curved inward like parentheses around his chest.

"Got the frequencies masked, Commander," he squeaks without looking up, his voice like gravel tumbling through a pipe. "Bouncing our telemetry off three different cell towers downtown. The High-Spire won't see a blip."

His workspace is cluttered with soldering irons, multicolored wires snaking across the concrete floor, and three half-empty coffee cups that smell stale enough to be considered hazardous waste. A pack of Marlboros peeks out from his breast pocket—they'll need changing soon if the smoke-stain pattern on his yellowed fingertips is any indication.

I slip my tactical gloves back on, feeling the synthetic leather mold to each knuckle. "Keep them safe, Fidget. Nobody gets in."

"Not even if they come with federal warrants?" His dark eyes finally flick toward me, sharp despite the perpetual redness that comes from inhaling too much solder smoke over too many decades.

"Especially then." I move closer to examine his setup—three separate laptops running parallel intrusion detection systems, all wired directly into the bunker's localized defense grid. If someone tries to breach this vault, he'll know before their boots hit the stairs.

Fidget nods once, short and definite. He taps something else into his PalmPilot, and I hear the heavy, echoing *thud* of the vault's deadbolts sliding into place. Just a test. The sound reverberates through the concrete chamber like a death knell.

"Four hours," I tell him, checking my watch. "If I don't check in by 04:00 HRS, you scramble the frequencies, lock this vault from the inside, and initiate Local 405 evacuation protocol. Understand?"

"Understood." He doesn't ask where I'm going or what I'm doing. Good. That would mean I chose poorly when selecting ward-crackers.

Behind us, one of the children begins to sob quietly. A woman's voice hushes them again.

I turn to look at the digital clock mounted on the concrete wall. The red LED numbers flip to 23:15 HRS.

Outside, rain has begun to fall harder against the ventilation grates. I can hear it now—a rhythmic drumming that promises no letup before dawn. The storm is moving in from the east, pushing across Newark Bay with the kind of force that turns streets into rivers and floods the Kearny Marshes until they remember what they were before civilization tried to tame them.

It is time to head to the pines. Time to meet the Butcher.

I move toward the vault entrance, but pause at the threshold, looking back at Fidget one last time. "You know what happens if I fail."

His fingers continue their dance across the keyboard. "Then these people die anyway. No sense borrowing trouble."

Wise old bastard. I follow the stairs up through darkness that smells of rust and decay, each step taking me further from safety and closer to whatever fresh hell awaits beneath the Pulaski Skyway.

The night swallows me whole.

---

## CHAPTER 3: CHAPTER 3

The pine forest breathes around me as I move through it, each step deliberate and silent despite the squelching mud that tries to suck my combat boots down into the saturated earth.

"Keep your head down, Cole," I whispered over the tactical frequency, clicking the transmit switch twice. "Thermal scope on the perimeter tower just swept the tree line. Two seconds on, five seconds off."

"I see 'em," Cole's rasp came back through the earpiece, low and gravelly, accompanied by the wet squelch of his boots behind me. "Old Westinghouse mercury-arc lamps. They've got blind spots wide enough to drive a flatbed through if you hug the ditch."

"We aren't driving a flatbed," I replied, checking the bismuth charge in my sidearm. "We're cutting the telluric feed to their main gate before the midnight shift changes. How are the grounding straps?"

"Holding at four ohms," he said. "Cold-iron wire's biting into my wrists, but it beats having my marrow cooked if we trip a subterranean lead. Move on my mark. Three... two... go." Rain isn't just falling—it's attacking, driving in horizontal sheets under the low-hanging clouds that have swallowed what little night there should be at this hour.

My tactical gear is already soaked through. Water beads off my canvas jacket like oil on water, but my face feels like someone's pressing ice needles into my skin, again and again. The cold seeps past every layer. November in North Jersey has teeth, and they're biting hard tonight.

Somewhere ahead, beyond the veil of rain and darkness, the Morvain Estate sprawls across acres of prime North District real estate. The perimeter wall catches sodium-vapor light from within—a sickly orange-yellow glow that makes everything look infected, diseased. Those lights pulse in rhythm with Telluric generators humming somewhere deep below ground. Old money, old magic, and older secrets all wrapped up in brick and mortar.

I don't need those lights though. Not really.

The 4th Law pulls at something deep in my chest, a faint tugging sensation that cuts through the white noise of the storm. It's like following a thread through a labyrinth, invisible except to those who know how to look for it. Cole Reyes bleeds frost-cobalt energy when he's killing. Right now, that thread feels different—warmer, less predatory. Still dangerous. Always dangerous where he's concerned.

A shadow detaches itself from a massive pine trunk maybe fifteen meters ahead.

My hand doesn't go to my weapon. Instead, I adjust my grip on my sidearm while keeping both hands visible as I step forward into the open space between trees. The rain hammers down harder here, the pine canopy offering no shelter. My breath comes out in steamy puffs.

"Commander Vance." His voice carries easily over the storm's percussion, low and rough-edged. "You're late."

"Not by much," I reply, matching his tone. "Traffic was shit on the Pulaski Skyway."

That's a lie. There was no traffic tonight. Hardly anyone drives after midnight anymore, not with the things that hunt the highways after dark. But I needed time to think, to prepare myself for this meeting.

Cole emerges fully from the shadows, and the cold disappears.

Not gradually—it vanishes. One moment I'm freezing, my muscles tensing against the bite of November rain. The next, warmth floods through me like someone just opened an oven door. It smells like burning wood and hot iron, with undertones of cedar and something else I can't quite place. Something wild and primal.

He's wearing a grease-stained mechanic's jacket over dark tactical pants, his pump-action shotgun slung across his back. Water cascades off the brim of his baseball cap, but his dark eyes are dry, locked onto mine with an intensity that makes my chest tighten.

There's no frost-cobalt bleeding off him right now—not the dead-silent, zero-remorse energy he reserves for when he's working. What I'm seeing instead is white-lilac, warm and almost gentle compared to what he usually projects. Still dangerous, still Cole Reyes, but… different.

"You look like hell, Commander," he says, taking a step closer.

"So do you, Reyes." Another step forward on my part, closing the distance between us until we're close enough to touch if either of us dared make that move. "But we've both seen worse."

The warmth radiating from him pushes back the November night completely now. Standing here in this pocket of heat while rain continues to hammer down around us feels surreal, like stepping into another dimension where normal rules don't apply.

"Morvain's got Telluric generators running at full capacity tonight," I say, needing to focus on something practical, something other than how easy it would be to lean into his space and let that fire-coal smell fill my lungs completely. "Probably knows we're here or suspects something."

Cole's jaw clenches. "Then we'd better make this quick." He glances past me toward where the sodium lights pulse weakly through the trees. "You sure about this play? After what happened last time—"

"I'm sure." The words come out harder than I intended. "We need what's inside that vault, and Morvain won't negotiate. Never does."

"What makes you think he'll talk after we take what we came for?"

I meet his gaze again, holding it even as every instinct screams at me to look away, to break eye contact before I lose myself in those dark eyes entirely. "Because he's not the one who's going to be doing the talking."

The 4th Law thrums between us now, our combined energy creating feedback loops that make the air shimmer with frost-cobalt and white-lilac, intertwining in ways that shouldn't be possible but somehow are when we're this close.

"This is a bad idea," Cole says quietly.

"You have a better one?"

He's silent for a long moment, studying my face like he's memorizing every detail by feel alone. When he finally speaks again, his voice drops even lower: "Yeah. We walk away right now and never look back."

My heart hammers against my ribs hard enough to hurt. Part of me wants to agree—to grab onto that lifeline and run before whatever this thing between us becomes something neither of us can control anymore.

But there are priorities beyond desire.

"There's no walking away from this, Reyes." My hand finally moves to rest on my sidearm—not threateningly, just acknowledging its presence. Grounding myself. "Not until Morvain pays for what he did to the Kearny Marshes."

Cole's expression shifts then, something cold and final settling into his features. The warmth doesn't fade—if anything it intensifies—but now there's an edge to it too. A promise of violence carefully controlled but still inevitable.

"Then let's get this done." He reaches behind him without looking, producing a small metal case from somewhere inside his jacket. "Brought you something."

I take it carefully—the thing is warm to the touch almost painfully so—and open it to reveal three crystalline vials filled with pulsing blue liquid. Telluric stabilizers, military grade.

"You shouldn't have," I murmur.

"I know." His smile doesn't reach his eyes. "That's why I did."

The rain continues hammering down around our pocket of warmth as we stand here at the edge of the Morvain Estate grounds—a commander and her most dangerous asset locked together in a moment that could be our last or the beginning of something much worse.

Whatever comes next, we'll face it together.

Or die trying.

* * *

The freezing rain hammers down harder now, each droplet stinging like tiny needles against my exposed skin. I pull up the sleeve of my BATC-issue tactical watch, the glowing green luminescence cutting through the darkness as I check the time—23:47 HRS. Two minutes until we move.

Cole stands beside me in the shadows between two ancient pines, the trees bent under the weight of accumulated snow and ice. He mirrors my movement, exposing his own wrist. Where mine is sleek black polymer and military-grade rubber, his is an ugly Casio covered in grease stains and scratches. The cheap watch face glows the same sickly green in the darkness.

As our bare fingers brush while synchronizing the time—exactly 23:48 HRS on both watches—the air crackles. A visible spark arcs between us, white-lilac and frost-cobalt energies colliding in a miniature aurora borealis. The collision creates heat where there should be none, pushing back the freezing rain in a small sphere around us both.

I look up at Cole's face, really seeing him for the first time in weeks. The heavy toll of his crusade is etched into every line around his eyes, every shadow beneath his cheekbones. His beard has grown wild, streaked with premature gray that wasn't there six months ago.

"This doesn't fix it, Mara," he says, his voice stripped of any romantic illusion. There's only raw truth left in it. "Dropping this grid tonight... it's a sliver of justice. It's not gonna scrape the black iron out of Danny's lungs. He's still gonna be strapped inside that brass-and-glass iron lung in Bram's sub-basement tomorrow."

He stares down at his hands—those scarred, calloused hands that know the feel of wrenching metal from engines and breaking bones from jawbones. Hands that have saved lives and ended them in equal measure over the last two years.

"It's never enough." His voice breaks slightly on those words, but only slightly. Two years of pain has taught him to keep most of it locked down deep. "But a sliver of justice for Danny, for those kids in the Vault... it's better than no justice for anyone."

The Morvain Estate looms ahead through the curtain of rain, its walls lit by strategic placement of our team's suppression devices. The perimeter is secure—we've already dealt with the outer ring of security. What lies beyond those walls is what matters now.

I watch as cedar wards—my signature energy—begin to wrap around Cole instinctively, drawn to him like iron filings to a magnet. They curl around his shoulders, his arms, offering their warmth against the freezing night.

"Then we take the sliver," I say quietly, holding his gaze. "And we make them bleed for the rest."

His eyes meet mine, and I see the warrior who burned half of Sub-Station Seven looking back. The man who became a weapon because the system failed people like Danny, like the kids in the Vault, like countless others whose names would never make police reports or news feeds.

"We burn it all down," he says. Not a question. A statement of fact.

"Yes." My hand moves to check my sidearm—the BATC-issued Glock 21, modified with frost-cobalt runes along the slide. Fully loaded. Ready. "We burn it all down."

The rain continues its assault, but inside our sphere of intertwined energies, the air remains warm. Frost-cobalt and white-lilac dance together, smelling heavily of hearth-coals and cedar, mixed with the acrid tang of gun oil and old engine grease that clings to Cole's leather jacket.

At exactly 23:50 HRS, we both move simultaneously. No words needed. Years of working together have made us a unit, our movements synchronized without conscious thought.

"For Danny," Cole whispers as we emerge from the tree line.

"For everyone they forgot," I answer as we begin our approach to the Morvain Estate walls.

The sliver of justice awaits. And if we're lucky—and ruthless enough—we might just carve it out of these bastards tonight.

* * *

The freezing rain hammers against my neck as I crouch beside the stone pillar, my fingers working the waterproof cable connector into the hidden data-port beneath the ivy. My breath comes out in white plumes that the wind tears apart before they rise two feet.

Cole's presence at my shoulder is a wall of cold heat—frost-cobalt energy bleeding from him like steam off winter pavement, but it doesn't make me shiver the way the November air does. If anything, standing this close creates a bubble of warmth that fights back against the downpour.

"My god, you're practically glowing," I mutter, not looking up from the PalmPilot screen. The harsh green glow reflects off my wet cheeks, casts shadows under my eyes that make me look like something dug up from a shallow grave. "They'll spot us from space."

"Then hurry." His voice is flat, controlled. Behind me, I hear the whisper-soft *shink* of metal on Kydex—a sound I've come to associate with impending violence.

The decryption sequence crawls across the bottom of the screen. TELLURIC MOTION SENSOR ARRAY - OUTER PERIMETER. AUTHENTICATION FAILED. REATTEMPTING...

"I know, I'm trying," I snap back, my thumb flying over the mini-keyboard. Each letter I type feels like it takes forever. The rain finds every gap in my tactical jacket. "The Morvain Estate's security is run by High-Spire elves. They don't believe in anything less than military-grade encryption."

"AREA DENIAL SYSTEMS DETECTED."

There it is. The real problem. Not just motion sensors—the whole perimeter is wired with tripwires that trigger automated defensive measures if anyone tries to bypass the gates properly. Smart.

I switch protocols, fingers dancing now with muscle memory developed over years of this kind of work. My other hand grips the pillar until my knuckles ache, grounding myself as I feel for the right sequence—not just disabling, but creating a blind spot. A dead zone where no alerts will fire.

"Sensors are blind," I whisper, disconnecting the hardline cable and pocketing both connector and PalmPilot in one fluid motion. I rise smoothly, water streaming off my shoulders. "We have a three-minute window before the sub-routine cycles and flags the dead zone."

Cole racks his shotgun.

The sound tears through the night like a gunshot, deafeningly loud against the sheeting rain. Birds scatter from the pines above us. I flinch despite myself, turning to see him lowering the weapon, his eyes already scanning the manicured grounds beyond the fence.

"Three minutes is plenty," he says.

He steps forward, combat knife held low and ready, blade gleaming even in the dim light—blood-iron, forged under conditions that would kill a normal human within seconds. The metal pulses faintly, reacting to his metahuman nature.

I move to follow when something catches my eye—a pulse of red along the iron bars nearest the gate. Runic wards, embedded in the wrought-iron itself. They're dying, fading to gray as whatever magic powers them succumbs to Mara's digital assault on their sensor network. But there's a moment of transition, a vulnerability.

"The wards," I say sharply. "They're—"

Cole doesn't wait. He drives the knife into the lock mechanism with brutal precision.

Metal screams. Frost-cobalt energy surges from his hand, meeting the physical force of his strike in an explosion of crackling power. The ancient locking mechanism—the kind designed to hold back things worse than intruders—shatters.

The heavy, wet click of the iron gate swinging open sounds impossibly loud in the sudden silence after the explosion of breaking metal. Well-oiled hinges make it smooth, silent. An invitation.

We slip through together into darkness deeper than the rain-soaked night outside.

And then—

Light.

A beam of high-intensity tactical illumination cuts through the downpour like a laser, sweeping across the lawn before slamming directly onto my chest. White-hot. Blinding.

"Contact right!" Cole barks.

From behind a sculpted hedge thirty yards out, three figures step into view. High-Spire Elven arc-guards, their charcoal suits remaining impossibly dry despite standing in the same deluge we just emerged from. Their movements are synchronized, practiced. MP7 submachine guns coming up in one fluid motion.

My hand goes to my sidearm.

Their weapons don't hesitate.

---

## CHAPTER 4: CHAPTER 4

The estate lawn erupts.

My world narrows to a strobe light of muzzle flashes—brilliant white-gold explosions in the darkness, each one painting the rain-soaked grass in violent bursts of illumination. I'm already moving when my brain registers the threat, muscle memory from a hundred firefights kicking in before conscious thought catches up.

Left. Dive left.

The wet grass hits me like a wall as I roll, feeling the impact of bullets chewing up turf inches behind where my body was. The sounds register separately—the sharp *crack* of supersonic rounds breaking the sound barrier, the wet thump of impacts, the high-pitched whine of a near-miss that sends my wards flaring in protest.

I come up on one knee, the cold weight of the MP5 familiar against my shoulder. My finger finds the trigger with practiced ease, and I don't hesitate—I never hesitate anymore. Three-round burst, center mass, the silver-jacketed hollow points trailing threads of arcane energy as they spin toward the lead guard.

The kinetic impact is beautiful in its brutality. The Elf's tailored charcoal suit does nothing to stop the hex-weaving rounds. His bio-armor, corporate-grade and supposedly impregnable, simply fails. He's thrown backward by the force of it, his tapetum lucidum eyes reflecting the muzzle flash even as life drains from them, shock freezing his flawless features into a mask of disbelief.

Cole moves differently than anyone I've ever seen.

He doesn't take cover. Doesn't dive for the ground or use the courtyard's ornate fountains for protection. Instead he closes distance with terrifying speed, his footsteps somehow silent despite the chaos around us. His frost-cobalt wards flare brilliantly blue-white as a round glances off his shoulder—he doesn't even flinch.

The shotgun comes up with fluid precision. One pump. Two. The booming thunder of it drowns out everything else—a deep, chest-vibrating roar that makes my teeth ache. The depleted-bismuth payload catches the second guard square in the torso, and I hear the sickening wet crunch even over the gunfire. The Elf's body does a grotesque pirouette before collapsing.

The third one drops his weapon immediately, hands coming up glowing with that sickly yellow corporate magic—rapid-transit spell already forming. "He's dialing out!" My voice cracks across the noise, raw with adrenaline. "I got him!"

But Cole's already moving past the statement. He drops the shotgun to its sling without checking if the target went down, draws his heavy 1911 in one seamless motion that would make any operator weep with envy. Two rounds. *Bam. Bam.* The 230-grain hollow points punch through the Elf's chest, dropping him instantly into a spreading puddle of blood and rainwater.

"Clear," Cole says, his accent thick enough to taste on my tongue. His voice is utterly flat, emotionless despite what just happened. "Move up."

I'm already running.

* * *

The moment our boots hit the cobblestones, everything went active.

I felt it first—a deep resonance in my bones, that telltale vibration of runecrafted machinery waking from sleep. Then came the sound: servo-motors grinding awake with mechanical hunger, hydraulic pistons hissing as armored panels slid open within marble statues that suddenly weren't just decorative anymore.

"Contact!" I barked, already raising both hands.

The turrets emerged fully deployed—heavy-caliber auto-guns mounted on articulated Dwarven frames, each one bristling with overlapping rune-etched barrels that glowed a sickening orange-red. Not Elvish elegance here. This was pure, brutal engineering, stamped with the marks of Local 405 Union workshops. I recognized Bram's craftsmanship instantly—the way those servos moved, the specific pattern of those runes.

They opened fire without hesitation.

My white-lilac ward erupted outward like a bubble catching bullets, and the courtyard became a chaos of hyperkinetic light. Heavy rounds slammed into my barrier, each impact sounding like someone driving railroad spikes through tempered glass. The force pushed against my consciousness, making my teeth ache and my sinuses burn.

Then Cole stepped into my aura, and everything changed.

His frost-cobalt energy didn't clash with mine—it *meshed*, weaving together like interlocking gears finding their perfect mesh. Blood-iron strength flooded into my construct, and the shield hardened visibly, sparks scattering wider as we held position beneath a hail of automated death.

"Local 405 tech!" I screamed over the gunfire, sweat mixing with rain on my face, dripping down my neck. "Heavy gauge! Bram's union brothers built this!"

The turrets kept tracking, their targeting algorithms coldly efficient as they walked fire across our position. Tracer rounds burned molten divots into the ancient cobblestones around us, superheating stone into glowing puddles of half-melted rock. The smell of burning marble mixed with ozone and cordite, cutting through even the cedar-scent of my magic.

Cole snarled, slamming a fresh tube into his shotgun—depleted-bismuth slugs that would punch through armor plating like paper. His frost-cobalt energy pulsed brighter, visible in the darkness as he recharged for another blast.

"Then we break it like union men," he growled, his voice carrying that edge it got when bloodlust really took hold. "Drop the shield on three! I'll take the left, you take the right!"

My heart hammered against my ribs. This was insane. Suicidal. But Cole was already counting down, his weapon raised.

"One."

I braced myself, feeling the strain in every muscle as I maintained the barrier while positioning for movement.

"Two."

The turret closest to me tracked its barrels toward where I'd be standing if I moved first—a trap, an algorithm trying to predict—

"THREE!"

I dropped the shield.

For one microsecond, we were exposed. For one impossible heartbeat, those heavy guns had clear shots at both of us while we sprinted forward into the kill zone.

But Cole was faster than their servos could track. He dove left, shotgun coming up in a smooth arc, and unleashed a point-blank blast that turned the leftmost turret into a shrieking fountain of sparks and twisted metal. Depleted-bismuth slugs ripped through the Dwarven engineering like it was tissue paper, shredding runes and shearing through hydraulic lines in a symphony of destruction.

I threw everything into my right hand, white-lilac energy condensing into a kinetic lance, and drove it point-first into the second turret's optical sensor array. The machine screamed—a high-pitched mechanical death rattle—as my magic boiled its targeting core, frying circuits and melting precision optics into slag.

Behind us, runic tripwires snapped to life across the courtyard floor, glowing that same furious orange, creating a grid of deadly detection fields.

We didn't slow down.

Cole kicked off a marble pedestal, spinning mid-air to put another round into a hidden panel I'd spotted near the fountain—the main control node for this section of defenses. It exploded in a shower of fragments and extinguished light.

Silence fell over the courtyard, broken only by the crackle of dying electronics and the steady drip of rain onto scorched stone.

My chest heaved as I caught my breath, white-lilac wards still flickering around my hands with residual energy. Beside me, Cole racked his shotgun, chambering fresh rounds with mechanical efficiency.

"Bram's going to hear about this," I muttered, looking at the smoking wreckage of his brothers' work.

"Tell him it's personal now," Cole replied flatly, already scanning for the next threat.

* * *

The white-lilac wards flare one final time before I let them collapse like a dying star going nova. The dome shatters into a million crystalline fragments that hang in the air for one impossible moment before dissolving into pure light.

"One... Two... Three!"

My command cuts through the chaos like a blade. In that split-second of sensor-blindness, as the automated turrets struggle to re-acquire us in the aftermath of my ward-dome's destruction, we strike.

I drop to one knee, MP5 rising smooth as silk, and sweep right. My rounds punch through the rain-soaked darkness—three precise shots that shatter the optical sensors of the two statues on my flank. They go dark instantly, heads lolling at unnatural angles as their internal mechanisms seize and die. Sparking wires drip molten metal down their stone faces.

Cole moves like he's reading my thoughts—because maybe he is. His boots slap against wet pavement as he steps forward into the gap I've created, his shotgun coming up in one fluid motion. The roar of his weapon tears through the night twice—a thunderclap of sound that makes my teeth ache.

Bismuth slugs don't just hit things; they *devour* them.

The heavy rounds slam into the reinforced armor plating of the left-side turrets with the force of artillery shells. There's no clean penetration—there's obliteration. The turret's internal ammunition feeds detonate in cascading explosions of sparks and grinding gears, the metallic scream of tortured machinery echoing off the courtyard walls. Molten casings rain down like deadly confetti.

Then silence.

Just the hiss of rain hitting hot metal.

"We're clear," Cole rumbles from beside me, breaking lock on his target. His frost-cobalt aura fades slightly, the immediate threat neutralized. "Move."

But I'm already moving, my boots carrying me toward those massive oak doors that guard the manor house entrance. The wood towers over us, ancient and thick, bound with iron straps that look more decorative than functional. Looks can be deceiving.

I press my palm flat against the grain, feeling the rough texture against my skin. Magic flows through me—not the bright, searing power of a ward-dome, but something more focused, more surgical. A localized detonation hex, small-scale but precisely targeted at the door's structural weak points.

Behind me, I hear Cole shift his weight back. He doesn't need words to understand what comes next.

Three seconds. That's all it takes for my hex to weave itself into the wood fibers, finding every stress fracture, every microscopic weak point accumulated across centuries of weather and time.

*BOOM.*

The concussive wave hits us both like a physical wall, even from this distance. Sawdust and splinters explode outward in a cloud of debris. The reinforced hinges groan—the sound of iron being tortured beyond its breaking point—and then give way with a series of sharp *CRACKS* that echo like gunshots.

The massive oak doors blow inward, crashing onto the polished marble floor inside with a thunderous impact that rattles my bones. The sound reverberates through the courtyard, swallowed by the storm behind us.

"Together," I say quietly, raising my MP5 to high ready position.

Cole nods once, his shotgun held low but deadly. We step through the threshold as one, leaving the storm-ravaged courtyard behind us.

The foyer that greets us is vast—cathedral-ceiling vast, oppressively so. Lightning flashes through tall windows set impossibly high on the walls, casting brief illuminations of the space between strikes. The opulence hits first: crystal chandeliers suspended on chains thick as wrists, oil paintings in gilded frames depicting scenes that make my stomach turn, marble floors so polished you could see your face in them if not for the shadows.

But there are no guards. No welcoming committee. No army waiting to cut us down.

Just silence. Heavy. Waiting.

"And here we go," Cole mutters beside me.

I don't respond. My eyes are already scanning the darkness ahead, searching for movement, for threats, for anything that might betray where Morvain has hidden himself in this monument to excess and depravity.

The High-Spire's true horror awaits us somewhere in these halls.

I can feel it breathing in the shadows.

---

## CHAPTER 5: CHAPTER 5

The rain hammers down like nails being driven into a coffin lid as Cole and I breach the main doors of the Morvain Estate.

"Door's reinforced oak over quarter-inch rolled steel," Cole muttered, running his calloused palm down the seam. "Deadbolt's linked to a telluric trip-wire. Touch the brass cylinder and it dumps five hundred amps through the handle."

"Stand back," I told him, sliding my ceramic probe into the keyway. The cold telluric current bit through my glove liner like ice water. "I'll ground the discharge through my white-lilac weave. You take the hinges with the sledge."

"You sure your heart-cage can eat that much juice, Vance?" he asked, raising the heavy sixteen-pound hammer with casual ease.

"I'm not sure of anything since Sub-Station Seven, Cole," I snapped, teeth gritted as the spark arced across my knuckles with a sharp, ozone-tinged crack. "Now hit it!"

The hammer swung with a deafening crash, the brass lock shearing off into the foyer. My boots hit the marble first—the sound absurdly loud in the suffocating silence that follows. Water streams from our tactical gear onto the pristine checkered floor, creating dark Rorschach stains that spread like spilled blood across white stone.

I don't lower my MP5. Can't. Not in this place.

The grand foyer stretches before us like a throat waiting to swallow us whole. A sweeping staircase curves up to the second floor, each step visible only as a dark silhouette against shadows thick enough to hide men with weapons. The archways branching off the main space yawn black, mouth-like, exhaling nothing but cold air that tastes of copper and lemon oil.

"This is wrong," I whisper, though I'm not entirely sure if I'm talking to Cole or myself. The words feel stolen from my mouth even as they leave it.

Cole's shotgun stays level, his movements economical as he covers the left flank. We move in concert—years of joint ops making our positioning instinctive. His wet rubber soles squeak against the marble with each calculated step. The sound echoes through the cavernous space, bouncing off walls decorated with paintings I can't quite see clearly. Their faces seem to turn away when I try to focus on them.

"Watch the corners," I say, voice tight as a wire about to snap. "This is too quiet. The internal grid should be screaming by now."

My wards flicker at the base of my skull—that familiar white-lilac burn that's been my constant companion since I made Aegis Commander. Right now they're misfiring, sputtering like a dying engine. The scent that usually accompanies them—the clean cedar smell of protective magic—has gone stale, replaced by something else. Something I haven't smelled in years.

Ash-gray static. Wet charred wool.

I push the sensation down, force it beneath layers of combat discipline. This isn't the time for whatever fucked-up psychological cascade is trying to surface.

"They know we're here," Cole replies softly, his voice carrying no inflection. He sweeps his shotgun barrel across an archway leading into what might be a sitting room—or an ambush site. "They're just waiting for us to walk into the kill box."

He doesn't sound afraid. That's what makes him good at this. He sounds like he's diagnosing a bad transmission: fact-based, fatalistic, utterly matter-of-fact about the possibility of dying in the next thirty seconds.

The grandfather clock in the corner ticks. Each second mark feels deliberate, measured—a countdown rather than time passing naturally. The massive brass mechanism's face gleams dully in the low light filtering through tall windows draped in heavy curtains. The hands read 12:17, though my watch shows 00:16.

Time gets weird around High-Spire estates. Always has.

"The library," I say, jerking my chin toward the main hallway stretching before us. According to the blueprints we acquired from that terrified architect in Newark Bay, the sub-vault entrance is hidden behind a false panel in the library. Standard Morvain construction: pretty on top, apocalyptic machinery below ground where their real operations run.

We move deeper into the house. My boots leave wet tracks across marble that should have been dusty with disuse but instead gleams as if freshly polished. Someone maintains this place despite it being abandoned by all official accounts.

The scent intensifies—lemon oil and old paper, those expensive smells of inherited wealth masking something underneath. Gunpowder residue from our breach adds a sharp chemical note, but beneath everything else, that phantom smell crawls up from some buried part of my brain.

Ash-gray static and wet charred wool.

The hallway narrows. Portraits line both sides now, faces I recognize from dossiers but somehow feel like I've known much longer than file review would suggest. Morvain bloodline, generations deep, all those calculating eyes following our progress toward the library doors at the end of the corridor.

Cole signals a halt with two fingers up. His shotgun never wavers from covering the space behind us.

"Commander." Just my rank. Never Mara. Professional distance even when we're alone in hostile territory.

I freeze mid-step, my boot hovering inches above the marble. The white-lilac wards flare warning hot at the base of my skull—a pulse of protective magic that sends ice down my spine because it's not responding to external threat.

It's responding to *memory*.

"This place," I start, then stop. Swallow hard against the taste of copper on my tongue. "We need to clear fast. Something's wrong with the magical signatures here."

Not exactly true. Not entirely false. What's wrong isn't the estate's defenses. It's what they're dredging up inside me just by existing.

The library doors loom ahead, twin oak panels carved with symbols that shift when I look directly at them. Behind those doors is our objective: access to whatever the Morvains have hidden below ground in their sub-vault. Probably weapons. Definitely something worth killing for.

Probably more dangerous than either of us realizes.

My finger rests alongside the MP5's trigger guard—not on the trigger, not yet, but close enough that muscle memory could pull it without conscious thought if shadows move wrong in this tomb-quiet hallway.

"We push through together," Cole says quietly. Not asking. Informed by years of watching how I operate under pressure. He knows something's off. Knows it's making me hesitate when hesitation gets people killed.

But he also knows I won't back down. Won't retreat. Not after everything it took to get here, not after the bodies we left cooling in Newark Bay to make this infiltration possible.

"On three," I whisper, and feel my wards try to stabilize even as that old smell fills my nostrils like I'm breathing through a grave.

* * *

The hallway stretches before us like a throat, all shadows and golden light bleeding between frames. My boots whisper against hardwood polished to a mirror sheen—I can see our distorted reflections fractured beneath our feet, warped by centuries of wax and footfalls.

Cole moves ahead, his rifle up, clearing corners with practiced efficiency. But I'm barely tracking him anymore.

My gaze has locked onto the portrait.

It hangs there, center-right, illuminated by that small brass sconce like some kind of profane altar. The painting depicts a woman—no, *the* woman—in evening dress from another era, her dark hair pinned in elaborate coils, her face pale and severe beneath a cascade of pearls. She wears a crimson gown that pools at her feet like frozen blood. Her eyes follow us down the corridor.

I recognize those eyes.

I recognize the curve of her cheekbone.

"Mara. Talk to me." Cole's voice cuts through my consciousness, sharp and insistent. He's positioned himself in front of me now, his broad shoulders blocking my line of sight to anything else. Scanning. Always scanning. But there's nothing to scan. Just paint. Just canvas. Just the past coming back to strangle me in my moment of weakness.

"What do you see?"

The MP5 dangles in my grip, forgotten. My thumb rests on the safety, but I don't remember moving it. The weight feels wrong suddenly—not the gun itself, but everything about this moment. The cedar scent of my wards has gone rancid, replaced by something older. Something that smells like ash-gray static and wet charred wool.

"I... I know this house," I hear myself say, and my own voice sounds distant, disconnected from the person speaking it. My jaw hangs loose, unprofessional as hell, but I can't seem to pull it shut. "I've been here before."

Cole spins toward me, and for just a second—the barest flicker—I catch something in his expression. Recognition? Fear? It's gone too fast to parse.

"That's not possible," he says, and even as he says it, we both know it is. We both feel it. The Morvain Estate isn't just a house. It's a wound in reality, a place where time bleeds sideways into itself like a corpse bleeding out onto snow.

He steps closer, reaches out like he wants to grab my shoulder, steady me. His hand stops an inch away—whether from professional restraint or some deeper instinct, I don't know.

"Commander, you need to focus." His eyes search mine, looking for the woman who led us through Sub-Station Seven, who held her ground against things that shouldn't exist. "We're exposed in this hallway. You're exposed. Talk to me."

But how do I explain that I'm five years old again? That I'm standing at the top of these stairs while grown men shout below? That I can smell my mother's perfume mixing with gunpowder and blood?

The portrait smiles at me.

No—that's impossible. Paint doesn't move. Dead women don't track your movements across centuries.

Yet she's watching. I *know* she's watching.

* * *

The oil painting hangs on the wall like an accusation.

I step closer, ignoring the warning hiss from Cole behind me. My combat instincts should be screaming danger—we're exposed in this hallway, vulnerable—but all I can see is *him*. Elias Morvain. Director of the Bureau of Arcane Threat Containment. The man who hired me three years ago after I washed out of police academy. The man whose signature appears on every paycheck, every commendation, every goddamn piece of paper that told me I was doing something meaningful with my life.

He's standing in the portrait, crystal glass held loosely in one hand, the other resting possessively on Julian Sterling's shoulder. My uncle. The Visible Head. The man Cole dismantled in a Newark warehouse six months ago, his organs spilling across concrete as he screamed about things I didn't understand then.

My white-lilac wards flicker, dying down to barely perceptible sparks around my fingers. The cedar scent goes stale and sour in my nostrils, replaced by that phantom smell again—the ash-gray static, the wet charred wool that haunted my childhood nights in foster homes where adults whispered about the Vance bloodline and what we'd *done* before we were scattered like dandelion seeds.

"The fuck," I breathe, reaching out with trembling fingers. Stopping just short of touching the canvas. The painted eyes of both men seem to follow my movement, lifelike and damning in their detail.

"That's Julian," Cole says behind me. His voice has gone flat, deadened into that absolute zero place the Butcher lives. He recognizes them both—the corpse he made, the director who sent us here. "And that's Morvain."

I nod slowly. Each confirmation hammers another nail into the coffin of everything I thought I knew. "They were together. From the beginning."

The mechanical grinding starts beneath our feet before I can process it fully. A deep, runic vibration that travels up through the floorboards, through the soles of our boots. Not alarms—something worse. Deliberate. The sound of a vault door unsealing somewhere in the sub-levels below this manor.

Cole's frost-cobalt wards snap to full intensity around him, ice crystals forming in the air like frozen daggers. "That wasn't locked. Someone just opened it for us."

Which means they know we're here.

Which means whoever's waiting down there knew we'd find this painting. Knew how it would break me.

---

## CHAPTER 6: CHAPTER 6

The library erupts in a storm of brass casings and ozone.

Cole's shotgun roars first, that deep-throated *BOOM* that makes my sinuses pop at fifteen feet.

"Clear left!" he barked, ejecting a smoking hull that clattered against the parquet floor. "Two down behind the librarian's desk! One more scrambled through the service elevator!"

"Hold your fire!" I shouted, sweeping my light across the ruined leather-bound volumes and shattered glass cases. "Smell that? It's not cordite."

Cole paused, nostrils flaring as he wiped a smear of soot from his jaw. "Phosphorus. And dried sage. Someone was burning ward-incense in here five minutes ago."

"Not just ward-incense," I said, crouching by the carved fireplace. "Look at the hearthstone. There's a hydraulic release set into the mantle. Morvain didn't take the elevator. He took the fire-stair down to the vault."

"Then let's go pay the landlord a visit," Cole pumped another round into the chamber, eyes hard as flint. "Ramos, watch our six at the threshold. Nobody leaves this wing alive except us." The sound slams into my chest cavity before I can process it, followed by the chemical punch of burning propellant. Cordite sharpens to needle-points in my nostrils as I slide left beneath his firing line, boots skidding across blood-slicked marble.

"Contact!" His voice cuts through the deafening report. Not yelling—command tone, matter-of-fact. Professional.

I don't answer. Can't. My breath is already fogging white in air that dropped ten degrees the moment he racked that Mossberg. Frost-cobalt resonance ripples outward from his position, a visible shimmer like heat haze in reverse. My own wards—the white-lilac and fresh cedar I've been maintaining since we kicked in those mahogany doors—flare at the edges where they intersect with his field. Sparks scatter across the ceiling, tiny fireworks against oil-painted baroque angels.

The rotary cannons mounted in the plasterwork cornices spin up with an industrial whine that sets my teeth on edge. Automated defense systems. Local 405 Dwarven engineering if I've ever seen it—all precisely machined iron and telluric runes that would make a proper artificer weep.

Bram Kovacs would certainly spit.

Not that I have time for sentimentality.

My silver warrant-stylus is already out, caught between my teeth as I shoulder-roll behind an overturned reading table. Iron-gall residue bleeds from bullet holes in the floorboards, staining the polished wood black-blue-black, like veining in obsidian. The smell hits me next—wet charred wool mixing with ozone. My throat constricts involuntarily.

*Sub-Station Seven. November 2007. Ash-gray static.*

No. Focus. *Now* is November 14th, 2007. Three years later. Different mission. Same job.

"Mara!"

Cole's shout snaps me back into the present just as my fingers find purchase on the floorboard rune. It's cold—colder than it should be, even accounting for Cole's localized frost effect. The stylus bites into the carved channel with a sound like grinding teeth. Ward-sense floods through my palm: Telluric currents, defensive protocols, and beneath it all...

The floor isn't solid.

It's illusion over steel.

I twist hard left, putting my whole body weight into the motion. Something cracks—a metal hinge beneath the mahogany veneer. The rune flares sickly amber before short-circuiting into dead copper. "Got it!" My voice sounds thin, distant even to myself.

The shotgun booms again. Twice. Four times.

The rotary cannons shriek and die mid-spin, their mounting brackets sheared clean through by depleted-bismuth slugs. Shrapnel pings off marble columns, shreds a leather-bound tome that explodes in a shower of vellum and gilt edges. A nearby desk—the kind of expensive mahogany executive furniture that screams 'High-Spire money'—takes a round square in its center. The 2007 Panasonic Toughbook sitting there doesn't stand a chance; the screen spiderwebs into crystalline fragmentation before the entire unit slides sideways and crashes onto scattered documents.

That was probably evidence.

Doesn't matter now.

The floor section beneath where I'm kneeling groans, a deep mechanical sound that reverberates up through my kneecaps. Illusion peels away like paint, revealing heavy steel plate beneath. Runes etched directly into the surface—these ones active, pulsing with faint blue light that syncs with the rhythmic hum coming from below.

Cole racks his shotgun. Shell casings scatter across blood-stained marble. He doesn't need to check them; muscle memory from hundreds of reloads makes it automatic. His breath fogs in the frosted air he's maintaining around our position.

"Help me lift this."

I'm already moving, fingers finding grip-points on the hatch's edge. It's cold enough to burn despite my tactical gloves. The steel rises six inches under our combined weight, just enough for the counterbalances to engage. Hinges creak—a sound that echoes down into darkness.

Down where necro-thermite pulses in sickly green-yellow rhythm.

Down where something massive breathes.

The stairwell spirals into that glow, concrete steps descending into what my ward-sense tells me is easily three levels beneath the estate proper. The Morvain Library. The collection everyone said was destroyed in '05.

Turns out everyone was wrong.

And whatever Torque Kaelen left down there? Whatever the Union Elders have been trying to keep buried?

We're about to find out.

Cole meets my eyes across the gap between us. No words needed. We've breached worse positions than this. We've both come back from things that should have killed us twice over.

My wards pulse steady: white-lilac, fresh cedar, frost-cobalt. His resonance holds firm against mine. Three years since Sub-Station Seven, and we've learned to move as a single unit.

I nod once, sharp.

He nods back.

Together, we descend into the dark.

* * *

My boot hits the first step, concrete dust spiraling up in my tactical red beam. The spiral descends into darkness thick enough to taste—metallic, like blood on tongue, laced with that fucking ozone stench that never quite left my nostrils after Sub-Station Seven.

"Stairwell secure," I whisper into my throat-mic, though the silence already screams otherwise. My .45 stays locked at chest height, suppressor gleaming under the sickly yellow wash of sodium-vapor lamps mounted every ten feet down the curve. They flicker. Everything here flickers, hesitates, like reality itself can't decide if it wants to exist in this place.

The walls aren't just concrete. They're *lined*—thick rubberized cabling snaking down alongside us, pulsing with stolen Telluric energy. I can feel it without even trying, that wrongness humming against my bio-wards. White-lilac and fresh cedar, they should be calm, controlled, but there's fraying at the edges now. Ash-gray static bleeding through from November 2005, when I held seventeen bodies that were still warm while the South Side grid died around them.

*Burning. Always burning.*

I don't want to look closer, but Commander doesn't mean shit if you can't stomach what you find.

I run a diagnostic weave. My white-lilac light—*our* light now, Cole's frost-cobalt braided so tight with mine we might as well share a circulatory system—spills across the nearest cable bundle. Data unfurls like intestines: municipal grid signatures, South Side markers, residential blocks I recognize from triage reports. The same grid that failed two years ago. The same grid feeding power to these monsters while half the Undercity scrabbles for generator fuel.

"You see this?" My voice cracks. I hate how it sounds. "They're siphoning direct from Sector Seven's recovery infrastructure."

Cole moves beside me, silent as winter. His hand—gloved, black leather, calloused in ways that speak of things before his BATC recruitment—brushes my shoulder. Not pushing, not pulling. Just *there*. His frost-cobalt ward bleeds into mine, and suddenly I smell hearth-coals instead of burning commuters. Warm instead of ash.

The Motorola Razr on my belt chirps. Vane Thorne, three minutes delayed on the encrypted channel:

`COMMANDER - THORNE - INTERESTING DEVELOPMENTS REGARDING THE FALLEN GNOME TELEMETRY CONTRACTORS STAY FROST 10-4`

Half the Undercity Gnome telemetry brokers must be on the payroll to mask a draw this massive. Or worse—they're *compromised*, their systems hijacked by whatever fucked technology Kaelen imported from the Breach.

"Commander." Cole's voice is dead-silent, zero-remorse frost. "Keep moving."

I want to argue. Want to stand here until my wards stabilize, until Sub-Station Seven stops bleeding ghost-commuters across my consciousness. But he's right. Always right about when hesitation becomes liability.

We descend.

Step after step, the cables multiply. Hundreds, thousands of rubberized veins pulsing with stolen life, all feeding downward into whatever nightmare waits at the bottom. The air gets colder—or maybe that's just the hearth-coal warmth of Cole's presence making everything else feel like meat locker temperatures.

Twenty feet down. Thirty. Forty.

My Razr chirps again: `DON'T ENGAGE KAELEN'S CONSOLE DIRECTLY - POTENTIAL FOR NEURAL CASCADE FAILURE PER M-B3 ANALYSIS`

The stairwell wall ends at landing forty-seven. Beyond it, an archway blasted clean through—concrete shattered and blackened like a throat wound—and past that, sodium-vapor yellow spills into darkness so complete it feels physical.

We reach the bottom.

I step through first, .45 sweeping the space beyond. The vault opens before us like a cathedral built for machines that learned God from pain. And in its center, dominating everything, the master console rises three stories tall—a brain of fire and iron fed by the corpse-light of the South Side grid.

"Mother of Christ," I whisper.

Cole's hand tightens on his own weapon. No words this time. None needed.

The true scale of the Syndicate's operation finally revealed, spreading out before us like a map of hell drawn in blue-black iron-gall residue and ozone smoke.

* * *

The sub-vault spreads beneath us like a cathedral built by mad engineers. Sodium-vapor lamps cast everything in that sickly orange-yellow glow—the kind that makes shadows pool thick and ugly in the corners where light can't reach properly. The air tastes like ozone mixed with something older, something that smells of paper yellowed by decades in basements, of burning metal that never quite cooled.

"Jesus Christ," Cole breathes beside me.

I don't answer. Can't. My eyes are locked on the master console rising from the center of this concrete bunker, and my chest feels suddenly too small to hold what I'm seeing.

It's alive. That's the only word that fits. A brain of fire and iron, and it's bleeding.

The console itself is a marvel of pre-2005 engineering—all brass fittings and glass tubes filled with fluids that shouldn't exist, conducting currents between copper nodes machined so precisely they catch the light like mirrors. But what catches my attention, what sends ice down my spine despite the heat radiating off the machine, are the seals.

Gold-Bismuth Seals. Chief Telluric Engineer Torque Kaelen's work.

Even corrupted, even dying, they're beautiful. Each seal is a perfect circle, about the size of a half-dollar, pressed into the console's core housing. The gold is 24-karat, I'd bet my pension on it, with intricate circuitry etched so fine you need magnification to see the individual lines. And threaded through each one, binding them to the console's heart: bismuth crystal rods that pulse with a steady rhythm—a heartbeat, almost. Perfect, mathematically precise pulses of energy flowing between the seals in a closed loop.

Torque machined these. His signature is all over the work—the obsessive attention to detail, the 0.02mm tolerances, the way everything fits together so perfectly it seems more art than machinery.

But someone's tried to murder his art.

Piercing through four of the twelve primary seals are jagged spikes of something that glows hot-white and sickly green. Necro-Thermite. Fucking Necro-Thermite spliced directly into Kaelen's harmonic dampeners. Where the thermite meets the gold-bismuth alloy, there's a reaction—I can see it in the way the metal around each puncture weeps molten droplets onto the console floor below. Sizzle. Sizzle. Sizzle.

"Commander." Cole's voice cuts through my analysis. He's moved to the vault's perimeter, MP5 up, scanning the shadows. "We got company?"

I shake my head without looking at him. Can't take my eyes off this thing. "No. But whoever did this had a full team. Look at the splice-work."

The thermite spikes aren't random. They're *hijacking* the dampeners—using Torque's own precision engineering against itself. The Syndicate didn't just break the console; they converted it. Stabilized their abyssal network by piggybacking on BATC infrastructure so sophisticated it could handle the backlash without collapsing entirely.

Which means they've been feeding power from Sub-Station Seven straight into the Between for... I don't even want to calculate how long. Months? Since November 2005?

My white-lilac wards pulse harder around me, reacting to the memory of that night—the ash-gray static creeping across my vision as Sub-Seven went dark. But beneath my bio-signature, I feel Cole's frost-cobalt resonance steadying mine, his warm hearth-coal warmth keeping the edges from fraying completely.

I move closer to the console, pulling out my PalmPilot. The screen glows green-backlit in the orange-yellow light, and I plug the data cable into an auxiliary port hidden behind a brass panel.

"Cole, keep your eyes open. If anything moves in those corners, you put ten rounds through it before asking questions."

"Already planned on it." His Nextel radio chirps with static—Grimjaw trying to reach us from surface level, but the signal won't penetrate this deep. He'll have to wait.

I tap the stylus pad, fingers flying across commands. The PalmPilot begins its diagnostic sweep of the console's encrypted ledger. Percentage counter appears: **0% DOWNLOADING...**

The Gold-Bismuth Seals thrum in perfect rhythm beside me. Thump-thump. Thump-thump. A heartbeat counting down seconds.

"What are we looking for exactly?" Cole asks, still scanning.

"Proof." My eyes are fixed on the screen. "Torque didn't build this to fail. Someone made it happen. And if we can get the ledger data, we'll know who had access, when they breached security, what they were running through these dampeners..."

**12% DOWNLOADING...**

The Necro-Thermite Spikes glow brighter, almost mockingly. Sickly green-white against gold that's weeping molten tears.

My ward smells suddenly sharp—fresh cedar cutting through ozone and burning metal. Reaction to stress. Controlled breathing. Focus.

**34% DOWNLOADING...**

"I got visuals," Cole says quietly. "Far corner, west wall. Looks like someone tried to hide equipment there. Cables running into the floor grates."

Note it mentally. Can't look away from the download now.

**58% DOWNLOADING...**

That's when the sodium-vapor lamps flicker.

Not just flicker—they cut out completely.

One second, we're standing in orange-yellow light with green backlit screens. Next second, absolute darkness except for one thing:

A red cherry glowing in the far shadows.

A cigar.

And behind that ember, someone inhales slowly, deliberately.

My hand moves to my sidearm as Cole's MP5 snaps toward the sound.

**99% DOWNLOADING...**

The PalmPilot beeps completion.

But I don't move. Don't breathe.

Because whoever's holding that cigar knows we're here, knows exactly where we stand, and has been watching us for God knows how long while we played at being the hunters in this tomb of fire and iron.

---

## CHAPTER 7: CHAPTER 7

The darkness hits like a physical blow.

One moment, the Sub-Vault's emergency lighting cast everything in sickly green, and then—nothing. Absolute. Complete. My white-lilac wards instinctively flare, throwing desperate tendrils of illumination into the void, but they're swallowed whole, eaten by something that shouldn't exist down here. Something wrong.

"Contact!" I snap, my hand already going for my sidearm as I rip the PalmPilot from its docking station. The device comes free with a wet *schlick*—plugged in too long, probably leaking data—but I don't care. It's evidence now, tucked hard against my tactical vest beneath my left arm.

Cole moves before I finish the word. I feel it more than see it—the temperature plummets so fast my breath becomes visible, frost spiderwebbing across the concrete floor in crystalline patterns. His blood-iron metallurgy hexes are already radiating outward, a defensive perimeter of razor-sharp temperature differentials. The air itself feels like it's cutting.

Then I smell it. Tobacco. Expensive. Cuban. Underneath the ozone stench and the metallic tang of disrupted electronics.

Footsteps. Slow. Measured. Deliberate.

Each echo bounces off the vault's far wall—a sound completely out of place in this controlled environment. Whoever's making them wants us to know they're there. Wants us to hear the expensive Italian leather soles striking concrete.

My sidearm clears its holster with a familiar weight. Safety off with a soft click that seems impossibly loud in the suffocating dark.

"Cole," I whisper, my voice tight. "You reading anything?"

"*Negative.*" His response is immediate, sharp-edged. "*No thermal signature. No Weave presence. This isn't—*"

The words cut off as my PTSD bleed surges through my wards—ash-gray static blooming across my vision, the ghost-scent of gunpowder and copper flooding my nostrils. My finger rests on the trigger guard, steady despite the way my heart hammers against my ribs.

"You always were a blunt instrument, Mr. Reyes."

The voice comes from everywhere and nowhere. Cultured. Educated. Completely unbothered by the fact that we're armed, that Cole's hexes could drop the temperature another twenty degrees and freeze water in our lungs, that my wards are screaming warnings I can't quite parse through the static.

"Identify yourself. *Now.*" Cole's voice drops into that dangerous rasp—the one that means he's already calculating firing solutions, already reaching for his own weapon. The frost continues spreading, and I feel it creeping up my neck like ice water poured down my spine.

Before either of us can press further, everything changes.

The auxiliary backup lights slam on with a mechanical groan and a harsh white glare that makes me flinch. One moment, darkness thick enough to choke. The next, the entire vault is illuminated in that unforgiving emergency lighting—cold, flat, revealing every detail of the concrete expanse.

And standing there, perhaps thirty meters away near the obsidian blast-doors, is a man.

He's holding a cigar, the red cherry glowing softly as he takes a slow drag, the ember bright against skin the color of polished mahogany. His suit is immaculate—charcoal gray, perfectly tailored, not a thread out of place despite the chaos around him. Silver hair, swept back, just a touch of gray at the temples. Age? Impossible to tell. Could be forty. Could be sixty.

But it's his eyes that catch me.

They reflect the light wrong. Just slightly off-axis. Like mirrors catching illumination at angles they shouldn't.

"Gentleman," he says, exhaling smoke that curls upward in perfect rings before dissipating into the cold air. "I do hope you'll forgive the dramatic entrance."

My wards are going haywire now—not PTSD bleed but genuine alarm signals. My bio-indicators spike. The man standing before us shouldn't exist according to any BATC database I've accessed.

Cole's hand hasn't moved from his weapon. "You're trespassing on secured federal property."

"I am?" The man's smile doesn't reach those mirror-eyes. He takes another pull from the cigar, the glow briefly illuminating features that seem to shift at the periphery of my vision. "How curious. I have paperwork suggesting otherwise."

* * *

The man across the vault makes no move toward cover.
