# BOOK #06: MOTHERS OF THE PERIMETER
### Bridge Duology Part 2 (MB-3)

---

## CHAPTER 1: THE IRON-LUNG RESERVE TANK

The sub-basement reeks of ozone and old motor oil, a smell I've come to associate with desperation. Brass gleams beneath the naked sixty-watt bulb hanging from the rafters.

"Valve three is sticking again, Cole," Bram Kovacs said without looking up from the drill press, his spectacles pushed up onto his bald, greasy forehead. "The brass seat's pitted from that dirty telluric gas you brought in Tuesday."

"It was the only cylinder I could pull out of the foundry supply yard without tripping the state alarms, Bram," I said, setting my toolbox on the bench with a heavy clatter. "How's Danny's oxygen saturation?"

"Holding at eighty-eight," Bram wiped his calloused hands on an oily rag, his voice dropping into that solemn, protective register he used whenever he spoke about my brother. "He had another coughing fit around four this morning. Coughed up three thimbles of black fluid, Cole. His lungs are calcifying."

"I'm getting him the new manifold tonight," I said, tightening the strap on my boots. "The syndicate's moving a shipment through the Morvain perimeter. Pure medical-grade brass regulators. The kind they reserve for the executive hospitals in Summit."

"That perimeter is suicide, boy," Bram warned, stepping between me and the tool locker, fixing me with bloodshot eyes. "Aegis has three sniper teams stationed on the water tower. You go in there with a shotgun and a pair of pliers, you're leaving Danny with an empty machine and nobody to bury you."

"Then pray my pliers don't slip, Bram," I said, pushing past him to grab the heavy cold-iron spikes from the rack. "Because I'm not watching my brother choke to death in this basement." under the overhead fluorescents, casting copper shadows across every surface. In the center of it all stands the Iron-Lung—a massive brass-and-glass contraption that looks like something torn from a Victorian madman's fever dream, all elaborate pipework and thick glass cylinders filled with swirling amber fluid.

Danny's inside. Eighteen years old, too young for what's happened to him. His chest rises and falls in that rhythmic *hiss-thump* that means he's still alive, still fighting whatever poison the South Side decided to breathe into his lungs during last week's chemical spill at the industrial park.

"Tolerances are tight tonight, Cole." Bram Kovacs doesn't look up from where he's seated cross-legged beside the lung's manifold, his calloused fingers working a wrench against a pressure valve with the kind of precision that comes from thirty years in Local 405. He's a Dwarf, stout and solid as a brick shithouse, his braided beard grease-stained and hanging over his faded union jacket. "I machined these gold-bismuth collars to 0.02 mil. If the city grid shits the bed, this reserve tank buys the kid exactly forty-eight hours."

I hand him another wrench without a word. The metal is already cold in my palm—my frost-cobalt wards bleeding into it, pulling the temperature down ten degrees below ambient. Bram takes it, grunts in acknowledgment, doesn't flinch when the chill hits his fingers. He's used to my little... quirks by now.

My eyes stay on Danny. Pale face pressed against the curved glass. Dark hair plastered to his forehead with sweat that shouldn't be there. The Iron-Lung's bellows keep their steady rhythm, but I can see the effort in each breath now, like watching someone drown in slow motion.

"Make it fifty," I say. My voice comes out flat, dead-silent—the way it does when I'm trying not to think about what happens if we lose power to this thing. "I'm not leaving anything to chance tonight."

Bram finally looks up at me, one bushy eyebrow raised. The green glow from the ruggedized Panasonic Toughbook he's running diagnostics on casts harsh shadows across his weathered features. Pressure graphs scroll across the screen, lines climbing and diving in hypnotic patterns.

"We're pushing tolerances as it is." He gestures at the new reserve tank—a heavy brass cylinder the size of an oil drum that's been welded into the system. "Any tighter and you'll need a goddamn miracle worker, not just a machinist."

"The reserves are enough."

It's not a question. Bram knows better than to argue when I get like this. He turns back to his work, the *click-click-click* of tools against metal filling the silence between us.

The smell hits different down here. Underneath the ozone and motor oil, there's something else—the sickening metallic tang of black iron, exhaled from Danny's failing lungs every time the Iron-Lung forces air through his system. It reminds me of blood and rust and things that should never have touched human flesh.

My phone buzzes in my pocket. I ignore it. Whatever Mara wants, whatever crisis she's got brewing in Newark Bay tonight, it can wait. This—this moment, this kid—it takes priority over everything except maybe stopping the world from ending.

Which, knowing my luck with the Morvain situation, might be what tonight actually comes down to.

The Toughbook chimes. A success tone, high-pitched and almost cheerful compared to the grim atmosphere in the sub-basement. Bram nods, starts typing commands into the keyboard with two fingers.

"Seal's good. Reserve pressure holding steady at 32 PSI. Kid's gonna make it through whatever bullshit's coming."

And then Danny spasms inside the glass cylinder.

A wet, rattling cough echoes through the chamber—not the mechanical *hiss-thump* of the lung's bellows, but something organic and wrong. His whole body convulses once, twice, limbs jerking against the restraints keeping him positioned for optimal airflow.

My blood runs cold.

"Danny?" I'm pressing against the glass before I realize I've moved, frost-cobalt wards spreading across the surface where my palms contact the cooled metal. Inside the cylinder, Danny's eyes flutter open—wide and white and terrified—and he tries to scream around a throat full of fluid.

Bram's already on his feet, hands flying across the Toughbook's keyboard. "Pressure spike! Shit, Cole, we're losing vacuum seal on the thoracic manifold!"

The Iron-Lung's rhythm stutters. The *hiss-thump* becomes irregular, uneven—like a heartbeat failing under strain.

And Danny keeps coughing that wet, drowning cough, his face turning purple behind the glass as my worst fears crystallize into absolute certainty:

Tonight just got a hell of a lot more complicated.

* * *

I place both palms flat against the glass of the Iron-Lung, feeling the cold seep through from my flesh into the chamber. My frost-cobalt hexes flare without conscious thought, tendrils of crystalline blue spreading across my forearms as I try to leech away even a fraction of Danny's fever. The glass fogs where my skin makes contact, condensation forming in delicate patterns that spread like frost across a winter window.

Inside the pressurized chamber, my little brother lies motionless on the padded surface, tubes snaking from his nose and mouth into the breathing apparatus. His chest rises and falls with mechanical precision—the rhythmic hiss-and-hump of the bellows system keeping him alive when his own lungs won't cooperate. But it's the sound that gets me every goddamn time: that wet, rattling gurgle amplified by the acoustics of the sealed environment. Like drowning heard from inside a bottle.

"Easy now," I whisper, though I know he can't hear me through three inches of reinforced glass and the constant white noise of his life support. "Breathe easy, *hermanito*. I'm going to make them pay for every ounce of this."

My voice cracks on the last word. I hate how it sounds. Hate the weakness. But standing here in this sub-basement, watching the boy who used to climb trees and terrorize the neighbor's cat slowly suffocate from black iron poisoning... it strips away the layers of ice I've built around myself since '99.

The residue is already forming on the inside of the access port—a faint mist of metallic particles that clings to the glass like some sick parody of morning dew. Black iron, the same shit that flooded the South Side when Apep's minions ruptured those reserve tanks back in '99. The stuff that got into Danny's bloodstream when he was just five years old, playing in puddles he shouldn't have been near.

I wipe at the stain with my thumb, pressing against the glass. The residue comes off as a gritty, charcoal-like powder, staining my fingertip black. I hold it up to the weak fluorescent light, watching the oily sheen coat my skin. This is what hatred looks like, I think. Not fire and rage like they show in movies. Something slow and corrosive. Something you carry in your marrow.

"Machine's holding steady." Bram's gruff voice cuts through my thoughts. The Dwarf has his back half-turned, adjusting the flow rate on the reserve tank with practiced efficiency. His gnarled fingers dance across the pressure gauges, dialing back the oxygen mix by point-five percent. "Brass and bismuth can only do so much against Apep's rot."

He doesn't look at me as he speaks. Doesn't need to. We've had this conversation a thousand times over the past nine years—ever since Danny started showing symptoms during puberty, when the black iron dormant in his system suddenly became active. The 1999 Sludge Flush didn't kill him outright like it did hundreds of others. No, it had to be slower. Crueler. A death sentence delivered in installments.

"The filters are clean," Bram continues, wiping his hands on a rag stained with motor oil and who-knows-what-else. "Changed them two hours ago. Pressure's stabilized at twelve-point-seven PSI. He'll be good for another six hours minimum before we need to cycle the scrubbers again."

I pull out my Motorola Razr, the blue backlight illuminating my face in the dim workshop. 20:57. Mara will be expecting me at the rendezvous point in thirteen minutes. Thirteen goddamn minutes to make peace with leaving Danny here, unconscious and slowly dying, while I go play vigilante in whatever fresh hell she's cooked up for tonight.

The Razr sits heavy in my palm, its plastic casing worn smooth from years of use. I could cancel. Tell Mara I'm not going. Stay here where I can watch the rise and fall of my brother's chest, listen to that terrible rattling breath, pretend that keeping vigil matters more than actually doing something about the sons of bitches responsible.

But I won't.

Because that's the difference between being a victim and being something else. Something harder. Something cold enough that the ice doesn't just cover your skin anymore—it gets inside you, becomes part of how you think, how you move through the world.

Thud. Thud. Thud.

Heavy footsteps on metal stairs. The distinct chirp of a Nextel walkie-talkie crackling to life somewhere above us in the chop-shop proper.

Grimjaw.

My hand instinctively moves toward the .38 Special holstered at my hip as Bram straightens up, his weathered features settling into something resembling alertness despite the casual slouch he'd maintained moments ago. We weren't expecting company this early. Not without a call ahead.

"The boss man around?" A voice bellows down the stairwell—not Grimjaw himself, but one of his lieutenants. Close enough. "We got business."

I meet Bram's eyes across the room. His beard twitches—the Dwarf equivalent of a grimace. Whatever conversation we were about to have just got postponed indefinitely.

"Stay with him," I tell Bram quietly, already moving toward the stairs. My frost-cobalt hexes pulse once, twice, the cold spreading down to my fingertips as I ready myself for whatever fresh complication has decided to crawl out of the woodwork tonight.

Danny's breathing continues its mechanical rhythm behind me.

Thirteen minutes.

The Iron-Lung hums its terrible song.

And somewhere above, Grimjaw's men are waiting.

* * *

The ceiling pipes rattled with steam pressure as Grimjaw's massive frame squeezed through the sub-basement door, forcing him to duck beneath the rust-stained conduit. He dropped the duffel bag with a heavy *thud* that echoed off concrete walls still slick from the morning's condensation. The metallic clink of depleted-bismuth shotgun slugs cascaded through the canvas—twelve-gauge rounds that'd punch through brick and bone alike.

I didn't turn from where I knelt beside Danny's cot, my hand resting on his shoulder blade, feeling the shallow rhythm of his breathing. The frost-cobalt in my blood made our sanctuary ten degrees colder than the rest of the chop-shop above, but Danny never complained. Never said a word about how the black iron sickness in his lungs seemed worse in the cold.

"Trunk of the '99 Vic is loaded, boss," Grimjaw rumbled, his voice like grinding machinery in the confined space. "C-4, thermite, and enough bismuth slugs to level a city block."

Still kneeling, I tilted my head slightly, acknowledging without words. My eyes stayed fixed on the rise and fall of Danny's back, watching the way his ribs expanded and contracted with mechanical precision. Each breath came harder than the last. The metallic tang of failing organs hung thick in the air despite the ozone sharpness from my hex.

"You're looking grim." It wasn't judgment from Grimjaw. Just statement. Fact.

I stood then, rolling my shoulders against the tight confines of the sub-basement. At six-foot-two, I had clearance here, unlike Grimjaw's seven-foot-two frame hunched below the ceiling pipes. Stepping close, I looked up into those tusked features, into eyes that had seen three decades of South Side tunnel work and knew exactly what kind of darkness we were wading into tonight.

"Listen to me, Grim." My voice dropped low, controlled. "If my ticker stops tonight... if I don't walk out of Morvain's estate..."

Grimjaw's expression hardened further, if that was possible. His scarred knuckles flexed at his sides.

"If I go down," I continued, each word measured, deliberate, "get Danny to the Watching Party. Don't wait for BATC. Don't trust the hospitals. Take him underground."

The Watching Party—what passed for a government among our kind. The syndicate council that supposedly kept order in North Jersey when the mundane authorities couldn't see past their noses. They operated out of the old Kearny marshworks, deep in tunnels beneath the Passaic where the river ran black and cold.

"They'll take him?" Grimjaw asked, though his tone suggested he already knew the answer.

"They have to." My jaw tightened. "Danny's got the iron-lung curse. If that black blood spreads, infects others..." I didn't finish. We both knew what happened to metahumans who came down with black iron sickness without proper containment. The Watching Party quarantined their own. Sometimes they even helped.

"Nobody touches the kid. On my life." Grimjaw tapped his chest twice—the sandhog oath, older than Local 405 itself.

I nodded once, sharp and definite. That would have to be enough.

My hand moved to the duffel bag, fingers closing around worn canvas. Inside: a cut-down Remington 870 loaded with those same bismuth slugs, three magazines for my Glock 23 converted to fire silver-jacket rounds, flashbangs, zip-ties, and more thermite charges than a sane man should carry into one building.

"Mara's already at the Morvain perimeter," I said, checking the Nextel clipped to my belt. The device chirped once—a pre-set alert from her. *"Position secure."* No emotion. Just facts.

Grimjaw grunted. "The ghost-bitch always is."

One last look at Danny's cot. His dark hair fanned across the thin pillow, lips slightly parted as he breathed through whatever nightmare haunted even his unconscious mind. Fourteen years old and already marked by the curse that'd kill him in months if we couldn't find a cure. If we could survive tonight long enough to keep looking.

I turned my back on him then, walking toward the stairs that led up through the chop-shop, through the South Side, toward whatever waited at the Morvain estate on the other side of Newark Bay.

Every step felt like wading deeper into cold water.

Behind me, Grimjaw's voice rumbled low: "Come back from this one, boss."

I didn't answer. Couldn't promise what I wasn't sure I could deliver.

The iron-lung sickness had taken enough from us already.

Tonight, it was going to take its final payment—or die trying.

---

## CHAPTER 2: THE THREEFOLD LEDGER

The chop-shop office smells like a corpse left too long in a locked room. Stale coffee grounds mixed with diesel fumes and wet sheepskin.

"I told you already, Reyes," Sal the Greek sneered from behind his formica desk, nervously shuffling a deck of greasy playing cards. "I don't know nothing about no delivery to the perimeter."

I didn't answer with words. I took two steps forward, grabbed the collar of his counterfeit leather jacket, and slammed his forehead down onto the desk, pinning his ear against the glass blotter.

"Jesus! Cole, wait!" he squealed, eyes bulging as I pressed the cold tip of an iron railroad spike against his temple. "Don't do it! I got kids!"

"Danny's a kid too," I growled into his ear, feeling the frantic flutter of his pulse beneath my thumb. "And right now his lungs sound like wet gravel in a concrete mixer. Where's the delivery truck heading tonight, Sal?"

"Culvert four!" he gasped, spit spraying across the blotter. "The old brickworks by the salt marsh! Midnight sharp! Two flatbeds loaded with reserve cylinders and security squads from Jersey City! That's all I know, I swear to the Virgin!"

"If there's an Aegis checkpoint waiting for me at that gate," I whispered, easing the pressure just enough for him to breathe, "I'm coming back here with a blowtorch and six feet of copper cable. Understand me?"

"I swear, Cole! No cops, just syndicate muscle!" he whimpered. "Now get out of here before somebody sees your truck!" and something else—something metallic and wrong that makes my sinuses burn. I've been sitting here for three hours now, watching the clock on the Toughbook screen flip through the seconds like they're counting down to something inevitable.

The Sony MiniDisc player in the corner hums its endless loop. Some shitty 90s rock track I can't even remember the name of anymore. It's just noise to fill the silence between thoughts. Between breaths. Between the man I was and the thing I've become.

I pull out the ledger.

The Threefold Cord. That's what Mara calls it when she's being poetic—which isn't often. The leather binding is cracked along the spine, held together by more duct tape than original material. Inside, the pages are thick, cream-colored paper that costs more per sheet than most people spend on groceries. I bought this book back in '03, right after the first time I came back from the dead. Thought maybe writing things down would make them real. Make them matter.

It didn't work then.

Doesn't work now.

But I keep doing it anyway.

I flip past page after page of names. Each one crossed out with a single black line dragged hard enough to leave grooves in the paper beneath. *Paid in full.* That's what each mark means. A debt settled. An account closed.

There's Dmitri Volkov on page forty-seven. Took me six months to get close enough to put two rounds in his skull behind the Ironbound warehouse district. His blood splattered across rust-streaked concrete while he screamed about his daughter.

Page sixty-two has Maria Castellanos. She tried to beg. Actually dropped to her knees and grabbed at my boots while I stood there holding the .45 level with her forehead. Didn't say anything. Just pulled the trigger.

Each name is a weight. A stone I carry around until I can drop it somewhere dark enough that nobody else will have to trip over it.

I stop on Julian Sterling. Page eighty-nine. His entry takes up half the page because I was detailed back then—younger, angrier, still thinking documentation mattered for something beyond my own memory.

*Julian Sterling. Age 52. Import/export consultant. Real job: laundering money for the Passaic River cartel. Orchestrated the hit on Marcus Reyes. Personal detail: favorite whiskey is Macallan 18. Allows himself exactly two fingers every night at 9 PM sharp.*

The last part came from surveillance. Three weeks of watching him through his office window while he went through the same boring ritual every goddamn evening like a creature of habit. Like someone who believed routines made you invisible.

They don't.

I drag the thick black marker across his name. The line comes out jagged and violent, tearing through the ink beneath.

Paid in full.

The page doesn't change. The weight doesn't lift.

It never does.

I turn to the next page. And there he is.

*Target #3 — Elias Morvain.*

My fingers hover over the name without touching it. Don't need to. The frost-cobalt wards woven into my skin are already reacting to what's stirring underneath my ribs—dark intent, Mara calls it. She has a term for everything. Professional terminology to keep the horror at arm's length.

But I'm not a psychiatrist. I'm not an analyst or a therapist or any other fancy title that makes killing sound clean.

I'm just a machinist who learned how to put things together and take them apart.

And right now, I'm taking apart the syndicate that burned half of Newark South Side to ash on October 3rd, 1999.

Elias Morvain isn't a man anymore. Not in my head. He's a load-bearing pillar in the architecture of that fire—a structural element holding up everything else. You knock him out, the whole rotten framework starts to collapse.

That's what keeps me moving forward when everything else wants to drag me down into cold earth where all the other victims are waiting.

I trace the name with my index finger, barely grazing the letters, and feel the blood-iron magic coiled tight in my bones start to leak from my fingertips like sweat.

Blue-black iron-gall residue hisses onto the paper, smoking as it burns into the fibers. The smell gets worse—sharper, more acidic, like burning antiseptic mixed with copper pennies.

The Toughbook screen glows harsh white against the cramped darkness of this office. Architectural blueprints of the Morvain Estate sprawl across the display: third-floor master bedroom, second-floor ballroom, ground-level service entrance, basement access points marked in red digital ink.

I've memorized every angle already. Could draw this place from memory if someone asked me to. Could walk through its halls blindfolded and know exactly which floorboards creak under pressure, which windows don't lock properly, which security cameras have dead zones big enough to hide an army in.

But knowing the structure doesn't mean I'm prepared for what's inside.

Not just Morvain himself—but what he represents. What that name means in the history of my family. In the ruins of what used to be home before October 3rd turned it all to dust and bone fragments.

My throat closes around something hot and bitter that isn't coffee or whiskey or any substance you could name.

Because Elias Morvain wasn't just some mid-level cartel lieutenant back in '99. He was the one who gave the order.

And Marcus Reyes—the father who taught me how to read blueprints instead of books, how to measure twice before cutting once, how to respect machinery because machines never lie about their intentions—they burned him alive in a warehouse on Newark Bay with forty-seven other people whose only crime was being born on the wrong side of everything that mattered to men like Morvain.

I stare at the name until my vision blurs at the edges.

*Elias Morvain.*

And beneath it, written smaller in my own handwriting from months ago:

*"The architect doesn't care about individual bricks. Only whether the wall stands."*

That's what Mara said when we first went over this file together. She has files on everyone—dossiers thick enough to strangle someone with if you folded them right. Photos, financial records, psychological profiles built from surveillance notes spanning years.

She called Morvain "the strategist." The planner. The man who thought three moves ahead while everyone else was still trying to figure out which way was forward.

Except that night in October.

Except when they forgot that some structures aren't meant to last forever no matter how carefully you lay the foundation.

The Sony MiniDisc player skips its track—same scratchy chorus bleeding into itself for the hundredth time tonight—and suddenly I'm not looking at architectural blueprints anymore but at photographs from the fire scene.

Marcus Reyes' body was never identified by dental records because there weren't any teeth left intact enough to match against charts. Just bone fragments and ash scattered across what used to be a textile warehouse employin fifty-three people before sunrise hit those ruins gold-red through smoke black

* * *

The sodium-vapor streetlight bleeds through the slatted blinds like weak, jaundiced eyes, casting rhythmic shadows across my office ceiling. I watch them slice back and forth, back and forth, a hypnotic metronome counting down to violence. The air is deathly cold—my frost-cobalt wards reacting to the intention crystallizing in my bones like shards of winter.

Stale coffee sits in a cracked mug beside the ledger. Diesel fumes seep through the gaps around my door, mixing with something sharper now—the acidic burn of blue-black iron-gall residue as it scorches into the pages. That smell always comes when I write names in this book. Always.

I lean back until my chair groans, staring at that ceiling, watching the shadows dance their endless waltz.

*"A sliver of justice,"* I whisper to the empty room.

My knuckles are white against the steel edge of my desk. The metal is ice-cold beneath my palms, grounding me in this moment, this decision. Through the floorboards, I feel the elevated train rumbling past—distant, mechanical thunder that vibrates up through my spine.

Danny Morales. Eighteen years old. Black iron in his lungs. His mother's face when she identified what was left of him in '99.

*"A sliver of justice."*

The words taste like ash and copper on my tongue.

It's never enough. I know that with the same certainty I know the Passaic River runs south. Killing Morvain won't scrape that black iron from Danny's dead lungs. Won't bring back the two dozen others who went down in the sludge flush. Won't resurrect the ghosts who haunt the Kearny Marshes, their voices lost in toxic mist.

But it will do for tonight.

Because a sliver of justice for one person is better than no justice for anyone. And a sliver is still more than these bastards have ever given anyone. Morvain won't see tomorrow because Danny didn't get to see his nineteenth birthday. That's the mathematics of this world—the only equation that matters in the dark places where men like me operate.

My PalmPilot buzzes sharply, vibrating across the scarred wood desk. The screen glows: *Target #3 confirmed on estate grounds. Undercity Gnome telemetry.*

I close my eyes. Let the frost spread from my fingers along the desktop, creeping outward like frost across a winter window. 

"Tonight," I say aloud, voice flat as blade-steel, "you pay for Danny's lungs."

With blood.

With bone.

With buried gold.

And then we'll see if any justice remains—slivered or otherwise—in whatever comes after.

* * *

The ledger sits open on my desk, its pages blackened with iron-gall residue that still sizzles faintly against the cheap particle board. I've been staring at it for three hours now, watching the names blur in the amber light of my Anglepoise lamp. The cold doesn't bother me anymore—not the kind that freezes your bones. That's just weather.

This cold is different. It comes from inside, where the frost-cobalt wards embedded in my skin are reacting to what's brewing in my chest. Dark intent, Mara calls it. She's got words for everything, clinical and clean, like she's cataloging a specimen instead of living through it. But I know what it really is.

It's the feeling right before you kill someone.

I push back from the desk, the chair scraping against concrete hard enough to make the rusted pipes overhead groan. My breath clouds in front of my face despite the space heater humming in the corner—useless piece of shit, but it runs off this old industrial power line so it doesn't show up on any utility grid. Off the books. Just like me.

Standing makes my knees crack. Forty-three years old and they sound like a goddamn bag of ice. I grab the ledger, flip it closed. The cover is scuffed leather, nothing fancy, but there's a blemish of dried blood along one edge. Not mine. Never mine.

Three names tonight. Three targets. The Morvain syndicate has been running arms out of an old factory complex near the Passaic River, shipping crates marked "agricultural equipment" that smell like ozone and copper filings. Corporate black market shit, the worst kind. The sort of evil that wears a suit and pretends it's about quarterly earnings while it bleeds people dry in warehouses.

I move to the weapons locker bolted into the wall. The combination lock clicks open with a satisfying thunk. Inside, everything's laid out like a surgeon's tray—not that I've ever seen one outside of TV, but I imagine this is how it goes. Methodical. Purposeful.

The twin MP5Ks sit nestled in cut foam, their receivers gleaming dully under the bare bulb. I lift them one at a time, feeling the familiar weight settle into my palms. These aren't your average subguns—they're modified down here in my shop over countless sleepless nights, the receivers etched with dwarven runes that look like broken spider webs to anyone who doesn't know better. Mara helped me with the sigil work back when we were still... well, back when things were different.

The runes bypass corporate kinetic shielding. Standard issue for security contractors who think they're untouchable because some VC firm paid extra for their force fields. They don't count on someone like me who learned to read the old texts before the Arcano-Industrial Complex made them proprietary.

*Clack.* The charging handle of the first MP5 slides home, the sound sharp and clean in the small office. *Clack.* The second one follows. I set them aside, grab the extended magazines from the rack above. Full loads—thirty rounds each, all hollow-point copper-jacketed 9mm. Good for flesh. Excellent for whatever passes as flesh these days.

But tonight calls for more than just stopping power.

I reach deeper into the locker and pull out the pump-action shotgun, the one customized with an eighteen-inch barrel and an extended tube magazine capable of holding six heavy rounds. My hands know exactly where to grip it, worn smooth by a hundred range sessions and twice as many dry practices. This isn't a gun you point at people unless you mean business.

Business is what's waiting for me across the Passaic.

I pull the bismuth slugs from their foam cradle—six of them, each one weighing almost two ounces, cast from depleted uranium alloy and coated in a layer of elemental bismuth. These aren't for stopping heartbeats. These are for shattering wards. For punching through arcane barriers that would laugh at normal ammunition. They cost me three weeks' rent per slug, but money means less than nothing when you're facing down a mage who thinks he's invincible behind his circle of protection.

The first slug slides into the magazine tube with a heavy *clunk*. Then another. And another. Each one adds weight, adds purpose. By the time I've loaded all six, my arm feels like it's holding a lead pipe—which, functionally, it is.

I work the pump action, chambering the first round. The metallic click echoes off the concrete walls. That sound means commitment. That sound means there's no backing out now.

My Motorola Razr vibrates against my hip, startlingly loud in the silence. I pull it out, squint at the T9 screen in the dim light. Mara's text glows green: *[In position. North Woods.]*

North Woods—that's her codename for the surveillance post overlooking the factory complex. She's got eyes on the perimeter, watching for patrols, counting vehicles. Doing the job she does better than anyone else I know because she actually believes we can make a difference. Me? I just believe in not letting the bastards win.

I tap back a reply with my thumb, the keys clicking under pressure: *[En route. Keep your head down.]*

*[Stay safe]* she sends back immediately.

I don't answer that one.

Instead, I holster the Razr and sling both MP5s across my chest, the straps settling over my shoulders with familiar weight. Then I grab my heavy leather coat from the hook by the door—the one that's been patched so many times it's more scar than jacket, but it'll stop a knife and maybe distract from a glancing bullet. It smells like gun oil and cold leather and rain-soaked asphalt.

The deadbolts slide home with their distinctive *thud-thud-thud*, three points of steel sealing this cramped sanctuary behind me. Outside, the October air hits like a slap—cold and wet, carrying the diesel stench of the Kearny Marshes somewhere to the east. Rain has stopped but everything's still slick, reflecting the sick orange glow of the streetlights.

My Crown Vic sits exactly where I left it, black and anonymous as a shadow. The '99 sedan isn't pretty anymore, but its V8 engine runs clean enough that the corporate scanners pass right over it, and nobody gives a second look to something so utterly forgettable.

I slide into the driver's seat, the suspension groaning under my weight plus the arsenal I'm carrying. My key turns in the ignition. The engine roars to life—not a polite purr but an actual roar, like some caged beast suddenly remembering what it's like to run free.

My hands grip the steering wheel, knuckles white against the cracked vinyl. Through the windshield, the city sprawls out before me: Newark Bay to the east, the Pulaski Skyway cutting through like a wound, the endless industrial sprawl of North Jersey spreading north toward where Mara is waiting.

Somewhere in all those lights are men who

## CHAPTER 3: THE MORVAIN FENCE

The Crown Vic died like something strangled beneath me, headlights cutting to black as I killed the ignition a half-mile from the perimeter gate.

"Kovacs, you got ears?" I whispered into the Nextel push-to-talk handset, the two-way beep chirping sharp in the dark cab.

"I'm here, Cole," Bram's voice rasped back, thick with the sound of grinding lathe-gears in the background at Local 405. "Scanning the county sheriff bands. Aegis patrol car twelve just passed the Belleville turnpike exit. You've got twenty minutes before they rotate the floodlights."

"The fence has two cut strands near culvert four," I said, checking the battery packs on my tool belt. "Someone dragged heavy wooden crates through the mud toward the old brickworks."

"That's the syndicate snatch-team," Bram muttered. "They're taking kids from the squatter camps along the salt marsh to juice the private generators in Sterling Manor. If you run into Matron Martha, don't draw iron until she sees your machinist union card. She's got two double-barrel tens loaded with rock-salt and silver dimes."

"Understood," I said, thumbing the handset off and stepping into the icy marsh water. "I'll bring 'em home, Bram." out. Through the windshield, I watched the Morvain Estate's perimeter fence materialize from darkness—a jagged silhouette against the sodium-vapor gloom bleeding through the North Woods' canopy. Rain hammered down harder now, turning the asphalt into liquid mercury that swallowed my parking spot whole.

I let the cruiser roll another thirty yards on momentum alone, then pushed open the door.

The deluge hit me like a bucket of ice water straight to the skull. Within seconds, my hair was plastered flat, rivulets running cold down the collar of my leather jacket. The smell of wet earth and decomposing leaf-matter filled my lungs as I stepped onto mud that squelched obscenely under my combat boots. Each footfall made those soft, sucking sounds that meant nobody would hear me coming.

Not unless they were listening for it.

I moved through the brush with practiced silence—low center of gravity, weight forward on the balls of my feet. These woods had been my hunting ground a dozen times over. Knew every twisted oak, every hollow where rats nested, every place the ground stayed soft enough to bury problems. The rain helped. Masked sound. Muted sight.

But not smell.

The fence came up fast in the jaundiced glow of distant highway lamps—that sickly orange light filtering through the trees like something diseased. Wrought iron, twelve feet tall minimum, topped with spiral spear-points that caught the rain and threw it off in constant streams. Beautiful work. Expensive work.

Corporate security.

My Nextel sat heavy in my palm, the green glow of its screen barely visible as I thumbed through encrypted frequencies. BATC chatter remained dead silent. Whatever Mara was doing inside that compound, she'd either managed to blind their surveillance network or they were pulling back for some reason.

Or she was already compromised.

I pocketed the radio and approached the fence line, eyes scanning for cameras. Found them quickly—thermal units mounted on the iron posts, their lenses dark but definitely active. High-Spire Elven tech. The kind that cost more than most people's houses. Humming just above audible range, casting those faint purple-tinted glows when you knew how to look.

Arcane tripwires crisscrossed the property line too. Felt them more than saw them—subtle tingle against my hex-sense, frost-cobalt reacting to whatever countermeasures Mara had woven into her wards. The cold in my chest flushed suddenly warmer, spreading down both arms in prickling waves.

Then I saw the shadow.

It detached itself from an oak tree maybe twenty yards along the fence—a human silhouette, weapon rising toward my chest with the smooth professionalism of someone who did this for a living. Suppressed. Aimed at center mass. My hand dropped instinctively toward the S&W on my hip before the scent hit me.

Lilac. White-lilac and cedar, warm as hearth-coals despite the freezing rain that should have killed any heat-signature dead.

"Cole."

Mara's voice cut through the drumming rain like a knife.

* * *

The rain hit different tonight.

I could feel it before I saw it—that electric tingle along my skin where water met flesh, turning to ice mid-air. My frost-cobalt hexes were singing their cold song, each droplet crystallizing on contact, forming a second skin of needle-sharp protection. The October chill that would've killed most men felt like a lover's caress.

Then she stepped out of the shadows.

Mara appeared at the edge of my peripheral vision—BATC Aegis tactical gear hugging her frame, rain beading off the ceramic plates like mercury on glass. She moved through the downpour without urgency, boots squelching in the mud, hands ready but not raised. Professional. Calculated.

Smart girl.

I didn't flinch when she stopped three feet away. Didn't even turn fully toward her. My MP5 stayed trained on the perimeter fence, finger resting light on the trigger guard. Old habits. Good habits.

But then—

*Fuck.*

The air between us *shifted*. Not gradually, not gently. It was like watching two angry dogs collide head-on and suddenly realize they're packmates instead of enemies. My dead-silent frost-cobalt blood-iron hexes, those hungry things that fed on death and iron, reached out instinctively. They found hers—white-lilac and fresh cedar, restorative and alive—and instead of the violent rejection I'd grown accustomed to from other Weavers, they...

*Meshed.*

Heat exploded outward from our combined signature. The freezing rain around us transformed in an instant—a warm mist rising where droplets should have been hitting frozen ground. Steam billowed up, obscuring everything beyond six feet. And the *smell*—Christ, the smell hit me next, overwhelming every other scent the marsh could throw at us.

Warm hearth-coals. Blooming white lilac. The kind of comfort you felt bone-deep after surviving something you weren't supposed to survive.

It made my chest ache where the phantom pain lived.

"Your wards are loud tonight, Commander," I murmured, voice gravel over rain, eyes still scanning the fence line even as my body registered the impossible warmth radiating between us. "Loud enough to wake the whole damn county."

Mara holstered her sidearm with a wet click of nylon against ceramic. When I finally looked down at her, orange streetlight catching in her eyes through the mist, she held my gaze without flinching.

"They're reacting to you, Reyes." Her voice carried that same professional edge, but there was something else underneath—recognition maybe, or resignation. "Try to keep your blood-iron in check. We need a clean breach, not a crater."

I racked the charging handle on my MP5. The metallic *snap* cut through the hiss of steam and rain.

"No promises."

She didn't argue. Instead, she shifted her weight, tactical boots finding purchase in the slick mud, and turned toward the fence. I followed her movement, starting to scan for weak points in the perimeter—looking for where the chain-link met oak tree, where the posts showed rot or damage, where...

My eyes caught something wrong.

A faint luminescence against dark bark. Unnatural. Wrong in a way that had nothing to do with rain or fog or the weird-ass ward-mesh happening between me and Mara.

The oak tree she'd been standing behind moments ago.

Still glowing.

Still *watching*.

* * *

The freezing rain finds every gap in my jacket, every space between the buttons where heat can escape. I'm shivering now, but it's different than before—the frost-cobalt hexes running through my veins are eating the cold, converting it into something sharp and crystalline that keeps my muscles from locking up completely.

I step closer to the oak, brushing aside a fern that's gone soggy with moisture. My boots squelch in the muddy leaf litter. The trunk is massive, old enough that it probably watched the first settlers hack their way through these woods. Water drips from the low-hanging branches in steady rhythm—plink, plink, plink—like some metronome keeping time with my heartbeat.

Then I see it.

Barely visible unless you're looking at it from exactly this angle, where the moonlight cuts through the canopy just right. A glyph etched into the bark, glowing with that sickly blue-green phosphorescence that makes my teeth hurt when I look at it too long. The lines are jagged, chaotic—not the clean corporate sigils I've learned to recognize, nothing like Morvain's sterile white-lilac architecture.

This is different.

"This is bad," I mutter, pointing my combat knife at the mark without actually touching it. The blade trembles slightly in my grip, more from exhaustion than fear, though maybe there's some of that too. "Blue-green phosphorescence. Copper-wire syntax."

Mara's beside me now, I hadn't even heard her move close. She's scanning the dark tree line beyond our position, her eyes reflecting what little light filters through the storm clouds overhead. The rain has soaked her hair flat against her skull, making her look almost skeletal in profile.

"Razor-Wire Elves?" she asks, her voice barely carrying over the sound of water hitting leaves and puddles. "Street runners? What are they doing all the way out here in the High-Spire zones?"

I grip my shotgun tighter, feeling its familiar weight settle into my hands. The weapon's almost a part of me by now, after everything we've been through tonight. "The Watching Party's been tracking Morvain too. We aren't alone out here." My jaw clenches as I force myself to think through the implications. "Which means we're walking into a potential three-way crossfire. Them, us, and whatever syndicate faction put this marker up."

"The fucking Razor-Wires don't play well with others," Mara says quietly. There's something in her tone—a memory or a past encounter she's not sharing. "If they're marking this place, they're either planning to hit it themselves or they're warning someone off."

"Yeah, well, warnings are for people who have time to listen." I'm already moving toward the wrought-iron gate at the estate perimeter, my boots leaving dark prints in the mud. The structure looms ahead of us—twelve feet tall, topped with those elegant spirals that scream 'old money' and 'fuck you.' The main electronic lock glows faintly red through the rain, a single eye watching our approach like some mechanical cyclops.

I press a block of C-4 against the mechanism, feeling the cold plastic stick slightly to my wet gloves. The explosive material is surprisingly light, almost deceptively so given what it can do. My thumb hovers over the detonator, and I meet Mara's eyes across the distance between us.

Three fingers. Two. One.

---

## CHAPTER 4: THE COURTYARD ENGINE

The detonator clicks cold and solid against my palm, its weight barely registering over the drumming pulse in my fingers.

"Hold your fire!" a voice hissed from the shadow behind the diesel storage tank. Sister Catherine stepped into the pale beam of my penlight, her woolen habit soaked with black mud, clutching a snub-nosed .38 revolver.

"I'm with the union, Sister," I kept my hands open where she could see the brass machinist ring on my knuckle. "Kovacs sent me. Where's Martha holding the children?"

"Beneath the packing plant," she whispered, her teeth chattering from the cold. "Two guards on the loading dock, both carrying telluric shock-staves. They've got four little girls locked in an insulated meat locker to keep their aura readings shielded from the state scanners."

"Not for long," I said, sliding two cold-iron spikes into the palm of my hand. "Get behind that concrete transformer pad. When the lights go out, run for the culvert and don't stop for anything."

"God protect you, Cole Reyes," she whispered.

"God isn't on the night shift in Newark, Sister," I told her. "Cold iron is."rs. Rain hammers down around us, each drop catching the distant city lights across Newark Bay like scattered diamonds on black velvet. The wrought-iron gate looms ahead, three stories of ornamental steel separating us from Morvain's inner sanctum.

"Thirty seconds," I mutter, thumb hovering over the red button.

Mara's already moving to position, her white-lilac wards humming that familiar low-frequency vibration that makes my teeth ache if I concentrate too hard. She's got her BATC sidearm out, mag inserted but hammer down—professional. Waiting.

The C-4 cluster I'd slapped onto the gate's support column is industrial-grade, stolen from a High-Spire construction site last week. Enough plastic explosive to level a small house, which right now feels about right for what we're walking into.

I press the button.

The world goes white-orange. The concussive blast slams into me like God's own fist, a pressure wave that lifts me off my feet and throws me backward into muddy earth. My ears ring with a high-pitched shriek that swallows every other sound. The heat washes over everything—a physical thing that sears through the rain and vaporizes it into scalding steam.

When my vision clears, there's nothing left of the gate but twisted metal screaming outward, chunks of iron suspended mid-air before gravity remembers them and sends them crashing into the manicured hedges lining the courtyard approach. Smoke pours from the breach, thick and greasy, catching the security lights mounted on the estate walls.

"Move!" I'm shouting, though I can barely hear my own voice. "Move, move!"

My pump-action's already coming up as I surge through the gap, boots slipping in the mud churned up by the blast. Three figures materialize from the smoke—High-Spire Elven arc-guards, their charcoal suits somehow still crisp despite the chaos, tactical rigs gleaming wet under the security lights. They've got MP7s trained on our position, and I can see the faint glow of kinetic shields rippling around them like heat mirages.

The lead guard spots us first. "Breach at the north gate! Suppressive fire!"

His words are crisp, corporate-accented English, completely calm. It makes me want to put him down twice as hard.

I don't hesitate. Can't afford to. The shotgun's stock settles against my shoulder, and I aim center-mass on the closest target. The depleted-bismuth slug tears out of the barrel with its own sound—different from standard buckshot, higher pitched, hungry. It hits his kinetic shield and the effect is exactly what we'd hoped: the barrier shatters like spun glass, that distinctive crystalline *crack* cutting through even the ringing in my ears. The slug keeps going, slamming into his shoulder and spinning him half-around before he hits the ground, blood painting the white stone facade behind him.

Mara's already firing, her sidearm bucking twice in rapid succession. The second guard jerks as both rounds punch through his chest, his shield sputtering out as he drops. She's moving as she shoots, angling right, covering space between her position and mine.

"Left!" I pump the shotgun, ejecting a smoking shell casing that clinks against wet pavement. "They're shielding up! Hit them with the bismuth!"

The third guard's trying to bring up some kind of localized stun-hex, his hands weaving patterns in the air that trail afterimages of violet light. But he's too slow. Heated. Probably thinks his corporate training and that shiny shield will carry him through this.

He doesn't have time to finish his cast.

I close the distance in three strides, the shotgun coming around butt-first. The stock connects with his jaw with a satisfying crunch that I feel in my arms all the way to my shoulders. Bone shatters. His head snaps sideways, neck bending at an angle that tells me we won't be having any more conversations with number three.

He hits the ground like a sack of wet cement.

"Moving right! Cover my flank!" Mara's voice cuts through the ringing, sharp as broken glass. She's already dropping a fresh magazine into her pistol, smooth and practiced. Seven-round extended mags—she likes them because they give her one clean shot left over from doubles if things go sideways.

The courtyard stretches ahead of us, all pristine lawns and geometric hedgerows designed by someone who thought beauty had anything to do with security. Wrong on every count.

Then the lawn shifts.

Grass parts like water around submerged rocks, earth opening up in precise geometric sections. Heavy metal housings rise from hidden compartments built into the estate's foundation—Dwarven sub-grid turrets, automated and lethal, their targeting lasers suddenly painting red dots across my chest.

"Contact!" I'm diving left, away from where those lasers are aimed. "Automated defenses!"

Mara's already rolling behind cover, her wards flaring bright white-lilac as she returns fire, trying to knock out the turret sensors before they can lock on properly.

* * *

The first bullet tears through the air where my head was half a second ago. Marble explodes in a cloud of white dust and needle-sharp fragments that sting every inch of exposed skin.

I'm already diving behind the fountain before my brain fully registers the sound—that deep, mechanical *chug-chug-chug* of heavy-caliber automation. Dwarven work. Brutal efficiency stripped down to its most lethal essence. No artistry here, just death-forged metal designed by engineers who understood that beauty is a luxury you can't afford when someone's trying to breach your perimeter.

"Contact left!" Mara's voice cuts through the chaos, sharp and controlled even as she drops to one knee behind an ornamental hedge, her rifle already tracking targets.

The courtyard has become a shooting gallery from hell. Three turrets mounted on industrial-grade swivels, each one bristling with barrel clusters that spit armor-piercing rounds at a rate that would make a machine gunner weep with envy. They're scanning in a synchronized pattern—methodical, relentless, programmed to cut down anything that moves across their kill zones.

My hands are moving before I think about it, pulling the thermite grenade from my rig. The weight of it is familiar, comforting even. South Side tech, union made, designed to burn hot enough to melt through tank armor.

*"Local 405!"* I shout over the gunfire, my throat raw from breathing in vaporized rain and ozone. *"They bought our fucking guns to protect their High-Spire rot!"*

Through the Weave, I don't need to see Mara to know what she's doing. Her intent washes through my mind like warm hearth-coals, tinged with the white-lilac scent of her wards. She's laying down suppressing fire, her rounds pinging off the turrets' thick armor plating in showers of blue-white sparks. Each impact makes those dwarven runes flicker—ancient script meant for something noble now defiled by corporate greed.

I feel her pull back just enough to create an opening.

That's all I need.

I break cover, sprinting low and fast across wet grass slick with condensation from the mist rolling off Newark Bay. The third bullet misses me by inches. The fourth chips stone near my feet. But I'm already committed, momentum carrying me forward as the nearest turret swivels to track my movement.

The gear housing is exposed on its left side—poor design choice, probably rushed production to meet some quarterly earnings projection. Perfect for someone who knows where to look.

I slide hard into the mud, feeling it soak through my clothes as I jam the thermite grenade directly into that vulnerable spot. My fingers work the safety pin while I'm still sliding, muscle memory taking over. Three seconds to detonation.

"Cole!"

I roll away, tucking my body tight against a decorative planter as the world turns magnesium-bright. The heat hits me like a furnace blast even at this distance—the air itself seems to shimmer and crackle. When I risk a glance back, the turret is collapsing into itself, metal running liquid-hot down its frame, pooling around the base like wax.

The smell is sickening—a combination of melting steel and burning grass that catches in the back of my throat. Smoke rises in thick gray columns, carrying embers that float lazily toward the night sky above the Passaic River.

But there are two more turrets.

Mara has already relocated, using the fountain's spray to mask her position. She's firing controlled bursts now, each shot measured, professional. Her rifle cracks three times in rapid succession, all three rounds hitting the same spot on the second turret's base.

*"Aim for the servos!"* she calls out. *"Armor's too thick up top!"*

Smart girl. She's seen the blueprints too.

I draw my MP5, switching from the thermite to something more immediate. The remaining turret is tracking us both now, its barrels moving with mechanical precision that would be beautiful if it wasn't trying to kill us. Rounds chew through the marble fountain behind which Mara is positioned—she ducks low, water spraying across her shoulders.

I open fire on the second turret's base, watching the dwarven runes flicker and die as my rounds shred the internal wiring. Sparks cascade from the damaged housing. The servo whines pitifully before locking up completely. The entire unit slumps forward with a groan of tortured metal, dead weight.

That leaves one.

But the heavy oak double doors of the manor suddenly blow open, revealing what waits beyond the sub-grid defenses.

Four Ogre-Kin retainers, each standing nearly eight feet tall and built like walking mountains of muscle beneath their black tactical armor. They carry riot shields emblazoned with Morvain's crest—a serpent consuming its own tail—and wield shock-mauls that crackle with contained electrical discharge.

The lead ogre's yellow eyes lock onto me. Its lips peel back from tusks the size of butcher knives.

"Intruders," it growls, voice like grinding stone. "You will not pass."

* * *

The rain screams like demons as I come around the corner of the Morvain estate, my shotgun ready, Mara's silhouette cutting through the downpour beside me. The courtyard spreads before us—flagstone wet with blood and lightning, an open killing ground.

"Three hostiles, twelve o'clock," Mara whispers, her voice barely audible over the storm. "Ogre-Kin retainers. Heavy armor. Electrified weapons."

I can see them now, massive figures descending the manor steps, shock-mauls crackling with violet energy that makes the air taste like ozone and burnt wiring. The largest one—I'm calling him Tank because fuck if I know anything else about him—stands nearly eight feet tall in his riot gear, the electrified weapon humming in both hands like some kind of sick tuning fork.

Mara's white-lilac wards flare to life around her shoulders, casting sickly purple light across the courtyard. My blood-iron hexes respond, rising from my skin like frost-cobalt smoke. When they mesh, there's a sound like grinding gears, two engines finding their rhythm.

We don't run. We push forward.

Tank swings first—a horizontal arc meant to take my head clean off. I drop low, sliding beneath the strike on wet stone, my shoulder screaming protest. The maul passes inches above my skull, close enough that I feel the static electricity raise the hairs on my scalp. I fire point-blank into his left knee, the bismuth slug punching through Kevlar and into meat and bone.

The giant Ogre goes down hard, stone steps cracking beneath him as he falls. But he's already reaching for his sidearm, those small pig eyes still locked on me behind his faceplate, grunting in thick North Jersey dialect: *"Crush the breacher! Hold the line!"*

No time for that shit.

I'm already rolling right, away from his falling bulk, my shotgun pumping out another round. Mara vaults over Tank's sprawled form like she's got springs in her legs, her compact pistol coming up smooth and fast. She fires twice—*crack crack*—the rounds striking the second retainer's faceplate with precise, angry impacts.

He stumbles back, one hand going to his helmet. That's all the opening I need. I bring the MP5 around from where it's mag-locked to my thigh, finger already on the trigger. Three-round burst to the throat, where armor plates meet vulnerable flesh.

The Ogre gurgles something unintelligible as he drops.

"Courtyard is clear," Mara says, landing beside me, breathing hard, smoke drifting from her pistol's barrel. "Stack on the door."

I kick a discarded shock-maul out of our path. My hands are steady despite the adrenaline flood, muscle memory taking over as I check both weapons—shotgun loaded, MP5 ready. The blood-iron hexes coil around my forearms like living things.

"Let's go find Target #3."

We move together toward the manor entrance, stepping over bodies slick with rain-washed blood. The heavy oak doors loom before us, carved with symbols I don't bother trying to decipher. Behind us, the storm rages on. Ahead, only darkness and silence.

The doors close behind us with a sound like a coffin lid.

And then we're inside Morvain Manor, two ghosts in the machine, hunting the ghost who started this whole fucking war.

---

## CHAPTER 5: THE FLOORBOARDS

The courtyard's carnage fades behind us like a bad dream. My boots squelch against pristine mahogany, leaving dark red prints across the polished foyer floor.

"Hallway clear," Mara Vance whispered, keeping her service weapon tucked tight against her chest plate, her tactical flashlight slicing through the smoke. "Two security monitors smashed on the console. Someone purged the hard drives before we breached."

"They weren't wiping cameras," I said, kneeling by the service entrance to inspect the lock. "They were venting the basement conduits. Look at the telluric soot on the baseboards."

"They're preparing to incinerate the evidence," Mara's eyes flashed with fierce, furious determination. "If they trip the self-destruct relay, every prisoner in the sub-vault will suffocate in thirty seconds."

"Where's the access hatch?" I demanded, thumbing two fresh slugs into the magazine tube.

"Beneath the kitchen pantry," she said, already moving down the corridor at a low tactical crouch. "Keep your safety on until we identify the hostages. Any stray spark could detonate the gas lines."

"Tell that to the bastards who locked 'em down there," I muttered, following close behind her.ts across floors probably worth more than my entire building. The silence hits me first—a different kind than death brings. This is the silence of money. Of people who've never heard gunfire except on television.

"Too quiet," Mara whispers, her voice cutting through the corporate stillness. She keeps her Glock raised, sweeping it in practiced arcs. "Internal security grid is dark. They know we're in here."

I don't lower my MP5. My eyes burn through the shadows between gilded frames and marble busts of men who died a hundred years ago, men whose faces were carved with the same smug certainty I see on every boardroom portrait downtown. The air tastes like lemon polish and ozone—the kind that clings to things that cost more than they're worth.

"Morvain's arrogant," I mutter, checking the corner where some Renaissance painting watches me with oil-painted judgment. "Thinks his money makes him untouchable. We're gonna prove him wrong."

My finger rests light on the trigger guard. Every step echoes in this tomb. Lightning flashes outside the floor-to-ceiling windows—another crack of white light turning night into day for half a second before plunging us back into shadow. Thunder follows, distant but building.

The frost-cobalt wards are bleeding out now. I can feel them, cold and sharp running up my spine, spilling from my shoulders like ice water. The temperature drops. I watch my breath become visible in front of me, small clouds that hang in the air between us. Mara notices immediately, her breath fogging too as the art gallery becomes colder, colder, until even the polished mahogany seems to hold a thin sheen of moisture.

"It's getting cold," she says, shifting weight from foot to foot.

I ignore her. Can't stop it. Not when I'm standing in the belly of the beast—when I'm breathing the same air that these vultures breathe while they sign off on plant closures and layoffs. When I'm walking past artifacts stolen from countries their corporations looted dry.

The flashlight beam sweeps across another wall—more paintings, more dead eyes looking down at me. And then it stops.

At the far end of the gallery, maybe forty yards away, hangs a tapestry. Massive thing, probably ten feet tall and twice that wide, woven gold thread against deep crimson. The edges are worn but carefully preserved, held by ornate bronze fixtures bolted directly into the wall.

And in the center of that tapestry is a symbol.

My blood goes cold for reasons that have nothing to do with my wards.

* * *

I move toward the tapestry like walking through ice water. Each step slows me down, drags at my legs. The gallery air thickens around me, that ozone stink mixing with something older—the musty decay of wool that's been hanging too long in darkness.

My frost-cobalt wards flare without conscious thought. The temperature drops hard. My breath becomes visible, small clouds escaping my lips as my body reacts before my mind can catch up.

The tapestry fills my vision now. Intricate weaving, silver thread against deep blue fabric so dark it's almost black. A wild boar rendered in perfect detail, tusks caught mid-glint, muscles coiled beneath its hide. Above it, fractured pieces of a crown float like broken stars.

Sterling's crest.

Julian Sterling's fucking crest.

My hands shake—just slightly—and I jam them into my jacket pockets, fingers finding the familiar weight of my mechanics tools. The metal is cold enough to bite. Grounding.

*"The boar and the crown,"* I whisper, and my voice sounds wrong in this place. Venomous. "Sterling."*

Mara moves closer beside me, her own breath now misting in the cold air my wards have created. She studies the tapestry with those sharp eyes of hers. *"Julian Sterling? The man you killed at the Manor? What is his crest doing here?"*

I don't answer immediately. Instead, I pull out the Toughbook, the harsh green glow illuminating my face as I navigate through encrypted files. Syndicate charts bloom across the screen—connections I'd mapped after Julian went down, after I'd put two rounds through his skull and left him bleeding out on marble floors while his daughter screamed.

Family trees.

Business associations.

And there it is. Hidden in plain sight because no one ever looks close enough at the High-Spire families. Everyone assumes they're separate entities—the Morvains, the Sterlings, the other old money dynasties. But that's what they want you to think.

*"They're family,"* I say, closing the Toughbook with a snap that echoes too loud in the gallery. *"Morvain and Sterling. It's a dynasty of butchers. And I'm going to end the bloodline tonight."*

Mara opens her mouth to respond, but I've already turned away from the tapestry. My mind is racing now, connecting dots I should have seen before. The '99 flush wasn't just corporate malice—it was family planning. Pruning the South Side so their interests could grow unopposed.

The floorboards creak beneath my boots as I shift my weight, taking a step toward where I'd left Elias Morvain unconscious near his desk. But my mechanic's ear catches something else—a sound that doesn't belong.

A metallic click.

Microsecond soft. Barely audible over my own heartbeat hammering in my ears.

My boot had landed on a specific board, and the sound came from directly beneath it—not wood on wood, but metal on metal. Something mechanical underneath the floor.

I freeze mid-step, every muscle locked tight.

Elias Morvain's last words echo back at me: *You think this is about you? You think any of this is about some vigilante justice?*

Not a panic room.

Something else entirely.

I turn slowly back toward Mara, but my eyes are scanning the floor now. Looking for irregularities. Seams that don't quite match. Boards slightly higher or lower than their neighbors.

There. Three boards down from where I'm standing. A hairline gap running perpendicular to the others. Almost invisible unless you're looking for it.

Almost invisible unless you spend your life listening to machinery, learning to hear the sounds that mean something's wrong with the works.

"Stay behind me," I say quietly, drawing my sidearm in one smooth motion. "And don't move unless I tell you."

The click came from below.

Which means whatever Elias Morvain really was—whatever he was protecting here in this gallery—wasn't just hiding in plain sight.

It was buried under our feet.

* * *

I freeze.

Every muscle locks solid. My boot hovers six inches above polished mahogany that catches the amber gallery lights like honey. Behind me, I hear Mara's footsteps stop abruptly—she must've seen my body language shift from casual to coiled steel.

My fingertips tingle with frost-cobalt wards, but I don't let them flare yet. Not yet. First, I need to read this room like a disassembled engine block.

The floor looks perfect. Immaculate. Worth more than most people make in three years, probably. But I'm not looking at aesthetics. I'm reading stress lines in varnish, micro-fractures that tell stories about weight distribution. My eyes trace an invisible grid across the hardwood, following the pattern of grain and sealant.

There.

A seam slightly too straight. Boards elevated by two micrometers on one side—a discrepancy you'd never see unless you spent half your life measuring tolerances between pistons and cylinders. I kneel slowly, balancing my weight forward onto my toes so I don't add even a gram of pressure where it shouldn't be.

My breath fogs the air as I lower myself down.

The wards finally spread from my fingertips, trailing silver-blue against dark wood. Temperature differential mapping—I learned this trick from studying how heat signatures move through engine blocks. The frost reads the thermal memory of the floorboards, tracing the cold mass of metal hidden beneath mahogany and subfloor.

Beneath us isn't just structure.

It's mechanical death.

I feel the thermite before I see its signature—bismuth lining, designed to create that specific kind of containment explosion that doesn't just destroy, but annihilates whatever organic matter happens to be in the kill box. And below that: Dwarven-forged pressure plates. The craftsmanship is exquisite. Whoever built this knew what they were doing.

"You're already standing in the center of the web," I whisper to myself.

"Cole?" Mara's voice cuts through the gallery's oppressive silence.

"Don't take another step." I hold up my left hand, palm out, without looking back at her. My right hand stays pressed to the floor, reading the temperature variations like braille. "Mara, listen to me very carefully. You are currently standing on what might be a safe zone. Don't test that theory."

"What is it?"

I finally look up, my eyes meeting hers across eight feet of trap-laden hardwood. Her face shows that perfect mixture of trust and terror—the kind of expression you see when someone realizes you know something life-or-death that they don't.

"Dwarven-forged pressure mechanics," I say, keeping my voice level despite the sweat now crawling down my spine. "Bismuth-lined thermite under the mahogany. The whole gallery is a containment trap. We take one wrong step, and we're ash."

She goes pale. Good. Fear makes people careful.

The ward-ice spreads wider from my palms, mapping out the grid beneath us with growing clarity. It's elegant, really—whoever set this up understood pressure distribution better than most engineers. The plates aren't just random. They're calibrated to create maximum overlap coverage while leaving specific narrow paths through the grid.

Like breadcrumbs made of explosive.

Or a chessboard where every square could be your last move.

"The perimeter path is too far," I mutter, more to myself than her. Even if I could find it—and I'm not sure I can—I'd have to guide Mara through step-by-step without either of us seeing the exact position our feet need to land. One miscalculation and the thermite ignites.

We're trapped in the middle of a killing field designed by someone who thought about how people walk.

Behind me, somewhere in the manor's guts, machinery hums to life. Air circulation changes—the ventilation system adjusting for... what? A new pressure differential? Someone coming?

Then I hear it: that faintest click. Microscopic but distinct. Like a marble dropping onto silk.

A plate just engaged.

Somewhere behind me, weight shifted on the floor. The pressure mechanics registered it.

And now they know exactly where we are.

"Cole?" Mara's voice pitches higher.

I don't answer immediately because I'm counting heartbeats, measuring the time between that click and any response from the system. Three seconds. Four. Five.

Nothing yet.

But it's coming.

A slow smile spreads across my face—not from happiness, but from recognition. This is Morvain's work. I've seen his signature before, back when I was still taking jobs from the Spire's lower tiers. He likes dramatic pauses. Builds suspense like he's conducting an orchestra.

"How much do you trust me?" I ask Mara, never taking my eyes off the floor grid I'm mapping with frost-ice.

"What?"

"How much do you trust me, Mara. Right now. In this moment."

She doesn't hesitate. "Completely."

"Good." I stand up slowly, redistributing my weight evenly across both feet—classic machinist technique for testing load-bearing surfaces. Nothing changes beneath me. "Because we're going to have to do something very specific, and if I'm wrong about this, we die together."

The PA system crackles to life overhead, filling the gallery with sound so clear it must be broadcasting directly into our ears through some kind of localized field array.

*Very good, Mr. Reyes.*

High-Spire accent. Upper-tier aristocracy. Someone who learned their consonants in finishing schools that cost more than most countries' GDP.

*You have an eye for architecture.* A pause, letting the compliment settle. *But you are already standing in the center of the web.*

"I know," I say out loud, addressing the voice even though I don't know where exactly it's coming from.

There's a chuckle—rich, aristocratic, dripping with condescension that makes my teeth hurt.

*Do tell.*

I look at Mara. Her breathing has gone shallow. She's trying not to show fear, but it bleeds through anyway—small movements, micro-adjustments of balance as her body unconsciously looks for escape routes that don't exist.

"We walk," I tell her simply.

"That's insane—"

"We walk," I repeat firmly, meeting her eyes. "I can see the path. It's narrow. There might be two safe spots between us and the wall. You'll have to trust my guidance completely. Don't think. Don't hesitate. When I say move, you move exactly how I tell you."

"Cole, there's got to be another way—"

"There isn't." The frost-cobalt wards flare brighter around my hands now, responding to the adrenaline spike in my bloodstream. The temperature drops perceptibly—I can see my breath forming clouds again. "This is what Morvain wants. He thinks he's cornered us like rats. But mechanics is about precise movement under pressure. This is just... extreme pressure."

The PA system hums with anticipation.

*The mechanic thinks himself clever,* the voice observes. *Very well. Let us see if your instincts serve you here, Mr. Reyes.*

I ignore him. Focus on the floor. The ward-
