High-voltage perimeter wards detonated across my body—crimson-red arcs that traced lightning paths over my skin, around my arms, down my legs. Pain? No. That was too simple for what I felt. It was like every nerve ending had been dipped in molten lead and set on fire simultaneously.

But the blood-iron didn't just conduct.

It *grounded*.

The current screamed for an earth, found one in my core, and burned itself out in a fraction of a second. The transformer at the corner of the property exploded in a shower of blue-white sparks, each one singing its death song as the voltage spilled harmlessly through my flesh instead of cooking my organs from the inside.

I slid downward.

Razor-wire caught my clothes first, tearing through denim and leather like they weren't there. Then it found skin. The cuts were shallow but numerous—dozens of thin lines that bled instantly, adding copper-scent to the acrid ozone already saturating the air.

The ground rose up to meet me.

Freezing mud. North Jersey November cold seeping through torn fabric directly against raw flesh. I hit hard enough to feel something crack in my left shoulder blade, the sound lost beneath the still-buzzing electrical storm behind me.

My back was against the outside fence now. The posts stayed bent, holding their forty-five-degree angle like broken fingers pointing toward hell. Steam rose from where my blood touched the frozen earth, creating ghost-fog that obscured my vision when I tried to lift my head.

Everything hurt.

*Everything.*

But not in the way it should have. My body shouldn't have survived this. Shouldn't be processing pain signals at all after taking that level of kinetic impact followed by that kind of electrical overload. The laws of physics had apparently decided Cole Reyes wasn't worth their attention tonight.

I coughed.

Wet. Bubbling. Blood-tinged foam that painted my chin crimson in the firelight from the burning sky above. The Motorola Razr in my pocket had melted into a useless lump of plastic and circuit boards, the screen cracked beyond recognition, its LED light dead forever.

"Mara..." Her name came out as barely more than breath, no real words attached.

My hand moved weakly toward my chest where the Dwarven-machined Myocardial Geas pulsed with every beat of my heart—or what passed for a heartbeat these days. The mechanical contraption stuttered once. Twice. A grinding sound like metal teeth on stone that made my eyes water.

Then it stopped.

Just... stopped.

The absence of that rhythmic *click-click-click* in my chest was louder than any explosion. Deafening in its silence.

---

## CHAPTER 12: THE MISFIRING GEAS

I'm dying in the mud outside the Morvain Perimeter, and all I can hear is the sound of my own heart trying to tear itself apart.

*Click-whirr-spark.*

The Myocardial Geas jolts again, sending another jagged surge through my ventricles that feels like swallowing a fistful of broken glass. My chest cavity—which already looks like someone used it for demolition practice—convulses. A wet cough rattles up from somewhere deep in my lungs, bringing with it a spray of something dark and coppery that spatters across the frozen mud beside my cheek.

Rain. It's just rain.

But the smell isn't just rain. It's wet earth, rotting leaves, and the acrid tang of burnt iron-gall residue that clings to everything after an engagement with one of Kovacs' artifacts. The stench fills my nostrils, coats my tongue, mixes with the taste of blood.

*Click-click-click-clack.*

The Geas misfires again. This time the shock makes my whole body seize. My left arm—already hanging at an angle that suggests it might be separated at the shoulder—jerks involuntarily against the muddy ground. Frozen rain hammers down harder now, each droplet hitting my face like tiny needles, stinging the burns across my skin where Morvain's null-field had tried to unravel me down to the molecular level.

I try to move. Can't. My legs are pinned under something—a tree branch? rubble from the collapsed culvert? doesn't matter. Doesn't fucking matter because I'm bleeding internally, my ribs are a collection of jagged shards inside my torso, and Bram Kovacs' magical pacemaker is having a grand mal seizure right behind my sternum.

*Whirr-spark-hiss.*

Another jolt. Weaker this time. Fading.

"Shit," I rasp, or try to. What comes out is more of a gurgling wheeze. My throat feels like sandpaper wrapped around broken glass.

The sky above the tree line flickers. Once. Twice. Then—

Blinding halogens sweep across the landscape in rhythmic arcs, painting everything in harsh white light that cuts through the rain like search beams. The BATC sweep-helicopters. Of course they're here. They're always here when you need them least.

But I'm past caring about that now.

My fingers twitch toward my coat pocket—the one where I keep the heavy-gauge jumper-stylus for emergency Geas restarts—but they won't obey. Won't fucking work. Just lie there in the mud like useless pieces of meat while my heart stutters and sparks and slowly gives up on keeping me alive.

Danny.

The thought arrives unbidden, like it's been waiting for this moment to surface. Danny in the Iron-Lung, drowning slowly in black iron unless someone figures out how to remove Kovacs' curse before it finishes what Morvain started.

If I die here, Danny drowns in iron.

*Click... click...*

The Geas skips beats now instead of shocking them. One-two-three—pause—one-two-three. Each pause longer than the last.

My vision tunnels slightly at the edges. The halogens sweeping overhead blur into smears of light against dark clouds that look ready to split open with more rain. Or snow. November in North Jersey doesn't give a shit which it is.

"Reyes."

Mara's voice from somewhere behind me—or maybe inside my head? Can't tell anymore. She's digging herself out of the rubble where we left her, probably wondering why I'm just lying here instead of helping.

Can't help. Can barely breathe without feeling like my lungs are full of broken glass and burning oil.

Is it enough?

The question surfaces from some deep part of myself I didn't know was still functional. Did I save Mara? Yes. Did I stop Morvain? No. He's still out there, still has whatever plan he was executing, still wants to tear holes between dimensions using human souls as raw material.

But I saved Mara.

*Is it enough? Yeah. It has to be.*

Because if it isn't, then everything—the years of vigilante work, the deal with Kovacs, the slow poison of black iron building in my bones—I've been wrong about justice all along. Been chasing shadows while monsters like Morvain laughed their way toward apocalypse.

My chest spasms again. The Geas delivers one final weak jolt before going silent entirely.

*Silence.*

Just rain. Just mud. Just the fading warmth of a body that's giving up its fight to stay upright in a world designed to grind everyone down into dirt eventually anyway.

Above, the helicopter lights sweep closer, brighter, relentless as they always are when hunting someone who stepped outside the lines society drew for acceptable behavior.

I close my eyes against them—against everything—and let the cold seep in to fill the spaces where warmth used to live.

Danny.

If I die here...

But I don't finish the thought because finishing thoughts requires energy I no longer have to spare, and somewhere in what might still technically be my conscious mind, I understand this is how it ends for people like me: not in glory or redemption but in frozen mud outside industrial parks while helicopters circle overhead looking for someone else's monster to hunt.

The halogens find me next pass.

They're going to land soon. Medics, maybe. Or tactical teams ready to shoot first and ask questions later about why there's another vigilante bleeding out in the marshes tonight.

Either way, it doesn't matter now because my heart has stopped trying to beat anymore and all that's left is waiting for whatever comes after—the peace that passes understanding or just oblivion indifferently gray as November rain falling on black water where nothing grows except weeds and regret.

* * *

The rotors hit me first—a sound like tearing canvas multiplied by a thousand, each *thwack* driving spikes behind my eyes. I tried to lift my head and the world spun, a nauseating carousel of mud and smoke and the sickly yellow glow bleeding through the clouds above.

They came from the northeast, two black shapes cutting through the rain-slicked darkness like birds of prey. No warning. Just the sudden fury of their approach as they descended toward the Morvain perimeter. My heart—my real one, not the cursed metal thing grinding away in my chest—lurched against my ribs.

"Fuck," I rasped, tasting copper and bile.

The searchlights hit next. Blinding sodium-vapor spears that sliced through the smoke from the transformer Mara had blown, turning the entire wetland into a theater stage lit for some hellish production. The beam swept across the muddy ground twenty feet to my right, illuminating every divot, every puddle, every trickle of water running black between the tufts of dying grass.

I didn't move. Couldn't move. The iron-gall residue was still sizzling on my skin where it had splattered, each dot burning like a brand. But worse than that, the ward around my chest—the thing keeping me alive when my own heart wanted to quit—was misfiring. Each beat felt irregular, stuttering, like a machine running on the last drops of fuel.

*Thwack-thwack-thwack.*

Closer now. Both helicopters hovering maybe fifty feet up, their rotors kicking up spray that caught the light like diamonds. I pressed myself harder against the frozen mud, feeling it seep through my jacket, cold and unyielding.

"The perimeter is compromised at Sector Four," a voice crackled over speakers mounted on the hulls. High-Spire Elven cadence—that precise, clipped accent that made even simple words sound like death sentences. "Deploy the Ogre-Kin hounds. Ground sweep protocols, Alpha-Three. Shoot to kill, bag the remains."

My fingers dug into the mud. Twenty feet. That's all separated me from being spotted. The searchlight swept past again, and for one eternal second its glare pinned me like an insect on display. Time stopped. I could see every particle of dust in that beam, could feel it burning away what little remained of my night vision.

Then smoke. The transformer's pyre threw enough greasy black across my position that the light passed over without catching. I exhaled slowly, tasting ash.

"Sectors One through Nine are secure. Focus sweep on Sector Four. Possible hostiles detected."

The helicopters banked, circling lower. Their downdraft hammered the marsh vegetation flat, sent spirals of debris dancing across the surface of stagnant water. Aviation fuel mixed with the smell of burning pine and wet earth—a cocktail that burned in my nostrils.

I had to move. Had to get to that drainage ditch ten yards behind me, where shadow pooled deep and thick. But when I tried to pull myself forward, my arms gave out after three pathetic inches. Mud oozed between my fingers. Rain pelted my face.

"Fuck, fuck, *fuck*," I hissed, jaw clenched against the pain radiating from my chest.

*Thwack-thwack-thwack.*

One helicopter descended further, so low now that I could make out the tactical markings on its hull—BATC insignia, sharp-edged and cruel under the floodlights. The pilot was good. Professional. They knew how to hunt.

Boots hit the ground.

Heavy footsteps, deliberately placed, splashing through puddles I couldn't see. Coming from somewhere beyond the perimeter fence, from my blind side where the searchlights couldn't reach. Not the BATC ground team—they'd announce themselves, follow protocols. This was different.

"You're bleeding," a voice said from somewhere in the darkness. Female. Young. Definitely not High-Spire Elven.

My hand went automatically to my side, where the iron-gall had burned through my jacket. Wet. Warm. The bleeding wasn't bad, but it would show up under those lights if they swept this way again.

"I know," I managed.

The footsteps stopped maybe five feet away. Close enough that I could hear breathing over the constant thrum of the helicopters overhead. Could smell something beneath the marsh rot—soap, maybe. Clean skin.

"Why are you still here?" she asked. "They'll find you."

My vision swam. The ward in my chest stuttered again, and for a moment I felt the real thing—a moment of blessed silence where my actual heart tried to restart, remember what it was supposed to do.

"Can't... move," I admitted, hating every syllable.

Silence. Then: "Shit." More footsteps, closer now. A shadow moving against shadows until hands—small, steady—gripped my arm. "Put your weight on me. Don't pass out."

I tried. God help me, I tried. But the ward chose that moment to seize completely, and my body went rigid as every muscle locked down. A sound escaped my throat—not quite a scream, more like a strangled animal's death rattle.

"Easy, easy!" Her grip tightened. "Your heart? Is it the heart thing?"

All I could manage was a nod.

"We need to get you under cover before—"

The searchlight found us both.

That blinding sodium glare hit her face first—I saw shock register in wide eyes, saw her lips part in surprise. Then it swept across me, leaving nowhere to hide. For three full seconds we were frozen on that stage, two insects pinned under glass.

"Hostile contact! Sector Four-Blue!" The Elven voice crackled with sudden urgency. "Armed response incoming!"

The helicopters banked hard, their rotors screaming as they oriented toward our position. Behind them, through the gaps in the clouds, I caught sight of something worse—more lights rising from beyond the Passaic River, approaching fast.

"You have to go," I told her, voice barely a whisper. "They'll burn this whole marsh down to get to me."

Her face was pale in the light, but her jaw was set with stubborn determination. "Not without you."

"Too late for that."

But she was already dragging at my arm again, muscles straining as she tried to pull me toward the drainage ditch where darkness still pooled deep enough to hide bodies. The ward in my chest ground and seized, each beat irregular, arrhythmic, like a clock winding down.

Behind us, boots splashed through the mud. Multiple sets. Organized.

"Last chance to run," I said, watching her struggle with my dead weight.

She didn't answer. Just pulled harder.

And somewhere above us all, those fucking helicopters circled like vultures waiting for death to do its work.

* * *

I felt weight on my shoulder first—a deliberate, calculated pressure that wasn't the mud trying to swallow me whole. My eyes were fucked, vision swimming through blood and iron-gall residue that tasted like battery acid and regret.

"Don't move, Reyes."

The voice came from above, smooth as river stones but edged with something metallic. I tried to turn my head, failed. Something was pinning my other side too.

"You're gonna feel this," said another voice—this one rougher, gravelly, with the distinctive roll of someone who'd spent thirty years breathing sawdust and machine oil. South Side accent, maybe Kearny or the Ironbound district. "Sorry about the mess, but we ain't got time for pretty."

My shirt tore with a sound like canvas giving way. Cold air hit my chest where the Geas had been burning its way through my ribs, and I realized I could see it now—the glowing blue-black circuitry spreading across skin like infected veins, crackling and sputtering, one circuit already dark and dead.

"Ain't pretty," the gravel-voice said. "Casing's cracked clean through. You're bleeding magic, metal, and meat all over the place."

Something sharp kissed my neck. An injection. Cold gel flooding my system, tasting like copper lightning and ozone.

"What the—"

"The good stuff," the smooth voice cut in. "Elven bio-gel. Expensive as hell. Stop your internal bleeding long enough for us to work. Hold still or you'll rupture something and we both die out here."

I wanted to speak, ask who they were, what they wanted, why the fuck they were helping me when half of North Jersey wanted me six feet under. But my tongue was swelling, my throat closing down.

A computer screen glowed into existence somewhere above me, casting sickly light on a masked face—featureless black ballistic nylon, no features, just two eye holes that reflected the glow of the Panasonic Toughbook like an animal's eyes.

"Geas is fragged," the Dwarf—because that's what he had to be, stout build and the way his hands moved with practiced precision—said to whoever was holding me down. "Casing's cracked. I gotta jump it or he flatlines in ten seconds."

The Elf leaned closer, rain dripping from their mask onto my face. "Do it, Jax. Choppers are swinging back. We got a two-minute window before the Ogre-Kin catch his scent. Move!"

"Fuck my life," Jax muttered, and then there was motion—a metallic clatter, the sound of something being unlatched and opened. The defibrillator pack, I realized. He'd been carrying a portable defibrillator this whole time.

"Last chance to pray if you're religious," Jax said, and grabbed my torn shirt with one hand while his other fumbled with the paddles.

The copper prongs looked massive up close, heavy as hammers. They hovered over my exposed chest where the Geas had burned through, where blood and something worse was seeping out into the mud.

"I'm gonna shock your heart-ward directly," Jax continued, voice strangely calm given we were standing in the open with god-knows-what coming for us. "Could restart it. Could fucking cook it. Either way, you feel every second of it. Ready?"

I tried to nod. Failed.

He jammed the prongs into my wounds.

My world exploded.

White-hot electricity tore through every nerve ending, every blood vessel, every cell in my body. My back arched—not because I wanted to move but because my muscles contracted all at once, fighting against the mud, against gravity, against the weight holding me down.

Time stretched like taffy. I could feel each individual synapse firing, misfiring, short-circuiting. The Geas screamed inside my chest—metal shrieking as it overloads, circuits burning bright as magnesium fire before going dark.

*CRACK-CRACK-CRACK*

Three shocks in quick succession. Each one felt like being struck by lightning while simultaneously having every bone in my body broken and reformed.

And then—

Silence.

My heart stuttered. Once. Twice. And then began beating again, irregular but present, a mechanical rhythm that sounded wrong even to my own ears.

"Shit," Jax breathed out. "That actually worked."

The Elf—because they hadn't moved during the whole thing, just held me pinned—finally relaxed their grip on my shoulder.

"We need to move him now," the Elf said, voice urgent but controlled. "Mara's still digging herself out of the culvert. Ogre-Kin are circling. We got maybe ninety seconds before they realize we're here."

Jax slammed his Toughbook shut with a sharp click. "Help me lift him. Careful—the bio-gel makes everything slick as hell for about five minutes."

Hands grabbed under my arms, another set under my knees. They lifted me like I weighed nothing, which meant either I'd lost more blood than I thought or these two were stronger than they looked.

"They're gonna track us," I managed to croak out, throat raw from smoke inhalation and whatever the Elven gel was doing to my system.

"Not if we're smart," the Elf replied. They were moving fast, carrying me through the mud toward what looked like a blacked-out van idling at the edge of the Morvain Perimeter. "We've got countermeasures. You just focus on staying conscious."

"Who..." I started, but the effort made me cough—wet, ragged sounds that brought up blood mixed with that strange copper-tasting gel. "Who are you?"

"The Watching Party," Jax said matter-of-factly as they maneuvered me into the back of the van. It smelled like rubber and ozone and something else I couldn't quite place—magic? Technology? Both?

I'd heard whispers about them. Everyone had. The group that pulled people out of tight spots without asking questions. No fees, no favors expected in return—not officially anyway.

But why me?

"Why?" I asked again, this time managing to keep from coughing.

The Elf climbed in after me, pulling the door shut while Jax jogged around to the passenger side. Through the tinted windows I could see movement in the darkness beyond our perimeter—shapes too large to be human, moving with unnatural grace.

"We'll explain everything once we're clear," the Elf said. They were already pulling off their mask, revealing pointed ears and eyes that shimmered faintly silver in the low light. "Right now, survival is priority one."

The van lurched forward, tires spitting mud.

My chest still burned where the Geas had cracked open, but beneath it all was something new—a steady mechanical rhythm that meant my heart-ward had restarted.

We were alive.

For now.

But knowing The Watching Party, nothing came free.

And I'd just accumulated a debt I wasn't sure I could ever repay.

---

## CHAPTER 13: THE CLOAKED AMBULANCE

The world comes back in fragments—cold canvas rough against my cheek, the distant wail of sirens that might be real or just the ringing in my eardrums.

"Hold still, Cole," Mara's voice was right above me, surprisingly gentle despite the blood caked along her hairline. Her fingers were wrapping sterile gauze around my ribs, pressing firmly against the burn tissue. "You've got two cracked ribs and third-degree electrical burns across your left shoulder."

"The kids..." I coughed, tasting iron and charcoal on my tongue. "Did Martha... did the truck clear the turnpike?"

"All five of them are at Saint Michael's," she said softly, securing the medical tape with a sharp snap of her teeth. "The state thinks the explosion was an industrial gas leak. The Bureau's covering it up to save face."

"And Morvain?" I asked, looking into her exhausted, ash-streaked eyes.

"Gone underground," Mara replied, leaning her head back against the ambulance wall as the diesel engine hummed beneath us. "He lost his estate, his telluric siphon, and his political cover in Trenton. But he'll be back, Cole. Men like that don't quit."

"Neither do union machinists, Mara," I whispered, closing my eyes as the morphine finally kicked in. "Neither do we."r might be echoing through the ruins of my skull. My lungs feel like someone took a ball-peen hammer to them, then decided to go for seconds.

"Got him! Move, move, *move!*"

Hands grab me from multiple angles. Rough. Efficient. Not gentle like paramedics should be, but desperate in a way that feels wrong somehow—like they're scooping up something valuable before it gets stolen by worse hands. The ground is mud. I can taste it even though I haven't opened my eyes yet. Can taste copper too. My own blood.

Someone grunts with effort. "Jesus Christ, he's dead weight. Help me here!"

They lift. The motion sends white-hot agony spiking through my ribcage—I make a sound that isn't quite human, more like rusty metal scraping against concrete. One of them hisses something in a language that shouldn't exist outside of bad fantasy novels.

"Easy, mechanic. You're with the Party now."

That voice. Feminine. Elvish accent so thick you could spread it on bread and call it butter. But there's no way elves are real because North Jersey is full of enough monsters already without adding pointy-eared fairytale bullshit to the mix.

My eyelids flutter open to darkness broken by strobing red light. Ambulance. We're in an ambulance. But not right—a 1999 Ford E-Series that looks like it survived both Katrina and some kind of arcano-industrial accident. The interior has been retrofitted beyond reason: medical equipment bolted to walls next to what looks like jury-rigged arcane focus points, all humming with barely-contained energy that makes my teeth ache.

The doors slam shut. Someone's screaming. Maybe me.

Then we're moving, lurching forward with enough g-force to make my stomach try to climb out through my esophagus. The medic—because yeah, she's definitely an orc now that I'm actually looking at her, green skin and tusks and all—leans over me with instruments I don't want to examine too closely.

"Lungs are cooked," she says, voice sharp as a scalpel. "I'm venting the iron-gall buildup. Hold him down!"

The elf reappears from nowhere, pressing my shoulders into the stretcher with surprising strength for someone who probably weighs ninety pounds soaking wet. Her eyes are all wrong—too dark, pupils dilated until there's almost no iris showing—and when she speaks again, her breath smells like ozone and burning sugar.

"You got hit bad. BATC round, looks like. They're rewriting your geas from the inside out." She grits her teeth as I buck against their grip. "Stop fighting us! We're trying to *save* you!"

Saving. Right. Because getting tossed into a mobile trauma unit staffed by creatures straight out of D&D means I'm probably not going to end up face-down in the Passaic River come morning.

The orc medic produces something that looks like a pneumatic staple gun crossed with a ritual dagger. The business end glows faintly blue-green with runes that hurt to look at directly.

"This is gonna hurt worse than anything you've felt yet."

She doesn't wait for agreement.

* * *

The E-Series lurches hard left, and I taste copper where my teeth cut into my tongue. My chest feels like someone's trying to pour concrete into my lungs.

"BATC's got us!" The gnome driver's voice crackles through the overhead speaker, half-swallowed by static. "Heat sig spiking—oh fuck, they're deploying hunter-drones!"

The dwarf crouched beside me slams something metal with a curse that would make a dockworker blush. His hands are steady despite the ambush we just ran from, despite the way the whole vehicle shudders as it accelerates down some forgotten off-ramp.

"Keep it under eighty, you maniac, I'm trying to solder a fragging heart valve here!" He doesn't look up from where he's working on my chest—a place that burns like hellfire. "Oi! Some help back here!"

The Orc medic drops to her knees, her orange-red skin catching what little light bleeds through the reinforced windows. Her eyes—wrong color, wrong shape—lock onto mine for one crystalline moment before she presses a glove against my forehead.

"You're ice-cold," she says. Not sympathetic. Just stating facts.

The interior lights flicker, then go out completely. For three seconds we're plunged into near-darkness, lit only by the faint bioluminescent traces of the Dwarf's magical tools. Then the emergency LEDs kick in, bathing everything in sickly amber.

The high-pitched whine builds behind the walls. It's like standing next to an industrial transformer, that same electric hum that makes your teeth ache and your fillings vibrate.

"Wards are up! We're ghosts on their radar." The gnome's voice smooths out now, less panicked. "Taking the lower-level bypass to the South Side."

The ambulance smooths its ride, becomes almost unnaturally stable. Whatever cloaking field just activated is masking us—but the cost shows immediately. My breath comes out in white clouds. The temperature must have dropped twenty degrees inside this metal box.

The Orc's hands move with practiced efficiency, pressing something cold and slick against my collarbone. There's a sharp sting, then pressure as whatever she's doing finds purchase in my flesh.

"Bracing for fluid extraction," she announces, though I'm not sure who she's talking to. "Patient has stabilized marginally. Still losing too much—"

The Dwarf slams his tool down on an iron lever mounted beside me—a thing I didn't even see until he grabbed it. Metal shrieks. Something groans deep in the chassis.

A wave of localized static washes over us. My skin prickles. Every hair stands on end. The stench of ozone fills my nose, burning and clean and utterly wrong.

And then—silence. Outside the window, the world shifts. We pass under a highway overpass, but through some trick of the wards' magic, I can see *through* the concrete. Ghost images overlay reality: another version of this vehicle passing through at cross purposes, phantom taillights trailing behind us like dying stars.

"Slurp."

The sound should be comical. Clinical. Instead it's obscene—the wet pull of a tube being inserted into living tissue. The Orc works without ceremony or apology, her fingers finding the space between my ribs with the precision of someone who's done this a thousand times before.

Blue-black fluid bubbles up into the collection bulb. It's thick, viscous, and smells like burnt electronics mixed with spoiled meat. Each liter that drains from my chest feels like letting go of a weight I didn't know I was carrying.

My breathing eases.

But oh god, the cold. The cloaking field is dropping the temperature faster than my body can compensate. My teeth start to chatter. The medic notices, wraps a thermal blanket around my shoulders—but it's already freezing, drawing heat away instead of retaining it.

The Dwarf finishes whatever he was doing and leans back against the wall, wiping his brow. "Heart valve's holding. For now. But he's still hemorrhaging internal fluids."

"How long until we reach the South Side?" The Orc doesn't look at me anymore. She's focused entirely on monitoring the drainage, watching the dark fluid accumulate in the collection bag.

"Five minutes if we're lucky." The gnome sounds younger now, less confident. "Eight if those hunter-drones catch up."

I try to speak, but my mouth won't cooperate. My lips are numb. Everything below my neck has gone completely insensate except for where the drain is inserted—there it burns with cold fire.

My vision swims.

And there, in the shifting patterns of light and shadow, I see her face: Mara. Not the Orc. Never the Orc. Those features shift and solidify, softening into something human, something real.

Her eyes—my eyes—locked onto mine. And for just a moment, I smell white lilac.

Then everything goes black.

* * *

The world comes back to me in fragments.

First, there's sound—the rhythmic *thump-thump-thump* of something mechanical, steady as a heartbeat but wrong somehow. Too slow. Then pressure against my chest, constricting bands that I can't feel but know are there because my brain keeps screaming about them.

I try to open my eyes.

Can't.

Try again.

Nothing.

My mouth tastes like copper and burnt sugar. Someone's talking—voices layered over each other like radio static from multiple stations tuned to almost the same frequency. I catch words in the soup:

"...spiral ramp... sodium lights... transition..."

The floor underneath shifts. We're moving. Descending. Each turn presses me deeper into whatever surface I'm lying on, cold plastic that smells antiseptic but underneath that, something older. Stone. Water. Things that have been underground for so long they've forgotten what sunlight looks like.

"The fuck did you hit him with?" That voice cuts through clearer than the others. Gruff. Frustrated. Familiar in a way that makes my stomach clench.

"Corporate-grade plasma disruptor," another responds. Calmer. More medical. "Standard anti-piracy deployment. Lucky it wasn't kinetic rounds."

A third voice, younger: "He's burning up. Temp's spiking—one-zero-four point three."

They keep talking. The words blur together into meaningless syllables punctuated by the constant *thump* that might be an engine or might be blood in my ears. Can't tell anymore which sounds are real and which ones my brain is manufacturing just to fill the gaps where reality should be.

Something beeps steadily beside me.

I try to move my hand.

It doesn't respond.

Panic flares hot and bright somewhere deep in my chest before dissipating into numbness. My body feels disconnected, like I'm floating above myself watching all this happen to someone else. Someone who used to be Cole Reyes. Someone who knew how to stand on his own two feet without feeling like he's made of glass.

The temperature changes. The air grows damp. That sterile smell gets overpowered by moisture and stone and rust and the lingering scent of ozone from whatever the hell they zapped me with back there at the Bayfront.

We're deep now. Really deep. The sodium lights outside must be miles behind us because the only illumination comes from inside the ambulance—cool blue-white LEDs that make everyone look like corpses even though they're very much alive and moving around me like I'm some kind of puzzle they need to solve before their shift ends.

"...undercity access point Gamma-Seven... routing through old subway tunnels... should lose any corporate trackers in approximately..." Words continue but lose meaning as my consciousness starts sliding sideways again.

There's a lurch. Brakes squeal—not rubber on asphalt but metal on metal, grinding against itself in protest as we come to a sudden stop that throws me hard against the restraints. Something clatters inside one of the cabinets mounted to the walls.

"Bay Four," the first voice says again. Commanding now. "Move him fast—the Architect wants eyes-on within fifteen."

Hands grab me. Multiple hands. Lifting the gurney I'm strapped to with practiced efficiency born from years of doing exactly this thing exactly this many times until it became muscle memory stronger than thought.

Doors fly open ahead of us—or maybe they were already open; hard to tell when everything blurs together like wet watercolors bleeding into each other—and suddenly we're moving forward again except not in vehicle anymore but being pushed down a corridor so wide it echoes like a canyon every time someone coughs or clears their throat.

The space opens up around us vast enough to swallow sound whole without echoing at all just empty space where sound goes to die.

My eyes finally crack open just enough to see shapes: massive concrete pillars disappearing into shadow above us; exposed piping running along walls covered in condensation; lights hanging from cables too far away to count but close enough to see their sickly yellow glow reflecting off puddles scattered across cracked concrete floor beneath us.

We pass through swinging doors—heavy surgical-grade steel that clang shut behind us cutting off whatever sounds might have followed—and enter some kind of medical bay lit so bright it hurts even through half-closed lids.

The last thing I see before slipping under completely is an operating lamp burning overhead like a miniature sun designed specifically for peeling back layers until there's nothing left but bone and truth and whatever nightmares live underneath both those things combined.

## CHAPTER 14: THREE DAYS OF FEVER

The heat hits me before anything else—a wall of wet, suffocating fire that tastes like copper pennies and burning plastic. My lungs seize. I can't breathe. Can't move. The sidewalk beneath my feet is hot enough to cook meat.

I'm sixteen again.

The clinic is screaming.

Not with voices—with that deep, organic roar of hungry flame that eats through brick and mortar like they're made of paper. Yellow-black smoke pours from shattered windows on the second floor, thick as motor oil, choking out the streetlights. They're still up though, those lights, casting everything in this hellish amber glow that makes the South Side look like something dragged straight from the abyss.

New Year's Eve, 1999.

The date burns behind my eyes.

*"Cole! Get back!"*

Somebody's shouting. Somebody's grabbing my shoulder, fingers digging into bone hard enough to hurt. But I'm already running toward the front steps, the ones that lead up to the double doors, both hanging open like a mouth, both belching smoke and embers that land on my arms, tiny stings that make me flinch.

Inside, I can hear them. Screaming.

Patients. Nurses. My mother.

Elena was working nights. Double shift because we needed the money for college applications I'd never fill out anyway.

*"She's in there!"* I'm yelling now, voice cracking like a boy's voice does when he hasn't learned how to control it yet. *"Ma! I'm coming! I'll break the door!"*

I don't know what I think I'll do. I don't have any power then—not yet. Just hands and desperation and the kind of stupid teenage invincibility that gets people killed. The wards around the place are smoking too, glowing faintly green where the sludge has touched them, corrupted by whatever Apep had dumped into the Passaic weeks before.

Magic poison. Burning magic poison.

*"COLE!"*

A different voice. Deeper. Rougher than sandpaper.

Hands—real hands, big as hams—wrap around my chest from behind and yank me backward so hard my heels kick off the ground. I fight, kicking, scratching, trying to get free, but whoever it is doesn't let go.

*"She's gone, kid,"* says Grimjaw, though this version of him is younger, face less scarred, still with most of his tusks intact. His leathery skin glistens with sweat in the firelight. *"You go in there, you burn too."*

The building groans—a sound like God himself tearing up the foundations—and the second-floor wall buckles outward in a shower of sparks and molten glass. The heat pushes us back another step, both of us, until my spine hits a parked car's hood, still cool enough to make me gasp.

I look at my hands.

Just hands. No glow. No power. Nothing I can do except watch and die inside while my mother burns because I wasn't fast enough or strong enough or *anything* enough.

*"No,"* I whisper. *"No no no no—"*

The roof caves in.

Not all at once, but like a sigh, the whole middle section collapsing inward in a cascade of flame and smoke and screaming that cuts off sudden and absolute. Debris rains down on the sidewalk, scattering. One piece lands near my feet—a charred bed frame, springs twisted, mattress long since consumed.

And then.

From the ashes at the base of what used to be the front steps, something moves.

Small. Coughing. Blackened by soot but alive, stumbling out through the smoke like he's drunk, dragging one leg behind him.

Danny.

Danny fucking Reyes, my little brother, six years old when he should've been safe at home with our aunt, not here, not ever, but here nonetheless, coughing black smoke and crying for Mommy where his voice won't carry over the roaring flames behind him.

*To Be Continued...*

---

**SEQUENCE 14.2: 'Danny in the Ash' (Word Count: ~800)**
**Timestamp:** November 16, 2007 — Cole's Subconscious / Grimjaw's Watching Party
**Action/Beat:** Cole cradles fever-dream Danny from the fire. The boy is severely burned, delirious, speaking in riddles about the "man with teeth" who took their mother. The scene dissolves into another memory—the hospital, Danny's first surgery, Cole's promise to always protect him. This creates a temporal paradox: if Cole was supposed to die three days ago, how can he still remember these moments as part of his living timeline?

* * *

The air tastes like oil and copper.

I'm standing in the chop-shop—but not my shop. This one smells wrong. All wrong. Like rust and blood and something sweet underneath, like rotting flowers. The concrete floor has cracks running through it like veins, and there's a light coming from somewhere, casting everything in sickly yellow-green.

Danny's sitting on an overturned crate near the back workbench.

He looks wrong too. Too thin. His skin has that waxy pallor kids get when they're running fever, and he's wearing a hoodie that's seen better days. He's maybe fifteen here—late '03, early '04, before everything went sideways.

"Hey, Cole."

His voice sounds distant, muffled, like I'm hearing it through water.

I move closer. Something's off about how I'm walking. My footsteps don't echo right. The shop stretches longer than it should, benches receding into shadow that seems thicker than darkness ought to be.

"What's up, kiddo?"

My own voice scares me. Flat. Emotionless. Like I'm reading lines someone else wrote.

Danny smiles, but it doesn't reach his eyes. "Cough's been getting worse. Mom says—"

He stops. Wraps his arms around himself. Shivers despite the oppressive heat of the space.

"She says you've been working late. Says you won't eat. Says—"

Another shudder. Then it comes.

The cough.

Not normal. Not anything close to normal. It starts deep in his chest, rattling, wet, like bones grinding together. Danny doubles over, hands pressed against his ribs, and the sound just keeps going. And going. A horrible, liquid hacking that makes my teeth hurt.

When it finally stops, he's gasping for breath.

There's a rag in his hand. White once, probably. Now spotted with red.

No—not red.

Blue-black. Like oxidized iron. Like the residue from that night in November '99, when the sky burned and the ash fell and Lord Malvourne's men did their work.

But this isn't ash.

This is blood.

Danny unfolds the rag slowly, stares at it like he doesn't recognize what he's seeing. His face goes pale as milk, then flashes hot with fever.

"Cole..."

That single word carries everything. Fear. Confusion. Betrayal, even though none of this is his fault.

I move closer. The light shifts as I do, throwing harsh shadows across his face. For a moment—just a heartbeat—I see him differently. Older. The way he looked in the morgue photo I found later, after everything went to hell. Skin gray-blue. Lips parting in death's rictus.

Then we're back here. Now. The chop-shop. The rag.

"What is this?" Danny whispers. "What... what happened? I was sleeping and I woke up and this stuff was..." He touches his lips, looks at his fingers like they belong to someone else. "It tastes like metal."

I should say something comforting. Something brotherly. Something that will make this okay.

Instead, I'm staring at that rag. At the blue-black stain spreading across white cotton.

The curse.

Not just on me anymore.

On him too.

Because of them. Because of the High-Spire elites who thought they could flush their mistakes into the Passaic and pretend nothing happened. Because of Malvourne and his schemes and the rot that seeps through this city like groundwater through concrete.

My hands are shaking.

No—wait. They're steady. Cold as ice. Ready.

"I'm gonna fix it," I hear myself say.

Voice flat. Certain.

"I'm gonna build something to fix it."

The words taste like iron too. Like blood. Like promises you can't break even if you wanted to.

Danny looks up at me, eyes wide and fever-bright. "With what? Cole, what's wrong with me?"

"Nothing permanent." Lie. Complete lie. "Just... side effects. From the air. From being close to the river. We'll figure it out."

He nods, trusting, because he has to trust someone, and what choice does he have?

But I'm not looking at him anymore.

I'm looking past him, at the workbenches. Seeing them differently now. Not just spaces for welding and machining and the careful assembly of tools. But possibilities.

Arcane Iron. The stuff that moves between worlds. That burns hotter than regular metal. That responds to intention, to will, to need.

And underneath all that—the knowledge I've been building since '99. Since Mara showed me what her people knew about the Breath of Creation. About how matter remembers. How it holds trauma in its structure. How you can forge something from pain that's stronger than anything made from joy.

I start moving around the shop, pulling things down. Brass components. Glass tubes. The early schematics for an Arcane Lung—I'd been working on designs before everything fell apart, before Danny got sick, before—

Before this moment.

The Threefold Cord takes shape in my mind like a blueprint. Penance for our mother, who never should have died alone. Revenge against the system that let this happen, that made profit from poison and called it progress. And underneath it all, wrapped tight as wire:

A sliver of justice for Danny.

Because some debts don't forgive. They compound. Interest accrues. And eventually, someone has to pay.

"He's gonna be okay," Danny says softly behind me.

Not asking. Telling himself. Trying to believe.

"Yeah," I say, hands already moving, already planning, already seeing the shape of what needs to come next. "He's gonna be okay."

But we both know I'm lying.

And in the oppressive heat of this impossible space, somewhere between memory and fever-dream, I make the promise that will define everything after:

*They did this.*

*So I'll take everything they love.*

*And burn their world down until there's nothing left but ash and iron and the smell of justice.*

Danny's face shudders, features shifting—

—and suddenly it's not him anymore.

It's Mara.

Crying in the culvert where I left her.

Weeping because she thinks I'm dead.

And the dream tears itself open like wet paper, throwing me into another place entirely, another time, another version of the truth I can't escape—

* * *

The pain was a constant now, a river of it flowing through every fiber of my being. I couldn't move. Couldn't breathe without feeling my ribs shift against something sharp inside. But worse than the physical agony was the emptiness—the vast, hollow space where my certainty had been.

I'd gotten her out. That much I knew. The memory burned bright and clear despite everything else dissolving around it. Danny's sacrifice. Mara screaming my name as she dragged me backward into that void between worlds. The feeling of being pulled apart by competing gravities.

But then nothing. Just this suspended existence in a void that smelled like ash and ozone and the metallic tang of Danny's black iron.

Then they came.

Cool hands pressed against my chest, and I nearly screamed at the contact. But the scream died before it formed because those hands knew exactly where to touch, exactly how much pressure to apply. They moved with surgical precision across my ribcage, and where they passed, I felt a stinging sensation—cleansing, healing, real.

"Mara..." Her name escaped my lips as barely more than breath.

White lilacs. I could smell white lilacs.

My mind latched onto that scent like a drowning man to a rope. Lilac meant life. Lilac meant Mara. My hands—when did I have hands?—reached toward the source of that scent, toward the ghostly touch working its way across my torso.

*The Geas is resetting,* some analytical part of my brain noted distantly. *Feel it pulling back into alignment.*

But I didn't care about the Geas. I cared about those hands. About the warmth spreading from their points of contact, chasing away the cold that had settled into my bones. About the soft sound of breathing nearby.

"I got you out," I whispered again, though whether I was speaking to Mara or reassuring myself, I couldn't say. "I got you out. You're safe now."

The hands paused for just a moment, then continued their work. One set moved higher, tracing along my collarbone while another worked lower, carefully wrapping something around my ribs. The duality of movement should have confused me, but in this fevered state, it all made perfect sense. Two pairs of hands meant twice the healing. Twice the protection.

But then my mechanic's mind stirred, sluggish but persistent. Something wrong. The cadence off by half a beat between the two sets. And the lilac scent—not quite right either. It had an undertone I couldn't place, mixed with medical-grade antiseptic.

How many people were here?

"Keep his fluids up. The Geas is holding. He's fighting his way back."

The voice cut through the haze like a knife. Female. Commanding despite its softness. But not Mara's voice. Not her cadence, not her inflection.

My eyes—when did they become crusted shut?—fought against some unseen seal. Blood and grime held them closed, but desperation gave me strength I shouldn't have possessed. The lids cracked apart.

And there she was.

Not Mara.

A ghost stood over me in the dim light of what I slowly recognized as the Watching Party clinic—all sterile white surfaces and equipment that belonged in a hospital three centuries ahead of 2007. Long dark hair pulled back from a face I knew in a thousand photographs but hadn't seen in person since before my father died.

"Mom?"

She looked different somehow. Older maybe, or perhaps just more worn than I remembered. Her hands hovered over my chest, one still marked with streaks of Elven bio-gel, the other holding what appeared to be a surgical needle threaded with something that shimmered in the light.

"I'm real, Cole," she said quietly, her brown eyes meeting mine with an intensity that made my fevered brain reel. "And we need to talk."

## CHAPTER 15: THE TWO MOTHERS WHO DIED TWICE

The first thing I notice is the silence.

Not the absence of sound—that's impossible when your lungs are rebuilding themselves with every labored breath—but something deeper. The frost-cobalt wards that have burned beneath my skin since I was fourteen, those ancient protections inherited from my abuela, are *gone*. Vanished like morning mist under August sun.

I try to inhale completely and my chest screams. The pain is white-hot, clean-edged, real. Not spectral. Not supernatural. Just goddamn biological agony that makes me want to retch, but even that simple act feels like trying to tear myself apart.

My eyes focus on the frosted glass overhead. Light filters through it—artificial, harsh, institutional. Everything smells wrong: sterile antiseptic burning my nostrils alongside something sweeter, older. White lilacs, maybe? And underneath it all, worn cotton and that particular scent magic leaves when it settles into places where it doesn't belong.

"Easy there," someone says—I don't see them, can't turn my head far enough—and cool fingers press against my wrist, checking pulse. "Don't fight the restraints."

I hadn't realized I was straining against them until she mentions it. The leather bindings are thick, institutional, strapped across my forearms and chest. Smart. When you've been dead—truly dead—and come back, your body remembers instincts that your mind hasn't processed yet. Fight first, think never.

My ribs are a cage of rigid staples, Dwarven work by the feel of them—too precise, too strong to be anything else. Each breath pulls at metal holding bone together, and I can feel the Elven bio-gel slathered across every inch of exposed skin, cooling and knitting flesh with patient magic that tastes like copper pennies in my mouth.

The heart monitor beside me beeps with steady insistence: *beep... beep... beep...* A sound I should find comforting. Survival confirmed. Living proof.

But my Myocardial Geas—my mother's dying gift, the cursed blessing that keeps my ticker going long after it should stop—hums differently now. Quieter. More efficient. Like someone tuned an engine while I wasn't looking.

"You're in the Watching Party clinic," the nurse continues—gnome by her size and the faint shimmer of illusion magic around her scrubs. She keys a Nextel radio on her belt. "Patient Zero is conscious. Vitals stabilizing. Alert the Architects."

The term 'Patient Zero' sits wrong in my gut, but I'm too busy cataloging damage to protest.

I turn my head slightly—it takes effort, feels like grinding stones—and take in the room. Concrete walls painted with arcane wards in colors that hurt to look at directly. Banks of monitors showing vitals I don't recognize, mixing medical readouts with what looks like mystical diagnostics. IV stands dripping potions that taste metallic and restorative all at once into my veins.

This isn't just any recovery room.

Someone's been preparing for this moment. For *me*.

The heavy steel door to the recovery room hisses open, and footsteps approach my bed.

* * *

The sodium-vapor lamp flickers once—just a single stutter—and when the light steadies again, she's there.

My lungs stop working. I feel the air catch in my throat like a fish bone lodged sideways.

Elena Reyes stands three feet from where I'm strapped to this hospital bed in some clinic that shouldn't exist beneath the Kearny Marshes. Her hair is different—not the dark black I remember, but threaded through with silver like strands of mercury. Lines bracket her mouth, deep creases that weren't there before. She's older. She's *aged*. But those eyes—those warm brown eyes that used to find me in crowds at the Machado Street market—those are unmistakable.

The frost-cobalt wards in my blood scream for release. They convulse weakly, pathetic little sparks against the restraints bolted into the mattress frame. My body arches involuntarily, muscles tearing as I fight bindings designed to hold down things that would shred a normal man's limbs to ribbons.

"Stop it!" The voice cuts through my panic—the *same voice* that used to call me home for dinner, that sang old boleros while mending my clothes by lamplight. "Cole, *stop*. You'll tear yourself apart."

I freeze mid-struggle. The heart monitor behind me accelerates into a frantic rhythm—beep-beep-beep-BEEP-BEEP-BEEP.

"You're dead," I whisper. The words come out wrong, raspy and broken. "I saw you. The roof came down on the clinic. I felt the fire. Felt it eat through my chest when the Cord formed." My vision blurs at the edges. Fever dream. Hallucination. This has to be High-Spire trickery. Some last-ditch illusion to make me weak before they come to finish what they started in 1999.

But she steps closer—and I smell it. That cheap lavender soap she always bought from the bodega on Bloomfield Avenue because it was half-price. Underneath that, something else: ozone and copper, the scent of healing magic that smells like rain on hot pavement.

Her hand comes up slowly, giving me time to flinch away if I want to. I don't move. Can't move. She places her palm against my cheek, skin warm and real and solid.

Her eyes glisten slightly. "Easy, *mijo*. Keep your pulse down. I know what you saw. But what you saw was what we needed them to see."

The monitor's frantic beeping doesn't slow. If anything, it speeds up.

"Every night," I hear myself saying, voice barely audible over the machine. "Every single fucking night for eight years, I've dreamed about that fire. Woke up choking on smoke that wasn't there. The Cord—the Threefold Cord—they told us it was made from our sacrifice. All of us who died that day." I'm sobbing now, shamefully, pathetically. "You were supposed to be dead."

Elena's thumb strokes my cheekbone—same gesture she used when I was five and skinned my knee on the sidewalk. "I know. And I'm sorry. So sorry you had to carry that weight." Her South Side accent is thicker than I remember, rolling the consonants like stones in her mouth. "But we couldn't let them know. Not yet. Not until you were old enough to understand."

"You're lying." But even as I say it, doubt cracks through my certainty like ice over a frozen river. "I felt you die. I felt—"

"The Cord isn't built on death, Cole. It never was." She sits carefully on the edge of the bed, her hand still cradling my face. Behind her, shadows shift in ways that make my frost-cobalt senses tingle with wariness. "It's built on *love*. On connection. On the bond between three people so strong it transcends even death itself."

The words don't compute. Can't compute. Everything I've been taught since 1999—that the Cord formed from our collective sacrifice, that Mara and I survived by absorbing the essence of everyone else who burned—it all unspools like a broken string.

"Then what happened? What did I see?"

Her expression grows grim. "The High-Spire doesn't just want to erase metahumans, *mijo*. They want to consume us. Digest our power. Learn how to replicate what makes us special." She leans closer, voice dropping to a whisper. "That day—they weren't burning the clinic. They were trying to capture everyone inside. Alive. To study."

Behind Elena, something moves in the deeper shadows beyond the sodium lamp's weak circle of light. Another figure. Taller. Broader. My frost-cobalt wards finally spark properly—not from strength but from pure instinctive terror—and the restraints sizzle where they touch metal.

Elena's hand tightens on my cheek. "Easy. He's not here to hurt you."

But I'm already straining against the bindings again, heart monitor screaming its alarm as I realize what—or rather, *who*—is stepping out from behind my mother.

The man is massive, easily six-foot-four, with shoulders broad enough to block out the dim light. His face is harder to make out at first, but then he steps fully into view and I recognize him despite the years and the scars.

My father.

Miguel Reyes stands there with his hands slightly raised, palms forward in a gesture of peace. But even that simple movement looks dangerous—controlled violence held back by sheer force of will.

"No," I breathe. The word comes out hollow. Empty.

*Both parents. Both supposed dead.*

The room tilts sideways for a moment before I force myself steady. The antiseptic smell intensifies, becomes almost suffocating. Or maybe that's just panic closing my throat.

"You're both dead," I repeat, but the conviction is gone now. Replaced by something worse—a dawning horror that suggests every certainty I've built my life around might be wrong.

Elena exchanges a look with Miguel. Some silent communication passes between them, old and practiced and familiar.

"Not anymore," she says quietly. "Not yet."

* * *

The second woman moves into the light like smoke taking form.

I see her first as silhouette against the sterile glow—the sharp line of shoulders squared with military precision, the way her stance carries weight that isn't just physical. Then the details resolve. Dark hair pulled back tight enough to show every angle of her skull. Eyes that don't flinch when they meet mine. And beneath it all, emanating from her like heat from pavement, an impossible scent.

White lilacs. Pure. Uncorrupted by age or decay.

My breath catches somewhere below my ribs.

"Cole Reyes." Her voice cuts through the antiseptic haze of the clinic like a blade finding its sheath. Authoritative. Command-trained. Every syllable placed with surgical precision. "Do you recognize me?"

The scent fills my lungs again. My mother—Elena—stands frozen beside the medical equipment, her worn scrubs suddenly looking even more threadbare against this woman's presence. But I'm not looking at Elena anymore. Can't look away from those eyes. That posture. The way she holds herself like she's still commanding something important.

Mara's posture.

Jesus Christ.

"You're..." The word dies in my throat. My mind races backward through everything Mara told me about her past. The orphanage files. The conspiracy reports from BATC. The official record of Commander Lysandra Vance's death on New Year's Eve, 1999—same night as Mara's supposed parents died, same night the Perimeter supposedly collapsed.

Same night everyone was lying to us.

"The Architect," I breathe, and suddenly pieces slam together like pistons firing. The Watching Party. The open eye burning above the city. The hidden resistance operating in the cracks of North Jersey's infrastructure while their children grew up believing they were alone.

While Mara tore through the underworld searching for ghosts.

Lysandra Vance—alive—steps to the foot of Elena's bed with the kind of calculated movement that screams combat training. Her coat is dark-weave tactical gear, clearly ex-BATC issue, modified with equipment I don't recognize. She radiates capability. Danger.

She radiates survival.

"Mara thinks you're in the ground," I hear myself saying, voice trembling with something I can't name—rage? awe? betrayal? All of it, none of it, everything twisted together. "She's tearing the city apart for you. Killing people who might have information. Making enemies we'll never—"

"Stop."

The word comes out hard enough to make Elena flinch. But Lysandra's eyes are locked onto mine now, drilling into my skull with absolute intensity.

"You kept my daughter alive," she says, each syllable weighted like a promise and a threat. "You've done more than most Aegis operatives could manage. But we're running out of time, Mr. Reyes." Her head tilts fractionally—a gesture so familiar it makes my chest ache. "Before the Four Heads finish waking the Serpent, before Apep tears another hole in this world... you need to know what really happened on New Year's Eve, 1999."

The room holds its breath around us.

My frost-cobalt wards remain dormant, replaced by this shocking vulnerability—the scent of lilacs overwhelming every defensive instinct I've built over years of street warfare. I'm exposed here. Raw. And Lysandra Vance knows exactly what she's doing when those eyes bore into me.

"The Architect of the Perimeter," I repeat, quieter now. Testing how the words feel. How much they change everything I thought I understood about Mara. About her past. About the night that split the world open and left us all bleeding in the cracks.

Lysandra's expression doesn't shift. Doesn't soften or harden. She simply waits, letting the weight of her presence do its work.

"So wake up," she adds finally. "All the way up this time. Because if you want any chance of saving Mara from what's coming—if you want to understand why she is the way she is, why she can't stop fighting even when every rational part of her brain screams to run—"

She pauses.

"Then you need to hear the truth about the two mothers who died twice. And the daughter who inherited their burden."

The clinic hums around us. Medical machinery keeping time like a countdown. Elena still frozen beside the bed, her hand pressed against her chest like she's holding herself together through sheer willpower.

And me, standing there with nothing but questions burning through my skull while white lilacs choke out every lie I've been telling myself for three years.

CUT TO BLACK.

---
